The consensus protocol for key operations in Bizur achieves consensus on key-value operations using a quorum-based protocol. For either a read or write operation, the client directs the request to the leader of the corresponding partition. The leader then processes the request in the following manner: 
1. **Write Operations:** For a write request, the leader assigns a unique, monotonically increasing version number to the operation. The leader then forwards the operation to the followers within the group and awaits acknowledgments from a majority. Upon receiving acknowledgments from a majority, the leader applies the operation locally and responds to the client. This ensures that the write operation is replicated across a quorum, maintaining consistency even in the event of replica failures.
2. **Read Operations:** For a read request, the leader directly serves the request from its local state. To ensure consistency, the leader verifies that it possesses the most recent version of the data by checking with a majority of the group. This quorum-based approach ensures that reads are consistent and up-to-date, even in the presence of concurrent writes. The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is one of the most extensively studied optimization problems in the fields of operations research and computer science. It is a classical combinatorial optimization problem where a set of cities is given, and the objective is to determine the shortest possible tour that visits each city exactly once and returns to the starting point. Despite its apparent simplicity, the TSP is NP-hard, meaning that no polynomial-time algorithm has been discovered to solve it exactly for all instances [1]. Over the decades, the TSP has served as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of optimization algorithms due to its relevance in real-world applications, such as logistics, manufacturing, and telecommunications, as well as its theoretical significance in computational complexity [2, 3]. The intractability of the TSP for large problem instances has led to the development of numerous heuristic and metaheuristic approaches aimed at finding high-quality, near-optimal solutions in a reasonable amount of time. Among these, methods such as genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, ant colony optimization, and greedy randomized adaptive search procedures (GRASP) have gained prominence for their ability to explore vast solution spaces efficiently [4, 5]. GRASP, in particular, is a multi-start metaheuristic that combines greedy construction with local search to iteratively refine solutions. While GRASP has been successfully applied to a wide range of combinatorial problems, its effectiveness is often constraind by its tendency to focus computational effort on specific solutions rather than exploiting shared structural features across high-quality solutions [6]. In this paper, we propose a novel population-based metaheuristic, the Fixed Set Search (FSS), which extends the capabilities of GRASP by incorporating a learning mechanism that emphasizes structural elements rather than indivdiual solutions. The core idea behind FSS is to identify and fix subsets of elements (in the case of the TSP, edges or connections between cities) that frequently appear in high-quality solutions. By focusing computational effort on exploring the solution space constrained by these fixed subsets, FSS aims to enhance the efficiency of the search process and improve solution quality. This approach diverges from traditional population-based metaheuristics, such as genetic algorithms, which rely on maintaining and evolving a diverse set of complete solutions. Instead, FSS operates on the premise that the structural building blocks of optimal or near-optimal solutions carry valuable information that can guide the search in a more meaningful direction. The motivation for developing FSS stems from the limitations of existing metaheuristics in balancing exploration and exploitation. While methods like GRASP excel at exploring diverse regions of the solution space, they often lack mcehanisms to effectively exploit the knowledge gained during the search process [7]. Conversely, methods such as tabu search focus on exploiting local neighborhoods but may suffer from premature convergence. FSS offers a complementary perspective by tarrgeting the structural components of high-quality solutions, thereby bridging the gap between exploration and exploitation. By concentrating on promising substructures and systematically refining the search within these constrained spaces, FSS seeks to achieve a more efficient trade-off between solution quality and computational effort. A key advantage of the proposed FSS approach lies in its simplicity and adaptability. Unlike many population-based metaheuristics that require extensive parameter tuning or complex solution encoding schemes, FSS can be seamlessly integrated into existing frameworks with minimal modifications. This simplicity not only facilitates its implementation but also ensures its scalability to larger problem instances. Furthermore, the modular nature of FSS allows it to be combined with other metaheuristics, leveraging their strengths to further enhance performance. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we introduce the conceptual framework of FSS and detail its integration with GRASP, illustrating how the learning mechanism is implemented to identify and fix subsets of structural elements. Second, we demonstrate the applicability and effectiveess of FSS in solving the TSP, presentign computational experiments that compare its performance to GRASP and the dynamic convexized method. Third, we provide insights into the impact of the fixed set size and other parameters on the performance of FSS, offering guidelines for practitioners seeking to apply this approach to related optimization problems. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a brief review of related work on metaheuristics for the TSP, with a focus on GRASP and its extensions. Section 3 introduces the Fixed Set Search methodology, outlining its key components and operational steps. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results, comparing FSS to existing methods across a set of benchmark TSP instances. Section 5 discusses the implications of the findings and suggests potential avenues for future research. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper, summarizing the mani contributions and highlighting the broader applicability of FSS beyond the TSP domain. By addressing the limitations of GRASP and other conventional metaheuristics, the Fixed Set Search represents a promising direction for advancing the state of the art in combinatorial optimization. Its focus on structural learning and its adaptability to diverse problem settings underscore its potential to become a valuable toool for tackling complex optimization challenges. Through this work, we aim to not only demonstrate the effectiveness of FSS on the TSP but also inspire furthher research into the development of metaheuirstics that leverage structural insights to enhance solution quality and computational efficiency. Moreover, the modular nature of FSS allows it to be easily integrated with othre metaheuristics, such as genetic algorithms or simulated annealing, to further enhance its performance. To validate the effectiveness of FSS, computational experiments were conducted on benchmark instances of the TSP, comparing its performance against standard GRASP and the dynamic convexized method [3]. The results demonstrated that FSS consistently outperformed the baseline approaches, achieving significantly better solution quality within comparable computational time. These findings highlight the potential of FSS as a robust and efficient metaheuristic for solving combinatorial optimization problems. This approach leverages the structural properties of the solution space to guide the search process, resulting in improved optimization performance. The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) has been a fundamental subject of investigation in the realms of operational research and computer science, exemplifying a paradigmatic optimization conundrum that has garnered extensive scrutiny. At its nucleus, the TSP entails the delineation of the shortest feasible itinerary that encompasses a series of cities, with each city being visited precisely once, prior to returning to the point of origin. This ostensibly straightforward objective, however, belies the intricate complexity that underlies the problem. Notwithstanding substantial advancements in computational capabilities and algorithmic methodologies, the TSP remains an NP-hard problem, denoting that no algorithm has been devised to yield an exact solution for all instances within a polynomial timeframe, as underscored in [1]. This inherent intractability has precipitated the widespread adoption of the TSP as a benchmark for evaluating the efficacy of optimization algorithms, given its pertinence to real-world applications in logistics, manufacturing, and telecommunications, as well as its theoretical significance in computational complexity, as elaborated upon in [2, 3]. Over the years, the intractability of large-scale TSP instances has spurred the development of a plethora of heuristic and metaheuristic approaches, whose primary objective is to identify high-quality, near-optimal solutions within a reasonable temporal framework. Among these, methodologies such as genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, ant colony optimization, and greedy randomized adaptive search procedures (GRASP) have emerged as particularly efficacious, owing to their capacity to efficiently navigate vast solution spaces, as noted in [4, 5]. GRASP, in particular, has garnered prominence as a multi-start metaheuristic that synergistically combines greedy construction with local search, thereby iteratively refining solutions. Although GRASP has been successfully applied to a diverse array of combinatorial problems, its effectiveness is often circumscribed by its propensity to concentrate computational effort on specific solutions, rather than leveraging shared structural features that typify high-quality solutions, a limitation highlighted in [6]. In response to these limitations, this paper proposes a novel population-based metaheuristic, termed the Fixed Set Search (FSS), which extends the capabilities of GRASP by incorporating a learning mechanism that emphasizes structural elements rather than individual solutions. The core concept underlying FSS involves the identification and fixation of subsets of elements (in the context of the TSP, these elements correspond to edges or connections between cities) that frequently recur in high-quality solutions. By concentrating computational effort on exploring the solution space constrained by these fixed subsets, FSS seeks to enhance the efficiency of the search process and augment solution quality. This approach diverges from traditional population-based metaheuristics, such as genetic algorithms, which rely on maintaining and evolving a diverse set of complete solutions. In contrast, FSS operates on the premise that the structural building blocks of optimal or near-optimal solutions carry valuable information that can guide the search in a more meaningful direction. The motivation for developing FSS stems from the limitations of existing metaheuristics in balancing exploration and exploitation. While methodologies like GRASP excel at exploring diverse regions of the solution space, they often lack mechanisms to effectively exploit the knowledge gained during the search process, as noted in [7]. Conversely, methodologies such as tabu search focus on exploiting local neighborhoods but may suffer from premature convergence. FSS offers a complementary perspective by targeting the structural components of high-quality solutions, thereby bridging the gap between exploration and exploitation. By focusing on promising substructures and systematically refining the search within these constrained spaces, FSS seeks to achieve a more efficient trade-off between solution quality and computational effort. A key advantage of the proposed FSS approach lies in its simplicity and adaptability. Unlike many population-based metaheuristics, which require extensive parameter tuning or complex solution encoding schemes, FSS can be seamlessly integrated into existing frameworks with minimal modifications. This simplicity not only facilitates its implementation but also ensures its scalability to larger problem instances. Furthermore, the modular nature of FSS allows it to be combined with other metaheuristics, leveraging their strengths to further enhance performance. The contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we introduce the conceptual framework of FSS and detail its integration with GRASP, illustrating how the learning mechanism is implemented to identify and fix subsets of structural elements. Secondly, we demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of FSS in solving the TSP, presenting computational experiments that compare its performance to GRASP and the dynamic convexized method. Thirdly, we provide insights into the impact of the fixed set size and other parameters on the performance of FSS, offering guidelines for practitioners seeking to apply this approach to related optimization problems. Section 3 introduces the Fixed Set Search methodology, outlining its key components and operational steps. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results, comparing FSS to existing methods across a set of benchmark TSP instances. Section 5 discusses the implications of the findings and suggests potential avenues for future research. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper, summarizing the main contributions and outlining potential future directions for research in this area, as referenced in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Once the fixed set \( \mathcal{F} \) is determined, FSS constructs a subproblem by fixing the elements in \( \mathcal{F} \) and re-optimizing the remaining parts of the solution. These compounds are frequently encountered as contaminants in crops such as cereals, nuts, fruits, and animal feed, where they are synthesized by fungi belonging primarily to the genera *Aspergillus*, *Fusarium*, and *Penicillium* [1]. Prolonged exposure to mycotoxins, even at low concentrations, can lead to acute and chronic toxic effects, including hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, genotoxicity, immunosuppression, and carcinogenicity [2]. In contrast, enzymatic detoxification has emerged as a more promising and sustainable alternative due to its high specificity, mild operating conditions, and ability to transform mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic metabolites without significant adverse effects on food composition [5]. These biocatalysts have evolved to metabolize mycotoxins as a means of survival in environments where these compounds are prevalent. For instance, soil-dwelling bacteria and fungi have develpoed ezymatic systems to degrade mycotoxins, enabling them to utilize these compounds as carbon or nitrogen sources [6]. Similarly, higher plants produce enzymes to neutralize fungal toxins as part of their innnate defense mechanisms against pathogenic fungi [7]. These natural systems provide a rich reservoir of enzymes with diverse catalytic properties and substrate specificities, which can be harnessed for biotechnological applications. Among microbial sources, bacterial genera such as *Bacillus*, *Pseudomonas*, and *Rhodococcus* have been extensively studied for their ability to degrade aflatoxins, ochratoxins, and trihcothecenes through enzymatic action [8]. Similarly, cetain fungal species, including *Trichoderma* and *Pleurotus* spp., produce enzymes capable of converting zearalenone and fumonisins into less harmful derivatives [9]. Oxidoreductases, hydrolases, and transferases are the primary enzyme classes involved in these processes. Oxidoreductases, including laccases, peroxidases, and cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, facilitate the oxidative degradation of mycotoxins by introducing hydroxyl groups or breaking aromatic rings, leading to the formation of less toxic metabolites [11]. For example, laccases have been shown to oxidize aflatoxins into non-toxic derivatives through radical-mediated electron transfer [12]. Hydrolases, such as esterases, proteases, and epoxide hydrolases, act by cleaving specific chemical bonds within mycotoxin molecules. This cllass of enzymes is particularly effective against ester- or epoxide-containing mycotoxins, such as zearalenone and fumonisins, converting them into less toxic hydrolysates [13]. Transferases, including glutathione-S-transferases (GSTs), catalyze the conjugation of mycotoxins with endogenous cellular molecules such as glutathione, thereby enhancing their solubility and facilitating their excretion or further degradation [14]. The catalytic efficiency and sustrate specificity of these enzymes are determined by their active site architecture and the molecular interactions between the enzyme and the mycotoxin. Advances in molecular modeling and docking studies have provided valuable insights into these mechanisms, enabling the rational design and engineering of enzymes with enhanced detoxification capabilities [15]. ### Multifunctional Enzyme Systems While individual enzymes exhibit promising detoxification activity, the complexity and diversity of mycotoxin structures often necessitate the use of multifunctional enzyme systems. Synergistic combinations of enzymes with complementary activities can target mutliple mycotoxins simultaneously or enhance the detoxification efficiency of a single mycotoxin through sequential transformations [16]. For instance, the coupling of oxidoreductases with hydrolases has been shown to achieve complete detoxification of zearalenone by first oxidizing the mycotoxin to an intermediate metabolite, which is subsequently hyddrolyzed [17]. Such multifunctional systems not only broaden the specrum of detoxifiable mycotoxins but also improve the robustness and adaptability of detoxification processes under varying environmental conditions. ### Challenges and Future Perspectives Despite significant progress in identifying and characterizing mycotoxin-detoxifying enzymes, severl challenges remain. The scalability of enzymatic detoxification processes for industrial applications is often hindered by the low stability, activity, or availability of these enzymes under practical conditions [18]. Additionally, the potential for enzymatic byproducts to exhibit residual toxicity must be carefully evaluated to ensure the safety of detoxified products. Advances in protein engineering, metagenomics, and synthetic biology are expected to address these limitations by enabling the development of tailored enzymes with improved performance and specificity [19]. Mycotoxins were selected based on their prevalence, toxicity, and economic impact, focusing on aflatoxins, ochratoxins, trichothecenes, fumonisins, zearalenone, and patulin [1, 2]. Enzymes were chosen based on prior reports of catalytic activity against these mycotoxins, with prioity given to enzyme families such as oxidoreductases, hydrolases, and transferases [3]. Protein sequences and structures were retrieved from publicly available databases, including UniProt and Protein Data Bank (PDB). Candidate enzymes from plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria were included to explore a wide range of potential biocatalysts. #### Molecular Docking and Structural Modeling Molecular docking was conducted to preict enzyme-substrate interactions and identify residues critical to catalytic activity. High-resolution three-dimensional structures of enzymes were obtained from the PDB whenever available. For enzymes lacking structural data, homology models were constructed using the SWISS-MODEL server [4]. Docking studies were carried out using AutoDock Vina [5]. Ligand structures of mycotoxins were retrieved from PubChem and prepared for docking by adding hydrogen atoms and optimizing geometry using PyMOL. Enzyme active sites were defined based on prior literature and structural annotations, and docking calculations were performed to estimate binding affinities and interaction modes. Results were analyzed to identify key residues involved in substrate recognition and catalytic action. #### Enzyme Activity Assays To validate the catalytic activity of selected enzymes, in vitro assays were peerformed using purified recombinant proteins. Enzyme genes were synthesized or cloned from respective organisms into bacterial expression vectors (pET system, Novagen). Recombinant proteins were expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) cells and purified using nickel-affinity chromatography under native conditions [6]. Protein purity was confirmed by SDS-PAGE, and concentrations were determined using the Bradford assay. Enzyme activity assays were designed for each class of mycotoxins. For aflatoxins and ochratoxins, oxidoreductase activity was monitored by measuring chagnes in absorbance at specific wavelengths corresponding to substrate oxidation or reduction. Hydrolysis assays for zearalenone and fumonisins involved monitoring the release of hydrolytic products using high-performance liiquid chromatography (HPLC) equipped with a UV detector [7]. Reaction conditions, including pH, temperature, and cofactors, were optimized for each enzyme based on previous reports and preliminary experiments. Neagtive controls without enzymes were included in all assays to account for non-enzymatic degradation of mycotoxins. #### Biochemical Characterization of Enzymes Enzyme kinetics were determined by analyzing substrate concentration-dependent reaction rates. Michaelis-Menten parameters (Km and Vmax) were calculated using nonlinear regression analysis in GraphPad Prism. Optimal pH and temperature for each enzyme were determined by conducting activity assays across a range of conditions. Enzyme stability was assessed by pre-incubating enzymes at various temperatures or pH levels before initiating the reaction. The effect of potential inhibitors, such as heavy metals or organic solvents, was also evaluated to assess enzyme robustness for practical applications [8]. #### Functional Annotation of Homologues To identify natural sources of active biocatalysts, hommologous enzymes from various organisms were analyzed. Protein sequences of selected enzymes were used as queries in BLAST searches against NCBI and UniProt databases. Phylogenetic trees were constructed using MEGA11 software to explore evolutionary relationships and identify conserved ressidues associated with catalytic activity [9]. Functional annotations were assessed using InterProScan and Pffam databases to identify domain structures and potential catalytic motifs. Expression patterns of homologues in different organisms were reviewed from transcriptomic and proteomic datasets to infer natural availability and practicality for large-scale applications. #### Combination of Enzymes for Multifunctional Detoxification To evaluate the potential of enzyme combinations for mycotoxin detoxification, selected enzymes were tested in tandem reactions. Sequential and simultaneous reaction setups were compared to determine the most efficient mode of action. For sequential reactions, substrates were first incubated with one enzyme, and reaction products were subsequently treated with the second enzyme. In simultaneous reactions, both enzymes were added to the substrate simultaneously. Reaction products were analyzed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to confirm complete degradation of mycotoxins and absence of toxic intermediates [10]. #### Statistical Analysis All experiments were performed in triplicate, and data are presented as means ± standard deviation. Statistical significance of differences between experimental conditions was determined using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.3.1). #### Ethical Considerations All experimental protocols involving recombinant DNA manipulation were approved by the institutional biosafety committee. The utilization of enzymes to mitigate the deleterious effects of mycotoxins, which are toxic secondary metabolites produced by fungi, has garnered significant attention in recent years. Mycotoxins, including aflatoxins, zearalenone, ochratoxin A, fumonisins, and trichothecenes, pose considerable threats to human health, animal welfare, and the economy due to their pervasive presence in food and feed [1, 2]. Consequently, the development of effective strategies to counteract these toxins is of paramount importance. In this context, enzymatic detoxification has emerged as a promising approach, leveraging the capabilities of enzymes to break down or modify mycotoxins, thereby rendering them non-toxic.

To elucidate the enzymatic mechanisms underlying mycotoxin detoxification, a comprehensive analysis of various enzyme classes was conducted. The results of this analysis revealed that oxidoreductases, hydrolases, and transferases were the most efficacious in modifying major mycotoxins. Specifically, oxidoreductases, such as laccases and peroxidases, demonstrated a high degree of efficacy in degrading aflatoxins through oxidative cleavage of the furan and coumarin rings, thereby rendering these mycotoxins non-toxic [1, 2]. Furthermore, molecular docking studies confirmed the strong binding affinity of aflatoxin B1 to the active sites of fungal laccases, with binding energies ranging from -6.8 to -8.2 kcal/mol, indicative of high substrate affinity. These findings are consistent with previous studies, which highlighted the potential of enzymatic approaches for mycotoxin detoxification [3].

In addition to oxidoreductases, hydrolases such as esterases and lactonases were found to facilitate hydrolytic cleavage of the lactone ring in zearalenone, leading to the formation of non-toxic metabolites such as zearalenone-diol. The catalytic mechanism involves nucleophilic attack on the lactone carbonyl group, with a critical role played by conserved serine residues in the active site [3]. Aminotransferases, on the other hand, were found to efficiently detoxify fumonisins by deaminating the tricarballylic acid side chain, thereby disrupting its toxic functionality. Docking simulations revealed that the active sites of bacterial aminotransferases had optimal spatial alignment with fumonisin B1, ensuring effective catalysis [4].

The detoxification of trichothecenes was predominantly achieved by epoxide hydrolases, which catalyze the hydrolysis of the epoxide group, a key structural feature responsible for cytotoxicity. Notably, bacterial epoxide hydrolases displayed higher catalytic efficiency than their fungal counterparts. The reaction mechanism involves an acid-base catalytic triad that facilitates protonation and subsequent ring opening [5]. Ochratoxin A detoxification was observed to proceed through hydrolysis of the amide bond by carboxypeptidases, yielding non-toxic phenylalanine and ochratoxin alpha. This reaction was confirmed via HPLC-MS analysis, which detected the reaction intermediates and final detoxified products [6].

To further elucidate the interactions between mycotoxins and enzymatic active sites, molecular docking studies were performed. For aflatoxin B1, fungal laccases exhibited the strongest binding affinity, with key residues such as His458 and Cys489 forming stable hydrogen bonds with the substrate. Similarly, docking of zearalenone with plant-derived lactonases revealed that the active sites of these enzymes had optimal spatial alignment with the substrate, ensuring effective catalysis.

In order to identify the most effective enzymes for mycotoxin detoxification, a comprehensive analysis of various enzyme classes was conducted. This analysis involved BLAST searches against NCBI and UniProt databases, as well as the construction of phylogenetic trees using MEGA11 software to explore evolutionary relationships and identify conserved residues associated with catalytic activity [9]. Functional annotations were assessed using InterProScan and Pfam databases to identify domain structures and potential catalytic motifs. Expression patterns of homologues in different organisms were reviewed from transcriptomic and proteomic datasets to infer natural availability and practicality for large-scale applications.

The combination of enzymes for multifunctional detoxification was also evaluated. Selected enzymes were tested in tandem reactions to determine the most efficient mode of action. For sequential reactions, substrates were first incubated with one enzyme, and reaction products were subsequently treated with the second enzyme. In simultaneous reactions, both enzymes were added to the substrate simultaneously. Reaction products were analyzed by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to confirm complete degradation of mycotoxins and absence of toxic intermediates [10].

The results of this study highlight the potential of enzymatic detoxification as a strategy for mitigating the risks associated with mycotoxin contamination in food and feed. By leveraging advances in protein engineering, metagenomics, and synthetic biology, it is possible to develop tailored enzymes with improved performance and specificity. The systematic approach employed in this study, which includes molecular docking, enzyme activity assays, and biochemical characterization, provides a comprehensive framework for identifying and optimizing enzymes for mycotoxin detoxification. Furthermore, the analysis of homologous enzymes and their expression patterns provides valuable insights into the natural availability and practicality of these biocatalysts for large-scale applications.

The ever-increasing demand for high-speed data communication continues to drive the development of advanced neetworking technologies. Optical networks, characterized by their immense bandwidth capacity and low latency, are at the forefront of this evolution. Among the various parradigms of optical networking, Optical Packet Switching (OPS) and Optical Burst Switching (OBS) haev emerged as proimsing approaches to accommodte the dynamic and diverse traffic demands of modern communication systems. These paradigms aim to combine the efficiency of packet-based data transport with the high throughput potential of optical transmission, offering a flexible and scalable solution for next-generation networks. OPS and OBS networks, however, face several critical challlenges that hinder their widespread deployment. Packet contention, which occurs when multiple packets compete for the same resources (such as wavelengths or time slots), is a persistent issue in these systems. Additionally, the lack of optical buffering capabilities and the inherent vulnerability of optical networks to failurse further exacerbate the problem. The dynamic nature of traffic and the distributed architecture of OPS/OBS netwoks make reliable data delivery and performance guarantees difficult to achieve. Furthermore, ensuring the security of data transmitted over optical networks is an important concern, particularly in light of increasing cyber threats and the growing need for privacy in data communication. In this context, effective transport mechanisms that address these challenges while leveraging the unique capabilities of optical networks are critical. Traditional mechanisms for improving network reliability and performance, such as retransmissions and error correction techniques, are often unsuitable for OPS/OBS networks due to their reliance on electronic processig and the associated latency. Alternative approaches, such as path diversity and cding schemes, offer a promising avenue for overcoming these limitations by exploiting the inherent parallelism and redundancy of optical networks. This paper introduces the Coded Packet Transport (CPT) scheme, a novel transport mechanism designed specifically for OPS/OBS networks. The CPT scheme addresses key issues such as packet loss due to contention and path failures, while simultaneously providing a degree of non-cryptographic secrecy. At its core, the CPT scheme integrates two complementary techniques: source coding using erasure codes and path diversity. Erasure coding, a well-established technique for enhancing data reliability, is employed at the ingrress node of the network to encode the original data into redundatn coded packets. These coded packets are then transmitted over multiple disjoint paths to an egress node, ensuring that the original data can be reconstructed even in the presence of packet loss or path failures. By distributing the coded packets across disjoint paths, the scheme not only improves survivability but also reduces the likelihood of contentions, thereby enhancing overall network performance. One of the defining features of the CPT scheme is its ability to provide a unified view of Quality of Service (QoS) in OPS/OBS networks by linking the interplay between survivability, performance, and secrecy. Survivability, which refers to the network's ability to maintain service continuity in the face of failures, is inherently improved through the use of redundant coded packets and path diversity. Performance, in terms of metrics such as packet delivery ratio and delay, is enhanced by reducing contention and leveraging the parallel nature of optical paths. Secrecy, meanwhile, is achieved by distributing coded packets across different paths, making it difficult for an adversary to intercept and reconstruct the original data without access to all the paths. The CPT scheme represents a departure from conventional approaches to QoS in optical networks, which oten adress these aspects in isolation. Instead, the CPT scheme demonstrates how survivability, performance, and secrecy can be interdependent and mutually reinforcing when viewed through the lens of erasure coding and path diversity. This holistic approach not only simplifies the design and management of OPS/OBS networks but also offers a scalable and efficient solution for addressing their challenges. To provide a rigorous evaluation of the CPT scheme, we develop analytical models that capture the key factors influencing its performance. These models take into account the number of disjoint paths available in the network, the overhead introduced by erasure coding, and the processing delays associated with encoding and decoding operations. The insights gained from these models illustrate the trade-offs inherent in the CPT scheme and provide guidelines for optimizing its parameters to met specific QoS requirements. The potential applications of the CPT scheme extend beyond traditional optical networking scenarios. In an era where data security and privacy are of paramount importance, the built-in secrecy of the CPT scheme makes it a compelling choice for sensitive applications such as financial transactions, healthcare data transmission, and milittary communications. Additionally, the scalable nature of the scheme positions it well to support emerging technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and 5G networks, which demand high reliability, low latency, and robust security mechanisms. The emergence of Optical Packet/Burst Switched (OPS/OBS) networks has brought about a multitude of complexities, including the need for reliable packet recovery, mitigation of path failures, and ensuring the confidentiality of sensitive data without relying on cryptographic techniques [17]. In response to these challenges, a novel approach has been devised, known as the Coded Packet Transport (CPT) scheme, which harnesses the combined strengths of erasure coding and path diversity to offer a holistic solution for Quality of Service (QoS) in these networks. This treatise aims to substantiate the practical viability and efficacy of the CPT scheme through a rigorous analytical modeling and performance assessment, thereby paving the way for its integration into future optical network architectures [1]. 

The CPT scheme is specifically designed to tackle several pivotal challenges inherent to OPS/OBS networks. Firstly, the loss of packets poses a significant threat to network performance, as the disappearance of even a single packet can lead to substantial performance degradation. Secondly, the failure of paths, which can be attributed to a variety of factors including network congestion, link failures, or node failures, can precipitate considerable disruptions within the network. Lastly, the provision of non-cryptographic secrecy is indispensable in OPS/OBS networks to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive information. The CPT scheme addresses these challenges by utilizing erasure coding at the point of entry into the OPS/OBS network, where data is encoded into redundant packets to enhance survivability and secrecy.

The erasure coding process is a fundamental component of the CPT scheme. Consider a data block comprising \( k \) original packets. By employing an erasure code, such as Reed-Solomon or Fountain codes, these \( k \) original packets are transformed into \( n \) coded packets, where \( n \geq k \) [2]. The erasure code guarantees that any \( k \) out of \( n \) coded packets are sufficient to reconstruct the original data block, thereby providing resilience against packet loss during transmission. The redundancy factor, defined as \( r = n/k \), is a crucial parameter in the CPT scheme, as it strikes a balance between the level of robustness and the associated overhead. A higher redundancy factor affords greater protection against packet loss but also increases the overhead associated with the transmission of redundant packets.

At the entry point of the network, the encoding process unfolds in the following manner: 1) the data block is segmented into \( k \) packets of equal size; 2) the erasure coding algorithm is applied to generate \( n \) coded packets, introducing redundancy by combining data from the original packets; and 3) each coded packet is assigned a unique identifier and metadata, including coding parameters and sequence information, to facilitate decoding at the exit point of the network. The computational complexity of the encoding process is directly related to the values of \( k \) and \( n \), with higher values resulting in increased computational demands [5].

Furthermore, the CPT scheme incorporates path diversity to enhance the survivability and secrecy of data transmission. By transmitting coded packets over diverse paths, the scheme mitigates the risk of path failures and unauthorized access to sensitive data [9]. The synergy between erasure coding and path diversity enables the CPT scheme to provide a unified framework for addressing the challenges of survivability, performance, and secrecy in OPS/OBS networks.

The performance evaluation of the CPT scheme is crucial to assessing its efficacy in addressing the challenges of OPS/OBS networks. Through analytical modeling and simulation, the CPT scheme has been shown to provide significant improvements in packet loss recovery, path failure mitigation, and non-cryptographic secrecy [10]. The results of the performance evaluation demonstrate the practical viability of the CPT scheme and its potential for adoption in next-generation optical networks.

In conclusion, the CPT scheme represents a substantial advancement in the design of transport mechanisms for OPS/OBS networks, offering a unified approach to addressing the challenges of survivability, performance, and secrecy in these systems. The scheme's ability to harness the combined strengths of erasure coding and path diversity makes it an attractive solution for ensuring the reliable and secure transmission of data in OPS/OBS networks. As the demand for high-reliability and low-latency networks continues to grow, driven by the emergence of the Internet of Things (IoT) and 5G networks, the CPT scheme is poised to play a critical role in the development of next-generation optical network architectures [17].

The quest for uncompromised Quality of Service (QoS) in Optical Packet/Burst Switched (OPS/OBS) networks is an ongoing endeavor, fraught with challenges stemming from packet loss, path failures, and the imperative to safeguard data secrecy. In tackling these hurdles, a novel approach has emerged under the moniker of Coded Packet Transport (CPT) scheme, which synergistically combines erasure coding and path diversity to present a holistic solution for QoS in OPS/OBS networks [3]. The incorporation of lightweight erasure coding techniques in the CPT scheme is pivotal, as it precludes the introduction of significant processing latencies, thereby rendering it apt for real-time applications [3]. Furthermore, the scheme's utilization of path diversity enables the dissemination of coded packets across multiple paths that are disjoint from the ingress to the egress node, mitigating the risk of correlated losses resulting from contentions or path failures within the network.

The process of path selection is multifaceted, involving a series of deliberate steps. Initially, the ingress node identifies a multitude of disjoint paths to the egress node, leveraging network topology information to inform its decisions [4]. Subsequently, coded packets are distributed across these disjoint paths in either a round-robin or random manner. The network control plane plays a critical role in dynamically monitoring the status of these paths and updating path assignments in response to failures or congestion, thereby ensuring the resilience and adaptability of the CPT scheme [4].

A critical parameter influencing the efficacy of the CPT scheme is the number of disjoint paths, denoted as \( p \). An increase in \( p \) enhances the scheme's resilience to path failures but may also introduce additional latency due to the heightened complexity of path management. This delicate balance underscores the need for careful consideration in the selection of \( p \) to optimize the performance of the CPT scheme.

At the egress node, the decoding process is initiated to reconstruct the original data block from the received coded packets, following a meticulous protocol. First, the egress node aggregates coded packets from all disjoint paths and identifies the subset of packets that have been successfully received [5]. If the number of coded packets received meets or exceeds a predetermined threshold, \( k \), the original data block is reconstructed using an erasure decoding algorithm; otherwise, the decoding process is deemed a failure, and the data block is considered lost [5]. The decoding process is designed with computational efficiency in mind, ensuring that the processing delay at the egress node is minimized, which is crucial for maintaining the real-time capability of the network [5].

The performance of the decoding process is inherently dependent on the packet loss rate in the network and the redundancy factor \( r \). By judiciously adjusting \( r \), the CPT scheme can achieve a desired level of reliability while minimizing the overhead associated with redundant packets, thereby optimizing the trade-off between reliability and efficiency [6].

To comprehensively evaluate the performance of the CPT scheme, we developed analytical models that meticulously quantify the QoS aspects of the scheme, including survivability, performance, and secrecy. These models are grounded in key parameters such as packet loss rate, redundancy factor, number of disjoint paths, and network topology [6]. The analytical models provide a robust framework for assessing the performance of the CPT scheme under a myriad of network conditions and traffic scenarios, offering valuable insights into its effectiveness and potential areas for optimization.

The findings from the analytical modeling and performance evaluation of the CPT scheme unequivocally demonstrate its efficacy in providing a unified framework for QoS in OPS/OBS networks. This novel approach addresses the dual challenges of packet loss and network security through the synergistic combination of erasure coding and path diversity, rendering it adaptable to the specific requirements of various applications [7]. The practicality and effectiveness of the CPT scheme, as evidenced by the analytical modeling and performance evaluation, pave the way for its integration into next-generation optical networks, where demands for high QoS, reliability, and security are paramount.

Future research endeavors should focus on the development of more efficient erasure coding techniques, the optimization of path selection algorithms to further enhance the resilience and efficiency of the CPT scheme, and the integration of the CPT scheme with other QoS mechanisms to provide a comprehensive framework for QoS in OPS/OBS networks [7]. This multifaceted approach will not only bolster the performance and reliability of OPS/OBS networks but also contribute significantly to the advancement of optical networking technologies, ultimately leading to more robust, efficient, and secure data transmission systems.

In the context of OPS/OBS networks, where packet loss, path failures, and ensuring data secrecy present significant challenges to maintaining high QoS metrics, the CPT scheme emerges as a promising solution. Its evaluation, focusing on key performance indicators such as packet loss recovery, survivability under path failures, non-cryptographic secrecy, and processing overhead, underscores its potential to address these challenges effectively.

To quantify the performance of the CPT scheme, several critical metrics were defined, including the Packet Loss Probability (PLP), which is derived as a function of the packet loss rate on individual paths, the number of disjoint paths \( p \), and the redundancy factor \( r \). This model comprehensively accounts for both independent and correlated losses across paths, providing a nuanced understanding of the scheme's robustness to packet loss [1]. Additionally, the analysis of the Packet Overhead introduced by the CPT scheme, as a function of \( r \) and the size of the metadata added to each coded packet, enabled an evaluation of the trade-off between overhead and reliability, a critical consideration in the design of efficient transport schemes for OPS/OBS networks [2].

The End-to-End Delay was meticulously modeled as the sum of the propagation delay, the queuing delay at intermediate nodes, and the processing delay at the ingress and egress nodes. This model facilitated an assessment of the impact of network conditions on the overall delay, thereby informing strategies to minimize latency and optimize network performance. The detailed examination of these metrics and their interplay within the CPT scheme contributes to a deeper understanding of its operational dynamics and potential for optimization, highlighting the scheme's versatility and capability to be tailored to the specific needs of various applications in OPS/OBS networks.

The allocation of resources to explore and engage with communities is a fundamental problem that arises in numerous real-world settings, ranging from online advertising campaigns to public health outreach and social network growth. Effectively distributing a limited budget to maximize the impact of exploration is a critical challenge faced by practitioners in these domains. For instance, in online advertising, advertisers often seek to identify and engage diverse audience groups by allocating their budget across multiple demographic or interest-based communities, while balancing trade-offs between exploratory and exploitative strategies. Similarly, in the context of social networks, community managers aim to expand their influence by interacting with various subgroups, often without complete prior knowledge of their size or engagement potential. This work introduces the *community exploration problem*, a framework that captures the essence of such scenarios. The problem can be described as follows: given a limited budget, an explorer must allocate resources across multiple communities to maximize the number of members encountered. The challenge lies in devising strategies that are both efficient and effective, particularly when the underlying characteristics of the communities, such as theiir sizes, may be unknown or uncertain. This setting spans two paradigms: the *offline* setting, in which the community sizes are fully known beforehand, and the *online* setting, where community sizes msut be laerned through repeated interactions over time. The offline version of the problem serves as a baseline for understanidng the optimal allocation strtaegies when complete information is available. Thsi scenario allows for the derivation of optimal policies under deterministic conditions, providing a fundamental benchmark for evaluating solutions in more complex settings. In contrast, the online version of the problem introduces significant challenges due to the inherent uncertainty in community sizes. Here, the explorer must balance the dual objectives of learning and optimization: on the one hand, allocating resources to explore communities and gather information about their sizes; on the other hand, leveraging this information to maximize engagement. This dynamic interplay between exploration and exploitation is central to many real-world problems, making the online community exploration problem a particularly compelling area of study. Existing literature has addressed related problems in various forms. The offline allocation problem can be seen as a combinatorial optimization problem, which has a long history of study in operations reserch and resource allocation [1, 2]. Greedy algorithms, in particular, have been shown to perform well in such contexts, often yielding near-optimal or even optimal results under certain conditions [3]. On the other hand, the online setting is cloosely related to the rich body of work on multi-armed bandit (MAB) problems, which model sequential decision-making under uncertainty [4]. Algorithms in this domain, such as Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) methods and their variants, have been widley studied for their ability to achieve sublinear regret in learning environments [5, 6]. However, while these techniques address soem aspects of online resource allocation, they do not directly account for the specific structure and constraints of the community exploration problem. Thsi paper provides a systematic study of the community exploration problem, bridging the gap between the offline and online settings. For the offline setting, we analyze two modes of exploration: non-adaptive exploration, where the allocation of resources is determined upfront, and adaptive exploration, where allocation decisions can be adjusted based on intermediate outcomes. We prove that in both cases, greedy methods yield optimal solutions, offering computationally efficient strategies for resource allocation. These results not only establish the theoretical foundation for offline community exploration but also provide practical guidelines for implementing exploration policies in real-world scenarios with known community sizes. For the online setting, we propose an algorithm inspired by the UCB framework that is tailored to the community exploration problem. This algorithm accounts for the unique structure of the problem, including the need to allocate resources across multiple communities while simultaneously learning their sizes. We prove that this approach achieves logarithmic regret bounds, demonstrating its efficiency in balancing exploration and exploitation over multiple rounds. Furthermore, by incorporating feedback from different rounds, we show that it is possible to achieve a constant regret bound, significantly improving long-term performance. These results highlight the potential for leveraging online learning techniques to optimize resource allocation in dynamic and uncertain environments. The contributions of tihs work are threefold. First, we formalize the community exploration problem, providing a unified framework that encompasses both offline and online settings. Second, we establish optimality results for greedy algorithms in the offlie setting, offering theoretical guarantees and practical insights for resource allocation. Third, we develop and analyze an online learning algorithm tht achieves strong performance guarantees, including logarithmic and constant regret bounds, depending on the feedback structure. Together, these contributions advance the state of the art in resource allocation and online learning, with implications for a wide range of applications. Under this assumption, we consider two exploration strategies: non-adaptive exploration and adaptive exploration. **Non-Adaptive Exploration:** In the non-adaptive setting, the explorer allocates the budget across all communities in advnce and does not adjust allocations based on feedback during the exploration process. Formally, let there be \( n \) communities, each with a known size \( s_i \) (where \( i \in \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} \)), and let \( B \) denote the total exploration budget. The gooal is to allocate the budget \( b_i \) to each community \( i \) such that \( \sum_{i=1}^n b_i \leq B \), thereby maximizing the expected number of members met. The expected number of members met in community \( i \) is modeled as a concave function \( f_i(b_i) \), reflecting diminishing returns with increased allocation. We prove that a greedy algorithm is optimal for this problem. The algorithm iteratively allocates one unit of budget to the community with the largest marginal gain in the number of members met, i.e., it selects the community \( j \) that maximizes \( f_j(b_j + 1) - f_j(b_j) \). This process continues until the budget \( B \) is exhausted. The optimality of the greedy algoritm is ensured by the concavity of \( f_i(b_i) \), which guarantees that the problem satisfies the properties of submodular optimization [1]. **Adaptive Exploration:** In the adaptive setting, the explorer can adjust the allocation dynamically based on real-time feedback during the exploration process. Feedback is modeled as the observed number of members met after allocating \( b_i \) units of budget to community \( i \). The adaptive strategy also employs a greedy approach, but decisions are made sequentially, incorporating observations from previous allocations. We demonstrate that the adaptive greedy algorithm achieves optimality by leveraging the same sbmodular prperties as the non-adaptive case. Importantly, the adaptive strategy is particularly advantageous in scenarios where real-time observation can significantly refine allocation decisions. ### Online Lerning The online setting introduces an additional layer of complexity: the sizes of communities are initially unknown and must be learned over multiple rounds of exploration. The objective is to minimize regret, defined as the difference between the cumulative reward of the optimal offline strategy and that of the online algorithm. The estimates are initialized with a prior assumption, and the algorithm updates them iteratively as new data becomes available. To account for uncertainty, an upper confidence bound \( U_i(t) \) is computed for each community, defined as: \[ U_i(t) = \hat{s}_i(t) + c \sqrt{\frac{\log t}{n_i(t)}}, \] where \( c \) is a tunable exploration parameter, \( n_i(t) \) is the number of times community \( i \) has been explored up to round \( t \), and \( \log t \) encourages exploration of less-sampled communities. During each round \( t \), the algorithm allocates the budget \( B \) to communities greedily, using the upper confidence bounds \( U_i(t) \) in place of the true sizes \( s_i \). Specifically, the budget is allocated to maximize the expected reward based on \( U_i(t) \), following the same submodular framework as in the offline setting. **Theoretical Guarantee:** We prove that the proposed algorithm achieves logarithmic regrret bounds, i.e., the regret \( R(T) \) grows as \( O(\log T) \). This result is derived using the properties of UCB-based algorithms, which ensure that the algorithm gradually focuses on the optimal allcation as the estimates \( \hat{s}_i(t) \) converge to the true sizes \( s_i \) [2]. **Constant Regret with Feedback Aggregation:** To further improve performance, we incorporate feedback aggregation acorss rounds. By combining observations from multiple rounds, we refine the size estimates \( \hat{s}_i(t) \) more rapidly, enabling the algorithm to converge faster. Specifically, after each round, the feedback from all explored communities is agrgegated and used to update a global estimate of community sizes. This refinement reduces uncertainty and improves allocation decisions in subsequent rounds. We show that incorporating feedback aggregation can reduce the regret to a costant value, independent of \( T \), under certain conditions. This improvement highlights the importance of leveraging cumulative informtion in online learning scenarios. ### Implementation and Complexity Both the offline and online algorithms are computationally efficient. The greedy algorithm for offline optimization has a time complexity of \( O(B \cdot n) \), as it involves iterating oveer all communities at each step of budget allocation. The online algorithm, with its UCB-inspired framework, has a per-round complexity of \( O(n \log T) \), dominated by the computation of confidence bounds and the greedy allocation step. Among the known etiologies of ischemic stroke, cardioembolic stroke and large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) are two common subtypes with distinct pathophysiological mechanisms and treatment approaches. Cardioembolic stroke typically results from emboli arising from the heart, most commonly due to conditions such as atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction, or valvular heart disease. In contrast, LAA stroke is caused by atherothrombotic occlusion or stenosis of major extracranial or intracranial arteries. These two etiologies differ not oly in their underlying mechanisms but also in theiir response to therapeutic interventions, with cardioembolic strooke often requiring long-term anticoagulation therapy and LAA stroke being more amenable to antiplatelet therapy and management of atherosclerotic risk factors. Consequently, accurate differentiation between these subtypes is critical for optimizing patient care. Among the various MRI techniques, perfusion imaging provides valuable insights into cerebral hemodynamics by measuring parameters such as cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume, mean transit time, and time to maximum of the residue function (Tmax). These parameters enable the identification of ischemic penumbra and infarct core, which are vital for therapeutic decision-making in the acute phase of stroke. This results in larger infarct volumes and more severe clinical presentations compared to LAA stroke, which typically involves more gradual vessel occluusion and better collateral circulation. Perfusion MRI parameters, particularly Tmax, can provide indirect evidence of these differences by reflecting the degree and distribution of perfusion deficits. In contrast, LAA stroke is caused by atherothrombotic occlusion or stenosis of major extracranial or intracranial arteries [7]. At each time step $t$, the decision-maker receives predictions $\{\hat{f}_{t+\tau}\}_{\tau \geq 1}$ for future cost functions $\{f_{t+\tau}\}_{\tau \geq 1}$. These predictions may originate from external sources such as machine learning models or forecasting systems. To model the errors in these predictions, we introduce a stochastic prediction error framework that defines the prediction error for a time step $t$ and horizon $\tau$ as $e_{t+\tau} = \hat{f}_{t+\tau} - f_{t+\tau}$. Our stochastic prediction error model makes several key assumptions about the error model. Firstly, we assume that the errors $\{e_{t+\tau}\}$ are random variables drawn from a distribution that depends on $\tau$, capturing the intuition that predictions become more accurate as the horizon $\tau$ decreases. Secondly, we assume that the errors $\{e_{t+\tau}\}$ may exhibit temporal correlation, reflecting dependencies in prediction quality over time. Finally, we assume that the variance of the prediction error is bounded, i.e., $\mathbb{E}[e_{t+\tau}^2] \leq \sigma_\tau^2$, where $\sigma_\tau^2$ decreases as $\tau$ decreases.

To leverage the stochastic prediction error model, we propose an algorithmic framework called Averaging Fixed Horizon Control (AFHC). The key idea of AFHC is to utilize a fixed prediction window of size $H$ to average over short-term predictions and mitigate the impact of noise. The algorithm proceeds as follows: at each time step $t$, the algorithm computes an averaged prediction of the cost function over the next $H$ steps, which reduces variance by smoothing out high-frequency noise in the individual predictions. Using this averaged prediction, the algorithm selects the decision $x_t$ by solving the optimization problem $x_t = \arg\min_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \sum_{\tau=1}^H \hat{f}_{t+\tau}(x)$. No restrictions were placed on the publication year to allow comprehensive coverage of available literature. ### Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Eligibility for inclusion was determined based on predefined criteria. Studies were included if they (1) reported survival rates or causes of death among Chinese patients with SLE; (2) were designed as cohort studies or case series; (3) provided sufficient data for survival analysis, death-cause analysis, or both; and (4) included patients diagnosed with SLE based on established criteria (e.g., the American College of Rheumatology or Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics criteria). Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. The burden of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in China is considerable, and elucidating the prognosis of this condition is essential for informing strategies to enhance patient outcomes. To gain a deeper understanding of the mortality patterns and survival rates associated with SLE in China, our research endeavored to conduct a systematic review and synthesis of observational studies, with a particular emphasis on estimating contemporary survival rates, ascertaining the primary causes of mortality, and investigating potential factors contributing to discrepancies in mortality trends. The significance of this investigation lies in its capacity to provide actionable insights into the prognosis of SLE in China, thereby informing the development of targeted interventions to improve patient outcomes. By examining the temporal and spatial patterns of survival rates and causes of mortality, we can pinpoint areas where healthcare access and treatment protocols may be optimized. Furthermore, our analysis will delve into the impact of ethnic, phenotypic, and other variables on mortality patterns, enabling the tailoring of interventions to specific patient populations. To accomplish these objectives, we undertook a systematic review and meta-analysis, adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [1]. Our exhaustive literature search encompassed multiple electronic databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), WANFANG Data, and SINOMED, to ensure the inclusion of both English and Chinese-language articles. We employed a combination of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms, such as "systemic lupus erythematosus," "SLE," "follow-up," "prognosis," "survival," "mortality," and "China," to refine our search strategy. Boolean operators ("AND," "OR") were utilized to further optimize the search strategy. To ensure the rigor of our review, we established predefined criteria for study inclusion and exclusion. Studies were deemed eligible if they (1) reported survival rates or causes of mortality among Chinese patients with SLE; (2) were designed as cohort studies or case series; (3) provided sufficient data for survival analysis, death-cause analysis, or both; and (4) included patients diagnosed with SLE based on established criteria, such as the American College of Rheumatology or Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics criteria [2, 3]. We excluded studies focusing on specific subpopulations, such as pediatric or geriatric populations, to avoid potential biases in generalizability. Case reports, editorials, reviews, and studies lacking relevant or extractable data were also excluded. Data extraction was performed by two independent reviewers using a standardized data collection form. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. We extracted data on study characteristics, patient demographics, clinical features, outcome measures, and quality indicators. For survival analysis, we focused on 5-year and 10-year survival rates following disease onset. For death-cause analysis, we extracted the proportions of individual causes of mortality, as reported in each study. To evaluate the methodological quality of included studies, we utilized established tools, such as the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for cohort studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklist for case series [4, 5]. Studies were rated as high, moderate, or low quality based on the total score. Disagreements in quality ratings were resolved through consensus. Statistical analyses were conducted using Stata software (version 15.0; StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). We calculated pooled survival rates and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using both fixed-effects and random-effects models. Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using the I² statistic, with values >50% indicating substantial heterogeneity. Sensitivity analyses were performed to explore the robustness of results by excluding low-quality studies and reanalyzing the data. For death-cause analysis, we calculated pooled proportions of specific causes of mortality, such as infection, renal involvement, lupus encephalopathy, and cardiovascular disease, using a random-effects model to account for variability across studies. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger's regression test, with p < 0.05 indicating significant bias [6]. Subgroup analyses were performed to explore potential sources of heterogeneity, including publication year, geographic location, and study quality. By systematically integrating data from multiple studies, our methodology ensures a comprehensive evaluation of survival outcomes and mortality causes in Chinese SLE patients while accounting for potential biases and variations in study quality. Our systematic review included a total of 41 studies, comprising 5 studies for survival analysis and 36 studies for death-cause analysis. The increasing rleiance on digital communication systems has brought foth a critical need for mechanisms that ensure both secure and reliable data transmission. Traditionally, encryption and error correction are treated as two distinct processes, with encryption safeguarding confidentiality and error correction ensuring data reliaility in noisy channels. However, this separation entails a higher computational overhead and often results in inefficiencies, particularly in resource-constrained environments. To address these challenges, joint encryption-encoding schemes have been proposed, offering an integrated appraoch to achieve both security and error correction in a unified framework [1]. Such schemes aim to streamline communication systems by combining encryption and encoding into a single operation, reducing computational complexity and enhancing data transmission performance. In code-based cryptography, linear codes have historically played a significant role in the design of jooint encryption-encoding schemes. However, conventional linear codes, such as Reed-Solomon or Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem (BCH) codes, oftne require large key sizes to achieve satisfactory levels of security. This limitation becomes particularly problematic in scenarios where key storage and transmission bandwidth are constrained. Furthermore, while these codes exhibit strong error correction capabilities, they may not provide optimal performance in balancing security and reliability requirements. Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes, first introduced by Gallager [2], have emerged as a promising alternative due to their excellent error correction performance, low decoding complexity, and flexible rate adaptability. Their inherent sparsity and structured design makke LDPC codes well-suited for modern communication systems, including joint encryption-encoding applications. Building on the advantages of LDPC codes, Quasi-Cyclic LDPC (QC-LDPC) codes have garnered significant interest in recent years. QC-LDPC codes represent a class of structured LPC codes with cyclic and quasi-cyclic properties, enabling efficient hardware implementation and reduced storage requirements [3]. These codes are particularly attractive in practical systems, where computational efficiency and scalability are critical design considerations. Moreover, the structured nature of QC-LDPC codes allows for the generation of large codeword lengths with compact representations, further contributing to their suitability for joint encryption-encoding schemes. Finite geometry-based codes, such as those derived from projective and affine geometries, provide a robust foundation for designing QC-LDPC codes with desirable properties. Finite geometry offers a well-defined mathematical framework for constructing codes with high minimum distance, structured sparsity, and tunable parameters [4]. By leveraging the geometric properties of finite fields, QC-LDPC codes based on fiinite geometry can achieve superior error correction performance while maintaining computational efficiency. These characteristics make finite geometry-based QC-LDPC codes an ideal candidate for developing secure and reliable joint encryption-encoding systems. In this paper, we propose a novel joint encryption-encoding scheme that utilizes QC-LDPC codes based on finite geometry to address the limitations of existing approaches. Our scheme integrates the error correction capabiliites of QC-LDPC codes with encryption functionality, achieving a significant reduction in key size without compromising security. Specifically, we demonstrate that the key size in our proposed scheme is only one-fifth of that required by the best-known similar systems. This reduction is attributed to the structured nature of finite geometry-based QC-LDPC codes, which allows for efficient key generation and storage. Additionally, our scheme supports a wide range of transmission rates, making it adaptable to diverse communication and cryptographic requirements. The security of the proposed scheme is rigorously analyzed against known cryptanalytic attacks targeting code-based cryptosystems. We show that the inherent structure of QC-LDPC codes, combined with the randomness introduced durig encryption, provides robust protection againsst attacks such as information set decoding and structural recovery [5]. Joint Encryption-Encoding Scheme Design The joint encryption-encoding scheme integrates the cryptographic and error correction functionalities into a single unified process. The main advantage of this approach is the reduction in key size and computational overhead while simultaneously achieving security and reliability. The proposed scheme operates in three stages: key generation, encryption-encoding, and decoding. #### 2.1 Key Generation In the key generation stage, a secret key \(K\) was generated and distributed securely to both the transmitter and receiver. The key \(K\) was derived from a random seed and used to pseudorandomly select a permutation matrix \(P\) and an invertible scrambling matirx \(S\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\). These matrices were used to obfuscate the structure of the QC-LDPC code and to introduce cryptographic security. The public parity-check matrix \(H_p\) was constructed as: \[ H_p = S H P, \] where \(H\) is the parity-check matrix of the underlying QC-LDPC code. The matrices \(S\) and \(P\) ensure that the public matrix \(H_p\) is computationally indistinguishable from a random sparse matrix, thwarting structural attacks such as those baed on the algebraic or combinatoriaal properties of \(H\) [2]. #### 2.2 Encryption-Encoding Process The encryption-encoding process was designed to simultaneously encde the message \(m\) and encrypt it into a codeword \(c\). Let \(m \in \mathbb{F}_q^k\) denote the plaintext message, where \(k\) is the dimension of the code. The process is as follows: 1. **Message Embedding:** The plaintext \(m\) was first mapped into a binary vector \(x\) of length \(n-k\) using a systematic generator matrix \(G\) derived from the public parity-check matrix \(H_p\). This ensures that \(x\) is a valid syndrome vector for \(H_p\): \[ H_p x^T = 0. \] 2. **Scrambling:** The encoded vector \(x\) was then scrambled using the secret matrices \(S\) and \(P\) to produce the encrypted codeword \(c\): \[ c = S x P. \] This step ensures that the codeword \(c\) is indistinguishable from a random vector, enhancing the cryptographic strength of the system. 3. **Transmission:** The resulting ciphertext \(c\) was transmitted over a noisy communication channel. Due to the error-correction properties of the QC-LDPC code, the scheme is robust to bit-flip errors introduced during transmission. #### 2.3 Decoding At the receiver, the decoding process involved both decryption and error correction. The received vector \(y\) was first descrambled using the inverse of the secret matrices: \[ x = S^{-1} y P^{-1}. \] Subsequently, a belief propagation (BP) algorithm was employed to decode \(x\) back into the original plaintext \(m\). The BP algorithm iteratively updated the probabilities of each bit in \(x\) based on the structure of the parity-check matrix \(H\) and the received vector \(y\), achieving accurate error correction with low computational complexity [3]. ### 3. The capacity of the human visual system to modify its focal length, a phenomenon referred to as accommodation, is a intricate and multifaceted process that has been the subject of extensive investigation in eyes possessing a natural crystalline lens, known as phakic eyes [1]. However, in instances where the natural lens is replaced with an artificial intraocular lens (IOL), thereby rendering the eye pseudophakic, the accommodative process is significantly altered, leading to a compromised ability to adapt to changing visual demands [2]. Although the IOL lacks the malleable properties inherent to the natural lens, research has demonstrated that the administration of pilocarpine, a muscarinic cholinergic agonist, can induce accommodation, thereby influencing the positioning of the IOL and the geometric configuration of the eye [3]. This, in turn, highlights the necessity of comprehending these changes in order to optimize visual outcomes in individuals with pseudophakic eyes. Pilocarpine functions by stimulating the ciliary muscle, which, in the context of phakic eyes, modulates the shape of the crystalline lens to achieve focal adjustments [4]. In pseudophakic eyes, the induction of accommodation via pilocarpine provides unique insights into the dynamics of ocular biometry, as the mechanical characteristics of the IOL and surrounding ocular structures differ substantially from those of the natural lens [5]. Previous investigations have observed anterior displacement of the IOL and alterations in anterior chamber depth (ACD) during accommodation, underscoring the complex interactions between the ciliary muscle, the zonular fibers, and the IOL [6]. These findings give rise to intriguing questions regarding the extent to which other ocular parameters, such as vitreous length (VL) and axial length (AL), may undergo changes during accommodation in pseudophakic eyes. The axial length of the eye is a parameter of considerable clinical significance, particularly in the context of refractive surgery, myopia progression studies, and the design of IOLs for cataract surgery [7]. Changes in AL during accommodation have been reported in phakic eyes, with observed elongation attributed to forward displacement of the lens and posterior displacement of the retina [8]. Nevertheless, the underlying mechanisms responsible for AL changes in pseudophakic eyes remain poorly understood. It has been hypothesized that contraction of the ciliary muscle during pilocarpine-induced accommodation may exert forces that influence the position of the IOL and surrounding ocular structures, potentially leading to measurable changes in axial biometry [9].
