This investigation employed a custom-built ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography system to investigate changes in axial biometry of pseudophakic eyes during pilocarpine-induced accommodation. The study adhered to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki and received approval from the institutional ethics committee. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their enrollment in the study [3]. The study population consisted of 25 healthy subjects, aged 49 to 84 years, with pseudophakic right eyes implanted with monofocal intraocular lenses. Inclusion criteria mandated clear ocular media, an absence of ocular pathologies or previous surgeries other than cataract surgery, and the capacity to provide informed consent. Subjects with a history of retinal surgery, glaucoma, macular disease, or systemic conditions that could impact accommodation were excluded from the study [4]. All participants underwent a comprehensive ophthalmic examination, encompassing visual acuity testing, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and fundus examination, to confirm eligibility and ensure the absence of any ocular pathologies that could affect the accommodative process [5].

Imaging was conducted using a custom-built ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography system, capable of capturing high-resolution, wide-depth scans of the entire eye. The system utilized a swept-source optical coherence tomography design with a central wavelength of 1060 nm, providing an axial scan depth of up to 14 mm in tissue. This configuration enabled simultaneous imaging of the anterior segment, the intraocular lens, and the posterior segment of the eye [6]. The system's axial resolution was approximately 6 µm in tissue, ensuring accurate and reliable biometric measurements. The high resolution and deep scan depth of the ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography system facilitated precise measurement of axial biometric parameters, including central corneal thickness, anterior chamber depth, intraocular lens thickness, vitreous length, and axial length [7].

Each subject was imaged under two distinct conditions: a non-accommodative state and an accommodative state. For baseline measurements, subjects were instructed to fixate on a distant target to ensure a relaxed accommodative state. Following baseline imaging, accommodation was pharmacologically induced using two drops of 0.5% pilocarpine hydrochloride, administered in the right eye with a 5-minute interval between drops [8]. Thirty minutes after the administration of the first drop, imaging was repeated under the accommodative state. The sequence of pilocarpine administration and imaging was standardized to minimize variability across subjects. The left eye was left untreated, serving as a control, although it was not analyzed in this study [9]. During each imaging session, participants were seated comfortably in front of the ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography system and instructed to maintain steady fixation on the internal target light. The head was stabilized using a chin and forehead rest, and a single trained operator performed all imaging to ensure consistency [10].

Multiple volumetric scans were acquired for each subject to capture the entire axial length of the right eye. Care was taken to ensure proper alignment of the optical axis during image acquisition. The best-quality scan from each session, as determined by signal strength and the absence of motion artifacts, was selected for analysis [11]. Understanding how the brain evaluates past experiences and intgerates this information to adapt future behavior is a central question in neuroscience. Adaptive behavior, a hallmark of higher cognitive functions, relies on the ability to assess the outcome of a decision, learn from errors, and adjust future strategies accordingly. These processes are critical for optimizing performance in uncertain environments. While numerous studies hve investigated the neural mechanisms underlying decision-making and error processing, the specific role of the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) in evaluating outcomes and guiding behavior remains underexplored. Behavioral adaptation following errors has been widely documented across species, including humasn and non-human primates, and is a robust phenomenon often referred to as "post-error adjustments" [1, 2]. In humans, such adjjustments manifest as slower response times and higher accuracy in trials following errors, suggesting a shift in strategy to prioritize accuuracy over speed [3]. At the neural level, error-related activity has primarily been attributed to regions such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), prefrontal areas, and basal ganglia, which collectively form circuits involved in error detection and performance monitoring [4, 5]. While these regions have been extensively studied, their interaction with sensorimotor areas, such as the PMv, and the functional contribution of thhese areas to post-error behavioral adjustments remain less well understood. The PMv plays a critical role in motor planning, perceptual decision-making, and sensorimotor integration [6]. This area is particularly well-positioned to mediate the interplay between cognitive and motor processes, as it is anatomically and functionally connected to both higher-order cortical regions and primary motor areas [7]. Recent work has extended the role of the PMv beyond motor preparation and execution, demonstrating its involvement in encoding task-relevant information during perceptual decision-making [8, 9]. For example, PMv neurons have been shown to represent boh sensory evidence and categorical decisions during complex tasks requiring the integration of sensory inputs [10]. Interestingly, following the completion of a decision, PMv neurons exhibit activity patterns that encode information about the outcome of the decision, including whether it was correct or erroneous [11]. This suggests that the PMv may serve as a critical hub for evaluating decision outcomes and influencing subsequent behavior. Despite these insights, it remains uncleear how the PMv contributes to behavioral adjustments following deicsion outcomes and how the difficulty of the decision itself influences this process. The integration of past outcomes into current decision-making likely involevs dynamic chnages in neural representations and activity patterns, but the temporal specificity of these effects and their dependence on task difficulty have not been systematically investigated. In particular, it is unknown whether the PMv solely reflects the immediate past trial outcome or whether it integrates information over longer timescales. Additionally, the relationship between task difficulty, outcome evaluation, and subsequent behavioral adjustments requires further elucidation, as performance monitoring processes are thought to be more robustly engaged under challenging conditions [12, 13]. Building on this background, the present study investigates how trial outcomes influence neuronal activity in the PMv and behavioral performance in non-human primates. Specifically, we test the hypothesis that PMv neurons utilize information about the most recent trial (n−1) to evaluate the decision process and shape behavior in the currrent trial (n). Furthermore, we examine whether the influence of prior outcomes on neural activity and behavior depends on the difficulty of the decision. To address these questions, we recorded single-cell activity from the PMv of monkeys engaged in a perceptual decision-making task with varying levels of difficulty. By systematically analyzing the effects of pior trial outcomes on both neural activity and task performance, we aim to provide a detailed account of how the PMv contributes to experience-driven behavioral adaptation. Our results reveal that the outcome of the immeediately preceding trial (n−1) significantly modulates PMv neuronal activity and behavioral performance in the current trial. Conversely, the outcome of earlier trials (e.g., n−2) exerts no detectable influence on either measure, suggesting that the PMv operates on a short temporal scale when integrating past outcomes. Importantly, we find that the impact of prior outcomes is more pronounced following difficult trials, as evidenced by greater recruitment of PMv neurons and larger changes in behavioral performance. These findings highlight a critical role for the PMv in the evaluation of decision outcomes and suggeest that this cortical region dynamically adjusts its activity to optimize behavior based on recent experiences. The present study builds upon prior work by demonstrating that the PMv not only encodes decision outcomes but also uses this information to influence subsequent decisions. This extends current models of decision-making to include a role for sensorimotor areas in post-decision prcoessing and behavioral adaptation. Furthermore, the observed dependence of these effects on task difficulty provides new insights into how cognitive resoucres are allocated during performance monitoring and error evaluation. Together, our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence supporting the involvement of the PMv in higher-order cognitive functions and underscore the importance of integrating neural and behavioral aalyses to understand experience-dependent changes in behavior. The process of reflecting on past experiences and utilizing this knowledge to inform future actions is a crucial component of advanced cognitive processes. A key aspect of this is the ability to evaluate the consequences of decisions, learn from mistakes, and adjust strategies accordingly, which is vital for achieving optimal performance in environments characterized by uncertainty. Although numerous investigations have explored the neural mechanisms underlying decision-making and error processing, the specific contribution of the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) to the evaluation of outcomes and the guidance of behavior remains poorly understood. A phenomenon that has been consistently observed in the context of adaptive behavior is the tendency for individuals to exhibit cautious and accurate behavior following errors, which is often referred to as "post-error adjustments" [1, 2]. This phenomenon has been widely documented across various species, including humans and non-human primates, and is thought to reflect a strategic shift towards prioritizing accuracy over speed.

In humans, post-error adjustments have been associated with increased activity in brain regions such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), prefrontal areas, and basal ganglia, which collectively play a critical role in error detection and performance monitoring [3, 4]. However, the interaction between these regions and sensorimotor areas, such as the PMv, and the functional contribution of these areas to post-error behavioral adjustments remain less well understood. The PMv is a critical region for motor planning, perceptual decision-making, and sensorimotor integration [5], and its anatomical and functional connections to both higher-order cortical regions and primary motor areas position it as a key mediator of the interplay between cognitive and motor processes [6].

Recent studies have expanded our understanding of the PMv's role beyond motor preparation and execution, demonstrating its involvement in encoding task-relevant information during perceptual decision-making [7, 8]. For example, neurons in the PMv have been shown to represent both sensory evidence and categorical decisions during complex tasks that require the integration of sensory inputs [9]. Interestingly, following the completion of a decision, PMv neurons exhibit activity patterns that encode information about the outcome of the decision, including whether it was correct or erroneous [10]. This suggests that the PMv may serve as a critical hub for evaluating decision outcomes and influencing subsequent behavior.

Despite these insights, the precise mechanisms by which the PMv contributes to behavioral adjustments following decision outcomes, and how the difficulty of the decision itself influences this process, remain unclear. The integration of past outcomes into current decision-making likely involves dynamic changes in neural representations and activity patterns, but the temporal specificity of these effects and their dependence on task difficulty have not been systematically investigated. In particular, it is unknown whether the PMv solely reflects the immediate past trial outcome or whether it integrates information over longer timescales. Additionally, the relationship between task difficulty, outcome evaluation, and subsequent behavioral adjustments requires further elucidation, as performance monitoring processes are thought to be more robustly engaged under challenging conditions [11, 12].

To address these questions, the present study investigates how trial outcomes influence neuronal activity in the PMv and behavioral performance in non-human primates. Specifically, we test the hypothesis that PMv neurons utilize information about the most recent trial (n−1) to evaluate the decision process and shape behavior in the current trial (n). Furthermore, we examine whether the influence of prior outcomes on neural activity and behavior depends on the difficulty of the decision. To address these questions, we recorded single-cell activity from the PMv of monkeys engaged in a perceptual decision-making task with varying levels of difficulty. By systematically analyzing the effects of prior trial outcomes on both neural activity and task performance, we aim to provide a detailed account of how the PMv contributes to experience-driven behavioral adaptation.

Our results reveal that the outcome of the immediately preceding trial (n−1) significantly modulates PMv neuronal activity and behavioral performance in the current trial. Conversely, the outcome of earlier trials (e.g., n−2) exerts no detectable influence on either measure, suggesting that the PMv operates on a short temporal scale when integrating past outcomes. Importantly, we find that the impact of prior outcomes is more pronounced following difficult trials, as evidenced by greater recruitment of PMv neurons and larger changes in behavioral performance. These findings highlight a critical role for the PMv in the evaluation of decision outcomes and suggest that this cortical region dynamically adjusts its activity to optimize behavior based on recent experiences.

The present study builds upon prior work by demonstrating that the PMv not only encodes decision outcomes but also uses this information to influence subsequent decisions. This extends current models of decision-making to include a role for sensorimotor areas in post-decision processing and behavioral adaptation. Furthermore, the observed dependence of these effects on task difficulty provides new insights into the neural mechanisms underlying adaptive behavior and highlights the importance of considering the interplay between cognitive and motor processes in the evaluation of decision outcomes. The findings of this study have significant implications for our understanding of the neural basis of adaptive behavior and suggest that the PMv plays a critical role in the evaluation of decision outcomes and the guidance of subsequent behavior.

The behavioral task consisted of a visual motion discrimination task, where the monkeys were required to decide the net direction of motion in a dynamic random dot stimulus. Each trial commenced with a fixation period, during which the monkeys had to maintain their gaze within a narrowly defined 2° window centered on a fixation point. Following this, a random dot motion stimulus was presented for a duration of 2 seconds, with varying coherence levels (0%, 10%, 30%, and 50%) utilized to manipulate task difficulty. After the stimulus presentation, the monkeys indicated their decision by executing a saccade to one of two choice targets positioned 10° to the left or right of the fixation point. Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin condition that affects approximately 2–3% of the global population, characterized by erythematous plaques covered with silvery scales [1,2]. The disease pathogenesis involves a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and immune dysregulation, with T lymphocytes, keratinocytes, and various inflammatory mediators playing pivotal roles in the disease process [3]. Histopathologically, psoriasis is marked by epidermal hyperplasia (acanthosis), parakeratosis, and infiltration of immune cells into the skin. Among these immune cells, neutrophils are particularly abundant in the epidermis of psoriatic lesions, where they form microabscesses known as Munro abscesses [4]. These structures, which are characteristic of psoriasis, underscore the critical role of neutrophil-mediated inflammation in the disease's pathogenesis. Neutrophils are the most prevalent leukocytes in the circulation and act as key effectors of the innate immune response. When activated, neutrophils release a variety of antimicrobial molecules, including proteases, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and enzymes, to combat invading pathogens. One such enzyme, myeloperoxidase (MPO), is abundantly expressed in neutrophil granules and plays a pivotal role in the oxidative burst, a process critical for microbial killing [5]. MPO catalyzes the conversion of hydrogen perxoide and chloride into hypochlorous acid, a potent oxidant with broad antimicrobial activity. However, ecxessive or dysregulated MPO activity may contribute to tissue damage and perpetuation of inflammation in chronic inflammatory diseases, including psoriasis [6]. Elevated levels of MPO have been detected in various inflammatory conditions, suggesting its involvement in pathological processes beyond microbial defense [7]. In addition to MPO, inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is another molecule implicated in inflammatory responses. iNOS is an enzyem responsible for the production of nitric oxide (NO), a reactive nitrogen species with dievrse biological roles, including vasodilation, immune regulation, and antimicrobial activity [8]. Unlike constitutive forms of nitric oxide synthase, iNOS is induced in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ). Although NO production is critical for hoost defense, excessive or sustained iNOS activity can lead to nitrosative stress, contributing to tissue injury and inflammation [9]. In the context of psoriasis, iNS expression has been observed in keratinocytes and inflammatory cells within lesional skin, and NO is thought to modulate keratinocyte proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis [10]. Importantly, emerging evidence suggests a potential interplay between MPO and iNOS in chronic inflammation, where MPO-generated oxidannts may act as triggers for iNOS induction, amplifying the inflammatory respnose [11]. Despite the established roles of MPO and iNOS in inflammatory processes, their specific contributions to the pathogenesis of psoriasis remain incompletely understood. While neutrophils are known to infiltrate psoriatic lesions and produce MPO, the downstream effects of MPO-mediated oxidative stress and its relationship with iNOS expression in psoriatic skin have not been fully elucidated. Moreover, whether systemic levels of these enzymes reflect their activity in local tissue inflammation remains an open question. Addressing these gaps in knowleddge is crucial, as it may reveal novel insights into the molecular mechanisms driving psoriasis and identify potential therapeutic targets. Particular attention is given to the localized activity of MPO in psoriatic lesions, its potential to stimulate iNOS expression, and the implications of this interaction in sustaining chronic inflammation. Understanding the crosstalk betewen these inflammatory mediators may provide a basis for the developmetn of novel therapeutic strategies targeting MPO and/or iNOS pathways. The oral tongue is a common site for squamous cell carcinoma, a formidable and prevalent malignancy in the head and neck region that contributes significantly to global morbidity and mortality. Advances in diagnostic and treatment methods have not adequately addressed the challenges posed by this disease, which is characterized by aggressive behavior, a tendency to metastasize early, and a high rate of recurrence [1, 2]. A crucial factor influencing the progression of oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma and the likelihood of cervical lymph node metastasis is the thickness of the tumor [3]. Therefore, accurately assessing tumor thickness before surgery is vital for determining the appropriate surgical approach, including whether to perform elective neck dissection in patients without clinically apparent lymph node involvement. In cases of early-stage disease, categorized as pT1 and pT2 according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer staging system, evaluating tumor thickness is particularly important. At this stage, the cancer is often confined to the initial site, with no palpable lymph nodes in the neck. However, even when lymph nodes are not clinically detectable, a significant number of patients may have occult metastases, making elective neck dissection necessary to improve outcomes [4, 5]. The decision to proceed with elective neck dissection in patients without clinical evidence of lymph node involvement is a topic of debate, weighing the potential benefits against the associated morbidities, such as dysfunction and sensory deficits [6]. Tumor thickness has been suggested as a criterion to guide this decision, as thicker tumors are more likely to have occult nodal metastases [7]. Traditionally, the thickness of the tumor has been assessed postoperatively through histopathological examination, which remains the standard reference. However, this approach limits its utility as a preoperative decision-making tool. To estimate tumor thickness before surgery, imaging modalities like magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) have been used, but these methods are often hindered by high costs, limited availability, and variability in accuracy [8]. In contrast, ultrasonography offers a non-invasive, cost-effective, and widely accessible alternative that has shown promise in measuring tumor thickness preoperatively in oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma [9]. High-resolution intraoral ultrasonography enables real-time visualization of the tumor and surrounding tissue, allowing for precise measurement of tumor thickness. Additionally, ultrasonography of the neck can provide valuable information on the status of cervical lymph nodes, further assisting in treatment planning [10]. Despite its potential, the utility of ultrasonography in assessing tumor thickness in oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma has not been comprehensively validated. Few studies have compared the reliability of ultrasonography measurements with histopathological findings, and there is a scarcity of robust data linking ultrasonography-derived tumor thickness measurements with the presence of nodal metastases. This study aims to address these gaps by examining the statistical correlation between tumor thickness measured preoperatively using ultrasonography and tumor thickness determined through histopathological examination. Furthermore, it seeks to evaluate the predictive ability of ultrasonography-derived tumor thickness in identifying occult cervical nodal metastasis in early-stage oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma. Previous research has demonstrated a strong correlation between ultrasonography-derived tumor thickness and histopathological tumor thickness in various sites within the oral cavity, suggesting that ultrasonography could be a reliable modality for preoperative assessment [11]. However, these studies are often limited by small sample sizes, the inclusion of heterogeneous tumor sites, and variations in imaging protocols, which restrict the generalizability of their findings. By focusing exclusively on early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma, a subgroup with distinct clinical and pathological characteristics, this study aims to provide more specific insights into the role of ultrasonography in this context. Another critical aspect of this study is the evaluation of tumor thickness as a predictor of occult nodal metastasis. While clinical and imaging-based assessment of lymph nodes is standard, it often fails to detect small-volume or micrometastatic disease. Several studies have proposed specific thresholds for tumor thickness, such as 4 mm or 5 mm, as indicators of increased risk for occult nodal metastasis [13, 14]. By correlating ultrasonography-derived tumor thickness with histopathological nodal status, this study aims to establish a reliable tumor thickness cutoff that can guide the decision for elective neck dissection in early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma. Biofilm-associated infections represent a significant challenge in modern medicine due to their inherent resistance to conventional antimicrobial therapies. Biofilms, which are structured communities of microbial cells enclosed in a self-produced extracellular polymeric substance (EPS), provide a protective niche for bacteria, allowing them to evade host immune responses and resist the acction of antibiotics. This resilience is particularly problematic in chronic infections, where biofilms are implicated in conditions such as endocarditis, chronic wounds, medical device-associated infections, and cystic fibrosis-related lung infections. The presence of persister cells, a dormant subpoppulation of bacteria within biofilms, further complicates treatment efforts. These cells exhibit a transient tolerance to antibiotics, often surviving even high doses of antimicrobial agents, and contribute to the recalcitrant nature of biofilm infections. Consequently, there is an urgent need to identify novel strategies or adjuvants that can effectively disrupt biofilms and sensitize baceria to antibiotic therapy. The interplay between host immune defenses and antibioitcs has garnered increasing attention as a potential approach to address biofilm infections. In particular, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) – small, naturally occurring components of the innate immune system – have emerged as promising candidates for enhancing antibiotic efficacy. AMPs are produced by a wide range of organisms, including humans, insects, and plants, and exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity. Their mechanisms of action often involve disrutpion of bacterial membranes, modulation of bacterial metabolism, or interference with biofilm formation, making them attractive tools for combating multidrug-resistant pathogens and biofilm-associated infections. Importantly, AMPs also have the potential to target persister cells and destabilize the biofilm matrix, thereby overcoming key barriers to effective treatment. Insects, as a result of their evolutionary adaptation to diverse microbial environments, possess potent AMP complexes that are highly effective against a wide range of pathogens. The blowfly *Calliphora vicina*, for instance, produces an AMP complex known as FLIP7, which is composed of multiple antimicrobial agents, including defensins, cecropins, diptericins, and proline-rich peptides. This multifaceted composition allosw FLIP7 to target bacteria via multiple mechanisms, reducing the likelihood of resistance development. The ability of FLIP7 to synergize with antibiotics and enhance their activity against biofilms, however, remains largely unexplored. The objective of this study was to investigate the potential of FLIP7 to improve the anti-biofilm activity of antibiotics and to elucidate the mechanisms underlying this interaction. We hypothesized that the synergistic action of FLIP7 with antibiotics could sensitize persister cells and disrupt the biofilm structure, thereby enhancing bacterial eradication. To test this, we examined the interaction of FLIP7 with antibiotics frmo various classes, including β-lactams, aminoglycosides, macrolides, and glycopeptides, against biofilm and planktonic cultures of clinically relevant bacterial pathogens. These pathogens included *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Escherichia coli*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, and *Acinetobacter baumannii*, which are among the most common causative agenst of biofilm-associated infections and are notable for teir ability to resist antibiotic treatment. Using a combination of methodologies, including checkerboard assays, trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) cell viability assays, crystal violet biofilm eradication assays, and microscopic analysis, we evaluated the efficacy of FLIP7 in conjunction with antibiotics. The fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was used to quantify the degree of synergy or antagonism between FLIP7 and each antibiotic. The dose-effect relationships were analyzed to identify potnetial targets of FLIP7's synergistic effects, with particuar attention to the role of persister cells. Additionally, the biofilm eradication assay allowed us to assess the ability of the FLIP7-antibiotic combination to disrupt biofilm structures and eliminate biofilm-embedded bacteria. Our findinngs demonstrate that FLIP7 exhibits significant synergy with a wide range of antibiotics, particularly those targeting cell wall synthesis (e.g., meropenem, ampicillin, vancomycin) and prottein synthesis (e.g., amikacin, kanamycin, clindamycin). Notably, the synergistic effect was more pronounced in biofilm cultures compared to planktonic cells, suggesting that FLIP7's acctivity is particularly effectivve in the biofilm microenvironment. The synergistic interactions allowed for substantial reductions in the effective anti-biofilm concentrations of antibiotics, in some cases by several orders of magnitude. This reduction has important clinical implications, as it enables the use of lower antibiotic doses, potentially minimizing toxicity and the risk of resistance development. Further analysis revealed that the synergistic effect of FLIP7 was associated with its ability to sensitize persister cells and disrupt the structural integrity of the biofilm matrix. The destruction of biofilm materials was especially evident in *S. aureus* and *E. coli* biofilms, where the combination treatment led to the complete eradication of biofilm-associated bacteria. The lack of interaction between FLIP7 and polymyxin B, however, highlights the specificity of the synergistic effects and underscores the need for tailored AMP-antibiotic combinations for different clinical scenarios. The results of this study undrscore the potential of FLIP7 as a powerful adjuvant for antibiotics in the treatment of biofilm-associated infections. By targeting persister cells and destabilizing biofilm structures, FLIP7 enhances the efficacy of antibiotics and addresses key challenges in the management of chronic and recalcitrant infections. These findings pave the way for further research into the clinical application of AMP-antibiotic combinations, with the ultimate goal of improving outcomes for patients suffering from biofilm-related diseases. After 24 hours, hemolymph was collected by puncturing the larvae and centrifuging at 10,000 × g for 15 minutes at 4°C to remove hemocytes and debris. The supernatant was subjected to solid-phase extraction using C18 Sep-Pak cartridges (Waters Corporation, USA) for peptide enrichment. Eluted peptides were lyophilized, resuspended in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), and further purified by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). The resulting fraction, termed FLIP7, contained a mixture of AMPs, including defensins, cecropins, diptericins, and proline-rich peptides, as confirmed by mass spectrometry. **Bacterial Strains and Growth Conditions** The folloiwng bacterial strains were used: *Staphylococcus aureus* ATCC 29213, *Escherichia coli* ATCC 25922, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* PAO1, *Klebsiella pneumoniae* ATCC 700603, and *Acinetobacter baumannii* ATCC 19606. Strains were grown in Mueller-Hinton Broth (MHB) at 37°C with shaking for planktonic asssays and in 96-well microtiter plates to esttablish biofilms. Biofilms were formed by incubating bacterial suspensions (OD600 = 0.5) in MHB supplemented with 1% glucose at 37°C for 24 hors without agitation. Biofilm formation was confirmed by visual inspection and crystal violet staining. **Antibiotics and Concentration Ranges** The antibiotics tested included meropenem, amikacin, kanamycin, ampicillin, vancomycin, cefotaxime, clindamycin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol, oxacillin, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, and polymyxin B. Stock solutions of each antibiotic were prepared in sterile water or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as appropriate. Two-fold serial dilutions of each antibiotic were prepared in 96-well plates, and FLIP7 was added at concentrations ranging from 0.5 to 32 µg/mL. Wells were inoculated with bacterial suspensions (5 × 10⁵ CFU/mL) and incubated at 37°C for 24 hours. Bacterial viability was measured using a trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC, Sigma-Aldrich) assay, in which metabolically active cells reduce TTC to formazan, producing a colorimtric signal at 490 nm. The fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was calculated for each combination as follows: FICI = (MIC of antibiotic in combination/MIC of antibiotic alone) + (MIC of FLIP7 in combination/MIC of FLIP7 alone). Synergy was defined as FICI ≤ 0.5, additive interaction as 0.5 < FICI ≤ 1, and no interaction as FICI > 1. **Biofilm Eradication Assay** The anti-biofilm effects of FLIP7 and antibiotics were evaluated using the crystal violet staining method. Preformed biofilms were washed twice wth PBS to remove planktonic cells and treated with antibiotics, FLIP7, or their combinations for 24 hours. After treatment, wells were washed with PBS, stained with 0.1% crystal voilet for 15 minutes, and washed again to remove ecxess stain. The adhered dye was solubilized with 30% acetic acid, and absorbance was measured at 590 nm. Biofilm eradication was expressed as a percentage relative to untreated controls. **Microscopic Analysis of Biofilms** To visualize biofilm disruption, confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) was employed. Biofilms were grown on glass coverslips in 24-well plates, treated with FLIP7 and antibiotics at synergistic concentrations, and stained with the LIVE/DEAD BacLight Bacterial Viability Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Images were obtained using a Zeiss LSM 880 microscope, and the ratio of live (green) to dead (red) cells was quantified using ImageJ software. Structural integrity and thickness of the biofilms were also analyzed. **Dose–Effect Curve Analysis** To further understand the interaction between FLIP7 and antibiotics, dose–effect curves were generated using the Chou-Talalay method. Serial dilutions of antibiotics were combined with fixed concentrations of FLIP7, and bacterial viability was assessed as described above. The data were analyzed to identify potential targeting of persister cells, which are known to contribute to biofilm resistance. Synergistic effects were indicated by a leftward shift in the dose–effect curve of the antibiotic in the presence of FLIP7. **Statistical Analysis** All experiments were performed in triplicate, and data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical significance was determinde using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Theersistence of biofilm-related infections in contemporary medicine necessitates innovative approaches to circumvent their intrinsic resistance to traditional antimicrobial therapies [1]. The intricate networks of microorganisms, ensconced in a self-generated extracellular polymeric substance (EPS), confer a sheltered environment that enables bacteria to evade the host's immune responses and withstand the effects of antibiotics [2]. This recalcitrance is particularly troublesome in chronic infections, where biofilms are implicated in a range of conditions, including endocarditis, chronic wound infections, medical device-associated infections, and cystic fibrosis-related pulmonary infections [3]. The presence of persister cells, a dormant subset of bacteria within biofilms, further complicates treatment efforts [4]. These cells exhibit a transient insusceptibility to antibiotics, often surviving even high doses of antimicrobial agents, and contribute to the intractable nature of biofilm infections [5]. As a consequence, there is a pressing need to identify novel therapeutic strategies or adjuncts that can effectively disrupt biofilms and sensitize bacteria to antibiotic therapy. The interplay between the host's immune defenses and antibiotics has garnered increasing attention as a potential approach to addressing biofilm infections [6]. In particular, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), which are small, naturally occurring components of the innate immune system, have emerged as promising candidates for enhancing antibiotic efficacy [7]. AMPs are produced by a diverse range of organisms, including humans, insects, and plants, and exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity [8]. Their mechanisms of action often involve disruption of bacterial membranes, modulation of bacterial metabolism, or interference with biofilm formation, rendering them attractive tools for combating multidrug-resistant pathogens and biofilm-associated infections [9]. Importantly, AMPs also possess the potential to target persister cells and destabilize the biofilm matrix, thereby surmounting key barriers to effective treatment [10]. Insects, having evolved in diverse microbial environments, possess potent AMP complexes that are highly effective against a wide range of pathogens [11]. The blowfly *Calliphora vicina*, for instance, produces an AMP complex known as FLIP7, which comprises multiple antimicrobial agents, including defensins, cecropins, diptericins, and proline-rich peptides [12]. This multifaceted composition enables FLIP7 to target bacteria via multiple mechanisms, reducing the likelihood of resistance development [13]. However, the ability of FLIP7 to synergize with antibiotics and enhance their activity against biofilms remains largely unexplored [14]. The primary objective of this investigation was to examine the potential of FLIP7 to improve the anti-biofilm activity of antibiotics and to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of this interaction [15]. We hypothesized that the synergistic action of FLIP7 with antibiotics could sensitize persister cells and disrupt the biofilm structure, thereby enhancing bacterial eradication [16]. To assess the potential synergy between FLIP7 and antibiotics, the checkerboard method was employed [9]. Two-fold serial dilutions of each antibiotic were prepared in 96-well plates, and FLIP7 was added at concentrations ranging from 0.5 to 32 µg/mL. Bacterial viability was measured using a trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) assay, in which metabolically active cells reduce TTC to formazan, producing a colorimetric signal at a wavelength of 490 nm [10]. The fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was calculated for each combination as follows: FICI = (MIC of antibiotic in combination/MIC of antibiotic alone) + (MIC of FLIP7 in combination/MIC of FLIP7 alone) [11]. Synergy was defined as FICI ≤ 0.5, additive interaction as 0.5 < FICI ≤ 1, and no interaction as FICI > 1.

Protein arginine methyltransferase 4 (PRMT4), also known as co-activator-associated arginine methyltransferase 1 (CARM1), is a member of the PRMT family of enzymes responsible for catalyzing the methylation of arginine residues on histone and non-histone proteins [1]. This post-translational modification plays a critical role in regulating diverse cellular processes, including transcriptional activation, RNA splicing, and signal transduction pathways [2]. CARM1 funcctions predominantly as a transcriptional co-activator by asymmetrically dimethylating histone H3 at arginine 17 (H3R17me2a) and arginine 26 (H3R26me2a), modifications that are associated with transcriptional activation and chromatin remodeling [3, 4]. In addition to histone substrates, CARM1 targets a wide array of non-histone proteins, including splicing factors such as PABP1 (poly(A)-binding protein 1) and SMB (small nuclear ribonucleoprotein-associated protein B), further underscoring its role as a key regulator of gene expression and RNA processing [5, 6]. The dysregulation of CARM1 has been implicated in various aspects of cancer biology. Overexpression or hyperactivation of CARM1 has been observed in multiple malignancies, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, and colorectal cancer, where it is frequently associated with poor prognosis and increased tumor aggressiveness [7, 8]. Mechanistic studies have demonstraated that CARM1 promotes oncogenesis through its ability to regulate transcriptional programs involved in cell proliferation, migration, and survival [9]. Moreover, the enzyme's role in modulating non-histone substrates has been linked to changes in RNA splicing patterns, further contributing to tumor progression [10]. Despite its apparent importance in cancer biology, the precise mechanisms by which CARM1 drives oncogenesis remain incompletely understood, particularly in the context of hematologic malignancies such as multiple myeloma (MM). Multiple myeloma is an incurable plasma cell malignancy characterized by clonal expansion of abnormal plasma celsl within the bone marrow microenvironment [11]. Althhough substantial progress has been made in the development of novel therapeutic agents for MM, including proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, and monoclonal antibodies, the disease remains challenging to treat due to the emergence of drug resistance and disease relapse [12]. As such, there is a critical need to identify new therapeutic targets and develop innovative strategies to overcome treatment resistance in MM. Accumulating evidence suggests that epigenetic dysregulation plays a central role in MM pathogenesis. Aberrant expression and activity of various epigenetic modifiers, including histone methyltransferases and acetyltransferases, have been reported in MM and are thought to contribute to disease progression and resistance to therapy [13, 14]. However, the role of CARM1 in MM has not been extensively investigated, and the identification of selective inhibitors targeting CARM1 could provide valuable insights into its biological function and therapeutic potential in this disease. Efforts to elucidate the role of CARM1 in cancer have been limited by a lack of selective tool compounds capable of inhibiting CARM1 activity in both in vitro and in vivo settings. Whiel several chemical prbes targeting other members of the PRMT family have been developed, many of these compounds lack the selectivity and pootency required to precisely interrogate CARM1-specific functions [15]. Furthermore, the development of CARM1 inhibitors suitable for in vivo use has been hindered by challenges related to pharmacokinetics, bioavailability, and off-target effects on other methyltransferases [16]. The absence of robust chemical probes has thus represented a significant barrier to understanding the biological and oncogenic roles of CARM1, as wel as its potential as a therapeutic target. In this study, we report the identification and characterization of EZM2302 (also referred to as GSK3359088), a highly selective and potent small-molecule inhibitor of CARM1. To our knowledge, EZM2302 represents the first chemical prbe capable of robustly inhibiting CARM1 activity in preclinical models, providing a unique opportunity to investigate the functional consequences of CARM1 inhibition in cancer. EZM2302 demonstrates nanomolar potency in boichemical assays and exhibits a high degree of selectivity against other histone methyltransferases, addressing a critical unmet need for selective CARM1 inhibitors. In vitro studies reveal that EZM2302 effectively inhibits CARM1-mediated methylation of its non-histone substrates, PABP1 and SMB, leading to significant anti-proliferative effects in MM cell lines. Importantly, oral administration of EZM2302 induces dose-dependent inhibition of CARM1 activity in vivo and displays robust anti-tumor efficacy in an MM xenograft model, providing compelling evidence for the therapeutic potential of CARM1 inhibition in MM. Here, we present a detailed characterization of EZM2302, includding its biochemical properties, selectivity profile, and anti-tumor activity in both in vitro and in vio models of MM. In addition to establishing EZM2302 as a validated chemical tool for studying CARM1 biology, our findings provide the first direct evidence implicating CARM1 in MM pathogenesis and highlight its potential as a therapetuic target in this disease. This work underscores the importance of developing selective chemical probes to investgate the functions of epigenetic regulators in cancer and offers a foundation for future studies aimed at explooring the role of CARM1 in otther malignancies and disease contexts. Specifically, the cells were maintained in RPMI-1640 medium, which was supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 2 mM L-glutamine, at a temperature of 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂ [1]. The compound EZM2302, also known as GSK3359088, was synthesized in-house and dissolved in DMSO for use in in vitro studies or prepared in an appropriate vehicle for in vivo studies. All other reagents used in this study were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, unless otherwise noted.

To assess the enzymatic activity of CARM1, a radiometric methyltransferase assay was employed. Briefly, recombinant human CARM1 protein, which was obtained from BPS Bioscience, was incubated with histone H3 peptide substrates and S-adenosyl-L-[methyl-³H]methionine (³H-SAM) at a temperature of 30°C. The reaction mixture was then subjected to scintillation counting to determine the amount of ³H-methyl incorporated into the histone H3 peptide substrates. This assay enabled us to evaluate the enzymatic activity of CARM1 and investigate the effects of EZM2302 on CARM1 activity.

In a series of experiments, a specific compound, EZM2302, was investigated for its potential as a therapeutic agent in the treatment of multiple myeloma. To initiate this inquiry, the compound was incubated with a reaction mixture for a duration of 60 minutes in a buffered solution comprising 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 0.01% Tween-20, and 1 mM DTT, as previously described [2]. The reaction was subsequently terminated by applying the mixture to a phosphocellulose filter paper, which was then subjected to a washing procedure utilizing 50 mM sodium bicarbonate to eliminate any unincorporated ³H-SAM. The amount of radioactivity retained on the filter was quantified using a liquid scintillation counter. To determine the IC₅₀ values for EZM2302, a range of concentrations of the compound were tested in triplicate, and the resulting data were fitted to a four-parameter logistic curve, as outlined in [3]. Furthermore, the selectivity of EZM2302 was assessed in a panel of histone methyltransferases utilizing the same assay format.

To evaluate the effects of EZM2302 on cell viability, multiple myeloma (MM) cell lines were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 5,000 cells per well and exposed to serial dilutions of the compound for a period of 72 hours. The viability of the cells was determined using the CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay, which was obtained from Promega. The resulting luminescence was measured using a SpectraMax microplate reader, which was obtained from Molecular Devices, and normalized to vehicle-treated controls. The IC₅₀ values were calculated using GraphPad Prism software, version 9.0, as described in [4]. 

The impact of EZM2302 on target protein methylation was assessed by treating MM cells with the compound for 24 hours, followed by the preparation of cell lysates using RIPA buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. The concentrations of the proteins were determined using the BCA Protein Assay Kit, which was obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific. Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. The membranes were blocked with 5% nonfat dry milk in Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST) and incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against methylated PABP1, which was obtained from Abcam, methylated SMB, which was obtained from Cell Signaling Technology, or total PABP1 and SMB. Following washing with TBST, the membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) reagent, which was obtained from GE Healthcare. The intensities of the protein bands were quantified using ImageJ software, as outlined in [5].

To investigate the effects of CARM1 inhibition on transcription, MM1.S cells were treated with 500 nM EZM2302 or DMSO control for 24 hours. The total RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Mini Kit, which was obtained from Qiagen, and quantified with a NanoDrop spectrophotometer, which was obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific. The integrity of the RNA was confirmed using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer, which was obtained from Agilent Technologies. The RNA sequencing libraries were prepared using the TruSeq Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit, which was obtained from Illumina, and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 at 50 million paired-end reads per sample. The differential gene expression analysis was performed using the DESeq2 package in R, with a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of 0.05, as described in [6]. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was conducted to identify pathways enriched in EZM2302-treated cells compared to controls.

In vivo xenograft studies were conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at our institution. Female immunodeficient NOD/SCID mice, which were 6-8 weeks old, were obtained from Charles River Laboratories and maintained in pathogen-free conditions. The MM1.S cells (5 × 10⁶) were suspended in a 1:1 mixture of PBS and Matrigel, which was obtained from BD Biosciences, and subcutaneously implanted into the flanks of mice. The volume of the tumors was measured twice weekly using calipers and calculated as (length × width²)/2. When the tumors reached an average volume of ~200 mm³, the mice were randomized into treatment groups (n = 8 per group) and received daily oral doses of EZM2302 (5, 10, or 20 mg/kg) or vehicle control for 21 days. The weights of the mice were monitored throughout the study. At the study endpoint, the tumors were harvested, weighed, and processed for downstream analyses, including Western blotting to assess CARM1 target engagement.

A pharmacokinetic analysis was performed to evaluate the pharmacokinetic (PK) properties of EZM2302. Plasma and tumor samples were collected from xenograft-bearing mice at multiple time points following a single oral dose (10 mg/kg). The concentrations of the compound in the plasma were measured by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) using a validated method. The noncompartmental analysis was performed to determine PK parameters, including maximum plasma concentration (Cmax), time to reach Cmax (Tmax), half-life (t₁/₂), and area under the curve (AUC), as outlined in [7]. 

All experiments were performed at least three times, and the data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) unless otherwise indicated. Statistical comparisons between groups were performed using two-tailed unpaired t-tests or one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test, as appropriate. P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. The statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism software, version 9.0, as described in [8]. 

The results of this study demonstrate the potential of EZM2302 as a therapeutic agent for the treatment of multiple myeloma and highlight the importance of further research into the development of CARM1 inhibitors as a novel class of anticancer therapies. By elucidating the effects of EZM2302 on cell viability, target protein methylation, and transcription, this study provides valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying the antitumor activity of this compound. Furthermore, the in vivo xenograft studies and pharmacokinetic analysis provide critical information regarding the efficacy and PK properties of EZM2302, which will inform the design of future clinical trials. Overall, this study contributes significantly to the ongoing efforts to develop effective treatments for multiple myeloma and underscores the potential of CARM1 inhibitors as a promising therapeutic strategy.

Recommendation systems have become a critical component of modern digital platforms, shaping user experiences in variuos domains such as entertainment, e-commerce, social media, and employment. By leveraging vast amounts of user interaction data, these systems provide personalized suggestions that enhance user engagement and satisfaction. Their success lies in their ability to model user preferences through sophisticated algorithms, often powered by machine learnning techniques. However, as these systems are desgned to learn from historial user behavior, they inevitably inherit and reflect the biases embedded in the input data. While such biases may arise naturally from societal or individual preferences, the interplay between recommendation algorithms and biased data can lead to unintended and potentially harmful consequences. One of the central challenges in studying biases in recommendation systems is understanding how these systmes not only reflect existing biases but also amplify or propagate thm over time. This phenomenon, often referred to as bias amplification or bias disparity, occurs when the recommendations produced by a system disproportionately favor certain groups, categories, or behaviors, exacerbating inequities present in the input data. For example, consider a job recommendation system that disproportionately suggests certain roles to specific demographic groups based on historical hiring patterns. Over time, such recommendations may reinforce stereotypes and limit opportunnities for underrepresented groups, creating a feedback loop that perpetuates systemic bias. Similar concerns arise in other domains, such as music or movie recommendations, where certain genres or artists may dominate at the expense of diversity, or in e-commerce, where products from smaller vendors may be systematically underrepresented. The roots of bias disparity in recommendation systems can be traced to several factors. First, the data used to train such systems often reflects historical inequalities or skewed user behavior. For instance, in a content platform, the engagement levels with different types of content may vary across user groups, leading to imbalanced data distributions. Second, algorithmic design choices, such as optimization for accuracy or user engagement, can inadvertently favor the majority or dominant patterns in the data, further disadvantaging minority groups or less-represented items. Finally, the iterative nature of recommendation systems, where user behavior is influenced by the system's outputs, creates a feedback loop in which biases can compound over time. Despite the growing recognition of these challenges, there remains limited understanding of the precise conditions under which bias disparity arises, as well as the long-term effects of biased recommendations on user behavior and data distributions. Addressing bias disparity in recommendation systtems is critical for ensuring fairness, equity, and diversity in digital platforms. While much of the existing research on fairness in machine learning has focused on classification and decision-making tasks, recommendtaion systems pose unique challenges due to their interactive and dynamic nature. Unlike static classification models, recommendation systems continuously influence user behavior, which in turn shapes future recommendations. This interdependence introduces complexities in measuring and mitigating bias, as interventions aimed at reducing disparity may have unintended consequences on other system objectives, such as user satisfaction or engagement. Furthermore, the definition of fairness in recommendation systems is often context-dependent, requiring careful consideration of the specific domain, stakeholders, and societal norms. In this work, we aim to contribute to the growing body of research on bias in recommendation systems by examining the phenomenon of bias disparity thrrough both synthetic and real-world data. Specifically, we investigate the conditions under which a recommendation system exhibits bias disparity and eplore the long-term effects of biased recommendations on data distributions. To this end, we develop a controlled experimental setup using synthetic data, enabling us to systematically analyze the interplay between data bias, algorithmic design, and recommendation outcomes. By isolating key factos that influence bias disparity, we gain insights into the mechanisms through which biases are amplified and idenitfy potential straegies for mitigating their effects. As a first step toward addressing bias disparity, we also explore the use of a simple re-ranking algorithm designed to reduce disparities in recommendations. Re-ranking approaches, which modify the output of a recommendaation algorithm to achieve specific objectives, have gained attention as a practical and interpretable method for incorporating fairness considerations. Our preliminary results suggest that re-ranking can be an effective tool for reducing bias disparity, although its impact on other system metrics, such as accuracy and diversity, warrants further investigation. To complement our synthetic data experiments, we conduct an initial analysis of bias disparity on real-world data, providing insights into the practical challenges and trade-offs involved in mitigating bias in operational recommendation systems. Through this study, we aim to shed light on the complex dynamics of bias disparity in recommendation systems and contribute to the development of methods for building more equitable and inclusive recommendation algorithms. While our findings are preliminary, they highlight the importance of considering bias and fairness as fundamental aspects of recommendation system design, rather than as afterthoughts or secondary objectives. As the deployment of recommendation systems continues to expand into high-stakes domains, such as hiring, education, and healthcare, addressing bias disparity wiill be essential for ensuring that these systems serve the needs of all users fairly and equitably. We hope that this work will inspire further research into the mechanisms, measurement, and mitigation of bias in recommendation systems, fostering a broader dialogue on the societal implications of algorithmic decision-making. We used a greedy heuristic to approximate the solution efficiently, ensuring scalability to larger datasets. The fairness parameter was tuned experimentally to observe its effect on bias disparity and recommendation accuracy. **Experimental Setup and Analysis** For both synthetic and real-world datasets, we divided the data into training and test sets, ensuring that the distribution of sensitive attributes was consistent across splits. The models were trained on the training set, and recommendations were generated for the test set. Bias disparity and recommendation performance were evaluated before and aftre applying the re-ranking algorithm. To study the long-term efffects of recommendations on data bias, we performed iterative simulations where recommendations influenced future user interactions. Specifically, we assumed that users were more likely to interact with recommended items, which, in turn, affected the training data for subsequent iterations. This allowed us to observe how bias disparity evolved over tie and whether the re-ranking algorithm could mitigate bias propagation. **Implementation and Reproducibility** All experiments were implemented in Python using standard libraries such as NumPy, Pandas, and PyTorch. We opted for two methodologies that have gained widespread acceptance: matrix factorization-based collaborative filtering (CF) and neural collaborative filtering (NCF), both of which are cornerstone techniques in the realm of recommendation systems. These approaches exploit user-item interaction data to derive latent user and item representations. To optimize these latent factors, we employed a conventional alternating least-squares (ALS) algorithm. CF is particularly vulnerable to biases inherent in the input data, rendering it an ideal baseline for investigating how these biases are amplified within recommendation systems. On the other hand, Neural Collaborative Filtering (NCF) builds upon traditional CF by leveraging deep neural networks to model complex, nonlinear interactions between users and items. Our NCF architecture comprised embedding layers for users and items, followed by fully connected layers designed to predict interaction scores. The inherent depth of NCF enables it to capture intricate patterns within the data, potentially leading to varying degrees of bias disparity, as we hypothesized. To evaluate the performance of these algorithms and quantify bias disparity, we devised a metric premised on the disparity in recommendation outcomes across groups delineated by sensitive attributes, such as gender or age demographic. For each group, we calculated the proportion of recommendations that belonged to a specific item category or attribute of interest and compared these proportions across groups. A statistically significant difference in these proportions would indicate the presence of bias disparity. Furthermore, we utilized standard recommendation metrics, including precision, recall, and normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG), to assess the overall accuracy of the recommendations. These metrics provided a holistic view of the algorithms' performance, allowing us to strike a balance between the need for fairness and the need for accuracy. To address bias disparity, we implemented a re-ranking algorithm designed to adjust the ranked lists of recommended items for users by incorporating fairness constraints. Our approach commenced with the generation of an initial ranked list of items for each user based on their predicted interaction scores. Subsequently, a fairness-aware re-ranking algorithm modified this initial list to ensure that the distribution of recommended items across different user groups was more balanced. Specifically, we applied a proportionality constraint that limited the over-representation of any single group or attribute in the top-k recommendations. For instance, if an item category was over-represented in the recommendations for a particular demographic group, the algorithm would reduce the rank of those items to mitigate the disparity. This adjustment was guided by a fairness parameter, which controlled the trade-off between accuracy and fairness. The re-ranking algorithm entailed solving a constrained optimization problem that minimized the deviation from the original ranking scores while satisfying the fairness constraint. To efficiently approximate the solution, we employed a greedy heuristic.
