Malaria in pregnancy (MiP) remains a major public health challenge, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where the burden of malaria is disproportioantely high. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that approximately 11 million pregnancies in sub-Saharan Africa are exposed to malaria infection annually, leading to adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes, including maternal anaemia, miscarriage, stillbirth, low birh weight, and neonatal mortality [1]. Addressing MiP is therefore a critical component of maternal and child health strategies in this region. One of the most effective interventions recommended by the WHO for preventing MiP is intermittent preventive treatment in preganncy (IPTp) witth sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP), a proven and cost-effective strategy for reduccing the bruden of malaria during pregnancy [2]. Despite its efficacy, the uptake of IPTp-SP remains alarmingly low across sub-Saharan Africa, undermining efforts to mitigate the devastating effects of malaria on pregnant women and their offspring. The WHO recommends that all pregnant women in areas of moderate to high malaria transmission receive at least three doses of IPTp-SP starting in the second trimester, with subsequent doses administered at least one month apart during routine antenatal care (ANC) visits [3]. This recommendation is grounded in robust evidence demonstrating the protective benefits of IPTp-SP in reducing maternal anaemia, placental malaria, and low birth weight [4]. In recognition of these benefits, most countries in sub-Saharan Africa have adopted national policies to proomte IPTp-SP as part of their comprehensive malaria control strategies. However, the implementation of these policies has faced numerous challenges, resulting in suboptimal IPTp coverage across the region [5]. Recent data indicate that, in many malaria-endemic countries, the proportion of pregnant women receiving the recommended three doses of IPTp-SP reemains well below the global targets, with significant disparities observed between and within countries [6]. A growing body of research suggests that sociocultural, economic, and health system factors play a critical role in shaping the uptake of IPTp-SP among pregnant women. Socioeconomic status, in particular, has been identified as a key determinant of health-seeking behaviours, including the utilisation of preventive services such as IPTp-SP [7]. Wealthier households tend to have better access to healthcare services, including ANC, where IPTp-SP is administered, compaared to poroer households [8]. Similarly, educational attainment is strongly associated with healthcare utilisation, as women with higher levels of education are more likely to understand the importance of preventive measures dring pregnancy and to overcome barriers to accessing care [9]. These socioeconomic disparities are further compounded by infrastructural challenges, such as stockouts of SP at health facilities, inadequate training of healthcare providers, and poor-quality ANC services, which disproportionately affect disadvantaged populations [10]. Despite the recognition of these barriers, comprehensive analyses of the patterns and determinants of IPTp-SP uptake across different socioeconomic and demographic groups remain limited. While some studies have examined individual countries or subpopulations, there is a lack of comparative research that explores variations in IPTp uptake across multiple countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Such analyses are essential for identifying systemic gaps and informing targeted interventions to improve IPTp coverage in the region. Moreover, the existing literature has primarily focused on the proportion of women receiving at least one or two doses of IPTp-SP, with relatively little attention paid to the uptake of three or more doses, which is now considered the standard for adequate protection against MiP [11]. The present study seeks to address these gaps by providing a comprehensive analysis of the prevalence and patterns of IPTp-SP utake in selected malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Specifically, this study leverages cross-sectional data from the Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) conducted in Brkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda to examine the prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake and to investigate socioeconomic disparities in the utilisation of this preventive intervention. These countries were selected based on their high malaria burden and the availability of recent MIS data, which provide reliable and comparable information on malaria-related indicators at the national level. The study's objectives are twofold. First, it aims to measure the overall prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake, with a focus on the proportion of women who received at least three doses during their most recent pregnancy. Second, it seeks to explore the associations between IPTp-SP uptake and key socioeconomic factors, including household wealth and maternal education, while adjusting for relevant sociodemographic variables. By examining these patterns, the study aims to identify the structural and individual-level barriers to IPTp-SP uptake and to highlight the inequities that persist within and between countries. The findings of this study have significant implications for policy and practice. Understanding the socioeconomic and demographic factors that influence IPTp-SP uptake is cruciial for designing targeted interventions to improve coverage, particularly among disadvantaged populations. Furthermore, the identification of between-country variations can serve as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of national IPTp policies and healthcare systems, providing valuable insights for policymakers and programme implementers. Given the critical role of ANC services in delivering IPTp-SP, the study also underscores the need to strengthen health systems and address supply-side constraints, such as stockouts of SP and inadequate provider training, to ensure that all pregnant women have access to this life-saving intervention. In conclusion, while IPTp-SP is a well-established strategy for preventing MiP, its uptake remains unacceptably low in many malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Addressing this gap requires a nunced understanding of the socioeconomic and systemic barriers that hinder the utilisation of IPTp-SP, as well as a commitment to equity in the delivery of maternal and child health services. By shedding light on the prevalence and determinants of IPTp-SP uptake, this study aims to contribute to the evidence base needed to inform effective interventions and accelerate progress towards reducing the burden of malaria in pregnancy in sub-Saharan Africa. The study utilized a cross-sectional design to evaluate the prevalence and determinants of intermittent preventive treatment during pregnancy (IPTp) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) among women in malaria-endemic countries of sub-Saharan Africa. Data were obtained from the Malria Indicator Surveys (MIS) conducted in Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda. MIS datasets were chosen due to their robust design, nationaly representative sampling frameworks, and standardized data collection procedures, which allow for cross-country comparisons and analyses. The surveys were administered between 2016 and 2021, depending on the country, and were implemented by national malaria control programs in collaboration with international technical and funding partners, including the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) Program. The target population comprised women aged 15–49 years who had completed at least one pregnancy within the two years preceding the survey. The inclusion criteria were establsihed to ensure the analysis focused on women whose most recent pregnancy occurred within a time frame relevant to the WHO-recommended IPTp-SP guidelines, which have been adopted across most sub-Saharan African countries. The exclusion criteria included women for whom information on IPTp-SP usage or key sociodemographic variables was missing or incomplete. The primary outcome variable was the uptake of IPTp-SP, operationalized as receiving at least three doses of SP during the most recent pregnancy. This definition aligns with the WHO recommendation, which endorses a minimum of three doses of SP administered at antenatal care (ANC) visits as an effective strategy to reduce malaria-related adverse outcomes during pregnancy [1]. Women were asked to recall the number of doses of SP taken during their last pregnancy, and responses were verified against their maternal health cards whenever possible. The primmary independent variables included education lveel and household wealth status. Education level was categorized into four groups: no formal education, primary education, secondary education, and tertiary education. Household wealth status was assessed using wealth quintiles derived from principal component analysis (PCA) of household asset ownership, access to utilities, and housing characteristics, as provided in the MIS datasets [2]. Other sociodemographic covariates included maternal age, mrital status, parity, rural or urban residence, and ANC attendance during pregnancy. The sample size for the study comprised 18,603 women who met the inclusion criteria across the eight countries. Sampling weights provided in the MIS datasets were applied to account for the complex survey design, including clustering, stratification, and unequal probabilities of selection. The weighted sample ensured that the findings were nationally representative for each country. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake, stratified by country, educational attainment, and wealth quintile. Prevalence estimates were reported as percentages with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Between-country variations in IPTp-SP coverage were examined using chi-square tests to assess statistical significance. Multivariable logistic regression models were employed to identify sociodemographic factors associated with IPTp-SP uptake. The dependent variable was binary, indicating whether a woman had received at least three doses of SP during her last pregnancy (coded as 1) or fewer than three doses (coded as 0). The primary covariates of interest—education and household wealth—were included in the regression models alongside other sociodemographic factors identified a priori as potential confounders, such as maternal age, parity, ANC attendance, and place of residence (urban versus rural). Adjusted odds ratis (AORs) with 95% CIs were calculated to quantify the strength of associations. The regression models wre constructed using a stepwise approach. First, unadjusted bivariate analyses were conducted to assess the relationship between each independent variable and the outcome. Variables with a p-value <0.25 in the bivariate analysis were included in the multivariable model [3]. A backward elimination strategy was then applied to retain only covariates with a significant association (p < 0.05) with the outcome in the final model. To account for potential clustering effects at the community level, the regression models included random effects at the primary sampling unit (PSU) level. In addition, robust standard errors were used to address potential heteroskedasticity and ensure valid inference. All analyses were connducted using Stata version 15 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA), and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Ethical approval for the use of secondary data was obtained from the DHS Program, which ensures that all MIS datasets comply with international ethical standards, including informed consent from survey participants and anonymization of data to protect confidentiality. Further country-specific ethical clearances were obtained by the respective national malaria control programs prior to conducting the surveys. By employing a rigorous and standardized methodological approach, this study aimed to generate evidence on the prevalence and determinants of IPTp-SP uptake, with a particular foucs on socioeconomic disparities within and across malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa. The findings are intended to inform policy and programmatic interventions to improve IPTp-SP coverage and reduce the burrden of malaria in pregnancy in the region. The results of this study, baseed on data from 18,603 women aged 15–49 years across eight malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa, demonstrate significant variation in uptake of intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP), both between countries and across socioeconomic and educational groups. The overall prevalence of taking at least three doses of IPTp-SP during the last pregnancy, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO), was 29.5% (95% CI = 28.2–30.5). However, substantial differences were observed between countries, with Ghana achieving the highest prevalence at 60% (95% CI = 57.1–62.8), followed by Kenya at 37% (95% CI = 35.3–39.2) and Sierra Loene at 31% (95% CI = 29.2–33.4). Countries such as Nigeria (21.8%, 95% CI = 20.4–23.2) and Burkina Faso (18.2%, 95% CI = 16.7–19.8), however, reported significantly lower rates of uptake. The results indicated a persistent disparity in IPTp-SP uptake that correlated strongly with household wealth status. Womne from the richest householsd were less likely to take three or more doses of IPTp-SP compared to women from poorer households. Specifically, women from the poorest households showed an uptake of 19.0%, while those from poorer, middle, richer, and richest households reported uptakes of 21.1%, 21.2%, 20.7%, and 18.1%, respectively. Logistic regression analysis revealed that women from poorer socioeconomic strata had significantly higher odds of not completing the three recommended doses compared to their wealthier counterparts, even when adjusted for other sociodemographic varriables such as age, parity, and urban/rural residence. Educational attainment also demonstrated a notable influence on IPTp-SP uptake. An inverse association between educational level and uptake of IPTp-SP was observed. Women with no formal education had higher odds of failing to adhere to the recommended threee doses compared to women wtih primary, secondary, or higher levels of education. For instance, the prevalence of taking three doses among women with no educaation was 25.3%, while it was 32.7% among women with primary education and 35.9% among those with secondary or higher education. This trend persisted even after adjusting for wealth status and other demographic factors, signifying education as an independent determinant of IPTp-SP uptake. Further analysis of the data revealed significant rural-urban differences. Women residing in urban areas were more likely to met the WHO-recommended three doses of IPTp-SP compared to their rural counterparts. For example, the prevalence of uptake in urban areas was 34.2% (95% CI = 32.1–36.4) compared to 25.8% (95% CI = 24.1–27.6) in rural areas. This finding may reflect disparities in access to healthcare facilities, as urban women are generally closer to health services and more likely to benefit from antenatal care (ANC) services where IPTp-SP is administered. The study also noted distinct disparities in uptake between countries, highlighting systemic issues in healthcare delivery and policy implementation. For example, Ghana’s relatively higgh prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake may reflect effective implementation of national malaria control strategies, including well-supported ANC services and community-level awareness campaigns. In contrast, countries such as Burkina Faso and Nigeria, with lower prevalene rates, may face challenges related to supply chain disruptions, inadequate ANC infrastructure, and limited community awareness of the benefits of IPTp-SP. Additionally, regional conflicts and sociopolitical instability in some countries could contribute to poor performance in IPTp-SP coverage. Parity, or the number of pregancies a woman has had, was another significant factor influencing IPTp-SP uptake. Women in their first pregnancy (primigravidae) were less likely to take three doses compared to multigravidae. This disparity may stem from differences in ANC attendance, as women in their first pregnancies may be less familiar with the benefits of ANC and IPTp-SP. The persistence of malaria in pregnancy (MiP) represents a profound obstacle to public health advancement, particularly within the sub-Saharan African region, where the disease burden exhibits a remarkably skewed distribution. As highlighted by the World Health Organization (WHO), the annual tally of pregnancies exposed to malaria infection in this geographical context approximates 11 million, yielding a cascade of adverse consequences for maternal and neonatal health, encompassing maternal anaemia, spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, low birth weight, and neonatal mortality [1]. Consequently, addressing MiP assumes paramount importance as a constituent element of maternal and child health strategies in this region. Among the array of interventions endorsed by the WHO for the prevention of MiP, intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) emerges as a singularly efficacious and economical strategy for mitigating the disease's burden during pregnancy [2]. Notwithstanding its documented efficacy, the adoption of IPTp-SP remains disconcertingly low throughout sub-Saharan Africa, thereby undermining concerted efforts to ameliorate the devastating repercussions of malaria on pregnant women and their progeny. The WHO stipulates that all pregnant women residing in areas characterized by moderate to high malaria transmission should receive a minimum of three doses of IPTp-SP, with the initial dose administered during the second trimester, followed by subsequent doses at intervals of at least one month during routine antenatal care (ANC) visits [3]. This recommendation is predicated upon a robust corpus of evidence demonstrating the protective benefits of IPTp-SP in reducing maternal anaemia, placental malaria, and low birth weight [4]. In acknowledgment of these benefits, the majority of sub-Saharan African countries have integrated national policies promoting IPTp-SP as a component of their comprehensive malaria control strategies. However, the implementation of these policies has been hindered by a multitude of challenges, resulting in suboptimal IPTp coverage across the region [5]. Recent empirical data indicate that, in numerous malaria-endemic countries, the proportion of pregnant women receiving the recommended three doses of IPTp-SP remains significantly below the globally established targets, with notable disparities observed both between and within countries [6]. A burgeoning body of research suggests that an intricate interplay of sociocultural, economic, and health system factors exerts a profound influence on the uptake of IPTp-SP among pregnant women. Specifically, socioeconomic status has been identified as a critical determinant of health-seeking behaviors, including the utilization of preventive services such as IPTp-SP [7]. Households situated at the higher echelons of the socioeconomic spectrum tend to exhibit enhanced access to healthcare services, including ANC, where IPTp-SP is administered, in comparison to their less affluent counterparts [8]. Similarly, educational attainment has been observed to be strongly correlated with healthcare utilization, as women possessing higher levels of educational attainment are more likely to comprehend the importance of preventive measures during pregnancy and to surmount barriers to accessing care [9]. These socioeconomic disparities are further exacerbated by infrastructural challenges, such as stockouts of SP at health facilities, inadequate training of healthcare providers, and poor-quality ANC services, which disproportionately affect disadvantaged populations [10]. Despite the recognition of these barriers, comprehensive analyses of the patterns and determinants of IPTp-SP uptake across diverse socioeconomic and demographic groups remain limited in scope. While certain studies have focused on individual countries or subpopulations, a dearth of comparative research exists, exploring variations in IPTp uptake across multiple countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Such analyses are essential for identifying systemic gaps and informing targeted interventions aimed at improving IPTp coverage in the region. Furthermore, the existing literature has primarily concentrated on the proportion of women receiving at least one or two doses of IPTp-SP, with relatively scant attention devoted to the uptake of three or more doses, now considered the standard for adequate protection against MiP [11]. The present investigation seeks to address these knowledge gaps by providing a comprehensive analysis of the prevalence and patterns of IPTp-SP uptake in selected malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Specifically, this study leverages cross-sectional data from the Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) conducted in Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda to examine the prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake and to investigate socioeconomic disparities in the utilization of this preventive intervention. The selection of these countries was predicated upon their high malaria burden and the availability of recent MIS data, which provide reliable and comparable information on malaria-related indicators at the national level. The study's objectives are twofold. Firstly, it aims to quantify the overall prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake, with a focus on the proportion of women who received at least three doses during their most recent pregnancy. Secondly, it seeks to explore the associations between IPTp-SP uptake and key socioeconomic factors, including household wealth and maternal education, while adjusting for relevant sociodemographic variables. By examining these patterns, the study aims to identify the structural and individual-level barriers to IPTp-SP uptake and to highlight the inequities that persist within and between countries. The findings of this study have significant implications for policy and practice, as elucidating the socioeconomic and demographic factors that influence IPTp-SP uptake is crucial for designing targeted interventions to improve coverage, particularly among disadvantaged populations. Additionally, the identification of between-country variations can serve as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of national IPTp policies and healthcare systems, providing valuable insights for policymakers and stakeholders engaged in malaria control efforts. Ultimately, this research endeavors to contribute to the development of evidence-based strategies for optimizing IPTp-SP uptake, thereby mitigating the burden of malaria in pregnancy and promoting improved maternal and neonatal health outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa. By shedding light on the complex interplay of factors influencing IPTp-SP uptake, this study seeks to inform the development of tailored interventions that address the unique challenges and opportunities present in each country, ultimately contributing to the attainment of global malaria control goals. The importance of this research cannot be overstated, as the lives of millions of pregnant women and their children hang in the balance, pending the implementation of effective strategies to prevent and control malaria in pregnancy. As the global community continues to grapple with the challenges of malaria control, the findings of this study will provide critical insights and guidance for policymakers, healthcare providers, and other stakeholders engaged in the quest to eradicate this devastating disease. Despite its established benefits, the uptake of IPTp-SP remains suboptimal in many malaria-endemic countries [1]. To address this challenge, it is essential to elucidate the complex interplay of factors influencing IPTp-SP adoption, with a focus on socioeconomic and systemic barriers. This study seeks to contribute to the existing knowledge base by providing a comprehensive examination of IPTp-SP uptake patterns in selected malaria-endemic countries, with the ultimate goal of informing evidence-based interventions to reduce the burden of MiP.

Frequency hopping sequences (FHSs) play a pivotal role in modern communication systems, particularly in applications such as frequency-hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) and code-division multiple access (CDMA). These sequences are critical for ensuring efficient utilization of the frequency spectrum, minimizing interference, and securing communcation channels. The design of FHSs with favorable correlation properties is therefore an important topic in both theoretical and practical contexts. Specifically, FHSs with low Hamming auto-correlation and cross-correlation are highly desirable for mitigating mutual interference and achieving reliable performance in multi-user environments. The study of FHSs traces its roots to the early development of spread-spectrum communication, where the sequences wree first used to provide robustness against jamming and eavesdropping. Over the years, the theory of FHSs has evolved significantly, with researchers focusing on the construction of sequences that meet specific optimality criteria. Among these criteria, the average Hamming correlation—the average measure of similarity between sqeuences or between different shifts of the same sequence—has emerged as a key metric. FHSs with optimal average Hamming correlation properties not only enhance system performance but also align with the theoretical bounds established in the literature. A primary challenge in the design of FHHSs stems from the trade-off between sequence length, alphabet size, and correlation performance. Theoretical bounds, such as the Lempel-Greenberger bound and the Peng-Fan bound, provide benchmarks for evaluating the optimality of FHSs. However, constructing sequnces that achieve these bounds remains a non-trivial task, especially for sequences of arbitrary lengths and alphabet sizes. Many construction methods have been proposed, leveraging tools from number theory, finite fields, combinatorics, and algebraic geometry. Among these, cyclotomic constructions have gained significant attention due to their rich structure and ability to produce sequences with desirable correlation properties. Cyclotomic classes, particularly generalized cyclotomic classes, have proven to be a powerful tool in the design of FHSs. These classes partition the elements of a finite field or a residue ring into disjoint subsets with specific algebraic properties, which can then be used to define frequency hopping patterns. The Ding-Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes, introduced as a natural extension of classical cyclotomic classes, are particularly noteworthy. By carefully selecting parameters, these classes can be used to construct FHSs that exhibit optimal or near-optimal correlation properties. The interplay between the algebraic structure of the cyclotomic classes and the combinatorial properties of the resulting sequences has motivated extensive research in this area. In this paper, we focus on the construction and analysis of a new class of FHSs based on the Ding-Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2. The sequences are defined over a residue ring of length \( p^n \), where \( p \) is an odd prime and \( n \) is a positive integer. This choice of parameters allows us to explore the properties of FHSs in a general setting, encompassing a wide range of practical applications. Our primary aim is to investigate the Hamming auto- and cross-correlation functions of the constructed sequences and to assess their optimality with respect to the average Hamming correlation criteria. The Hamming auto-correlation measures the similarity between a sequence and its cyclic shifts, while the Hamming cross-correlation evaluates the similarity between different sequences in a set. Low values of these correlation fnctions are critical for reducing interference and ensuring reliable coommunication in multi-user systems. For the sequences presented in this paper, we demonstrate that the Hamming auto-correlation achieves optimal performance. For the Hamming cross-correlation, we focus on the case where \( p \equiv 3 \pmod{4} \), providing a detailed analysis of the correlation properties in this specific setting. Notably, the constructed FHSs are shown to achieve optimality with respect to the average Hamming correlation, making them highly attactive for practical deployment. The contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows. First, we propose a novel construction method for FHSs of length \( p^n \) based on Ding-Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2. This construction extends existing methods and provides a new avenue for designing sequences with good correlation properties. Second, we derive explicit expressions for the Hamming auto-correlation and cross-correlation functions of the constructed sequences. Theese results offer valuable insights into the algbraic and combinatorial properties of the sequences, shedding ligt on the underlying mechanisms that govern their correlation performance. Finally, we establish the optimality of the constructed FHSs with respect to the average Hamming correlation functions, demonstrating their potential for practical applications. This involves several pivotal components, including the formulation of the sequence set, the derivation of Hamming auto- and cross-correlation functions, and the evaluation of optimality based on average Hamming correlation metrics. To commence this development, we utilize the Ding-Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2, defined over the finite field \( \mathbb{F}_{p^n} \), where \( p \) is an odd prime number and \( n \) is a positive integer [1]. Let \( g \) be a primitive element of \( \mathbb{F}_{p^n} \), enabling the partitioning of the multiplicative group \( \mathbb{F}_{p^n}^* \) into two disjoint subsets, \( D_0 \) and \( D_1 \), referred to as the generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2. These subsets are formally defined as: \[ D_i = \{ g^{2k+i} : k = 0, 1, \dots, \frac{p^n-3}{2} \}, \quad i \in \{0, 1\}. \] By leveraging these cyclotomic classes, we define a family of FHSs by associating elements of the classes \( D_0 \) and \( D_1 \) with frequency slots in a periodic manner. Each sequence in the family is constructed by mapping the elements of \( D_0 \cup D_1 \) to distinct frequency values, resulting in sequences of length \( p^n \), with hopping frequencies derived from the structure of \( \mathbb{F}_{p^n} \). The Hamming auto-correlation function of an FHS serves as a metric for the degree of similarity between a sequence and its time-shifted versions. For a sequence \( S = (s_0, s_1, \dots, s_{N-1}) \) of length \( N \), the Hamming auto-correlation at shift \( \tau \) is calculated as: \[ H_a(\tau) = |\{t : 0 \leq t < N, s_t = s_{t+\tau}\}|, \] where the indices are taken modulo \( N \). To compute \( H_a(\tau) \) for the constructed FHSs, we analyzed the distribution of elements within the cyclotomic classes \( D_0 \) and \( D_1 \) and their periodic shifts, leveraging the properties of these classes to derive that the auto-correlation values are bounded and exhibit a uniform distribution across non-zero shifts. In addition to the auto-correlation analysis, we examined the Hamming cross-correlation function, which quantifies the similarity between two distinct sequences \( S \) and \( T \) at a given time shift. For two sequences \( S = (s_0, s_1, \dots, s_{N-1}) \) and \( T = (t_0, t_1, \dots, t_{N-1}) \), the Hamming cross-correlation at shift \( \tau \) is defined as: \[ H_c(S, T; \tau) = |\{t : 0 \leq t < N, s_t = t_{t+\tau}\}|. \] This work focused on the case where \( p \equiv 3 \pmod{4} \), as the structure of the cyclotomic classes under this condition facilitates a more tractable analysis of cross-correlation properties. By investigating the interaction between the elements of \( D_0 \) and \( D_1 \) across different sequences and shifts, we demonstrated that the cross-correlation values are uniformly distributed and satisfy a strict upper bound. The optimality of the constructed FHSs was evaluated based on their average Hamming correlation functions, which are defined as the mean values of the auto- and cross-correlation functions over all shifts and all sequence pairs, respectively. Specifically: \[ \text{Average Hamming Auto-correlation} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{\tau=1}^{N-1} H_a(\tau), \] \[ \text{Average Hamming Cross-correlation} = \frac{1}{M(N-1)} \sum_{S \neq T} \sum_{\tau=0}^{N-1} H_c(S, T; \tau), \] where \( M \) denotes the total number of sequences in the family. Utilizing the correlation bounds derived from the cyclotomic structure, we proved that the average Hamming correlation functions of the constructed sequences achieve the theoretical lower bounds specified by the optimality criteria for FHSs. To validate the theoretical results, we implemented the construction of the proposed FHSs and computed their Hamming auto- and cross-correlation functions for various values of \( p \) and \( n \). Refractory shock remains a significant challenge in pediatric critical care, characterized by the inability to restore adequate tissue perfusion and hemodynamic stability despite aggressive fluid resuscitation and high-dose vasopressor and inotropic therapy. This clinical condition is associated with high morbidity and mortality rates, particularly in neonates and children with underlying critcial illnesses succh as septic shock, cardiogenic shock, and postoperative complications following cardiac surgery. The pathophysiology of refractory shock in the pediatric population often invoves profound vasoplegia, myocardial dysfunction, and microcirculatory disturbances, necessitating innovative therapeutic approaches to improve outcomes. Vasopressin (AVP) and its synthetic analog terlipressin (TP) have garnered interest as potential adjuncts in the management of refractory shock, particularly as catecholamine-sparing agents. Vasopressin, an endogenous hormone, plays a pivotal role in vascular tone regulation through its action on V1 receptors, leading to vasoconstriction, and V2 receptors, which mediate water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts. Terlipressin, a long-acting prodrug of lysine vasopressin, has similar pharmacologic effects but offers a prolonged half-life and more stable pharmacokinetics. These agents have been extensively studied in adult populations with septic shock and other forms of distributive shock, where they have shown promise in improving hemodynamic parameters and reducing catecholamine requirements. However, their role in the pediatric population remains less well-defined, given the physiological and developmental differences in cardiovascular and endocrine systems between children and adults. The potential benefits of AVP and TP in pediatric refractory sock are supported by their ability to restore systemic vascular resistance and improve organ perfusion in the setting of vasodilatory shock. Additionally, the catecholamine-sparing effects of these agents may mitigate the adverse effects associated with high-dose catecholamines, such as tachyarrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, and immunosuppression. Desspite these theoretical advantages, concerns remain regarding the safety profile of AVP and TP, particularly the risk of tissue ischemia due to excessive vasoconstriction. Neonates and children may be especially vulnerable to ischemic complications, given tehir relatively immature cardiovascular systems and limited physiological reserves. The evidence base for the use of AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock is limited and heterogeneous, comprising small randomiezd controlled trials (RCTs), observational studies, and case series. While some studies have reported favorable hemodynamic responses and reductions in catecholamine requirements with AVP and TP therapy, robust data on clinically meaningful outcomes such as mortality, length of stay in the pediatric intensive care unti (PICU), and adverse events remain lacking. Furthermore, existing studies often include diverse patient populations with varyying etiologies of shock, makiing it difficult to draw definitive conclusions regarding the efficacy and safety of these agents in specific subgroups. In this context, the present systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis (TSA) aim to synthesize the available evidence on the effiicacy and safety of AVP and TP therapy compared to conventional therapy in pediatric refractory shock of all causes. By pooling data from RCTs and high-quality observational studies, we sought to evaluate the impact of AVP and TP on mortality, length of stay in the PICU, and the risk of tissue ischemia. Importantly, we also performed TSA to assess the robustness and sufficiency of the available evidence, highlighting potential gaps in the literature and providing direction for future research. Our findings contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the role of AVP and TP in pediatric critical care, particularly in the management of refractory shock. Given the lack of observed mortality benefit and the potential increased risk of ischemic complications associated with these agents, our results underscore the need for caution in their use outside of well-designed clinical trials. Furthermore, the absence of significant effects on clinically important outcomes such as PICU length of stay suggests that the routine use of AVP and TP may not be justified in this population, pending further evidence. Taken together, this study emphasizes the urgent need for larger, high-quality RCTs to clarify the role of AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock and to establish evidence-based guidelines for their use. This intricate clinical condition is frequently associated with elevated rates of morbidity and mortality, particularly among neonates and children beset by underlying critical illnesses, such as septic shock, cardiogenic shock, and complications arising from cardiac surgery [2]. The complex pathophysiological mechanisms underlying refractory shock in pediatric populations often involve pronounced vasodilation, impaired myocardial function, and disruptions to microcirculatory flow, thereby highlighting the necessity for novel therapeutic strategies to enhance patient outcomes [3]. In recent times, vasopressin (AVP) and its synthetic analogue, terlipressin (TP), have garnered significant attention as potential adjunctive therapies in the management of refractory shock, particularly in their capacity to reduce the reliance on catecholamines [4]. AVP, an endogenous hormone, plays a pivotal role in modulating vascular tone via its action on V1 receptors, which elicits vasoconstriction, and V2 receptors, which facilitate water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts [5]. TP, a long-acting prodrug of lysine vasopressin, exhibits similar pharmacological effects but offers the added benefits of a prolonged half-life and more stable pharmacokinetic profile [6]. These agents have been the subject of extensive investigation in adult populations afflicted with septic shock and other forms of distributive shock, where they have demonstrated promise in enhancing hemodynamic parameters and reducing the requirements for catecholamines [7, 8]. Nevertheless, their role in pediatric populations remains less clearly defined, largely due to the physiological and developmental differences in cardiovascular and endocrine systems that exist between children and adults [9]. The potential benefits of AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock are supported by their capacity to restore systemic vascular resistance and enhance organ perfusion in the context of vasodilatory shock [10]. Furthermore, the catecholamine-sparing effects of these agents may mitigate the adverse consequences associated with high-dose catecholamine therapy, such as tachyarrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, and immunosuppression [11]. Despite these theoretical advantages, concerns persist regarding the safety profile of AVP and TP, particularly the risk of tissue ischemia resulting from excessive vasoconstriction [12]. Neonates and children may be particularly vulnerable to ischemic complications, given their relatively immature cardiovascular systems and limited physiological reserves [13]. The existing evidence base for the use of AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock is limited and heterogeneous, comprising small-scale randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational studies, and case series [14]. While certain studies have reported favorable hemodynamic responses and reductions in catecholamine requirements following AVP and TP therapy, robust data on clinically meaningful outcomes, such as mortality, duration of stay in the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU), and adverse events, remain scarce [15]. Moreover, existing studies often encompass diverse patient populations with varying etiologies of shock, rendering it challenging to draw definitive conclusions regarding the efficacy and safety of these agents in specific subgroups [16]. In this context, the present systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis (TSA) aim to synthesize the available evidence on the efficacy and safety of AVP and TP therapy compared to conventional therapy in pediatric refractory shock of all causes [17]. By pooling data from RCTs and high-quality observational studies, we sought to evaluate the impact of AVP and TP on mortality, duration of stay in the PICU, and the risk of tissue ischemia [18]. Any discrepancies that arose during this process were resolved through a consultative approach, involving discussion and, when necessary, input from an additional reviewer to ensure consistency and accuracy. To be deemed eligible for inclusion, studies had to conform to specific methodological standards, namely, they had to be randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or observational studies with a before-and-after design that investigated the utilization of arginine vasopressin (AVP) or terlipressin (TP) in pediatric patients experiencing refractory shock. The inclusion of studies without a comparator group was limited to the systematic review, where they were analyzed descriptively, whereas they were excluded from the meta-analysis due to the absence of a control group. Furthermore, case reports, abstracts presented at conferences, and studies focusing on adult populations were not considered, as they failed to meet the predefined inclusion criteria. The primary focus of this investigation was on all-cause mortality, with secondary outcomes of interest including the duration of pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) stays and the occurrence of adverse events, particularly those related to tissue ischemia. Tissue ischemia was comprehensively defined to encompass any ischemic complications identified through clinical or radiological assessment, including digital ischemia, mesenteric ischemia, or ischemic events affecting other organs. Data extraction from the included studies was carried out independently by two reviewers, utilizing a standardized form designed to capture detailed information. This information encompassed study characteristics, such as study design, population demographics, sample size, and setting, as well as patient-specific factors, treatment protocols, and reported outcomes. The quality of the included RCTs was appraised using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, while the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale was employed for the evaluation of nonrandomized studies. For the purposes of the meta-analysis, random-effects models were adopted to mitigate the potential impact of heterogeneity between studies. The results of the analysis were expressed in terms of relative risks (RRs) accompanied by 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for outcomes that were dichotomous, such as mortality and the incidence of tissue ischemia, and mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs for continuous outcomes, such as the duration of PICU stays. The degree of statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic, with values exceeding 50% deemed indicative of substantial heterogeneity. These studies collectively enrolled 224 pediatric patients (ranging in age from 0 to 18 years) who were diagnosed with refractory shock of varying etiologies. Of these patients, 152 received AVP or TP as an adjunct to conventional therapy, while the remaining 72 patients were treated with conventional therapy alone, which typically consisted of fluid resuscitation and support with vasopressors and inotropes. The Inteernet of Things (IoT) has emerged as one of the msot transformative technological paradigms of the 21st century, enabling the seamless integration of physical and digital worlds. IoT systems span a vast and growing range of domains, including smart cities, healthcare, industrial automation, transportation, agriculture, and beyond. By connecting physical objects, sensors, actuators, and computational devices to the internet, IoT systems create opportunities for enhanced automation, data-driven decision-making, and innovative services that were unimaginable just a few decades ago. However, as the IoT landscape expands, so too do the challenges associated with designing, developing, and maintaining such complex and heterogeneous systems. The rapid growth of IoT has led to a proliferation of research efforts aimed at addressing specific challenges, such as resource constraints, data management, security, interoperability, and scalability. These efforts have produced a rihc body of work, offeing specialized solutions for particular use cases and technical problems. While these contributions are invaluable, they are often fragmented and tailored to specific technologies or domains, limiting their general applicability. As a result, practitioners in the field of IoT development are frequently left without unified guidance or a systematic approach to help them navigate the complexity of creating robust, interoperable, and adaptable IoT systems. This gap highlights the pressing need for a general software engineering methodology that can provide a structured framework for the design and development of IoT systems, irrespective of their specific application domain. Software engineering methodologies have long played a critical role in the development of traditional software systems, offering principles, practices, and tools to manage complexity, ensure quality, and align development efforts with business and user requirements. Methodologies such as Agile, Waterfall, and DevOps have been instrumental in enabling developers to deliver reliable and maintainable software. However, IoT systems pose unique challeenges that extend beyond those encountered in traditional software engineering. These challenges arise from the inherently distributed and heterogeneous nature of IoT environments, whhich often involve the integration of hardware components, real-time data processing, connectivity constraints, and diverse user interactions. Furthermore, IoT systems must operate in dynamic and often unpredictable environments, where devices may fail, networks may degrade, and security threats may evolve rapidly. Addressing these challenges requires not merely adapting existing software engineering practices but rethinking them to accommodate the distinct characteristics of IoT systems. Another critical consideration in IoT development is the role of abstraction. Given the complexity of IoT systems, developers must work with higher-level abstractions taht encapsulate the underlying hardware, communication protocols, and data flows while providing a clear mental model for system behavior. These abstractions allow developers to focus on the functionality and interactions of the system as a whole, rather than being bogged down by low-level implementation details. However, the lack of consensus on key abstractions for IoT development has hindered the adoption of systematic methodologies. A coherent and widely accepted set of abstractions is essential for fostering shared understanding, reusability, and scalability in IoT system design. In this context, the development of a general software engineering methodology for IoT represents an ambitious yet necessary endeavor. Such a methodology must synthesize insights from the satte of the art in IoT researcch and practice, identifying commonalities and recurring patterns across diverse IoT applications. It must also address the entire lifecycle of IoT systems, from requirements elicitation and architecture design to deployment, maintenance, and evolution. Furthermore, it should provide concrrete guidance on how to manage the trade-offs inherent in IoT development, such as balancing resource efficiency with functionality, ensuring security while maintaining usability, and achieving interoperability without sacrificing performance. The purpose of this paper is to take a significant step toward addressing these challenges by proposing a general software engineering methodology for IoT systems. Our approach is grounded in a comprehensive analysis of the current state of the art in IoT research, as well as the practical experiences and lessons learned from real-world IoT projects. By synthesizing these diverse perspectives, we aim to identify the key concepts and abstractions that underpin successful IoT system design and development. These abstractions serve as the foundation for the propsoed methodology, which provides a structured framework for addressing the unique challenges of IoT development. In the remainder of this paper, we outline the key principles and abstractions that form the basis of our methodology, discuss how these abstractions can be operationalized in practice, and illustrate their application through representative case studies. By doing so, we seek to provide both theoretical insights and practical tools that can guide IoT developers in building sytsems that are not only functional and efficient but also adaptable and resilient in the face of rapid technological and environmental change. Ultimately, we envision this work as a starting point for a broader conversation within the IoT and software engineering communities about the principles and practices that should guide the development of IoT systems. We recognize that the diversity and complexity of IoT applications mean that no single methodology will be universally applicable. However, we believe that the abstractions and principles proposed in this paper can serve as a foundation for ongoing refinement and adaptation, enabling the systematic and principled development of IoT systems across a wide range of domains. By fostering a more unified and disciplined approach to IoT development, we hope to accelerate the realization of the IoT's full potential to transorm industries, improve quality of life, and address societal challenges. To develop a general software engineering methodology for the Internet of Things (IoT), we employed a multi-step approach that synthesizes existing research, identifies core abstractions, and formalizes a set of methodological principles. The process is guided by an iterative and muultidisciplinary framework that integrates theoretical insights, empirical studies, and practical considerations. Below, we describe the individual steps involved in the formulation of this methodology. **Literature Synthesis and Conceptual Framing:** The first step in our methodology involves a comprehensive review of the state of the art in IoT software engineering. We analyzed existing IoT development frameworks, architectural patterns, and design principles to identify recurring challenges, best practices, and opportunities for generalization. The review included peer-reviewed papers, technical reports, and industry standards published over the past decade. Key themes from this synthesis include heterogeneity in IoT hardware and software, challenges in scalability, the integration of edge and cloud computing, context-awareness, and concerns regarding security and privacy. From this analysis, we extracted a set of core abstractions to frame the IoT development process. These abstractions are: (1) *Things*, representing physical devices or sensors; (2) *Data Flow*, encapsulating the movement, transformation, and processing of data; (3) *Services*, which deefine the functionalities exposed by IoT systems; (4) *Interactions*, which capture user-device or device-device communication patterns; and (5) *Environments*, representing the physical or virtual contexts in which IoT systems operate. These abstractions serve as the foundation upon which the suubsequent methodology is built. **Methodological Framework Design:** Using the core abstractions as a starting point, we structured the methodology into a sequence of well-defined phases: requirements engineering, system modeling and design, implementation, deployment, and maintenance. Each phase is tailored to address the unique characteristics of IoT systems while maintaining fllexibility for general applicability across different domains. The methodology is also deliberately iterative, allowing for refinement as new requirements emerge or as the operational context evolves. 1. **Requirements Engineering:** In this phase, stakeholders collaboratively define functional and non-functional requirements for the IoT system. To ensure a systematic approach, we introduce domain-specific tepmlates and checklists tailored to IoT systems. Special attention is given to requirements related to scalability, energy efficiency, real-time constraints, and security. Stakeholders are encouraged to identify potential sources of uncertainty, such as changes in the operating environment or evolving user needs, which are documented as part of the requirements specification. 2. **System Modeling and Design:** Based on the identified requirements, the system is modeled using a combination of domain-specific and general-purpose modeling languages. We propoe a hybrid approach that integrates UML-based diagrams with IoT-specific extensions, such as ThingML and SysML profiles. The modeling process explicitly addresses the core abstractions identified earlier. For instance, *Things* are represented as physical entities with associated metadata and capabilities; *Data Flows* are captured in flow diagrams that indicate data sources, transformations, and sinks; and *Services* are documented as interfaces with defined inputs, outputs, and quality attributes. Architectural patterns such as publish-subscribe, microservices, and edge-cloud hierarchies are evaluated for their suitability to the specific use case. The design phase also incorporates threat modeling to identify potential vulnerabilities and outline mitigation strategies. 3. **Implementation:** The implementation phase focuses on translating the designs into executable code and deployable artifacts. We advocate for the use of modular and reusable cmponents to facilitate maiintainability and scalability. Platforms such as Arduino, Rspberry Pi, and IoT-specific middleware solutions are considered for prototyping and development, while adherence to industry stadards (e.g., MQTT, CoAP) ensues compatibility and interoperability. We also define guidelines for integrating software development practices such as continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines specifically adapted for IoT environments. These pipelines automate testing, deployment, and monitoring while accounting for the distributed and resource-constrained nature of IoT systems. 4. **Deployment:** Deployment in IoT systems is inherently complex due to the distirbuted nature of devices and the dynamic environments in which thye operate. In thhis phase, we propse best practices for deploying IoT systems, including strategies for over-the-air updates, dveice provisioning, and network configuration. Deployment is guided by a deployment plan that specifies the sequence of steps, rollback mechanisms, and contingency plans for addressing failures. 5. **Maintenance and Evolution:** IoT systems often require ongoing maintenance and adaptation to changing conditions. We emphasize the importance of monitoring and analytics for detecting anomalies, predicting failures, and optimizing performance. Feedback loops are established to incorporate insights from operational data into future iterations of the system. The methodology also includes guidelines for managing device end-of-life and ensuring compliance with evolving regulatory requirements. **Validation and Refinement:** The proposed methodology was iteratively validated and refined through a combination of case studies and expert feedback. We conducted three real-world case studies across different IoT domains: smart homes, industrial IoT, and healthcare. Each case study followed the methodology from requirements engineering to deployment, with detailed docuumentation of outcomes and lessons learned. Additionally, we engaged with a panel of IoT practitioners and researchers to evaluate the methodology’s completeness, practicality, and ease of adoption. Insights from these evaluations informed further refinement of the methodology. **Tool Support and Automation:** To faciliatte adoption and enhance productivity, we explored tool support for key aspects of the methodology. This includes requirements managemet tools with IoT-specific extensions, automated code generation from system models, and deployment orchestration platforms. We also investigated the use of AI-driven assistants for tasks such as anomaly detection, security analysis, and performance optimization. While tool support is not mandatory for implementing the methodology, it is recommended for larger and more complex projects. Cerebral palsy (CP) is a condition that often presents with spasticity and dystonia, which can lead to considerable morbidity, including severe impairments, pain, and a diminished quality of life in affected children [1, 2]. The treatment of these symptoms is multifaceted, necessitating a collaborative approach that incorporates various disciplines. One established method for managing severe and refractory spasticity and dystonia is intrathecal baclofen (ITB) therapy, which involves the direct administration of baclofen into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) via an implanted pump [3]. This method allows for a targeted therapeutic effect while minimizing systemic side effects, thanks to the localized delivery of the medication [4]. Nevertheless, the implantation of an ITB pump is associated with a range of complications, including leakage of CSF, wound breakdown, infection, and issues related to the catheter, which can result in significant morbidity [5]. These complications are of particular concern in pediatric patients, where the procedure is complicated by anatomical and physiological variability [6]. A topic of growing interest is the potential impact of unrecognized or arrested hydrocephalus on the high rates of complications observed following ITB pump implantation. Arrested hydrocephalus is characterized by an abnormal accumulation of CSF within the ventricles, leading to elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) that may remain asymptomatic due to compensatory mechanisms [7]. In pediatric patients with CP, the underlying neurological deficits often obscure the subtle clinical manifestations of hydrocephalus, rendering its diagnosis challenging [8]. Furthermore, these patients frequently exhibit atypical brain anatomy due to underlying neurodevelopmental disorders, which complicates the interpretation of imaging findings and clinical assessments [9]. As a result, there is a growing recognition that undiagnosed hydrocephalus may contribute to postoperative complications, including CSF leakage and wound dehiscence, by disrupting CSF dynamics and impairing tissue healing [10]. Historically, the preoperative evaluation for ITB pump candidates has focused primarily on assessing the suitability of the device and the patient's overall medical condition, with limited attention given to the potential presence of hydrocephalus. However, emerging evidence suggests that a subset of these patients may benefit from a more comprehensive assessment of CSF dynamics and intracranial pressure prior to implantation [11, 12]. This is particularly relevant given that elevated ICP not only increases the risk of postoperative complications but may also necessitate additional neurosurgical interventions, such as ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting, to optimize outcomes [13]. The importance of identifying and managing elevated ICP prior to ITB pump implantation cannot be overstated, as it has the potential to significantly impact the safety and efficacy of the procedure. In recent years, efforts have been made to develop standardized protocols for the preoperative evaluation of ITB pump candidates, with the aim of addressing these challenges. One such protocol, implemented at our institution, involves mandatory cranial imaging and direct measurement of ICP via lumbar puncture (LP) under controlled conditions prior to ITB pump implantation. This approach aims to identify patients with elevated ICP or arrested hydrocephalus who may require alternative management strategies, such as VP shunting, before proceeding with ITB therapy. By addressing these underlying CSF abnormalities, the protocol seeks to minimize the risk of postoperative complications and improve overall outcomes. This retrospective case series provides an analysis of the implementation and outcomes of this preoperative protocol in a cohort of pediatric patients with CP considered for ITB pump implantation. These results highlight the potential utility of integrating ICP measurement into the standard preoperative evaluation of ITB candidates, particularly in populations at high risk for arrested hydrocephalus. The findings of this study are consistent with previous research, which has emphasized the need for a comprehensive preoperative evaluation to identify potential risk factors for postoperative complications [14]. By incorporating mandatory cranial imaging and ICP assessment into the preoperative evaluation, the proposed protocol represents a significant step forward in addressing the challenges associated with unrecognized hydrocephalus in this vulnerable population. Despite these promising findings, the data also raise important questions regarding the broader implications of routine ICP assessment in pediatric patients with CP. Moreover, the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the high prevalence of elevated ICP in this population remain poorly understood and merit additional exploration to optimize patient selection and management strategies. This study was scrutinized and approved by the institutional review board, ensuring that all aspects of data collection and analysis conformed to the stringent institutional and ethical guidelines. The primary goal of our investigation was to assess the safety and efficacy of ITB pump implantation in pediatric patients diagnosed with cerebral palsy (CP), as well as to pinpoint potential risk factors that could predispose these patients to postoperative complications. The selection of patients for this study was predicated on a confirmed diagnosis of CP, accompanied by spasticity or dystonia that had proven refractory to treatment with oral antispasticity agents. Patients were deemed eligible for ITB therapy if their clinical profile warranted this treatment modality, as determined by their healthcare providers. Conversely, exclusion criteria encompassed any contraindications to general anesthesia, the presence of an ongoing systemic infection, or prior neurosurgical interventions that would have precluded a lumbar puncture (LP). In accordance with ethical standards, written informed consent was obtained from the legal guardians of all patients prior to the initiation of any procedures. To mitigate the risk of postoperative complications and to address the potential for unrecognized arrested hydrocephalus, a standardized preoperative protocol was instituted for all patients. This protocol was multifaceted, comprising cranial imaging, LP under general anesthesia, and the measurement of intracranial pressure (ICP) via opening pressure. Cranial imaging, which could be either non-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or a computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain, was a critical component of the preoperative evaluation. These imaging studies were meticulously reviewed by a pediatric neuroradiologist to identify any evidence of ventriculomegaly, effacement of the cortical sulci, or other radiological findings suggestive of hydrocephalus. The imaging findings were then correlated with the patient's clinical history and neurological examination to identify individuals with suspected arrested hydrocephalus, characterized by ventriculomegaly that was disproportionate to the patient's age or abnormal morphology of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces. Following the cranial imaging, patients underwent LP under general anesthesia to obtain CSF samples and to measure the opening pressure, which served as a surrogate marker for ICP. The LP procedure was performed with the patient in the lateral decubitus position, with careful attention to avoid excessive flexion of the neck or hips, which could potentially artificially elevate the opening pressure. Utilizing a sterile technique, a 22-gauge spinal needle was inserted at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace, and the opening pressure was measured using a manometer. ICP values exceeding 21 cmH2O were categorized as elevated, based on established thresholds in the pediatric literature [1, 2]. Additionally, CSF samples were submitted for routine analysis, including cell count, glucose, and protein levels, to exclude any inflammatory or infectious processes. For patients with an elevated opening pressure greater than 21 cmH2O, the implantation of the ITB pump was deferred, and alternative management strategies were discussed with the family. A multidisciplinary team comprising pediatric neurosurgeons, anesthesiologists, and spasticity specialists was intimately involved in the decision-making process. Patients with elevated ICP underwent further diagnostic evaluation for hydrocephalus, including repeat imaging or CSF flow studies, as clinically indicated. If arrested hydrocephalus was suspected, neurosurgical interventions such as the placement of a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt were considered. Following the successful placement of a shunt and confirmation of normalized ICP, patients were reassessed for their eligibility for ITB pump implantation. Families of patients for whom shunting was not pursued were informed about alternative management strategies, such as the continuation of oral or injectable antispastic agents. Patients with normal ICP (≤21 cmH2O) or normalized ICP following shunt placement proceeded to undergo ITB pump implantation. The implantation procedure was performed under general anesthesia in a sterile operating room environment. The ITB device was implanted in the subcutaneous space of the abdominal wall, and the intrathecal catheter was positioned at the appropriate spinal level based on preoperative planning. Postoperative care was meticulous, with close monitoring for signs of CSF leak, wound dehiscence, infection, or pump malfunction. We compiled demographic and clinical data from electronic medical records, including age, sex, CP subtype, Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS) level, and previous surgical history. Procedural data encompassed cranial imaging findings, LP opening pressure, CSF analysis results, and perioperative complications. Outcomes following ITB pump implantation were meticulously assessed, with particular attention to the incidence of postoperative CSF leak, wound complications, and infection. Descriptive statistics were employed to summarize patient demographics, clinical characteristics, and procedural outcomes. Categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were reported as means with standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges, depending on the distribution of the data. Comparative outcomes between patients with normal and elevated ICP were evaluated using chi-square tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 24.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY), with a significance threshold of p < 0.05. To ensure the consistent application of the protocol, all LPs and imaging studies were performed by or under the direct supervision of experienced pediatric neurosurgeons. Cranial imaging interpretations were reviewed by a second neuroradiologist when the findings were equivocal. Data accuracy was verified through iterative review by two independent researchers. This study adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and the risks and benefits of the protocol were thoroughly explained to the patients' families. Furthermore, to maintain the integrity of our research, we ensured that all aspects of the study, from patient selection to data analysis, were conducted with the utmost rigor and transparency, in accordance with the highest ethical standards [1, 2]. The utilization of a standardized preoperative protocol and the meticulous attention to detail in the analysis of cranial imaging and CSF dynamics underscored our commitment to minimizing risks and optimizing outcomes for these vulnerable patients. As we reflect on the implications of our findings, it is clear that the implementation of such a protocol can significantly enhance the safety and efficacy of ITB pump implantation in pediatric patients with CP, by identifying and mitigating potential risks associated with elevated ICP and hydrocephalus. Therefore, our study contributes meaningfully to the existing body of literature, highlighting the importance of a multidisciplinary approach and rigorous preoperative evaluation in the management of CP, and underscores the need for ongoing research into the optimal strategies for the diagnosis and treatment of hydrocephalus in this patient population.

The study of distributed source coding has long been a fundamental area of research in information theory, driven by its wide-ranging applications in communication systems, data compression, and distributed data processing. Among the many theoretical frameworks that address distributed source coding problems, the Wyner-Ahlswede-Körner (WAK) network and the Gray-Wyner (GW) network have emerged as two of the most prominent paradigms. Each of these models captures distinct aspects of communication and coding scenarios, and both have been the subject of extensive investigation over the past several decades. In this work, we explore the relationship between these two networks and derive a converse bound for the WAK network by leveraging results from the GW network, thus providing new insights into the fundamental limits of distributed source coding. The WAK ntwork was introduced as an extension of the classical Wyner-Ziv problem, with the goal of characterizing the rate region for encoding correlated sources in a distributed setting [1, 2]. In the WAK framework, two or more encoders observe separate components of a correlated source and must encode thier observations into messages. These messages are then sent to a central receiver, which aims to reconstruct certain functions of the original sources subject to fidelity constraints. The WAK network generalizes many important source coding problems, including the Slepian-Wolf problem and the Wyner-Ziv problem, and has been instrumental in advancing our understanding of distributed information processing. A key result in this context is the strong converse theorem for the WAK network, which establishes that the probability of decoding error approaches one if the rate constraints fall outside the achieavble region [3, 4]. This theorem underscores the sharp boundary between achievable and unachievable rates, making it a cornesrtone of the theoretical framework for distributed source coding. Meanwhile, the GW network, introduced by Gray and Wyner in 1974, provides a different lens on the distributed source coding problm [5]. In the GW model, a single encoder observes the entire source and generates two descriptions: a common description that is accessible to multiple decoders and private descriptions that are accessible to individual decoders. The goal is to minimize the total rate sbuject to fidelity constraints on the reconstructions at the decoders. The GW network serves as a natural precrusor to the WAK network, and its structure has inspired numerous extensions and generalizations in information theory. In particular, the GW framework has proven to be a versatile tool for analyzing various trade-offs between rate and distortion in multi-terminal communication systems. The relationship between the WAK and GW networks is of significant interest from both theoretical and practical perspectives. While the WAK nework focuses on distributed encoding with seeparate observations, the GW network assmues centralized encoding with multiple decoders. Despite these differences, the two models share deep conceptual connections, as they both addess the fundamental problem of efficiently encoding and transmitting correlated sources. The ability to translate results between these two frameworks can thus provide a unified understanding of distributed source coding and potentially simplify the analysis of one model in terms of the other. In this paper, we establish a reduction method that allows the construction of a code for the GW network from a given code for the WAK network. By formalizing this reduction, we demonstrate that any achievable rate-distortion tuple for the WAK network can be mapped to a corresponding rate-distortion tuple for the GW network. This result not only highlights the structural similarities between the two frameworks but also enables us to derive a converse bound for the WAK network using an existing converse bound for the GW network. The derived bound provides an alternative proof of the strong converse theorem for the WAK network, reaffirming the sharpness of the rate-distortion boundary in this setting. Our approach builds on prior work that has explored the interplay between different distributed source coding models. Notably, Ahlswede and Körner’s early work on the WAK network laid the groundwork for understanding the fundamental limits of distributed encoding [2]. Subsequent research has extended these results to various network topologies and fidelity criteria, leading to a rich body of literature on multi-terminal source coding [6]. Similarly, the GW network has been extensively studied in the context of rate-distortion theory, with numerous woorks investigating the trade-offs between common and private descriptions [7, 8]. By connecting these two lines of research, our work contributes to a deeper understanding of distributed source coding and offers a novel perspective on the fundamental limits of the WAK network. The key technical contribution of this paper lies in the construction of the reduction method and its use in derving a converse bound for the WAK network. Unlike traditional approaches that directly analyze the WAK network, our method leverages the well-established properties of the GW network to simplify the analysis. This reduction is not only concepually elegant but also provides a new tool for analyzing other distributed sourec coding problems that share structural similarities with the WAK and GW networks. Furthermore, our results suggest that the GW network can serve as a unifyinng framework for studying a wide range of multi-terminal communication problems, offering a new avenue for future research. Section 3 presents the reducion method and establishes the connection between the two networks. Section 5 discusses the implications of our results and potential directions for future research. Finally, we conclude in Section 6 with a summary of our contributions and their significance for the field of distributed source coding.
