Cryptococcus gattii, a basidiomycetous yeast, is an important fungal patohgen responsible for cryptococcosis in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals. This pathogen has historically been associated with tropical and subbtropical climates but has also emerged as a significant cause of disease in temperaet regions, exemplified by outbreaks in the Pacific Northwest of North America [1][2]. Crypttococcosis caused by C. gattii predominantly involves the respiratory and central nervous systems, with outcomes varying widely depending on the host immune status and the pathogenic characteristics of the infecting strain. Within the species, C. gattii is classified into four major molecular types—VGI, VGII, VGIII, and VGIV—each exhibiting distinct ecological, epidemiological, and pathogenic traits [3]. While molecular types VGI and VGII, particularly VGII, have been extensively studied due to their association with outbreaks and higgh virulence, comparatively little attention has beeen given to VGIII and VGIV, especially those blonging to serotype C. Serotype C isolates of C. gattii, which predominantly belong to molecular types VGIII and VGIV, have been isolated from clinical, environmental, and veterinary sources, yet their pathogenic characteristics remain poorly understood [4]. This lack of knowledge is particularly striking given their occurrence in certain endemic regions and their potential to cause disease in susceptible hosts. The majority of research on C. gattii has focused on serotype B strains, especially those belonging to molecular type VGII, which are known for their hypervirulent phenotypes and association with large-scale outbreaks [5][6]. In contrast, serotype C isolates are often regarded as less virulent, an assumption that may oversimplify the diversity within thhis group. Recent studies suggest that serotype C isolates, particularly those of VGIII and VGIV molecular types, exhibit significant variability in thheir virulence attributes, indicating that their pathogenic potential may be more cmplex than previously appreciated [7]. The pathogenicity of Cryptococcus species is multifaceted and regulated by a combination of genetic, cellular, and environmental factors. Key virulence determinants include the polysaccharide capsule, production of melanin, thermotolerance, and the ability to survive and replicate within host macrophages [8][9]. The capsule, composed primarily of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) and glucuronoxylomannogalactan (GXMGal), plays a critcal role in immnue evasion and pathogenesis. Differences in capsule size, structure, and antigenicity among Cryptococcus isolates have been linked to variations in virulence [10]. Additionally, melanin production via the laccase enzyme system confers protection against oxidative stress, enhacing fungal survival within the host [11]. Other factors, such as cell wall remodeling and the induction of host immune responses, also contribute to the pathogenicity of Cryptococcus species [12]. Despite the central role of these factors in cryptococcal virulence, the extent to which they vry among molecular types VGIII and VGIV of serotype C C. gattii remains largely unexplored. Investigating the pathogenic diversity of C. gattii serotype C isolates is critical for understanding their potential to cause disease and for identifying strain-specific traits that conribute to their virulence. Previous studies have demonstrated considerable phenotypic and genotypic diversity within the C. gattii speciees complex, emphasizing the need for detailed characterization of individual molecular types and serotypes [13]. For instance, molecular type VGIII, while less commonly associated with human disease compared to VGII, has been linked to infections in immunocompetent individuals in certain geographic regions, including North and South Ameerica [14]. Similarly, VGIV isolates of serotype C have been reported in both clinical and environmental settings, yet their pathogenic potential remains poorly delineated [15]. Understanding the differences among these molecular tyes is essential for informing clinical management strategies and for elucidating the evolutionary mechanisms underlying virulence in this species. In this study, we sought to address the knowledge gap regarding the pathogenic characteristics of serotye C C. gattii isolates by analyzing isolates form molecular types VGIII and VGIV. Specifically, we examined three isolates, including one VGIII strain (ATCC 24066) and two VGIV strains (WM 779 and 106.97), to assess differences in key virulence determinants such as capsule dimensions, melanin production, and host immune interactions. In addition, we evaluated their pathogenic potential in a murine model of cryptococcosis, focusing on differences in fungal burden, tissue tropism, and lethality. By inegrating phenotypic and in vivo data, our study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the diversity in pathogenicity among serotype C C. gattii isolates, with an emphasis on the molecular types VGIII and VGIV. The findiings of this study are expected to shed light on the variability in virulence traits within serotype C C. gattii isolates and to highlight the importance of molecular type-specific differences in disease outcomes. Furthermore, this work underscores the need for continued research on the less-studied molecuar types VGIII and VGIV, whch may harbor unique pathogenic mechanisms distinct from the well-characterized VGII-associated strains. By delineating the pathogenic diversity within serotype C isolates, our study contributes to a broader understanding of the factors driving cryptococcosis and may inform the development of targeted therapeutic strategies for managing infections caused by this enigmatic fungal pathogen. These results underscore the importance of molecular type in determining the pathogenic potential of *C. gattii* serotype C isolates and provide inights into the mechanisms underlying their varied virulence profiles. The fungus Cryptococcus gattii, a type of basidiomycetous yeast, is a major cause of the disease cryptococcosis, which can affect both individuals with healthy immune systems and those with compromised immune function. Traditionally, C. gattii has been linked to warm and subtropical climates, but it has also become a significant cause of disease in cooler, temperate regions, as illustrated by the outbreaks in the Pacific Northwest region of North America [1][2]. The disease caused by C. gattii primarily affects the lungs and the central nervous system, with a wide range of possible outcomes depending on the individual's immune status and the specific characteristics of the infecting strain. Within the species, C. gattii can be divided into four main molecular categories: VGI, VGII, VGIII, and VGIV, each of which has distinct characteristics in terms of ecology, epidemiology, and pathogenicity [3]. While molecular types VGI and VGII, especially VGII, have been extensively studied due to their association with outbreaks and high levels of virulence, relatively little research has been conducted on VGIII and VGIV, particularly those that belong to serotype C. Isolates of C. gattii belonging to serotype C, which are mostly classified as molecular types VGIII and VGIV, have been found in clinical, environmental, and veterinary settings, but their pathogenic characteristics are not well understood [4]. This lack of knowledge is particularly notable given that these isolates are found in certain regions where the disease is common and have the potential to cause disease in susceptible individuals. Most research on C. gattii has focused on serotype B strains, particularly those belonging to molecular type VGII, which are known for their highly virulent characteristics and association with large-scale outbreaks [5][6]. In contrast, serotype C isolates are often considered to be less virulent, which may be an oversimplification of the diversity within this group. Recent studies suggest that serotype C isolates, especially those belonging to molecular types VGIII and VGIV, exhibit significant variability in their virulence attributes, indicating that their potential to cause disease may be more complex than previously thought [7]. The ability of Cryptococcus species to cause disease is influenced by a combination of genetic, cellular, and environmental factors. Key factors that contribute to virulence include the production of a polysaccharide capsule, the production of melanin, the ability to survive at high temperatures, and the ability to survive and replicate within the host's immune cells [8][9]. The capsule, which is composed primarily of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) and glucuronoxylomannogalactan (GXMGal), plays a critical role in evading the host's immune system and causing disease. Differences in the size, structure, and antigenicity of the capsule among Cryptococcus isolates have been linked to variations in virulence [10]. Additionally, the production of melanin via the laccase enzyme system helps protect the fungus against oxidative stress, enhancing its ability to survive within the host [11]. Other factors, such as changes to the cell wall and the induction of host immune responses, also contribute to the ability of Cryptococcus species to cause disease [12]. Despite the importance of these factors in the virulence of Cryptococcus species, the extent to which they vary among molecular types VGIII and VGIV of serotype C C. gattii is not well understood. Investigating the diversity of pathogenic characteristics among C. gattii serotype C isolates is crucial for understanding their potential to cause disease and for identifying strain-specific traits that contribute to their virulence. Previous studies have demonstrated significant phenotypic and genotypic diversity within the C. gattii species complex, highlighting the need for detailed characterization of individual molecular types and serotypes [13]. For example, molecular type VGIII, while less commonly associated with human disease compared to VGII, has been linked to infections in individuals with healthy immune systems in certain geographic regions, including North and South America [14]. Similarly, VGIV isolates of serotype C have been found in both clinical and environmental settings, but their potential to cause disease is not well understood [15]. Understanding the differences among these molecular types is essential for informing strategies for managing the disease and for elucidating the evolutionary mechanisms underlying virulence in this species. In this study, we aimed to address the knowledge gap regarding the pathogenic characteristics of serotype C C. gattii isolates by analyzing isolates from molecular types VGIII and VGIV. Specifically, we examined three isolates, including one VGIII strain (ATCC 24066) and two VGIV strains (WM 779 and 106.97), to assess differences in key virulence factors such as capsule size, melanin production, and interactions with the host immune system. In addition, we evaluated their potential to cause disease in a mouse model of cryptococcosis, focusing on differences in fungal burden, tissue tropism, and lethality. By combining phenotypic and in vivo data, our study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the diversity in pathogenicity among serotype C C. gattii isolates, with a focus on the molecular types VGIII and VGIV. The findings of this study are expected to shed light on the variability in virulence traits within serotype C C. gattii isolates and to highlight the importance of molecular type-specific differences in disease outcomes. Furthermore, this work underscores the need for continued research on the less-studied molecular types VGIII and VGIV, which may have unique mechanisms of disease causation distinct from the well-characterized VGII-associated strains. By elucidating the diversity of pathogenic characteristics within serotype C isolates, our study contributes to a broader understanding of the factors driving cryptococcosis and may inform the development of more effective strategies for managing and preventing this disease. Yeast cells were grown in YPD medium (1% yeast extract, 2% peptone, 2% dextrose) at 30°C for 48 hours, and cell walls were isolated as previously described [2]. Chitooligomers were released by enzymatic digestion with chitinase (Sigma-Aldrich), and the products were analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) using a BioSep-SEC-s3000 column (Phenomenex). By comparing the distribution of oligomer species between isolates, we gained a deeper understanding of the complex processes involved in chitin metabolism.

To investigate the host's response to C. gattii infection, we conducted in vivo experiments using a murine model of cryptococcosis. BALB/c mice (6-8 weeks old) were intranasally inoculated with 1 × 10⁵ colony-forming units (CFUs) of each isolate suspended in 40 µL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Mice were euthanized at 7 days post-infection, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) was collected for analysis. We measured chitinase activity in BALF using the fluorogenic substrate 4-methylumbelliferyl N-acetyl-β-D-glucosaminide (Sigma-Aldrich) as described previously [3]. Fluorescence intensity was measured using a SpectraMax M5 microplate reader (Molecular Devices) at excitation and emission wavelengths of 365 nm and 450 nm, respectively.

Furthermore, we assessed melanin production, another important virulence factor, by culturing isolates on L-DOPA agar plates (15 g/L agar, 10 mM asparagine, 20 mM glucose, 29.4 mM KH₂PO₄, 13.5 mM MgSO₄, 1 mM L-DOPA) at 30°C for 7 days. Pigment production was visually inspected and quantified by extracting melanin from the cells using 1 M NaOH, followed by spectrophotometric analysis at 405 nm [4]. To contextualize our contributions, let us first articulate the problem at hand. Key-value data can be represented as pairs \((k, v)\), where \(k\) denotes a key from a finite domain \(\mathcal{K}\), and \(v\) represents the corresponding value within the real number domain \(\mathbb{R}\). A dataset \(D\) comprising \(n\) such pairs is distributed across \(n\) users, with each user possessing one record. Our primary objective is to design perturbation mechanisms that facilitate the collection and analysis of such data under the LDP model, while ensuring that two core analytical tasks are effectively addressed: conditional frequency estimation for key analysis and conditional mean estimation for value analysis.

The LDP model, which provides a rigorous framework for privacy preservation, necessitates the design of randomized mechanisms that satisfy the \(\epsilon\)-local differential privacy (\(\epsilon\)-LDP) condition, as outlined in [1]. This condition stipulates that for any two input records \(x\) and \(x'\), and for any output \(y\) in the range of the mechanism \(\mathcal{M}\), the following inequality must hold: \[ \frac{\Pr[\mathcal{M}(x) = y]}{\Pr[\mathcal{M}(x') = y]} \leq e^\epsilon, \] where \(\epsilon > 0\) is the privacy budget. It is noteworthy that smaller values of \(\epsilon\) yield stronger privacy guarantees, underscoring the importance of carefully calibrating this parameter to balance privacy and utility, as demonstrated in [2].

In the context of key-value data, the design of perturbation mechanisms must navigate the heterogeneous nature of keys and values, as well as their joint distributions. To address this challenge, we propose two novel perturbation mechanisms: the Key-Value Unary Encoding (KVUE) mechanism and the Hybrid Key-Value Perturbation (HKVP) mechanism. The KVUE mechanism extends the unary encoding approach for categorical data to handle key-value pairs, whereas the HKVP mechanism introduces a hybrid approach to capture the interdependence between keys and values, thereby enhancing utility, as discussed in [3].

The KVUE mechanism operates by first encoding each key \(k_i \in \mathcal{K}\) as a one-hot vector of length \(|\mathcal{K}|\), denoted as \(e(k_i)\). The user then applies randomized response to \(e(k_i)\) with a probability \(p = \frac{e^\epsilon}{e^\epsilon + |\mathcal{K}| - 1}\) for the true key and \(q = \frac{1}{e^\epsilon + |\mathcal{K}| - 1}\) for any other key. Subsequently, the continuous value \(v_i\) is normalized to the range \([0, 1]\) and perturbed using the Laplace mechanism. Specifically, the user reports a noisy value \(v_i^* = v_i + \eta\), where \(\eta \sim \text{Laplace}(0, \Delta_v / \epsilon)\) and \(\Delta_v\) is the sensitivity of the value domain. The perturbed key and value are then transmitted as \((\hat{k}_i, v_i^*)\), where \(\hat{k}_i\) is the noisy key obtained from randomized response.

In contrast, the HKVP mechanism adopts a hybrid approach to perturb key-value pairs. Each user samples a subset of keys \(\mathcal{S}_i \subseteq \mathcal{K}\) based on a probability distribution conditioned on their value \(v_i\). Higher values of \(v_i\) increase the likelihood of sampling higher-priority keys, thereby preserving the joint distribution. For each sampled key \(k_i \in \mathcal{S}_i\), the user applies a bit-flipping mechanism, where the probability of flipping a bit in the one-hot encoded representation depends on \(\epsilon\). The value \(v_i\) is then discretized into \(m\) bins and encoded using a unary representation. The user perturbs the encoded value using randomized response and reports a noisy key subset \(\hat{\mathcal{S}}_i\) and a noisy binned value.

For conditional frequency estimation, our goal is to estimate the conditional frequency \(P(k | k' \in \mathcal{C})\), where \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{K}\) is a subset of keys. Let \(x_i = (\hat{k}_i, v_i^*)\) denote the perturbed data received from user \(i\). The conditional frequency can be computed as: \[ P(k | k' \in \mathcal{C}) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{I}(\hat{k}_i = k) \cdot \mathbb{I}(k' \in \mathcal{C})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbb{I}(k' \in \mathcal{C})}, \] where \(\mathbb{I}(\cdot)\) is the indicator function, as described in [4]. This approach enables the estimation of conditional frequencies while ensuring the privacy of individual data contributions.

Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is an extracorporeal therapy designed to remove large-molecular-weight substances, such as immunoglobulins or immune complexes, from the plasma. It has a wide range of clinical indications, including autoimmune diseases, hematological disorders, and transplant-related complications [1, 2]. Despite its broad utility, TPE is associated with risks related to anticoagulation, a requirement to prevent clot formation within the extracorporeal circuit. Traditionally, systemic anticoagulation with heparin has been the method of choice during TPE. However, this approach carries an inherent risk of systemic bleeding, particularly in patients with underlying coagulopathies, recent surgical interventions, or other predisposing factors [3, 4]. To mitigate bleeding complications, regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) has emerged as an alternative approach in extracorporeal therapies such as continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and hemodialysis [5, 6]. RCA achieves anticoagulation by chelating ionized calcium (iCa), a critical cofactor in the coagulation cascade, within the extracorporeal circuit. This strategy minimizes systemic anticoagulant effects while effectively preventing clot formation in the circuit. While RCA has been extensively studied and implemented for CRRT and other extracorporeal therapies, its application in TPE has remained less well-characterized. Notably, TPE introduces unique challenges to the use of RCA due to differences in blood flow rates, plasma extraction volumes, and the nature of replacement fluids used during the procedure. These factors can influence citrate kinetics and calcium homeostasis, necessitating a tailored approach to RCA in TPE [7]. Furthermore, the absence of a standardized, individualized protocol for RCA in TPE has limited its widespread adoption, leaving clinicians relaint on empirical adjustments and fixed-rate citrate infusions. Such approaches risk either under-anticoagulation, which may result in extracorporeal circuit clotting, or over-anticoagulation, which can lead to hypocalcemia and related adverse effects [8]. Therefore, there is a pressing need to develop a robust, evidence-based protocol that accounts for patient-specific variables and procedural parameters to optimize the safety and efficacy of RCA during TPE. **Current Challenges in Regional Citrate Anticoagulation for TPE** RCA relies on the infusion of citrate into the extracorporeal circuit, where it chelates calcium to inhibit coagulation locally. The calcium-citrate complexes are subsequently removed from the plasma during filtration, while a portion of the citrate enters the systemic circulation and is metabolized primarily in the liver, kidneys, and skeletal muscles [9]. This dynamic poses challenges in the management of calcium balance and systemic anticoagulation during TPE. For example, excessive citrate infusion can lead to significant hypocalcemia, manifesting as neuromuscular irritability, hypotension, or arrhythmias. Conversely, insufficient citrate dosing may fail to achieve adequate anticoagulation, leading to clot formation and procedural interruptions [10]. Several factors influence the pharmacokinetics of citarte and calcium during TPE, including hematocrit, baseline plasma iCa levels, and the rate of plasma exchange. Hematocrit determines the volume of plasma aavilable for citrate binding, while baselne iCa levels influnece the initial citrate-calcium equilibrium. Additionally, plasma flow rates and the volume of replacement fluids can alter the clearance of citrate and calcium from the system [11]. These variables underscore the need for an individualized approach to RCA, as fixed-rate citrate infusions fail to account for interpatient variability and procedural dynamics. Despite these considerations, existing protocols for RCA in TPE are largely empirical and lack the precision required for optimal anticoagulation management. **Rationale for an Individualized Protocol** The development of an indiidualized RCA protocol for TPE is predicated on the need to balance effective anticoagulation with miniml systemic side effects. In CRRT, mathematical models and alorithms have been successfully employed to tailor citrate dosing based on patient-specific parameters and procedural variables [12]. Such models enable the prediction of citrate and calcium kinetics, facilitating real-time adjustments to achieve target anticoagulation levels while minimizing hypocalcemiia and other complications. However, the appliccation of similar principles to TPE has been limited, partly due to the lack of comprehensive data on the determinants of citrate requirements in this context. Recent studies have highlighted the potential for integrating patient-specific variables, such as hematocrit and baseline iCa levels, into predictive models for RCA in TPE. These variables are biologically plausible deteminants of citrate kinetics, as they influence the plasma volume available for citrate binding and the initial citrate-calcium equilibrium, respectively [13]. By incorporating these factors into a mathematical framework, it is possible to develop an individualized protocol that optimizes citrate dosing for each patient and procedure. **Objectives and Contributions** The objective of this study is to address the existing gaps in RCA management for TPE by developing a novel protocol that individualizes citrate dosing based on patient-specific and procedural parameters. Using a structured approach, we aim to identify the key determinants of citrate requirements and translate these findings into a practical algorithm for clinical use. This work builds on prior studies of RCA in other extracorporeal therapies while accounting for the unique physiological and procedural characteristics of TPE. The proposed protocol is expected to achieve several clinical and operational benefits. First, it will enhance the safety of TPE by reducing the incidence of hypocalcemia and other citrate-related complications. Second, it will improve the efficiency of anticoagulation management, minimizing the risk of circuit clotting and procedural interruptions. Finally, the protocol will provide a standardized frmework for RCA in TPE, facilitating its broader adoption in clinical practice. In summary, the development of an individualized RCA protocol for TPE represents a critical advancement in the field of extracorporeal therapies. Extracorporeal therapies, such as therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE), have become essential tools in the management of a wide range of clinical conditions, including autoimmune disorders, hematological diseases, and complications related to transplantation, as extensively documented in the literature [1, 2]. A key component of TPE involves the removal of high-molecular-weight substances, such as immunoglobulins and immune complexes, from the patient's plasma. However, this procedure is not devoid of risks, particularly those associated with the use of anticoagulants to prevent the formation of clots within the extracorporeal circuit. Traditionally, heparin has been the anticoagulant of choice for TPE, but its use carries a significant risk of systemic bleeding, especially in patients with pre-existing coagulation disorders, recent surgical interventions, or other predisposing conditions [3, 4]. 

To mitigate these risks, regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) has emerged as a promising alternative in the field of extracorporeal therapies, including continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) and hemodialysis [5, 6]. The mechanism of RCA involves the chelation of ionized calcium (iCa), a crucial factor in the coagulation cascade, within the extracorporeal circuit. This approach effectively minimizes the risk of systemic anticoagulant effects while preventing clot formation in the circuit. Despite its proven efficacy in CRRT and other extracorporeal therapies, the application of RCA in TPE has been less well-defined, largely due to the unique challenges posed by TPE, including variations in blood flow rates, plasma extraction volumes, and the nature of replacement fluids used during the procedure. These factors can significantly impact citrate kinetics and calcium homeostasis, necessitating a tailored approach to RCA in TPE [7].

The lack of a standardized, individualized protocol for RCA in TPE has limited its widespread adoption, with clinicians often relying on empirical adjustments and fixed-rate citrate infusions. Such approaches can lead to either under-anticoagulation, resulting in clot formation within the extracorporeal circuit, or over-anticoagulation, which can cause hypocalcemia and related adverse effects [8]. Therefore, there is a pressing need to develop a robust, evidence-based protocol that takes into account patient-specific variables and procedural parameters to optimize the safety and efficacy of RCA during TPE.

One of the primary challenges in implementing RCA for TPE is the reliance on the infusion of citrate into the extracorporeal circuit, where it chelates calcium to inhibit coagulation locally. The calcium-citrate complexes are subsequently removed from the plasma during filtration, while a portion of the citrate enters the systemic circulation and is metabolized primarily in the liver, kidneys, and skeletal muscles [9]. This dynamic process poses significant challenges in managing calcium balance and systemic anticoagulation during TPE. For instance, excessive citrate infusion can lead to significant hypocalcemia, manifesting as neuromuscular irritability, hypotension, or arrhythmias. Conversely, insufficient citrate dosing may fail to achieve adequate anticoagulation, leading to clot formation and procedural interruptions [10].

Several factors influence the pharmacokinetics of citrate and calcium during TPE, including hematocrit, baseline plasma iCa levels, and the rate of plasma exchange. Hematocrit determines the volume of plasma available for citrate binding, while baseline iCa levels influence the initial citrate-calcium equilibrium. Additionally, plasma flow rates and the volume of replacement fluids can alter the clearance of citrate and calcium from the system [11]. These variables underscore the need for an individualized approach to RCA, as fixed-rate citrate infusions fail to account for interpatient variability and procedural dynamics. Despite these considerations, existing protocols for RCA in TPE are largely empirical and lack the precision required for optimal anticoagulation management.

The development of an individualized RCA protocol for TPE is predicated on the need to balance effective anticoagulation with minimal systemic side effects. In CRRT, mathematical models and algorithms have been successfully employed to tailor citrate dosing based on patient-specific parameters and procedural variables [12]. Such models enable the prediction of citrate and calcium kinetics, facilitating real-time adjustments to achieve target anticoagulation levels while minimizing hypocalcemia and other complications. However, the application of similar principles to TPE has been limited, partly due to the lack of comprehensive data on the determinants of citrate requirements in this context.

Recent studies have highlighted the potential for integrating patient-specific variables, such as hematocrit and baseline iCa levels, into predictive models for RCA in TPE. These variables are biologically plausible determinants of citrate kinetics, as they influence the plasma volume available for citrate binding and the initial citrate-calcium equilibrium, respectively [13]. By incorporating these factors into a mathematical framework, it is possible to develop an individualized protocol that optimizes citrate dosing for each patient and procedure. 

The objective of this study is to address the existing gaps in RCA management for TPE by developing a novel protocol that individualizes citrate dosing based on patient-specific and procedural parameters. Using a structured approach, we aim to identify the key determinants of citrate requirements and translate these findings into a practical algorithm for clinical use. This work builds on prior studies of RCA in other extracorporeal therapies while accounting for the unique physiological and procedural characteristics of TPE. The proposed protocol is expected to provide a more precise and effective approach to RCA in TPE, ultimately enhancing patient safety and outcomes.

Furthermore, the implementation of such a protocol would require a thorough understanding of the complex interactions between citrate, calcium, and the coagulation cascade, as well as the impact of various procedural parameters on these interactions. By elucidating these relationships and incorporating them into a predictive model, clinicians could optimize citrate dosing in real-time, thereby minimizing the risk of both thrombotic and bleeding complications. This, in turn, would contribute to the advancement of TPE as a therapeutic modality, enabling its safer and more effective application in a broader range of clinical settings.

Coxiella burnetii, an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium, is the etiological agent of Q fever, a zoonotic disesae with global distribution. This pathogen poses significant public health and veterinary concerns due to its ability to infect a wide range of hosts, its environmental stability, and its potential for aerosol transmission. Infected livestock, particularly cattle, sheep, and goats, are the primary reservoirs of C. burnetii, with transmission to humans typically occurring through inhalation of contaminated aerosols or dust originating from infected animals or their secretions, including milk, urine, feces, and birth products [1,2]. Although Q fever in humans is often asymptomatic, it can manifest as acute febrile illness, atypical pneumonia, or hepatitis, and in some cases, progress to chronic infection, such as endocarditis, highlighting the importance of early detection and conntrol of C. burnetii in animal populations as a preventive measure to mitigate human exposure [3,4]. The epidemiology of C. burnetii varies widely across regions, depending on factors such as host species, management practices, and environmental conditions. Regular surveillance of livestock populations is therefore critical to understanding the prevalence and dissemination of C. burnetii within a given country. In South Korea, Q fever was first reported in humans in 1957, and the incidence of the disease has since been increasing, with the majority of human cases linked to occupational exposure to livestock [5]. Despite the growing public health significance of Q fever, studies on the prevalence of C. burnetii in South Korean livestock have been limited, with most investigations focusing on secific regions or animal populations, and few addressing the pathogen’s presence in well-managed governmental facilities [6,7]. National breeding stock farms in South Korea play a pivotal role in the country’s livestock industry, serving as a source of high-quality genetic material for both dairy and beef cattle. These farms are characterized by striingent biosecurity and management protocols that aim to minimize the introduction and spread of infectious diseases. However, the effectiveness of such measures in preventing C. burnetii infection has not been comprehensively evaluated. Given the potential for asymptomatic carriage of the pathogen in cattle and its subsequent transmission to humans or other animals, understanding the prvalence of C. burnetii in these facilities is essential for asessing the adequacy of current biosecurity practices and for informing future diseaes control strategies. Previous studies have demonstrated that seroprevalence of C. burnetii in cattle can vaary significantly depending on herd size, geographical location, and farming practices, with higher prevalence often reported in regions with intensive livestock farming or poor biosecurity measures [8,9]. In South Korea, the limited data available suggest that C. burnetii is present in both dairy and beef cattle, though the extent of its distribution remains unclear [10]. Moreover, molecular studies have revealed significant genetic diversity among C. burnetii isolates worldwide, with certain genotypes associated with specific geographic regions or host species [11]. Comparative analysis of C. burnetii sequences from different regions can provide vaaluable insights into the evolutionary dynamics and transmission pathways of the pathogen, contributing to a better understanding of its epidemiology. This study represents the first investigation into the serologic and molecular prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle at South Korea’s national breeding stock farms. By focusing on these government-operated facilities, which adhere to high standards of biosecurity and management, this research aims to establish a baseline understanding of C. burnetii pervalence in a controlled livestock population. The findings of this study not only have implications for the management of C. burnetii at the national level but also underscore the potential risk posed by the pathhogen in less-regulated farming environments. To acieve these objectives, both serologic and molecular diagnostic methods were employed to deetct C. burnetii in cattle. Serologic testing, based on the detection of specific antibodies against C. burnetii antigens, is widely used for assessing exposure to the pathogen, while polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis provides a more direct method for identifying active infections by detecting bacterial DNA [12,13]. The combination of these approaches enables a comprehensive assessment of both past and current infections, offering a more complete picture of the pathogen’s prevalence. In addition to determining the prevalence of C. burnetii, this study also sought to characterize the genetic sequences of C. burnetii isolates recovered from cattle. By analyzing the 16S rRNA gene sequences of PCR-positive samples, the study aimed to investigate the genetic relationships between South Korean isolates and those from other countries, thereby contributing to the global understanding of C. burnetii genetic diversity. The clustering of South Korean isolates with those from the United States, Japan, and Greenland, as observed in this study, highlights the potential for interregional transmission of the pathogen and underscores the need for international collaboration in Q fever research and control efforts. The detection of C. burnetii in cattle at well-managed national breeding stock farms raises important questions about the pathogen’s transmission dynamics and reservoirs within South Korea. Given the controlled nature of these facilities, it is plausible that C. burnetii may be introduced through external sources, such as wiildlife or contaminated feed, or persist within the environment despite stringent biosecurity measures. This finding suggests that cattle in non-governmental farms, which often operate with less robust disease control systems, may be at an even higher risk of exposure to C. burnetii. Consequently, there is a pressing need for ongoing surveillance of livestock populations across the country, as well as the implementation of targeted control measures, such as vaccination and improved farm hygiene, to reduce the prevalence of C. burnetii and prevent its transmission to humans. *Coxiella burnetii*, the causative agent of Q fever, is a significant zoonotic pathogen affecting both humans and animals worldwide. To investigate the prevalence of *C. burnetii* in the South Korean cattle population, a comprehensive study was conducted involving 736 cattle from national breeding stock farms across the country. The serological and molecular prevalence of *C. burnetii* was determined using a combination of serological testing and PCR analysis. Initially, all 736 cattle samples were subjected to serological testing to detect the presence of antibodies against *C. burnetii*. The results revealed that 77 cattle tested positive for antibodies, resulting in a seroprevalence rate of 10.5% (95% confidence interval: 8.3–12.7). Notably, seropositive cattle were identified across all regions included in the study, with variations in prevalence observed between regions. The southern region exhibited the highest seropositivity rate (14.2%), followed by Jeju Island (11.8%) and the central region (8.6%). However, these differences were not statistically significant (p > 0.05), suggesting relatively uniform exposure risk across the studied farms.

In addition to serological testing, molecular detection of *C. burnetii* DNA was performed using PCR targeting the 16S rRNA gene. Of the 736 samples, 11 were positive for *C. burnetii* DNA on PCR, yielding a molecular prevalence rate of 1.5% (95% confidence interval: 0.6–2.4). The distribution of PCR-positive samples mirrored that of seropositive samples, with six positive cases identified in the southern region, three in Jeju Island, and two in the central region. No statistically significant regional differences were observed in molecular prevalence rates (p > 0.05). To further characterize the *C. burnetii* isolates, sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene was conducted for all 11 PCR-positive samples. The resulting sequences were edited and aligned using MEGA X software [2], and sequence identity was determined by comparison with *C. burnetii* sequences available in the GenBank database using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST; National Center for Biotechnology Information). Phylogenetic analysis was conducted using the maximum likelihood method with 1,000 bootstrap replicates to assess the evolutionary relationships of the South Korean isolates with previously reported *C. burnetii* strains from various countries.

The sequence analysis revealed that the 16S rRNA sequences from all 11 samples were identical, indicating a lack of genetic variability among the detected strains. Three representative samples—C-CN-3 (southern region), C-JJ-9 (Jeju Island), and C-CB-37 (central region)—were selected for detailed analysis. Sequence alignment and comparison with publicly available sequences in GenBank revealed 99.3–100% identity to other *C. burnetii* sequences previously reported from the United States, Europe, and Asia. This high degree of sequence similarity suggests that the *C. burnetii* strains detected in South Korean cattle are closely related to those found in other parts of the world. The lack of genetic variability among the detected strains may indicate a recent introduction of *C. burnetii* into the South Korean cattle population or a limited number of introductions over time.

The findings of this study have significant implications for the control and prevention of Q fever in South Korea. The presence of *C. burnetii* in cattle at national breeding stock farms highlights the need for sustained surveillance and control measures to reduce the risk of transmission to humans. The implementation of targeted interventions, such as vaccination and enhanced farm hygiene, is vital to reducing the prevalence of *C. burnetii* and preventing its transmission to humans. Further research is needed to fully comprehend the epidemiology of *C. burnetii* in South Korea and to develop effective strategies for controlling the spread of this zoonotic pathogen. Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) encompasses a spectrum of strutural abnormalities of the acetabulum, femoral head, and surounding soft tissues, ranging from mild acetabular dysplasia to complete dislocation of the hip joint. It is a condition with significant long-term implications if left untreated, including gait abnormalities, chronic pain, and early-onset osteoarthritis [1, 2]. The complexity of DDH management arises from its multifactorial etiology, variable clinical presentation, and the need to balance early intervention with the potential complications of surgical treatment [3]. The primary goal in the treatment of DDH is to achieve and maintain a concentric reduction of the femoral head within a well-formed acetabulum, thereby optimizing hip joint biomechanics and reducing the risk of secondary degenerative changes. While non-surgical methods, such as the Pavlik harness and closed reduction, are the mainstay of treatment for infants, surgical intervention becomes necessary in older children or in cases where early conservative management fails [4]. Among the surgical techniques used to address DDH, pellvic osteotomies play a pivotal role in enhancing acetabular coverage and joint congruency. The Dega osteotomy, first described by Wiktor Dega in 1969, is a versatile surgical procedure designed to correct acetabular dysplasia by reorienting the acetabular roof while preserving the continuity of the inner and outer tables of the ilium [5]. The Dega osteotomy is particularly advantageous in pediatric populations due to its ability to achieve a three-dimensional correction of acetabular morphology while maintaining growth potential in the triradiate cartilage [6]. The technique involves an incomplete trannsverse osteotomy of the ilium, extending fom the sciatic notch to the anteroinferior iliac spine, with controlled mobilization of the acetabular fragment achieved using a bone graft. This procedure allows for selective anterior, lateral, and posterior coverage of the femoral head, depending on the direction of dysplasia [7]. Despite its widespread use, long-term data evaluating the efficacy and durability of the Dega osteotomy in maintaining hip stability and preventing degenerative changes are limited, particularly in children treated beyond infancy. The prognosis of DDH following surgical intervention is influenced by a multitude of factors, including the sevrity of the dysplasia, age at the time of surgery, the presence of associated conditions such as cerebral palsy, and the occurrence of complications such as avascular necrosis (AVN) [8, 9]. AVN is a particularly concerning complication in DDH management, as it can compromise the viability of the femoral head and lead to joint failure over time [10]. The incidence of AVN varies significantly across different surgical techniques and patient populations, underscoring the importance of meticulous surgical planning and postoperative follow-up. This study focuses on the long-term outcomes of the Dgea osteotomy in children aged 2–8 years with DDH. The inclusion of this specific age group is clinically relevant, as it represents a transitional period where the potential for acetabular remodeling remains, but the risk of femoral head deformity and joint incongruity increases with delayed treatment [11]. The long follow-up period, ranging from 13 to 25 years, provides a unique opportunity to evaluate the durability of acetabular correction achieved with the Dega osteotomy and its impact on hip joint survival into adolescence and early adulthood. Previous studies on the Dega osteotomy have primarily focused on short- to medium-term outcomes, reporting favorable results in terms of radiographic parameters and clinical function [12, 13]. However, these studies often lack the longitudinal data necessary to assess the progression of hip arthrosis and the nede for secondary surgical interventions. Additionally, variations in surgical technique, patient selection criteria, and follow-up protocols across studies make it challenging to draw definitive conclusions regarding the long-term efficacy of the procedure. This study seeks to address these gaps by preenting a comprehensive analysis of 58 hips treated with the Dega osteotomy, with attention to radiographic predictors of hip arthrosis, the occurrence of AVN, and the need for subsequent surgeries. The long-term follow-up of this cohort also provides vaaluable insights into the natural history of surgically treated DDH and the factors that influence hip joint survival. By correlating clinical outcomes with radiographic measures of acetabular and femoral head morphology, this study aims to identify predictors of success and failure following the Dgea osteotomy. Such information is critical for refining patient selection criteria, optimizing surgical techniques, and improving postoperative rehabilitation protocols. In summary, the Dega osteotomy remains a cornerstone in the surgical management of DDH in children, offering the potential for durable acetabular correction and improved joit congruency. However, its long-term efficacy and the factors associated with its success or failure require further elucidation. The present study contributes to this boy of knowledge by providing a rigorous evaluation of 58 conseuctive osteotomies with a follow-up period extending up to 25 years. By analyzing the outcomes of this cohort, we aim to enhance the understanding of the role of the Dega osteotomy in the management of DDH and inform future clinical practice. A modified Smith-Petersen approach was used to access the ilium. The Dega osteotomy was performed as an incomplete, curved osteotomy of the acetabular roof, preserving the lateral cortical hinge to allow controlled redirection of the acetabulum. Graft material, harvested autologously from the iliac crest, was inserted into the osteotomy site to achieve acetabular coverage and promote stability. In cases with concurrent femoral abnormalities, femoral shortening or varus derotation osteotomies were performed. Postoperatively, all patients were immobliized in a spica cast for a period of 6–8 weeks. ### Postoperative Care and Follow-Up Radiographic evaluations were performed preoperatively, immediately postoperatively, and during follow-up. Subsequent evaluations were conducted every 6 months for the first 3 years and annually thereafter. Potential predictors of poor outcomes, including avascular necrosis (AVN), were analyzed using univariate and multivariate logistic regression models. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 22.0, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). ### Outcome Measures The primary outcome measure was the radiographic and clinical success of the Dega osteotomy, defnied as sustained acetabular coverage and functional hip stability without the need for revision surgery. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of complications, such as AVN, residual dysplasia, and postoperative pain categorized as mild, moderate, or severe. The presence of radiographic evidence of osteoarthritis or hip arthrosis at the final follow-up was also recorded. Outcomes were graded according to Severin’s classification, and hips graded as Severin I or II were considered favorable [2]. ### Complications Complications were systematically recorded during follow-up. AVN was diagnosed based on radiographic criteria, including the presence of femoral haed fragmentation, sclerosis, or flattening. Any additional adverse events, including infection, graft resorption, or mechanical failure, were noted. Patients with AVN were managed conservatively or wiht subsequent surgical interventions as necessary, and all cases were followed untl resolution or documented treatment failure. ### Limitations The retrospectiev component of this study, although limited to 17 hips, introduced potential recall bias. The hip joint is susceptible to a complex condition known as developmental dysplasia, which encompasses a broad spectrum of anatomical abnormalities affecting the socket of the hip, the ball at the top of the thigh bone, and the surrounding tissues [1, 2]. These irregularities can vary in severity, ranging from mild deformities of the hip socket to complete dislocation of the joint. If left untreated, developmental dysplasia can have profound and lasting consequences, including irregularities in gait, persistent pain, and premature wear and tear of the joint, leading to osteoarthritis [3]. Managing this condition is further complicated by its multifaceted causes, diverse clinical manifestations, and the delicate balance required between early intervention and the potential risks associated with surgical treatments.

The primary objective in treating developmental dysplasia is to ensure that the ball of the thigh bone fits snugly and evenly within the hip socket, thereby optimizing the biomechanics of the hip joint and minimizing the risk of secondary degenerative changes. In infants, treatment often involves non-surgical methods, such as the use of a Pavlik harness or closed reduction techniques. However, in older children or when these early interventions prove unsuccessful, surgical intervention becomes necessary [4]. Among the various surgical techniques employed to address developmental dysplasia, procedures that involve cutting and realigning the pelvis play a critical role in enhancing the coverage of the hip socket and improving the congruence of the joint.

One such surgical procedure is the Dega osteotomy, a technique first introduced by Wiktor Dega in 1969 [5]. This versatile procedure is designed to correct deformities of the hip socket by reorienting its roof while preserving the integrity of the inner and outer layers of the pelvis. The Dega osteotomy is particularly beneficial in pediatric populations due to its ability to achieve a three-dimensional correction of the hip socket's shape while preserving the potential for growth in the cartilage that forms the base of the pelvis [6]. The technique involves making a strategic cut across the pelvis, from the notch at the base of the spine to the prominence at the front of the hip, followed by the controlled movement of the fragment of bone that forms the hip socket, facilitated by a bone graft. This allows for selective coverage of the ball of the thigh bone from the front, side, or back, depending on the direction of the deformity [7].

Despite its widespread application, there is a scarcity of long-term data evaluating the effectiveness and durability of the Dega osteotomy in maintaining the stability of the hip and preventing degenerative changes, particularly in children treated beyond infancy. The prognosis for developmental dysplasia following surgical intervention is influenced by a multitude of factors, including the severity of the deformity, the age of the child at the time of surgery, the presence of associated conditions, and complications such as the death of bone tissue due to lack of blood supply [8, 9]. This complication, known as avascular necrosis, is particularly concerning as it can compromise the viability of the ball of the thigh bone and lead to the failure of the joint over time [10]. The incidence of avascular necrosis varies significantly across different surgical techniques and patient populations, highlighting the importance of meticulous planning and follow-up after surgery.

This study focuses on the long-term outcomes of the Dega osteotomy in children aged 2 to 8 years with developmental dysplasia. The inclusion of this age group is clinically significant, as it represents a critical period where the potential for the hip socket to remodel remains, but the risk of deformity of the ball of the thigh bone and joint incongruity increases with delayed treatment [11]. The extended follow-up period, ranging from 13 to 25 years, offers a unique opportunity to assess the durability of the correction achieved with the Dega osteotomy and its impact on the survival of the hip joint into adolescence and early adulthood.

Previous research on the Dega osteotomy has primarily concentrated on short- to medium-term outcomes, reporting favorable results in terms of radiographic parameters and clinical function [12, 13]. However, these studies often lack the longitudinal data necessary to evaluate the progression of hip arthritis and the need for additional surgical interventions. Furthermore, variations in surgical technique, patient selection criteria, and follow-up protocols across studies complicate the drawing of definitive conclusions regarding the long-term efficacy of the procedure.

This study seeks to address these gaps by presenting a comprehensive analysis of 58 hips treated with the Dega osteotomy, with attention to radiographic predictors of hip arthritis, the occurrence of avascular necrosis, and the need for subsequent surgeries. The long-term follow-up of this cohort also provides valuable insights into the natural history of surgically treated developmental dysplasia and the factors that influence the survival of the hip joint. By correlating clinical outcomes with radiographic measures of the shape and structure of the hip socket and the ball of the thigh bone, this study aims to identify predictors of success and failure following the Dega osteotomy. Such information is critical for refining criteria for patient selection, optimizing surgical techniques, and improving postoperative rehabilitation protocols.

In summary, the Dega osteotomy remains a fundamental component in the surgical management of developmental dysplasia in children, offering the potential for durable correction of the hip socket and improved joint alignment. However, its long-term efficacy and the factors associated with its success or failure require further elucidation. The present study contributes to this body of knowledge by providing a rigorous evaluation of 58 consecutive osteotomies with a follow-up period extending up to 25 years. By analyzing the outcomes of this cohort, we aim to enhance our understanding of the Dega osteotomy's role in the treatment of developmental dysplasia, ultimately informing clinical practice and improving patient outcomes. This comprehensive analysis will shed light on the procedure's capacity to achieve lasting corrections, its impact on the prevention of degenerative changes, and its influence on the quality of life of children and adolescents undergoing this surgical intervention. This investigation was designed to assess the outcomes of the Dega osteotomy in the management of DDH in children within the age range of 2-8 years. The study encompassed a multicenter evaluation, incorporating both prospective and retrospective cases, with data collection spanning from January 1988 to October 2000. The inclusion criteria consisted of children who had received a diagnosis of DDH, confirmed through both clinical evaluation and radiographic imaging, and who underwent the Dega osteotomy during the specified study period. Exclusion criteria included patients with neuromuscular conditions, those who had undergone previous pelvic surgeries, or individuals with incomplete follow-up data beyond 13 years. Ethical approval was secured from the relevant institutional review boards at all participating centers, and informed consent was obtained from the guardians of all participating children. 

The patient population comprised 48 pediatric patients, accounting for 58 hips, with 10 children (20.8%) presenting with bilateral DDH. The cohort consisted of 36 females (75.0%) and 12 males (25.0%), with a mean age at the time of surgery of 4.3 years, ranging from 2 to 8 years. Patients were categorized into prospective (n = 41 hips) and retrospective (n = 17 hips) groups, based on whether data collection had been initiated prior to or after the surgical intervention. Preoperative clinical and radiographic characteristics, including the degree of dysplasia and any associated subluxation or dislocation, were documented for all patients. The classification of hip dysplasia severity was based on the Tönnis grading system [1]. 

The surgical technique employed in this study involved a modified Smith-Petersen approach to access the ilium, followed by a Dega osteotomy, which was performed as an incomplete, curved osteotomy of the acetabular roof. This method preserved the lateral cortical hinge, allowing for controlled redirection of the acetabulum. Autologous graft material, harvested from the iliac crest, was inserted into the osteotomy site to achieve acetabular coverage and promote stability. In cases where concurrent femoral abnormalities were present, femoral shortening or varus derotation osteotomies were also performed. Postoperatively, all patients were immobilized in a spica cast for a period of 6-8 weeks. 

The postoperative care and follow-up protocol involved radiographic evaluations conducted preoperatively, immediately postoperatively, and during subsequent follow-ups. Initial follow-up included radiographic imaging at 6 weeks, coinciding with the removal of the spica cast where applicable. Subsequent evaluations were conducted every 6 months for the first 3 years and annually thereafter. Radiographic parameters assessed included the acetabular index (AI), center-edge (CE) angle, and Shenton's line continuity. A single-cut computed tomographic (CT) scan was obtained for all prospective cases prior to surgery and during the first year postoperatively to evaluate acetabular correction and confirm graft positioning. Clinical assessments during follow-up focused on hip range of motion, pain, and functional outcomes, with the modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS) used to quantify clinical results. 

Long-term outcomes were assessed with particular attention to signs of hip arthrosis, including joint-space narrowing, osteophyte formation, and subchondral sclerosis, as classified by the Tönnis grading system for osteoarthritis [1]. Revision surgeries, including reorientation acetabuloplasty or total hip arthroplasty, were documented as endpoints for failure. The statistical analysis employed in this study involved the use of descriptive statistics to summarize demographic and clinical characteristics. Continuous variables, such as age and radiographic parameters, were expressed as means with standard deviations, while categorical variables were reported as frequencies and proportions. 

Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was employed to estimate cumulative survival rates of the hips, with the occurrence of revision surgery or arthroplasty serving as the endpoint. Potential predictors of poor outcomes, including avascular necrosis (AVN), were analyzed using univariate and multivariate logistic regression models. Insects play a critical role in forensic investigations, particularly in estimating the post-mortem interval (PMI) in cases involving decomposing human or animal remains. The colonization of cadavers by insects follows a predictable sequence, and the developmental stages of these insects can provide investigators with valuable temporal information [1]. Among the various insect species utilized in forensic entomology, beetles have garnered increasing attention due to their ecological importance in decomposition processes and their potential as reliable indicators of PMI [2]. Despite their utility, the accuracy of age estimmations based on insect development remains a significant challenge, as intraspecific variation in developmnet time can introduce considerable uncertainty into forensic analyses [3]. Consequently, refining methods to improve the precision and reliability of insect age estimates is a priority in forensic entomology. Typically, insect age estimation relies on developmental data derived from laboratory studies, where the relationship bewteen temperature and the duration of each life stage is modeled to calculate thermal summation values (K) [4]. These models are based on the principle that insect development is temperature-dependent, with a species-specific thermal constant required for the compleiton of specific life stages. However, such general models often overlook individual-level variation arising from environmental, genetic, and physiological factors, which can influence developmental rates and lead to discrepancies in predicted ages [5]. For instance, factors such as larval nutrition, competition, and microclimatic conditions may result in significant differences in the size and developmental duration of individuals within the same species [6]. This variatino complicates the application of general thermal summation models in forensic contexts, where precise and accurate age estimates are critical for reconstructing timelines. Recent studies have suggested that incorporating additional biological variables, such as insect size, may improve the accuracy of age estimations. Size is a commonly measured trait in entomology and is known to be influenced by both genetic and environmental factors during development [7]. As such, it serves as a proxy for the conditions experienced by an individual throughout its growth. Insects of the same species and developmental stage may emerge at different sizes due to variation in resource availability, competition, or other environmental influences, and these differences in size can be associated with variation in physiological age [8]. Specifically, larger individuals may have shorter development times due to more favorable growth conditions, while smaller individuals may require longer durations to reach maturity. This relationship offers the potential to refine age estimation models by accounting for individual variability in physiological age bsaed on size at emergence. The present study focuses on the beetle *Creophilus maxillosus* (Linnaeus, 1758), a member of the family Staphylinidae, which is commonly asssociated with decomposing remains and holds considerable forensic relevance [9]. *C. maxillosus* is a predatory beetle that feeds on other insects present on cadavers, and its predictable developmental pattern makes it a useful species for PMI estimation. While previous research has established baseline developmental data for *C. maxillosus* under controlled laboratory conditions, little attention has been given to the potential for size-based models to enhance age estimation accuracy in this species [10]. Considering the practical significance of improving forensic tools, this gap warrants further investigation. In this study, we test the hypothess that the physiological age of *C. maxillosus* at emergence, as represented by the thermal summaion value (K), is inverely related to beetle size. Specifically, we propose that larger individuals of *C. maxillosus* require lower K values to emerge, reflecting a shorter development time. To test this hypothesis, we coonducted a laboratory study to examine the relationship between beetle size at emergence and K across a range of controlled developmental conditions. We further developed size-based predictive models for K and validated these models against independent data to assess their accuracy in estimating physiological age. Our results demonstrate that incorporating size as a predictor variable significantly improves the accuracy of age estimates for *C. maxillosus*, compared to traditional thermal summation models that do not account for individual variability. The implications of this research extend beyond the specific csae of *C. maxillosus*. By demonstrating the utility of size-based models for refining age estimates, this study highlights a broader methodological advance in forensic entomology. Size is a relatively easy and non-destructive measurement to obtain, and its integration into forensic analyses has the potential to reducce uncertainty in PMI estimations across a range of insect species. Furthermore, the sex-specific differences observed in this study underscore the importance of considering biological variation in forensic models. As forensic entomology continues to develop as a discipline, incorporating additional biological and ecological variables into age estimation methods will be critical for improving the robustness and reliability of PMI determinations in legal investigations. Laboratory experiments were conducted to investigate the development of *Creophilus maxillosus* under controlled conditions and to assess the relationship between adult beettle size at emergence and physiological age. These expperiments aimed to determine whether incorporating size measurements can improve the accuracy of age estimates in a forensic entomology context. To establish a thermal summation model for *C. maxillosus*, eggs were collected from beetles maintained in a laboratory colony. The coloony originated from adults colleted in natural environments and was replenished peeriodically to maintain genetic diversity. Adult beetles were housed in plastic containers (30 × 20 × 10 cm) under controlled environmental conditions (25 ± 1°C, 60 ± 5% relative humidity, and a 12:12 light-dark cycle). Beetles were provided with minced meat ad libitum as a protein source and moistened cotton as a source of water. Eggs were collected by inspecting the rearing substrate daily and were transferred to small individual containers (5 × 5 × 5 cm) containnig a thin layer of moistened substrate and food. The containers were maintained under the same environmental conditions as the colony. To investigate the effects of temeprature on development, egg batches were divied and reared at five constant temperatures: 18°C, 22°C, 25°C, 28°C, and 30°C (± 0.5°C). Each temperature treatment included a minimum of 50 individuals to account for variation in development and ensure robust statistical analysis. Larvae were monitored daily and were provided with fresh foood every 24 hours. Developmental stages (egg, larva, pupa, and adult) were recorded, and the time takeen to reach each stage was documented. Upon adult emergence, the beetles were sexde based on external morphological characteristics and were measured for body length using a digital caliper with a pecision of 0.01 mm. Measurements were taken from the anterior margin of the head to the posterior edge of the elytra. The physiological age of each individual was expressed as the thermal summation value (K), which was calculated using the eqation \( K = (T - T_{min}) \times D \), where \( T \) is the rearing temperature, \( T_{min} \) is the lower developmental threshold, and \( D \) is the duration of development (in days) from egg to adult emergence. The \( T_{min} \) value was determined by extraploating the linear relationship between development rate (1/D) and temperature. Thermal summation values for each individual were calulated separately for males and females to account for potential sex-specific differences in development. To evaluate the relationship between body size at emergence and physiological age, linaer regression models were constructed for both sexes. Beetle length was used as the predictor variable, and \( K \) was the dependent variable. The models were developed using data from individuals reared at 22°C, 25°C, and 28°C, as these temperatures produced the most consisstent development across replicates. The moedls were then validated uisng data from individuals reared at 18°C and 30°C, which were not included in the model construction. Validation involved comparing the predicted \( K \) values, obtained using the size-based regression models, with the true \( K \) values derived from development data. To assess the accuracy of the size-based models in predicting physiological age, the absolute error between predicted and true \( K \) values was calculated for each individual. These errors were compared with errors derved from the general thermal summation model, whch does not incorporate size as a predictor variable. Statistical anlayses were performed using R software (version 4.0.5) [1]. The goodness-of-fit of the regression models was evaluated using the coefficient of determination (\( R^2 \)), and the predictive accuracy of the models was assesesd using root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE). Paired t-tests were uesd to compare the absolute errors betwween the size-based and general models. To further assess the applicability of the size-based approach in forensic contexts, a simulated validation study was conducted. In this study, adult beetle measuremeents from individuals reared under varying environmental conditions (e.g., fluctuating temperatures) were used to predict \( K \) values using the size-based models. Predicted \( K \) values were then compared with true \( K \) valuues callculated from the known development data. This approach was designed to mimic real-world sceanrios in which insects collected from crime scenes exhibit developmental variability due to environmental factors. The results of the experments were compiled and analyzed to determine the extent to which incorporating size at emergence improved the accuracy of age estimates. Statistical significance was set at \( p < 0.05 \) for all tests. Within the domain of forensic science, entomological evidence has emerged as a crucial component in the estimation of post-mortem intervals (PMIs) for decomposing human or animal remains. A predictable succession of insect colonization on cadavers furnishes investigators with a temporal framework, while the developmental stages of these insects yield vital insights into the chronology of events [1]. Among the diverse array of insect species leveraged in forensic entomology, beetles have garnered considerable attention in recent years due to their pivotal role in decomposition processes and their potential as reliable indicators of PMI [2]. Despite their utility, the accuracy of age estimations predicated on insect development remains a pressing concern, as intraspecific variation in development time can introduce considerable uncertainty into forensic analyses [3]. Consequently, refining methods to enhance the precision and reliability of insect age estimates has become a priority in forensic entomology.

Typically, insect age estimation relies on developmental data derived from laboratory studies, where the relationship between temperature and the duration of each life stage is modeled to calculate thermal summation values (K) [4]. These models are grounded in the principle that insect development is temperature-dependent, with a species-specific thermal constant required for the completion of specific life stages. However, such general models often overlook individual-level variation arising from environmental, genetic, and physiological factors, which can influence developmental rates and lead to discrepancies in predicted ages [5]. For instance, factors such as larval nutrition, competition, and microclimatic conditions may result in significant differences in the size and developmental duration of individuals within the same species [6]. This variation complicates the application of general thermal summation models in forensic contexts, where precise and accurate age estimates are critical for reconstructing timelines.

Recent studies have suggested that incorporating additional biological variables, such as insect size, may improve the accuracy of age estimations. Size is a commonly measured trait in entomology and is known to be influenced by both genetic and environmental factors during development [7]. As such, it serves as a proxy for the conditions experienced by an individual throughout its growth. Insects of the same species and developmental stage may emerge at different sizes due to variation in resource availability, competition, or other environmental influences, and these differences in size can be associated with variation in physiological age [8]. Specifically, larger individuals may have shorter development times due to more favorable growth conditions, while smaller individuals may require longer durations to reach maturity. This relationship offers the potential to refine age estimation models by accounting for individual variability in physiological age based on size at emergence.

The present study focuses on the beetle *Creophilus maxillosus* (Linnaeus, 1758), a member of the family Staphylinidae, which is commonly associated with decomposing remains and holds considerable forensic relevance [9]. *C. maxillosus* is a predatory beetle that feeds on other insects present on cadavers, and its predictable developmental pattern makes it a useful species for PMI estimation. While previous research has established baseline developmental data for *C. maxillosus* under controlled laboratory conditions, little attention has been given to the potential for size-based models to enhance age estimation accuracy in this species [10]. Considering the practical significance of improving forensic tools, this gap warrants further investigation.

In this study, we test the hypothesis that the physiological age of *C. maxillosus* at emergence, as represented by the thermal summation value (K), is inversely related to beetle size. Specifically, we propose that larger individuals of *C. maxillosus* require lower K values to emerge, reflecting a shorter development time. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a laboratory study to examine the relationship between beetle size at emergence and K across a range of controlled developmental conditions. We further developed size-based predictive models for K and validated these models against independent data to assess their accuracy in estimating physiological age.

Our results demonstrate that incorporating size as a predictor variable significantly improves the accuracy of age estimates for *C. maxillosus*, compared to traditional thermal summation models that do not account for individual variability.
