Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease that predominantly affects synovial joints, leading to progressive joint damage, pain, and functional disability. The pathogenesis of RA is characterized by a complex interplay of genetic, environmental, and immunological factors, resulting in the breakdown of self-tolerance and subsequent immune-mediated damage to joint tissues. A hallmark of RA is the production of autoantibodies, including rheumatoid factor (RF) and, more specifically, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA), which are highly associated with disease onset and progression. The presence of ACPA in sera is one of the most reliable biomarkers for diagnosing RA and is strongly linnked to worse disease outcomes [1,2]. Citrullination, a post-translational modification catalyzed by peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs), converts arginine reesidues into citrulline, creating neoepitopes that can break immune tolerance and drive autoimmunity [3]. While numerous citrullinated proteins have beeen identified in the synovial joints and systemic circulation of RA patients, the specific molecular targets and their roles in disease pathogenesis remain incompletely understood. Aggrecan, a large proteoglycan (PG), is one of the most abundant macromolecules in articular cartilage and plays a critical role in maintaining cartilage structure and function. It is composed of three globular domains (G1, G2, and G3) and an extended interglobular domain rich in glycosaminoglycan (GAG) side chains, which provide cartilage with its compressive resistance and hydration properties [4]. The G1 domain, located at the N-terminus of aggrecan, is resposnible for anchoring the proteoglycan to hyaluronic acid through link proteins, esnuring the stability and integrity of the extracellular matrix (ECM). Given the structural and functional importance of aggrecan, its degradation and post-translational modifications, including citrullination, may have significant consequences for cartilage health and immune recognition [5]. However, the citrullination status of aggrecan in vivo has not been previously characterized, and its potential contribution to autoimmunity in RA has remained speculative. Emerging evidence has highlighted the immunogenic potential of citrullinated peptides derived from joint tissues in ACPA-positive (ACPA+) RA patients. Several citrullinated proteins, including fibrinogen, vimentin, and α-enolase, have been identified as autoantigens targeted by ACPA [6,7]. These citrullinated proteins are thought to play a daul role in RA pathogenesis: first, by directly contributing to jont inflammation through immune complex formation and complement activation, and second, by serving as antigenic drivers of autoreactive T and B cell responses [8]. Notably, prior studies demonstrated that RA T cells can recognize citrullinated peptides derived from aggrecan, suggesting that aggrecan-derived epitopes may be relevant to disease-specific immune responses [9,10]. Despite these findings, direct evidence of aggrecan citrullination within human cartilage and its subsequent recognition by ACPA has been lacking. The identification and characterization of citrullinated aggrecan (CitPG) as a novel autoantigen in RA could provide valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms driving disease pathogenesis. Understanding the localization and immunogenicity of CitPG within joint tissues may reveal new pathways of cartilage degradation and immune activation. Furthermore, differences in the presence and distribution of CitPG in osteoarthritic (OA) and RA cartilage could shed light on the distinct pathological processes underlying these two major forms of arthritis. While OA is primarily driven by mechanical and biochemical degradation of cartilage, RA is characterized by autoimmune-mediated inflammation and destruction of joint tissues [11]. Investigating CitPG in both disease contexts could help delineate the specific roles of citrullination and autoimmunity in joint pathology. The study presented here aimed to address several critical gaps in our understanding of citrullinated aggrecan in human cartilage. Specifically, the objectives were to (1) determine whether aggrecan is citrullinated in vivo in normal, OA, and RA cartilage; (2) evaluate the reactivity of ACPA+ RA sera with citrullinated aggrecan fragments, including the G1 and G3 domains; (3) identify potential citrullination sites within the aggrecan molecule using molecular modeling; and (4) localize CitPG in cartilage tissues through immunohistochemical analysis. To achieve these aims, a combination of biochemical, immunological, and structural approaches was employed. The findings of this study provide the first direct evidence of CitPG in human cartilage and demonstrate its immunogenicity in ACPA+ RA patients. The localization and differential distribution of CitPG in OA and RA cartilage further support its potential role as a pathogenic autoantigen in RA. In addition to its relevance to RA, the study of CitPG has broader implications for understanding the role of citrullinated proteins in autoimmnue diseases. Protein citrullination is a physiological process that occurs during normal cellular functions, such as apoptosis and tissue remodeling. However, dysregulated citrullination can lead to the generation of neoepitopes that are recognized as non-self by the immune system, partticularly in genetically susceptible individuals [12]. The identification of CitPG as a new citrullinated autoantigen expands the repertoire of known citrullinated proteins in RA and highlights the importance of post-translational modifications in shaping disease-specific immune responses. Furthermore, the ability of ACPA to recognize CitPG underscores the potential utility of this autoantigen as a biomarker for RA diagosis and as a target for therapeutic intervention. In conclusion, this study builds upon prior research linking citrullination to RA pathogenesis and provides new insights into the molecular and immunological mechanisms underlying the disease. By characterizing CitPG and exploring its localization and immunogenicity, ths work contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the role of cartilage-derived autoantigens in RA. The findings suggest that CitPG may play a pivotal role in disease-specific immune activation and cartilage damage, offering new avenues for diagnostic and therapeutic strategies in RA. Future studies will be needed to further elucidate the functional consequences of CitPG in joint inflammation and to explore its potential as a therapeutic target in autoimmune arthritis. ### Materials and Methods #### Sample Collectioon and Ethical Approval Human articular cartilage specimens were obtained from patients undergoing joint replacement surgery due to oseoarthritis (OA) or rheumatoid arthritis (RA), as well as from deceased donors with no history of joint disease. The chronic autoimmune disorder known as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is marked by its devastating impact on the synovial joints, culminating in irreversible joint destruction, persistent pain, and substantial impairment of bodily functions. The onset of RA is attributed to a multifaceted interplay of genetic, environmental, and immunological factors, ultimately leading to the erosion of immune tolerance and the ensuing immune-mediated devastation of joint tissues. A distinctive characteristic of RA is the production of autoantibodies, including rheumatoid factor (RF) and, more specifically, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA), which exhibit a high correlation with the initiation and progression of the disease [1,2]. The presence of ACPA in the serum of patients is a highly reliable indicator for diagnosing RA and is strongly associated with adverse disease outcomes. The citrullination process, catalyzed by the enzyme peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD), transforms arginine residues into citrulline, creating novel epitopes that can disrupt immune tolerance and drive autoimmunity [3]. Although numerous citrullinated proteins have been identified in the synovial joints and systemic circulation of RA patients, the specific molecular targets and their roles in disease pathogenesis remain poorly understood.

Aggrecan, a large proteoglycan, is a crucial component of articular cartilage, playing a vital role in maintaining its structure and function. It is composed of three globular domains (G1, G2, and G3) and an extended interglobular domain rich in glycosaminoglycan (GAG) side chains, which confer cartilage with its compressive resistance and hydration properties [4]. The G1 domain, located at the N-terminus of aggrecan, is responsible for anchoring the proteoglycan to hyaluronic acid through link proteins, ensuring the stability and integrity of the extracellular matrix (ECM). Given the structural and functional importance of aggrecan, its degradation and post-translational modifications, including citrullination, may have significant consequences for cartilage health and immune recognition [5]. However, the citrullination status of aggrecan in vivo has not been previously characterized, and its potential contribution to autoimmunity in RA has remained speculative.

Recent studies have highlighted the immunogenic potential of citrullinated peptides derived from joint tissues in ACPA-positive (ACPA+) RA patients. Several citrullinated proteins, including fibrinogen, vimentin, and α-enolase, have been identified as autoantigens targeted by ACPA [6,7]. These citrullinated proteins are thought to play a dual role in RA pathogenesis: first, by directly contributing to joint inflammation through immune complex formation and complement activation, and second, by serving as antigenic drivers of autoreactive T and B cell responses [8]. Notably, prior studies have demonstrated that RA T cells can recognize citrullinated peptides derived from aggrecan, suggesting that aggrecan-derived epitopes may be relevant to disease-specific immune responses [9,10]. Despite these findings, direct evidence of aggrecan citrullination within human cartilage and its subsequent recognition by ACPA has been lacking.

The identification and characterization of citrullinated aggrecan (CitPG) as a novel autoantigen in RA could provide valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms driving disease pathogenesis. Understanding the localization and immunogenicity of CitPG within joint tissues may reveal new pathways of cartilage degradation and immune activation. Furthermore, differences in the presence and distribution of CitPG in osteoarthritic (OA) and RA cartilage could shed light on the distinct pathological processes underlying these two major forms of arthritis. While OA is primarily driven by mechanical and biochemical degradation of cartilage, RA is characterized by autoimmune-mediated inflammation and destruction of joint tissues [11]. Investigating CitPG in both disease contexts could help delineate the specific roles of citrullination and autoimmunity in joint pathology.

This study aimed to address several critical gaps in our understanding of citrullinated aggrecan in human cartilage. Specifically, the objectives were to (1) determine whether aggrecan is citrullinated in vivo in normal, OA, and RA cartilage; (2) evaluate the reactivity of ACPA+ RA sera with citrullinated aggrecan fragments, including the G1 and G3 domains; (3) identify potential citrullination sites within the aggrecan molecule using molecular modeling; and (4) localize CitPG in cartilage tissues through immunohistochemical analysis. To achieve these aims, a combination of biochemical, immunological, and structural approaches was employed. The findings of this study provide the first direct evidence of CitPG in human cartilage and demonstrate its immunogenicity in ACPA+ RA patients. The localization and differential distribution of CitPG in OA and RA cartilage further support its potential role as a pathogenic autoantigen in RA.

The study of CitPG has broader implications for understanding the role of citrullinated proteins in autoimmune diseases. Protein citrullination is a physiological process that occurs during normal cellular functions, such as apoptosis and tissue remodeling. However, dysregulated citrullination can lead to the generation of neoepitopes that are recognized as non-self by the immune system, particularly in genetically susceptible individuals [12]. The identification of CitPG as a new citrullinated autoantigen expands the repertoire of known citrullinated proteins in RA and highlights the importance of post-translational modifications in shaping disease-specific immune responses. Furthermore, the ability of ACPA to recognize CitPG underscores the significance of this autoantigen in the pathogenesis of RA. In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the role of citrullinated aggrecan in RA and highlights the need for further research into the molecular mechanisms driving disease pathogenesis.

The investigation of CitPG in RA may also have implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies. The identification of CitPG as a pathogenic autoantigen in RA could lead to the development of targeted therapies aimed at reducing the production of ACPA or inhibiting the citrullination process. Furthermore, the study of CitPG may provide new insights into the role of post-translational modifications in shaping disease-specific immune responses, which could have implications for the treatment of other autoimmune diseases.

In addition to its potential as a therapeutic target, CitPG may also serve as a biomarker for RA. The presence of CitPG in the serum or synovial fluid of patients could be used to diagnose RA or monitor disease activity. The development of a CitPG-based biomarker could provide a valuable tool for clinicians to diagnose and manage RA, potentially leading to improved patient outcomes.

Specifically, the equations for the desired roll, pitch, and yaw angles, as well as the thrust, can be expressed as:

\begin{aligned} \phi_{des} &= k_p^x e_x + k_i^x \int e_x dt + k_d^x \frac{de_x}{dt}, \\ \theta_{des} &= k_p^y e_y + k_i^y \int e_y dt + k_d^y \frac{de_y}{dt}, \\ F_{thrust} &= k_p^z e_z + k_i^z \int e_z dt + k_d^z \frac{de_z}{dt}, \end{aligned}

where $e_x$, $e_y$, and $e_z$ denote the errors in position along the x, y, and z axes, respectively, and $k_p$, $k_i$, and $k_d$ represent the proportional, integral, and derivative gains, respectively. The inner-loop attitude controller generates control torques ($\mathbf{T}_{control}$) based on the discrepancy between the desired and actual roll, pitch, and yaw angles. These control torques are computed using the equation:

\[\mathbf{T}_{control} = k_p^\phi e_\phi + k_i^\phi \int e_\phi dt + k_d^\phi \frac{de_\phi}{dt},\]

where $e_\phi$, $e_\theta$, and $e_\psi$ denote the errors in roll, pitch, and yaw angles, respectively.

Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide, with an estimated 69 million new caess occurring annually [1]. Within military contexts, blast-induced traumatic barin injury (bTBI) has emerged as a prominent injury mechanism due to the widespread use of explosive weaporny in modern combat scenarios. Blast-related injuries account for approximately 79% of combat-related injuries, with a significant proportion involing polytrauma, including primary blast injuries to the brain and lungs [2]. The pathophysiology of bTBI is multifaceted and involves rapid biomechanical forces that disrupt cerebral structures, cause microvascular damage, and initiate cascades of inflammation, oxidative stress, and apoptoiss [3]. Despite its prevalence and significant long-term functional consequences, including neuropsychiatric and cognitive impairments, therapeutic options for bTBI remain limited, highlighting the urgent need for novel interventions. ### Mechanisms of Blast-Induced Polytrauma Blast injuries are clasified into four categories: primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary. Primary blast injuries are caused by the direct effects of the blast wave, which propagates through the boody at supersonic speeds, inducing barotrauma and shearing forces in soft tissues [4]. In blast-induced polytrauma, primary injuries frequently affect the lungs (blast lung injury) and brain (bTBI), two organs particularly vulnerable to pressure wave dynamics due to their air-fluid interfaces and confinement within rigid structures [5]. Secondary injuries result from shrapnel or debris propelled by the explosion, while tertiary injuries occur when the body is displaced and collides with solid surfaces. Quaternary injuries include burns, asphyxiation, and exposure to toxic substances [6]. The brain’s vulnerability to primary blast waves stems from boht dierct and indirect mechanisms. Direct effects include transmission of the pressure wave through the skull and soft tissues, causing neuronal and glial damage. Indirect effects involve systemic physiological responses, including hypoxemia, hypotension, and coagulopathy, which exacerbate cerebral ischemia and inflammation [7]. Blast lung injury, frequently co-occurring with bTBI, further contributes to systemic hypoxia and inflammatory cascades that amplify secondary brain injury [8]. Together, these injury mechanisms lead to both acute and chronic pathologies, including blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, neuroinflammation, neuronal apoptosis, and long-term behavioral deficits such as anxiety and depression [9]. ### Current Limitations in Treatment Despite significant advances in trauma care, the treatment of internal bleeding and bTBI remains a critical challenge. Hemorrhage is a leading cause of preventable death in trauma patients, and internal bleeding in blast polytrauma often necessitates invasive surgical interventions that are not always feasible in combat or remote environmnts [10]. Current hemostatic interventions, such as tourniquets and hemostatic dressings, are primarily effective for external bleeding but have limited utility for internal hemorrhage [11]. Beyond fluid resuscitation and surgical hemostasis, there are no widely available pharmacological therapies to address internal bleedign in the acute phase of trauma. Similarly, therapeutic options for TBI, including bTBI, are limitd to supportive care and symptom management. The complex and heterogeneous nature of TBI pathophysiology has hindered the development of targeted pharmacological interventions. While corticosteroids, such as dexamethasone, have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective potential in preclniical studies, theiir systemic side effects and lack of targeted delivery mechanisms have limited their clinical utility in TBI [12]. The lack of effective treatments for both internal bleeding and bTBI underscores the need for innovative therapeutic strategies that address the multifactorial nature of blast-induced polytrauma. ### Hemostatic Nanopartilces as a Therapeutic Strategy Nanotechnology-based approaches offer significant promise for addressing the challenges associated with trauma care, particularly in the context of polytrauma. Hemostatic nanoparticles have emerged as a novel class of materials designed to enhance clot formation and reduce internal bleeding. These nanoparticles are often engineered to mimic the natural coagulation process by interacting with activated platelets and fibrinogen at sites of vascular injury [13]. Preclinical studies have demonstrated the ability of hemostatic nanoparticles to reduce bleeding and improve survival in modles of hemorrhaagic shock, suggesting their potential applicability in trauma settings [14]. In addition to their hemostatic properties, nanoparticles provide a versatile platform for the targeted dellivery of therapeutic agents. Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanoparticles, in particular, have been widely studied due to their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and aility to encapsulate a wide range of drugs [15]. By encapsulating dexamethasone within PLGA-based hemostatic nanoparticles, it is possible to combine the benefits of hemostasis with localized anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects. Such an approach has the potential to mitigate both systemic and central nervous system (CNS) inflammation, thereby addressing two critical components of blast-induced polytrauma pathophysiology. ### Rationale for the Present Study The present study builds upon the foundational principles of nanoparticle-based hemostasis and targeted drug delivery to address the dual challenges of internal bleeding and bTBI in blast polytrauma. We hypothesize that the administration of PLGA-based hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs) immediately after blast exposure will improve survival, reduce neuropathological damage, and alleviate long-term behavioral deficits. The rationale for this approach is threefold: first, the hemostatic properties of the nanoparticles will address internal bleeding and prevent hypoxic damage; second, the localized delivery of dexamethasone will reduce inflammation and neuronal appotosis in the CNS without the systemic side effects associated with corticosteroids; and third, the combination of these effects will mitigate seconary injury mechanisms that contribute to chronic neuropsychiatric outcomes, such as anxiety and depression. ### Objectives and Scope The objectives of this study are to (1) evaluate the effects of hDNPs on survival in a rodent model of blast-induced polytrauma, (2) assess their impact on neuropathological outcomes, including apoptosis and BBB integrity, and (3) determine their efficacy in alleviating long-term behavioral deficits, with a focus on anxiety-like behaviors. By addressing these objectives, we aim to provide preclinical evidence supporting the translational potential of hDNPs as a dual-function therapeutic platform for blast-induced polytrauma. This study represents a significant step toward the development of targeted interventions that address the complex interplay between systemic and CNS pathologies in trauma. ### Refernces [1] Dewan, M. The global burden of traumatic brain injury (TBI) is staggering, with approximately 69 million new cases reported every year [1]. In the context of military operations, the incidence of blast-induced TBI (bTBI) has increased significantly due to the prevalent use of explosives in contemporary combat zones. A substantial proportion of combat-related injuries, approximately 79%, are attributed to blast exposure, with many cases involving multiple injuries, including primary blast injuries to the brain and lungs [2]. The pathophysiological mechanisms underlying bTBI are complex and multifaceted, involving rapid mechanical forces that disrupt cerebral structures, cause microvascular damage, and trigger a cascade of inflammatory, oxidative, and apoptotic responses [3]. Despite the prevalence and long-term functional consequences of bTBI, including cognitive and neuropsychiatric impairments, the therapeutic options available for its management are limited, emphasizing the urgent need for innovative interventions.

The pathophysiology of blast-induced polytrauma is multifaceted and can be categorized into four distinct classes: primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary injuries. Primary blast injuries result from the direct effects of the blast wave, which propagates through the body at supersonic velocities, inducing barotrauma and shearing forces in soft tissues [4]. The lungs and brain, due to their unique air-fluid interfaces and confinement within rigid structures, are particularly susceptible to primary blast injuries, including blast lung injury and bTBI [5]. Secondary injuries, on the other hand, are caused by shrapnel or debris propelled by the explosion, while tertiary injuries occur when the individual is displaced and collides with solid surfaces. Quaternary injuries encompass a range of other effects, including burns, asphyxiation, and exposure to toxic substances [6].

The brain's vulnerability to primary blast waves is attributed to both direct and indirect mechanisms. Direct effects involve the transmission of the pressure wave through the skull and soft tissues, resulting in neuronal and glial damage. Indirect effects, by contrast, involve systemic physiological responses, including hypoxemia, hypotension, and coagulopathy, which exacerbate cerebral ischemia and inflammation [7]. The frequent co-occurrence of blast lung injury with bTBI further contributes to systemic hypoxia and inflammatory cascades that amplify secondary brain injury [8]. Collectively, these injury mechanisms lead to both acute and chronic pathologies, including blood-brain barrier disruption, neuroinflammation, neuronal apoptosis, and long-term behavioral deficits, such as anxiety and depression [9].

The current limitations in treating blast-induced polytrauma are a significant concern. Despite advances in trauma care, the management of internal bleeding and bTBI remains a critical challenge. Hemorrhage is a leading cause of preventable death in trauma patients, and internal bleeding in blast polytrauma often necessitates invasive surgical interventions that may not be feasible in combat or remote environments [10]. Current interventions for hemorrhage control, such as tourniquets and hemostatic dressings, are effective primarily for external bleeding but have limited utility for internal hemorrhage [11]. Beyond fluid resuscitation and surgical hemostasis, there are no widely available pharmacological therapies to address internal bleeding in the acute phase of trauma. Similarly, therapeutic options for TBI, including bTBI, are limited to supportive care and symptom management. The complex and heterogeneous nature of TBI pathophysiology has hindered the development of targeted pharmacological interventions. While corticosteroids, such as dexamethasone, have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective potential in preclinical studies, their systemic side effects and lack of targeted delivery mechanisms have limited their clinical utility in TBI [12].

The lack of effective treatments for both internal bleeding and bTBI underscores the need for innovative therapeutic strategies that address the multifactorial nature of blast-induced polytrauma. Recent advances in nanotechnology have led to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for addressing the challenges associated with trauma care, particularly in the context of polytrauma. Hemostatic nanoparticles have emerged as a promising class of materials designed to enhance clot formation and reduce internal bleeding. These nanoparticles are often engineered to mimic the natural coagulation process by interacting with activated platelets and fibrinogen at sites of vascular injury [13]. Preclinical studies have demonstrated the ability of hemostatic nanoparticles to reduce bleeding and improve survival in models of hemorrhagic shock, suggesting their potential applicability in trauma settings [14]. In addition to their hemostatic properties, nanoparticles provide a versatile platform for the targeted delivery of therapeutic agents. Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanoparticles, in particular, have been widely studied due to their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and ability to encapsulate a wide range of drugs [15].

By encapsulating dexamethasone within PLGA-based hemostatic nanoparticles, it is possible to combine the benefits of hemostasis with localized anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects. Such an approach has the potential to mitigate both systemic and central nervous system (CNS) inflammation, thereby addressing two critical components of blast-induced polytrauma pathophysiology. This study aims to build upon the foundational principles of nanoparticle-based hemostasis and targeted drug delivery to address the dual challenges of internal bleeding and bTBI in blast polytrauma. We hypothesize that the administration of PLGA-based hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs) immediately after blast exposure will improve survival, reduce neuropathological damage, and alleviate long-term behavioral deficits. The rationale for this approach is threefold: first, the hemostatic properties of the nanoparticles can help to control internal bleeding, thereby reducing the risk of hemorrhagic shock and improving overall survival. Second, the localized delivery of dexamethasone can help to mitigate CNS inflammation and promote neuroprotection, thereby reducing the risk of long-term cognitive and neuropsychiatric impairments. Finally, the combination of hemostasis and neuroprotection can help to address the multifactorial nature of blast-induced polytrauma, thereby improving overall outcomes in affected individuals [1-15]. To investigate the effects of hDNPs on blast-induced polytrauma, we utilized a rodent model of primary blast-induced polytrauma. Male Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly assigned to one of three experimental groups: a sham group (uninjured, untreated), a control group (blast-injured, treated with vehicle), or an hDNPs group (blast-injured, treated with hemostatic dexamethasone nanoparticles). Each group consisted of 8-10 animals to ensure adequate statistical power for both survival and histological analyses. The hDNPs were synthesized using a double emulsion solvent evaporation method, and their physical and chemical properties were characterized using dynamic light scattering and high-performance liquid chromatography. The fabrication of hDNPs involved the emulsification of a dexamethasone solution in a poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) solution, followed by the formation of a double emulsion and solvent evaporation. The resulting nanoparticles were collected by centrifugation, washed, and lyophilized for storage. The encapsulation efficiency of dexamethasone was determined to be 78 ± 3%, and the average particle size and zeta potential were measured to be 240 ± 15 nm and −20 ± 5 mV, respectively.

To model primary blast-induced polytrauma, we employed a custom-built Advanced Blast Simulator (ABS) to generate a single blast wave. The ABS consisted of a compressed helium-driven shock tube with adjustable driven and driver sections, and the experimental parameters were calibrated to produce a peak overpressure of 200 kPa (±5%) with a positive phase duration of 3 milliseconds. Rats were anesthetized with isoflurane and positioned longitudinally within the blast tube, restrained in a prone position on a custom-designed platform to ensure uniform exposure to the blast wave. Sham animals underwent identical handling but were not exposed to the blast wave. Immediately following blast exposure, rats in the hDNPs group received an intravenous (IV) bolus injection of the nanoparticles (1 mg/kg dexamethasone equivalent) suspended in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Control group animals received an equivalent volume of PBS without nanoparticles. Sham animals received no injections. All injections were administered via the tail vein using a 27-gauge needle within 30 minutes post-blast. The dose of dexamethasone was selected based on prior studies demonstrating efficacy in reducing inflammation and neuroprotection in rodent models of traumatic brain injury [1, 2].

The efficacy of hDNPs in alleviating long-term behavioral deficits was assessed using the elevated plus maze (EPM) and open field test (OFT) to evaluate anxiety-like behavior at 7 and 14 days post-injury. The EPM is a well-established model of anxiety-like behavior in rodents, and it involves placing the animal in the center of a plus-shaped apparatus with two open and two enclosed arms elevated above the floor. The OFT is another commonly used model of anxiety-like behavior, and it involves placing the animal in a large, open arena and measuring its locomotor activity and exploratory behavior. By utilizing these behavioral models, we aim to gain a deeper understanding of the effects of hDNPs on anxiety-like behavior in a rodent model of blast-induced polytrauma.

Cancer is a highly complex and heterogeneous disease, characterized by a wide array of genetic and molecular alterations that drive tumor development, progression, and response to therapy. Advances in next-generation sequencing (NGS) and other high-throughput molecular profiling technologies have enabled the comprehensive characterization of thousands of cancer genomes, leading to the identification of numerous driver genes and pathways associated with speific tumor types. These large-scale efforts, such as those led by The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC), have provided invaluable insights into the molecular basis of cancer, revealing the intricate landscape of somatic mutations, copy number alterations, structural rearrangements, epigenetic modifications, and transcriptomic changes underlying tumorigenesis. However, while these population-based studies have significantly advanced our understanding of cancer biology, they highlight a critical challenge in the era of precision oncology: the interpretation of genomic alterations at the level of individual patients. The need for patient-centric approaches in cancer genomics arises from the inherent variability of tumors, even within the same histological subtype. Tumor genomes are shaped by a combination of factors, including the tissue of origin, environmental exposures, and the evolutionary dynamics of clonal selection. As a result, the repertoire of driver mutations and other clinically relevant alterations can vary widely between patients. In practice, this means that the actionable insights derived from cohort-level studies are not always directly transferable to inividual cases. For example, while certain alterations, such as mutations in TP53 or KRAS, are recurrent and well-studied across multiple tumor types, many patients harbor rarre or even unique mutations whose functional and clinical significance remains unclear. Furthermore, the interplay between genomic alterations and the tumor microenvironment adds an additional layer of complexity, influencing tumor behavior and therapeutic response. To address these challenges, there is an urgent need for tools and resources that can bridge the gap between population-level knowledge and patient-specific interpretation. Cancer PanorOmics is one such resource, designed to provdie a comprehensive and integrative molecular view of personal cancer genomes. By contextualizing the genomic alterations detected in an individual tumor within the broader body of scientific and clinical evidence, Cancer PanorOmics aims to facilitate the identification of actionable alterations and support clinical decision-making. The Cancer PanorOmics platform offers two complementary perspectives for analyzing personal cancer genomes: a cohort-centric view and a patient-centric view. The cohort-centric view leverages daa from large-scale studies to assess the prevalence and significance of genomic alterations across 26 tumor types, thus providing a benchmark against which individual findings can be evaluated. This perspective enables users to identify alterations that are known to be recurrent and potentially pathogenic in specific cancer types, as well as those that are rare or novel. The patient-centric view, on the other hand, focuses on the individual tumor, integrating genomic data with functional annotations, pathway analyses, and clinical evidence. This dual approach ensures that both the broader context and the unique characteristics of the tumor are taken into account during the interpretation process. One of the distinguishing features of Cancer PanorOmics is its ability to explore the cellular environment of mutations. Genomic alterations do not occur in isolation; their functional impact is oftne mediated by interactions with other molecules within the cellular network. To capture this complexity, Cancer PanormOics maps mutations onto the human interactome, a comprehensive representation of protein-protein and protein-DNA interactions. By examining the network-level context of mutations, the platform can identify potential downstream effects, such as dysregulation of signaling pathways or disruption of protein complexes. Additionally, whenever sttructural information is available, Cancer PanorOmics provvides quasi-atomic details of the mutations, offering insights into their effects on protein structure and function. This molecular-level analysis is particularly valuable for understanding the mechanisms of action of rare or poorly characterized alterations, as well as for identifying potential therapeutic targets. The ultimate goal of Cancer PanorOmics is to enaable precision oncology by facilitating the translation of genomic data into clinically actionable insights. Precision oncology relies on the ability to tailor treatment strategies to the specific molecular profiile of a patient’s tumor, a process that requires the integration of genomic, functional, and clinical data. By providing a holistic view of personal cancer genomes, Cancer PanorOmics can help to identify alterations that may predict sensitivity or resistance to specific therapies, guide the selection of targetd treatments, and inform the design of combination strategies. Importantly, the platform is intended to complement, rather than replace, the expertise of clinicians and genetic counselors, who play a critical role in interpreting genomic findings and integrating them into the broader context of patient care. In addition to its clinical applications, Cancer PanorOmics has the potential to advance cancer research by enabling the systematic study of rare and patient-specific alterations. While large-scale studies have primarily focused on recurrent events, rare mutations and other less common genomic features may hold important clues about cancer biology and therapeutic vulnerabilities. By aggregating and analyzing data from individual cases, Cancer PanorOmics can contribute to the discovery of novel drivers, pathways, and biomarkers, ultimately broadening the scope of therapeutic opportunities. Among these responses, neointimal hyperplasia—a proliferative process involving smooth muscle cells and extracellular matrix deposition—plays a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of restenosis and can be visualized using advanced imaging modalities. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) has emerged as a powerful intravascular imaging tool that allows for high-resolution visualization of stent struts and surrounding tissue. OCT enables detailed assessment of neointimal characteristics, including the morphology and intensity patterns of tissue around the stent struts. One specific finding detectable by OCT is the peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA), characterized by a low-intensity signal around the stent struts surrounded by higher-intensity neointimal tissue. This distinct imaging feature has garnered attention in recent years due to its potential association with underlying biological processes, such as inflammation, lipid accumulation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. However, the clinical implications of PLIA, including its genesis, risk factors, and impact on long-term prognosis, remain poorly understood. Several studies have investigated the morphological features of neointima following stent implantation, yet the specific factors associated with the development of PLIA are not well established. It is hypothesized that the presence of PLIA may reflect localized alterations in the vascular environment, possibly influenced by systemic factors such as lipid metabolism, inflammatory processes, or patient comorbidities. Notably, elevated levels of serum lipids, including triglycerides and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), are well-recognized contributors to atherosclerotic progression and may play a role in the genesis of PLIA. Similarly, a history of cerebrovascular disease—often accompanied by systemic vascular inflammation and endothelial dysfunction—may predispose patients to distinct patterns of neointimal response. The initial clinical presentation of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and the timing of OCT evaluation relative to stent implantation may also influence the prevalence and charatceristics of PLIA, reflecting the dynamic nature of vascular healing and remodeling over time. Despite its frequent occurrence, the prognostic significance of PLIA remains an area of active investigation. Previous studies have suggested that abnormal neointimal patterns observed by OCT, including PLIA, may be linked to addverse clinical outcomes such as restenosis or stent thrombosis. However, robust data on the long-term impact of PLIA on patient outcomes are lacking. In particular, whether PLIA is associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), including myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death, remains unclear. Furthermore, the potential relationship between PLIA and unstable angina (UA)—a clinical manifestation of myocardial ischemia—warrants further exploration, as understanding this link could proivde valuable insights into risk stratification and management strategies for patients undergoing stent implantation. To address these knowledge gaps, this study aimed to systematically evaluate the clinical characteristics, predictors, and long-term prognosis of PLIA as detected by OCT in patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). By prospectively analyzing a cohort of patients with documented neointimal hyperplasia on OCT reexamination, we sought to identify factors associated with the development of PLIA and assess its impact on subsequent clinical outcomes. Specifically, we examined the relationship between PLIA and key parameters such as serum lipid levels, history of cerebrovascular disease, initial presentation with ACS, and stent implantation time. Additionally, we evaluated the incidence of MACEs and UA during long-term follow-up to determine whether PLIA confers an increased risk of adverse clinical events. This study provides novel insights into the pathophysiological underpinnings of PLIA and its implications for patieent management following PCI. By elucidating the predictors and prognostic significance of this unique imaging feature, our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence aimed at optimizing the assessment and treatment of patients with CAD. Understanding the clinical relevance of PLIA may ultimately inform tailored theerapeutic approaches to improve outcomes in this high-risk population. This study was conducted as a prospective observational analysis to evaluate the clinical characteristics and prognostic implications of peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA) detected by optical coherence tomography (OCT) following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Patients were recruited from a single-center registry between January 2009 and December 2011 based on eligibility criteria outlined below. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Ethical approval for the study protocol was obtained from the institutional review board. Patients aged ≥18 years who had undergone successful PCI with stent implantation and demonstrated neointimal hyperplasia on routine follow-up OCT reexamination were included in the study. Exclusion criteria consisted of incomplete stent apposition, stent fracture, restenosis requiring revasccularization at the time of OCT reexamination, or poor-quality OCT images precluding detailed analysis. Patients with significant systemic inflammatory or autoimmune diseases, end-stage renal disease, or life expectancy less than one year were also excluded. Baseline demographic and clinical data, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), comorbid conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease), smoking status, medication history, and the initial clinical presentation (acute coonary syndrome [ACS] or stable angina), were colected at the time of index PCI. Serum levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) were measured during the index hospitalization. Procedural characteristics, including the type, size, and length of the stent as well as post-procedural angiographic findings, were also recorded. OCT reexaminations were performed at 6 to 12 months post-PCI using a frequency-domain OCT system (C7-XR, St. Jude Medical, St. Paul, MN, USA). Following intracoronary administration of nitroglycerin (100–200 µg), a 0.014-inch imaging catheter was positioned distal to the stented segment, and the vessel was flsuhed with contrast media at a rate of 3–5 mL/s to achieve blood clearance. Automated pullback at a speed of 20 mm/s was performed to acquire cross-sectional images of the stented segment at 100-µm intervals. OCT images were analyzed offline by two independent investigators blinded to clinical and procedural data. The pirmary parameter of interest was the peri-strut intensity pattern of the neointima. Using image analysis software (LightLab Imaging, St. Jude Medical), the intensity of the neointimal layer surrounding each stent strut was categorized as low-intensity (PLIA) or high-intensity baseed on signal attenuation characteristics. Neointimal thickness and stent coverage were also quantified. Patients were classified into two groups based on the presence or absence of PLIA. Comparative analyses of baseline demographic, clinical, and procedural characteristics were performed between the two groups to identify predictors of PLIA. Logistic regression models were used to evaluate the independent associations between clinical variables and the presece of PLIA. Variables with P < 0.10 in univariate analysis were included in multivariate models to adjust for potential confounders. Following OCT reexamination, patients who did not require immediate revascularization were enrolled in long-term follow-up. Clinical follow-up was conducted via outpatient visits or telephone interviews at least annually to assess the occurrence of adverse events. The primary outcome of interest was the inidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), defined as a composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, or target lesion revascularization. The secondary outcome was the incidence of unstable angina (UA), defined as new or worsening chest pain with evidence of myocardial ischemia but without myocardial infarction. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were constructed to evaluate the cumulative incidence of MACEs and UA during the follow-up period. A two-tailed P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. Interobserver agreement for OCT image interpreattion was assessed using the kappa statistic. Assuming an incidence of PLIA of approximately 15% and a relative hazard of 3.0 for UA in patients with PLIA, a minimum of 120 patients was required to achieve 80% power at a significance level of 0.05. Additionally, the prevalence of PLIA decreases with longger stent implantation time. The advent of stent implantation has revolutionized the field of interventional cardiology, offering a highly effective solution for the treatment of coronary artery disease (CAD) by facilitating the restoration of blood flow and mitigating the risk of myocardial ischemia. Over the course of several decades, the technological advancements in stent design, particularly the introduction of drug-eluting stents (DES), have led to a substantial decrease in the incidence of in-stent restenosis and other related complications when compared to the use of bare-metal stents [1]. Nevertheless, the long-term efficacy of stent implantation remains contingent upon the vascular environment's response to the stent, as well as the biological processes that ensue. One such process, neointimal hyperplasia, which involves the proliferation of smooth muscle cells and the deposition of extracellular matrix, plays a crucial role in the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying restenosis [2]. The visualization of this process is facilitated by advanced imaging modalities, such as optical coherence tomography (OCT), which has emerged as a powerful tool for intravascular imaging [3]. OCT enables the high-resolution visualization of stent struts and the surrounding tissue, thereby allowing for a detailed assessment of neointimal characteristics, including the morphology and intensity patterns of the tissue in the vicinity of the stent struts. A specific finding that can be detected using OCT is the peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA), which is characterized by a region of low signal intensity surrounding the stent struts, juxtaposed with neointimal tissue of higher intensity [4]. This distinctive imaging feature has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its potential association with various underlying biological processes, including inflammation, lipid accumulation, and extracellular matrix remodeling [5]. However, the clinical implications of PLIA, including its genesis, risk factors, and impact on long-term prognosis, remain poorly understood. While several studies have investigated the morphological features of neointima following stent implantation, the specific factors associated with the development of PLIA are not well established [6]. It is hypothesized that the presence of PLIA may reflect localized alterations in the vascular environment, potentially influenced by systemic factors such as lipid metabolism, inflammatory processes, or patient comorbidities [7]. Notably, elevated levels of serum lipids, including triglycerides and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), are well-recognized contributors to the progression of atherosclerosis and may play a role in the genesis of PLIA [8]. Similarly, a history of cerebrovascular disease, which is often accompanied by systemic vascular inflammation and endothelial dysfunction, may predispose patients to distinct patterns of neointimal response [9]. The initial clinical presentation of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and the timing of OCT evaluation relative to stent implantation may also influence the prevalence and characteristics of PLIA, reflecting the dynamic nature of vascular healing and remodeling over time [10]. Despite its frequent occurrence, the prognostic significance of PLIA remains an area of active investigation. Previous studies have suggested that abnormal neointimal patterns observed by OCT, including PLIA, may be linked to adverse clinical outcomes such as restenosis or stent thrombosis [11]. However, robust data on the long-term impact of PLIA on patient outcomes are lacking. In particular, whether PLIA is associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), including myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death, remains unclear [12]. Furthermore, the potential relationship between PLIA and unstable angina (UA), a clinical manifestation of myocardial ischemia, warrants further exploration, as understanding this link could provide valuable insights into risk stratification and management strategies for patients undergoing stent implantation [13]. To address these knowledge gaps, this study aimed to systematically evaluate the clinical characteristics, predictors, and long-term prognosis of PLIA as detected by OCT in patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Professional values are fundamental principles that guide nurses in providing ethical, high-quality, and patient-centered care. These values serrve as a cornerstnoe for decision-making, interactions with patients, and the overall practice of nursing. They are essential not only for safeguarding patients' rights and dignity but also for maintaining the integrity and credibility of the nursing profession. In today’s complex healthcare systems, where nurses face growing ethical challenges, the recognition and application of professional values have become increasingly critical. Nurses' perspectives on these values are particularly important, as they directly influence their clinical judgments, behaviors, and the quality of care they provide [1,2]. Professional values in nursing encompass a wide array of ethical principles, such as respecting patient autonomy, maintaining confidentiality, safeguarding privacy, and advocating for patients' rights. These valus also extend to broader professional responsibilities, including participation in nursing research, adherence to evidence-based practice, and involvement in shaping healthcare policies [3]. However, the extent to which individual nurses prioritize and apply these values in their daily practice can vary significantly based on personal, cultural, and organizational factors. Understanding the perspectives of clinical nurses regarding the importance of professional values is essential for identifying potential gaps in their knowledge and practice, as well as for designing effective educational interventions to address these gaps. Previous studies have highlighted the integral role that professional valus play in ensuring ethical and safe patient care. For instance, adherence to professional values has been linked to improved patient outcomes, enhanced trust between nurses and patients, and greater job satisfaction among nurses themselves [4]. Moreover, professional values provide nurses with a framework for navigating ethical dilemmas, which are increasingly prevalent in modern healthcare settings due to factors such as technological advancements, resource limitations, and diverse patient populations [5]. Despite the recognized importance of professional values, studies have also reported variations in the prioritization of thhese values among nurses, with some ethical principles receiving less attention than others [6]. Such variations underscore the need for a deeper exploration of nurses' perspectives to better understand the factors influencing their prioritization of professsional values. In the Iranian healthcare context, cultural and religious norms play a significant role in shaping nurses' ethical perspectives and practices. Islamic ethical principles, which emphasize compassion, justice, and respect for human dignity, align closely with the core values of the nursing profession [7]. However, the rapid evolution of healthcare systems in Iran, coupled with increasing ethical challenges, has highlighted the need for greater awareness and reinforcement of professional values among nurses. Studiees in Iran have shown that while nuses generally demonstrate a strong commitment to ethical principles, certain aspects of professional values, such as participation in research and policy-making, are often perceived as less important [8]. These findings point to potential areas for improvement in nursing education and professional development programs. This instrument encompasses a comprehensive range of ethical principles, enabling rsearchers to gain insights into how nurses prioritize different aspects of professional values in their practice [9]. The NPVS-R has been adaptd and validated in variosu cultural contexts, including Iran, where it has been translated into Persian to facilitate its use among Iranian nurses [10]. By employing this tool, researchers can identify not only the overall importance that nurses assign to professional values but also specific areas where further education or support is needed. The foundational principles of nursing practice are rooted in a distinct set of values that serve as the linchpin for delivering exceptional, patient-focused care. These values act as a lodestar, guiding nurses' interactions with patients and informing their decision-making processes, ultimately shaping the fabric of nursing practice. The importance of these values cannot be overstated, as they play a pivotal role in safeguarding patients' rights and dignity, while also maintaining the integrity and credibility of the nursing profession as a whole. In the contemporary healthcare landscape, where nurses are increasingly confronted with complex ethical challenges, the recognition and application of these values have become more critical than ever. The perspectives of nurses themselves are particularly salient in this regard, as they have a direct impact on clinical judgments, behaviors, and the quality of care provided to patients [1,2]. The spectrum of professional values in nursing is remarkably broad, encompassing a wide range of ethical principles, including the respect for patient autonomy, the maintenance of confidentiality, the safeguarding of privacy, and the advocacy for patients' rights. These values also extend to more expansive professional responsibilities, such as participation in nursing research, adherence to evidence-based practice, and involvement in shaping healthcare policies [3]. Nevertheless, the degree to which individual nurses prioritize and apply these values in their daily practice can vary significantly, influenced by a complex interplay of personal, cultural, and organizational factors. Gaining a deeper understanding of the perspectives of clinical nurses regarding the importance of professional values is crucial for identifying potential gaps in their knowledge and practice, as well as for designing effective educational interventions to address these gaps. A plethora of previous studies has consistently underscored the integral role that professional values play in ensuring ethical and safe patient care. For instance, adherence to professional values has been linked to improved patient outcomes, enhanced trust between nurses and patients, and greater job satisfaction among nurses themselves [4]. Furthermore, professional values provide nurses with a framework for navigating the ethical dilemmas that are increasingly prevalent in modern healthcare settings, due to factors such as technological advancements, resource limitations, and diverse patient populations [5]. Despite the recognized importance of professional values, studies have also reported variations in the prioritization of these values among nurses, with some ethical principles receiving less attention than others [6]. Such variations highlight the need for a more nuanced exploration of nurses' perspectives to better comprehend the factors influencing their prioritization of professional values. In the Iranian healthcare context, cultural and religious norms exert a significant influence on shaping nurses' ethical perspectives and practices. Islamic ethical principles, which emphasize compassion, justice, and respect for human dignity, align closely with the core values of the nursing profession [7]. However, the rapid evolution of healthcare systems in Iran, coupled with increasing ethical challenges, has underscored the need for greater awareness and reinforcement of professional values among nurses. Studies conducted in Iran have demonstrated that while nurses generally exhibit a strong commitment to ethical principles, certain aspects of professional values, such as participation in research and policy-making, are often perceived as less important [8]. These findings point to potential areas for improvement in nursing education and professional development programs. The Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R), developed by Weis and Schank, is a widely utilized tool for assessing nurses' perspectives on professional values. This instrument encompasses a comprehensive range of ethical principles, enabling researchers to gain insights into how nurses prioritize different aspects of professional values in their practice [9]. The NPVS-R has been adapted and validated in various cultural contexts, including Iran, where it has been translated into Persian to facilitate its use among Iranian nurses [10]. By employing this tool, researchers can identify not only the overall importance that nurses assign to professional values but also specific areas where further education or support is needed. The present study seeks to investigate the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses working in educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences in Iran. Given the critical role that nurses play in the delivery of healthcare services, understanding their views on professional values is essential for informing strategies to enhance ethical practice and patient care quality. While previous research has provided valuable insights into nurses' adherence to professional values, most studies have focused on specific ethical principles or have been conducted in limited geographical settings. This study aims to build upon existing knowledge by providing a comprehensive assessment of professional values as perceived by clinical nurses in a diverse range of hospital settings. In addition to exploring the overall importance of professional values, this study examines the relationship between nurses' perspectives and demographic factors such as age, work experience, and participation in professional ethical training programs. Previous research has suggested that these factors may influence nurses' ethical attitudes and behaviors [11,12]. For example, older nurses or those with more years of experience may place greater emphasis on certain professional values due to their increased exposure to complex patient care scenarios and their heightened awareness of the importance of ethical decision-making. Conversely, younger nurses or those with less experience may require additional support and education to develop a deeper understanding of professional values and their application in practice. By investigating the relationships between these demographic factors and nurses' perspectives on professional values, this study aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of the complex factors that influence nurses' ethical attitudes and behaviors. Ultimately, this knowledge can inform the development of targeted educational interventions and professional development programs designed to enhance nurses' understanding and application of professional values, thereby improving the quality of patient care and promoting a stronger, more ethical nursing profession. To achieve this objective, the present study employed a cross-sectional design to evaluate the importance of professional values from the perspective of clinical nurses working in educational hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences, Iran. Conducted in 2016, the study adhered to the ethical principles of research, including obtaining informed consent from all participants and maintaining the confidentiality of their data, in accordance with established guidelines [1]. The target population comprised all clinical nurses employed in the four educational hospitals of Kerman University of Medical Sciences, chosen for their dual role in providing educational and clinical services, thereby offering a comprehensive setting for studying nurses' professional values. Inclusion criteria stipulated that participants must have had a minimum of one year of clinical experience and be actively engaged in direct patient care during the study period. To ensure the relevance of the data to clinical practice, nurses who were on leave or engaged in administrative roles without regular clinical responsibilities were excluded from the study. The sample size was calculated using Cochran's formula for cross-sectional studies, assuming a 95% confidence level and a margin of error of 5%, as recommended in similar studies [1]. Based on an expected standard deviation of scores derived from analogous investigations, the required sample size was determined to be 250 participants. To ensure adequate representation of nurses from all four hospitals, stratified random sampling was employed, with each hospital considered a stratum. The proportion of nurses sampled from each hospital was proportional to its total number of clinical nurses. Within each stratum, participants were randomly selected using a table of random numbers, thereby minimizing bias and ensuring the generalizability of the findings. Data collection was conducted using the Persian version of the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R), originally developed by Weis and Schank [2]. This instrument has been widely utilized to assess nurses' perceptions of professional values and consists of 26 items distributed across five dimensions: caring, activism, trust, professionalism, and justice. Each item is rated on a five-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (not important) to 5 (very important), thereby providing a nuanced understanding of nurses' perspectives on professional values. The NPVS-R has been validated in various contexts, demonstrating its reliability and validity in assessing professional values among nurses. The use of this instrument in the present study enables the comparison of findings with those of previous investigations, contributing to the development of a comprehensive understanding of professional values in nursing. To investigate this phenomenon, the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R) was utilized, which comprises a comprehensive set of items that are rated on a scale of 1 to 5, with higher scores denoting greater importance attributed to professional values [2]. The NPVS-R has consistently demonstrated robust reliability and validity in preceding research [3, 4], and its Persian adaptation was validated by experts, exhibiting excellent internal consistency in a pilot study involving 30 nurses, as evidenced by a Cronbach's alpha coefficient of 0.89.

Prior to initiating the data collection process, ethical approval was secured from the Research Ethics Committee of Kerman University of Medical Sciences, with the assigned Ethics Code being IR.KMU.REC.1395.123. Participants provided written informed consent, which ensured the confidentiality and anonymity of their responses, and were informed that their participation was entirely voluntary, with the option to withdraw from the study at any time without facing any repercussions. Trained research assistants distributed the NPVS-R questionnaires to participants in person during their work shifts, providing a concise explanation of the study's objectives and instructions for completing the questionnaire.

To minimize potential response bias, participants were encouraged to complete the questionnaires individually and return them in sealed envelopes to designated drop boxes located in each hospital ward. The data collection process spanned two months, ensuring sufficient time for all selected nurses to participate. Demographic information, including age, gender, level of education, years of work experience, and history of participation in professional ethical training programs, was collected using a separate form. This information was utilized to explore potential associations between demographic variables and the importance of professional values as perceived by the nurses.

Data analysis was conducted using SPSS software version 21, with descriptive statistics, including means, standard deviations, frequencies, and percentages, employed to summarize the demographic characteristics of the participants and their responses to the NPVS-R items. To identify the most and least important professional values from the nurses' perspective, the mean scores for each item were calculated and ranked. Inferential statistical analyses, including independent t-tests and one-way ANOVA, were performed to examine differences in NPVS-R scores based on demographic variables such as age, work experience, and participation in ethical training programs. Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to examine the relationship between demographic variables and NPVS-R scores.

Cohesin, a multisubunit protein complex, plays a central role in maintaining genomic integrity by mediating sister chromatid cohesion, DNA condensation, and repair. Central to cohesin’s function is its ability to tether two DNA molecules, a process that is essential for accurate chromosome segregation during mitosis and meiosis. The established model posits that a single cohesin complex encircles sister chromatids, forming a physical link that resists the pulling forces of the spindle apparatus. However, emerging evidence suggests that the molecular mechanisms underlying cohesin function may be more complex than previously appreciated, with multiple cohesin complexes potentially interacting to execute their biological roles. Understanding how cohesin complexes cooperate or interact on DNA is crucial for elucidating the molecular basis of cohesion and condensation and for defining how defects in these processes contribute to genomic instability and disease. Cohesin’s core structure is composed of four subunits: Smc1, Smc3, Scc1 (also called Rad21 or Mcd1 in yeast), and Scc3 (SA1/SA2 in vertebrates). Smc1 and Smc3 are members of the structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) protein family, and together, they form a V-shaped heterodimer via their coiled-coil arms and hinge domains. The Scc1 protein connects the ATPase head domains of Smc1 and Smc3, forming a tripartite ring that topologically entraps DNA. Scc3 serves as a regulatory subunit, interacting with Scc1 and other cohesin-associated factors to modulate cohesin’s activity. The cohesin complex is loaded onto chromosomes during the S phase of the cell cycle, and its association with DNA is tightly regulated by a network of accessory proteins and post-translational modifications, including acetylation of Smc3 and phosphorylation of Scc1. Despite significant progress in elucidating cohesin’s composition and basic mechanisms, fundamental questions remain about how cohesin complexes work together to achieve their diverse biological functions. Interallelic complementation is a genetic phenomenon in which two different mutant alleles of a gene, each of which is defective on its own, can restore function when expressed together in the same cell. Thsi phenomenon is typically observed in proteins that form multimers or interact in a cooperative manner. In the context of cohesin, interallelic complementation has the potential to reveal novel functional interactions between cohesin complexes on DNA. While a single cohesin complex is sufficient to mediate sister chromatid cohsion in simple models, the possibility that cohesin complexes cooperate or interact in a more dynamic and coordinated manner has been hinted at in several studies. For example, cohesin has been shown to cluster at specific chromosomal loci, such as centromeres and sites of double-strand breaks, raising the intriguing possibility that these clusters represent functional assemblies of multiple cohesin complexes. However, direct evidence for cohesin-cohesin interactions and their functional significance has been lacking. In this study, we provide functional evidence for cohesin-cohesin interactions on chromatin through the identification and characterization of inerallelic complementation events involving cohesin mutants. We describe three distinct examples in which two different mutant cohesin complexes, each harboring a unique defect, can interact to reestore cohesin function. These finings challenge the prevailing view of cohesin as a solitary actor on chromatin and instead support a model in which multiple cohesin complexes interact physically or functionally to mediate sister chroatid cohesion and higher-order chromatin organization. By combining genetic, biochemical, and cell biological approaches, we demonstrate that these interactions are not random but reflect specific and functionally significant cooperativity between cohsein complexes. Our results have important implications for understanding the mechanisms of cohesin function and regulation. The ability of cohesin mutants to complement each other suggests that cohesin complexes may form higher-order assemblies on DNA, potentially through direct physical interactions or via bridging factors. Such assemblies might enhance the robustness of sister chromatid cohesion, particularly in regions of the genome that are subjected to high mechanical stress or require precise spatial organization. Furthermore, our findings raise the possibility that defects in cohesin function assoociated with human diseases, suh as cohesinopathies and certaiin cancers, might involve disruptions in cohesin-cohesin interactions. Interallelic complementation could thus provide a framework for exploring therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring cohesin function in these contexts. In addition to shedding light on cohesin biology, our study underscores the utility of interallelic complementation as a tool for probing protein-protein interactions and functional cooperativity in other macromolecular complexes. The approach we employed—systematically combinng different cohesin mutants and assessing their capacity to restore function—could be extended to other systems to uncover novel mechanisms of protein interaction and regulation. Finally, the possibility that cohesin operates as part of a dynamic, multicomplex network raises exciting questions about how suuch networks are assembled, maintained, and disassembled during the cell cycle and in response to cellular signals. In summary, this work chlalenges the traditional view of cohesin as a single, self-sufficient moleecular ring and provides compelling evidence for functional interactions between cohesin complexes on DNA. By leveraging interallelic complementation as a genetic tool, we demonstrate that cohesin-cohesin interactions are critical for mediating sister chromatid cohesion and condensation. These findings open new avenues for investigating the molecular mechanisms of cohesin function and their relevance to human health and disease.
