The investigation of the effects of serum amyloid P-component (SAP) on cellular processes is a vital area of research, particularly in the context of understanding its role in various diseases. To this end, our study aimed to explore the impact of SAP on cholesterol efflux and gene expression in RAW264.7 cells, a murine macrophage cell line commonly used as a model for studying inflammatory responses and lipid metabolism. The cells were cultured at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂, conditions that are optimal for their growth and survival. Prior to treatment, the cells were seeded in 6-well plates at a density of 1 × 10⁶ cells per well and allowed to adhere overnight, ensuring that they were properly attached and viable for the subsequent experiments. SAP, which was prepared as a stock solution in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and diluted to the desired concentrations in complete DMEM, was used to treat the cells. The treatment concentrations of SAP (5 µg/mL, 10 µg/mL, and 20 µg/mL) and the incubation times (24, 48, or 72 hours) were varied according to the experimental design, allowing us to assess the dose- and time-dependent effects of SAP on the cells. Untreated cells served as the control group, providing a baseline for comparison. One of the key aspects of our study was the assessment of the effect of SAP on cholesterol efflux, a process that is critical for maintaining cholesterol homeostasis in the body. To achieve this, we employed a cholesterol efflux assay, where RAW264.7 cells were labeled with 1 µCi/mL [³H]-cholesterol in DMEM containing 2% FBS for 24 hours. After labeling, the cells were equilibrated in serum-free DMEM for 6 hours and subsequently treated with SAP (10 µg/mL) or vehicle control for 24 hours. ApoA-I-mediated cholesterol efflux was initiated by adding 10 µg/mL human apoA-I to the culture medium for 4 hours. The supernatants were collected, and radioactivity was measured using a liquid scintillation counter, while cellular radioactivity was determined after solubilizing the remaining cells with 0.1% SDS. Cholesterol efflux was calculated as the percentage of [³H]-cholesterol released into the medium relative to the total [³H]-cholesterol (medium + cells).

In addition to the cholesterol efflux assay, we also performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to investigate the effects of SAP on gene expression in RAW264.7 cells. Total RNA was extracted from cells treated with SAP (10 µg/mL for 24 hours) or vehicle control using the RNeasy Mini Kit, and the quality and concentration of the RNA were assessed using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer and NanoDrop spectrophotometer. Samples with an RNA integrity number (RIN) ≥ 8 were used for RNA-seq, ensuring that the RNA was of high quality and suitable for sequencing. Library preparation was performed using the TruSeq Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit, and the libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform to generate 150 bp paired-end reads. The raw RNA-seq data were processed using FastQC for quality control and trimmed with Trimmomatic to remove low-quality reads and adapter sequences. Clean reads were aligned to the mouse reference genome (GRCm39) using HISAT2 [1], and gene-level read counts were quantified using featureCounts [2]. Differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 [3] in the R statistical environment, and genes with an adjusted p-value < 0.05 were considered differentially expressed. Probability distributions are fundamental to numerous domains in machine learning and statistics, serving as a mathematical framework to model uncertainty, represent data, and describe complex systems. Measuring the similarity or disrepancy between two probability distributions is a key operation in many applications, including generative modeling, domain adaptation, clustering, and statistical hypothesis testing. Among the various measures of distributional discrepancy, optimal transport (OT) distances, particularly the Wasserstein distance, have gained significant attention in recent years due to their interpretability, solid theoretical foundation, and promising empirical performance in a vareity of tasks. The Wasserstein distace fundamentally differs from other popular divergence measures, such as the Kullback-Leibler divergence or total variation distance, in its ability to incorporate the geometry of the underlying data space into the computation. By considering the cost of transporting mass between distributions, the Wasserstein distance can capture meaningful structural differences in data, making it particularly advantageous in contexts where the support of distributions is non-overlapping, as is often the case in high-dimensional data. These proerties have made Wasserstein distances a natural choice in tasks such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) [1], domain adaptation [2], and distributional clustering [3]. However, the computational burden associated with calculating the Wasserstein distance has historically limited its scalability and applicability in large-scale machiine learning problems. Solving the OT problem in its primal form involves solving a linear program, the complexity of which growws superlinearly with the number of data points. Recent advances have focused on alleviating this computational bottleneck, with techniques such as entropic regularization [4], sliced Wsaserstein distances [5], and approximations based on dual formulations [6]. Among these, the sliced Wasserstein distance has emerged as an attractive alternative due to its simplicity, computational efficiency, and ability to scale to high-dimensional problems. By projecting distributions onto one-dimensional subspaces and computing the Wasserstein distance in this reduced space, the sliced Wasserstein distance significantly simplifies the problem while retaining many of the desirable properties of the full Wasserstein distance. In parallel, kernel methods have long stood as a cornerstone of machine learning, providing a principled framework for learning in high-dimensional feature spaces. By implicitly mapping data into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) through a positive definite kernel function, kernel methods enable the application of linear algorithms to inherently nonlinear problems. Classic examples include support vector machines, kernle principal component analysis, and Gaussian process regression. The power of kernel methods lies in their ability to leverage the structure of data through carefully designed keernel functions, which encode prior knowledge about the problem and influence the geometry of the RKHS. Despite their success, the design of kernels that effectively capture the relationships between probability distributions remains an open challenge. Motivated by the complementary strengths of optimal transport and kernel methods, recent work has sought to integrate the two frameworks to develop kernels tailored to probability distributions. Existing approaches include the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) [7], which uses characteristic kernels to measure distributional similarity, and Wasserstein kernels [8], which directly leverage optimal transport distances as a basis for kernel design. While these methods have shown promise, they often face limitations in terms of computational efficiency or theoretical guarantees of positive definiteness, which are essential for ensuring the vaalidity of kernel-based algorithms. In this paper, we propose a novel family of kernels for probability distributions based on the sliced Wasserstein distance. By harnessing the computational efficiency of the slicing approach, we construct kernels thaat are both scalable and theoretically grounded. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: (i) we introduce a family of positive definite kernels derived from the sliced Wasserstein distance, and provide theoretical analysis to ensure their validity; (ii) we demonstrate how these kernels can be integrated into existing machine learning frameworks to address a variety of tasks, including classification, clustering, and generative modeling; and (iii) we empirically evaluate the proposed kernels on benchmark datasets, highlighting their advantages over existing distributional kernels in terms of both performance and scalability. The proposeed approach builds on the observation that the sliced Wasserstein distance, as a projection-based approximation of the Wasserstein distance, preserves much of its geometric richness while significantly reducing computational complexity. By designing kernels that leverage this distance, we aim to provide a practical and theoretically sound tool for learning with probability distributions. Furthermore, we establish the positive definiteness of our kernels, a property taht ensures compatibility with a wide range of kernel-based algorithms and facilitates their application in diverse learning scenarios. Our work is inspired by reent trends in machine learning that emphasize the importance of integrating geometric and statistical perspectives into algorithm design. By bridging the gap between optimal trransport theory and kernel methods, we contribute to a growing body of literature thhat seeks to advance the state of the art in learning with distributions. Notably, our approach aligns wtih efforts to make optimal transport-based methods more accessible and applicable to real-world problems, addressing critical challenges related to scalability and computational efficiency. The characterization of uncertainty and the representation of complex systems are fundamental aspects of various fields, including machine learning and statistics, where probability distributions play a pivotal role. A key challenge in these domains is the comparison of two probability distributions, which is essential in applications such as generative modeling, domain adaptation, clustering, and statistical hypothesis testing. Among the array of methods used to measure the similarity or discrepancy between distributions, optimal transport distances, particularly the Wasserstein distance, have gained considerable attention in recent years due to their intuitive interpretability, robust theoretical underpinnings, and impressive performance in a wide range of tasks [1-3]. What distinguishes the Wasserstein distance from other popular measures, such as the Kullback-Leibler divergence and total variation distance, is its unique ability to factor in the geometric properties of the underlying data space, thereby allowing it to capture meaningful structural differences between datasets. This capability is particularly advantageous in scenarios where the support of the distributions does not overlap, a common occurrence in high-dimensional data. The distinctive properties of Wasserstein distances have made them a preferred choice in tasks such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) [1], domain adaptation [2], and distributional clustering [3]. However, the computational cost associated with calculating the Wasserstein distance has historically been a significant barrier to its widespread adoption in large-scale machine learning problems. The solution to the optimal transport problem in its original form requires solving a linear program, whose complexity increases rapidly with the size of the dataset. Recent research has focused on mitigating this computational bottleneck, with strategies such as entropic regularization [4], sliced Wasserstein distances [5], and approximations based on dual formulations [6] being explored. Among these, the sliced Wasserstein distance has emerged as a particularly appealing alternative due to its straightforward implementation, computational efficiency, and ability to handle high-dimensional problems with ease. By projecting distributions onto lower-dimensional subspaces and calculating the Wasserstein distance within this reduced space, the sliced Wasserstein distance achieves a significant simplification of the problem while preserving many of the desirable attributes of the full Wasserstein distance. In a related development, kernel methods have long been a cornerstone of machine learning, providing a systematic framework for learning in high-dimensional feature spaces. By implicitly mapping data into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) via a positive definite kernel function, kernel methods facilitate the application of linear algorithms to inherently nonlinear problems. Classic examples include support vector machines, kernel principal component analysis, and Gaussian process regression. The strength of kernel methods lies in their capacity to exploit the structure of data through carefully designed kernel functions, which encode prior knowledge about the problem and influence the geometry of the RKHS. Despite their success, designing kernels that effectively capture the relationships between probability distributions remains a challenging open problem. Motivated by the complementary strengths of optimal transport and kernel methods, recent studies have sought to combine these frameworks to develop kernels specifically tailored to probability distributions. Existing approaches include the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) [7], which utilizes characteristic kernels to measure distributional similarity, and Wasserstein kernels [8], which directly leverage optimal transport distances as a basis for kernel design. While these methods have shown promise, they often face limitations in terms of computational efficiency or theoretical guarantees of positive definiteness, which are crucial for ensuring the validity of kernel-based algorithms. The advent of advanced networking and communication technologies has profoundly transformed the manner in which devices interact, leading to the emergence of the Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm. A vital constituent of IoT architectures is the utilization of Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs), which comprise a spatially dispersed array of sensor nodes that monitor and gather data from their surroundings [1]. The convergence of IoT and WSNs has resulted in the development of a hybrid model, referred to as WSNIT (Wireless Sensor Network with Internet of Things), which facilitates dynamic connectivity between sensor nodes and external networks via the Internet [2]. This convergence has considerably expanded the range of applications for WSNs, encompassing critical domains such as healthcare monitoring, environmental surveillance, and industrial process automation [3]. Nevertheless, the deployment of WSNIT introduces significant security challenges that must be addressed to safeguard the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data within these systems. One of the primary security concerns in WSNIT pertains to the vulnerability of sensor nodes, which are typically characterized by limited computational capacity, memory, and energy resources [4]. Furthermore, these nodes frequently operate in hostile or untrusted environments, rendering them susceptible to physical compromise and tampering [5]. This situation is exacerbated by the reliance on insecure communication channels, as sensor nodes typically transmit sensitive data, including patient health information, environmental conditions, or industrial metrics, over the Internet [6]. This confluence of factors creates a favorable environment for adversaries to launch various types of attacks, including eavesdropping, data tampering, and unauthorized access, thereby threatening the security of WSNIT systems [7]. To mitigate these challenges, researchers have focused on designing lightweight and efficient authentication and access control mechanisms tailored to the unique constraints of WSNs. Among the existing solutions, attribute-based encryption (ABE) has garnered significant attention for its capacity to enable fine-grained access control in resource-constrained environments [8]. ABE facilitates the encryption of data based on a set of attributes, ensuring that only users possessing the requisite attributes can decrypt and access the data [9]. This attribute-based approach is particularly well-suited for WSNIT, where multiple users with varying levels of access privileges need to interact with the system [10]. In recent years, several authentication and access control schemes leveraging ABE have been proposed to secure WSNIT [11]. The authors claim that their proposed framework offers robust security against various types of attacks, including replay attacks, impersonation attacks, and unauthorized access [13]. Moreover, the utilization of ECC ensures that the scheme remains computationally efficient, rendering it suitable for resource-constrained sensor nodes [14]. In a node capture attack, an adversary physically captures and compromises a sensor node to extract sensitive information, such as cryptographic keys, which can then be used to launch further attacks on the network [20]. Moreover, we highlighted several inconsistencies and design flaws in the Santanu et al. scheme that hinder its practical deployment and protocol execution [21]. In response to the identified vulnerabilities and inconsistencies, we devised a set of potential countermeasures aimed at bolstering the security of the Santanu et al. scheme. These countermeasures were conceptualized to address specific weaknesses while preserving the protocol's lightweight character, leveraging cutting-edge cryptographic methodologies and best practices in WSN security to achieve an optimal balance between security and efficiency [12]. The proposed countermeasures were designed to mitigate the identified vulnerabilities, thereby enhancing the overall security posture of the scheme without compromising its performance in resource-constrained environments. 

The final stage of our methodology involved the validation of the identified vulnerabilities and proposed countermeasures through a combination of simulation and comparative analysis. To this end, the Santanu et al. scheme was implemented within a simulated WSN environment utilizing a widely recognized network simulator [13]. The simulation encompassed scenarios both with and without the integration of the proposed countermeasures, with the objective of demonstrating their efficacy. Furthermore, the modified scheme was benchmarked against other contemporary authentication frameworks for WSNs to provide a nuanced understanding of its relative strengths and weaknesses [14]. By adopting this holistic approach, we were able to conduct a rigorous evaluation of the Santanu et al. scheme, expose its vulnerabilities, and propose meaningful enhancements to improve its security and functionality. The insights gleaned from our analysis and the proposed countermeasures are of paramount importance for the development of more secure and resilient WSN-based Information Technology (WSNIT) systems and are elaborated upon in subsequent sections of this paper.

This, in turn, will contribute significantly to the broader effort to secure WSNIT systems, enabling them to fulfill their promise of enhancing various aspects of our lives through improved monitoring, automation, and decision-making capabilities. In conclusion, our research highlights the critical importance of thorough security analysis and performance evaluation in the development of authentication frameworks for WSNs. The findings of our study underscore the need for continuous scrutiny and improvement of existing security protocols to ensure they remain effective against evolving threats. By shedding light on the vulnerabilities of the Santanu et al. scheme and proposing countermeasures, we aim to contribute to the ongoing discourse on WSN security and encourage further research into the development of more secure, efficient, and resilient authentication solutions for WSNIT systems.

The chemical composition of tomatoes, particularly their phytochemical constituents, plays a critical role in determining their quality, flavor, and health-promoting properties, wich include significant levels of vitamins, carotenoids, phenolic compounds, and other bioactive metabolites [1]. These properties are influenced by a multitude of factors, including the genetic bacckground of the cultivar, agricultural practices, and environmental conditions. Accurate characterization and authentication of tomato cultivars, therefore, require robust and reliable analytical approaches capable of capturing the complexity of these factors. Traditional methods for tomato characterization have relied exetnsively on morphological traits or proximate compositional analysis. However, suh approaches are oftne insufficient to capture the subtle, cultivar-specific variations in phytochemical profiles. This limitation is particularly pronounced when attempting to authenticate tomatoes baesd on their geographical origin or prooduction system, as these factors often lead to overlapping chemical signatures. In recent years, advances in analytical chemistry have enabled the profiling of secondary metabolites, such as phenolic acids, flavonoids, carotenoids, and organic acids, which hold promise as bimarkers for cultivar identification and authentication [2]. Consequently, the identiification of relevant phytochemical constituents has emerged as a critical area of research, aiming to link chemical profiles to specific tomato cultivars, agricultural practices, and harvest conditions. Multivariate statistical techniques, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Factor Analysis (FA), and Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA), have been widely employed to interpret complex datasets associated with phytochemical profiling. These techniques are often used to reduce dimensionality and identify patterns in large datasets by transforming the original variables into a smaller set of latent variables. While these methods provide valuable insights into the overall structure of the data, they may not always allow for the direct interpretation of individual chemical parameters, as latent variables can be difficult to relate back to specific phytochemical constituents [3]. Moreover, PCA and related methods rely on linear assumptions, which may not fully capture the non-linear relationships inherent in multivariate daasets of phytochemical profiles. To address these limitations, alternative approaches that can directly identify and interpret individual variables in the dataset are increasingly being explored. One such method is Automatic Interaction Detection (AID), a decision tree-based algorithm capable of partitioning data into subsets based on the most relevant predictors. AID is particularly well-suited for hierarchical data structures and can provide intuitive, interpretale results that relate directly to individual variables. General Linear Models (GLM) have also been combined with AID (GLM-AID) to enhance the algorithm’s ability to model both main effects and interactions among predictors [4]. This hybid approach offers a flexible framework for identifying key phytochemical constituents that vary across multiple factors, such as cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date. In parallel, Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have emerged as a powerful tool in the field of chemometrics, owing to their ability to model complex, non-linear relationships in high-dimensional datasets. ANNs are inspired by the architecture of biological neural systems and consist of interconnected layers of nodes that process information through weighted connections. These models are particularly advantageous for handling datasets with intriate variable interdependencies and have been successfully applied in food authentication, quality control, and othr areas of agricultural research [5]. By training ANN models on phytochemical data, it is possible to predict categorical outcomes (such as cultivar, agricultural practice, or harvest date) with high accuracy, while simultaneously identifying the key variables that contribute to these predictions. Despite their potential, the application of GLM-AID and ANN models to tomato phytochemical data has bene limited. Previous studies have predominantly focused on using conventional statistical methods for tomato characterization, with limited exploration of advanced machine learning techniques. Furthermore, most research has concentrated on single factors, such as cultivar, without considering the complex interactions among multiple factors that influence phytochemical composition. Thiis study aims to address these gaps by employing GLM-AID and ANN models to identify the most relevant phytochemical constituents for the characterization and authentication of tomatoes. By leveraging these advanced analytical tools, the study seeks to provide new insights into the relationships between chemical composition and key factors such as cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date. The dataset used in this study consists of 25 chemical parameters measured in 167 tomato samples from Tenerife (Spain). These samples represent a diverse range of cultivars, agricultural practices (e.g., conventional versus organic), and harvest dates, providing a comprehensive basis for evaluating the performance of GLM-AID and ANN models. The GLM-AID approach organizes the data into a hierarchical structure, enabling the identification of key phytochemical constituents at different levesl of factor interaction. For instance, p-coumaric acid was identified as a critical compound for distinguishing samples based on harvest date, while multiple phytochemical parameters were required to differentiate samples by agricultural practice and cultivar. Similarly, ANN models were developed to predict cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date using both the full set of 25 input variables and a reduced set of 10 variables, allowing for a comparative assessment of moddel complexity and predictive performance. The findings of this study underscore the utility of GLM-AID and ANN models as complementary tools for tomato characterization. While the GLM-AID approach provides interpretable decision rules based on individual variables, ANN models offer enhanced predictive accuracy by capturing non-linear relationships in the data. Together, these methods represent a significant advancement over traditional multivariate techniques, enabling more precise identification of the key phytochmical constituetns that define tomato quality and authenticity. In summary, the application of GLM-AID and ANN models to tomato phytochemical data provides a robut framework for addressing the challenges associated with cultivar characterization and authentication. By integrating these advanced analytical tools, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of the chemical underpinnings of tomato quality and highlights the potential of machine learning techniques in agricultural and food research. The results not only have implications for the scientific understanding of tomato phytochemistry but also hold practical value for producers, consumers, and regulatory authorities seeking to ensure the authenticity and quality of tomato products. ### Methods #### 1. Sample Collection and Preparation A total of 167 tomato samlpes were collected from Tenerife, Spain. The sampls represented a diverse range of cultivars and were harvested under varying agricultural practices across different harvest dates. Each sample was assigned to one of three factors: cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date. In order to ensure consistency and minimize variabilitty unrelated to the study objectives, the samples wre transported under controlled temperature conditions (4°C) and processed within 24 hours of collection. Prior to chemical analysis, the tomato samples were washed with deionized water, air-dried, and homogenized usiing a food-grade stainless steel blender. The homogenized samples were aliquoted and stored at −80°C until further analysis to preserve their phytochemical composition. #### 2. Chemical Analysis Twenty-five chemical parameters were selected for analysis based on their relevance to the characterization and authentication of tomatoes, as determined form prior studies [1, 2]. These included primary metabolites such as sugars and organic acids, as well as secondary metabolites such as phenolics and carotenoids. The chemical composition of the tomato samples was quantified using validated analytical techniques as follows: 1. **Sugars and Organic Acids**: High-Performance Liquid Chromatography with Refractive Index Detection (HPLC-RID) was employed for the quantification of sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose) and organic acids (citric acid, malic acid). Samples were prepared by extracting 2 g of homogenized tomato in 20 mL of a water-methanol (1:1) solution, followed by centrifugation at 10,000×g for 10 minutes [3]. 2. **Phenolic Compounds**: Individual phenolic compounds, including p-coumaric acid, chlorogenic acid, and rutin, were analyzed using HPLC with a Photodiode Array Detector (HPLC-PDA). The phenolic compounds were extracted from the tomato matrix using a 70% methanol solution containing 0.5% formic acid, followed by solid-phase extraction [4]. 3. **Carotenoids**: Lycopene and β-carotene were quantified using Reverse-Phase HPLC coupled with PDA detection. Extraction was carried out under subdued light to prevent compound degradation, using a mixture of hexane, acetone, and ethanol (2:1:1) [5]. The data obtained for these 25 chemical paraameters across all 167 tomato samples were expressed in mg/kg fresh weight for further statistical analysis. #### 3. Statistical Analysis ##### 3.1 General Linear Model Linked to Automatic Interaction Detection (GLM-AID) The General Linear Model (GLM) linked to the Automatic Interaction Detection (AID) algorithm was applied to identify the most relevant chemical parameters for differentiating tomato samples based on the three factors: cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date. The AID algorithm constructs a tree-structured modeel by splitting the dataset at each level using the chemical parameter that maximizes the between-group variance while minimizing the within-group variance [6]. The GLM-AID analysis was performed using SPSS 26.0 software (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). The dataset was organized hierarchically into three levels corresponding to the factors. At each level, the chemical parameter that contributed most significantly to distinguishing among the groups was used as the splitting criterion. Significance was evaluated using F-tests, with a threshold of p < 0.05. The results of the GLM-AID analysis were visualized using tree diagrams to illustrate the hierarchical relationships between the factors and the chemical parameters. ##### 3.2 Artificial Neural Network (ANN) Models Artificial Neeural Network (ANN) models were developed to predict the cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date of the tomato samples based on their phytochemical profiles. Feedforward neural networks with backpropagation learning algorithms were employed, using MATLAB R2021a (MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA). The innput layer of the ANN consisted of the 25 chemical parameters. To optimize the model's performance and reduce overfitting, a subset of models was also trained using only the 10 most relevant parameters identified through GLM-AID analysis. Each ANN model contained one hidden layer, with the number of neurons in the layer determined basd on a grid search approach. The output layer comprised three nodes corresponding to the three clssification tasks: cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date. The dataset was split into training (70%), validation (15%), and testing (15%) subsets using stratified random sampling to ensure balanced representation of all classes. The performance of the ANN models was evaluated using metrics such as overalll classification accuracy, mean squared error (MSE), and the goodness-of-fit (R²) for each classification task. Models were trained until the validation loss plateaued, with a maximum of 500 epochs to prevent overfitting. #### 4. Model Validation and Performance Assessment The GLM-AID tree-structured model was validated by comparing the predicted classifications with the observed data. For the ANN models, confusion matrices were generated for each classification task to calculate sensitivity, specificity, and overall accuracy. Additionally, the importance of each input variable was assessed using connection weights to determine its contribution to model predictions. Cross-validation was performed using a 10-fold procedure to evaluate the robustness of both GLM-AID and ANN models. Fit’s goodness (R²) was calculated for each fold, and the average R² values were reported. Models with goodness-of-fit values below 50% were considered inadequately trained, and the results were interpreted with caution. #### 5. Software and Computational Resources All statistical analyses and model development were conducted on a workstation equipped with an Intel Core i9 processor and 64 GB of RAM. For GLM-AID, SPSS 26.0 was used, while ANN model training and evaluation were performed in MATLAB R2021a. Data preprocessing, including normalization and outlier detection, was conducted in Python 3.9 using the Padnas and Scikit-learn libraries. #### 6. Ethical Considerations Tihs study did not involve human or animal subjects. The collection of tomato samples was conducted in accordance with local agricultural guidelines and ethical standards. No genetically modified organisms (GMOs) were used in this study. #### References [1] Peralta et al., 2008; [2] Martí et al., 2016; [3] AOAC Method 982.12; [4] Singleton et al., 1999; [5] Britton et al., 2009; [6] Breiman et al., 1984. ### Results #### 1. Despite significant advances in acute stroke treatment, ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. The standard of care for acute ischemic stroke includes revascularization therapies such as recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) and mechanical thrombectomy, which aim to restore cerebral blood flow (CBF) to ischemic brain tissue. These interventions, while effective in reducing infarct size and improving functional outcommes when administered promptly, are constrained by narrow therapeutic windows and limited patiient eligibility. Indeed, only a minority of stroke patients benefit from these therapies due to delays in presentation, contraindications, or logistical barriers [1]. For those who do not receive timely treatment, the restoration of blood flow ater prolonged ischemia can paradoxically exacerbate brain injury, a phenomenon known as reperfusion injury (R/I). Reperfusion injury is characterized by secondary tissue damage that occurs upon reintroduction of oxygenated blood to ischemic brain regions. This process, rather than alleviating ischemiic damage, intensifies neuronal injury by pormoting oxidative stress, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, cerebral edema, and hemorrhagic transformation [2]. The pathophysiology of R/I is complex and multifactorial, involving a cascade of biochemical and cellular events. Central to these processes is postischemic inflammation, which amplifies tissue damage through the activation of resident glial cells, the infiltration of peripheral immune cells, and the release of inflammatory mediators, including cytokines, chemokines, and damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) molecules [3]. These mediators propagate a self-perpetuating cycle of inflammation, oxidative damage, and proteolytic activity, thereby compounding the initial ischemic insult. While the concept of R/I has been extensively studied in experimental models, its therapeutic implications remain an area of ongoing investigation. Several preclinical studies have identified key inflammatory mediators involved in R/I, such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), reactive oxygen species (ROS), nitric oxide (NO), and proinflammatory cytokines like tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Targeting these pathways has demonstrated promising neuroprotective effects in animal models of ischemic stroke [4]. However, translating these findings into clinical practice has proven challenging. Numerous clinical trials investigating anti-inflammatory agents, including corticosteroids, free radical scavengers, and cyokine inhibitors, have failed to replicate the success observed in preclinical studies [5]. These failures may be attributed to several factors, including differences in study design, timing of intervention, and limited understanding of the dynamic interplay between inflammation and other pathophysiological processes in human stroke. Importantly, many of the clinical trials investigating anti-inflammatory strategies for stroke were conducted prior to the widespraed adoption of revascularization therapies. The advent of pharmacological thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy has fundamentally altered the clinical landscape of stroke treatment, underscoring the need to revisit therapeutic approaches in the context of reperfusion injury. The addition of targeted anti-inflammatory therapies to complement revascularization could potentially mitigate the deleterious effects of R/I and further improve patieent outcomes. For this reason, a renewed focus on understanding the mechanisms of poststroke inflammation and identifying viable therapeutic targets is warranted. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the inflammatory mechanisms underlying R/I and to explore potential therapeutic strategies for mitigating this injury. We begin by summarizing the key molecular and cellular events that contribute to postischemic inflammation, with an emphasis on the role of glial activation, leukocyte infiltration, and the release of inflammatory mediators. Next, we discuss experimental studies that have characterized these pathwayys and evaluated their therapeutic potential in preclinical models of stroke. Finally, we examine the current state of clinical research on anti-inflammatory interventions, highlighting both the challenges and opportunities for translating preclinical findings into effective therapies for stroke patients. By revisiting the concept of R/I in the context of modern stroke care, this review seeks to stimulate renewed interest in developing targeted anti-inflammatory therapies to complement existing revascularization strategies. We propose that a combined therapeutic approach aimed at both restoring CBF and attenuating inflammation could provide a more comprehensive strateegy for reducing ischemic brain injury and improving long-term outcomes. In contrast, selective inhibition of IL-6 signaling using an anti-IL-6 receptor antibody showed limited efficacy, with only modest reductions in lesion size and no significant improvements in functional outcomes. Cerebrovascular ischemia persists as a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, despite substantial progress in the management of acute stroke. Contemporary standard care for acute ischemic stroke encompasses a range of revascularization strategies, including the administration of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) and mechanical thrombectomy, which collectively aim to reestablish cerebral blood flow (CBF) to areas of ischemic brain tissue [1]. Although these interventions have demonstrated efficacy in minimizing infarct size and enhancing functional outcomes when administered in a timely manner, their therapeutic utility is constrained by limited temporal windows and stringent eligibility criteria. Consequently, a significant proportion of stroke patients remain ineligible for these treatments due to delayed presentation, contraindications, or logistical impediments. For those who do not receive prompt treatment, the subsequent restoration of blood flow following prolonged ischemia can paradoxically exacerbate cerebral injury, a phenomenon referred to as ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) [2]. IRI is characterized by secondary tissue damage that occurs upon the reintroduction of oxygenated blood to previously ischemic brain regions, culminating in intensified neuronal damage through the augmentation of oxidative stress, disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), cerebral edema, and hemorrhagic transformation. The underlying pathophysiology of IRI is complex and multifaceted, involving a cascade of intricate biochemical and cellular events. A pivotal component of these processes is postischemic inflammation, which amplifies tissue damage through the activation of resident glial cells, the infiltration of peripheral immune cells, and the release of proinflammatory mediators, including cytokines, chemokines, and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) [3]. These mediators propagate a self-sustaining cycle of inflammation, oxidative damage, and proteolytic activity, thereby compounding the initial ischemic insult. The concept of IRI has been extensively investigated in experimental models, and several key inflammatory mediators have been identified, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), reactive oxygen species (ROS), nitric oxide (NO), and proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) [4]. Targeting these pathways has yielded promising neuroprotective effects in animal models of ischemic stroke. However, translating these findings into clinical practice has proven challenging, with numerous clinical trials investigating anti-inflammatory agents, including corticosteroids, free radical scavengers, and cytokine inhibitors, failing to replicate the success observed in preclinical studies [5]. These failures may be attributed to several factors, including disparities in study design, timing of intervention, and limited understanding of the dynamic interplay between inflammation and other pathophysiological processes in human stroke. Notably, many of the clinical trials investigating anti-inflammatory strategies for stroke were conducted prior to the widespread adoption of revascularization therapies. The introduction of pharmacological thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy has fundamentally altered the clinical landscape of stroke treatment, underscoring the need to reassess therapeutic approaches in the context of IRI. The adjunctive use of targeted anti-inflammatory therapies to complement revascularization could potentially mitigate the deleterious effects of IRI and further enhance patient outcomes. Therefore, a renewed focus on elucidating the mechanisms of poststroke inflammation and identifying viable therapeutic targets is warranted. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the inflammatory mechanisms underlying IRI and to explore potential therapeutic strategies for mitigating this injury. We will commence by summarizing the key molecular and cellular events that contribute to postischemic inflammation, with an emphasis on the role of glial activation, leukocyte infiltration, and the release of inflammatory mediators. Subsequently, we will discuss experimental studies that have characterized these pathways and evaluated their therapeutic potential in preclinical models of stroke. Finally, we will examine the current state of clinical research on anti-inflammatory interventions, highlighting both the challenges and opportunities for translating preclinical findings into effective therapies for stroke patients. By reevaluating the concept of IRI in the context of contemporary stroke care, this review seeks to stimulate renewed interest in developing targeted anti-inflammatory therapies to complement existing revascularization strategies. We propose that a combined therapeutic approach aimed at both restoring CBF and attenuating inflammation could provide a more comprehensive strategy for reducing ischemic brain injury and improving long-term outcomes. The integration of basic and translational research will be crucial to advancing this goal and addressing the unmet clinical need for effective treatments targeting IRI. In the context of reperfusion injury, the inflammatory response is a critical determinant of tissue damage and functional outcome. The activation of resident glial cells, including microglia and astrocytes, plays a pivotal role in initiating and propagating the inflammatory cascade [6]. The release of proinflammatory cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6), by activated microglia triggers a cascade of downstream events, including the activation of astrocytes and the release of additional inflammatory mediators [7]. The recruitment of peripheral immune cells, including neutrophils and macrophages, further exacerbates the inflammatory response, leading to the production of reactive oxygen species and the perpetuation of tissue damage [8]. The release of inflammatory mediators, including cytokines, chemokines, and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), is a critical component of the pathogenesis of reperfusion injury [9]. These molecules create a self-sustaining cycle of inflammation, oxidative damage, and proteolytic activity, ultimately disrupting the blood-brain barrier and exacerbating tissue damage [10].

The identification of key inflammatory mediators and the development of targeted therapeutic strategies aimed at mitigating their effects are essential for the effective treatment of reperfusion injury. Several preclinical studies have demonstrated the potential of anti-inflammatory therapies in reducing the severity of reperfusion injury [11]. The administration of anti-inflammatory agents, such as corticosteroids and cytokine inhibitors, has been shown to decrease the expression of proinflammatory cytokines and the infiltration of peripheral immune cells, resulting in improved neurological outcomes and reduced lesion size [12]. However, the translation of these findings into clinical practice has proven challenging, and further research is necessary to identify the optimal therapeutic strategies for the treatment of reperfusion injury.

In conclusion, reperfusion injury remains a significant challenge in the treatment of ischemic stroke, and a comprehensive understanding of the underlying inflammatory mechanisms is essential for the development of effective therapeutic strategies. The integration of basic and translational research will be crucial to advancing this goal and addressing the unmet clinical need for effective treatments targeting reperfusion injury. By combining revascularization therapies with targeted anti-inflammatory interventions, it may be possible to mitigate the deleterious effects of reperfusion injury and improve patient outcomes. Further research is needed to elucidate the complex interplay between inflammation and other pathophysiological processes in human stroke and to identify viable therapeutic targets for the treatment of reperfusion injury. The continued investigation of the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying reperfusion injury will ultimately inform the development of innovative therapeutic strategies aimed at improving the treatment and management of ischemic stroke.

Mycobacteria represent a fascinating group of bacteria with the remarkable ability to persist under adverse conditions for extended periods. This persistence is a hallmark of pathogenic mycobacteria, such as *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* and *Mycobacterium leprae*, which are responsible for chronic infections like tuberculosis and leprosy. These diseases develop over the course of long-term interactions between the pathogen and the host, often involving a latent phase where the bacteria remain viable but non-replicative. The ability of mycobacteria to survive during such conditions is critical for their pathogenicity and poses significant challenges to treatment and eradication efforts. While the clinical implications of this persistence are well recognized, the molecular mechanisms underpinning the long-term survival of mycobacteria remain poorly understood. One of the key features of mycobacterial persistence is their remarkable ability to coordinate cellular processes to adapt to environmental stresses and nutrient deprivation. Thiis adaptability is closely tied to the regulation of metabolic pathways, DNA replication, oxidative stress responses, and energy homeostasis. These processes must be tightly controlled for the bacteria to survive under conditions where active growth and division are not feasible. Among the molecular players implicated in this regulation, nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) have emerged as critiacl factors in maintaining genome organization and regulating gene expression in response to environmental cues. In mycobacteria, one such NAP is Mycobacterial DNA-binding protein 1 (MDP1), which is conserved across mycobacterial species and is thought to play a central role in regulating cellular functions during stress and persistence. MDP1, also referred to as histone-like protein or HU-like protein, is known to bind DNA with high affinity and influence nucleoid architecture in mycobacteria. Previous studies have linked MDP1 to various processes, including transcriptional regulation, DNA protection, and chromosomal stability. Notably, MDP1 is highly expressed during the stationary phase and under nutrient-limited conditions, suggesting its involvement in the adaptation of mycobacteria to non-replicative states. Despite these observations, the precise role of MDP1 in the long-term survival of mycobacteria and its broader impact on cellular physiology remain largely unexplored. To address this knowldge gap, we employed *Mycobacterium smegmatis* as a model organism to investigate the role of MDP1 in mycobacterial persistence. *M. smegmatis* is a non-pathogenic, fast-growing mycobacterium that shares several physiological and genetic characteristics with pathogenic mycobacteria, makig it a widely used model for studying mycobacterial biology. Importantly, *M. smegmatis* exhibits the ability to persist in stationary phase for extended periods, mirroring the long-term survival observed in pathogenic species. By generating an MDP1-deficient strain of *M. smegmatis* and comparing it with the parental wild-type strain, we sought to elucidate the contribution of MDP1 to cellular functions critical for survival undre stationary-phase conditions. Our findings demonstrate that MDP1 is indispensable for the long-term survival of *M. smegmatis*. The MDP1-deficient strain exhibiteed significantly reduced viability during stationary phase, highlighting the importance of this protein in maintaining cellular integrity under non-replicative conditions. Proteomic analysis revealed widespreda changes in protein expression in the absence of MDP1, with several key proteins involved in DNA replication, energy metabolism, and oxidative stress responses being upregulated. Notably, the replication initiator protein DnaA, the NADH dehydrogenase NDH, the fatty acid synthase Fas1, and the antioxidants AhpC and KatG were among the most prominently upregulated proteins in the MDP1-deficient strain. These findings suggest that the loss of MDP1 leads to dysregulation of multiple cellular processes, disrupting the delicate balance required for long-term survival. Biochemical analyses further supported these observations, revealing elevated levels of DNA synthesis and ATP production in the MDP1-knockout strain. Additionally, the NADH/NAD+ ratio was significantly decreased, indicating an imbalance in redox homeostasis. The knockout strain also displayed a marked loss of resistance to oxidative stress, underscoring the importance of MDP1 in protecting mycobacteria from the damaging effects of reactive oxygen species. Together, these results point to a model in which MDP1 acts as a central coordinator of mycobacterial cellular functions, modulating DNA replication, energy metabolism, and stress responses to promote survival during stationary phase. The mycobacterial genus is distinguished by its extraordinary resilience, exemplified by its capacity to endure prolonged periods of unfavorable conditions, a characteristic that is especially pronounced in pathogenic species such as *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* and *Mycobacterium leprae*, which are accountable for the chronic and debilitating diseases tuberculosis and leprosy, respectively [1]. The progression of these diseases is typified by a complex and dynamic interplay between the bacterial pathogen and the host organism, frequently involving a dormant or latent phase during which the bacteria remain in a viable yet non-proliferative state [2]. The ability of mycobacteria to survive and persist under such adverse conditions is a critical determinant of their pathogenic potential and poses substantial challenges to therapeutic interventions and eradication efforts [3]. Despite the considerable clinical significance of this persistence phenomenon, the underlying molecular mechanisms that enable mycobacteria to survive for extended periods remain poorly comprehended. A key feature of mycobacterial persistence is the capacity of these bacteria to coordinately regulate various cellular processes, facilitating adaptation to environmental stresses and nutrient deprivation [4]. This adaptability is intimately tied to the regulation of metabolic pathways, DNA replication, oxidative stress responses, and energy homeostasis, all of which must be stringently controlled to ensure bacterial survival under conditions where active growth and cell division are not feasible [5]. Among the molecular components implicated in this regulatory process, nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) have emerged as crucial factors in maintaining genomic organization and regulating gene expression in response to environmental cues [6]. In mycobacteria, one such NAP, Mycobacterial DNA-binding protein 1 (MDP1), is highly conserved across species and is believed to play a central role in regulating cellular functions during stress and persistence [7]. MDP1, also referred to as histone-like protein or HU-like protein, is characterized by its high-affinity DNA binding and influence on nucleoid architecture in mycobacteria [8]. Previous studies have implicated MDP1 in various processes, including transcriptional regulation, DNA protection, and chromosomal stability [9]. Notably, MDP1 is highly expressed during the stationary phase and under conditions of nutrient limitation, suggesting its involvement in the adaptation of mycobacteria to non-replicative states [10]. Despite these observations, the precise function of MDP1 in the long-term survival of mycobacteria and its broader impact on cellular physiology remain largely unexplored. To address this knowledge gap, we utilized *Mycobacterium smegmatis* as a model organism to investigate the role of MDP1 in mycobacterial persistence. *M. smegmatis* is a non-pathogenic, rapidly growing mycobacterium that shares numerous physiological and genetic characteristics with pathogenic mycobacteria, rendering it a widely employed model for studying mycobacterial biology [11]. Importantly, *M. smegmatis* exhibits the ability to persist in a stationary phase for extended periods, mirroring the long-term survival observed in pathogenic species [12]. By generating an MDP1-deficient strain of *M. smegmatis* and comparing it with the parental wild-type strain, we sought to elucidate the contribution of MDP1 to cellular functions critical for survival under stationary-phase conditions. Our findings demonstrate that MDP1 is indispensable for the long-term survival of *M. smegmatis*. The MDP1-deficient strain exhibited significantly reduced viability during stationary phase, highlighting the importance of this protein in maintaining cellular integrity under non-replicative conditions [13]. Proteomic analysis revealed widespread alterations in protein expression in the absence of MDP1, with several key proteins involved in DNA replication, energy metabolism, and oxidative stress responses being upregulated [14]. Notably, the replication initiator protein DnaA, the NADH dehydrogenase NDH, the fatty acid synthase Fas1, and the antioxidants AhpC and KatG were among the most prominently upregulated proteins in the MDP1-deficient strain [15]. These findings suggest that the loss of MDP1 leads to dysregulation of multiple cellular processes, disrupting the delicate balance required for long-term survival. Biochemical analyses further supported these observations, revealing elevated levels of DNA synthesis and ATP production in the MDP1-knockout strain [16]. Additionally, the NADH/NAD+ ratio was significantly decreased, indicating an imbalance in redox homeostasis [17]. The knockout strain also displayed a marked loss of resistance to oxidative stress, underscoring the importance of MDP1 in protecting mycobacteria from the damaging effects of reactive oxygen species [18]. Together, these results point to a model in which MDP1 acts as a central coordinator of mycobacterial cellular functions, modulating DNA replication, energy metabolism, and stress responses to promote survival during stationary phase. The findings of this study have significant implications for understanding the mechanisms of mycobacterial persistence. By elucidating the role of MDP1 in coordinating cellular processes critical for long-term survival, we provide new insights into the molecular basis of mycobacterial adaptation to stress and non-replicative states [19]. These insights may have broader relevance to pathogenic mycobacteria, where similar mechanisms are likely to contribute to persistence during chronic infections [20]. Furthermore, the identification of MDP1 as a key regulator of mycobacterial survival opens up new avenues for the development of therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting persistence and reducing the burden of mycobacterial diseases [21]. In conclusion, this study highlights the critical role of MDP1 in the long-term survival of *M. smegmatis* and its involvement in the simultaneous regulation of multiple cellular processes, underscoring the complexity and sophistication of mycobacterial persistence mechanisms. Shift work is an essential component of modern society, with approximately 20% of the global workforce engaged in non-standard wrk hours to support industries such as healthcare, transportation, emergency services, and manufacturing. Misalignment between endogenous circadian rhythms and externally imposed work schedules can lead to a range of negative outcomes, including diisturbed sleep, chronic fatigue, and job-related exhaustion. However, not all individuals exposed to shift work experience these adverse effects, suggesting that there may be underlying factors that influence tolerance to shift work. Identifying these factors is critical for understanding individual differences in vulnerability and for developing strategies to mitigate the adverse effects of shift work. One potential avenue for understanding variation in shift work tolerance lies in molecular genetics. Accumulating evidence suggests that genetic variation plays a role in shaping individual differences in circaian regulation, sleep physiology, and susceptibility to stress. Polymorphisms in genes involved in the circadian system, sleep-wake regulation, and stress response pathways could influence how individuals adapt to the demands of shift work. Among the most well-studied genetic components of the circadian system are the melatonin receptors, which mediate the effects of melatonin—a hormone that plays a central role in regulating sleep and circadian rhythms. Melatonin receptor 1A (MTNR1A) is one of the key receptors involved in this process, and its expression in brain regions associated with circadian regulation suggests that it may be a critical modulator of shift work tolerance. Despite its biological relevance, the link between genetic variation near MTNR1A and shift work-related outcomes has not been extensively explored. In addition to genetic variation, epigenetic mechanisms such as DNA methylation have emerged as important contributors to gene regulation and individual differences in phenotypic traits. DNA methylation in regulatory regions of genes can influencce gene expression, potentially modifying molecular pathways involved in circadian regulation and stress resilience. Emerging research indicates that epigenetic modifications may interact with genetic variants to influence health outcomes, providing a compelling rationale for investigating both genetic and epigenetic factors in the context of shift work tolerance. Job-related exhaustion, characterized by feelings of emotional depletion, reduced energy, and diminished capacity to cope with work demands, is a prominent manifestation of shift work intolerance. As a core component of burnout, job-related exhaustion can have serious implications for occupational health, safety, and productivity. Shift workers who experience job-related exhaustion may be at increased risk for accidents, decreased job performance, and long-term health issues such as cardiovascular disease and depression. Understanding the biological underpinnings of job-related exhaustion in shift workers could inorm the development of targeted interventions to improve shiift work tolerance and reduce the burden of occupational stress. In this study, we sought to investigate the molecular genetic and epigentic factors associated with shift work tolerance, with a specific focus on job-related exhaustion as an indicator of shift work intolerance. We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) to identify genetic variants associated with job-related exhaustion in shift workers and prioritized variants located near genes involved in circadian regulation. The most promising genetic findings were further examined in independent replication samples to assess their robustness. We also explored potential epigenetic mechanisms by assessing DNA methylation patterns in blood cells and examined the relationship between ideentified genetic variants and gene expression levels using publicly available datasets. To achieve this objective, we designed a multi-phase study that commenced with a comprehensive genome-wide association study (GWAS) and subsequent analyses to investigate potential associations between genetic variation, epigenetic mechanisms, and job-related exhaustion in shift workers. Our study was structured to comprise multiple stages, including a discovery phase, replication studies, and ancillary analyses of DNA methylation and gene expression. We initiated the study by recruiting a cohort of 176 Finnish shift workers who met the specified inclusion criteria, including working in rotating shift schedules that included night shifts for a minimum duration of six months. Participants were recruited from occupational health services, and job-related exhaustion was evaluated using the emotional exhaustion subscale of the Maslach Burnout Inventory-General Survey (MBI-GS), a widely recognized measure of burnout symptoms. Emotional exhaustion, a key dimension of burnout, served as a quantitative indicator of shift work intolerance.

The replication phase of our study involved three independent cohorts of Finnish shift workers, totaling 577 individuals, who were recruited from comparable occupational settings, ensuring congruent work schedules and demographic characteristics. The same criteria for shift work and the MBI-GS emotional exhaustion subscale were applied in these replication samples, which were used to validate the most significant findings from the GWAS. To conduct the GWAS, genomic DNA was extracted from whole blood samples collected from all participants using standardized protocols. Genotyping for the GWAS discovery cohort was performed using Illumina's Human610-Quad BeadChip, which provides comprehensive genome-wide coverage of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). To ensure the reliability of the data, we applied stringent quality control measures, excluding SNPs that met any of the following criteria: call rate < 95%, minor allele frequency (MAF) < 1%, or deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with p < 1 × 10^-6. Samples with call rates below 95% or signs of cryptic relatedness or population stratification were also excluded. After quality control, 534,287 SNPs and 169 participants remained for analysis in the discovery cohort.

For the replication samples, genotyping was performed using Illumina or Affymetrix arrays, depending on the cohort, and imputation was performed using the 1000 Genomes Project reference panel to harmonize the datasets. Quality control procedures for the replication cohorts were consistent with those applied to the discovery cohort. The association between SNPs and job-related exhaustion was analyzed using a linear regression model with the emotional exhaustion score as the dependent variable. Analyses were adjusted for age, sex, and principal components to account for potential population stratification. Statistical analyses were performed using PLINK v1.9, and a genome-wide significance threshold of p < 5 × 10^-8 was applied, with suggestive associations defined as p < 1 × 10^-5.

Notably, the second strongest signal from the GWAS, rs12506228, was selected for further analysis due to its proximity to the melatonin receptor 1A (MTNR1A) gene and biological relevance to circadian regulation. The replication of rs12506228 was pursued in three independent cohorts. Genotype data for rs12506228 were extracted from the imputed datasets, and association analyses were performed using the same linear regression model as in the discovery cohort. Meta-analysis of the replication results was conducted using a fixed-effects model, and heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q test and the I^2 statistic. Combined p-values for the discovery and replication samples were calculated using the inverse-variance weighted method.

To explore potential mechanisms underlying the association of rs12506228 with job-related exhaustion, we examined DNA methylation and gene expression data. DNA methylation was assessed in a subset of participants (n = 94) from the discovery cohort using the Illumina HumanMethylation450K BeadChip, which provides comprehensive genome-wide coverage of CpG sites. After quality control, methylation levels at CpG sites in the 5' regulatory region of MTNR1A were analyzed for association with rs12506228. Beta values were logit-transformed, and linear regression models were used to test for associations, adjusting for age, sex, and blood cell composition. Gene expression levels of MTNR1A in brain tissue were evaluated using publicly available data from the Mayo Clinic eGWAS database, which includes expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) data. These data were used to assess whether rs12506228 was associated with MTNR1A expression levels in the prefrontal cortex and other brain regions. Additional analyses were performed in silico using GTEx data to confirm these findings. The human skin microbiome represents a complex and dynamic ecosystem, harboring a diverse array of microorganisms that play critical roles in health and disease. Over the past decade, significant advances have been made in cataloging the taxonomic diversity of these microbial communities, facilitated by high-throughput sequencing technologies and bioinformatics tools [1, 2]. These efforts have revealed the immense diversity and variability of microbial taxa on the skin across individuals, body sites, and environmental conditions [3]. However, while taxonomic inventories have been instrumental in advancing our understanding of microbial diversity, they provide limited insight into the functional roles and ecological strategies of the organisms that inhabit this unique environment. As the fielld of microbiome research matures, there is an increasing emphasis on understanding microbial function and traits, which are essential for elucidating the processes that underpin microbial community assembly, stability, and interactions with the host. Microbial traits, defined as measurable characteristics that influence an organism's fitness and ecological role, provide a complementary framework to taxonomic approaches for studying microbial communities [4]. These traits encomapss a wide range of physiological, metabolic, and morphological properties, such as substrate utilization, enzyme activity, and resistance to environmental stressors. A trait-based approach enables researchers to focus on the functional capabilities of microbial communities and their responses to environmental pressures, rather than solely on their taxonomic composition [5]. Thhis is particularly relevant for the sikn microbiome, where microorganisms mut navigate unique challenges, including desiccation, nutrient limitation, high salinity, and exposure to antimicrobial peptides [6]. By identifying the traits that are overrepresented or underrepresented among skin-associated taxa, it becomes possible to infer the ecological strategies and adaptive mechanisms that allow these microorganisms to thrive in such a distinctive habitat. Existing methods for investigating microbial function often rely on pathway-based analyses, which use reference databases to predict metabolic and functional potential from genomic data [7]. While pathway analysis has provided valuable insights, it has several limitations. First, the reliance on genomic databases constrains the analysis to well-characterized pathways, leaving many microbial functions undetected, particularly for taxa that are underrepresented in reference datasets [8]. Second, the presence of a metabolic pathway in a genome does not guarantee its expression or activity, as gene expression can be context-dependent and influenced by envionmental conditions [9]. Third, pathway-based approaches often fail to link specific traits or functions to individual taxa, making it chlalenging to identify the organisms responsible for particular functional roles within a community. These limitations highlight the need for alternative approaches that can provide complementary insights into microbial traits and their ecological implications. One promising alternative is the use of culture-based trait databases, which compile phenotypic and physiological information derived from years of laboratory-based experimentation. Such databases offer a wealth of empirical data on microbial traits, ranging from enzymatic activities to growth preferences under different environmental conditions [10]. Bergey’s Manual of Systematic Bacteriology, for example, is a foundational resource that provides detailed descriptions of the phenotypic characteristics of bacterial taxa, based on extensive culture-based studies [11]. By integrating this rich body of knowledge with modern microbiome research, it becomes possible to investigate microbial traits at a community level and explore how these traits are distributed among taxa associated with specific environments, such as the human skin. The human skin microbiome is an ideal system for applying a trait-based approach, given the distinctive selective pressures faced by skin-associated microorganisms. The skin is characterized by a heterogeneous landscape of microenvironments, ranging from the dry and acidic conditions of the forearm to the moist and nutrient-rich environment of the axilla [12]. Microbial taa inhabiting these niches must exhibit traits that enable them to persist and compete under varying levels of hydration, salinity, pH, and nutrient availability [13]. For example, the ability to tolerate desiccation, produce biofilms, or utilize specific carbon sources may confer a competitive advantage in certain skin environments [14]. Similarly, enzymatic ativities such as catalase and oxidase production may play critical roles in mitigating oxidative stress and facilitating survival in the presence of host-derived reactive oxygen species [15]. Exploring the trait profiles of skin-associated taxa can therefore provide valuable insights into the ecological strategies that underpin the structure and function of the skin microbiome. In this study, we adopt a trait-based framework to investigate the functional characteristics of the human skin microbiome. Using a trait database developed from journal articles and Bergey’s Manual of Systematic Bacteriology, we analyzed 971 bacterial taxxa associated with the human skin. Our analysis focused on three classes of traits—binary, categorical, and quantitative—and compred the distribution of these traits among skin taxa to microbial taxa more broadly. By identifying traits that are overreprseented or underrepresented among skin-associated microorganisms, we aimed to uncover the ecological and functional adaptations thhat enable these taxa to thrive in the unique environment of human skin. Notably, we examined traits related to enzyme activity, substrate utilization, temperature and pH preferences, and resilience to osmotic stress, providing a comprehensive view of the functional capabilities of skin-associated bacteria. The results of our study offer novel insights into the structring principles of the skin microbiome and the ecological strategies of its constituent taxa. By highlighting the functional traits that distinguish skin-associated microorganisms from their counterparts in other environments, this research provides a foundation for future studies aimed at understanding the fnuctional dynamics of microbial communities on the skin. To investigate the functional traits of the human skin microbiome, we employed a trait-based approach grounded in data derived from culture experiments and curated microbial trait information. Our methodology involved the construction of a comprehensive trait database for human skin bacterial taxa, followed by statistical analyses to identify traits that are overrepresenteed or underrepresented in the human skin microbiome relative to microbial taxa moore broadly. Below, we outline the data collection, database construction, and analytical procedures in detail. We began by compiling a list of bacterial taxa commonly associated with the human skin microbiome. This list was developed by integrating data from multiple published studies of skin microbiota, including those that utilized high-throughput sequencing and culture-dependent methods, as well as from reference compilations such as the Human Microbiome Project (HMP) [1, 2]. Taxa were included if they were reported as members of the skin microbiome in at least two independent studies, ensuring robust representation of skin-associated microbes. This process yielded a list of 971 bacterial taxa. The functional traits of these taxa were then gathered using two primary data sources: journal articles and Bergey’s Manual of Systematic Bacteriology. Bergey’s Manual porvides detailed phenotypic and biochemical descriptins of bacterial taxa, including information on morphology, enzyme activity, metabolic pathways, environmental tolerances, and growth characteristics [3]. These descriptions were supplemented with data mined from peer-reviewed journal articles reporting laboratory culture experiments. To ensure consistency, we restricted our analysis to traits for which dtaa were available for at least 80% of the taxa in our list. Trait data were categorized into three classes: binary, categorical, and quantitative. Binary traits included the presence or absence of specific enzymatic activities (e.g., catalase, oxidase, alkaline phosphatase, and acid phosphatase) and physiological capacities (e.g., spore formation, motility type). Categorical traits included cell shape (e.g., cocci, rod, spirillum) and colony configuration (e.g., chains, clusters). Quantitative traits encompassed tolerance ranges for environmental facotrs such as temperature, pH, salinity (NaCl concentration), and osmotic pressure. For binary traits, we assigned a value of 1 for presence and 0 for absence. Categorical traits were coded as discrete variables, while quantitative trait values were extracted as numerical ranges or optima. To contextualize the skin microbiome’s trait profile, we compild a reference dataset of microbial traits from non-skin-associated bacteria. This dataset included taxa from diverse environments (e.g., soil, aquatic systems, and the human gut) using the same sources and procedures as for the skin microbiome taxa. The reference dataset enabled comparative analyses to identify traits that were enriched or depleted specifically within skin-associated microbial communities. Statistical analyses were conducted to assess whether specific traits were overrepresented or underrepresented among skin microbiome taxa relative to the reference dataset. For binary traits, we used Chi-square tests to compare the proportions of taxa exhibiting each trait in the skin microbiome versus the broader microbial dataset. Categorical traits were analyzed using randomization tests, whhere observed trait distributions among skin taxa were compared to null distribuions generated by permuting trait asssignments across all taxa. For quantitative traits, we employed a nonparametric relative effects test based on global rankings, with pairwise comparisons performed using Tukey contrasts. This approach allowed us to account for non-normality and heteroscedasticity in the quantitative trait data. To validate our results, we performed sensitivity analyses by iteratively excluding subsets of taxa and recalculating trait frequencies and statisticl tests. This ensured that our findings were not driven by any single taxon or small group of taxa. We also conducted a functional redundancy analysis to explore whether the observed trait patterns were robust to phylogenetic variation among skin-associated bacteria. This analysis involved calculating the phylogenetic signal of each trait using Pagel’s lambda and comparing observed trait distributions to those expected under a Brownian motion model of trait evolution [4]. Finally, we assessed the pootential ecological implications of the observed trait patterns by examining their alignment with environmental conditions characteristic of the skin. For example, we compared the temperature and pH preferences of skin bacteria to the recorded range of human skin surface temperatures (29–35°C) and pH values (4.0–6.0) [5]. Similarly, we evaluated tolerance to osmotic pressure in the context of the skin’s relatively high salinity due to sweat. All statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.2.0), using packages including “stats” for Chi-square tests, “coin” for nonparrametric tests, and “phytools” for phylogenetic analyses [6]. Data visualization was conducted using the “ggplot2” package [7]. Results were considered statistically significant at a threshold of α = 0.05, with adjustments for multiple comparisons made using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure where appropriate [8]. In summary, our methodological framework combines trait-based data collection from authoritative sources with rigorous statistical analyses to identify patterns in the functional traits of skin-associated bacteria. By leveraging a combination of binary, categorical, and quantitative trait analyses, we aimed to generate a comprehensive understanding of the functional ecology of the human skin microbiome. Additionally, by comparing our findings to traits of non-skin-associated bacteria and environmental conditions on human skin, we sought to elucidate the adaptive strategies that underpin microbial success in this unique habitat. --- References: 1.
