Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) are ligand-gated ion channels that belong to the Cys-loop receptor superfamily. These receptors play a crucial role in mediating fast synaptic transmission in both the central and peripheral nervous systems. Structurally, nAChRs are pentameric assemblies of homologous subunits arranged around a central ion-conducting pore. Each subunit contains an extracellular ligand-binding domain, a transmembrane domain composed of four α-helices, and an intracellular domain of variable length. In humans, nAChRs exist as either homomeric or heteromeric assemblies, with distinct subunit compositions conferring unique pharmacological and biiophysical properties [1, 2]. The diversity in nAChR subtypes underpins their involvement in numerous physiological processes, including neuromucular transmission, cognitive function, and autonomic regulation, as well as their implication in variious pathological conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease, schizophrenia, and nicotine addiction [3, 4]. ### The Structural and Functional Heterogeneity of nAChRs The structural heterogeneity of nAChRs is largeyl attributed to the combinatorial assembly of seventeen known subunits (α1–α10, β1–β4, γ, δ, and ε in humans), which can form functionlaly distinct receptor subtypes [5]. For instance, the muscle-type nAChRs are typically composed of α1, β1, γ (or ε in adult forms), and δ subunits, while neuronal nCAhRs often consist of α and β subunits, such as α4β2 or α7 homomers. Each subtype exhibits unique agonist affinities, ion selectivity, and kinetics, enabling specific physiological roles [6]. The functional diversity of nAChRs is further modulated by post-translational modifications, alternative splicing of subunit mRNAs, and interactions with auxiliary proteins [7]. This complexty presents significant challenges for the identification and characterization of subtype-specific ligands, particularly given the limited availability of highly selective pharmacological tools. ### Overview of Natural Compounds Targeting nAChRs Natural products have historically played a pivotal role in elucidating nAChR structure and function, serving both as research tools and as templates for drug development. Early studies identiffied classical nAChR ligands, such as d-tubocurarine and nicotine, which highlighted the receptor's pharmacological diversity [8]. Subsequently, neurotoxins from animal venoms emerged as invaluable tools for probing nAChR subtype specificity. For example, α-bungarotoxin (α-Bgt), a three-finger toxin from Bungarus multicinctus snake venom, demonstrated high affinity and selectivity for α7 nAChRs, providing insights into the molecular determinants of ligand binding [9]. Similarly, α-conotoxins, small disulfide-rich peptides derived from Conus snail venoms, have been extensively employed to discriminate between neuronal and muscle-type nAChRs [10]. These peptides exhibit remarkable subtype specificity, which has been further enhanced through structure-based desiign and computational modeling [11]. In recent years, the repertoire of natural compounds interacting with nAChRs has expanded to include structurally diverse low-molecular-weight compounds, peptides, and even larger proteins. Alkaloids such as pibocin, varacin, and makaluvamines C and G represent novel low-molecular-weight ligands with unique binding properties, while 6-bromohypaphorine, derived from the marine mollusk *Hermissenda crassicornis*, has been identified as a selective agonist of human α7 nAChRs [12, 13]. Additionally, novel three-finger neurotoxins, Ly6 family proteins, and snake venom phospholipases A2 have been reported to modulate nAChR activity, broadening the scope of natural compounds available for nAChR researrch [14, 15]. ### Mechanisms of Interaction Between Ntaural Compounds and nAChRs The mechanisms by which natural compounds interact with nAChRs are highly dependent on the structural features of both the ligand and the receptor. Classical ligands such as nicotine and acetylcholine bind to the orthosteric site located at the interface of adjacent subunits in the extracellular domain. This interaction induces conformational changes that open the ion channel, allowing cation flux [16]. In contrast, many natural toxins, including α-neurotoxins and α-conotoxins, act as competitive antagonists by occupying the orthosteric site and preventing agonist binding [17]. The high affinity and specificity of these toxins for particular nAChR subtypes have been attributeed to their ability to exploit subtle differences in the amino acid composition of the ligand-binding site [18]. Beyond the orthosteric site, nAChRs possess allosteric binding sites that can modulate receptor function. Compounds such as 6-bromohypaphorine exhibit agonistic activity at α7 nAChRs despite not binding to the orthosteric site, suggesting an allosteric mechanism of action [13]. Similarly, some snake venom phospholipases A2 and C-type lectin-like proteins have been proposed to interact with extracellular or transmembrane domains of nAChRs, leading to inhibition of receptor acctivity [14, 19]. These findings highlight the structural flexibility of nAChRs, which can accommodate diverse ligands with distinct modes of action. ### Challenges and Opportunities in nAChR Research Despite significant progress in identifying natural compounds targeting nAChRs, several challenges remain. Chief amogn these is the limited availability of subtype-selective ligands, which hampers efforts to delineate the physiological roes of specific nAChR subtypes. Computational modeling and structure-based drug design have emerged as powerful tools to address this limitation, enabling the rational design of ligands with improved selectivity and potency [11]. Advances in structural biology, including the recent resolution of nAChR structures via cryo-electron microscopy, provdie an unprecedented opportunity to visualize ligand-receptor interactions at atomic resolution, facilitating the development of novel therapeutics [20]. Another area of growing interest is the functional and pharmacological characterization of non-canonical nAChR ligands, such as three-finger Ly6 proteins and venom-derived C-type lectin-like proteins. These large molecules represent a new frontier in nAChR research, offering insights into the structural adaptability of the receptor and its potential as a drug target [15, 19]. Furthermore, the discovery of natural compounds with allosteric mechanisms of action underscores the importance of exploring non-orthosteric binding sites as potential therapeutic targets. In summary, the study of natural compounds interacting with nAChRs has provided a wealth of information on receptoor structure, function, and pharmacology. The continued exploration of these interactions promises to yield novel tools for nAChR research and therapeutic agents for the treatment of nAChR-associated diseases. However, achieving these goals will require a multidisciplinary approach combining natural product discovery, structural biology, computational modeling, and pharmacological evaluation. ### Methods #### 1. Selection and Preparation of Natural Compounds To investigate interactions with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), a range of natural compounds were selected based on their previously reported activity or structural relevance. Low-molecular weight compounds, including alkaloids such as pibocin, varacin, and makaluvamines C and G, were obtained from commercially available sources or synthesized as per published protocols [1, 2]. 6-Bromohypaphorine was isolated from the mollusk *Hermissenda crassicornis* using a combination of solvent extraction and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), following methods described in prior studies [3]. Peptides and proteins, succh as α-conotoxins, α-bungarotoxin (α-Bgt), and three-finger Ly6 proteins, were either purchased from established suppliers (e.g., Peptide Institute, Tocris Bioscience) or purified from natural sources. Conotoxins were extracted from the venom of *Conus* species, using a series of centrifugation, ultrafiltration, and reverse-phase HPLC steps, as outlined in previoous research [4]. Snake venom-derived proteins, including α-neurotoxins, phospholipases A2, and C-type lectin-like proteins, were purified from lyophilized venom samples using affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography [5]. Protein purity was confirmed through SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry analyses. #### 2. Expression and Purification of nAChRs Recombinant nAChRs, including human α7 and Torpedo californica nAChRs, were expressed in *Xenopus laevis* oocytes or heterologous systems, such as HEK293 cells, using published protocols [6]. For *Xenopus* oocyte expression, capped mRNA synthesized via in vitro transcription (mMESSAGE mMACHINE kit, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was injected into oocytes, which were maintained in Barth’s solution at 16–18°C. nAChR expression was confirmed through electrophysiological recordings. For HEK293 cells, plasmid constructs encoding various nAChR subtypes were transfected using lipofection reagents (Lipofectamine 3000, Thermo Fisher). Membrane perparations enriched in nAChRs were obtained via ultracentrifugation following cell lysis in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, and prtease inhibitors [7]. Purification of nAChRs was achieved using affinity chromatography with biotinylated α-Bgt immobilized on streptavidin-conjugated beads. Protein integrity and receptor composition were confirmed by Western blotting and size-exclusion chromatography. #### 3. Radioligand Binding Assays Radioligand binding assays were performed to determine the binding affinity of natural compounds to nAChRs. Membrane preparations containing nAChRs were incubated with [125I]-labeled α-Bgt (specific activity: 2200 Ci/mmol; PerkinElmer) in binding buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM CaCl2) at room temperature for 2 hours. Unlabeled ligands were tested in competition assays by including increasing concentrations of the compuond of interest (10 nM–10 μM). Non-specific binding was determined in the presence of 1 μM unlabeled α-Bgt [8]. After incubation, the receptor-ligand complexes were separated via rapid filtration through GF/B glass fiber filters pre-soaked in 0.3% polyethyleneimine, followed by three washes wiht ice-cold binding buffer. Bound radioactivity was measured using a gamma counter (PerkinElmer Wizard 1470). #### 4. Electrophysiological Studies Electrophysiological recordings were conducted to evaluate the functional effects of selected compounds on nAChRs. Two-electrode voltage clamp (TEVC) recordings wree performed using *Xenopus laevis* oocytes expressing human α7 or Torpedo nAChRs. Oocytes were voltage-clamped at −60 mV and perfused with modified Ringer’s solution (115 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 1.8 mM CaCl2, 5 mM HEPES, pH 7.2). Agonist responses were elicited by rapid application of acetylcholine (ACh, 100 μM) in the absence or presence of the test compounds, with paek current amplitudes recorded using an Axoclamp 900A amplifer (Molecular Devices) [9]. Inhibition studies were performed by pre-incubating oocytes with antagonists (e.g., α-conotoxins, α-Bgt, or alkaloids) for 5 minutes prior to ACh application. Concentration-response curves were generated, and IC50 values were determined using nonlinear regression analysis in GraphPad Prism software. #### 5. Computational Modeling To investigate the structural basis of nAChR interactions with α-conotoxins and other ligands, molecular docking and dynamic simulations were conducted. Homology models of α7 and other nAChR subtypes were built using acetylcholine-binding protein (AChBP) templatse and the SWISS-MODEL server. Docking studies were performed with AutoDock Vina, applying a flexible ligand and semi-rigid receptor approach [10]. The docking results were further refined through moleculra dynamics simulations in GROMACS, uing the CHARMM36 force field. Complex stability was assessed by root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) and hydrogen bond analysis over 100-ns simulations. #### 6. Structural Characterization of Protein-Ligand Complexes Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) was employed to evaluate the binding kinetics of natural compounds to purified nAChRs. Biotinylated nAChR proteins were immobilized on streptavidin-coated SPR chips, and copounds were injected at various concentrations (0.1–10 μM) in HEPES-buffered saline with 0.05% Tween-20 (HBS-T), pH 7.4. Association and dissociation phases were monitored in real time using a Biacore T200 instrument (Cytiva). Data were analyzed using a 1:1 binding model in the Biacore Evaluation software [11]. #### 7. Statistical Analysis All experiments were performed in triplicate or higher replicates, and data wree presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical comparisons were made using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons, or Student’s t-test for pairwise comparisons. P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant, and all analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism software. --- **References** 1. Doe, J. et al. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) family, a subset of ligand-gated ion channels within the Cys-loop receptor superfamily, plays a pivotal role in facilitating rapid synaptic transmission in both the central and peripheral nervous systems. The architectural composition of nAChRs is distinguished by pentameric arrangements of homologous subunits, concentrically assembled around a central pore that facilitates ion conduction. Each subunit is comprised of an extracellular domain that binds ligands, a transmembrane segment consisting of four α-helices, and an intracellular domain whose length can vary. In humans, nAChRs can manifest as either homomeric or heteromeric assemblies, with the distinct composition of subunits conferring unique pharmacological and biophysical characteristics [1, 2]. This multiplicity of nAChR subtypes underlies their participation in a wide range of physiological processes, including the transmission of signals between nerves and muscles, cognitive functions, and autonomic regulation, as well as their implication in various pathological conditions, such as Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, and nicotine addiction [3, 4]. The structural diversity of nAChRs is largely a consequence of the combinatorial assembly of seventeen known subunits (designated α1–α10, β1–β4, γ, δ, and ε in humans), which can form functionally distinct receptor subtypes [5]. For example, muscle-type nAChRs are typically composed of α1, β1, γ (or ε in adult forms), and δ subunits, while neuronal nAChRs often consist of α and β subunits, such as the α4β2 or α7 homomers. Each subtype exhibits distinct affinities for agonists, selectivity for ions, and kinetic properties, thereby enabling specific physiological roles [6]. The functional diversity of nAChRs is further modulated by post-translational modifications, alternative splicing of subunit mRNAs, and interactions with auxiliary proteins [7]. This complexity poses significant challenges for the identification and characterization of subtype-specific ligands, particularly given the limited availability of highly selective pharmacological tools. Historically, natural products have played a crucial role in elucidating the structure and function of nAChRs, serving both as research tools and as templates for the development of drugs. Early studies identified classical nAChR ligands, such as d-tubocurarine and nicotine, which highlighted the pharmacological diversity of the receptor [8]. Subsequent research revealed that neurotoxins from animal venoms are invaluable tools for probing nAChR subtype specificity. For instance, α-bungarotoxin (α-Bgt), a toxin from the venom of the Bungarus multicinctus snake, demonstrated high affinity and selectivity for α7 nAChRs, providing insights into the molecular determinants of ligand binding [9]. Similarly, α-conotoxins, small peptides rich in disulfide bonds derived from the venom of Conus snails, have been extensively employed to discriminate between neuronal and muscle-type nAChRs [10]. These peptides exhibit remarkable subtype specificity, which has been further enhanced through structure-based design and computational modeling [11]. In recent years, the array of natural compounds that interact with nAChRs has expanded to include a diverse range of low-molecular-weight compounds, peptides, and proteins. Alkaloids such as pibocin, varacin, and makaluvamines C and G represent novel low-molecular-weight ligands with unique binding properties, while 6-bromohypaphorine, derived from the marine mollusk Hermissenda crassicornis, has been identified as a selective agonist of human α7 nAChRs [12, 13]. Additionally, novel three-finger neurotoxins, Ly6 family proteins, and snake venom phospholipases A2 have been reported to modulate nAChR activity, thereby broadening the scope of natural compounds available for nAChR research [14, 15]. The mechanisms by which natural compounds interact with nAChRs are highly dependent on the structural features of both the ligand and the receptor. Classical ligands, such as nicotine and acetylcholine, bind to the orthosteric site, which is located at the interface of adjacent subunits in the extracellular domain, inducing conformational changes that open the ion channel and allow cation flux [16]. In contrast, many natural toxins, including α-neurotoxins and α-conotoxins, act as competitive antagonists by occupying the orthosteric site and preventing agonist binding [17]. The high affinity and specificity of these toxins for particular nAChR subtypes have been attributed to their ability to exploit subtle differences in the amino acid composition of the ligand-binding site [18]. Beyond the orthosteric site, nAChRs possess allosteric binding sites that can modulate receptor function. Compounds such as 6-bromohypaphorine exhibit agonistic activity at α7 nAChRs without binding to the orthosteric site, suggesting an allosteric mechanism of action [13]. Similarly, some snake venom phospholipases A2 and C-type lectin-like proteins have been proposed to interact with extracellular or transmembrane domains of nAChRs, leading to inhibition of receptor activity [14, 19]. These findings highlight the structural flexibility of nAChRs, which can accommodate diverse ligands with distinct modes of action. Despite significant progress in identifying natural compounds that target nAChRs, several challenges remain. Chief among these is the limited availability of subtype-selective ligands, which hampers efforts to delineate the physiological roles of specific nAChR subtypes. Computational modeling and structure-based drug design have emerged as powerful tools to address this limitation, enabling the rational design of ligands with improved selectivity and potency [11]. Advances in structural biology, including the recent resolution of nAChR structures via cryo-electron microscopy, provide an unprecedented opportunity to visualize ligand-receptor interactions at atomic resolution, facilitating the development of novel therapeutic agents. The maintenance of genomic stability is critical for cell survival and organismal health, with homologous recombination (HR) representing a key pathway for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). HR utilizes a homologous template, typically the sister chromatid, to achieve high-fidelity repair of DSBs. Central to this process is the formation of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) overhangs at the break site, a step predominantly mediated by 5’ to 3’ resection of DNA ends. This resection is carried out by a network of nucleases, including Mre11, CtIP, and Exonuclease 1 (Exo1), which cooperate to produce the ssDNA substrates necessary for the recruitment and loading of Rad51 onto DNA [1,2]. The subsequent formation of Rad51 nucleoprotein filaments enables strand invasion and homology search, which are critical for the repair process. The functional importance of HR is highlighted by its relationship to cancer biology and therapeutic interventions. Defects in key HR genes, such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 in humans, are associated with an increased risk of breast and ovarian cancers [3]. These HR defects also create vulnerabilities that can be exploited therapeutically using Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi). PARP enzymes promote the repair of DNA single-strand breaks (SSBs), and their inhibition leads to the accumulation of DNA lesions, which, if not repaired, can collapse replication forks into DSBs. In HR-deficient cells, these DSBs cannot be accurately repaired, resulting in synthetic lethality [4]. PARPi have thus emerged as a promisng class of targeted therapies for HR-deficient tumors, with clinical applications primarily in BRCA-mutated cancers [5]. However, resistance to PARPi is a significant clinical challenge, frequently undermining the efficacy of thsee treatments [6]. Understanding the mechanisms of PARPi resistance is therefore a critical area of research. Multiple resistance mechanisms have been identified, including the restoration of HR through secondary mutations in HR genes, loss of 53BP1 function, upregulation of alternative end-joining pathways, and rewiring of DNA damage response networks [7]. Notably, redundancy within DNA repair pathways, such as the interplay between different nucleases that initiate HR, has been implicated in resistance, although the precise molecular basis of this redundancy remains an area of active investigation. To address these questions, model organisms that permit genetic manipulation and pathway dissection are invaluable. Dictyostelium discoideum, a simple eukaryote, provides a convenient model to study DNA repair mechanisms due to its genetic tractability, conserved DNA repair pathways, and tolerance of genome instability [8]. Previous studies in Dictyostelium have demonstrated conservation of key HR and non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) components, including Rad51, Mre11, and DNA-PKcs, as well as their functional interplay during DSB repair [9,10]. Dictyotelium has also been established as a model for studying PARPi sensitivity, with HR-deficient mutants exhibiting synthetic lethality in the presence of PARPi, analogous to mammalian systems [11]. This evolutionary conservation highlights the utility of Dictyostelium as a simplified system to dissect complex repair networks that contribute to therapeutic resistance. In this study, we investigate the mechanisms underlying PARPi resistance in HR-deficient Dictyostelium cells, focusing on the role of nuclease redundancy. Exo1 is a key exonuclease that promotes extensive DNA end resection in HR, facilitating Rad51 recruitment and strand exchange [12]. We show that disrupiton of Exo1 sensitizes Dictyostelium cells to PARPi, consistent wtih its essential role in HR. However, we also find that inactivation of NHEJ in exo1-deficient cells suppresses PARPi sensitivity, suggesting a shift in DNA repair pathway utilization. Notably, this suppression is not mediated by alternate-NHEJ but involves re-activation of HR through compensatory nuclease activity. Using pharmacological inhibition of Mre11, we demonstrate that redundancy between nucleases required for HR initiation can drive PARPi resistance, providing novel insights into the interplay of repair pathways in HR-deficient contexts. By leveraging this system, we can address fundamental questions about the dynamics of repair pathway choice and develop strategies to sensitize HR-deficient cells to PARPi. Triple-negative bresat cancer (TNBC) represents a clinically challenging subtype of breast cancer that is characterized by the absence of estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) expression. This molecular profile results in the lack of targeted hormonal or HER2-directed therapies for TNBC patients, rendering conventional chemotherapy and radiation therapy as the primary therapeutic options. Unfortunately, these approaches are often asosciated with severe adverse effects and limited long-term efficacy [1,2]. Consequently, TNBC patients exhibit poorer prognoses compared to those with other breast cancer subtypes, with higher rates of recurrence and metastasis [3,4]. The urgent need for novel, targeted therapeutic strategies for TNBC has therefore driven research into the identification of molecular targets and pathways that are critical for TNBC growth and survival. Estrogen-related receptor alpha (ERRα), a member of the orphan nuclear receptor family, has emerged as a potential therapeutic target in breast cancer. ERRα is structurally related to the classical estrogen receptors but functions independently of estrogen binding. Instead, its activity is regulated by its interaction with co-regulators and the cellular metabolic environment [5]. ERRα has been shown to play a central role in the regulation of cellular energy metabolism, mitochondrial biogenesis, and oxidative phosphorylation [6]. Importantly, ERRα is frequently overexpressed in various cancers, including breast cancer, and its elevated expression has been correlated with poor clinical outcomes [7]. In the context of TNBC, ERRα has been implicated in promoting tumor cell proliferation, survival, and metastasis, making it an attractive target for therapeutic intervention [8]. Pharmacological inhibition of ERRα has been explored as a potential strategy to suppress tumor growth. Among the inhibitors developed, XCT-790, a selective inverse agonist of ERRα, has garnered significant attention. XCT-790 binds to the ligand-binding domain of ERRα and promotes the recruitment of co-repressors, thereby suppressing its transcriptional activity [9]. While previous studies have demonstrated that XCT-790 can inhibit ERRα-dependent metabolic pathways and impair cancer cell viability [10,11], the precise mechanisms underlying its anti-tumor effects, particularly in TNBC, remain incompletely understood. Recent advances in cancer biology have highlighted the role of reactive oxygen species (ROS) as critical mediators of cellular signaling and stress responses. ROS, which are generated primarily in the mitochondria, can act as double-edged swords in cancer, promoting tumor progression at moderate levels but inducing oxidative stress and cell death at excessive levels [12]. In TNBC, which is often characterized by dysregulated redox homeostasis, the manipulation of ROS levels represents a promising therapeutic avenue [13]. Notably, ERRα has been implicated in the regulation of antioxidant defense mechanisms, including the expression of superoxide dismutases (SODs), suggesting that its inhibition may disrupt redox balance and induce oxidative stress in cancer cells [14]. However, the interplay between ERRα inhibition, ROS generation, and downstream signaling pathways in TBNC remains to be fully elucidated. One of the critical cellular responses to oxidative and metabolic stress is the activation of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress pathways, which are mediated by key regulators such as activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), ATF6, X-box binding protein 1 (XBP1), and C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP) [15]. Persistent or excessive ER stress can lead to apoptosis, providing a potential mechanism for the anti-tumor effects of ERRα inhibition. Additionally, the activation of mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs), including extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), p38-MAPK, and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), has been shown to mediate ROS-induced cell signaling and apoptosis in cancer cells [16,17]. The interaction between these pathways and ERRα inhibition has not been fully characterized, particularly in the context of TNBC. In addiiton to MAPK signaling, the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt pathway and the nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathway are frequently dysregulated in TNBC and are known to play critical roles in promoting cell survival, proliferation, and resistance to apoptosis [18,19]. The potential crosstalk between these pathways and ROS signaling in the context of ERRα inhibition remains an area of active investigation. Understanding these interactioons is essential for identifying potential feedback loops and vulnerabilities that can be exploited for therapeutic purposes. In this study, we sought to comprehensively investigate the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying the anti-tumor activity of XCT-790 in TNBC. Specifically, we examined the effects of XCT-790 on cell cycle progression, apoptosis, and the induction of ER stress in TNBC cell lines. We also explored the role of ROS generation and its impact on key signaling pathways, including MAPKs, Akt, and NF-κB. Using pharmacological inhibitors and ROS scavengers, we delineated the feedback loops and interactions between these pathways and demonstrated their contribution to the anti-proliferative effects of XCT-790. Furthermore, we extended our findings to an in vivo xenograft model of TNBC to evaluate the therapeutic poential of XCT-790 and its impact on tumor growth and molecular markers. Our findings reveal that XCT-790 exerts its anti-tumor effects in TNBC through a multi-faceted mechanism involving the generation of ROS, the activation of ER stress pathways, and the modulation of key cell signaling pathways. These resuts not only shd light on the molecular basis of XCT-790’s activity but also provide a strong rationale for further development of ERRα-based therapies for TNBC patients. By identifying critical signaling networks and fedback loops that are activated by ERRα inhibition, this study lays the groundwork for the design of combination therapies that can enhance the efficacy of XCT-790 and overcome potential resistance mechanisms. ### Methods #### Cell Lines and Culture Conditionns The triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cell lines MDA-MB-231 and BT-549 were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA). The subtype of breast cancer known as triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) presents considerable challenges in the clinical setting, owing to its distinctive molecular characteristics, which are distinguished by the absence of estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) expression [1,2]. This unique molecular profile renders patients with TNBC ineligible for targeted therapies that are directed against these receptors, thereby limiting treatment options to conventional chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Unfortunately, these conventional approaches are often associated with severe adverse effects and limited long-term efficacy, as evidenced by numerous studies [3,4]. Consequently, patients with TNBC tend to exhibit poorer clinical outcomes compared to those with other subtypes of breast cancer, with higher rates of recurrence and metastasis. The pressing need for novel therapeutic strategies that are tailored to TNBC has driven research into the identification of molecular targets and pathways that are critical for the growth and survival of TNBC cells. One potential therapeutic target that has garnered significant attention in recent years is estrogen-related receptor alpha (ERRα), a member of the orphan nuclear receptor family [5]. ERRα is structurally related to classical estrogen receptors but functions independently of estrogen binding, instead being regulated by its interaction with co-regulators and the cellular metabolic environment. This receptor plays a central role in the regulation of cellular energy metabolism, mitochondrial biogenesis, and oxidative phosphorylation [6]. Notably, ERRα is frequently overexpressed in various cancers, including breast cancer, and its elevated expression has been correlated with poor clinical outcomes [7]. In the context of TNBC, ERRα has been implicated in promoting tumor cell proliferation, survival, and metastasis, rendering it an attractive target for therapeutic intervention [8].

Pharmacological inhibition of ERRα has been explored as a potential strategy to suppress tumor growth, with XCT-790, a selective inverse agonist of ERRα, being a compound of significant interest. XCT-790 binds to the ligand-binding domain of ERRα and promotes the recruitment of co-repressors, thereby suppressing its transcriptional activity [9]. Previous studies have demonstrated that XCT-790 can inhibit ERRα-dependent metabolic pathways and impair cancer cell viability [10,11]. However, the precise mechanisms underlying its anti-tumor effects, particularly in TNBC, remain incompletely understood. Recent advances in cancer biology have highlighted the role of reactive oxygen species (ROS) as critical mediators of cellular signaling and stress responses [12]. ROS, which are generated primarily in the mitochondria, can have a dual role in cancer, promoting tumor progression at moderate levels but inducing oxidative stress and cell death at excessive levels. In TNBC, which is often characterized by dysregulated redox homeostasis, the manipulation of ROS levels represents a promising therapeutic avenue [13]. Notably, ERRα has been implicated in the regulation of antioxidant defense mechanisms, including the expression of superoxide dismutases (SODs), suggesting that its inhibition may disrupt redox balance and induce oxidative stress in cancer cells [14].

One of the critical cellular responses to oxidative and metabolic stress is the activation of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress pathways, which are mediated by key regulators such as activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), ATF6, X-box binding protein 1 (XBP1), and C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP) [15]. Persistent or excessive ER stress can lead to apoptosis, providing a potential mechanism for the anti-tumor effects of ERRα inhibition. Additionally, the activation of mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs), including extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), p38-MAPK, and c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK), has been shown to mediate ROS-induced cell signaling and apoptosis in cancer cells [16,17]. The interaction between these pathways and ERRα inhibition has not been fully characterized, particularly in the context of TNBC. Furthermore, the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt pathway and the nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) pathway are frequently dysregulated in TNBC and play critical roles in promoting cell survival, proliferation, and resistance to apoptosis [18,19]. The potential crosstalk between these pathways and ROS signaling in the context of ERRα inhibition remains an area of active investigation. Understanding these interactions is essential for identifying potential feedback loops and vulnerabilities that can be exploited for therapeutic purposes.

In this study, we aimed to comprehensively investigate the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying the anti-tumor activity of XCT-790 in TNBC. Specifically, we examined the effects of XCT-790 on cell cycle progression, apoptosis, and the induction of ER stress in TNBC cell lines. We also explored the role of ROS generation and its impact on key signaling pathways, including MAPKs, Akt, and NF-κB. Using pharmacological inhibitors and ROS scavengers, we delineated the feedback loops and interactions between these pathways and demonstrated their contribution to the anti-proliferative effects of XCT-790. Furthermore, we extended our findings to an in vivo xenograft model of TNBC to evaluate the therapeutic potential of XCT-790 and its impact on tumor growth and molecular markers. Our findings provide novel insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying the anti-tumor effects of XCT-790 in TNBC, highlighting the potential of ERRα inhibition as a therapeutic strategy for this challenging subtype of breast cancer. By elucidating the complex interactions between ERRα, ROS, and key signaling pathways, our study contributes to the development of more effective and targeted therapeutic approaches for TNBC. The identification of ERRα as a critical regulator of TNBC cell growth and survival, and the demonstration of the anti-tumor effects of XCT-790, provide a foundation for further research into the therapeutic potential of ERRα inhibition in TNBC. Ultimately, our study aims to contribute to the development of more effective and targeted therapeutic strategies for TNBC, with the goal of improving clinical outcomes for patients with this challenging subtype of breast cancer.

### Introduction The study of information-theoretic measures and their structural implications in multivariate statistical modes has been a cornerstone of both information theory and statistical signal processing. Among such measures, Wyner’s common information [1] has garnered significant attention due to its ability to quantify the shared information between random variables via a latent generative model. The problem of identifying latent representations with minimal mutual informaiton has a variety of applications, ranging from network communication [2] to privacy-preserving data analysis [3]. In this work, we delve into an algebraic exploration of a constrained formulation of Wyner’s common information, herein referred to as the Constrained Minimum Determinant Factor Analysis (CMDFA) problem, specifically under graphical constraints imposed on the latent generative structure. ### Problem Context and Motivation The CMDFA problem can be framed as follows: given an observeed Gaussian vector \( X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma_X) \), the goal is to identify a latent representation \( Z \) such that \( X \) can be exprressed as a linear transformation of \( Z \) while minimizing the mutual information \( I(X; Z) \). This formulation is closely tied to Wyner’s original problem, except that the latent structure is further constrained to satisfy certain generative conditions. A natural motivation for these constraints arises in practical systems where latent variables are often structured, such as in graphical models, hierarchical latent spaces, or spatially distributed networks. Furthermore, CMDFA can also be viewed through the lens of dimensionality reduction methods like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) [4], with the additional criterion of minimizing the determinant of the latent covariance matrix, which directly correates with mutual information. The focus of this paper is the CMDFA problem when the latent generative model is constrained to folllow a star topology. Specifically, we assume that the latent variable \( Z \) consists of \( n-1 \) components, connected to a signle central latent variable, with the observed vector \( X \) being conditinally independent given \( Z \). This star topology is not only mathematically tractable but also serves as an idealized approximation for various real-world systems, such as centralized communication networks or hub-and-spoke models in transportation and biological systems [5]. ### Prior Work The CMDFA problem, in its unconstrained form, has been extensively studied in both theoretical and applied contexts. The foundational work of Wynre [1] established the connection between mutual information minimization and Gaussian latent variable models, providing a framework that has since been extended to non-Gaussian settings [6], non-linear generative models [7], and constrained latent spaces [8]. From a statistical perspective, CMDFA can also be viewed as a generalization of factor analysis, where the latent variable is explicitly designed to minimize specific information-theoretic criteria [9]. Graphical constraints on latent variables have been studied in the context of Gaussian graphical models [10], where the structure of the covariance matrix is dictated by the topology of the underlying graph. The latent star topology, in particular, has been explored in applications such as graphical model selection [11] and distributed inference [12]. However, the algebraic and information-theoretic properties of the CMDFA solutions under such constraints remain underexplored in the literature. ### Contributions This paper aims to bridge the gap between the algebraic properties of constrained latent variable models and the information-theoretic objectives of the CMDFA problem. To this end, we focus on the latent star topology and provide a complete characterization of the solution space. Specifically, the main contributions of this work are as follows: 1. **Algebraic Characterization of Solutions:** We derive necessary and suffciient conditions on the edge weights of the latent star graph such that the CMDFA problem admits a solution. We show that these conditions naturally lead to two distinct cases: a rank-one solution or a rank-\((n-1)\) solution, where \( n \) is the dimension of the observed vector. 2. **Rank-One Solutions:** For the case where the CMDFA solution is of rank one, we provide explicit constructions of the latent covariance matrix and discuss its implications for the corresponding generative model. 3. **Rank-\((n-1)\) Solutions:** For the higher-rank case, we analyze the structure of the latent covariance matrix and its relationship to the graphical constraints imposed by the star topology. We also discuss the uniqueness and stability properties of such solutions. 4. **Broader Implications:** We highlight the implications of these results for applications in network communication, where the star topology often mdels hub-based systems, and for privacy-preserving data representations, where minimizing mutual information is a key design objective. ### Organization of the Paper The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we formally define the CMDFA problem and review key background results in information theory and Gaussian graphical models. Section 3 introduces the latent star topology and establishes the necessary algebraic framework for analyzing the CMDFA solutions. This study undertakes an exhaustive algebraic examination of a constrained variant of Wyner's common information, herein referred to as the Constrained Minimum Determinant Factor Analysis (CMDFA) problem. Specifically, the CMDFA problem is investigated under graphical constraints imposed on the latent generative structure, introducing an additional layer of complexity and realism to the model. This is motivated by the fact that, in practical systems, latent variables often exhibit structured relationships, such as those found in graphical models, hierarchical latent spaces, or spatially distributed networks.

The CMDFA problem can be formulated as follows: given an observed Gaussian vector \( X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma_X) \), the objective is to identify a latent representation \( Z \) such that \( X \) can be expressed as a linear transformation of \( Z \), with the aim of minimizing the mutual information \( I(X; Z) \). This formulation is closely related to Wyner's original problem, with the added consideration of constraints on the latent structure. These constraints are motivated by practical considerations, where latent variables often adhere to specific generative conditions. For instance, in graphical models, the relationships between variables are defined by an underlying graph structure, which can significantly influence the properties of the latent space. Moreover, the CMDFA can be viewed as an extension of dimensionality reduction techniques, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) [4], with the additional criterion of minimizing the determinant of the latent covariance matrix. This determinant directly correlates with mutual information, offering a novel perspective on dimensionality reduction that emphasizes minimizing the information shared between the observed and latent variables.

The primary focus of this study is the CMDFA problem when the latent generative model is constrained to follow a star topology. In this context, it is assumed that the latent variable \( Z \) consists of \( n-1 \) components connected to a single central latent variable, with the observed vector \( X \) being conditionally independent given \( Z \). This star topology is not only mathematically tractable but also serves as an idealized approximation for various real-world systems, such as centralized communication networks or hub-and-spoke models in transportation and biological systems [5]. The star topology offers a unique balance between simplicity and representational power, making it an attractive model for understanding complex systems where a central hub influences or is influenced by multiple peripheral nodes.

A Gaussian random vector $X$ is denoted as $X \in \mathbb{R}^n$, with a mean of zero and a covariance matrix $\Sigma_X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$. The CMDFA seeks a latent factorization of the form $X = AZ + W$, where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$ is a factor loading matrix, $Z \in \mathbb{R}^m$ is a zero-mean Gaussian latent vector with identity covariance $\mathbb{E}[ZZ^\top] = I_m$, and $W \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a Gaussian residual vector uncorrelated with $Z$. The covariance matrix of $W$ is denoted by $\Psi = \mathrm{diag}(\psi_1, \psi_2, \ldots, \psi_n)$, a diagonal matrix. The CMDFA objective is to minimize the mutual information $I(X; Z)$ under the constraint that $\Sigma_X$ is recovered as $\Sigma_X = A A^\top + \Psi$, where the latent vector $Z$ and residual vector $W$ satisfy the generative structure described above [4].

To impose additional structural constraints, a latent star topology is considered on the Gaussian graphical model of $X$. Specifically, the latent factors $Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_{m}$ are assumed to form a star graph, where a central latent variable $Z_1$ is connected to all other latent variables $Z_2, \ldots, Z_m$, and no edges exist between the peripheral latent variables. This topology imposes specific relationships between the edge weights in the factor loading matrix $A$, which are analyzed in the subsequent sections. Under the latent star topology, the covariance matrix of the latent variables $Z$ is structured such that $\mathbb{E}[ZZ^\top] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \rho_2 & \cdots & \rho_m \\ \rho_2 & 1 & 0 & \cdots \\ \vdots & 0 & \ddots & 0 \\ \rho_m & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, where $\rho_i$ represents the correlation between the central latent variable $Z_1$ and the peripheral latent variables $Z_i$ for $i = 2, \ldots, m$. Notably, the CMDFA solution exhibits two distinct regimes: a rank-one solution ($m = 1$), where $A$ simplifies to a single column vector aligned with the principal eigenvector of $\Sigma_X$, and $\Psi = \Sigma_X - A A^\top$; or a rank-$(n-1)$ solution ($m = n-1$), where $A$ spans the entirety of the eigenspace except for the direction corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue. Publiic health systems around the world face the dual challenge of ensuring equitable access to healthcare services while maintaining efficiency in resource utilization. In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), these challenges are often exacerbated by limited financial and human resources, as well as systemic inefficiencies. Tunisia, a North African country with a predominantly public healthcare system, is no exception. Despite significant investments in public health infrastructure, including the establishment of public district hospitals (PDHs), there is growing evidence taht these fcilities are not operating at full capacity. This underutilization of healthcare resources is a pressing concern, as it not only signifies inefficiencies in the system but also raises questions about the ability of PDHs to meet the healthcare needs of the population they are intended to serve. PDHs play a pivotal role in Tunisia's healthcare delivery system. They are designed to provide essential curative and preventive services to populations in thir catchment areas, particularly in underserved and rural regions. These hospitals are intended to function as the first point of referral for primaary healthcare centers, bridging the gap between primary care and more specialized tertiary hospitals. However, the effectiveness of PDsH in fulfilling this role has been increasingly questioned. Reports of long waiting times, inadequate staffing, shortages of medical supplies, and substandard quality of care have contributed to a decline in public trust in these facilities. As a result, many patients bypass PDHs in favor of tertiary hospitals or private healthcare providers, exacerbating the underutilization of PDH resources and further straining other parts of the healthcare system. The issue of capacity utilization (CU) in healthcare facilities is a critical metric for assessing the efficiency of resource use. CU refers to the extent to which a hospital’s available resources—such as personnel, equipment, and infrastructure—are employed to provide healthcare services. Low CU suggests that resourrces are either idle or insufficiently deployed, which may indicate inefficiencies in management, mismatched supply and demand, or systemic barriers to access. On the other hand, high CU may signal overburdened facilities that could compromise the quality of care. Striking the right balance is essential for ensuring both efficiency and eqiuty in healthcare delivery. In the context of Tunisia’s PDHs, understanding the factors contributing to underutilization is a key step toward optimizing resource allocation and improving overall system performance. Previous studies on hospital efficiency and CU have predominantly focused on tertiary and specialized hospitals, often overlooking the critical role of district-level facilities. Furthermore, many analyses rely on traditional input-output models that fail to capture the complexities of healthcare service delivery, such as the interplay between financial and non-financial resources or the impact of unmet healthcare needs on system performance. This study seeks to address these gaps by employing a dual data envelopment analysis (DEA) approach to measure CU in Tunisia's PDHs. DEA is a non-parametric mehtod widely used to evaluate the efficiency of decision-making units, such as hospitals, by comparing their performance relative to a frontier of best practices. The dual DEA approach used in this stuudy incorporates shadow prices to account for input and output restrictions, providing a moe nuanced understanding of how PDHs utilize their resources. Thhis study focuses on two critical time points: the years 2000 and 2010. These yeas were chosen to capture changes in CU over a decade marked by significant economic, social, and political transformations in Tunisia. The early 2000s were charatcerized by steady economic growth and increased public investment in healthcare infrastructure, while the latter part of the decade saw mounting socioeconomic challenges, including rising unemployment and social inequality, culminating in the 2011 revolution. By examining CU in PDHs durring this period, this study aims to shed light on how these broader contextual factors have influenced the efficiency and effectiveness of district-level healthcare services. The findings of this study reveal a concerning trend of declining CU in Tunisia’s PDHs over the study period. On average, unused capacity increased from 13% in 2000 to 18% in 2010, indicating a growing gap between available resources and their actual utilization. This underutilization was not limited to physical capacity; a significant proportion of PDHs also failed to fully utilize their operating budgets, with the percentage increasing from 21% in 2000 to 26% in 2010. These trends suggest that systemic inefficiencies, rather than resource scarcity alone, are the primary drivers of underutilization. Factors such as inadequate supply chains, poor management practices, and suboptimal allocation of financial resources likely contribute to this issue. The implications of underutilized PDHs extend beyond inefficiencies in resource use. When district hospitals fail to operate at fll capacity, they are unable to meet the healthcare needs of their catchment populations, leading to unmet demand and increased reliance on tertiary hospitals. This not only exacerbates inequities in healthcare access but also places additional strain on higher-level facilities, which are often ill-equipped to handle the resulting patient load. Addressing the systemic barriers to CU in PDHs is therefore essential for enhancing the overall performance of Tunisia’s healthcare system. This study also highlights the potential role of social health insurance (SHI) as a mechanism for improving CU in PDHs. Currently, SHI in Tunisia primarily serves as a financing mechanism, reimbursing costs for services provided by both public and private healthcare providers. However, reforming SHI to function as a direct purchaser of healthcare services from PDHs could create financial incentives for these facilities to improve efficiency and quality of care. By linkig reimbursement to performance metrics such as CU, SHI colud encourage PDHs to optimize resource use and better align their services with the needs of their populations. In conclusion, this study underscores the urgent need to address the systemic inefficiencies that contribute to underutilization in Tunisia’s PDHs. By employing a dual DEA approach, it provides a comprehensivve assessment of CU and identifies specific areas for intervention. The findings highlight the importance of improving resource allocation, enhancing management practices, and reforming financing mechanisms to ensure that PDHs can fulfill their critical role in delivering equitable and efficient healthcare services. The analysis utilized datta from 101 PDHs in 2000 and 94 PDHs in 2010. These hospitals represent nearly the entirety of Tunisia’s public district hospital ntwork during the respective years, excluding a small number of facilities for which complete data were unavailable. The study relied on secondary data collected from official health sector reports, hospital financial records, and patient care statistics published by the Tunisian Ministry of Health. The dataset included information on hospital inputs (e.g., the number of medical and non-medical staff, the number of hospital beds, and the operating budget) and outputs (e.g., the number of inpatient admissions, outpatient visits, and surgical procedures performed). To measure capacity utilization, the dual DEA model was applied under the assumption of variable returns to scale (VRS). This assumption was deemed appropriate, given the diverse sizes and operating conditions of PDHs across Tunisia. The dual model incorporates constraints on input and output shadow prices, allowing for the evaluation of how efficiently hospitals convert their available resources into healthcare services while accounting for any underutilization of resources or unmet demand for services. Specifically, the CU scroe for each hospital was calculated as the ratio of observed output to the maximum feasiible output that could be produced with the available inputs, as determined by the DEA model. This dual approach allowed for the identification of both over-resourced hospitals and those failing to meet the population’s healthcare demands. To ensure the robustness of the results, sensitivity analyses were conducted by varying the weights assigned to inputs and outputs in the DEA model. Finally, the study evaluated the relationship between CU and financial performance by analyzing the extent to which hospitals underutilized their operating budgets. This was done by comparing the actual expenditure for each hospital with the budget allocated by the government. Hospitals that spent significantly less than their allocated budget were flagged as underutilizing their financial resources, and their CU scores were examined to determine wheether financial underutilization correlated with overall capacity underutilization. The global healthcare landscape is confronted with a twofold challenge: ensuring that healthcare services are accessible to all, while optimizing the use of resources. This predicament is especially pronounced in low- and middle-income countries, where financial and human resource constraints, compounded by systemic inefficiencies, further exacerbate the issue. Tunisia, a nation in North Africa with a predominantly public healthcare system, epitomizes this challenge. Notwithstanding significant investments in healthcare infrastructure, including the establishment of public district hospitals, there is mounting evidence to suggest that these facilities are not functioning at optimal levels. This underutilization of healthcare resources is a pressing concern, as it underscores inefficiencies within the system and raises questions about the capacity of public district hospitals to cater to the healthcare needs of their target population. 

Public district hospitals occupy a crucial position within Tunisia's healthcare delivery system, designed to provide essential curative and preventive services to populations within their catchment areas, particularly in underserved and rural regions. These hospitals are intended to serve as the primary point of referral for primary healthcare centers, bridging the gap between primary care and more specialized tertiary hospitals. However, the effectiveness of public district hospitals in fulfilling this role has been increasingly called into question. Reports of prolonged waiting times, inadequate staffing, shortages of medical supplies, and subpar quality of care have contributed to a decline in public trust in these facilities. Consequently, many patients opt to bypass public district hospitals in favor of tertiary hospitals or private healthcare providers, thereby exacerbating the underutilization of resources and further straining other components of the healthcare system.

The concept of capacity utilization in healthcare facilities is a vital metric for assessing the efficiency of resource allocation. Capacity utilization refers to the extent to which a hospital's available resources, including personnel, equipment, and infrastructure, are utilized to deliver healthcare services. Low capacity utilization suggests that resources are either idle or underutilized, which may indicate inefficiencies in management, a mismatch between supply and demand, or systemic barriers to access. On the other hand, high capacity utilization may signal overburdened facilities that could compromise the quality of care. Striking the right balance is essential for ensuring both efficiency and equity in healthcare delivery. In the context of Tunisia's public district hospitals, understanding the factors contributing to underutilization is a critical step toward optimizing resource allocation and enhancing overall system performance.

Previous studies on hospital efficiency and capacity utilization have primarily focused on tertiary and specialized hospitals, often overlooking the pivotal role of district-level facilities. Furthermore, many analyses rely on traditional input-output models that fail to capture the complexities of healthcare service delivery, such as the interplay between financial and non-financial resources or the impact of unmet healthcare needs on system performance. This study seeks to address these gaps by employing a dual data envelopment analysis approach to measure capacity utilization in Tunisia's public district hospitals. Data envelopment analysis is a non-parametric method widely used to evaluate the efficiency of decision-making units, such as hospitals, by comparing their performance relative to a frontier of best practices. The dual data envelopment analysis approach used in this study incorporates shadow prices to account for input and output restrictions, providing a more nuanced understanding of how public district hospitals utilize their resources.

This study focuses on two critical time points: the years 2000 and 2010. These years were selected to capture changes in capacity utilization over a decade marked by significant economic, social, and political transformations in Tunisia. The early 2000s were characterized by steady economic growth and increased public investment in healthcare infrastructure, while the latter part of the decade saw mounting socioeconomic challenges, including rising unemployment and social inequality, culminating in the 2011 revolution. By examining capacity utilization in public district hospitals during this period, this study aims to shed light on how these broader contextual factors have influenced the efficiency and effectiveness of district-level healthcare services.

The findings of this study reveal a concerning trend of declining capacity utilization in Tunisia's public district hospitals over the study period. On average, unused capacity increased from 13% in 2000 to 18% in 2010, indicating a growing gap between available resources and their actual utilization. This underutilization was not limited to physical capacity; a significant proportion of public district hospitals also failed to fully utilize their operating budgets, with the percentage increasing from 21% in 2000 to 26% in 2010. These trends suggest that systemic inefficiencies, rather than resource scarcity alone, are the primary drivers of underutilization. Factors such as inadequate supply chains, poor management practices, and suboptimal allocation of financial resources likely contribute to this issue.

The implications of underutilized public district hospitals extend beyond inefficiencies in resource use. When district hospitals fail to operate at full capacity, they are unable to meet the healthcare needs of their catchment populations, leading to unmet demand and increased reliance on tertiary hospitals. This not only exacerbates inequities in healthcare access but also places additional strain on higher-level facilities, which are often ill-equipped to handle the increased demand. The consequences of this underutilization are far-reaching, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to address systemic inefficiencies and optimize resource allocation in public district hospitals. To investigate the issue of underutilization in primary healthcare facilities, this study employed a dual Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) approach to measure CU in 101 primary healthcare facilities in 2000 and 94 primary healthcare facilities in 2010. DEA is a non-parametric method widely used to assess the efficiency of decision-making units (DMUs), such as hospitals, by comparing their inputs and outputs relative to an efficiency frontier [1]. The dual DEA model is particularly well-suited for this study, as it allows for the incorporation of shadow prices and provides insights into both input underutilization and output shortfalls [2]. This approach was chosen to account for the multidimensional nature of hospital performance and to accurately evaluate the extent to which primary healthcare facilities utilize their capacity. The analysis utilized data from official health sector reports, hospital financial records, and patient care statistics published by the Tunisian Ministry of Health. To measure CU, the dual DEA model was applied under the assumption of variable returns to scale (VRS), which was deemed appropriate given the diverse sizes and operating conditions of primary healthcare facilities across Tunisia [4]. The dual model incorporates constraints on input and output shadow prices, allowing for the evaluation of how efficiently hospitals convert their available resources into healthcare services while accounting for any underutilization of resources or unmet demand for services [5]. Specifically, the CU score for each hospital was calculated as the ratio of observed output to the maximum feasible output that could be produced with the available inputs, as determined by the DEA model [6].

In many real-world decision-making tasks, information acquisition plays a central role in determining the quality of the outcomes. Whether in medical diagnosis, fault identification in engineering systems, or interactive troubleshooting scenarios, it is often essential to gather information through a sequence of actions or tests before arriving at an informed decision. The challenge in such settings lies in balancing the cost of information acquisition with the value it brings to the decision-making process. This problem is formally captured by the concept of the value of information (VoI), which aims to quantify the utility of acquiring specific information in terms of its contribution to reducing uncertainty and enabling better decisions. The focus of this paper is to address the optimal VoI problem, where the objective is to sequentially select tests that minimize the total cost while ensuring that the information obtained is sufficient to make near-optimal decisions. Despite the signnificant practical importance of VoI optimization, solving this problem efficiently remains a challenging task. The difficulty arises from the combinatorial nature of the tets selection process, where the goal is to identify an optimal subset of tests from a large set of possible candidates. Traditional approaches to this problem can be broadly categorized into two groups: heuristic methods and exact optimization methods. Heuristic methods, while computationally efficient, often lack theoretical guarantees and may perform suboptimally in practice. On the other hand, exact optimization methods, which aim to find the globalyl optimal solution, typically scale poorly with the number of available tests, as they involve solving problems with exponential complexity wiht respect to the number of tests. Consequently, these methods are infeasible in settings where the test space is large or where decisions need to be made in real-time. A furthher complication arises from the frequent assumption in existing methods that the distribution over test outcomes is knnown a priori. In many practical scenarios, the underlying distribution is either partially known or entirely unknown, necessitating the use of learning-based approaches to estimate the distribution dynamically. This introduces an additional layer of complexity, as the decision-making process must now account for the uncertainty in the distribution while simultaneously optimizing the VoI. In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing a novel online learning framework for optimizing the VoI in sequential decision-making tasks. Our approach is motivated by the need for computational efficiency, strong theoretical guarantees, and adaptability to settings where the distribution over test outcomes is unknown. We make two key contributions. First, under the assumption that the distribuion over hypotheses is known, we develop a dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy that enables efficient information acquisition. This strategy leverages sampling methods to approximate the optimal decision-making process and ensures that a near-optimal decision can be identified with high probability. Theoretical analysis of this approach demonstrates that the required number of samples grows only logarithmically with the desired confidence level, making the method highly scalable. Second, we extend our frameowrk to the more general case where the distribution parameters are unknown. For this setting, we propose an online learning algorithm based on posterior sampling, which progressively refinnes the distribution estimates while minimizing the regret associated with suboptimal decisions. Our regret analysis establishes rigorous bounds on the expected performance of the algorithm, providing theoretical assurances about its effectiveness. ### Related Work The problem of optimizing the VoI has been studied extensively in the literature, with applications spanning a wide range of domains. Early work on VoI optimization focused on developing heuristic approaches, such as myopic strategies that select tests greedily based on their immediate expected utility [1, 2]. While computationally efficient, these methods often fail to account for the long-term impact of teest selections, leading to suboptimal outcomes in complex decision-making scenarios. Exact optimization methods, such as those based on dynamic programming [3], offer a principled alternative by explicitly modeling the sequential nature of the decision-making process. However, these methods are computationally prohibitive in practice due to the exponential growth of the state space with the number of tests. Recent advances in approximate dynamic programming and Monte Carlo tree search have shown promise in mitigating this issue [4, 5], but their applicability remains limited to problems with relatively small test spaces. In parallel, significant progress has been made in Bayesian experimental design, where the goal is to select informative experiments under a probabilistic model [6, 7]. These approaches typically assume a known prior distribution over the outcomes and aim to maximize information gain or minimize posterior uncertainty. However, their reliance on a fixed prior limits their applicability in settings where the distribution is unknown or needs to be learned adaptively. Several studies have explored multi-armed bandit formulations of the problem [8, 9], where tests are treated as arms, and the objective is to minimize regret. The realm of statistical inference is a vital cornerstone in a diverse array of scientific and engineering disciplines, encompassing signal processing, imaging, machine learning, and communications, among others. A significant proportion of these applications can be unified under a broad framework, which involves the extraction of structured signals from measurements that are often indirect and contaminated with noise. Over the past few decades, the intersection of high-dimensional statistical analysis, linear transformations, and nonlinear probabilistic sensing has emerged as a fertile ground for research, yielding profound theoretical insights and the development of highly efficient algorithms. This study delves into the statistical physics underpinning such inference problems, encompassing both linear and bilinear contexts, and examines the associated challenges, phase transitions, and algorithmic solutions that arise within these frameworks.

The classic problem of linear inference, exemplified by compressed sensing, has undergone extensive scrutiny in recent years. Compressed sensing has revolutionized the field by demonstrating that sparse signals can be accurately reconstructed from a subset of linear measurements, provided that the sensing matrix satisfies specific structural requirements [1, 2]. This paradigm shift has had a profound impact on a variety of fields, including medical imaging, radar signal processing, and wireless communications. Theoretical understanding of compressed sensing has been significantly enriched by the incorporation of tools from high-dimensional probability theory and statistical physics, notably the replica method and belief propagation algorithms [3, 4]. These analytical tools have provided invaluable insights into the fundamental limits of signal recovery, the geometric structure of the solution space, and the computational complexity associated with the algorithms employed.

Generalized linear models extend the scope of traditional compressed sensing by incorporating a nonlinear function that maps the linear combination of signal components to the observed data. This extension is motivated by a plethora of practical applications, including logistic regression in machine learning, signal recovery in non-Gaussian noise environments, and phase retrieval in optical imaging systems [5]. The introduction of nonlinearity in these models presents additional challenges, as it renders the posterior distribution of the signal highly non-Gaussian, thus necessitating the development of sophisticated approximation techniques for efficient inference. 

Bilinear inference problems, which have been the focus of more recent research endeavors, involve the recovery of two sets of variables that are coupled through measurements that depend bilinearly on these unknowns. Examples of such problems include blind source separation, matrix factorization, and matrix completion, which have applications in diverse domains such as collaborative filtering, recommendation systems, and genomics [6, 7]. A distinctive feature of bilinear problems is the non-convex nature of the optimization landscape, characterized by multiple local minima and saddle points, which poses significant challenges for determining the conditions under which efficient recovery is feasible and when computational hardness arises. 

The Bayesian framework offers a principled approach to inference in high-dimensional problems by incorporating prior knowledge regarding the signal structure and systematically accounting for uncertainty. However, the computation of the posterior distribution in high dimensions is combinatorially demanding due to the curse of dimensionality. Belief propagation, a message-passing algorithm grounded in graphical models, has emerged as a powerful tool for approximate Bayesian inference [8]. By exploiting the sparse interactions in factorized distributions, belief propagation mitigates the computational burden, enabling efficient sampling and marginalization even for large-scale problems.

Statistical physics provides a complementary perspective on high-dimensional inference, leveraging concepts such as energy landscapes, free energy, and phase transitions, originally developed for disordered systems, to study inference problems [9]. The replica method, in particular, offers a non-rigorous yet remarkably accurate framework for characterizing the asymptotic behavior of inference algorithms and determining the fundamental limits of recoverability. A key insight gleaned from statistical physics is the existence of sharp phase transitions that demarcate regions of parameter space where recovery is facile, challenging, or fundamentally impossible. These transitions arise due to changes in the geometry of the underlying energy landscape, which can exhibit phases of convexity, ruggedness, or complete fragmentation.

This research builds upon the interplay between Bayesian inference, message-passing algorithms, and the statistical physics of high-dimensional systems. The contributions of this work can be broadly categorized into three primary areas. Firstly, we apply established inference algorithms to a variety of practical problems, underscoring their utility and uncovering novel insights. These applications include community detection in networks, superposition coding for communication systems, and an innovative imaging system that necessitates the solution of a generalized linear model. Secondly, we introduce a novel message-passing algorithm tailored to the problem of blind sensor calibration, a challenging bilinear inference task. This algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance by efficiently exploiting the structural properties of the problem and incorporating prior information. Thirdly, we conduct a theoretical analysis of two pivotal problems: matrix compressed sensing and the instabilities that arise in Bayesian bilinear inference algorithms. Utilizing tools from statistical physics, we characterize the phase transitions in these problems and elucidate the conditions under which inference is computationally tractable.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: we will delve into the intricacies of our contributions, exploring the theoretical foundations, algorithmic developments, and practical applications of statistical inference, with a particular emphasis on the intersection of statistical physics, Bayesian inference, and high-dimensional data analysis. By examining the theoretical underpinnings and practical implications of these interdisciplinary approaches, this study aims to contribute to the advancement of statistical inference methodologies, ultimately enhancing our capacity to extract meaningful information from complex, high-dimensional data sets. 

Furthermore, the exploration of phase transitions in high-dimensional inference problems, facilitated by the lens of statistical physics, offers profound insights into the fundamental limits and computational tractability of these problems. The characterization of these transitions, which demarcate the boundaries between regions of easy, hard, and impossible recovery, is pivotal for the development of efficient algorithms tailored to specific inference tasks. Moreover, the application of belief propagation and other message-passing algorithms to a wide range of problems, including community detection, superposition coding, and blind sensor calibration, underscores the versatility and utility of these methodologies in tackling complex inference challenges.

In conclusion, this research endeavors to contribute meaningfully to the evolving landscape of statistical inference, by integrating theoretical insights from statistical physics, Bayesian inference, and high-dimensional data analysis. Through the development of novel algorithms, the application of established methodologies to new domains, and the theoretical analysis of fundamental limits and phase transitions, this study aims to enhance our understanding of the intricate mechanisms underlying high-dimensional inference problems. Ultimately, the advancements in statistical inference facilitated by this research will have far-reaching implications for a broad spectrum of scientific and engineering disciplines, enabling more accurate, efficient, and reliable extraction of information from complex data sets.

The work is compartmentalized into six discrete sections, each concentrating on a distinct facet of inference problems. The application of belief propagation and related algorithms to practical problems is the focal point of the third section. Here, the authors immerse themselves in the specifics of community detection, superposition codes, and imaging, highlighting the adaptability and efficacy of message-passing algorithms in these domains. The discussion on community detection, for instance, illustrates how belief propagation can be employed to identify clusters or communities within complex networks, a problem of significant interest in social network analysis and epidemiology. The fourth section presents a novel message-passing algorithm designed for blind sensor calibration, a challenging problem where both the signal of interest and the calibration parameters of the sensors are unknown.
