The land plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA) is a key regulator of various physiological processes, including seed dormancy, stomatal closure, and adaptation to environmental stresses such as drought, salinity, and low temperature [1,2]. In these organisms, ABA is recognized by PYR/PYL/RCAR receptors, which in turn inhibit type 2C protein phosphatases, leading to the activation of SnRK2 kinases and downstream transcriptional programs [3,4]. However, ABA is not exclusive to land plants, as it is also synthesized by a diverse range of organisms outside the land plant lineage, including algae, fungi, bacteria, and metazoans, where it has been implicated in stress responses, development, and immune responses [5,6]. The presence of ABA in organisms that lack the canonical PYR/PYL/RCAR receptors suggests that ABA perception and signaling mechanisms are more diverse than those found in angiosperms, and that ancient ABA-responsive pathways may still be awaiting discovery [7].

Tetrapyrroles, which include chlorophyll, heme, siroheme, and phycobilin chromophores, are essential for photosynthesis, respiration, and redox metabolism. In photosynthetic eukaryotes, the tetrapyrrole biosynthesis pathway commences with the formation of 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) from glutamate in plastids, followed by a series of enzyme-catalyzed reactions that ultimately yield protoporphyrinogen IX (Proto IX) [8]. The pathway then diverges, with ferrochelatase (FeCh) inserting Fe²⁺ to form protoheme, and magnesium-chelatase (comprising the ChlH, ChlD, and ChlI subunits) inserting Mg²⁺ to form Mg-protoporphyrin IX (Mg-Proto IX), the first committed intermediate in chlorophyll synthesis [9]. Due to the photoreactive nature of free tetrapyrrole intermediates, which can generate reactive oxygen species, the flux through the pathway must be tightly coordinated with demand. Regulation of the pathway occurs at multiple levels, including transcriptional control by light and circadian cues, feedback inhibition of ALA synthesis by heme, and post-translational control of glutamyl-tRNA reductase stability [10,11].

Tetrapyrrole intermediates, such as Mg-Proto IX and heme, have also been proposed to act as retrograde signals between plastids and the nucleus, although the details of this process remain the subject of debate [12,13]. Heme occupies a unique position as both a prosthetic group and a signaling molecule, with unbound or loosely associated "regulatory" heme modulating transcription, translation, ion channel activity, and protein stability in various organisms [14,15]. Control of the size of this labile heme pool is therefore physiologically important and may be achieved by regulating synthesis, degradation, export, or sequestration by heme-binding proteins.

The unicellular red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae has emerged as a valuable model organism for studying tetrapyrrole metabolism and its regulation. This alga inhabits acidic hot springs and has a minimal cellular organization, with a single nucleus, one mitochondrion, and one chloroplast [16,17]. Its genome is small and fully sequenced, with few introns and limited gene redundancy, making it an ideal system for genetic and biochemical analysis [18,19]. The cell division of C. merolae can be synchronized by light–dark cycles, and efficient transformation and gene-targeting methods are available, allowing for precise manipulation of gene expression and function [20]. Studies in C. merolae have shown that heme plays a critical role in regulating cell-cycle progression, with heme synthesized in plastids and exported to the cytosol promoting entry into the cell cycle, and inhibition of heme synthesis or sequestration of free heme delaying or blocking cell-cycle initiation [21,22]. This observation has placed tetrapyrrole metabolism directly within the regulatory network governing proliferation in this alga.

Interestingly, C. merolae responds to exogenous ABA, despite lacking obvious homologs of the canonical PYR/PYL/RCAR receptors [23]. ABA treatment causes accumulation of heme and delays cell-cycle initiation, suggesting a complex interplay between ABA signaling, heme metabolism, and cell-cycle control. A recent study indicated that this arrest is not simply the consequence of heme shortage, as ABA induces tryptophan-rich sensory protein-related protein O (TspO), which binds heme and thereby titrates the unbound, signaling-competent heme pool [24]. This model accounts for the apparent paradox of increased heme content accompanied by cell-cycle inhibition but leaves open the question of how ABA increases total heme in the first place. Plausible explanations include enhanced synthesis, reduced consumption by competing pathways, or decreased turnover. Because the heme and chlorophyll branches share Proto IX, the relative activities of FeCh and magnesium-chelatase are expected to determine partitioning of the common precursor, so ABA-dependent changes in the expression of these and other biosynthetic genes could alter the distribution of tetrapyrroles.

Although ABA is known to influence tetrapyrrole metabolism in land plants, for example by affecting the expression of genes such as *CHLH*, which has been reported to encode a candidate ABA-binding protein [25,26], little is known about how ABA modulates the tetrapyrrole pathway in algae. Therefore, the aim of the present study was to examine whether the ABA-induced accumulation of heme in C. merolae can be explained by transcriptional regulation of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes. We quantified transcript levels of genes encoding enzymes across the pathway, including the FeCh and magnesium-chelatase subunits, after ABA addition, and measured the cellular contents of heme, Mg-Proto IX, and Proto IX under identical conditions. By relating changes in transcript levels and metabolite contents, we sought to elucidate the mechanisms underlying ABA-induced changes in tetrapyrrole metabolism in C. merolae.

To investigate the effects of ABA on tetrapyrrole metabolism in C. merolae, we first examined the expression of genes involved in the tetrapyrrole biosynthesis pathway. We found that ABA treatment led to increased transcript levels of several genes, including those encoding FeCh and magnesium-chelatase subunits. We also observed changes in the cellular contents of heme, Mg-Proto IX, and Proto IX, which suggested that ABA treatment altered the partitioning of tetrapyrroles between the heme and chlorophyll branches. Our results indicate that ABA-induced changes in tetrapyrrole metabolism in C. merolae are mediated by transcriptional regulation of biosynthetic genes, and that the relative activities of FeCh and magnesium-chelatase play a key role in determining the distribution of tetrapyrroles.

The finding that ABA treatment leads to increased transcript levels of genes involved in the tetrapyrrole biosynthesis pathway in C. merolae is consistent with previous studies in land plants, which have shown that ABA can regulate the expression of genes involved in tetrapyrrole metabolism [25,26]. However, the mechanisms underlying ABA-induced changes in tetrapyrrole metabolism in algae are not well understood, and our study provides new insights into the regulation of this pathway in C. merolae. Our results suggest that ABA treatment leads to increased synthesis of heme, which is then sequestered by TspO, leading to a decrease in the unbound, signaling-competent heme pool. This decrease in signaling-competent heme leads to delays in cell-cycle initiation, highlighting the importance of tetrapyrrole metabolism in regulating cell-cycle progression in C. merolae.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that ABA-induced changes in tetrapyrrole metabolism in C. merolae are mediated by transcriptional regulation of biosynthetic genes, and that the relative activities of FeCh and magnesium-chelatase play a key role in determining the distribution of tetrapyrroles. Our findings provide new insights into the regulation of tetrapyrrole metabolism in algae and highlight the importance of this pathway in regulating cell-cycle progression. Hypoparathyroidism is a relatively uncommon disorder of the endocrine system, marked by abnormally low levels of calcium in the blood, elevated phosphate levels, and insufficient or inappropriate production of parathyroid hormone (PTH) [1,2]. The majority of cases arise from damage to or surgical removal of the parathyroid glands during operations on the neck, which can precipitate a range of complications. Nonetheless, hypoparathyroidism can also result from non-surgical factors, including autoimmune disorders, genetic conditions, and diseases that infiltrate various organs. In certain instances, the condition is classified as sporadic idiopathic hypoparathyroidism (SIH) when no underlying surgical, familial, syndromic, or autoimmune cause can be pinpointed. SIH is a comparatively prevalent form of non-surgical hypoparathyroidism in numerous regions, including the Indian subcontinent, where it is frequently diagnosed in individuals lacking a clear underlying cause [3]. Conventionally, the management of hypoparathyroidism entails the administration of calcium supplements and active vitamin D analogues, which can help alleviate symptoms associated with low calcium levels. However, this therapeutic approach does not replicate the physiological effects of PTH, and patients may continue to experience fluctuations in calcium levels, increased excretion of calcium in the urine, and a persistent elevation of the calcium-phosphate product [4]. This can have significant repercussions for mineral metabolism and vascular health, as disrupted calcium and phosphate homeostasis contributes to the calcification of vascular tissues and increased stiffness of the arteries. For example, in chronic kidney disease, elevated phosphate levels and an increased calcium-phosphate product can promote the transformation of vascular smooth muscle cells into bone-like cells and the deposition of hydroxyapatite in the arterial wall, leading to increased mortality due to cardiovascular disease [5,6]. Even in individuals with normal kidney function, higher serum phosphate and calcium concentrations within the normal range have been linked to the calcification of coronary arteries and increased risk of cardiovascular events [7,8]. Furthermore, PTH itself may exert influence on the cardiovascular system, as PTH receptors are expressed in heart muscle cells, endothelial cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells, and PTH has been shown to have vasodilatory effects and other impacts on vascular tone [9]. Primary hyperparathyroidism, for instance, is associated with high blood pressure, thickening of the left ventricle, impaired endothelial function, and increased thickness of the carotid intima-media [10,11]. However, the cardiovascular consequences of PTH deficiency are less clearly defined. The absence of PTH, combined with prolonged exposure to calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D analogues, could plausibly impact the vascular system, but existing evidence from experiments and clinical studies is inconsistent. Some research suggests that low PTH levels may be associated with vascular calcification or adverse cardiovascular outcomes, whereas other studies have found no increased cardiovascular risk [12,13]. Studies examining cardiovascular morbidity in hypoparathyroidism have yielded mixed results. Data from registries in Denmark and Sweden reported increased overall morbidity, with higher risks of kidney disease, infection, and, in certain analyses, cardiovascular disease, particularly in non-surgical hypoparathyroidism [14,15]. Other cohorts found no increase in cardiovascular mortality, and some reported a lower risk of ischemic events in postsurgical disease [16]. Abnormal calcification is common in hypoparathyroidism, particularly in the basal ganglia, and has also been observed in the kidneys, heart valves, and blood vessels [17]. Small-scale imaging studies have reported impaired endothelial function, increased arterial stiffness, and altered left ventricular function in treated patients [18,19]. However, these studies are heterogeneous in terms of etiology, treatment, and methodology, and many combined postsurgical and non-surgical cases. Data specific to SIH, in which the disease is typically long-standing and not complicated by neck surgery or autoimmune comorbidity, are scarce. Given the uncertainty surrounding vascular risk in hypoparathyroidism, the lack of data in SIH, and the dearth of information on aortic and renal arterial involvement, further research is required in this area. The thickness of the intima-media layer, measured by high-resolution ultrasonography, is a validated, non-invasive indicator of subclinical atherosclerosis and future cardiovascular risk. The carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) is the most extensively studied site, and increased CIMT predicts myocardial infarction and stroke independently of traditional risk factors [20,21]. Atherosclerosis is a diffuse process, and measuring intima-media thickness at additional vascular sites may provide complementary information. Abdominal aortic intima-media thickness (AIMT) correlates with the burden of coronary disease and conventional risk factors, and may reflect early atherosclerotic changes even when CIMT is normal [22]. Renal artery intima-media thickness (RIMT) is a less commonly used measure that has been associated with hypertension, metabolic syndrome, and chronic kidney disease, and may indicate renal vascular involvement [23]. Evaluating multiple arterial territories in the same patient therefore provides a more comprehensive assessment of vascular involvement than a single site. Reports on intima-media thickness in hypoparathyroidism are limited, and a few studies have examined CIMT in postsurgical or mixed cohorts, yielding conflicting findings. Data on aortic and renal arterial intima-media thickness in any form of hypoparathyroidism are, to our knowledge, lacking [19,24]. In SIH, the combination of lifelong PTH deficiency and long-term calcium and vitamin D therapy, with frequent biochemical fluctuations, offers a unique model in which to examine the vascular effects of altered mineral homeostasis in the absence of confounding by surgery or autoimmune disease. The objective of our study was to measure CIMT, AIMT, and RIMT in patients with SIH and compare them with healthy controls, and to investigate whether clinical and biochemical parameters, including serum calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D levels, as well as PTH levels, are associated with intima-media thickness in this population. We also aimed to explore the relationship between intima-media thickness and cardiovascular risk factors, such as blood pressure, lipid profiles, and markers of inflammation, in patients with SIH. Furthermore, we sought to examine the impact of long-term calcium and vitamin D therapy on vascular health in SIH, and to investigate whether any potential vascular effects are mediated by changes in mineral metabolism or other mechanisms. By addressing these questions, our study aimed to contribute to a better understanding of the vascular consequences of hypoparathyroidism, particularly in the context of SIH, and to inform the development of more effective therapeutic strategies for managing this condition. The study's findings have important implications for the management of hypoparathyroidism, particularly in terms of monitoring and treating cardiovascular risk factors, and highlight the need for further research into the vascular effects of altered mineral homeostasis in this population. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the relationship between hypoparathyroidism and cardiovascular disease will enable clinicians to provide more effective care for patients with this condition, and to reduce the risk of cardiovascular complications in this vulnerable population. 

In conclusion, hypoparathyroidism is a complex disorder with significant implications for mineral metabolism and vascular health. The condition is characterized by low calcium levels, elevated phosphate levels, and insufficient or inappropriate production of PTH, and can result from a range of causes, including surgical and non-surgical factors. The management of hypoparathyroidism typically involves the administration of calcium supplements and active vitamin D analogues, but this therapeutic approach does not replicate the physiological effects of PTH, and patients may continue to experience fluctuations in calcium levels and increased cardiovascular risk. Further research is required to fully understand the vascular consequences of hypoparathyroidism, particularly in the context of SIH, and to inform the development of more effective therapeutic strategies for managing this condition. By examining the relationship between hypoparathyroidism and cardiovascular disease, and by investigating the impact of long-term calcium and vitamin D therapy on vascular health, our study aimed to contribute to a better understanding of the vascular effects of altered mineral homeostasis in this population, and to highlight the need for further research into the management of this complex and multifaceted disorder. The complexities of hypoparathyroidism, a condition characterized by an insufficient production of parathyroid hormone (PTH), have been the subject of extensive investigation, owing to its multifaceted implications on vascular health. Previous studies have underscored the associations between various factors, including phosphate levels, the calcium-phosphate product, PTH concentrations, the duration of the disease, and the intensity of treatment, with intima-media thickness (IMT) at critical vascular sites [1]. Our investigation, conducted within the Department of Endocrinology at a tertiary care teaching hospital in northern India, was specifically designed to delve into the vascular repercussions of sporadic idiopathic hypoparathyroidism (SIH) and to explore the potential interrelations between clinical, biochemical parameters, and IMT in this patient demographic. The protocol for this study received approval from the institutional ethics committee, and all participants provided their written informed consent prior to enrollment, in adherence to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki.

The design and setting of our study were deliberately chosen to yield a comprehensive understanding of the vascular effects of SIH and to elucidate the potential relationships between various clinical and biochemical indices and IMT in patients with this condition. Ultimately, the findings of our study are anticipated to offer invaluable insights into the cardiovascular sequelae of PTH deficiency and the potential advantages of early intervention and treatment in patients with SIH. By scrutinizing the relationships between clinical and biochemical parameters and IMT, we aim to identify potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets for the prevention and treatment of cardiovascular disease in hypoparathyroidism, thereby improving the management and outcomes of patients with SIH and reducing their risk of cardiovascular complications.

Hypoparathyroidism is a complex disorder associated with significant cardiovascular risks, and the paucity of data on SIH, particularly regarding its impact on aortic and renal arterial health, underscores the need for further research in this area. Our study seeks to address these knowledge gaps by providing a comprehensive understanding of the vascular effects of SIH. The implications of our research are profound, as they hold the potential to inform the development of novel treatment strategies and management guidelines for patients with SIH. Enhancing our understanding of the cardiovascular consequences of PTH deficiency and the benefits of early intervention and treatment can lead to a reduction in the risk of cardiovascular complications and improved patient outcomes. Moreover, our study's findings are expected to have broader implications for the management of hypoparathyroidism and other disorders of mineral metabolism, highlighting the necessity for a comprehensive and multidisciplinary approach to patient care.

Future research should focus on fully elucidating the relationships between PTH deficiency, mineral metabolism, and cardiovascular disease through large-scale, longitudinal studies examining the effects of PTH deficiency on cardiovascular outcomes and the potential benefits of early intervention and treatment. Additionally, molecular mechanism studies that explore the interplay between PTH, mineral metabolism, and cardiovascular disease are essential for identifying therapeutic targets and informing the development of new treatments. By continuing to advance our understanding of hypoparathyroidism and its cardiovascular consequences, we can improve patient management and outcomes, reducing the risk of cardiovascular complications.

Our study population consisted of 30 consecutive patients with sporadic idiopathic hypoparathyroidism who attended our outpatient clinic. The diagnosis of hypoparathyroidism was established based on persistent hypocalcemia, defined as an albumin-corrected serum calcium level below the reference range, accompanied by hyperphosphatemia or high-normal phosphate levels, and low or inappropriately normal intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH) levels, with a disease duration of at least one year [1]. To be classified as idiopathic, patients had to have no history of neck surgery, radiation, or infiltrative disease, and no evidence of syndromic features, a family history of hypoparathyroidism, or other autoimmune endocrinopathies that might suggest an autoimmune polyglandular syndrome. Patients with a known genetic cause of their hypoparathyroidism, such as DiGeorge syndrome or autosomal dominant hypocalcemia, were excluded.

Other exclusion criteria included age below 18 years, diabetes mellitus, established hypertension, dyslipidemia requiring treatment, chronic kidney disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate <60 mL/min/1.73 m²), chronic liver disease, smoking, known coronary or peripheral vascular disease, vasculitis, malabsorption, and the use of medications that could influence vascular or mineral metabolism, except for standard hypoparathyroidism therapy (e.g., glucocorticoids, bisphosphonates, thiazides). The control group comprised healthy volunteers recruited from hospital staff and relatives of patients, matched to the patients for age, sex, and body mass index (BMI). These controls had normal serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH levels and met the same exclusion criteria as the patients.

To estimate the required sample size, we referenced published data regarding carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) differences between hypoparathyroidism and control populations [2], assuming a mean difference of 0.07 mm, a standard deviation of 0.09 mm, a power of 80%, and a two-sided alpha of 0.05. Based on these calculations, we aimed to recruit approximately 26 participants per group. Ultimately, our study's outcomes are poised to contribute significantly to the existing body of knowledge on hypoparathyroidism, guiding future clinical practice and research endeavors aimed at mitigating the cardiovascular risks associated with this condition. To mitigate potential participant attrition and technical issues, our study recruited 30 individuals. Each participant underwent an exhaustive clinical assessment, utilizing a standardized template to gather information on demographic characteristics, duration of illness, age at diagnosis, symptoms, seizure history, and the dosage and duration of calcium and active vitamin D (calcitriol or alfacalcidol) treatments. The cumulative exposure to these therapies was estimated through a combination of medical records and patient recall. Standardized methods were employed to measure anthropometric parameters, including height, weight, waist circumference, and body mass index (BMI), while blood pressure was recorded as the average of two readings taken in a seated position after a 5-minute period of rest. Biochemical analyses were performed on fasting venous blood samples collected in the morning, and included measurements of serum total calcium, albumin, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, creatinine, glucose, and lipid profiles (including total cholesterol, triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol) using standardized colorimetric methods on an automated analyzer. Calcium levels were adjusted for albumin concentration. Intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels were determined using electrochemiluminescence immunoassay, and the calcium-phosphate product was calculated. Additionally, 24-hour urinary calcium and creatinine levels were measured in patients. Where applicable, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein was determined using immunoturbidimetry. To evaluate long-term biochemical control, mean serum calcium and phosphate levels over the preceding year were extracted from clinic records. Ultrasonographic measurements of intima-media thickness were performed by an experienced radiologist blinded to the participant's group allocation and clinical and biochemical details. A high-resolution ultrasound machine equipped with a 7-12 MHz linear array transducer was used for carotid artery measurements, while a 3.5-5 MHz curvilinear probe was employed for abdominal aorta and renal artery measurements. Participants were examined in the supine position after an overnight fast, and the examination was conducted in a quiet environment. Carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) was measured bilaterally with the head slightly extended and turned 45° away from the side being examined. In accordance with established guidelines [3], CIMT was measured on the far wall of the distal 1 cm of the common carotid artery, proximal to the bulb, in plaque-free segments, as the distance between the leading edge of the lumen-intima interface and the leading edge of the media-adventitia interface. Three measurements on each side were taken, and the mean of the right and left averages was used for analysis. Focal wall thickening exceeding 1.5 mm was defined as plaque and was not included in the measurement. Aortic intima-media thickness (AIMT) was measured in the abdominal aorta, imaged longitudinally in the supine position, 1-2 cm proximal to the bifurcation, at the infrarenal level. The thickness of the posterior (far) wall was measured using the same lumen-intima and media-adventitia criteria, as the mean of three measurements [4]. Renal artery intima-media thickness (RIMT) was measured in the main renal arteries, identified by color Doppler from the aorta to the renal hilum. The intima-media thickness of the proximal segment of the renal artery was measured in a longitudinal view of the artery in a plaque-free area, and the average of three measurements from each side was calculated, followed by the mean of both sides. To assess the reproducibility of our measurements, ten randomly selected participants were scanned twice by the same operator on separate days, and the intraobserver coefficient of variation and intraclass correlation coefficient were calculated. The primary outcomes of our study were CIMT, AIMT, and RIMT in patients compared with controls. Secondary outcomes included the comparison of clinical and biochemical parameters between the two groups, as well as the evaluation of potential correlations between intima-media thickness and various clinical and biochemical variables. By investigating these outcomes, we aimed to gain a deeper understanding of the vascular implications of hypoparathyroidism and to explore potential avenues for the prevention and treatment of cardiovascular complications in this patient population. Our study examined the relationship between intima-media thickness values and various clinical and biochemical variables in patients with sporadic idiopathic hypoparathyroidism (SIH). The correlations we examined included those with age, disease duration, body mass index (BMI), blood pressure, lipid levels, mean serum calcium, phosphate, calcium-phosphate product, intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH), 25-hydroxyvitamin D, urinary calcium, and the doses of calcium and vitamin D supplements. To analyze our data, we utilized SPSS (version 23.0, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) for statistical analysis. We first tested the distribution of continuous variables using the Shapiro-Wilk test to determine whether they followed a normal distribution. Normally distributed variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation, while skewed variables are presented as median (interquartile range). Categorical variables, on the other hand, are expressed as numbers and percentages. To compare differences between patients and controls, we used the independent-samples t-test or the Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables, and the chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables. We evaluated correlations between intima-media thickness and clinical and biochemical variables using Pearson's or Spearman's correlation coefficients, as appropriate. A two-sided P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Our research aimed to contribute to the existing body of knowledge on hypoparathyroidism, a condition characterized by the underproduction of parathyroid hormone, which plays a crucial role in regulating calcium and phosphate levels in the body. By examining the relationship between intima-media thickness and various clinical and biochemical variables, we sought to shed light on the vascular implications of hypoparathyroidism and identify potential risk factors for cardiovascular disease in this patient population. The findings of our study have important implications for the management and treatment of hypoparathyroidism, and highlight the need for regular monitoring of cardiovascular risk factors in patients with this condition. Furthermore, our research underscores the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to the management of hypoparathyroidism, involving close collaboration between endocrinologists, cardiologists, and other healthcare professionals. By working together, we can improve our understanding of the complex relationships between hypoparathyroidism, cardiovascular disease, and other comorbidities, and develop effective strategies for preventing and treating cardiovascular complications in this patient population. In conclusion, our study demonstrates the importance of intima-media thickness as a marker of cardiovascular risk in patients with hypoparathyroidism, and highlights the need for further research into the vascular implications of this condition. By exploring the relationships between intima-media thickness, clinical and biochemical variables, and cardiovascular disease, we can gain a deeper understanding of the complex pathophysiology of hypoparathyroidism and develop effective strategies for improving cardiovascular outcomes in this patient population. Future studies should aim to build on our findings, exploring the relationship between intima-media thickness and cardiovascular disease in larger, more diverse populations, and examining the potential benefits of interventions aimed at reducing cardiovascular risk in patients with hypoparathyroidism. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the development of personalized treatment strategies for patients with hypoparathyroidism, tailored to their individual needs and risk profiles. By working together, we can improve the health and wellbeing of patients with hypoparathyroidism, and reduce the burden of cardiovascular disease in this vulnerable population.

Modern distributed file-systems must serve metadata and data at a scale of hundreds of servers while preserving strong consistency and predictable latency. Internally, such systems rely on a small set of services whose state must be consistent despite server crashes, network partitions, and message loss: lock managers, service locators, namespace and configuration stores, and similar components. The standard way to build such services is state machine replication [1], in which replicas apply the same deterministic sequence of commands, with the sequecne agreed upon through a consensus protocol such as Paxos [2], Viewstamped Replication [3], Zab [4], or Raft [5]. Systems such as Chubby [6], ZooKeeper [4], and etcd are built on this pattern, and many distributed file-systems depend on them for their critical state. **Limitations of log-based consensus** The abstraction these protocols provide is a totally ordered, replicated log. This abstraction is general, since any deterministic service can be replicated on top of it, but the generality has a cost. First, the log imposes a single serialization point. Every update, even one touching state unrelated to all other updates, is ordered with respect to every other update. In Raft and Zab, a single leader sequences all writes, so its CPU, network, and storage bandwidth bound system throughput regardless of the number of replicas. Second, log entries must be committed and applied in order. A slow or lost entry delays all subsequent entries (head-of-line blocking), which inflates tail latency. Third, failures are expensive. Leader failure halts the service until a new leader is elected and its log is reconciled with those of the followers. Log truncation, snapshotting, and catch-up of lagging replicas add further complexity and can interfere with foreground operations. Optimizations such as batching, pipelining, and multi-instance Paxos [7] mitigate some of these costs but do not remove the underlying serialization. Many services built atop consensus do not need a general log. A lock manager, a service locator, or a metadata directory is naturally expressed as a collection of independent objects addressed by key. Operations on distinct keys commute, so no ordering between them is required for correctness. Imposing a global order on them creates artificial contention points that serve no semantic purpose. **Our approach** This paper presents Bizur, a consensus algorithm that exposes a key-value interface rather than a replicated log. Bizur partitions the key space into a fixed set of buckets and reaches consensus independently on the state of each bucket. Each bucket has its own elected leader and its own replicated value state, with a versioned, per-bucket election and replication protocol. Operations on different buckets proceed fully in parallel and never wait for one another. Consequently, there is no global log to order, truncate, snapshot, or replay, and no single node whose failure stalls the whole service. Leadership is distributed across the cluster, so load is spread among servers. When a server fails, only the buckets it led must elect a new leader, and recovery of each bucket is independent and lazy, requiring the reading and repaair of a single bucket's state rather than the reconstruction of a whole log. Bizur provides strong consistency, specifically linearizable reads and writes on individual keys, under the usual asynchronous crash-recovery model with message loss, in which progress requires a majority of replicas to be available. We do not claim to support multi-key transactions as primitives; we argue that for the targeted class of services, per-key atomicity is sufficient, and that where it is not, higher-level mechanisms can be layered on top. **Context: a scalable file-system** Bizur was designed as the foundation for the metadata and configuration services of a distributed file-system that scales to hundreds of servers and delivers millions of IOPS of both data and metadata with consistently low latency. In such a deployment, a log-based service would becoe the bottleneck as the cluster grows, and a leader failure wuld produce a visible latency spike for clients. Building the system on Bizur let the coordination layer scale with the rest of the file-system and degrade gracefully, rather than abruptly, during failures. We report our experience and measurements from this setting. **Contributions** This paper makes the following contributions: 1. We identify the artificial contention points that arise when a distributed log is used to replicate services that are inherently key-value based, and we characterize how they affect throughput, latency, and failure handling. 2. We present Bizur, a consensus algorithm that reaches agreement independently per key (at bucket granularity), including its normal-operation protocol, leader election, and rceovery procedures, and we argue its safety properties. 3. We describe how Bizur is used within a production distributed file-system and the practical engineering concerns involved, such as bucket sizing, leadership distribution, and persistence. 4. We evaluate Bizur against log-based alternatives, showing higher throughput and lower latency during normal operation, and notably smaller disruption during failures. **Organization** Section 2 reviews background and related wok on consensus and replicated key-value stores. The architecture of contemporary distributed file systems presents substantial hurdles, particularly in terms of efficiently managing metadata and data across hundreds of servers while ensuring robust consistency and reliable latency. At the core of these systems are a limited number of vital components, including lock coordinators, service detectives, namespace and configuration repositories, which must maintain consistency despite server failures, network fragmentations, and message losses. The conventional methodology for constructing such services relies on replicating state machines [1], where identical replicas execute the same deterministic sequence of instructions, with the sequence agreed upon through consensus protocols like Paxos [2], Viewstamped Replication [3], Zab [4], or Raft [5]. Noteworthy examples of systems built using this approach include Chubby [6], ZooKeeper [4], and etcd, which are extensively employed in numerous distributed file systems for managing critical state. Nevertheless, the utilization of log-based consensus protocols in these systems has multiple limitations. The abstraction provided by these protocols is a completely ordered, replicated log, which, while versatile and applicable to any deterministic service, incurs significant costs. Firstly, the log imposes a single point of serialization, where every update is ordered relative to every other update, regardless of whether the update affects state unrelated to other updates. This can result in substantial performance bottlenecks, as observed in Raft and Zab, where a single leader sequences all writes, thus limiting system throughput by its CPU, network, and storage bandwidth, regardless of the number of replicas. Secondly, log entries must be committed and applied sequentially, which can lead to head-of-line blocking, where a slow or lost entry delays all subsequent entries, thereby inflating tail latency. Thirdly, failures are costly, as leader failure halts the service until a new leader is elected and its log is reconciled with those of the followers. Additional complexities, such as log truncation, snapshotting, and catch-up of lagging replicas, can interfere with primary operations and contribute to the overall overhead. Although optimizations like batching, pipelining, and multi-instance Paxos [7] can alleviate some of these costs, they do not eliminate the underlying serialization point. Many services constructed atop consensus protocols do not require a general log. For instance, a lock coordinator, a service detective, or a metadata directory can be naturally represented as a collection of independent objects addressed by key, where operations on distinct keys are commutative, and no ordering between them is necessary for correctness. Imposing a global order on these operations creates artificial contention points that serve no semantic purpose and can significantly impact system performance. This paper introduces Bizur, a novel consensus algorithm that presents a key-value interface rather than a replicated log. Bizur partitions the key space into a fixed set of buckets and achieves consensus independently on the state of each bucket. Each bucket has its own elected leader and its own replicated value state, with a versioned, per-bucket election and replication protocol. This design enables operations on different buckets to proceed entirely in parallel and never wait for one another. As a result, there is no global log to order, truncate, snapshot, or replay, and no single node whose failure stalls the entire service. Leadership is distributed across the cluster, spreading the load among servers and ensuring that the failure of a server only affects the buckets it led, which must then elect a new leader. Recovery of each bucket is independent and lazy, requiring only the reading and repair of a single bucket's state, rather than the reconstruction of a whole log. Bizur provides robust consistency, specifically linearizable reads and writes on individual keys, under the usual asynchronous crash-recovery model with message loss, where progress requires a majority of replicas to be available. While we do not claim to support multi-key transactions as primitives, we argue that for the targeted class of services, per-key atomicity is sufficient, and where it is not, higher-level mechanisms can be layered on top. The development of Bizur was motivated by the need for a scalable and performant coordination layer in a distributed file system that scales to hundreds of servers and delivers millions of IOPS of both data and metadata with consistently low latency. In such a deployment, a log-based service would become the bottleneck as the cluster grows, and a leader failure would produce a visible latency spike for clients. By building the system on Bizur, we were able to create a coordination layer that scales with the rest of the file system and degrades gracefully, rather than abruptly, during failures. We report our experience and measurements from this setting, highlighting the benefits of using Bizur in a real-world distributed file system. This paper makes several key contributions. Firstly, we identify the artificial contention points that arise when a distributed log is used to replicate services that are inherently key-value based and characterize the limitations of log-based consensus protocols in this context. Secondly, we present the design and implementation of Bizur, a novel consensus algorithm that overcomes these limitations by providing a key-value interface and partitioning the key space into independent buckets. Thirdly, we evaluate the performance and scalability of Bizur in a real-world distributed file system, demonstrating its ability to scale with the rest of the system and provide consistently low latency. Finally, we discuss the implications of our work for the design of distributed file systems and the development of scalable and performant coordination layers. By providing a more efficient and scalable consensus algorithm, Bizur has the potential to improve the performance and reliability of a wide range of distributed systems, from cloud storage and databases to social media and online services. As the demand for scalable and performant distributed systems continues to grow, the need for efficient and reliable consensus algorithms like Bizur will become increasingly important. Our work highlights the importance of rethinking the design of consensus protocols and exploring new approaches that can provide better performance and scalability in modern distributed systems. By doing so, we can create more efficient, reliable, and scalable distributed systems that can meet the needs of a rapidly growing and increasingly complex digital landscape. The quest for optimal performance in distributed systems has led to a profound examination of consensus protocols, with a particular focus on their impact on throughput, latency, and failure handling mechanisms. This endeavor has culminated in the development of Bizur, a pioneering consensus algorithm that facilitates agreement on a per-key basis, with each key mapped to a specific bucket, thereby ensuring a granular level of control and efficiency. The Bizur protocol encompasses a multifaceted approach, including a normal-operation protocol designed to optimize performance under typical conditions, a leader election process tailored to minimize latency and maximize throughput, and recovery procedures aimed at ensuring swift mitigation of failures. Furthermore, the safety properties of Bizur have been meticulously evaluated to guarantee the integrity and consistency of the distributed system. 

In addition to its theoretical underpinnings, the practical application of Bizur within a production distributed file system has been explored, highlighting the critical engineering considerations necessary for its successful implementation. These considerations include the optimal sizing of buckets to balance load and reduce overhead, the strategic distribution of leadership roles across servers to prevent bottlenecks, and the implementation of persistence mechanisms to ensure durability in the face of failures. The integration of Bizur into such a system demonstrates its potential to address the limitations inherent in traditional log-based consensus protocols, which often suffer from scalability issues and increased latency due to the sequential nature of their operation.

A comprehensive evaluation of Bizur, comparing its performance against that of log-based alternatives, reveals significant advantages. Notably, Bizur exhibits higher throughput and lower latency during normal operation, attributes that are crucial for supporting high-performance applications. Moreover, in the event of failures, Bizur demonstrates a marked reduction in disruption, ensuring that the system can rapidly recover and resume operation with minimal impact on overall performance. These findings underscore the effectiveness of Bizur in enhancing the performance and scalability of distributed file systems, positioning it as a viable solution for systems requiring high availability and efficiency.

At its core, Bizur is built upon the principles of asynchronous communication, acknowledging that in distributed systems, messages can be lost, delayed, duplicated, or reordered. The protocol assumes a failure model where servers can crash but may subsequently recover with their persistent state intact, excluding Byzantine behavior where nodes may act arbitrarily. Similar to traditional Paxos-style protocols [1,2], Bizur guarantees safety even under conditions of arbitrary asynchrony, although liveness is contingent upon a majority of servers being correct and maintaining mutual connectivity for a sufficient duration. The replicated state managed by Bizur is that of a key-value store, where operations are linearizable on a per-key basis, and cross-key transactions are not considered within the foundational algorithm.

To achieve efficient consensus, the key space in Bizur is partitioned into a fixed number of buckets, denoted as B, which is substantially larger than the number of servers. Each bucket serves as an independent unit of consensus, containing a set of keys, an election state unique to that bucket, and a replication state. The replication of buckets across the same group of servers ensures high availability, with each bucket having at most one leader at any given time. To distribute the load evenly and prevent any single server from becoming a bottleneck, preferred leaders are assigned to buckets in a balanced manner. A critical aspect of Bizur's design is the lack of ordering constraints between buckets, meaning that no total order over operations is maintained across different buckets. This approach diverges from traditional consensus protocols like Multi-Paxos, Zab, and Raft [1–3], which serialize all updates through a single log.

Each replica in the Bizur system maintains detailed information for every bucket, including the key-value pairs associated with that bucket, the highest election term for which the replica has voted (`electid`), the term of the leader that most recently updated the bucket (`lastWrite`), and a version number (`ver`) used to order values within a term. The ordering of values is determined by the pair (`electid`, `ver`), ensuring that updates are properly sequenced and applied. To ensure durability and persistence, all updates to a replica's state are made persistent before any response is sent, safeguarding against data loss in the event of failures.

The leader election process in Bizur is performed independently for each bucket, allowing for concurrent leadership elections without interference between them. When a server seeks to become the leader of a bucket b, it initiates the process by selecting a term that exceeds any previously observed term for that bucket. It then sends a *PleaseVote* request to all replicas, which grant their vote if the proposed term is higher than their stored `electid` for b. Upon voting, a replica persists the new `electid`, replies with its current bucket content and version, and await further instructions. Once a majority of votes is secured, the candidate for leadership adopts the highest-versioned bucket content from the replies as the authoritative state, a process known as the "read-repair" phase. This state is then written back to a majority of replicas under the new term, confirming the candidate's role as the bucket leader. The design of this process ensures that the adopted state encompasses every committed write, as the quorum of votes intersects with every earlier write quorum, thereby guaranteeing consistency.

Bizur's replication protocol is engineered to facilitate efficient and concurrent writes to different buckets without head-of-line blocking, allowing writes to different buckets to proceed independently without delay. For a write operation to key k within bucket b, the leader of b assigns the next version number, disseminates a *Write(b, term, ver, content)* message to all replicas, and awaits acknowledgments from a majority. A replica accepts the write if the term matches its `electid` for b, or if it exceeds the `electid`, prompting the replica to update its `electid`. The operation is considered complete once a majority of replicas have acknowledged it, a process that typically requires a single round trip in the steady state. This mechanism ensures that writes to different buckets can be issued and acknowledged concurrently, without any bucket's write operation impeding the progress of another, thus optimizing overall system throughput and responsiveness.

To guarantee linearizability, even in scenarios where leadership changes may have occurred unnoticed, a leader serving a read request first contacts a majority of replicas to verify its leadership status for the current term. Only after confirmation does it return the local value, ensuring that the returned value is the most recent and consistent with the system's state. This approach obviates the need for synchronized clocks or leases, allowing buckets unaffected by leadership changes to continue serving read and write requests without interruption, while buckets impacted by a failed leader are efficiently re-elected.

In the event of a failure, Bizur's recovery procedures are designed to minimize disruption and rapidly restore the system to a consistent state. By leveraging its bucket-level consensus and independent leader election, Bizur can isolate the impact of failures to specific buckets, allowing other buckets to continue operation without interruption. This capability, combined with its high throughput and low latency, positions Bizur as a critical component in the development of highly performant and resilient distributed file systems. In the event of a failure, our system is engineered to facilitate a swift and efficient recovery process. When a bucket leader failure is detected through heartbeat timeouts, any replica can initiate an election process for the affected bucket. This targeted approach ensures that only the buckets previously led by the failed server undergo recovery, with the scope of recovery being proportional to the data contained within the bucket. As a server recovers, it rejoins the system with its persisted state intact, and any stale content is reconciled in a lazy manner, either when the bucket is next elected or when a write operation from the leader brings the replica up to date. To prevent the formation of recovery hotspots, elections for different buckets are distributed across multiple servers. Furthermore, membership changes are managed through a separate configuration mechanism, which leverages the same bucket-level protocol but utilizes a distinguished configuration bucket. Following reconfiguration, the bucket-to-leader map is rebalanced to ensure optimal system performance. We demonstrate the correctness of our system by establishing invariants on a per-bucket basis [1,2]. Specifically, we show that at most one leader can successfully complete the election process for a given bucket, thereby guaranteeing that the system maintains a consistent and linearizable state. Our approach yields a robust and efficient consensus protocol for replicated key-value stores, emphasizing scalability, fault tolerance, and performance. Achieving consensus and maintaining linearizability are critical for ensuring data consistency and correctness in distributed systems. Bizur addresses these challenges by employing a novel approach to consensus and key management. This section delves into the technical intricacies of Bizur's design and implementation, as well as our methodology for evaluating its performance. At its core, Bizur's consensus protocol ensures that all operations on a given key are confined to a single bucket, thereby guaranteeing linearizability for each key. This is achieved through three primary mechanisms: (1) votes are granted once per term, with a majority required to acknowledge a value; (2) any value acknowledged by a majority in term t is visible to every election quorum in terms greater than t, due to the intersection of quorums; and (3) after a replica votes for term t′, it rejects writes from smaller terms, preventing stale leaders from committing afterwards [1]. These mechanisms, in conjunction with the eventual stabilization of a single candidate per bucket under randomized backoff of election timeouts, as described in [2,3], ensure liveness and linearizability for each key. Furthermore, we observed that Bizur's performance advantage was consistent across various workloads and key distributions, demonstrating its versatility and scalability. In addition to its performance benefits, Bizur also provides strong consistency guarantees, ensuring that all operations on a given key are linearizable and that the system maintains a consistent state even in the presence of failures. Graphs are a natural abstraction for relational data in domains such as social networks, citation networks, biological systems, and recommender systems. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for learning from such data, and models including GCN [1], GraphSAGE [2], GAT [3], and GIN [4] have achieved strong results on node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. Most of these architectures follow a message-passing scheme: each node iteratively aggreates information from its neighbors and transforms the aggregated signal with learnable weights, so that the resulting representation reflects both local topology and node attributes. Despite this progress, the quality of the learned representations dpeends heavily on the input node features. In many real-world graphs, node features are high-dimensional and sparse. Bag-of-words vectors in citation networks, one-hot encoded categorical attributes in e-commerce and social platforms, and user-profile fields in online services all yield feature matrices in which only a small fraction of entries are non-zero. Under such conditions, a standard GNN layer applies a linear transformation to the feature vector and then propagates the result. Each feature therefore contributes to the representation largely independently and additively. This design has two limitations. First, sparse features provide little signal per node, so the estimated weights of rarely active features are noisy and poorly trained. Second, the model cannot directly capture *feature interactions*, namely the joint effect of several features that is not recoverable from their individual effects. For example, in a social network the co-occurrence of two particular interests may be far more indiative of a community than either interest alone. Although stacking nonlinear layers can in principle approximate such interactions, doing so implicitly is inefficient, especially when data are sparse, and it is prone to overfitting and over-smoothing as depth increases [5]. The importance of feature interactions has been well established in other fields. In click-through-rate prediction and recommendation, factorization machines [6], Wide&Deep [7], DeepFM [8], AutoInt [9], and related models explicitly model low-order and high-order interactions among sparse categorical features, with substantial gains over methods that treat features independently. These methods, however, assume that samples are independent and ignore the relational structure connecting them. Conversely, GNNs exploit graph structure but typically lack explicit mechanisms for modeling feature interactions. Several recent works have combind the two directions, for instance by modeling interactions within a graph over feature fields [10] or by ading interaction terms to neighborhood aggregation [11]. Yet these appproaches tend to treat all interactions as equally important, rely on a fixed, global interaction pattern shared across nodes, or are tailored to a specific architecture or task. Because the number of possible interactions grows combinatorially with feature dimension, and because most interactions are uninformative or even harmful, indiscriminately including them introduces noise and computational burden. These observations motivate our central question: *how can we identify and exploit informative feature interactions in a node-specific manner within general GNNs on feature-sparse graphs?* Answering this question raises three challenges. (1) **Informativeness:** among a combinatorially large set of candidate interactions, only a small subset is useful for a given task, and this subset must be selected without manual engineering. (2) **Personalization:** the relevance of an interaction depends on the node and its neighborhood context, so a single global interaction pattern is inadequate. (3) **Compatibility:** the mechanism should integrate with diverse GNN backbones without redesigning their aggregation functions, and should remain scalable on large graphs. To address these challenges, we propose Feature Interaction-aware Graph Neural Networks (FI-GNNs), a plug-and-play framework that enriches node representations with informative feature interactions. FI-GNNs model the interactons among the active features of each node explicitly, and use a personalized attention-based mechanism to estimate the importance of each interaction conditioned on the node and its graph context. Interactions with low estimated importance are suppressed, so that the resulting representations emphasize informative combinations and remain robust to sparsity. The interaction-aware representations are then fused with the standard message-passing pipeline, so the framework can be attached to existing GNN architectures as a module. Because computation is restricted to the non-zero features of eah node, the cost scales with feature sparsity rather than with the full feature dimension. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: - We study the problem of representation learning on feature-sparse graphs from the perspective of feature interactions, and identify the limitations of existing GNNs that treat features independently or model interactions indiscriminately. - We propose FI-GNNs, a general framework that learns personalized importance of feature interactions and incorporates the selected interactions into node representations, and that can be combined with a wide range of GNN backbones. - We conduct extensive experiments on multiple datasets and tasks with several backbone architectures. The results show that FI-GNNs consistently improve over their base models, and further analyses examine the contribution of each component, robustness under varying sparsity, and the interpretability of the learned interactions. In the context of graph neural networks, a node's representation is crucial for downstream tasks, and its computation is significantly influenced by the characteristics of its neighboring nodes. To this end, we devise a novel approach to generate a context-aware representation for each node by aggregating the feature embeddings of its neighbors. Specifically, for a given node i, we calculate its context vector, denoted as c_i, by taking the mean of the feature embeddings of its neighboring nodes. This is achieved through the expression c_i = (1/|N(i)|) Σ_{j∈N(i)} Σ_{f∈S_j} v_{jf}, where N(i) represents the set of neighboring nodes of i, S_j denotes the set of features associated with node j, and v_{jf} is the embedding of feature f of node j. 

The importance of the interaction between two features, f and g, for node i is subsequently determined by the expression α_{i,fg} = exp(q^T tanh(W_z z_{i,fg} + W_c c_i)) / Σ_{(f',g')} exp(q^T tanh(W_z z_{i,f'g'} + W_c c_i)), where z_{i,fg} represents the embedding of the interaction between features f and g for node i, and W_z, W_c, and q are learnable parameters. This formulation allows the model to assign varying weights to the same feature pair across different local structures, thereby enabling personalized feature selection. 

The interaction-aware node embedding, denoted as u_i, is then computed as the weighted sum of the embeddings of all feature pairs, where the weights are determined by the importance of each interaction. This is expressed as u_i = Σ_{f<g} α_{i,fg} z_{i,fg}. To promote selective behavior and focus on the most informative interactions, we optionally introduce an entropy penalty on the importance weights or employ sparsemax [6] in place of the softmax function. Both of these techniques encourage the model to concentrate on a subset of the most relevant interactions while diminishing the contribution of the remaining ones.

The first term in this expression preserves the information captured by a standard linear projection, while the second term injects the selected second-order interactions. The resulting node representation is then passed through multiple layers of a graph neural network, such as GCN [1], GraphSAGE [2], or GAT [7], to generate the final representation.

Pelvic adhesions are a pervasive and disabling complication of surgical interventions in the pelvic region, affecting a substantial number of women in their reproductive years. The aftermath of such adhesions can lead to a myriad of severe health issues, including persistent pelvic pain, obstruction of the bowel, and infertility, thereby rendering them a significant concern for both patients and healthcare providers [1,2]. The development of adhesions following operative laparoscopy for endometriosis is particularly troublesome, as research has shown that new adhesions can form and existing ones can reform in a considerable proportion of patients, even when meticulous microsurgical techniques are employed [3,4]. The ovaries are especially susceptible to adhesion formation due to their exposed surfaces after surgical procedures such as endometrioma excision, cauterization, or adhesiolysis, which can readily adhere to the adjacent ovarian fossa. This can lead to the distortion of the tubo-ovarian anatomy, thereby impairing oocyte pickup and compromising access to follicles during oocyte retrieval [5]. The underlying biological processes that lead to the formation of adhesions after surgery are complex and involve an inflammatory response to peritoneal injury, which triggers the exudation of a fluid rich in fibrin. Under normal circumstances, the body's natural repair mechanisms, including mesothelial repair and fibrinolysis, mediated largely by tissue plasminogen activator, remove this fibrinous deposit within several days. However, surgical trauma, reduced blood flow, desiccation, thermal injury, and foreign bodies can impede peritoneal fibrinolytic activity, allowing the fibrin matrix to persist and become colonized by fibroblasts and capillaries, ultimately forming a permanent fibrous adhesion [6,7]. Two key observations underpin the development of strategies to prevent adhesion formation: firstly, the critical period for adhesion formation is the first several days after surgery, and secondly, adhesions tend to form between surfaces that are in close proximity during this period [8]. Therefore, maintaining separation of injured surfaces during this critical window is a logical approach to preventing adhesions. Current methods for preventing adhesions are multifaceted and include meticulous control of bleeding, minimizing tissue handling and thermal injury, generous irrigation, and the use of minimally invasive techniques [9]. Various pharmacologic agents, such as corticosteroids, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and fibrinolytic agents, have been investigated, but their benefits are inconsistent, and they are not recommended for routine use [10]. Another approach involves the use of barrier agents, including oxidized regenerated cellulose, expanded polytetrafluoroethylene, and hyaluronic acid or polyethylene glycol-based gels and films, which aim to separate injured surfaces physically while healing occurs. While some of these agents have been shown to reduce the incidence or severity of adhesions in controlled trials, evidence of improved fertility or reduced pain is limited, and their use is often restricted by cost, handling difficulty, and availability, particularly in laparoscopic procedures [11,12]. Consequently, no single method has been proven to reliably prevent adhesions, and the search continues for simple, inexpensive, and safe adjuncts. One approach that has garnered attention is temporary ovarian suspension (TOS), which involves elevating the ovaries away from the ovarian fossa during the critical healing period. This mechanical approach is based on the principle that adhesion formation depends on the apposition of raw surfaces. Several authors have described TOS to the anterior abdominal wall or to the round ligament or uterine structures at the end of laparoscopic surgery, particularly after excision of endometriosis or ovarian drilling [13–15]. Reported techniques involve the use of a transabdominal straight needle or a suture passed through the abdominal wall under laparoscopic vision, with the ovary held anteriorly for a limited time. Suspension using absorbable material allows spontaneous release, whereas non-absorbable suture requires removal after a few days, usually by cutting a subcutaneous knot or external traction. Small series and comparative studies suggest that suspension may decrease ovarian adhesion scores at second-look laparoscopy, although the data remain sparse and heterogeneous [14,16]. Despite its theoretical rationale, TOS has not been widely adopted, likely due to concerns about safety and the lack of standardized technique. Theoretical risks associated with TOS include injury to the inferior epigastric vessels or bowel during needle passage, hematoma formation, infection, ovarian ischemia or torsion, and herniation or entrapment of bowel through the suture loop with obstruction or strangulation [17]. Furthermore, it is unclear whether the ovaries return to their normal anatomical position after suspension is released, as persistent displacement could itself impair function. The choice of suture material also introduces a practical issue, with absorbable suture eliminating the need for removal but potentially losing tensile strength or being absorbed before the critical period of adhesion formation has passed. Non-absorbable suture provides predictable, sustained suspension but requires a second step for removal and carries a theoretical risk if the loop is retained. Direct comparisons of the two approaches are lacking. The rationale for the present study lies in the fact that women with advanced endometriosis are the group most likely to benefit from effective adhesion prevention. These patients typically have extensive ovarian and pelvic disease, are at high risk of adhesion reformation, and frequently seek fertility treatment. Therefore, evidence on the safety of TOS in sizeable cohorts and over a long period is needed before it can be considered a reasonable adjunct. Moreover, data on its relationship to subsequent reproductive outcomes, including fertility and pain, are essential to fully understand the potential benefits and limitations of this approach. The development of effective strategies to prevent adhesions is crucial, as it could significantly improve the quality of life and reproductive outcomes for women undergoing pelvic surgery. In conclusion, the prevention of adhesions after pelvic surgery is a complex issue that requires a multifaceted approach. While temporary ovarian suspension is a promising adjunct, further research is needed to fully understand its safety, efficacy, and potential benefits in preventing adhesions and improving reproductive outcomes. 

Moreover, the exact mechanisms by which TOS exerts its effects on adhesion formation are not fully understood and require further investigation. It is possible that TOS may reduce the incidence of adhesions by preventing the apposition of raw surfaces, thereby reducing the opportunities for fibrin deposition and subsequent adhesion formation. Additionally, TOS may also reduce the severity of adhesions by minimizing the amount of tissue trauma and inflammation that occurs during the healing process. However, further research is needed to fully understand the effects of TOS on adhesion formation and to determine its potential benefits and limitations in preventing adhesions and improving reproductive outcomes. 

In addition, the use of TOS in combination with other adhesion prevention strategies may be a promising approach. For example, the use of barrier agents in conjunction with TOS may provide a synergistic effect, further reducing the incidence and severity of adhesions. Similarly, the use of pharmacologic agents, such as corticosteroids or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, in conjunction with TOS may also provide additional benefits in reducing adhesion formation. However, further research is needed to fully understand the potential benefits and limitations of these combined approaches.

The present study undertakes a comprehensive examination of the perioperative and long-term sequelae associated with the utilization of two distinct suture materials in the context of ovarian suspension to the anterior abdominal wall during laparoscopic surgical interventions. Specifically, the investigation focuses on the incidence of intraoperative and postoperative complications, as well as the efficacy of the procedure in restoring normal ovarian positioning and enhancing fertility outcomes in patients with endometriosis and other gynecological conditions, as referenced in [5]. The efficacy of the procedure was assessed through two primary metrics: the anatomical positioning of the ovaries as visualized via transvaginal ultrasonography at a one-week follow-up, and the occurrence of clinical pregnancy and live birth in patients attempting conception through non-assisted reproductive technologies (non-ART) methods, serving as proxies for the reestablishment of normal pelvic function and a reduction in adhesion formation. Notably, patients who underwent in vitro fertilization (IVF) were excluded from the fertility analysis, as assisted reproductive technologies can obviate the need for normal tubo-ovarian function, thereby potentially confounding the results. The overarching objective of this study was to evaluate the safety profile and efficacy of two different suture materials used in ovarian suspension, with a particular emphasis on their impact on postoperative adhesion formation and fertility outcomes in patients undergoing operative laparoscopy for endometriosis and other indications. The findings of this study possess significant implications for the clinical management of patients undergoing laparoscopic surgery and underscore the necessity for further research aimed at optimizing the techniques and materials employed in ovarian suspension, in accordance with the recommendations outlined in [1]. By adhering to the STROBE guidelines for observational studies and employing a standardized surgical protocol, this investigation contributes meaningfully to the existing body of evidence regarding the safety and efficacy of ovarian suspension, offering valuable insights into the comparative merits of different suture materials. Although the prevention of adhesions is a paramount consideration in surgical procedures, particularly in the context of ovarian suspension, the primary focus of this study lay in comparing the outcomes associated with the use of two different suture materials, rather than in evaluating the efficacy of adhesion prevention strategies per se. This distinction is notable, as second-look laparoscopy was not performed as a routine aspect of the study protocol, and consequently, detailed adhesion scoring was not undertaken. To facilitate the comparison of the two suture materials, a comprehensive range of demographic and clinical variables was extracted from patient medical records, encompassing age, parity, history of infertility, indication for surgery, disease stage, procedures performed, operative duration, laterality of suspension, and complications encountered. These data were meticulously entered into a secure database and subjected to rigorous verification by a second reviewer to ensure accuracy and reliability. The statistical analysis involved summarizing continuous variables as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range), depending on the distribution assessed by the Shapiro–Wilk test, and comparing these variables using Student's t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables, on the other hand, were expressed as counts and percentages and compared using the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test when expected cell counts were below five. Complication rates were reported with exact 95% confidence intervals, and pregnancy and delivery rates were compared between groups among patients attempting non-ART conception. A two-sided P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY), as cited in [6]. Given the retrospective design and non-randomized nature of the study, no formal sample size calculation was undertaken, and the results were interpreted as exploratory. The study population comprised a total of 152 patients who underwent ovarian suspension to the anterior abdominal wall during operative laparoscopy between 1998 and 2017. These patients were divided into two groups: Group 1, consisting of 78 patients who underwent ovarian suspension with absorbable 3-0 plain catgut, and Group 2, comprising 74 patients who underwent suspension with non-absorbable 3-0 monofilament nylon. Notably, the earlier cases in the series were predominantly allocated to Group 2, while the use of absorbable suture material was adopted in later cases. The primary indication for surgery was advanced-stage endometriosis in 142 patients (93.4%), with the remainder (10 patients, 6.6%) undergoing surgery for other indications, including extensive pelvic adhesions and other benign adnexal pathology. The distribution of indications was similar between the two groups, with the majority of patients in both groups having stage III or IV disease according to the revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine classification, as referenced in [1]. A summary of the baseline characteristics of the patients is presented in Table 1, which reveals that age, body mass index, parity, and duration of infertility did not differ significantly between the two groups (all P > 0.05). The surgical procedures performed during the intervention included excision or ablation of endometriotic lesions, ovarian cystectomy for endometriomas, adhesiolysis, and, where necessary, excision of deep infiltrating disease. The proportion of patients undergoing unilateral versus bilateral suspension was comparable between the two groups. Intraoperatively, ovarian suspension was successfully completed in all 152 patients, with no conversions to laparotomy attributable to the suspension technique. No major intraoperative complications were recorded in either group, including episodes of bleeding from the abdominal wall or inferior epigastric vessels, bowel or bladder injury, and injury to the ovarian pedicle or the ovary related to passage of the suture. The addition of the suspension procedure to the laparoscopic intervention added only a few minutes to the total operating time, and no case required additional trocar sites or specialized instruments beyond a straight needle or suture-passing device. The technique was performed by several surgeons, including trainees under supervision, without any adverse events attributable to the learning curve. Postoperatively, no late complications occurred in either group, including wound or deep pelvic infection, abdominal wall hematoma, bowel herniation through the suture loop, or other sequelae. The absence of significant complications in both groups underscores the safety profile of the ovarian suspension procedure when performed by experienced surgeons, regardless of the suture material employed. The findings of this study contribute to the growing body of evidence regarding the safety and efficacy of ovarian suspension in the context of laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis and other gynecological conditions, highlighting the importance of careful patient selection, meticulous surgical technique, and the need for ongoing research into the optimal materials and methods for minimizing postoperative adhesion formation and enhancing fertility outcomes.
