Massive multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) is a key technology for fifth generation (5G) and beyond wireless networks. By equipping the base station (BS) with a large number of antennas, serving many users simultaneously on the same time-frequency resource becomes possible, yielding substantial gains in spectral and energy efficiency [1], [2]. As the number of BS antennas grows, the channel vectors of different users become increasingly orthogonal under favorable propagation, and simple linear processing such as maximum-ratio or zero-forcing (ZF) approaches the performance of optimal nonlinear schemes [3]. Small-scale fading is also averaged out, a phenomenon known as channel hardening, which relaxes the demands on scheduling and power control [4]. These benefits rely on accurate channel state information (CSI) at the BS. In time division duplex (TDD) operation, which is the favored mode for massive MIMO, CSI is acquired from uplink (UL) pilots and exploted through reciprocity for both UL detection and downlink (DL) precodinng [1]. The CSI is therefore only valid for a limited period. Between the instant of channel estimation and the instant of use, the channel evolves because of user mobility and movement of scatterers. This inherent propagation and processing delay produces channel aging, in which outdated CSI degrades the effective signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio and causes inaccuracies in detection and precoding [5], [6]. The effect is particularly harmful for DL precoding, since the delay between estimation and transmission is generally longer than that for UL detection, and the interference nulling of ZF is sensitive to errors in the channel estimate. In extreme cases, only the UL may remain usable. The temporal behavior of massive MIMO channels is therefore cetnral to assessing practical deployments, determining pilot overhead, frame structure, and the feasible mobility range. Much of the literature on mobility in massive MIMO has been theoretical. Analyses based on autoregressive channel models, Jakes' Doppler spectrum, and the associated temporal correlation have been used to derive achievable rates under aging and to design predictors or robust precoders [5]–[7]. These studies typically assume independent and identically distributed Rayleigh fading across antennas and users, and an isotropic scattering environment. Real channels deviate from these assumptions: propagation is often dominated by line-of-sight (LOS) components, scatteers are spatially clustered, and the Doppler shifts experienced across a large array may differ between antennas and between users. Such features influence how rapidly the composite channel vector decorrelates, and they cannot be fully captured by simplified models. Measurements are thus indispensable. Several massive MIMO testbeds have been developed, including the Lund University LuMaMi systm [8], the Argos platform [9], and the Bristol-Lund system used in this wok [10]. Measurement campaigns have studied favorable propagation, channel hardening, spatial correlation, and capaciy in indoor and outdoor settings, mostly with static or nomadic users [11]–[13]. Studies of the effect of mobiliyt on real massive MIMO channels remain comparatively scarce. Some real-time prototypes have demonstrated operation with moving terminals [8], [14], and a few measurement-based works have examined channel aging at low speeds, but a systematic characterization of temporal correlation for a large array serving multiple users in a realistic LOS environment with moving vehicles and pedestrians is lacking. In particular, it is not well understood how the array size affects the rate at which the multi-user channel must be updated, nor how it influencs the rate at which power control must be refreshed. The two effects of array size are expected to work in opposite directions. On one hand, the channel vector of a user with many antennas is high dimensional, and its correlation with an earlier snapshot may fall more quickly, since small phase changes accumulate coherently across antennas and the narrower beams are more sensitive to user displacement. This suggests that CSI for precoding and detection must be refreshed more often as the array grows. On the other hand, channel hardening makes the channel gain, and hence the large-scale quatity relevant to power control, vary much more slowly, so that power control updates could be less frequent. Quantifying both effects with measured data would give system designers concrete guidance. This paper presents, to the authors' knowledge, the first measured results on the temporal behavior of a LOS massive MIMO channel with moderate mobility. Using a 100-antenna BS operating at 3.7 GHz and seerving 8 users, measurements were taen in an outdoor environment with moving cars and pedestrians, with vehicle speeds up to 29 km/h. We examine the temporal correlation of the MIMO channel vector, and evaluate how the correlation, and thus the required update interval, changes with the numbeer of BS antennas. The contributions are as follows: 1. We describe a measurement campaign with a 100-antenna array and 8 simultaneously active mobile users in a LOS scenario at 3.7 GHz. 2. We characterize the temporal correlation of the channel vector and show that, relative to an 8-antenna system, the CSI update rate for the 100-antenna system may need to increase by a factor of about 7. 3. We investigate channel hardening in time and show that, relative to a single-antenna system, the power control update rate can be reduced by at least a factor of 5. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the measurement system and scenario. Section III defines the metrics used for temporal analysis. Section IV presents and discusses the results, and Section V concludes the paper. The emergence of next-generation wireless networks, specifically fifth-generation (5G) and beyond, has sparked a surge of interest in the development of massive multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) technology, which promises to revolutionize the field of wireless communication. By equipping base stations (BS) with an extensive array of antennas, it becomes feasible to serve multiple users concurrently on the same time-frequency resource, thereby achieving significant enhancements in spectral and energy efficiency [1], [2]. As the number of BS antennas increases, the channel vectors corresponding to different users become increasingly orthogonal under favorable propagation conditions, enabling simple linear processing techniques, such as maximum-ratio or zero-forcing (ZF) approaches, to approximate the performance of optimal nonlinear schemes [3]. Additionally, the phenomenon of channel hardening occurs, where small-scale fading is averaged out, which in turn relaxes the demands on scheduling and power control [4]. Nevertheless, these benefits are contingent upon the availability of accurate channel state information (CSI) at the BS. In time division duplex (TDD) operation, which is the preferred mode for massive MIMO, CSI is acquired from uplink (UL) pilots and utilized through reciprocity for both UL detection and downlink (DL) precoding [1]. However, the CSI remains valid only for a limited duration, as the channel evolves over time due to user mobility and the movement of scatterers. This inherent propagation and processing delay gives rise to channel aging, which degrades the effective signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio and causes inaccuracies in detection and precoding [5], [6]. The impact of channel aging is particularly detrimental for DL precoding, as the delay between estimation and transmission is generally longer than that for UL detection, and the interference nulling of ZF is sensitive to errors in the channel estimate. In extreme cases, only the UL may remain usable. Therefore, understanding the temporal behavior of massive MIMO channels is crucial for assessing practical deployments, determining pilot overhead, frame structure, and the feasible mobility range. Much of the existing literature on mobility in massive MIMO has been theoretical, with analyses based on autoregressive channel models, Jakes' Doppler spectrum, and the associated temporal correlation used to derive achievable rates under aging and to design predictors or robust precoders [5]–[7]. These studies typically assume independent and identically distributed Rayleigh fading across antennas and users, and an isotropic scattering environment. However, real-world channels deviate from these assumptions, as propagation is often dominated by line-of-sight (LOS) components, scatterers are spatially clustered, and the Doppler shifts experienced across a large array may differ between antennas and between users. Such features influence the rate at which the composite channel vector decorrelates, and they cannot be fully captured by simplified models. Consequently, measurements are essential for gaining a deeper understanding of the temporal behavior of massive MIMO channels. Several massive MIMO testbeds have been developed, including the Lund University LuMaMi system [8], the Argos platform [9], and the Bristol-Lund system used in this work [10]. Measurement campaigns have investigated favorable propagation, channel hardening, spatial correlation, and capacity in indoor and outdoor settings, mostly with static or nomadic users [11]–[13]. However, studies of the effect of mobility on real massive MIMO channels remain relatively scarce. Some real-time prototypes have demonstrated operation with moving terminals [8], [14], and a few measurement-based works have examined channel aging at low speeds, but a systematic characterization of temporal correlation for a large array serving multiple users in a realistic LOS environment with moving vehicles and pedestrians is lacking. In particular, it is not well understood how the array size affects the rate at which the multi-user channel must be updated, nor how it influences the rate at which power control must be refreshed. The two effects of array size are expected to work in opposite directions. On one hand, the channel vector of a user with many antennas is high dimensional, and its correlation with an earlier snapshot may fall more quickly, since small phase changes accumulate coherently across antennas and the narrower beams are more sensitive to user displacement. This suggests that CSI for precoding and detection must be refreshed more often as the array grows. On the other hand, channel hardening makes the channel gain, and hence the large-scale quantity relevant to power control, vary much more slowly, so that power control updates could be less frequent. Quantifying both effects with measured data would provide system designers with concrete guidance on how to optimize the performance of massive MIMO systems. This paper presents, to the authors' knowledge, the first measured results on the temporal behavior of a LOS massive MIMO channel with moderate mobility. Using a 100-antenna BS operating at 3.7 GHz and serving 8 users, measurements were taken in an outdoor environment with moving cars and pedestrians, with vehicle speeds up to 29 km/h. We examine the temporal correlation of the MIMO channel vector and evaluate how the correlation, and thus the required update interval, changes with the number of BS antennas. The contributions of this work include the analysis of the temporal behavior of massive MIMO channels, the evaluation of the impact of array size on the required update interval, and the provision of insights into the optimization of massive MIMO system performance. Furthermore, the results of this study can be used to inform the design of future massive MIMO systems, particularly in terms of pilot overhead, frame structure, and power control strategies. By understanding the temporal behavior of massive MIMO channels, system designers can create more efficient and effective systems that can support the growing demands of wireless communication. In this context, our research investigates the temporal characteristics of massive MIMO channels, with a particular focus on the update rates required for power control and CSI. To conduct our measurements, we utilized the Lund University massive MIMO testbed (LuMaMi), a software-defined radio platform based on NI hardware and operating in Time Division Duplexing (TDD) mode [1]. The system was configured with 100 transceiver chains connected to a 160-element dual-polarized patch antenna array, centered at 3.7 GHz with a 20 MHz bandwidth. The signal employed Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) with 2048 subcarriers, of which 1200 were active, and a subcarrier spacing of 15 kHz, similar to the Long-Term Evolution (LTE) numerology. The frame structure consisted of 10 ms frames, divided into slots in which uplink pilots and data were transmitted.

The array was mounted on the exterior of a building roof, approximately 20 m above ground level, and was oriented towards the measurement area. The measurement campaign was conducted in an outdoor environment with a predominantly Line-of-Sight (LOS) setting in an open car park area adjoining the BS building. The area contained parked cars, trees, and surrounding buildings that acted as potential scatterers. Eight single-antenna user terminals were served simultaneously, with each terminal consisting of a software-defined radio connected to an omnidirectional monopole antenna. Two groups of users were used: some terminals were carried by pedestrians walking at approximately 3–5 km/h, while others were mounted on vehicles driven along predefined routes at speeds up to 29 km/h. 

In addition to the intentionally moving users, other cars and pedestrians moved in the vicinity, producing time-varying scattering. Each user was synchronized to the BS through a dedicated pilot and over-the-air time and frequency references, and their transmissions used orthogonal pilot resources (frequency-interleaved subcarriers) so that the channels of all 8 users could be estimated in each pilot symbol. For each pilot opportunity, the least-squares estimate of the channel was obtained per subcarrier and per BS antenna. The channel for user k at time t and subcarrier f is represented by the vector h_k(t,f) ∈ C^{M×1}, where M = 100 is the number of active BS antennas.

The channel sounding repetition interval was 0.5 ms, providing a Doppler-unambiguous sampling at the speeds considered. Using a carrier frequency f_c = 3.7 GHz, the maximum Doppler shift for a 29 km/h (8.06 m/s) user is f_D = v f_c / c ≈ 99 Hz, which corresponds to a coherence time of approximately 0.423/f_D ≈ 4.3 ms according to the usual rule of thumb [2]. Measurements were recorded in snapshots of several seconds, and the data were normalized to remove the effect of the automatic gain control and hardware calibration offsets. Reciprocity calibration was not required for the temporal analysis of the uplink (UL) channel, but it is relevant for the downlink (DL) interpretation of the results [3].

To quantify the temporal behavior of the channel, we employed two key metrics. First, the normalized temporal correlation coefficient of the channel vector was computed as ρ_k(τ) = |E[h_k^H(t) h_k(t+τ)]| / (E[‖h_k(t)‖²]^{1/2} E[‖h_k(t+τ)‖²]^{1/2}), where the expectation was approximated by averaging over time t and over the subcarriers within the measured band. This metric represents the vector generalization of the conventional scalar autocorrelation function, and for M = 1, it reduces to the single antenna case. 

To determine the dependence on the number of antennas, ρ_k(τ) was evaluated for subsets of M = 1, 8, 20, 50, and 100 antennas, selected with different random and contiguous configurations, and the results were averaged. The channel is considered decorrelated when ρ_k(τ) falls below a threshold, here 0.9 for CSI-update purposes, which corresponds to a limited loss in beamforming gain [4]. The CSI update interval was taken as the lag τ at which this threshold was crossed.

Second, to assess the effect of the temporal variation on power control, the large-scale (average) received power was separated from the instantaneous channel gain by averaging ‖h_k(t)‖² over a sliding window of 20 wavelengths in length. This allowed us to quantify the impact of channel variations on power control and CSI update rates. By analyzing these metrics, we can gain a deeper understanding of the temporal behavior of massive MIMO channels and the requirements for advanced channel estimation and prediction techniques.

Mycotoxins are low-molecular-weight secondary metabolites produced mainly by filamentous fungi of the genera Aspergillus, Fusarium, Penicillium, and Alternaria. They contaminate a wide range of agricultural commodities, including cereals, nuts, spices, fruits, and animal feed, both in the field and during storage [1,2]. The Food and Agriculture Organization has estimated that a considerable share of the world's food crops is contaminated with mycotoxins at detectable levels, causing substantial economic losses and risks to human and animal health [3]. Climate change is expected to alter the geographical distribution of toxigenic fungi and the patterns of contamination, so the problem is likely to intensify [4]. Several hundred mycotoxins are known, but only a few groups are of major concern: aflatoxins, ochratoxins, trichothecenes (deoxynivalenol, T-2 toxin), zearalenone, fumonisins, patulin, and ergot alkaloids. Their toxic efects are diverse. Aflatoxin B1 is a potent hepatocarcinogen after metabolic activation to an epoxide that forms DNA adducts [5]. Ochratoxin A is nephrotoxic, immunotoxic, and possibly carcinogenic [6]. Trichothecenes inhibit eukaryotic protein synthesis by binding the ribosomal peptidyl transferase center [7]. Zearalenone mimics estrogen and disrupts reproductive function [8]. Fumonisins inhibit ceramide synthase and disturb sphingolipid metabolism [9]. Co-occurrence of several mycotoxins in one matrix is common, and addiitive or synergistic effects complicate risk assessment [10]. Regulatory limits for mycotoxins have been established in many countries, and strategies for preventing contamination include good agricultural practices, resistant cultivars, biocontrol, and optimized storage [11]. Once toxins are formed, however, they must be removed or inactivated. Physical and chemical methods such as sorting, milling, thermal treatment, ammonization, ozonation, and the use of adsorbents have limited efficiency. They may impair the nutritional value and organoleptic properties of the product, generate toxic residues, or lack specificity [12,13]. Adsorbents such as aluminosilicates and activated carbon work well for aflatoxins but poorly for many other toxins, including zearalenone, fumonisins, and trichothecenes, and they may bind vitamins and minerals [14]. Biological detoxification using microorganisms or their enzymes is regarded as a more promising alternative because it can be specific, mild, and environmentally friendly. Enzymatic transformation permits the conversion of mycotoxins into less toxic or nontoxic products under moderate conditions without affecting feed quality. Application of enzymes as feed additives has been recognized by regulators; in the European Union, for example, fumonisin esterase and trichothecene-detoxifying biotransforming agents have been authorized as technological additives [15]. Compared with whole-cell preparations, purified or recombinant enzymes offer defined composition, controllable dosage, and absence of undesirable microbail metabolites. The enzymes known to act on mycotoxins belong to various classes. Oxidoreductases, including laccases, peroxidases, cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, and dehydrogenases, oxidize or redue functional groups of aflatoxins, deoxynivalenol, and other toxins [16,17]. Hydrolases such as lactonases, carboxypeptidases, esterases, and amidases cleave lactone, amide, or ester bonds in zearalenone, ochratoxin A, and fumonisins, respectively [18–20]. Transferases, such as glucosyltransferases, glutathione S-transferases, and acetyltransferases, conjugate mycotoxins with sugars, glutathione, or acetyl groups, which is the basis of plant self-protection against trichothecenes [21]. Epoxide-cleaving and de-epoxidating enzymes, including the recently described DepA/DepB system and related proteins, remove the toxophoric epoxide group of trichothecenes [22]. Despite these discoveries, the activity of many enzymes remains low, and their substrate specificity, stability, and mechanisms of action are not fully understood. Mayn reports describe enzymatic activity without sequence or structural information, and the metabolites formed are not always identified or tested for residual toxicity [23]. Understanding catalytic mechanisms is essential for rational selection and engineering of mycotoxin-converting enzymes. Structural studies, site-directed mutagenesis, and computational approaches, particularly molecular docking and molecular dynamics, make it possible to identify key residues in the active center, explain substrate specificity, and predict the effect of amino acid substitutions [24]. Such knowledge has already been applied to improve the thermostability and activity of zearalenone hydrolases and aflatoxin-degrading oxidases [25]. Moreover, comparison of homologous proteins from plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria can reveal the distribution of such activities in nature and suggest new, easily accessible sources of biocatalysts, including enzymes with other primary functions that show promiscuous activity toward mycotoxins [26]. Previous reviews have mainly focused on individual toxins or on microorganisms capable of detoxification, and they often present enzymes as lists of activities without analyzing the underlying chemistry [27,28]. A comprehensive analysis combining biochemical mechanisms, structural modeling, and phylogenetic distribution is still lacking. In addition, because contamination with several toxins at once is typical, the possible use of multifunctional enzyme combinations deserves attention. The realm of mycotoxins encompasses a diverse array of low-molecular-weight secondary metabolites predominantly synthesized by filamentous fungi, notably species belonging to the genera Aspergillus, Fusarium, Penicillium, and Alternaria. The pervasive impact of these toxins is evident in their ability to contaminate a wide range of agricultural commodities, including cereals, nuts, spices, fruits, and animal feed, at various stages of growth and storage [1,2]. Estimates provided by the Food and Agriculture Organization suggest that a substantial proportion of the world's food crops are tainted with mycotoxins at detectable levels, resulting in considerable economic losses and posing significant risks to human and animal health [3]. The situation is anticipated to deteriorate due to the effects of climate change, which is expected to alter the geographical distribution of toxigenic fungi and the patterns of contamination [4]. Among the numerous mycotoxins identified, a select few, including aflatoxins, ochratoxins, trichothecenes (such as deoxynivalenol and T-2 toxin), zearalenone, fumonisins, patulin, and ergot alkaloids, are of primary concern due to their toxicological significance. The detrimental effects of these mycotoxins are multifaceted and can have severe consequences. For instance, aflatoxin B1 is a potent hepatocarcinogen that, upon metabolic activation to an epoxide, forms DNA adducts [5]. In contrast, ochratoxin A is known to exhibit nephrotoxic, immunotoxic, and potentially carcinogenic properties [6]. Trichothecenes inhibit eukaryotic protein synthesis by binding to the ribosomal peptidyl transferase center [7], whereas zearalenone mimics estrogen, thereby disrupting reproductive function [8]. Fumonisins inhibit ceramide synthase, leading to disturbances in sphingolipid metabolism [9]. Furthermore, the co-occurrence of multiple mycotoxins in a single matrix is a common phenomenon, and the potential for additive or synergistic effects complicates risk assessment [10]. To mitigate the risks associated with mycotoxins, regulatory limits have been established in many countries, and various strategies for preventing contamination have been implemented, including the adoption of good agricultural practices, the use of resistant cultivars, biocontrol, and optimized storage [11]. However, once mycotoxins are formed, they must be removed or inactivated. Traditional physical and chemical methods, such as sorting, milling, thermal treatment, ammonization, ozonation, and the use of adsorbents, have limited efficacy and can compromise the nutritional value and organoleptic properties of the product, generate toxic residues, or lack specificity [12,13]. Adsorbents like aluminosilicates and activated carbon are effective against aflatoxins but less so against other toxins, including zearalenone, fumonisins, and trichothecenes, and they may also bind vitamins and minerals [14]. In contrast, biological detoxification using microorganisms or their enzymes is considered a more promising alternative, as it can be specific, mild, and environmentally friendly. Enzymatic transformation allows for the conversion of mycotoxins into less toxic or nontoxic products under moderate conditions without affecting feed quality. The application of enzymes as feed additives has been recognized by regulators, and in the European Union, for example, fumonisin esterase and trichothecene-detoxifying biotransforming agents have been authorized as technological additives [15]. Purified or recombinant enzymes offer several advantages over whole-cell preparations, including defined composition, controllable dosage, and the absence of undesirable microbial metabolites. The enzymes known to act on mycotoxins belong to various classes, each with distinct mechanisms of action. Oxidoreductases, including laccases, peroxidases, cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, and dehydrogenases, oxidize or reduce functional groups of aflatoxins, deoxynivalenol, and other toxins [16,17]. Hydrolases, such as lactonases, carboxypeptidases, esterases, and amidases, cleave lactone, amide, or ester bonds in zearalenone, ochratoxin A, and fumonisins, respectively [18–20]. Transferases, including glucosyltransferases, glutathione S-transferases, and acetyltransferases, conjugate mycotoxins with sugars, glutathione, or acetyl groups, which is the basis of plant self-protection against trichothecenes [21]. Despite these discoveries, the activity of many enzymes remains low, and their substrate specificity, stability, and mechanisms of action are not fully understood. Understanding the catalytic mechanisms of these enzymes is essential for the rational selection and engineering of mycotoxin-converting enzymes. Structural studies, site-directed mutagenesis, and computational approaches, particularly molecular docking and molecular dynamics, make it possible to identify key residues in the active center, explain substrate specificity, and predict the effect of amino acid substitutions [24]. One promising approach involves the utilization of enzymes with complementary specificities as antidotes, which can selectively target and degrade specific mycotoxins. To investigate this concept, we conducted an exhaustive literature search and selection of enzymes, focusing on publications from 1990 to 2022 that reported on the enzymatic conversion of mycotoxins. Our search terms combined the names of major mycotoxins, such as aflatoxins, zearalenone, ochratoxin A, fumonisins, trichothecenes, patulin, citrinin, and ergot alkaloids, with keywords related to enzyme activity, biotransformation, degradation, and detoxification [1,2]. We included studies that reported the use of purified or recombinant enzymes, identified reaction products, and demonstrated a decrease in toxicity or provided a clear structural rationale for it. The degradation of mycotoxins, which are toxic compounds produced by fungi, is a critical process for ensuring the safety of food and feed. Recent advances in understanding the enzymatic mechanisms underlying the breakdown of these toxic compounds have been significant. A thorough review of the existing literature has been conducted, and the data have been harmonized to provide a consistent and accurate understanding of the various enzyme mechanisms involved. This review has focused on the major mycotoxin groups, including aflatoxins, ochratoxins, zearalenone, trichothecenes, fumonisins, patulin, and others. The enzyme mechanisms that act on these mycotoxins can be broadly categorized into several groups, including hydrolytic, oxidative, conjugation and transferase, reductive, and eliminative mechanisms. Hydrolytic mechanisms involve the cleavage of chemical bonds using water, and examples of enzymes that utilize this mechanism include lactonases, carboxypeptidases, and amidohydrolases. For instance, lactonases such as ZHD101 from *Clonostachys rosea* are capable of opening the macrocyclic lactone ring of zearalenone (ZEN), resulting in the formation of a decarboxylated and non-estrogenic compound [1,2]. The catalytic mechanism of ZHD101 involves a Ser–His–Asp catalytic triad, where the nucleophilic serine attacks the lactone carbonyl, forming an acyl-enzyme intermediate that is subsequently hydrolyzed by water. In contrast, carboxypeptidases and amidohydrolases cleave the amide bond of ochratoxin A (OTA), resulting in the formation of non-toxic ochratoxin α and L-phenylalanine [3,4]. These enzymes utilize a zinc ion to polarize the amide carbonyl and activate a water molecule, which then attacks the amide bond. Additionally, carboxylesterases and fumonisin esterases (FumD) remove the tricarballylic acid side chains of fumonisin B1 (FB1), resulting in the formation of hydrolyzed FB1, which is less toxic [5,6]. Epoxide hydrolases have also been reported to open the epoxide ring of aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) metabolites and trichothecenes, although their activity towards the trichothecene 12,13-epoxide is limited [7]. Oxidative mechanisms, on the other hand, involve the transfer of electrons, resulting in the formation of reactive oxygen species. Laccases, which contain four copper atoms, are capable of oxidizing the phenolic groups of AFB1, ZEN, and OTA, often with the assistance of redox mediators [8]. The resulting radical intermediates can couple or fragment, leading to the formation of products with reduced toxicity. Manganese peroxidases and versatile peroxidases act on aflatoxins through a similar one-electron mechanism [9]. Aflatoxin-degrading reductases, such as AFO from *Armillaria tabescens*, oxidize the furan ring of AFB1 [10]. Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases hydroxylate or epoxidize aflatoxins, ZEN, and trichothecenes, although this route can also lead to the formation of toxic metabolites, such as the 8,9-epoxide of AFB1 [11]. Conjugation and transferase mechanisms involve the transfer of a functional group from one molecule to another. UDP-glucosyltransferases, such as HvUGT13248 from barley, transfer glucose to the C3 hydroxyl of DON and ZEN, resulting in the formation of glucosides [14]. These conjugates are less toxic, although they can be hydrolyzed back to their toxic forms in the gut. Glutathione S-transferases form conjugates with the AFB1 epoxide and trichothecenes, and they play a role in cellular detoxification [15]. Acetyltransferases, such as Tri101, acetylate the C3 hydroxyl of trichothecenes, reducing their ribosomal toxicity [16]. Sulfotransferases and kinases phosphorylate ZEN or add sulfate groups, resulting in similar effects [17]. Reductive and eliminative mechanisms involve the removal of functional groups or the reduction of double bonds. De-epoxidases, such as DepA/DepB and the cobalamin-dependent system of *Eubacterium* BBSH 797, convert the 12,13-epoxide of DON to the non-toxic DOM-1 [18]. This is the most effective detoxification route for trichothecenes, as the epoxide is the main toxicophore. Reductases also reduce the lactone-conjugated double bond of ZEN, and patulin is converted by short-chain dehydrogenases to the less toxic desoxypatulinic acid and ascladiol [19]. Molecular docking studies have provided valuable insights into the mechanisms of enzyme action and have helped to explain the specificity of enzyme-mycotoxin interactions. For example, the docking of ZEN into the active center of ZHD101 revealed that the enzyme's catalytic triad plays a crucial role in recognizing and binding the mycotoxin [1]. These findings highlight the importance of considering the structural and biochemical properties of enzymes in the development of efficient detoxification strategies. Furthermore, the examination of enzyme combinations and their compatibility under different reaction conditions can provide valuable insights into the development of effective mycotoxin degradation processes. The use of enzymes in feed and food processing has the potential to improve the safety of these products, reducing the risk of mycotoxin contamination and the associated health risks. However, further research is needed to fully exploit the potential of enzymes in mycotoxin detoxification, including the development of novel enzymes and the optimization of existing ones. Additionally, the development of efficient and cost-effective methods for the production and purification of these enzymes is crucial for their practical application. In conclusion, the enzymatic degradation of mycotoxins is a complex process that involves a variety of enzyme mechanisms and interactions. The understanding of these mechanisms and the development of efficient detoxification strategies are critical for ensuring the safety of food and feed products. Further research is needed to fully explore the potential of enzymes in mycotoxin detoxification and to develop novel and effective solutions for the degradation of these toxic compounds.

Depression is among the most prevalent mental disorders worldwide and a leading contributor to the global burden of disease. The World Health Organization estimates that more than 300 million people live with depression, and the condition is a major cause of disability, reduced productivity, and premature mortality through suicide and comorbid medicaal illness [1,2]. Its burden is not confined to psychiatric settings. Depression frequently coexists with chronic physical conditions such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and chronic pain, where it worsens prognosis, reduces adherece to treatment, and increases healthcare utilisation [3,4]. Consequently, patients with depression commonly present first to non-psychiatric clinicians, who are often the only professionals they encounter. **Depression in primary and non-psychiatric care** Because mental health specialists are scarce in many countries, integration of mental haelthcare into general medical services is a centrl strategy for narrowing the treatment gap [5]. Non-psychiatric physicians, including family physicians, internists, surgeons, and other specialists, are therefore expected to recognise depressive symptoms, initiate first-line treatment, and refer appropriately. Evidence nonetheless indicates that depression is under-recognised and under-treated in these settings, with a substantial proportion of cases going undetected or receiving inadequate management [6,7]. The reasons are multifactorial and include time constraints, limited training in mental health, the somatic presentation of depression, and patient reluctance to disclose psychological distress. Clinician attitudes are an additional and potentially modifiable determinant. Physicians who regard depression as untreatable, as a personal weakness, or as outside their professional remit may be less likely to screen, to diagnose, or to engage patients in management [8]. **Stigma and attitudes among health professionals** Stigma towards mental illness is well documented in the general population, and health professionals are not immune to it [9]. Negative attitudes among clinicians may manifest as pessimism about prognosis, social distancing, diagnostic overshadowing, or reluctance to treat, and they may compound the self-stigma experienced by patients and discourage help-seeking [10]. Non-psychiatric physicians may be particularly susceptible, given their more limited exposure to psychiatric education and practice. Studies from Europe, Asia, and elsewhere have reported variable levels of confidence, optimism, and professional comfort among general practitioners and hospital doctors in managing depression, with training and experience repeatedly associated with more favourable attitudes [11,12]. Assessing these attitudes is therefore a prerequisite for designing educational and service interventions. **Measuring attitudes: the Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire** The Depression Attitude Questionnaire (DAQ) was developed to assess professionals' views on depression, and was subsequently revised and psychometrically validated as the Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ) [13]. The R-DAQ is a 20-item instrument that captures multiple dimensions, including generalist perspectives on managing depression, professional confidence, optimism or pessimism about prognosis, beliefs about the identification of depression, and perceived professional boundaries between physical and mental halth care. It has been applied across diverse professional groups and cultural contexts, which facilitates cross-study comparison [14,15]. **The Saudi context** In Saudi Arabia, mental disorders constitute a considerable public health concern. National survey data suggest that a substantial share of the population experriences a mental disorder at some point in life, with major depressive disorder among the most common, yet only a minority seek or receive treatment [16]. Cultural and religious interpretations of mental distress, concerns about family reputation, and fear of social labelling continue to contribute to stigma and delayed help-seeking [17]. The Saudi healthcare system has taken steps to expand mental healtth services, including through national mental health strategies and efforts to integrate mental health into primary care [18]. The success of such integration depends heavily on the preparedness and attitudes of the non-psychiatric workforce. Existing Saudi studies of attitudes towards depression and mental illness have largely focused on primary care physicians, medical students, or the general public, and have often been restricted to single institutions or regions [19,20]. Less is known about the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians working across specialties in large tertiary hospitals in the capital, Riyadh, where complex patients wiht comorbid physical and mental illness are frequently managed and where many trainees receive their education. Evidence from this group is neded to identify training needs and to inform referral pathways and collaborative care models. **Aim and significance of the study** This sudy aimed to investigate the attitudes of non-psychiatric physicians towards depression in four tertiary centres in Riyadh using the R-DAQ. It further sought to exaamine how these attitudes relate to professional characteristics, including specialty, seniority, and clinical experience, where such factors may shape confidence and willingness to manage depression. By characterising optimism, confidence, and perceived professional roles within tihs population, the study provides locally relevant evidence to guide undergraduate and postgraduate mental health education, to support the integration of mental health into general hospital care, and to contribute to efforts to reduce stigma within the medical profession itself. **Study design and setting** A descriptive, cross-sectional, questionnaire-based survey was conducted between [month/year] and [month/year] in four tertiary care centres in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The centres were selected because they are large teaching hospitals with broad specialty coverage and receive referrals from across the central region. The study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for cross-sectional studies [1]. **Study population and eligibility** The target population comprised non-psychiatric physicians working at the participating centres. Eligible participants were consultants, specialists, residents, and medical interns/registrars from any non-psychiatric specialty (e.g., internal medicine, faily medicine, surgery, paediatrics, obstetrics and gynaecology, emergency medicine, and their subspecialties) who were in active clinical practice during the data collection period. Psychiatrists and psychiatry residents were excluded because the study focused on attitudse among clinicians without specialist mental health training. Physicians who were on extended leave or who declined to take part were also excluded. **Sample size and sampling technique** The required sample size was calculated using the formula for estimating a single proportion, n = Z²P(1−P)/d², assuming a 95% confidence level (Z = 1.96), an expected proportion of 50% to maximise variance, and a margin of error of 5%. This yielded a minimum of 384 respondents. A finite population correction was considered based on the estimated number of eligible physicians across the four centres. The target was inflated to account for incomplete responses. A convenience sampling approach with quota allocation proportional to each centre's physician workforce was used to distribute questionnaires. In total, 380 completed questionnaires were included in the final analysis. **Study instrument** Data were collected using a self-administered questionnaire consisting of two parts. *Part 1: Sociodemographic and professional characteristics.* This section captured age, gender, nationality, marital status, specialty, professional rank, years of clinical experience, and primary workplace. It also asked about prior training in mental health or depression management, personal or family history of depression, and previous experience treating patients with depression. *Part 2: Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ).* Attittudes towards depression were measured using the R-DAQ, developed by Haddad and colleagues from the original Depresison Attitude Questionnaire [2,3]. The R-DAQ comprises 20 items rated on a five-point Likert scale from "strongly disagree" (1) to "strongly agree" (5). Its validated factor structure includes five subscales: (i) professional confidence in managing depression, (ii) professional identification and therapeutic optimism or pessimism, (iii) generalist perspective on depression (that depression is a condition managed within general clinical practice), (iv) the perception that depression is difficult to identify or distinguish from normal distress, and (v) the perception of depression as a mental disorder with a biological or psychosocial aetiology [3]. Positively and negatively worded items were scored accordingly, with reverse scoring applied where required so that higher scors consistently reflected the construct measured by each subscale. The instrument has shown acceptable reliability and construct validity in studies of general practitioners and other clinicians across several countriies [3,4]. No major modifications were required, and pilot data were excluded from the analysis. **Data collection procedure** Following institutional approvals, trained data collectors visited clinical departments and distributed the questionnaires, either on paper or through a seure online link (according to departmental preference). Participants received an information sheet describing the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of participation, and assurances of anonymity. Completion of the questionnaire was taken as implied consent. No personal identifiers were collected, and completed forms were stored securely, accessible only to the research team. Reminders were issued at one-week and two-week intervals to improve the response rate. **Variables and outcome measures** The primary outcome was the attitude towards depression, expressed as the total R-DAQ score and the five subscale scores. Attitudes were interpreted according to published scoring guidance, with higher subscale scores indicating greatr confidence, more therapeutic optimism, stronger generalist orientation, greater perceived difficulty in identification, or stronger endorsement of a mental disorder model, respectively [3]. Independent variables included demographic and professional characteristics, specialty, previous training, and personal or faimly exposure to depression. **Statistical analysis** Data were entered and analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics (version [XX]) [5]. Data were screeneed for missing values and outliers. Categorical variables were summarised as frequencies and percentages, and continuous variables as means with standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges, depending on distribution, whicch was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test and visual inspection of histograms. Item-level responses were described as the proportion agreeing (agree/strongly agree), neutral, or disagreeing (disagree/strongly disagree). Associations between R-DAQ scores and participant characteristics were examined using independent-samples t-tests or Mann–Whitney U tests for two groups, and one-way ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis tests for three or more groups, with post hoc comparisons adjusted using the Bonferroni correction. Associations between categorical variables were tested using the chi-square or Fisher's exact test. Pearson or Spearman correlation coefficients were used for continuous variables such as age and years of experience. Multiple linear regression was used to identify independent preditcors of R-DAQ subscale scores, including variables with p < 0.20 in bivariate analysis. Statistical significance was set at a two-tailed p-value < 0.05, and 95% confidence intervals were reportd where appropriate. **Ethical considerations** The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board of each paricipating centre (approval numbers [XX]). The study adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki [6]. Participation was voluntary, responses were anonymous and confidential, and participants could withdraw at any time before submission without consequence. Respondents had a mean age of 34.6 years (SD = 8.2; range 25–62), and 231 (60.8%) were male. Saudi nationals accounted for 248 participants (65.3%). The global prevalence of depression, a complex and crippling mental health disorder, is staggering, with estimates suggesting that over 300 million individuals worldwide are affected [1,2]. The far-reaching consequences of depression extend beyond the realm of psychiatric care, often coinciding with chronic physical ailments, such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and chronic pain, which can exacerbate prognosis, hinder treatment adherence, and increase healthcare utilization [3,4]. As a result, individuals with depression frequently present to non-specialist healthcare providers, who may be their sole point of contact with the healthcare system. This highlights the imperative of incorporating mental health services into primary care, particularly in regions where specialist mental health professionals are scarce [5]. In primary care and non-psychiatric settings, the burden of recognizing depressive symptoms, initiating treatment, and referring patients to specialized care when necessary falls on non-psychiatric physicians, including general practitioners, internal medicine specialists, surgeons, and other specialists. However, evidence suggests that depression is frequently underdiagnosed and undertreated in these settings, with a significant proportion of cases going undetected or receiving inadequate management [6,7]. The reasons for this are multifaceted, encompassing time constraints, limited mental health training, the presentation of depression with somatic symptoms, and patient reluctance to disclose psychological distress. Furthermore, the attitudes of healthcare providers play a significant role, as those who view depression as intractable, a personal failing, or outside their professional scope may be less inclined to screen, diagnose, or engage patients in management [8]. The stigma surrounding mental illness is a well-documented phenomenon in the general population, and healthcare professionals are not immune to it [9]. Negative attitudes among healthcare providers can manifest as pessimism regarding prognosis, social withdrawal, diagnostic overshadowing, or reluctance to treat, ultimately exacerbating the self-stigma experienced by patients and discouraging help-seeking behavior [10]. Non-specialist physicians may be particularly vulnerable to these attitudes, given their limited exposure to psychiatric education and practice. Studies conducted in diverse regions, including Europe and Asia, have reported varying levels of confidence, optimism, and professional comfort among general practitioners and hospital-based physicians in managing depression, with training and experience consistently linked to more favorable attitudes [11,12]. Assessing these attitudes is therefore crucial for designing effective educational and service interventions. To this end, the Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ) has been developed and psychometrically validated as a reliable tool for assessing healthcare professionals' views on depression [13]. The R-DAQ is a 20-item instrument that captures multiple dimensions, including generalist perspectives on managing depression, professional confidence, optimism or pessimism regarding prognosis, beliefs about identifying depression, and perceived professional boundaries between physical and mental healthcare. The R-DAQ has been applied across diverse professional groups and cultural contexts, facilitating cross-study comparisons and enabling researchers to identify areas for improvement [14,15]. In the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, mental health disorders constitute a significant public health concern, with national survey data indicating that a substantial proportion of the population experiences a mental health disorder at some point in their lifetime, and major depressive disorder is among the most prevalent [16]. Cultural and religious interpretations of mental distress, concerns about family reputation, and fear of social labeling continue to contribute to stigma and delayed help-seeking behavior [17]. The Saudi healthcare system has implemented measures to expand mental health services, including the development of national mental health strategies and efforts to integrate mental health into primary care [18]. However, the success of these initiatives is heavily dependent on the preparedness and attitudes of the non-specialist workforce. Existing studies in Saudi Arabia have primarily focused on primary care physicians, medical students, or the general public, and have often been restricted to single institutions or regions [19,20]. Consequently, there is a need for evidence on the attitudes of non-specialist physicians working across specialties in large tertiary hospitals in the capital, Riyadh, where complex patients with comorbid physical and mental illness are frequently managed and where many trainees receive their education. This study aimed to investigate the attitudes of non-specialist physicians towards depression in four tertiary centers in Riyadh using the R-DAQ. It also sought to examine the relationship between these attitudes and professional characteristics, including specialty, seniority, and clinical experience, which may shape confidence and willingness to manage depression. By characterizing optimism, confidence, and perceived professional roles within this population, the study provides locally relevant evidence to inform undergraduate and postgraduate mental health education, support the integration of mental health into general hospital care, and contribute to efforts to reduce stigma within the medical profession itself. The study was designed as a descriptive, cross-sectional, questionnaire-based survey, conducted between [month/year] and [month/year] in four tertiary centers in Riyadh. The survey aimed to recruit a representative sample of non-specialist physicians working across various specialties, with the goal of gathering insights into their attitudes towards depression and identifying areas for improvement in their education, training, and practice. By exploring the attitudes of non-specialist physicians in Saudi Arabia, this study contributes to the growing body of research focused on understanding the complexities of depression and its management in diverse cultural and clinical contexts. Furthermore, the study's findings have significant implications for the development of targeted interventions aimed at improving the recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of depression in non-specialist settings, ultimately enhancing patient outcomes and reducing the burden of mental health disorders on individuals, families, and society as a whole. The integration of mental health services into primary care is a critical step towards addressing the complex needs of patients with depression, and the attitudes of non-specialist physicians play a vital role in this process. By promoting a culture of understanding, empathy, and evidence-based practice, healthcare providers can work towards reducing stigma, improving patient outcomes, and enhancing the overall quality of care for individuals with depression. Ultimately, the study's findings underscore the need for continued research, education, and training in mental health, as well as the importance of addressing the complex interplay between cultural, social, and clinical factors that influence the recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of depression in diverse contexts. Conducted across four large tertiary care centers in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, this study was strategically positioned to capture a broad spectrum of medical specialties due to the centers' size, comprehensive specialty coverage, and role as referral hubs for the central region. In conformity with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for cross-sectional studies [1], the primary objective was to examine the perceptions of depression among non-psychiatric physicians practicing in these centers. The study population consisted of consultants, specialists, residents, and medical interns/registrars from a variety of non-psychiatric specialties, including but not limited to internal medicine, family medicine, surgery, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, and emergency medicine, along with their subspecialties. However, the study deliberately excluded psychiatrists and psychiatry residents, as the focus was squarely on clinicians lacking specialized mental health training. Additionally, physicians on extended leave or those who declined participation were also excluded from the study. To calculate the required sample size, a formula for estimating a single proportion was employed, n = Z²P(1−P)/d², assuming a confidence level of 95% (Z = 1.96), an anticipated proportion of 50% to maximize variability, and a margin of error of 5%, yielding a minimum of 384 respondents. Furthermore, a finite population correction was applied, based on the estimated number of eligible physicians across the four centers, and the target was adjusted to account for potential incomplete responses. A convenience sampling strategy, augmented by quota allocation proportional to each center's physician workforce, was utilized to distribute questionnaires, ultimately resulting in 380 completed questionnaires being included in the final analysis. The research instrument comprised a self-administered questionnaire, divided into two sections. The first section gathered sociodemographic and professional data, including age, gender, nationality, marital status, specialty, professional rank, years of clinical experience, and primary workplace. It also inquired about previous training in mental health or depression management, personal or family history of depression, and prior experience in treating patients with depression. The second section of the questionnaire incorporated the Revised Depression Attitude Questionnaire (R-DAQ), developed by Haddad and colleagues from the original Depression Attitude Questionnaire [2,3]. The R-DAQ consists of 20 items rated on a five-point Likert scale, ranging from "strongly disagree" (1) to "strongly agree" (5), with a validated factor structure comprising five subscales: (i) professional confidence in managing depression, (ii) professional identification and therapeutic optimism or pessimism, (iii) generalist perspective on depression, (iv) the perception of depression as challenging to identify or distinguish from normal distress, and (v) the perception of depression as a mental disorder with a biological or psychosocial etiology [3]. Items were scored in a manner that ensured higher scores consistently reflected the construct measured by each subscale, with appropriate reverse scoring applied where necessary. The instrument has demonstrated acceptable reliability and construct validity in studies involving general practitioners and other clinicians across several countries [3,4]. Given that English is the predominant language of medical education and practice in Saudi Arabia, the questionnaire was administered in English, with permission to utilize the instrument obtained from the authors. The internal consistency of the instrument in the present sample was evaluated using Cronbach's alpha for the total scale and subscales, with values ≥0.70 deemed acceptable. Prior to the primary survey, the questionnaire underwent pilot testing among approximately 20 physicians not included in the final sample to assess clarity, completion time, and feasibility. No substantial modifications were deemed necessary, and pilot data were excluded from the analysis. The data collection process involved trained data collectors visiting clinical departments and distributing the questionnaires, either in paper form or via a secure online link, in accordance with departmental preferences. Participants received an information sheet outlining the study's purpose, the voluntary nature of participation, and assurances of anonymity. Completion of the questionnaire served as implied consent. No personal identifiers were collected, and completed forms were stored securely, accessible solely to the research team. Reminders were issued at one-week and two-week intervals to enhance the response rate. The primary outcome of the study was the attitude towards depression, expressed as the total R-DAQ score and the five subscale scores. Attitudes were interpreted in accordance with published scoring guidance, with higher subscale scores indicating greater confidence, more therapeutic optimism, stronger generalist orientation, greater perceived difficulty in identification, or stronger endorsement of a mental disorder model, respectively [3]. Independent variables included demographic and professional characteristics, specialty, previous training, and personal or family exposure to depression. Community structures are ubiquitous in real-world networks, and exploiting them is central to many applications. Consider online advertising: an advertiser who wants to promote a product may purchase advertising slots on different platforms or websites, each of which attracts a distinct community of users. The advertiser has a limited budget and must decide how to allocate it across communities so as to reach as many distinct users as possible. A similar scenario arises wheen a sales representative visits organizations, when a researcher recruits participants from different groups, or when a marketer sends promotions through different social channels. In each case, an explorer allocates a limited budget among communities, each exploration reaches a member of a community, and the objective is to maximize the number of distinct members met. Because the same member may be encountered repeatedly, the problem exhibits diminishing returns, and the allocation must balance exploring large communities against avoiding redundant encounters. We formalize this setting as the *community exploration problem*. There are several disjoint communities, and the explorer has a budget of exploration opportunities. Each exploration of a community returns a member drawn uniformly at random from it. The explorer wishes to maximize the expected number of distinct members met. We study two variants. In *non-adaptive exploration*, the allocation of the budget across communities is fixed in advance. In *adaptive exploration*, the explorer observes the outcome of each exploration, such as whether the encountered membeer is new, and uses this information to choose the next community to explore. We further consider the problem in two regimes: an offline regime where community sizes are known, and an online reegime where sizes are unknown and must be learned through repeated rounds of exploration. The problem is related to several lines of work but differs from each. Classical resource allocation and budgeted maximization problems often admit constant-factor approximations through greedy algorithms, relying on submodularity [1, 2]. The expected number of distinct members is a concave-like function of the allocation to each community, suggesting that greedy methods should perform well, but it is unclear whether they achieve exact optimality. Adaptive submodularity [3] provides guarantees for adaptive greedy policies, yet typically yields approximation ratios rather than optimality. The problem also resembles the coupon collector problem [4] and species richnss estimation [5], where one samples with replacement to discover distinct items, but these works do not consider allocating a budget across multiple populations to maximize coverage. On the online side, our setting is connected to multi-armed bandits [6, 7] and especially combinatorial multi-armed bandits [8, 9, 10], in which a learner selects a set of base arms and receives semi-bandit feedback. The unknown community sizes play the role of unknown parameters, and the reward is a nonlinear function of both the sizes and the allocation. However, the feedback here has a distinctive structure: the observations are collisions among sampled members, from which sizes must be inferred, and standard analyses do not directly apply. Our contributions are as follows. First, for the offline setting with known community sizes, we show that the greedy algoirthm is optimal for non-adaptive exploration. The key is to prove that the marginal gain of allocating an additional exploration to a community is decreasing in the number of explorations already allocated, so that incremental selection of the largest marginal gain yields a globally opimal allocation. For adaptive exploration, we prove that the greedy policy, which at each step explores the community with the largest expected probability of yielding a new member, is also optimal. This result is stronger than the approximation guarantees usually available for adaptive submodular problems. We also compare the adaptive and non-adaptive optima, quantifying the benefit of adaptivity. Second, for the online setting in which community sizes are unknown, we consider a multi-round game where in each round the explorer alloates a budget, observes the members met, and updates estimates of the sizes. We propose an upper-confidence-bound-style algorithm that builds confidence intervals for the community sizes from the collisions observed within each round and plays the offline greedy solution aaginst optimistic estimates. We prove that this algorithm achieves a regret bound that is logarithmic in the number of rounds, for both the non-adaptive and adaptive versions. Our analysis handles the nonlinearity of the reward and the dependence between estimation error and allocation. Third, we show that regret can be reduced substantially by combining feedback across rounds. Because members encountered in different rounds can be matched, the collisions among all previously observed members provide far more information about community sizes than the collisions within a single round. Exploiting this, we design an algorithm whose regret is bounded by a constant independent of the number of rounds. To our knowledge, this is a rare case in combinatorial bandits in which constant regret is achievable without special assumptions on the reward gap, and it arises from the structure of the feedback. Finally, we complement the theory with experiments on synthetic data and real-world data, which confirm that greedy allocations match optimal values, that the proposed algorithms attain the predicted regret behavior, and that cross-round feedback yields markedly lower regret. The existence of distinct groups within complex networks has far-reaching consequences for various fields, including digital marketing and social media analysis. For example, consider a company seeking to promote a product to a broad and diverse group of people. To achieve this, the company must distribute its limited resources across multiple online platforms, each of which caters to a unique set of users. The primary objective is to reach the maximum number of unique individuals while minimizing redundant interactions. This challenge is not unique to marketing; similar problems arise in fields such as sales and research, where a researcher must allocate limited resources to engage with as many distinct community members as possible. In each of these cases, the researcher faces a fundamental dilemma between exploring large communities and avoiding unnecessary interactions. This dilemma, which we refer to as the *community exploration problem*, can be formally defined as follows: given a set of distinct communities and a limited budget for exploration, the goal is to maximize the expected number of unique members encountered. We examine two variants of this problem: *non-adaptive exploration*, where the allocation of resources is predetermined, and *adaptive exploration*, where the researcher observes the outcome of each interaction and adjusts the allocation accordingly. The community exploration problem is related to several existing areas of research, but it differs from each in significant ways. Traditional problems of resource allocation and budgeted maximization often yield to constant-factor approximations using greedy algorithms, which rely on the concept of submodularity [1, 2]. However, the expected number of unique members encountered is a function of the allocation to each community that exhibits concave-like behavior, suggesting that greedy methods may perform well, but it is unclear whether they achieve optimal results. Adaptive submodularity [3] provides guarantees for adaptive greedy policies, but typically yields approximation ratios rather than optimal solutions. The problem also bears resemblance to the coupon collector problem [4] and species richness estimation [5], where one samples with replacement to discover unique items, but these works do not consider allocating resources across multiple populations to maximize coverage. In the context of online learning, our setting is connected to multi-armed bandits [6, 7] and combinatorial multi-armed bandits [8, 9, 10], where a learner selects a set of base arms and receives semi-bandit feedback. The unknown community sizes play the role of unknown parameters, and the reward is a nonlinear function of both the sizes and the allocation. However, the feedback in our setting has a distinct structure, where the observations are collisions among sampled members, from which sizes must be inferred, and standard analyses do not directly apply. Our contributions are threefold. Firstly, for the offline setting with known community sizes, we demonstrate that the greedy algorithm is optimal for non-adaptive exploration. The key insight is that the marginal benefit of allocating an additional interaction to a community decreases as the number of interactions already allocated increases, so that selecting the largest marginal gain incrementally yields a globally optimal allocation. For adaptive exploration, we prove that the greedy policy, which at each step explores the community with the highest expected probability of yielding a new member, is also optimal. This result is stronger than the approximation guarantees typically available for adaptive submodular problems. We also compare the adaptive and non-adaptive optima, quantifying the benefits of adaptivity. Secondly, for the online setting in which community sizes are unknown, we consider a multi-round game where the researcher allocates resources, observes the members encountered, and updates estimates of the sizes in each round. We propose an algorithm that builds confidence intervals for the community sizes from the collisions observed within each round and plays the offline greedy solution against optimistic estimates. We prove that this algorithm achieves a regret bound that is logarithmic in the number of rounds, for both the non-adaptive and adaptive versions. Our analysis accounts for the nonlinearity of the reward and the dependence between estimation error and allocation. Thirdly, we show that regret can be substantially reduced by combining feedback across rounds. Since members encountered in different rounds can be matched, the collisions among all previously observed members provide far more information about community sizes than the collisions within a single round. By exploiting this, we design an algorithm whose regret is bounded by a constant independent of the number of rounds. To our knowledge, this is a rare case in combinatorial bandits where constant regret is achievable without special assumptions on the reward. Overall, our work provides a comprehensive framework for addressing the community exploration problem, with implications for a wide range of applications. By formalizing the problem and developing efficient algorithms for both offline and online settings, we provide a foundation for optimizing resource allocation in community-based networks. Our results demonstrate the power of combining feedback across rounds and adapting to the observed outcomes, leading to significant improvements in the expected number of unique members encountered. Furthermore, our work highlights the importance of considering the structure of the feedback and the nonlinearity of the reward when designing algorithms for community exploration. By doing so, we can develop more effective strategies for allocating resources and engaging with diverse communities, ultimately leading to better outcomes in various fields, from marketing and sales to research and social media analysis. Tackling complex network optimization problems requires leveraging insights from submodularity, adaptive submodularity, and combinatorial bandits. A particularly intriguing challenge is the allocation of limited resources to explore multiple communities in order to maximize the expected number of unique individuals encountered. This problem is inherently complex due to the structure of the feedback received during the exploration process. To address this challenge, we have developed a comprehensive framework that encompasses both offline and online settings, as well as non-adaptive and adaptive exploration strategies. Our approach is validated by experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, which demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed algorithms and confirm that they achieve the predicted regret behavior. The remainder of this paper is organized into several sections, each of which explores a specific aspect of our research. Section 2 introduces the underlying model and notation used throughout the paper, while Section 3 provides an in-depth examination of the offline problem for both non-adaptive and adaptive exploration strategies.
