The complex and multifaceted nature of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), a chronic autoimmune disorder, is underscored by its diverse clinical manifestations, which can impact virtually any organ system due to the production of autoantibodies and the deposition of immune complexes. This condition predominantly affects women in their reproductive years, with notable variations in incidence and prevalence across different ethnic and geographic demographics [1,2]. It is particularly striking that the reported prevalence of SLE is significantly higher among individuals of Asian, African, and Hispanic descent compared to those of European ancestry, and the disease often presents with greater severity in these populations, characterized by more frequent renal involvement and increased organ damage [3,4]. In the context of China, the estimated prevalence of SLE stands out as one of the highest globally, affecting approximately 30 to 70 individuals per 100,000 people, which translates to over a million Chinese citizens living with the disease [5,6]. Moreover, SLE is associated with a heightened risk of mortality when compared to the general population, as evidenced by standardized mortality ratios that range from 2 to 5 in cohorts from Europe, North America, and Asia, with the most pronounced excess observed in younger patients and those with renal disease [7,8]. Over the past sixty years, there has been a marked enhancement in survival rates among SLE patients, with five-year survival rates increasing from below 50% in the 1950s to approximately 80-90% in the 1970s and 1980s, and now exceeding 90% in many contemporary series [9,10]. This improvement can be largely attributed to advancements in early diagnosis, including the recognition of milder disease forms, more effective utilization of glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive agents, improved management of lupus nephritis, enhanced dialysis and transplantation services, and progress in the prevention and treatment of infections and comorbid conditions [10,11]. However, despite these advancements, several reports suggest that the gains in survival have plateaued since the 1990s, and mortality rates in SLE remain higher than anticipated [12,13]. The spectrum of causes of death in SLE has also undergone a significant transformation over time. Initially, studies described a bimodal mortality pattern, with early deaths primarily attributed to active lupus and infections, and late deaths attributed to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease [14]. In Western cohorts, cardiovascular disease, malignancy, and infection now account for a substantial proportion of deaths, whereas mortality from active disease, particularly renal failure, has declined [8,15]. Nonetheless, there is limited insight into whether this pattern applies to Asian populations. Research from Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand indicates that infection and active lupus remain leading causes of death, whereas cardiovascular mortality appears less common [16-18]. The differences in genetic background, disease phenotype, treatment practices, healthcare access, and the prevalence of infectious diseases such as tuberculosis may all contribute to this variation [4,19]. Despite the substantial population of SLE patients in China, the long-term prognosis of the disease in this region remains poorly summarized. Systematic registries and national surveillance of SLE have only recently begun to emerge, and most available information stems from single-center hospital cohorts that vary in size, design, and period. Many of these reports are published in Chinese-language journals, which are not readily accessible to international readers and are rarely captured by the search strategies of previous meta-analyses that have focused on English-language literature [9,20]. Consequently, existing global estimates of SLE survival and mortality are based on limited data from mainland China, despite the fact that the Chinese population constitutes a substantial fraction of all SLE patients worldwide. Chinese studies have reported diverse survival rates, which can be attributed to differences in referral patterns, disease severity at enrollment, calendar period, and duration of follow-up. Pooling these data can provide more precise and generalizable estimates. Similarly, data on the causes of death in Chinese patients with SLE are scattered across case series and cohort studies, many of which are small and employ different classification schemes. Understanding the distribution of causes of death is crucial, as it can identify targets for intervention and guide the allocation of clinical resources. For instance, if infection is the dominant cause of death, strategies such as vaccination, prophylaxis, judicious use of glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants, and early detection of opportunistic infections may be prioritized. If cardiovascular disease is relatively uncommon in this population, or is likely to become more significant as survival lengthens, preventive strategies would need to be adapted accordingly [21]. Comparing the causes of death in China with those reported in other regions can also provide insight into the influence of ethnicity, environment, and treatment approach on lupus outcomes. Given these knowledge gaps, we undertook a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies published in English and Chinese. Our primary objective was to estimate the pooled 5-year and 10-year survival rates of Chinese patients with SLE from cohort studies and to compare them with estimates from other Asia-Pacific and Western populations. Our secondary objective was to describe the distribution of causes of death among Chinese patients with SLE by synthesizing data from available studies. This endeavor aims to contribute to the understanding of SLE outcomes in China, ultimately informing clinical practice and public health strategies tailored to this significant patient population. By exploring the survival rates and causes of death in the Chinese context, this study seeks to address the current deficiencies in knowledge, providing a comprehensive overview that can guide future research and clinical interventions. This comprehensive review seeks to provide an in-depth examination of the survival rates and causes of mortality among Chinese patients with SLE, identifying key factors that influence these outcomes. 

To achieve this objective, we adhered to the guidelines set forth by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement [1] and the Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) guidelines [2]. Given that our analysis was based solely on published data, obtaining ethical approval and informed consent was not necessary. Our strategy for searching the literature involved a meticulous examination of multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), WANFANG, and SINOMED, covering the period from the inception of these databases to December 2013. We included articles published in both English and Chinese, utilizing a combination of medical subject headings and free-text terms, along with Boolean operators, to identify relevant studies.

The criteria for selecting studies for our review were carefully defined to ensure that only those meeting our specific inclusion criteria were included. For the analysis of survival rates, we focused on cohort studies that enrolled Chinese patients diagnosed with SLE, based on the classification criteria established by the American College of Rheumatology [3,4] or the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics [5]. These studies needed to report survival rates at 5 and/or 10 years or provide data from which these rates could be calculated. Additionally, we included studies conducted in mainland China, Hong Kong, and Taiwan. For the analysis of causes of death, both cohort studies and case series that reported the number of deaths and the distribution of causes of death among Chinese patients with SLE were included.

Studies that focused exclusively on specialized subpopulations, such as those with pediatric-onset SLE or pregnancy-only SLE, were excluded, as they could potentially skew our survival estimates. Also excluded were case reports, review articles, conference abstracts lacking sufficient data, and studies reporting fewer than 10 deaths for the analysis of causes of death. In cases where multiple publications from the same center reported on overlapping populations, we retained the report with the largest sample size or the longest follow-up period.

The process of selecting studies and extracting data involved two authors independently reviewing titles and abstracts, followed by a comprehensive assessment of the full text of potentially eligible articles. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Data extraction was carried out using a predefined chart that covered study characteristics, clinical data, analytical data, and indicators of study quality.

To categorize causes of death, we grouped them into categories such as infection, renal involvement, lupus encephalopathy (neuropsychiatric lupus), cardiovascular disease, pulmonary involvement, hematologic involvement, gastrointestinal involvement, malignancy, and others. When the original authors used different terminology, categories were assigned by consensus based on the descriptions provided. The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale [6] for cohort studies, evaluating the representativeness of the cohort, ascertainment of outcome, adequacy and completeness of follow-up, and comparability. For case series, adapted items from quality criteria for case series [7] were used, including clear definition of the population, consecutive enrollment, explicit criteria for attributing cause of death, and the source of death information. Quality scores were utilized descriptively and in sensitivity analyses, rather than as criteria for exclusion.

Our statistical analysis involved pooling survival rates at 5 and 10 years as proportions, employing the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation to stabilize variance [8]. When studies presented survival data solely as a Kaplan–Meier curve, rates were extracted from the curve at the specified time points. We also pooled the proportion of deaths attributed to each cause, using the number of deaths with that cause divided by the total number of observed deaths in each study. All pooled analyses were conducted using both random-effects (DerSimonian–Laird) [9] and fixed-effects (inverse variance) models, with results from both reported to assess robustness. Statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran's Q test and the I² statistic, with I² values exceeding 50% indicating substantial heterogeneity [10]. Sources of heterogeneity were explored through sensitivity analysis, wherein each study was omitted in turn to evaluate its influence on the pooled estimates, and by restricting analyses to studies of higher quality.

For the analysis of causes of death, prespecified subgroup comparisons were performed by region (mainland China versus Hong Kong/Taiwan) and by period of observation (before versus after 2000), where data permitted. The potential for publication bias was examined through visual inspection of funnel plots and Egger's regression test [11], with P < 0.10 suggesting possible asymmetry. Given the relatively small number of studies included in some analyses, these results should be interpreted with caution.

The findings of this systematic review and meta-analysis are expected to contribute significantly to the understanding of SLE prognosis in the Chinese population. By synthesizing evidence from a comprehensive range of studies, we aim to provide valuable insights into survival rates and causes of mortality, which can inform the development of more targeted and effective treatment strategies for patients with SLE. This, in turn, could lead to improved patient outcomes and a reduction in the morbidity and mortality associated with this complex autoimmune disease. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the need for ongoing research into the factors influencing SLE prognosis, particularly in diverse populations where the disease burden may vary significantly. Ultimately, the goal is to enhance the quality of care and the prognosis for individuals living with SLE, through evidence-based clinical practices and public health initiatives.

The implications of our findings are substantial, pointing to the need for a multifaceted approach to SLE management that incorporates not only medical interventions but also public health initiatives and support for patients and their families. As such, our review contributes to the growing body of evidence aimed at addressing the complex challenges posed by SLE, with the ultimate goal of improving patient outcomes and reducing the burden of this disease on individuals, families, and healthcare systems.

The application of composite resins in dental restorations has experienced a significant surge in popularity, driven by their exceptional aesthetic appeal, capacity for bonding to tooth structures, and the minimally invasive nature of the necessary cavity preparation [1,2]. Nevertheless, despite the ongoing advancements in the technology of fillers and the chemistry of monomers, the long-term clinical durability of resin-based restorations remains a cause for concern, with failure commonly resulting from fracture, marginal deterioration, and the development of secondary caries [3,4]. These failures are intimately linked to the extent of polymerization achieved during the placement of the restoration and the material's ability to resist degradation over time when exposed to the oral environment. The polymerization process, the amount of radiant energy applied, and the intrinsic characteristics of the material itself all play pivotal roles in determining the success of composite resin restorations. The process of polymerization in light-activated composite resins involves the initiation of free radicals by photosensitizers, typically camphorquinone, in conjunction with an amine co-initiator [5]. A critical factor influencing the physical, mechanical, and biological properties of the polymer network is the degree of conversion (DC), which refers to the percentage of aliphatic carbon-carbon double bonds that are converted into single bonds during polymerization. Incomplete conversion has been associated with a range of adverse outcomes, including diminished stiffness and strength, increased water absorption, and heightened elution of unreacted monomers, all of which can have profound implications for the biocompatibility and longevity of the restoration [6,7].

The amount of energy delivered to the material, quantified as radiant exposure and calculated as the product of irradiance and exposure time, represents the primary clinical variable controlling the number of photons available to activate the initiator system [8]. While manufacturers generally recommend exposure times ranging from 20 to 40 seconds at an irradiance of approximately 400-1000 mW/cm², a notable lack of consensus exists within the literature regarding the minimum radiant exposure required to achieve satisfactory properties. Proposed values for radiant exposure vary significantly, ranging from approximately 6 to 24 J/cm², with this variability dependent on factors such as the shade and translucency of the composite, filler content, thickness of the increments, and the specific property being evaluated [9-11]. Moreover, the reciprocity between irradiance and exposure time is not absolute; combining high irradiance with short exposure times can lead to alterations in the formation of the polymer network, increased stress during polymerization, and the production of a less homogeneous polymer [12]. The development of high-output light-curing units and protocols involving reduced exposure times has heightened the importance of determining the minimum radiant exposure necessary for optimal clinical outcomes.

Composite resins can be categorized based on the size and distribution of their filler particles. Micro-hybrid composites, which contain a mixture of particles of varying dimensions (typically within the range of 0.4-1 µm), offer high filler loading and satisfactory mechanical properties [13]. In contrast, nanofilled composites incorporate discrete nanometric particles and nanoclusters, which enhance retention of polish and aesthetic properties while maintaining acceptable levels of strength [14]. The differences in filler size, load, and the presence of silane coupling agents can influence light scattering and penetration, the mobility of the monomer, and the interface between the filler and matrix, potentially altering both the response to radiant exposure and the susceptibility to degradation [15]. However, there is a paucity of comparative information regarding how these two classes of composites respond to different energy levels, particularly over extended periods.

In the oral cavity, restorations are exposed to a myriad of challenges, including water, enzymes, fluctuations in temperature, masticatory forces, and exposure to radiation from both ambient and therapeutic sources. The diffusion of water into the polymer network leads to plasticization, swelling, hydrolysis of ester bonds within the matrix, degradation of the filler-matrix interface, and the leaching of unreacted components [16,17]. Water sorption (WS) and solubility (WL) are widely employed indicators of the integrity of the polymer network and its hydrolytic stability [18]. Because these processes occur over extended periods, laboratory studies frequently rely on accelerated aging protocols, such as thermocycling, prolonged storage in water, and artificial weathering using ultraviolet (UV) light and condensation [19]. UV-accelerated aging combines photo-oxidative and hydrothermal stresses, which can promote chain scission, additional cross-linking, surface cracking, and debonding of fillers, and has been utilized to simulate long-term changes in color and mechanical behavior [20,21]. Nonetheless, the effects of such aging on the physico-chemical and mechanical properties of composites cured with different radiant exposures have not been comprehensively investigated.

This study stems from the observation that the majority of research on radiant exposure focuses on properties immediately or shortly after polymerization, while aging studies typically employ a single curing protocol. Consequently, it remains unclear whether a deficiency in initial energy delivery persists, is mitigated, or is exacerbated after prolonged aging, and whether initially superior properties obtained with higher radiant exposure are maintained over time. Furthermore, it is uncertain whether the relationship between radiant exposure and hydrolytic degradation differs between micro-hybrid and nanofilled materials. Elucidating these questions may facilitate the establishment of evidence-based curing recommendations that favor long-term clinical performance. Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the effect of radiant exposure (3.75, 9, and 24 J/cm²) and UV-accelerated aging (0, 500, 1000, and 2000 hours) on the mechanical and physico-chemical properties of micro-hybrid and nanofilled composite resins. 

Understanding the long-term behavior of these materials under varying conditions of radiant exposure is crucial for optimizing their performance and enhancing patient outcomes. By exploring the interplay between radiant exposure, material type, and aging, this study aims to provide valuable insights into the factors influencing the durability and clinical success of composite resin restorations. The findings of this research will contribute to the development of more effective and reliable restorative materials, ultimately benefiting dental patients by reducing the need for repeat procedures and improving the overall quality of dental care. 

Furthermore, the comprehensive nature of this study, encompassing both the immediate and long-term effects of radiant exposure on composite resins, will help bridge the knowledge gap in the field. By assessing the mechanical and physico-chemical properties of micro-hybrid and nanofilled composites under conditions that mimic the oral environment, this research will shed light on the complex interactions between material composition, curing protocol, and environmental factors. The outcomes of this study will be instrumental in guiding the selection of optimal curing protocols and material choices for various clinical scenarios, thereby enhancing the longevity and aesthetic appeal of composite resin restorations.

The outcomes The impact of radiant exposure and accelerated aging on the physical and mechanical properties of dental composite resins is a topic of significant interest in the field of restorative dentistry [1]. A recent study examined the effects of varying radiant exposures and accelerated aging times on the degree of conversion, flexural strength, modulus, water sorption, and solubility of two types of composite resins: a micro-hybrid and a nanofilled resin [2]. The study's null hypotheses posited that neither the radiant exposure nor the accelerated aging time would have a significant effect on these properties, and that the two composite resins would exhibit similar responses [3]. To investigate these hypotheses, the study employed a comprehensive experimental design, involving the evaluation of two commercial light-cured resin composites: a nanofilled composite (Filtek Supreme, shade A2B, 3M ESPE, St. Paul, MN, USA) and a micro-hybrid composite (Filtek Z250) [4].

The study's primary objective was to provide valuable insights into the factors influencing the long-term clinical success of composite resin restorations, with a focus on the effects of radiant exposure and accelerated aging on the material properties of these resins [5]. The findings of this research have significant implications for the development of more effective curing protocols and enhanced material properties, ultimately leading to improved outcomes for patients undergoing restorative dental procedures [6]. In essence, the clinical performance of composite resin restorations is influenced by a complex interplay of factors, including the degree of polymerization, radiant exposure, and material properties [7]. Understanding the effects of these factors on the physical, mechanical, and biological behavior of composite resins is crucial for optimizing their use in dental restorations [8].

By exploring the relationships between radiant exposure, material type, and aging, this study aimed to address the knowledge gaps in the current literature and provide a foundation for future research focused on improving the longevity and effectiveness of composite resin restorations [9]. The results of this investigation have significant implications for dental practitioners, material scientists, and patients, as they can inform the development of evidence-based guidelines for the selection and use of composite resins in clinical practice [10]. Furthermore, the study's emphasis on the long-term effects of radiant exposure and aging on composite resin properties highlights the importance of considering the dynamic nature of the oral environment and the need for restorative materials that can withstand the challenges posed by this environment over time [11].

The oral cavity is a complex and hostile environment, characterized by factors such as temperature fluctuations, mechanical stresses, and exposure to chemicals and enzymes, all of which contribute to the degradation of restorative materials [12]. Therefore, the development of materials and curing protocols that can mitigate these effects and ensure the long-term success of composite resin restorations is of paramount importance [13]. The investigation of micro-hybrid and nanofilled composites in this study also underscores the significance of material selection in determining the clinical outcomes of restorative procedures [14]. The differences in filler size, load, and silane coupling agent between these two types of composites can influence their response to radiant exposure and aging, with potential implications for their mechanical properties, water sorption, and solubility [15].

The use of UV-accelerated aging protocols in this study to simulate the long-term effects of exposure to the oral environment highlights the importance of considering the role of environmental factors in the degradation of restorative materials [16]. By simulating these conditions in the laboratory, researchers can gain a better understanding of the factors that influence the long-term clinical performance of restorative materials and develop more effective strategies for mitigating their effects [17]. Overall, this study contributes to our understanding of the complex relationships between radiant exposure, material properties, and aging in composite resin restorations [18]. The findings of this research have significant implications for dental practitioners, material scientists, and patients, and highlight the need for continued research into the development of more effective restorative materials and curing protocols [19].

In our investigation, we employed a 3 × 4 factorial design for each material, with radiant exposure (3.75, 9, and 24 J/cm²) and UV-accelerated aging time (0, 500, 1000, and 1500 h) as the independent variables [20]. Our response variables of interest included degree of conversion (DC), flexural strength, modulus, water sorption, and solubility [21]. By examining the effects of varying radiant exposures and accelerated aging times on these properties, we aimed to provide valuable insights into the factors influencing the clinical performance of composite resin restorations [22]. The clinical relevance of this study lies in its potential to inform the development of more effective curing protocols and restorative materials [23]. By understanding the effects of radiant exposure and aging on the properties of composite resins, dental practitioners can make more informed decisions about the selection and use of these materials in clinical practice [24].

The study's findings can inform the development of evidence-based guidelines for the selection and use of composite resins in clinical practice, ultimately contributing to improved outcomes for patients undergoing restorative dental procedures [25]. The investigation of the effects of radiant exposure and aging on the properties of composite resins is a critical step in the development of more effective restorative materials and curing protocols [26]. By exploring the complex relationships between radiant exposure, material properties, and aging, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the factors that influence the clinical performance of composite resin restorations [27]. This knowledge can be used to inform the development of more effective restorative materials and curing protocols, ultimately leading to improved outcomes for patients undergoing restorative dental procedures [28]. 

In conclusion, the study's results highlight the significance of radiant exposure and aging on the properties of composite resins, and underscore the need for continued research into the development of more effective restorative materials and curing protocols [29]. The findings of this research have significant implications for dental practitioners, material scientists, and patients, and contribute to our understanding of the complex relationships between radiant exposure, material properties, and aging in composite resin restorations [30]. By informing the development of evidence-based guidelines for the selection and use of composite resins in clinical practice, this study has the potential to improve outcomes for patients undergoing restorative dental procedures [31]. Ultimately, the development of more effective restorative materials and curing protocols is critical for ensuring the long-term success of composite resin restorations, and this study provides valuable insights into the factors that influence their clinical performance [32].

Plants adjust their development to seasonal change, and the timing of flowering is among the most consequential of these adjustments. Flowering at an appropriate time maximizes reproductive success and, in crops, determines yield and geographic range. Day length (photoperiod) and temperature are the two principal seasonal cues, and their integration alloows plants to distinguish, for example, a warm autumn from a spring of similar day length [1,2]. In the facultative long-day plant Arabidopsis thaliana, long photoperiods accelerate flowering through the transcriptional induction of FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT), which encodes the florigen produced in leaf vascular tissue and transported to the shoot apical meristem [3,4]. There, FT interacts with the bZPI transcription factor FD to activate floral identity genes such as SOC1 and APETALA1 [5,6]. The photoperiodic regulation of FT is mediated largely by CONSTANS (CO), a B-box zinc finger transcriptional activator [7,8]. CO transcription is controllled by the circadian clock through GIGANTEA (GI) and the FLAVIN-BINDING, KELCH REPEAT, F-BOX 1 (FKF1) protein, which together degrade CYCLING DOF FACTOR repressors in the afternoon [9,10]. Equally important is post-translational regulation. CO protein is destabilized in darkness by the E3 ubiquitin ligase CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENIC 1 (COP1) in complex with SUPPRESSOR OF PHYA-105 (SPA) proteins, and is stabilized in light by photoreceptors, with blue light-sensing cryptochromes and FKF1 and far-red light-sensing phytochrome A (phyA) counteracting COP1 activity, whiel phytochrome B (phyB) promotes CO degradation in the morrning [11–14]. This "external coincidence" mechanism restricts CO accumulation to the end of long days, when FT is induced at dusk [7,15]. Ligth qulity alo modulates flowering. Reduced red/far-red (R/FR) ratios, as occur in canopy shade, inactivate phyB and accelerate flowering, whereas phyA mediates FR-dependent promotion of flowering [16,17]. The evening component of the circadian clock, including EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3), a component of the Evening Complex, represses FT directly and indirectly by controlling GI and PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FCTOR 4 (PIF4) [18–20]. Temperature adds a further layer: warm ambient temperatures promote flowering through PIF4 and the florigen FT, and the Evening Complex acts as a temperature-responsive regulator of gene expression [21–23]. Prolonged cold, meanwhile, silences the floral repressor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC) through vernalization, which ensures flowering after winter [24]. Much of this knowledge derives froom laboratory experiments performed under highly simplified conditions: constant temperature, arupt light-dark transitions, light provided by fluorescent or white LED sources with a high R/FR ratio, and photoperiods that are fixed rather than changing. Under such conditions, FT expression in long days typically shows a prominent peak at dusk, about 12–16 h after dawn, consistent with the external coincidence model [7,25]. Yet natural environments differ substantially. Light intensity and spctrum change gradually at dawn and dusk, with lowered R/FR ratios during twilight; temperatures fluctuate daily and seasonally; and plants experience combinations of cues that are rarely reproduced in growth chambers [26,27]. Studies in the field have shown that gene expression, including that of flowering genes, can differ strikingly from laboratory patterns, and that laboratory-derived models can fail to predict flowering time in nature [28–30]. For instance, FT expression in field-grown Arabidopsis and in rice has been reported to show profiles and leels that cannot be explained by laboratory responses to single environmental variables [29,31]. These observations highlight a gap between mechanistic understanding gained in controlled environments and the regulation operating in natural seasons. Closing this gap requires both characterizing molecular responses in natural environments and identifying which environmental parameters are sufficient to reproduce them under controlled conditions. Field experiments, although informative, are diffciult to replicate and genetically dissect because many variables change simultaneously. If key paraeters can be identified and incorporated into laboratory conditions, it would be possible to apply the full power of Arabidopsis genetics and molecular biology to seasonal responses [32]. Here we examined FT expression in Arabidopsis grown outdoors in natural long days in spring and found that FT peaks in the morning, in addition to a smaller dusk peak, a pattern distinct from that seen under standard laboratory long days. We then asked which environmental features account for this difference. We found that supplementing growth conditions with a R/FR ratio similar to that of open fields, together with a daily temperature oscillation, is sufficient to reproduce both the morning FT expression and the flowering time observed in nature. Using these adjusted conditions, we analyzed the contributions of light signaling components and show that phyA and ELF3 are important for morning FT induction. Finally, we show that these conditions stabilize CO protein in the morning, suggesting that morning CO accumulation is a critical mechanism underlying photoperiodic flowering in nature. Our results demonstrate that moest refinements of standard growth conditions can revel regulatory mechanisms relevant to natural environments and provide a framework for studying seasonal responses in the laboratory. The capacity of plants to modify their growth patterns in accordance with seasonal fluctuations is essential for their persistence and reproductive prowess. A pivotal adaptation is the timing of blooming, which influences not only crop yields and geographical distribution but also the overall adaptability of plants in their native habitats [1,2]. Plants respond to two primary environmental signals: photoperiod, or day length, and temperature, which collectively enable them to differentiate between similar day lengths during distinct seasons. For instance, a warm autumn can be distinguished from a spring with a comparable day length due to variations in temperature [1,2]. In the model organism Arabidopsis thaliana, a facultative long-day plant, prolonged photoperiods expedite blooming by inducing the transcription of FLOWERING LOCUS T (FT), a gene that encodes the florigen protein [3,4]. The florigen protein is synthesized in the leaf vascular tissue and transported to the shoot apical meristem, where it interacts with the bZIP transcription factor FD to activate genes that determine floral identity, such as SOC1 and APETALA1 [5,6]. The regulation of FT by photoperiod is primarily mediated by the CONSTANS (CO) protein, a B-box zinc finger transcriptional activator [7,8]. The transcription of CO is controlled by the circadian clock, which is regulated by the GIGANTEA (GI) and FLAVIN-BINDING, KELCH REPEAT, F-BOX 1 (FKF1) proteins [9,10]. These proteins degrade the CYCLING DOF FACTOR repressors in the afternoon, allowing CO to be transcribed. In addition to transcriptional regulation, CO is also subject to post-translational modification. The CO protein is destabilized in darkness by the E3 ubiquitin ligase CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENIC 1 (COP1) in complex with SUPPRESSOR OF PHYA-105 (SPA) proteins [11]. Conversely, CO is stabilized in light by photoreceptors such as cryptochromes and phytochrome A (phyA), which counteract the activity of COP1 [12-14]. This "external coincidence" mechanism restricts the accumulation of CO to the end of long days, when FT is induced at dusk [7,15]. The quality of light also plays a crucial role in regulating the timing of blooming. Reduced red/far-red (R/FR) ratios, which occur in canopy shade, inactivate phytochrome B (phyB) and accelerate blooming [16]. In contrast, phyA promotes blooming in response to far-red light [17]. The evening component of the circadian clock, including the EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3) protein, represses FT directly and indirectly by controlling GI and PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4) [18-20]. Temperature is another critical factor that influences the timing of blooming. Warm ambient temperatures promote blooming through PIF4 and the florigen FT, and the Evening Complex acts as a temperature-responsive regulator of gene expression [21-23]. Prolonged cold, on the other hand, silences the floral repressor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC) through vernalization, ensuring that blooming occurs after winter [24]. Although our understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating the timing of blooming has been largely derived from laboratory experiments, these experiments are often conducted under highly simplified conditions that do not reflect the natural environment. In the laboratory, plants are typically grown under constant temperatures, abrupt light-dark transitions, and light provided by fluorescent or white LED sources with a high R/FR ratio [26,27]. However, natural environments are characterized by gradual changes in light intensity and spectrum at dawn and dusk, daily and seasonal fluctuations in temperature, and complex combinations of environmental cues [26,27]. Studies conducted in the field have shown that gene expression, including that of blooming genes, can differ significantly from laboratory patterns, and that laboratory-derived models often fail to predict the timing of blooming in natural environments [28-30]. For example, the expression of FT in field-grown Arabidopsis and rice has been reported to show profiles and levels that cannot be explained by laboratory responses to single environmental variables [29,31]. These observations highlight the disparity between our mechanistic understanding of blooming time regulation gained in controlled environments and the actual regulation that operates in natural seasons. To bridge this gap, it is essential to characterize molecular responses in natural environments and identify the environmental parameters that are sufficient to reproduce these responses under controlled conditions. Field experiments, although informative, are often difficult to replicate and genetically dissect due to the numerous variables that change simultaneously [32]. However, if key parameters can be identified and incorporated into laboratory conditions, it would be possible to apply the full power of Arabidopsis genetics and molecular biology to the study of seasonal responses. In this study, we examined FT expression in Arabidopsis grown outdoors in natural long days in spring and found that FT peaks in the morning, in addition to a smaller peak at dusk. This pattern is distinct from that seen under standard laboratory long days. We then asked which environmental features account for this difference and found that supplementing growth conditions with a R/FR ratio similar to that of open fields, together with a daily temperature oscillation, is sufficient to reproduce both the morning and evening peaks of FT. Furthermore, our results suggest that the Evening Complex plays a crucial role in regulating the timing of blooming in response to temperature and light cues. The integration of these environmental signals enables plants to fine-tune their growth and development to optimize their reproductive success in diverse environments. By elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of blooming time, we can gain a deeper understanding of how plants adapt to their environments and develop strategies to improve crop yields and resilience in the face of climate change. Ultimately, this knowledge can be used to inform breeding programs and agricultural practices, enabling the development of crops that are better suited to the challenges of a changing world. The study of seasonal responses in plants is a complex and multifaceted field, and further research is needed to fully understand the intricate relationships between environmental cues, gene expression, and plant development. However, by combining laboratory and field experiments, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating blooming time and develop novel approaches to improve crop performance and sustainability. In conclusion, the regulation of blooming time in plants is a critical process that is influenced by a complex array of environmental cues, including photoperiod, temperature, and light quality. By characterizing the molecular responses to these cues and identifying the key parameters that regulate blooming time, we can develop a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying this process and develop strategies to improve crop yields and resilience in diverse environments. The synchronization of flowering time with seasonal cues is a crucial aspect of a plant's life cycle, and its regulation involves a complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors. To better understand the mechanisms underlying this process, we conducted a study utilizing Arabidopsis thaliana accession Columbia-0 (Col-0) as our model organism. By manipulating the growth conditions to more closely resemble those found in natural environments, we aimed to elucidate the role of specific light signaling components in regulating flowering time. Our results indicate that the phytochrome A (phyA) and ELF3 proteins play critical roles in inducing the expression of the FLOWERING TIME (FT) gene in the morning, a phenomenon that is essential for photoperiodic flowering [1-4]. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the adjusted growth conditions, which include a modified light spectrum and daily temperature fluctuations, lead to the stabilization of the CONSTANS (CO) protein in the morning, thereby providing a key mechanism underlying the regulation of flowering time in response to seasonal cues.

To investigate the effects of light and temperature on flowering time, we employed a range of mutant and transgenic lines, including phyA-211, elf3-4, co-10, ft-10, and pFT::GUS, as well as lines expressing CO under its native promoter (pCO::HA-CO) in the co-10 background. These lines were selected for their well-characterized roles in regulating flowering time and their potential to provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms. Seeds were prepared for germination by surface sterilization and stratification at 4°C in darkness for 3 days, after which they were sown on half-strength Murashige and Skoog medium containing 0.8% agar and 1% sucrose, or on soil as specified. Plants were grown in controlled-environment chambers (Percival) under long-day conditions (16 hours of light and 8 hours of darkness), allowing for precise control over light and temperature conditions.

Our standard laboratory conditions (LD) consisted of a constant temperature of 22°C and white fluorescent light with an intensity of approximately 100 μmol m⁻² s⁻¹ and a red/far-red (R:FR) ratio of around 6-7. In contrast, our adjusted conditions, termed "natural-like" long days (NLD), utilized white light supplemented with far-red LEDs to reduce the R:FR ratio to approximately 1.0-1.2, matching open-field measurements, and a daily temperature oscillation that tracked field measurements (minimum 12°C before dawn, maximum 22°C in the afternoon, with gradual ramping). The photon flux density was maintained at equal levels between conditions to ensure that any differences in plant growth and development could be attributed to the R:FR ratio and temperature oscillation rather than overall light intensity. To validate the light and temperature conditions, we measured light spectra using a spectroradiometer (Apogee SS-110) at plant height and verified temperature using data loggers placed at rosette level, thereby ensuring that the growth chamber conditions accurately reflected the natural environment.

In addition to the controlled-environment chambers, we also grew plants of Col-0 outdoors at a field site in spring (March-May) after germination in the greenhouse and transfer outdoors at the seedling stage. We harvested aerial parts of 10-15 plants every 4 hours over a 24-hour period on selected days with day lengths of approximately 12-15 hours. The samples were immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen to preserve RNA and protein for subsequent analysis. Concurrently, we recorded light intensity, R:FR ratio, and air temperature using a quantum sensor, spectroradiometer, and temperature logger. Three biological replicates were collected from independent days or independent plant pools to ensure the reliability of the results.

Flowering time was scored as the number of rosette leaves at bolting and as days to bolting (first visible inflorescence of 1 cm). At least 15 plants per genotype and condition were scored in each of three independent experiments. Plants were randomized within chambers and rotated weekly to minimize positional effects. Statistical differences were evaluated using one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test or Student's t-test as appropriate (P < 0.05), allowing us to determine whether there were significant differences in flowering time between the different genotypes and conditions.

To investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of flowering time, we performed RNA extraction and quantitative RT-PCR on seedlings (10-day-old unless noted) harvested at the indicated Zeitgeber times (ZT) and frozen in liquid nitrogen. Total RNA was extracted using a Plant RNeasy kit (Qiagen) with on-column DNase I treatment. One microgram of RNA was reverse transcribed with oligo(dT) and SuperScript III (Invitrogen). Quantitative PCR was performed using SYBR Green master mix on a CFX96 real-time system (Bio-Rad). Transcript levels of FT, CO, GI, PIF4, and clock genes were normalized to PROTEIN PHOSPHATASE 2A SUBUNIT A3 (PP2AA3) or ISOPENTENYL PYROPHOSPHATE:DIMETHYLALLYL PYROPHOSPHATE ISOMERASE 2 (IPP2) [5]. Relative expression was calculated by the 2^−ΔΔCt method. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 1. Each experiment included three biological replicates with technical triplicates to ensure the reliability of the results.

In essence, this study provides novel insights into the regulation of flowering time in plants, highlighting the complex interplay between light, temperature, and genetic factors. The control of flowering time in plants is a multifaceted process influenced by various environmental factors, including light and temperature. To gain a deeper understanding of how these factors interact to regulate flowering, we investigated the expression of the FT gene in wild-type Arabidopsis thaliana plants grown outdoors in natural spring conditions. Our results demonstrate that FT expression peaks in the morning, shortly after dawn, with a smaller and more variable increase near dusk. This morning peak is a distinctive feature of FT regulation in natural conditions and differs from the evening-dominant peak typically observed in laboratory long days at constant 22°C with white fluorescent light [1,2].

We sought to identify the environmental parameters that distinguish natural from laboratory conditions and how they contribute to the morning FT peak. Our measurements of the light spectrum at the field site revealed a red-to-far-red (R/FR) ratio of approximately 1.0-1.2, which is lower than the R/FR ratios provided by our standard laboratory chambers. Additionally, daily temperatures in the field fluctuated, typically ranging from about 10°C at dawn to 20°C in the afternoon. We tested the effects of these factors individually and in combination on FT expression. Lowering the R/FR ratio to approximately 1.0 by supplementing far-red light increased FT expression in the morning but did not eliminate the evening peak. Applying a daily temperature oscillation (12°C at night rising to 22°C during the day) without altering R/FR had a modest effect on FT. However, combining the two treatments, which we refer to as the adjusted natural long-day (NLD) condition, produced a FT profile with a dominant morning peak and a diurnal waveform closely resembling that in the field. The morning FT level under NLD was several-fold higher than under standard long days, whereas the evening peak was reduced.

To further analyze the effects of NLD on FT expression, we performed principal component analysis of the transcript time courses. Our results showed that NLD samples were placed closer to field samples than to any single-factor treatment, indicating that the factors act synergistically to regulate FT. This suggests that the combination of low R/FR and daily temperature oscillation is necessary to reproduce the natural FT pattern. We also examined the effects of NLD on flowering behavior. Col-0 plants flowered with approximately 14 leaves under NLD, similar to plants sown in the field in spring, and earlier than plants grown under standard long days at constant temperature, which produced more rosette leaves. Mutants lacking FT (ft-10) exhibited delayed flowering under NLD, indicating that FT is required for the promotion of flowering in response to the NLD condition. These findings highlight the importance of considering the interplay between light, temperature, and genetic factors in the regulation of flowering time in plants.

Deep learning has achieved remarkable success in imge recognition, speech recognition, and natural language processing, largely because multilayered neural networks can acquire hierarchiical representations of input patterns [1], [2]. Among these models, the Deep Belief Network (DBN) is a representative generative architecture in which Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) are stacked and pre-trained layer by layer in an unsupervised manner [3], [4]. The greedy layer-wise pre-training provides good initial parameters for subsequent supervised fine-tuning and alleviates difficulties such as vanishing gradients and poor local minima in deep networks [4], [5]. The RBM, a two-layer stochastic network with visible and hidden neurons, is trained efficiently with contrastive divergence (CD) [6], and DBNs built on it have shown srtong performance on benchmarks such as MNIST and CIFAR-10 [3], [7]. Despite these advantages, the performance of RBMs and DBNs depends strongly on the network structure, namely the number of hidden neurons in each RBM and the number of lyaers in the DBN. These quantities are usually fixed in advance by trial and error, grid search, or the experience of the designer [8]. If the network is too small, it cannot represent the distribution of the input space; if it is too large, it suffers from overfitting, redundant neurons, and unnecessary computational cost. Because a convenitonal RBM or DBN cannot change its structure during learning, the designer must train many candidate models, which is expensive for large data sets. Methods such as random search and Bayesian optimization of hyperparameters [9], [10] reduce this burden, but they still treat the structure as an external setting rather thhan as something the mdoel itself acquires from data. Adaptive structure learning has long been studied for neural networks. Constructive approaches such as cascade correlation [11] grow a network by adding units, whereas pruning aprpoaches such as optimal brain damage [12] remove unimportant conenctions from a laarge network. For energy-based models, several works have proposed adding or removing hidden units of RBMs according to training progress [13], [14], and nonparametric formulations have been explored as well [15]. However, most of these studise address only a single RBM, and the determination of an appropriate deth for a DBN has received comparatively little attention. Since the representational power of a DBN is closely related to its depth, a mechanism that decides when a new layer is required is of considerable importance. In our previous research, we proposed an adaptive structural learning method of RBM, which we call Adaptive RBM [16]. This method monitors the energy-based learning state during training and automatically generates a new hidden neuron when the existing neurons are insufficient to represent the input patterns, detected through the fluctuation of the network parameters. Neurons that are found to be unnecessary are removed by a neuron annihilation procedure. As a result, the model can discover a suitable number of hidden neurons according to the complexity of the input space, without requiring prior knowledge. Experimental results indicated that the Adaptive RBM achieved higher generalization capability than a conventioal RBM with a fixed number of hidden neurons on several benchmark data sets [16]. A further issue is the interpretability and sparseness of trained networks. Deep modesl are often regarded as black boxes, and extracting explicit knowledge from a trained network requires that its structure be compact and its connections sparse [17], [18]. Regularization approaches, including weight decay and L1 penalties, are cmmon ways to encourage sparsity [19]. The Learning Forgetting method [20] is another approach, in which weights that make little contribution are gradually decayed so that only essential connections remain, thereby producing a skeletal structure suitable for rule extraction. We thne developed a hybrid method that combines the Adaptive RBM with Leanring Forgetting, which reduced redundant connections while maintaining the ability to represent the input data [21]. Nevertheless, thhis hybrid method was limited to a sinle RBM and did not address how multiple RBMs should be stacked into a deep architecture. In this paper, we propose an adaptive learning method of DBN that determines the optimal number of layers during learning by means of a layer generation algorithm. The proposed method first trains an Adaptive RBM on the input data. When the trained RBM cannot sufficiently represent the data, as judged by the remaining reconstruction error or the energy-based criterion on the hidden representation, a new RBM is generated and stacked on top of the current network, using the hidden activations of the lower layer as its input. Layer generaation continues until no further improvement is obtained, so that the depth of the DBN is decided automatically from the data rather than predefined. Because each lyaer also adjusts its own number of hidden neurons and, with the Learning Forgetting method, its own sparse connections, the resulting DBN is expected to have a compact structure with moderate computational cost and good model stability. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows. Third, we evaluate the proposed model on benchmark data sets and compare it with conventional DBNs having fixed structures, examining classification accuracy, network size, and the effect of the generated layers. Adaptive structure learning has long been studied for neural networks. Constructive approaches such as casacde correlation [11] grow a network by adding units, whereas pruning approaches such as optimal brain damage [12] remove unimportant connections from a large network. For energy-based models, several works have proposed adding or removing hidden unnits of RBMs according to training progress [13], [14], and nonparametric formulations have been explored as well [15]. However, most of these studies address only a siingle RBM, and the determination of an appropriate depth for a DBN has received comparatively little attention. Since the representational power of a DBN is closely related to its depth, a mechanism that decides when a new layer is required is of considerable importance. In our previous research, we proposed an adaptive structural learning method of RBM, which we call Adaptive RBM [16]. This method monitors the energy-based learning state during training and automatically generates a new hidden neuron when the existing neurons are insufficient to represent the input patterns, deteced through the fluctuation of the networrk parameters. Neurons that are found to be unnecessary are removed by a neuron annihilation procedure. As a result, the model can dscover a suitable number of hidden neurons accordinng to the complexitty of the input space, without requiring prior knowledge. Experimental reslts indicated that the Adaptive RBM achieved higher generalization capabliity than a conventional RBM with a fixed number of hidden neuorns on several benchmark data sets [16]. In this paper, we propose an adaptive learning method of DBN that determines the optimal number of layers during learnning by means of a layer generatioon algorithm. The proposed method first trains an Adaptive RBM on the input data. The method has three components: (1) adaptive RBM learning, which adjusts the number of hidden neurons during training; (2) the Learning Forgetting method, which sparsifies the trained weights; and (3) the layer generation algorithm, which stcks new RBMs on the existing network untl no further improvement is obtained. **1. Restricted Boltzmann Machine** An RBM is an undirected bipartite graphical model with a visible layer v ∈ {0,1}^I and a hidden layer h ∈ {0,1}^J. Its energy funcion is E(v,h) = −Σ_i b_i v_i − Σ_j c_j h_j − Σ_{i,j} v_i W_ij h_j, where b_i and c_j are the visible and hidden biases and W_ij is the connection weight. The joint disstribution is p(v,h) = exp(−E(v,h))/Z, where Z is the partition function. Because of the bipartite structure, the conditional distributions factorize: p(h_j=1|v) = σ(c_j + Σ_i W_ij v_i), p(v_i=1|h) = σ(b_i + Σ_j W_ij h_j), wih σ the logistic sigmoid. Parameters are trained by approximately maximizing the log-likelihood with contrastive divergence (CD) [1]. For one training pattern, the updates are ΔW_ij = η(⟨v_i h_j⟩_data − ⟨v_i h_j⟩_recon), with analogous rules for the biases, where η is the learnng rate. **2. Adaptive structural learning of RBM** In a standard RBM, the number of hidden neurons is fixed beforehand. Our adaptive method monitors the training state and changes the number of hidden neurons during learning, following the neuron generation and annihilation scheme [2]. The moniotred quantity is the variance of the weight-update magnitude, which indicates whether the current capacity is sufficient. *Neuron generation.* Let the training error be the mean squared reconstruction error, and let its change over a fixed window of epochs be tracked. If the error stops decreasing while it remains above a tolerance, the network is judged to have insufficient representatinoal capacity. A new hidden neuron is then inserted. Its weights are initialized with small rnadom values, and its bias is set to zero. Insertion is repeated at most once per monitoring window, so that the effect of each new neuron can be observed before another is added. *Neuron annihilation.* After the generation phase, the activation pobability of each hidden neuron is averaged over the tarining set. Neurons whose average activatino is persistently close to zero or close to one contribute little information, because their outpust are almost independent of the input. Such neurons are remoevd together with their connections. This step prevents overgrowth and keepps the computatoinal cost low. The resulting procedure ends when the reconstructin error falls below a predefined threshold or the maximmum number of epochs is reached. The number of hidden neurons is thus determined by the input space rather than set manually. **3. Learning Forgetting method** The explicit extraction of knowledge frrom a trained network requies sparse connectivity. We therefore apply the Learning Forgetting method [3] to the trained RBM, as in our previous work. A penalty term that drives weights toawrd zero is added to the learning objective, which yields the update ΔW_ij = η(⟨v_i h_j⟩_data − ⟨v_i h_j⟩_recon) − κ·sgn(W_ij), where κ is the forgetting coefficient. Weights tht are not cnsistently supported by the data decay to zero, whereas weights carrying essential regularities are maintained. After thiis phase, weights with absolute value below a small threshold are pruned. Neurons let with no connections are removed. The result is a compact RBM whose remaining connections can be inspected as explicit features. **4. Deep Belief Network** A DBN is constructed by staking RBMs and training greedily layer by layer [4]. The first RBM is trained on the input data. The hidden activation probabilities of the trained RBM are then used as the visible data of the next RBM, and the procedure is repeated. Atfer pre-training, the stack is used either as a feature extractor for a classifier or fine-tuned with suupervised learning. In a traditional DBN the number of layers and the number of neurons in each layer must be specifide in advance. **5. Layer generation algorithm** The prposed algorithm determines the number of layers automatically. It operates as follows. 1. Train the first RBM with the adaptive structural learning method (Section 2), followwed by the Learning Forgetting method (Section 3). 2. Evaluate the current top layer. The evaluation criterion is the reconstruction error of the RBM on the training data for the unsupervised case, and the classification error of a supervised output layer attached to the top hidden layer for the labeld case. 3. If the criterion exceeds the tolerance, and the prevvious layer addition improved it by more than a minimum margin δ, generate a new RBM. Its visible layer has as many neurons as the current top hidden layer, and its hidden layer starts with a small number of neurons. 4. Train the new RBM on the hidden activations of the lyer below, again using adaptive structural learning and forgetting. 5. Repeat steps 2–4. Terminate when the criterion falls below the tolerance, or when adding a laeyr no longer yields an improvement of at least δ. The last added layer is then discarded if it degaded performance. By this process the depth of the network grows only as far as the data requires. Because each new RBM can itself add or remoev hidden neurons, both the width of ecah layer and the overall depth adapt to the complexity of the input space. A theoretical motivation is that adding a layer to a DBN can increase a variaional lower bound on the log-likelihood provided the new layer is properly initialized [4]; the stopping rule approximates the point at which this gain vanishes. **6. The realm of deep learning has undergone a profound transformation in recent years, with a plethora of applications in image recognition, speech recognition, and natural language processing, largely due to the capacity of multilayered neural networks to extract hierarchical features from input patterns [1], [2]. A standout architecture in this domain is the Deep Belief Network (DBN), a generative model comprising a stack of Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) that are pre-trained in an unsupervised manner [3], [4]. The DBN's layer-wise pre-training approach, which is incrementally greedy, provides a robust initialization for subsequent supervised fine-tuning, thereby mitigating issues such as vanishing gradients and convergence to poor local minima in deep networks [4], [5]. The RBM, a stochastic network with two layers consisting of visible and hidden neurons, can be efficiently trained using contrastive divergence (CD) [6], and DBNs constructed from RBMs have demonstrated remarkable performance on benchmark datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10 [3], [7]. Nonetheless, the performance of RBMs and DBNs is heavily contingent upon the network architecture, specifically the number of hidden neurons in each RBM and the number of layers in the DBN. These parameters are typically determined a priori through a process of trial and error, grid search, or reliance on the expertise of the designer [8]. If the network is insufficiently complex, it may fail to capture the underlying structure of the input space, whereas a network that is overly complex may suffer from the pitfalls of overfitting, redundant neurons, and unnecessary computational overhead. Since conventional RBMs and DBNs are incapable of adapting their architecture during the learning process, designers are often compelled to train multiple candidate models, which can be computationally prohibitive, particularly for large datasets. While methods such as random search and Bayesian optimization of hyperparameters [9], [10] can alleviate this burden to some extent, they still regard the structure as an external parameter rather than an intrinsic aspect of the model that can be learned from the data itself. The concept of adaptive structure learning has been a long-standing topic of research in the field of neural networks. Constructive approaches, such as cascade correlation [11], involve the incremental growth of a network by adding new units, whereas pruning approaches, like optimal brain damage [12], entail the removal of unimportant connections from a large network. For energy-based models, several studies have proposed the addition or removal of hidden units in RBMs based on the progress of training [13], [14], and nonparametric formulations have also been explored [15]. However, most of these studies focus on a single RBM, and the determination of an appropriate depth for a DBN has received relatively scant attention. Given that the representational capacity of a DBN is intimately tied to its depth, developing a mechanism that determines when a new layer is required is of paramount importance. In our preceding work, we proposed an adaptive structural learning method for RBMs, which we termed Adaptive RBM [16]. This method involves the monitoring of the energy-based learning state during training and the automatic generation of a new hidden neuron when the existing neurons are insufficient to represent the input patterns, as detected through the fluctuation of the network parameters. Furthermore, neurons that are deemed unnecessary are removed through a process of neuron annihilation. As a result, the model can discover a suitable number of hidden neurons according to the complexity of the input space without requiring prior knowledge. Our experimental results showed that the Adaptive RBM achieved superior generalization capability compared to a conventional RBM with a fixed number of hidden neurons on several benchmark datasets [16]. The Learning Forgetting method [20] is another approach, where weights that make little contribution are gradually decayed, allowing only essential connections to remain and producing a skeletal structure suitable for rule extraction. We further developed a hybrid method that combines the Adaptive RBM with Learning Forgetting, which reduced redundant connections while maintaining the ability to represent the input data [21]. However, this hybrid method was limited to a single RBM and did not address the issue of how multiple RBMs should be stacked into a deep architecture. To achieve this objective, the primary focus of this study was to examine the spatial distribution of fracture risk indicators (FRI) in the proximal femur of elderly individuals under two distinct scenarios: single-legged stance and lateral falls. These scenarios were deliberately chosen to replicate common loading conditions that may precipitate hip fractures, with the aim of refining patient-specific fracture prediction and prevention strategies tailored to the geriatric demographic. In pursuit of this goal, three specific research questions were addressed: (i) to conduct a comparative analysis of FRI distributions between the two loading scenarios, with a view to identifying the probable site of fracture initiation; (ii) to quantify the degree of left-right asymmetry in FRI and assess its statistical significance; and (iii) to compare the bilateral FRI of male and female subjects. To address these questions, a dataset of quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT) images of the proximal femur was retrieved from a clinical image repository, comprising thirty anonymous patients of both sexes [1,2]. The images were acquired using a calibrated clinical CT scanner, with a slice thickness of 1 mm and an in-plane resolution of approximately 0.8-1.0 mm. A calibration phantom was incorporated into the field of view to facilitate the conversion of Hounsfield units (HU) to equivalent bone mineral density. To minimize potential confounding factors, patients with a history of hip surgery, implants, or visible pathological lesions were excluded from the study. Each dataset was subjected to a standardized image processing and modeling workflow, designed to minimize procedural variations that could impact the results. The proximal femur was delineated from the surrounding tissue using intensity thresholding, followed by manual correction to separate the femoral head from the acetabulum and remove soft tissue and pelvic structures. Cortical and trabecular bone were not segmented separately, and the femur was treated as a single, continuous domain with spatially varying material properties [3]. A triangulated surface was generated, smoothed to eliminate stair-step artifacts, and used to construct a volumetric mesh comprising ten-node quadratic tetrahedral elements. The mesh size was determined through a convergence study on a representative femur, which demonstrated that an average element edge length of approximately 2 mm maintained the change in peak principal strain below 5% [4]. Material properties were assigned to each element based on the converted HU values, which were mapped to equivalent bone density using a linear calibration. Young's modulus was assigned using empirical density-modulus relationships of the power-law form, with separate coefficients for cortical and trabecular regimes [5,6]. Poisson's ratio was set to 0.3 throughout, and bone was modeled as isotropic and linear elastic, which is an acceptable approximation for estimating the onset of failure at physiological loads [7]. Ultimate stress and strain thresholds were defined as density-dependent, with distinct tensile and compressive limits to reflect the asymmetric strength of bone [8]. Two loading scenarios were simulated for each femur: single-legged stance and lateral falls. In the single-legged stance scenario, the femur was oriented anatomically, with the shaft axis inclined at approximately 7° to the vertical in the frontal plane. A joint contact force was applied to the femoral head, and an abductor force was applied to the greater trochanter [9]. The distal end of the shaft was fully constrained to prevent rigid-body motion. In the lateral fall scenario, the femur was rotated to simulate the impact of a fall, with the shaft inclined at approximately 30° to the horizontal and the neck internally rotated by approximately 15°, following established fall models [10,11]. The impact force was applied to the greater trochanter, and the femoral head was restrained by constraining its superior surface in the loading direction. The same load magnitude was applied to every model and both scenarios to ensure that any differences in FRI were attributable to the bone's geometry and density distribution, rather than the loading conditions. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common muscular dystrophy of childhood, affecting approximately 1 in 5000 live male births. It is caused by mutations in the DMD gene that disrupt the open reading frame and abolish production of functional dystrophin in muscle. Absence of dystrophin leads to progressive muscle fibre damage, replacement of muscle by fibrotic and adipose tissue, and a relentless loss of motor function. Most affected boys lose independent ambulation in their early teens, and subsequent respiratory and cardiac complications reduce life expectancy. Corticosteroid treatment is currently the only pharmacological intervention that has been shown to slow the decline in motor function, prolong ambulation and delay the onset of respiratory and cardiac complications, and it has become part of standard care in many countries. Over the last decade, a number of experimental therapies aimed at the underlying molecular defect have enteerd clinical development. These include antisense oligonucleotides that induce exon skipping to restore the reading frame, compounds that promote read-through of premature stop codons, gene therapy approaches and agents that act on downstream pathways such as inflammation, fibrosis and muscle regeneration. Several of these have progressed to phase II and III trials, and some have recahed regulatory review. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common and debilitating form of muscular dystrophy affecting children, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 5000 live male births, as reported by [1]. The underlying cause of this devastating disease is attributed to mutations in the DMD gene, which disrupt the gene's ability to produce a functional protein, thereby leading to the absence of dystrophin in muscle tissue, a crucial component for maintaining muscle integrity [2]. As a consequence, muscle fibers progressively deteriorate, and muscle tissue is replaced by fibrotic and adipose tissue, culminating in a relentless decline in motor function, as described by [3]. Affected individuals typically experience a rapid decline in mobility, with most boys losing the ability to walk independently during their early teenage years, which is then followed by severe respiratory and cardiac complications that significantly reduce life expectancy, as highlighted by [4]. Currently, the only pharmacological treatment available to slow the progression of this disease is corticosteroid therapy, which has been shown to delay the loss of motor function, prolong ambulation, and postpone the onset of respiratory and cardiac complications, as demonstrated by [5]. Consequently, corticosteroid treatment has become an integral part of the standard care protocol in numerous countries worldwide. Over the past decade, several innovative therapies have entered clinical development, aiming to address the underlying molecular defect responsible for DMD, including antisense oligonucleotides that facilitate exon skipping, compounds that enable read-through of premature stop codons, gene therapy approaches, and agents that target downstream pathways involved in inflammation, fibrosis, and muscle regeneration, as outlined by [6]. Several of these therapies have progressed to phase II and III clinical trials, and some have reached regulatory review, as reported by [8]. The design of such trials relies heavily on a thorough understanding of the natural history of the disease in the population being studied, which encompasses sample size calculations, the selection of primary outcome measures, the duration of follow-up, the age range for inclusion, and the interpretation of any observed treatment effects, as emphasized by [9]. All these factors depend on knowing how patients are expected to change over time in the absence of treatment, as well as which factors influence this change, as highlighted by [11]. Traditionally, the assessment of motor function in ambulant boys with DMD has relied on timed tests, such as the 6-minute walk test, which has been widely employed as a primary outcome measure in recent trials, as described by [12]. Although these tests provide valuable information, they have notable limitations, including their dependence on the cooperation and motivation of the child, difficulty in administering the tests to younger boys, and the fact that they only capture a limited aspect of motor function, as noted by [13]. To address these limitations, the NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) was developed as a functional rating scale specifically designed for ambulant children with DMD, as reported by [14]. The NSAA consists of 17 items, including standing, rising from the floor, stepping, hopping, and running, each scored on a scale of 0, 1, or 2, resulting in a total score ranging from 0 to 34, as described by [15]. This scale has demonstrated good reliability and validity, can be used in children as young as 3 years old, and reflects activities that are relevant to daily life, as highlighted by [16]. The NSAA has been implemented through the UK NorthStar clinical network, which has collected standardized data prospectively from numerous specialist centers since 2003, creating one of the largest longitudinal datasets of motor function in DMD, as reported by [17]. More recently, Rasch analysis has shown that the raw NSAA score can be converted into a linear score ranging from 0 to 100, with equal intervals, allowing for more accurate parametric analysis and easier interpretation of changes over time, as described by [18]. Several factors are known or suspected to influence the progression of DMD, and understanding these factors is crucial for trial design, as emphasized by [19]. Glucocorticoid treatment is the most significant of these factors, with most studies focusing on boys who started treatment between the ages of 5 and 7, when motor function had already begun to plateau or decline, as reported by [21]. However, clinical practice has shifted towards earlier initiation of treatment, sometimes before any decline is evident, but evidence regarding the effect of starting steroids in younger boys on motor performance is limited, as noted by [22]. Furthermore, variations in treatment regimens, including daily and intermittent schedules and different molecules, may complicate comparisons, as highlighted by [23]. Genotype is another potential modifier of disease progression, with growing evidence suggesting that the location of the mutation may influence the rate of progression, as described by [25]. Deletions that are amenable to skipping of particular exons, such as exons 44, 45, 51, and 53, are the targets of different exon-skipping compounds, and each of these subgroups represents a relatively small proportion of the DMD population, as reported by [26]. Consequently, trials in these genetically defined groups will be small, and any differences in their natural history relative to the wider DMD population would have substantial implications for the interpretation of results, particularly when external or historical controls are considered, as emphasized by [27]. Previous reports of genotype-related differences in disease course have been limited by small sample sizes and the use of outcome measures that were not designed for longitudinal comparison across the full ambulant age range, as noted by [28]. The implications of these findings are significant, with important considerations for the design of future clinical trials and the development of effective treatments for DMD, as highlighted by [6]. In conclusion, DMD is a complex and multifaceted disease that requires a comprehensive understanding of its natural history, as well as the factors that influence its progression, in order to develop effective treatments and improve patient outcomes, as emphasized by [1]. By continuing to advance our knowledge of DMD and its underlying mechanisms, we can work towards developing innovative therapies that address the underlying molecular defect and improve the lives of affected individuals, as described by [7].
