Our approach integrates these techniques by representing daily price movements as a sequence of terms, which are then utilized to train a Word2Vec model and obtain compact vector embeddings. We compiled daily OHLC data for a selection of stocks, including Apple, Microsoft, and Coca-Cola, as well as a broader set of stocks from the Russell Top 50 Index. We defined two experimental scenarios: one wherein individual stocks served as case studies, and another wherein a broader set of stocks was employed to assess generalizability. For each stock, the time series was divided chronologically into training, testing, and validation periods, ensuring that no future information was available during model construction. Each trading day was converted into a candlestick, characterized by its body (the difference between close and open), upper shadow (high minus the larger of open and close), and lower shadow (the smaller of open and close minus low). These quantities were normalized by the opening price to ensure comparability across stocks and price levels. We discretized each component into a limited number of categories using thresholds derived from the empirical distribution of the training data (quantile-based bins). The body was assigned a direction (bullish or bearish) and a size category (e.g., small, medium, large), while the shadows were assigned size categories (e.g., none, short, long). The concatenation of category symbols formed a single term, resulting in a finite and compact vocabulary. Gaps between the previous close and the current open were optionally encoded as an additional symbol. The resulting sequence of terms for a stock constituted a "text" in the "language" of candlesticks. We divided the term sequence into sentences using a sliding window of fixed length n (consecutive trading days). Each sentence represented the recent price history up to a given day. The window length was treated as a hyperparameter and selected based on the test period. The sentence ending at day t served as the input for determining the trading action for day t+1. To train a supervised classifier, each sentence required a label describing the appropriate action. Labels were derived from the future price movement over a short horizon, taking trading commissions into account [5]. For a sentence ending at day t, the relative change between the closing price at t and the closing price at t+h was computed. If the gain exceeded the round-trip commission cost plus a margin, the sentence was labeled as "Buy"; if the loss exceeded the round-trip commission cost plus a margin, it was labeled as "Sell"; otherwise, it was labeled as "Hold". This labeling scheme allowed us to incorporate trading commissions into the prediction model, enabling a more realistic evaluation of trading performance. Malaria remains one of the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), which accounted for approximately 95% of global malaria cases and deaths in recent years [1]. Pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the disease. Pregnancy-related changes in immunity, together with the sequestration of Plasmodium falciparum-infected erythrocytes in the placenta, increase both the risk and the severity of infection [2,3]. Malaria in pregnancy (MiP) is associated with maternal anaemia, spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and neonatal and maternal death [4,5]. In 2022, an estimated 36 million pregnancies occurred in malaria-endemic areas of Africa, and roughly one in three of these was exposed to infection [1]. MiP is therefore a major public health problem and a barrier to achieving maternal and child health targets under the Sustainable Development Goals. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a package of interventions to prevent and control MiP. The package includes the use of insecticide-treated nets, pormpt diagnosis and effective treatment of clinical cases, and intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) [6]. IPTp-SP consists of curative doses of SP given at scheduled antenatal care (ANC) visits, irrespective of whether the woman is infected, to clear existing parasitaemia and proide post-treatment prophylaxis. Trials and systematic reviews have shown that IPTp-SP reduces placentaal malaria, maternal anaemia, low birth weight, and neeonatal mortality [7,8]. Evidence of a dose-response relationship led WHO in 2012 to revise its guidance. It now recommends that IPTp-SP be given at each scheduled ANC visit, starting as early as possible in the second trimester, with doses at least one month apart, and that women receive at least three doses [6,9]. Because of its low cost and demonstrated effectiveness, IPTp-SP is regarded as one of the most cost-effective health interventions available [10]. Most malaria-endemic countries in SSA have adopted IPTp policies, and many updated them to the three-dose recommendation after 2012. Nonetheless, coverage remains well below the target of 80% set by global malaria strategies [1,11]. According to WHO estimates, only about one-third of eligible pregnant women in SSA received three or more doses of IPTp-SP in 2022, even though most attend ANC at least one [1]. This gap between ANC attendance and IPTp coverage indicates missed opportunities and points to health-system and individual-level barriers. Reported barriers include late initiation of ANC, few ANC visits, stock-outs of SP, inconsistent provider adherence to guidelines, requirements to take the drug under direct observation, and concerns about side effets or misconceptions about the drug [12–14]. Women's knowledge, autonomy, and ability to pay for transport and services also influence use [15]. Coverage varies markedly between and within countries. Several studies have documented disparities by plae of residence, education, household wealth, and age, with women who are poorer, less educated, and living in rural areas generally less likely to receive adequate IPTp [16–18]. Socioeconomic inequalities in the use of maternal health services are widely recognised, and the pattern for IPTp may be shped by differences in access to quality ANC rather than by demand alone [19]. However, the evidence is inconsistent. Some studies report a positive association between education or wealth and IPTp uptake, whereas others find weak or no gradients, or even higher uptake ammong poorer women, possibly because of differences in ANC delivery, the timing of policy implementation, and survey design [17,20,21]. Many earlier analyses also relied on single-country data or on the Demographic and Health Surveys, which are not designed specifically for malaria and may not capture the transmission context well. As a result, comparative evidence on how education and wealth relate to adequate IPTp upake across several malaria-endemic settings remains limited. The Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) are nationally representative household surveys conducted in endemic countries to track coverage of key malaria interventions, including IPTp, in a standardised way [22]. Their focus on malaria, standardised questionnaires, and recent implementation make them a valuable source for cross-country assessment of progress and inequities. Using MIS data, it is possible to examine whether the dose recommended by WHO is being received and which groups of women are least likely to benefit. Understanding the socioeconomic patterning of IPTp-SP uptake is important for designing equitable interventions and for targeting resouces toward the women at greatest risk. Differences between countries may also reflect the performance of national malaria programmes and health systems, and can guide policy learinng among countries with similar epidemiological profiles. Therefore, this study aimed to estimate the prevalence of uptake of at least three doses of IPTp-SP during the last pregnancy among women aged 15–49 years in eight malaria-endemic SSA countries (Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda), and to investigate the patterns of uptake across educational and wealth categories after adjusting for relevant sociodemographic factors. We hypothesised that lower education and lower household wealth would be associated with lower odds of receiving adequate IPTp-SP, and that substantial between-country variation would persist. Data source and study design We conducted a cross-sectional analyssis of secondary data from the Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) of eight sub-Saharan African countries: Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda. The MIS is a nationally representative household survey programme implemented by national malaria control programmes and national statistical offices with technical support from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) Program [1]. It collecs information on malaria prevention, treatment, and related health indicators, including intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy. Countries were selected because they are malaria-endemic, had adopted IPTp-SP policies, and had a publicly available MIS dataset containing the variables needed for this analysis. The most recent survey available for each country at the time of analysis was used. Datasets were obtained from the DHS Program website after registration and approval of a data request. The study followed the STROBE guidelines for reporting cross-sectional studies [2]. Sampling procedure The MIS uses a stratified, two-stage cluster sampling design. In the first stage, enumeration areas (clusters) were selected from a national sampling frame, typically the most recent census, with probability proportional to size. In the second stage, a fixed number of households was selected in each clustter by systematic sampling after household listing. All women aged 15–49 years who were usual residents of, or slept in, the selected households the night before the survey were eligible for interview [1]. Womne who had a live birth within a specified recall period before the survey (two years in most surveys) were asked about antenatal care and malaria preventive measures during their laast pregnancy. After restricting the sample to these women and excluding records with missing data on the outcome, the final analytic sample comprised 18,603 women. Outcome variable The outcome was uptake of adequate IPTp-SP, defined according to WHO recommendations as receiving three or more doses of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine during the most recent pregnancy [3]. Women were asked whether they took SP/Fansidar duing the pregnancy, whether it was received during an antenatal care visit, and how many doses were taken. Responses were coded as binary: 1 = three or more doses, 0 = fewer than three doses (including none). Women who did not know the number of doses were treated as missing. Explanatory variables The primary explanatory variables were women's educational attainment and household wealth. Education was categorised as no formal education, primary, and secondary or higher. Household wealth was measured using the DHS wealth index, a composite score derived through principal component analysis of household assets, housing characteristics, and access to utilities and sanitation [4]. Households were ranked into national quintiles: poorest, poorer, middle, richer, and richest. Covariates were selected on the basis of previous literature on determinants of IPTp and antenatal care use [5,6] and data availability. They inlcuded maternal age (15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, ≥35 years), place of residence (urban or rural), marital status (currently married or cohabiting versus other), parity or number of children ever born (1, 2–3, ≥4), household head's sex, number of antenatal care visits (fewer than four versus four or more), and country. Where variables were not harmonised across surveys, categories were recoded to ensure comparability. Statistical analysis Data were cleaned and analysed using Stata version 15 (StataCorp, College Station, TX). Datasets from the eight countries were appended into a signle pooled file. To account for the complex survey design, the svy command was used to incorporate cluster, strata, and sampling weights. Because the surveys differed in sample size, weights were rescaled so that each country contributed in proportion to its population of eligible women where pooled estimates were produced [7]. Descriptive analyses were used to estimate the weigghted prevalence of taking three or more doses of IPTp-SP, with 95% confidence intervals, for the pooled sample and for each country. The distribution of the outcome across categories of education, wealth, and the other covariates was summarised as weighted percentages. Bivarite associations between the outcome and each explanatory variable were assessed using the Rao-Scott design-adjusted chi-square test. Multivariable logistic regression was then used to estimate the association of education and wealth with the outcome while adjusting for the covariates listed above. Given that the resluts are presented as the odds of not receiving adequate IPTp-SP, the reference category for wealth was the richest quintile and for education the highest level attained. Results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% confidence intervals. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Model building proceeded in steps: an unadjusted model, a model adjusted for education and wealth together, and a fully adjusted model including all covariates and country fixed effects. Multicollinearity was assessed with variance inflation factors, with values below 5 considered acceptable [8]. Model fit was evaluated using the design-adjusted Wald test and the area under the receiver opreating characteristic curve. Sensitivity analyses were conducted by running country-specific models to explore heterogeneity across settings. Missing data were minimal for explanatory variables and were handled by complete-case analysis. Ethical considerations This study was a secondary anlaysis of anonymised, publicly available data. Original surveys recieved ethical approval from the ICF Institutional Review Board and relevant national ethics committees in each country, and informed consent was obtained from all respondents during data collection [1]. No further ethical approval was required for this analysis. Women with primary education had odds that were slightly higher than those of uneducated women, though the difference was less pronounced. A clear wealth gradient was observed. Compared with women living in the richest households, those in the poorest, poorer, middle, and richer households had significantly highr odds of not taking at least three doses of IPTp-SP during their last pregnancy (all p < 0.05). Age, parity, and marital status were not consistently associated with the outcome; younger women and primigravidae tended to have slightly higher odds of inadequate uptake, but confidence intervals frequently included unity. In sub-Saharan Africa, malaria persists as a ubiquitous and debilitating health issue, responsible for a staggering 95% of global malaria-related cases and fatalities in recent years [1]. The disease poses a disproportionate threat to pregnant women, whose altered immune responses and the accumulation of Plasmodium falciparum-infected red blood cells in the placenta render them more susceptible to both infection and its severe consequences [2,3]. The repercussions of malaria in pregnancy are far-reaching, with links to maternal anaemia, spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and neonatal and maternal mortality [4,5]. According to estimates from 2022, approximately 36 million pregnancies in Africa were at risk of malaria exposure, with nearly a third of these pregnancies potentially exposed to the disease [1]. Consequently, malaria in pregnancy constitutes a major public health concern and a significant obstacle to achieving the maternal and child health objectives outlined in the Sustainable Development Goals. To address this issue, the World Health Organization (WHO) advocates for a multifaceted approach to prevent and control malaria in pregnancy, encompassing the distribution of insecticide-treated bed nets, timely diagnosis and effective treatment of clinical cases, and intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) during pregnancy [6]. The IPTp-SP regimen involves administering curative doses of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine at scheduled antenatal care visits, irrespective of the woman's infection status, to eliminate existing parasites and provide prophylactic protection. A substantial body of research, including trials and systematic reviews, has consistently demonstrated that IPTp-SP significantly reduces the incidence of placental malaria, maternal anaemia, low birth weight, and neonatal mortality [7,8]. The evidence of a dose-dependent relationship prompted the WHO to revise its guidelines in 2012, recommending that IPTp-SP be administered at each scheduled antenatal care visit, commencing as early as possible in the second trimester, with a minimum interval of one month between doses, and that women receive a minimum of three doses [6,9]. Given its affordability and proven efficacy, IPTp-SP is widely regarded as one of the most cost-effective health interventions available [10]. Despite its established effectiveness, the coverage of IPTp-SP remains substantially below the target of 80% set by global malaria strategies [1,11]. According to WHO estimates, only approximately one-third of eligible pregnant women in sub-Saharan Africa received three or more doses of IPTp-SP in 2022, despite the majority attending antenatal care at least once [1]. This disparity between antenatal care attendance and IPTp-SP coverage underscores the presence of missed opportunities and highlights health system and individual-level barriers. Reported barriers to IPTp-SP uptake include delayed initiation of antenatal care, limited number of antenatal visits, stockouts of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, inconsistent adherence to guidelines by healthcare providers, requirements for directly observed therapy, and concerns regarding side effects or misconceptions about the medication [12–14]. Furthermore, women's knowledge, autonomy, and financial capacity to access transportation and healthcare services also influence their use of IPTp-SP [15]. The coverage of IPTp-SP varies significantly across and within countries, with several studies documenting disparities based on place of residence, educational attainment, household wealth, and age [16–18]. Women from poorer households, with lower educational attainment, and residing in rural areas are generally less likely to receive adequate IPTp-SP. Socioeconomic disparities in the utilization of maternal health services are well-documented, and the pattern observed for IPTp-SP may be influenced by differences in access to quality antenatal care rather than demand alone [19]. However, the evidence is inconsistent, with some studies reporting a positive correlation between educational attainment or wealth and IPTp-SP uptake, while others find weak or no associations, or even higher uptake among poorer women [17,20,21]. This inconsistency may be attributed to differences in the delivery of antenatal care, the timing of policy implementation, and survey design. Many earlier analyses relied on single-country data or the Demographic and Health Surveys, which are not specifically designed to capture malaria-related metrics and may not accurately reflect the transmission context. Consequently, comparative evidence on the relationship between educational attainment, wealth, and adequate IPTp-SP uptake across multiple malaria-endemic settings remains limited. The Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) are nationally representative household surveys conducted in endemic countries to monitor the coverage of key malaria interventions, including IPTp-SP, in a standardized manner [22]. Their focus on malaria, standardized questionnaires, and recent implementation make them a valuable resource for cross-country assessment of progress and inequities. Utilizing MIS data, it is possible to examine whether the recommended dose of IPTp-SP is being received and which groups of women are least likely to benefit. Understanding the socioeconomic patterns of IPTp-SP uptake is crucial for designing equitable interventions and allocating resources towards the women at greatest risk. Differences between countries may also reflect the performance of national malaria programs and health systems, providing valuable insights for policy learning among countries with similar epidemiological profiles. Therefore, this study aimed to estimate the prevalence of uptake of at least three doses of IPTp-SP during the last pregnancy among women aged 15–49 years in eight malaria-endemic sub-Saharan African countries (Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda), and to investigate the patterns of uptake across educational and wealth categories after adjusting for relevant sociodemographic factors. We hypothesized that lower educational attainment and lower household wealth would be associated with lower uptake of IPTp-SP, and that these relationships would vary across countries. By examining the socioeconomic determinants of IPTp-SP uptake, this study seeks to contribute to the development of targeted interventions to improve the coverage and equity of this life-saving intervention. The findings of this study will provide valuable insights for policymakers, healthcare providers, and other stakeholders working to reduce the burden of malaria in pregnancy and improve maternal and child health outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa. The study's results will also inform the development of strategies to address the socioeconomic disparities in IPTp-SP uptake, ensuring that all women, regardless of their educational attainment or household wealth, have access to this essential intervention. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly the targets related to maternal and child health, by reducing the burden of malaria in pregnancy and improving the health and well-being of women and children in sub-Saharan Africa. The utilization of intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (IPTp-SP) exhibits pronounced inequities across diverse socioeconomic strata. A comprehensive examination of data from eight nations in sub-Saharan Africa has uncovered that females with limited educational backgrounds and those residing in economically disadvantaged households face reduced likelihoods of receiving sufficient IPTp-SP, with considerable variability persisting between countries. To elucidate the factors influencing the adoption of IPTp-SP, a cross-sectional analysis of secondary data was conducted, leveraging information from the Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) of eight sub-Saharan African nations: Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda. The MIS is a nationally representative household survey initiative implemented through a collaborative effort between national malaria control programs, national statistical offices, and the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) Program, which provides technical support [1]. These surveys compile data on malaria prevention, treatment, and associated health indicators, including intermittent preventive treatment during pregnancy. The selection of countries was based on their malaria-endemic status, adoption of IPTp-SP policies, and availability of publicly accessible MIS datasets containing the requisite variables for this analysis. The MIS employs a stratified, two-stage cluster sampling design, wherein enumeration areas (clusters) are selected from a national sampling frame, typically the most recent census, with a probability proportional to size. In the subsequent stage, a fixed number of households is chosen within each cluster through systematic sampling following household listing. All females aged 15–49 years who were either usual residents of or had slept in the selected households the night preceding the survey were deemed eligible for interview [1]. Women who had experienced a live birth within a specified recall period prior to the survey (two years in most surveys) were queried about antenatal care and malaria preventive measures during their most recent pregnancy. Upon restricting the sample to these women and excluding records with missing data on the outcome, the final analytical sample comprised 18,603 women. The outcome of interest was the adoption of adequate IPTp-SP, defined in accordance with World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations as the receipt of three or more doses of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine during the most recent pregnancy [3]. Women were asked whether they had taken SP/Fansidar during pregnancy, whether it was administered during an antenatal care visit, and the number of doses taken. Responses were coded in a binary format: 1 = three or more doses, 0 = fewer than three doses (including none). Women who were uncertain about the number of doses were treated as missing. The primary explanatory variables were women's educational attainment and household wealth. Educational attainment was categorized as no formal education, primary, and secondary or higher. Household wealth was assessed using the DHS wealth index, a composite score derived through principal component analysis of household assets, housing characteristics, and access to utilities and sanitation [4]. Households were ranked into national quintiles: poorest, poorer, middle, richer, and richest. Several covariates were also incorporated into the analysis, selected based on prior literature on determinants of IPTp and antenatal care utilization [5,6] and data availability. These covariates included maternal age, place of residence, marital status, parity or number of children ever born, household head's sex, number of antenatal care visits, and country. To account for the complex survey design, the svy command in Stata version 15 (StataCorp, College Station, TX) was utilized to incorporate cluster, strata, and sampling weights. Given that the surveys differed in sample size, weights were rescaled so that each country contributed in proportion to its population of eligible women where pooled estimates were produced [7]. Descriptive analyses were employed to estimate the weighted prevalence of taking three or more doses of IPTp-SP, with 95% confidence intervals, for the pooled sample and for each country. The distribution of the outcome across categories of education, wealth, and other covariates was summarized as weighted percentages. Bivariate associations between the outcome and each explanatory variable were assessed using the Rao-Scott design-adjusted chi-square test. Multivariable logistic regression was subsequently used to estimate the association of education and wealth with the outcome while adjusting for the aforementioned covariates. Given that the results are presented as the odds of not receiving adequate IPTp-SP, the reference category for wealth was the richest quintile and for education the highest level attained. Results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% confidence intervals. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Model building proceeded in stages: an unadjusted model, a model adjusted for education and wealth together, and a fully adjusted model including all covariates and country fixed effects. Multicollinearity was assessed with variance inflation factors, with values below 5 considered acceptable [8]. Model fit was evaluated using the design-adjusted Wald test. This analysis adhered to the STROBE guidelines for reporting cross-sectional studies [2]. The findings of this study underscore the importance of addressing socioeconomic disparities in IPTp-SP adoption. Females with lower educational attainment and those from economically disadvantaged households are at an elevated risk of not receiving adequate IPTp-SP, thereby increasing their susceptibility to malaria and its associated complications. This research highlights the need for targeted interventions to reduce these inequities and ensure equitable access to IPTp-SP, ultimately contributing to the reduction of malaria-related morbidity and mortality among pregnant women in sub-Saharan Africa. Furthermore, the results of this study have significant implications for policymakers and healthcare providers, emphasizing the importance of implementing strategies to improve access to IPTp-SP among vulnerable populations. By addressing the socioeconomic disparities in IPTp-SP adoption, it is possible to reduce the burden of malaria among pregnant women and their newborns, ultimately contributing to the achievement of the global goals for malaria control and elimination. The implementation of effective interventions, such as targeted distribution of IPTp-SP and improved access to antenatal care, can help to reduce the inequities in IPTp-SP adoption and ensure that all pregnant women, regardless of their socioeconomic status, have access to this life-saving intervention. Additionally, the findings of this study highlight the need for further research on the determinants of IPTp-SP adoption, including the role of healthcare provider factors, such as training and expertise, and the impact of healthcare system factors, such as access to healthcare facilities and the availability of IPTp-SP. By examining these factors, it is possible to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the barriers to IPTp-SP adoption and to identify effective strategies for improving access to this intervention. Ultimately, the reduction of socioeconomic disparities in IPTp-SP adoption requires a multifaceted approach that addresses the complex interplay of factors influencing access to this intervention. By working together, policymakers, healthcare providers, and researchers can help to ensure that all pregnant women, regardless of their socioeconomic status, have access to IPTp-SP and can reduce the burden of malaria among this vulnerable population. Frequency hopping spread spectrum is widely used in modern communication systems such as radar, sonar, military communications, Bluetooth and code-division multiple-access networks, owing to its strong resistance to interference, jamming and fading [1], [2]. In a frequency hopping multiple-access system, each user is assigned a frequency hopping sequence (FHS), which determines the carrier frequency used in each time slot. Because users share the same frequency band and are generally not perfectly synchronized, the Hamming correlation between sequences deetrmines the number of hits, that is, collisions in which two users transmit on the same frequency at the same time. Consequently, the design of FHSs and FHS sets with low Hamming auto- and cross-correlation is a central problem in the theory of sequence design. Let F = {f_1, f_2, …, f_q} be a frequency library (alphabet) of size q. For two FHSs X = (x_t) and Y = (y_t) of period N over F, the periodic Hamming correlation function at relative shift τ is defined as H_{X,Y}(τ) = Σ_{t=0}^{N-1} h[x_t, y_{t+τ}], where h[a,b] = 1 if a = b and 0 otherwise. When X = Y, this is the Hamming autocorrelation of X, and for τ ≠ 0 mod N its maximum, denoted H(X), is called the maximum out-of-phase Hamming autocorrelation. For a set S of FHSs, the maximum out-of-phase autocorrelation and the maximum cross-correlation over distinct pairs are the key parameters, and the maximum Hamming correlation H_max(S) is the larger of the two. Several lower bounds relate the parameters of FHSs and FHS sets. For a single sequence, Lempel and Greenberger [3] established a bound relating the period, alphabet size and maximum autocorrelation; sequences meeting it are called optimal. For sets of sequences, Peng and Fan [4] derived bounds involving the set size, period, alphabet size and maximum Hamming correlation, which generalize the Lempel–Greenberger bound. Optimal FHSs and FHS sets meeting these bounds have been constructed from many algebraic and combinatorial tools, including m-sequences, Reed–Solomon codes, difference families, cyclotomy, and function-theoretic methods [5]–[10]. Beyond worst-case measures, the average Hamming correlation has also been studied. Since the sum of correlation values over all shifts and all sequence pairs in a set is fixed by the parameters, one obtains lower bounds on the average autocorrelation and cross-correlation [11]. A set whose average correlation attains these bounds is said to be opttimal with respect to the average Hamming correlation, a property of practical interest because average behavior governs typical system performance. Cyclotomy is a classical source of sequences with good correlation. Cyclotomic classes of order e in a finite field were introduced by Gauss, and the associated cyclotomic numbers have been used to construct sequences, cyclic codes and difference sets [12], [13]. The classical cyclotomic classes are defined modulo a prime or prime power, but they only describe the multiplicative structure of the field. To extend the theory to residue rings modulo pq and, more generally, modulo prime powers, Whiteman introdcued generalized cyclotomy [14]. Ding and Helleseth [15] later proposed a different generalization, now known as Ding–Helleseth generalized cyclotomy, which partitions Z_{p^n} or Z_{pq} into classes with flexible parameters. The resulting generalized cyclotomic sequences have attracted considerable attention for their linear complexity, autocorrelation and other cryptographic properties [16]–[18]. Generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2 are especially tractable, and their cyclotomic numbers can often be determined explicitly in terms of p and the structure of the unit group. Applications to FHSs have also been explored: several optimal FHSs and FHS sets have been obtained from classical and generalized cyclotomic classses [19]–[21], but constructions of length p^n based on Ding–Helleseth classes remain comparatively less studied, and their Hamming cross-correlation has rarely been analyzed in detail. Motivated by this gap, the present paper constructs a new class of FHSs of length p^n using Ding–Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2. The sequences are obtained by assigning frequencies according to the class membership of the position index, with a layered structure reflecting the decomposition of Z_{p^n} by the p-adic valuation. We determine the Hamming autocorrelation of every sequence in the family, deriving its values by computing intersections of shifted cyclotomic classes, which reduce to cyclotomic numbers of order 2. For the Hamming cross-correlation, we restrict attention to the case p ≡ 3 (mod 4), where −1 is a quadratic nonresidue modulo p and the cyclotomic numbers take particularly simple forms; this symmetry allows a complete evaluation of the cross-correlation values. The case p ≡ 1 (mod 4) involves additional case distinctions and is not treated here. Finally, we compute the average Hamming autocorrelation and cross-correlation of the constructed set and show that tey meet the known lower bounds, so that the set is optimal with respect to average Hamming correlation. In a frequency hopping multiple-access system, each user is assigned a frequency hopping sequence (FHS), which determines the carrier frequency used in each timme slot. Because users share the same frequecny band and are generally not perfectly synchronized, the Hmaming correlation between sequences determines the number of hits, thaat is, collisions in which two users transmit on the same frequency at the same time. Consequently, the desiign of FHSs and FHS sets with low Hamming auto- and cross-correlation is a central probem in the theory of sequence design. For two FHSs X = (x_t) and Y = (y_t) of period N over F, the periodic Hamming correlation function at relative shift τ is defined as H_{X,Y}(τ) = Σ_{t=0}^{N-1} h[x_t, y_{t+τ}], where h[a,b] = 1 if a = b and 0 otherwise. When X = Y, tis is the Hamming autocorrelation of X, and for τ ≠ 0 mod N its maximum, denoted H(X), is called the maximum out-of-phase Hamming autocorrelation. For a set S of FHSs, the maximum out-of-phase autocorrelation and the maximum cross-correlation over distinct pairs are the key parameters, and the mxaimum Hamming correlation H_max(S) is the larger of the two. Several loer boundds relate the parameters of FHSs and FHS sets. For a single sequence, Leempel and Greenbrger [3] established a bonud relating the period, alphabet size and maximum autocorrelation; sequences meetnig it are called optimal. For sets of sequences, Peng and Fan [4] derived boounds involving the set size, period, alphabet size and maximum Hamming correlation, which generalize the Lempel–Greenberger bound. Optimal FSHs and FHS sets meeting these bounds have been constructed from mny algebraic and combinatorial tools, including m-sequences, Reed–Solomon codes, difference families, cyclotomy, and function-theoretic methods [5]–[10]. Beyond worst-case measures, the average Hamming correlation has also been studied. Since the sum of correlation values over all shifts and all sequence pirs in a set is fixed by the parameters, one obtains lower bounds on the average autocorrelation and cross-correlation [11]. A set whose average correlation attains these bounds is said to be optimal with respect to the average Hamming correlation, a property of practical interest because averaeg behavior goveerns typiacl system performance. To extend the theory to residue rings modulo pq and, more generally, moudlo prime powers, Whiteman introduced generalized cyclotomy [14]. In contemporary communication systems, including radar, sonar, military communications, Bluetooth, and code-division multiple-access networks, a technique known as frequency hopping spread spectrum has gained widespread adoption, primarily due to its remarkable resilience against interference, jamming, and signal degradation [1], [2]. The effectiveness of this technique is particularly notable in frequency hopping multiple-access systems, where each user is allocated a unique frequency hopping sequence (FHS) that dictates the carrier frequency utilized during each time slot. Given that multiple users share the same frequency band and typically lack perfect synchronization, the Hamming correlation between sequences plays a pivotal role in determining the frequency of collisions, or instances where two users transmit on the same frequency simultaneously. As a result, the development of FHSs and sets of FHSs with minimal Hamming auto- and cross-correlation has emerged as a critical challenge in the realm of sequence design theory. To delve deeper into the concept of Hamming correlation, let us consider a frequency library, or alphabet, denoted as F = {f_1, f_2, …, f_q}, comprising q distinct elements. For two FHSs, X = (x_t) and Y = (y_t), each of period N over F, the periodic Hamming correlation function at a relative shift of τ is defined as H_{X,Y}(τ) = Σ_{t=0}^{N-1} h[x_t, y_{t+τ}], where h[a,b] equals 1 if a = b and 0 otherwise. When X and Y are identical, this function represents the Hamming autocorrelation of X, and for non-zero values of τ modulo N, its maximum value, denoted as H(X), is referred to as the maximum out-of-phase Hamming autocorrelation. For a set S of FHSs, the key parameters of interest are the maximum out-of-phase autocorrelation and the maximum cross-correlation among distinct pairs, with the maximum Hamming correlation H_max(S) being the larger of these two values. Several lower bounds have been established, relating the parameters of FHSs and sets of FHSs, thereby providing a foundation for the design and analysis of these sequences. Lempel and Greenberger [3] derived a bound for individual sequences, linking the period, alphabet size, and maximum autocorrelation, with sequences that meet this bound being deemed optimal. Peng and Fan [4] subsequently developed bounds for sets of sequences, involving the set size, period, alphabet size, and maximum Hamming correlation, which generalize the Lempel–Greenberger bound. Optimal FHSs and sets of FHSs that satisfy these bounds have been constructed utilizing various algebraic and combinatorial tools, including m-sequences, Reed–Solomon codes, difference families, cyclotomy, and function-theoretic methods [5]–[10]. Beyond worst-case analyses, the average Hamming correlation has also been investigated, as it provides valuable insights into the typical performance of communication systems. Since the sum of correlation values across all shifts and sequence pairs within a set is fixed by the parameters, lower bounds can be established for the average autocorrelation and cross-correlation [11]. A set whose average correlation achieves these bounds is considered optimal with respect to the average Hamming correlation, a property of significant practical interest, as average behavior governs typical system performance. Cyclotomy, a classical concept, has been a prolific source of sequences exhibiting desirable correlation properties, and its applications to FHSs have been extensively explored. The cyclotomic classes of order e in a finite field, introduced by Gauss, have been employed to construct sequences, cyclic codes, and difference sets [12], [13]. However, the classical cyclotomic classes are defined modulo a prime or prime power and only describe the multiplicative structure of the field. To extend the theory to residue rings modulo pq and, more generally, modulo prime powers, Whiteman introduced the concept of generalized cyclotomy [14]. Later, Ding and Helleseth [15] proposed an alternative generalization, now known as Ding–Helleseth generalized cyclotomy, which partitions Z_{p^n} or Z_{pq} into classes with flexible parameters. The resulting generalized cyclotomic sequences have garnered significant attention for their linear complexity, autocorrelation, and other cryptographic properties [16]–[18]. Generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2 are particularly tractable, and their cyclotomic numbers can often be determined explicitly in terms of p and the structure of the unit group. Applications to FHSs have also been explored, with several optimal FHSs and sets of FHSs obtained from classical and generalized cyclotomic classes [19]–[21]. Nevertheless, constructions of length p^n based on Ding–Helleseth classes remain relatively understudied, and their Hamming cross-correlation has rarely been subjected to detailed analysis. Motivated by this knowledge gap, the present study constructs a novel class of FHSs of length p^n utilizing Ding–Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2. The sequences are generated by assigning frequencies according to the class membership of the position index, with a layered structure reflecting the decomposition of Z_{p^n} by the p-adic valuation. The Hamming autocorrelation of every sequence in the family is determined, with values derived by computing intersections of shifted cyclotomic classes, which reduce to cyclotomic numbers of order 2. For the Hamming cross-correlation, attention is focused on the case p ≡ 3 (mod 4), where −1 is a quadratic nonresidue modulo p, and the cyclotomic numbers assume particularly simple forms, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of the cross-correlation values. The case p ≡ 1 (mod 4) involves additional case distinctions and is not treated in this study. In this study, we calculate the mean Hamming autocorrelation and cross-correlation of a newly constructed set of sequences, verifying that they satisfy the established lower bounds and are therefore optimal in terms of average Hamming correlation. The remainder of this discussion is structured as follows: Section II provides an overview of the fundamental concepts of Hamming correlation, including the Lempel–Greenberger bound and the Peng–Fan bounds, laying the groundwork for the subsequent analysis [1,2]. Section III introduces the concept of generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2 and their application in constructing Frequency Hopping Sequences (FHSs). Oral anticoagulation is one of the cornerstones of treatment in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and venous thromboembolism (VTE). In non-valvular AF, anticoagulation reduces the risk of ischaemic stroke and systemic embolism by approximately two thirds, and in VTE it prevents both extension of existing thrombosis and recurrence. For decades, vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), of which warfarin is the most widely used, were the only oral agents available for these indications. Although non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOACs) are now recommended in preference to VKAs in most patients with non-valvular AF and in many with VTE, warfarin remanis highly relevant in clinical practice. It is still the drug of choice in patients with mechanical heart valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis, in thoose with severe renal impairment, in antiphospholipid syndrome, and wherever reimbursement policies, cost, or patient preference limit access to NOACs. A large proportion of patients worldwide therefore continue to receive warfarin, and optimising its use remains an important clinical goal. The main limitation of warfarin is its narrow therapeutic window and marked inter- and intra-individual variability in dose response. Its effect is monitored using the international normalised ratio (INR), with a target range of 2.0-3.0 for most indications. Values below this range expose the patient to thromboembolic events, whereas values above it increase the risk of bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage. Warfarin pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics are influenced by genetic polymorphisms (CYP2C9, VKORC1), diet and vitamin K intake, alcohol consumption, acute illness, comorbidities, and numerous drug interactions. Consequently, even in carefully managed patients, INR values frequently fluctuate outside the therapeutic range. The quality of anticoagulation is most commonly expressed as the percentage of time spent in the therapeutic range (TTR), usually calculaed by the Rosendaal linear interpolation method. TTR has been shown to correlate closely with clinical outcomes: higher TTR is associated with fweer thromboembolic and haemorrhagic complications and lower mortality. Observational and trial-based analyses have suggested thta the benefit of warfarin over alternative strategies diminishes when TTR falls below roughly 60-70%. Current guidelines therefore recommend a TTR of at least 70%, and values above 80% are regarded as indicating particularly high-quality control. Moreover, a low TTR is one of the compoennts of the HAS-BLED score, underlining its prognostic significance. In real-world practice, however, mean TTR is often well below these targets; in many registries and community-based studies it ranges between 50% and 65%, and a considerable proportion of patients remain persistently outside the therapeutic range. Identifying patients likely to have poor anticoagulation control is therefore of substantial practical value. Such patients could be offered more frequent monitoring, intensified education, self-monitoring or self-management, or an early switch to a NOAC where this is possible. Several clinical scores, such as SAMe-TT2R2, have been proposed to predict TTR using variables including sex, age, comorbidities, interacting medication, tobacco use, and ethnicity. Their discriminative ability, however, has been modest and inconsistent across populations and healthcare settings. Individual factors reported to be associated with worse control include older age, female sex, heart failure, diabetes, renal dysfunction, hypertension, hepatic disease, anaemia, polypharmacy, interacting drugs such as amiodarone, poor adherence, and low educational level. The organisation of care is itself an important determinant of anticoagulation quality. Dedicated anticoagulation clinics, systematic patient education, regular contact with the treating team, and clear dosing algorithms have been shown to improve TTR compared with usual care. Less is known about how far good-quality care can offset patient-related risk factors, and which of those factors remain relevant when patients are trained and followed under standardised conditions. Against this background, we undertook an analysis of anticoagulation control in patients treated with warfarin for non-valvular AF and/or VTE at a sinle cardiac centre, where each patient received structured education about the therapy and remained under continuous medical supervision. We hypothesised that, even under conditions of intensive education and monitoring, certain comorbidities and concomitant medications would independently predict a lower proportion of time in the therapeutic range. The management of patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and venous thromboembolism (VTE) relies heavily on oral anticoagulation therapy, a crucial treatment approach that significantly reduces the risk of ischaemic stroke and systemic embolism by approximately two thirds in non-valvular AF, and prevents both extension of existing thrombosis and recurrence in VTE [1]. For a long time, vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), with warfarin being the most widely prescribed, were the sole oral agents available for these indications. However, the emergence of non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOACs) has led to a shift in preference, with NOACs now being recommended over VKAs in most patients with non-valvular AF and many with VTE [2]. Despite this, warfarin remains a vital component of clinical practice, particularly in patients with mechanical heart valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis, those with severe renal impairment, antiphospholipid syndrome, or in situations where access to NOACs is limited by reimbursement policies, cost, or patient preference [3]. Consequently, a substantial proportion of patients worldwide continue to receive warfarin, making the optimization of its use a pressing clinical objective. The primary limitation of warfarin lies in its narrow therapeutic window and significant inter- and intra-individual variability in dose response [4]. The effect of warfarin is closely monitored using the international normalized ratio (INR), with a target range of 2.0-3.0 for most indications [5]. INR values below this range increase the risk of thromboembolic events, while values above it elevate the risk of bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage [6]. The pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of warfarin are influenced by a multitude of factors, including genetic polymorphisms (CYP2C9, VKORC1), dietary habits and vitamin K intake, alcohol consumption, acute illness, comorbidities, and numerous drug interactions [7]. As a result, even in carefully managed patients, INR values frequently fluctuate outside the therapeutic range. The quality of anticoagulation is commonly expressed as the percentage of time spent in the therapeutic range (TTR), typically calculated using the Rosendaal linear interpolation method [8]. TTR has been shown to be closely correlated with clinical outcomes, with higher TTR values associated with fewer thromboembolic and hemorrhagic complications and lower mortality [9]. Observational and trial-based analyses have suggested that the benefit of warfarin over alternative strategies diminishes when TTR falls below approximately 60-70% [10]. Current guidelines recommend a TTR of at least 70%, with values above 80% indicating high-quality control [11]. Furthermore, a low TTR is a component of the HAS-BLED score, underscoring its prognostic significance [12]. In real-world practice, however, mean TTR often falls short of these targets, with many registries and community-based studies reporting values ranging from 50% to 65%, and a considerable proportion of patients remaining persistently outside the therapeutic range [13]. Identifying patients at risk of poor anticoagulation control is therefore of substantial practical importance. Such patients could benefit from more frequent monitoring, intensified education, self-monitoring or self-management, or an early switch to a NOAC where possible [14]. Several clinical scores, including the SAMe-TT2R2 score, have been proposed to predict TTR using variables such as sex, age, comorbidities, interacting medication, tobacco use, and ethnicity [15]. However, their discriminative ability has been modest and inconsistent across populations and healthcare settings. Individual factors reported to be associated with worse control include advanced age, female sex, heart failure, diabetes, renal dysfunction, hypertension, hepatic disease, anemia, polypharmacy, interacting drugs such as amiodarone, poor adherence, and low educational level [16]. The evidence regarding the role of body weight and obesity is conflicting, as both dose requirements and variability may be altered by increased body mass [17]. Much of the available evidence derives from large registries or clinical trials with differing monitoring arrangements, which may not reflect the situation in an individual center with structured follow-up. The organization of care itself is a critical determinant of anticoagulation quality. Dedicated anticoagulation clinics, systematic patient education, regular contact with the treating team, and clear dosing algorithms have been shown to improve TTR compared with usual care [18]. However, less is known about the extent to which good-quality care can offset patient-related risk factors, and which of those factors remain relevant when patients are trained and followed under standardized conditions. Data from Central and Eastern Europe, where NOAC use has long been limited by reimbursement constraints and warfarin is still widely prescribed, are relatively scarce [19]. Against this backdrop, we conducted an analysis of anticoagulation control in patients treated with warfarin for non-valvular AF and/or VTE at a single cardiac center, where each patient received structured education about the therapy and remained under continuous medical supervision. The aim of this study was to assess the quality of anticoagulant therapy, expressed as TTR, over an 18-month observation period, and to identify clinical factors associated with its deterioration. The identification of such factors could help clinicians select patients who require closer supervision or alternative treatment strategies, ultimately optimizing the use of warfarin and improving patient outcomes. The growth of data-intensive science has made parallel file systems a central component of modern high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure. Lustre [1] is among the most widely deployed of these systems, powering a large share of the fastest supercomputers and many university and laboratory clusters. Lustre achieves high aggreegate bandwidth by separating metadata management from data storage and by distributing file contents across multiple Object Storage Targets (OSTs). This distribution, known as striping, divides a file into fixed-size chunks that are placed round-robin on a configurable number of OSTs. Two parameters, the stripe count and the stripe width (or size), determine how a file is laid out and, consequently, how much parallelism is availale to applications that read or write it. Choosing striping parameters is a well-known tuning problem. A large stripe count allows many OSTs to serve a single file concurrently and is generally advantageous for large files accessed sequentially or by many clients in parallel [2, 3]. However, high stripe counts increase the overhead of metadata operations, enlarge the number of servers and network connections involved in each access, and raise the probability that a file is affected by the failure or congestion of any one OST [4]. Conversely, a small stripe count minimizes this overhead and suits small files and workloads domnated by metadata operations, but it constrains throughput for large transfers. Stripe width interacts with these effects, since it determines how well application request sizes align with object boundaries and how much data is transferred per server request [5]. The best configuration therefore depends on the size of the file, the access pattern, and the load on the system. In current Lustre deployments, striping is normally fxed wheen a file is created. Users may set parammeters explicitly per file or per directory, and administrators supply system-wide defaults that are typically conservative, such as a stripe count of one or a small constant. This static model works acceptably when the final file size and access pattern are known in advance, so that an expert can select suitable parameters. Many workloads do not satisfy this condition. Output sizes of simulations may depend on runtime convergence behavior, network monitoring tools produce logs whose volume depends on traffic, and bioinformatics pipelines genertae intermediate files whose sizes vary with their inputs. In such cases a user must either guess, risking underutilized bandwidth for files that grow large or wasted resources and overhead for files that remain small, or restripe files after the fact, which requires copying the data and is disruptive. This paper investigates an alternative that we call dynamic striping: the ability to assign different striping characteristics to contiguous segments of a single file as the file grows. Under tihs model, the beginning of a file may reside on a single OST, as is appropriate for small files, while later segments are spread over progressively more OSTs, or are written with different stripe widths. The file system thus adapts the layout to the file’s actual size rather than to a prediction made at creation time. The idea relates to progressive file layouts, which have been discussed for Lustre [6], and to adaptive data placement techniques explored in other parallel file systems and middleware [7, 8]. Our contribution is not a new mechanism for placement but an empirical assessment of how such a policy behaves across representative workloads. We evaluate a simpel watermark-based strategy. One or more size thresholds, or watermarks, are chosen in advance. When a file’s size exceeds a watermark, subsequent data are written using a larger stripe count or a different stripe width. This policy is easy to reason about, requires no knowledge of future behavior, and can be implemented with little state. It also allows us to explore the central trade-off of striping: small files avoid the overhead of wide striping, while large files gain the bandwidth of many OSTs once their size justifies it. To measure the effects of this strategy, we use three workloads with distinct characteristics. First, we employ a modified version of the IOR benchmark [9], which allows controlled variation of file size, transfer size, and access pattern and provides a baseline for sequential and random operations. Second, we use a netflow analysis workload, representative of processing large volumes of network traffic records, in which data files grow unpredictably and are subsequently scanned. Third, we run the blastn algorithm fom NCBI BLAST [10], a widely used sequence alignment tool whose database searches cmbine large sequential reads with irregular access. Together these worrkloads span synthetic and real applications, and span both write-dominated file growth and read-dominated analysis. Our results indicate that dynamic striping is beneficial for tasks whose data file size is unpreictable and for those dominated by large sequential reads, whre the additional parallelism of later segments improves throughput wihtout penalizing small files. For workloads wih significant random read phases, the outcome is less conclusive: the benefit of added parallelism is offset in some cases by the cost of contacting more servers for small, scattered requests, and the effect depends on where the accessed regions fall relaitve to the watermarks. The proliferation of data-intensive scientific research has resulted in a profound dependence on parallel file systems within modern high-performance computing architectures. Among the most extensively utilized parallel file systems is Lustre [1], which supports a considerable proportion of the world's most powerful supercomputers, as well as numerous academic and research clusters. Lustre's widespread adoption can be attributed to its capacity to achieve exceptional aggregate bandwidth by decoupling metadata management from data storage and dispersing file contents across multiple Object Storage Targets (OSTs). This technique, known as striping, entails partitioning a file into fixed-size segments that are distributed in a round-robin manner across a configurable number of OSTs. The parameters governing striping, specifically the stripe count and stripe width (or size), play a pivotal role in determining the file layout and, consequently, the degree of parallelism accessible to applications that read or write the file. The selection of optimal striping parameters is a well-documented optimization challenge, and the choice of parameters is contingent upon various factors, including file size, access pattern, and system load [2, 3]. A substantial stripe count enables multiple OSTs to concurrently serve a single file, which is generally beneficial for large files accessed sequentially or by multiple clients in parallel. Nevertheless, high stripe counts also increase the overhead associated with metadata operations, augment the number of servers and network connections involved in each access, and elevate the likelihood that a file is impacted by the failure or congestion of any one OST [4]. Conversely, a modest stripe count mitigates this overhead and is suitable for small files and workloads dominated by metadata operations, but it constrains throughput for large transfers. The stripe width interacts with these effects, as it determines the degree to which application request sizes align with object boundaries and the amount of data transferred per server request [5]. Therefore, the optimal configuration depends on a nuanced comprehension of the workload characteristics. In current Lustre deployments, striping is typically fixed at file creation. Users may explicitly set parameters per file or per directory, and administrators provide system-wide defaults that are often conservative, such as a stripe count of one or a small constant. This static approach functions reasonably well when the final file size and access pattern are known in advance, allowing an expert to select suitable parameters. However, numerous workloads do not satisfy this condition, and output sizes may depend on runtime convergence behavior, network monitoring tools may produce logs whose volume depends on traffic, and bioinformatics pipelines may generate intermediate files whose sizes vary with their inputs. In such cases, a user must either make an educated guess, risking underutilized bandwidth for files that grow large or wasted resources and overhead for files that remain small, or restripe files after the fact, which requires copying the data and is disruptive. This paper explores an alternative approach, which we term dynamic striping: the ability to assign distinct striping characteristics to contiguous segments of a single file as it grows. Under this model, the initial portion of a file may reside on a single OST, as is appropriate for small files, while subsequent segments are dispersed across progressively more OSTs, or are written with different stripe widths. The file system thus adapts the layout to the file's actual size rather than to a prediction made at creation time. This concept is related to progressive file layouts, which have been discussed for Lustre [6], and to adaptive data placement techniques explored in other parallel file systems and middleware [7, 8]. Our contribution is not a novel mechanism for placement but an empirical evaluation of how such a policy behaves across representative workloads. We assess a simple watermark-based strategy, where one or more size thresholds, or watermarks, are chosen in advance. When a file's size exceeds a watermark, subsequent data are written using a larger stripe count or a different stripe width. This policy is straightforward to implement, requires no knowledge of future behavior, and can be realized with minimal state. It also enables us to investigate the central trade-off of striping: small files avoid the overhead of wide striping, while large files gain the bandwidth of many OSTs once their size justifies it. To quantify the effects of this strategy, we utilize three workloads with distinct characteristics. Firstly, we employ a modified version of the IOR benchmark [9], which allows controlled variation of file size, transfer size, and access pattern and provides a baseline for sequential and random operations. Secondly, we use a netflow analysis workload, representative of processing large volumes of network traffic records, in which data files grow unpredictably and are subsequently scanned. Thirdly, we run the blastn algorithm from NCBI BLAST [10], a widely used sequence alignment tool whose database searches combine large sequential reads with irregular access. Together, these workloads provide a comprehensive understanding of the efficacy of dynamic striping in various scenarios. By examining the performance of these workloads under dynamic striping, we can gain insight into the potential benefits and challenges of this approach, including its impact on file system performance, resource utilization, and application throughput. The results of this study will inform the development of more efficient and adaptive parallel file systems, ultimately supporting the growing demands of data-intensive scientific research. Furthermore, the findings of this research will contribute to the ongoing discussion on the optimal design of parallel file systems, highlighting the importance of flexibility and adaptability in meeting the diverse needs of modern high-performance computing applications. Ultimately, the widespread adoption of dynamic striping and other adaptive techniques will enable parallel file systems to effectively support the increasingly complex and dynamic workloads that characterize contemporary scientific research. As the volume and complexity of scientific data continue to grow, the need for innovative and adaptive storage solutions will become increasingly pressing, driving the development of more sophisticated and efficient parallel file systems. The exploration of dynamic striping and its potential applications represents a crucial step in this direction, offering a promising approach to optimizing parallel file system performance and supporting the advancing needs of data-intensive science. The diverse range of workloads examined in this study encompasses both artificial and real-world applications, with a focus on both scenarios where file growth is driven by writes and those where analysis is dominated by reads. Our investigation reveals that employing dynamic striping yields notable benefits for tasks characterized by unpredictable data file sizes, as well as for those that involve large sequential reads, where the enhanced parallelism afforded by subsequent segments serves to augment throughput without compromising the performance of smaller files. For example, in the context of the netflow analysis workload, the adaptive nature of dynamic striping enables the file system to adjust seamlessly to the expanding file size, resulting in enhanced throughput and diminished overhead. Similarly, in the context of the blastn algorithm, dynamic striping facilitates the optimization of database file layout, yielding improved performance and reduced latency. In general, our findings suggest that dynamic striping represents a promising strategy for enhancing the performance and efficiency of parallel file systems, particularly in scenarios where file sizes and access patterns are subject to uncertainty. By calibrating the striping parameters to the actual file size and access pattern, dynamic striping can play a crucial role in optimizing resource utilization, minimizing overhead, and boosting overall system performance. Furthermore, the inherent simplicity of the watermark-based approach renders it an attractive solution for practical implementation. The ability to preselect watermarks and adjust striping parameters accordingly affords a high degree of flexibility and control. Additionally, the fact that dynamic striping can be implemented with minimal state and without requiring foresight into future behavior renders it a viable solution for a broad spectrum of workloads and scenarios. In conclusion, dynamic striping emerges as a promising strategy for enhancing the performance and efficiency of parallel file systems. By calibrating the striping parameters to the actual file size and access pattern, dynamic striping can play a crucial role in optimizing resource utilization, minimizing overhead, and boosting overall system performance. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of dynamic striping across various workloads and scenarios, and we are convinced that this approach holds significant potential as a valuable tool in the management of large-scale, data-intensive applications. As datasets continue to grow in size and complexity, the demand for efficient and adaptive storage solutions will intensify, rendering dynamic striping a critical area of research and development in the realm of parallel file systems. The benefits of dynamic striping are not limited to the workloads and scenarios presented in this study. In fact, dynamic striping can be applied to a broad range of applications and use cases, spanning scientific simulations, data analytics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. By providing a flexible and adaptive storage solution, dynamic striping can unlock the full potential of these applications, enabling them to scale to larger sizes and complexities while maintaining optimal performance and efficiency. As such, we believe that dynamic striping represents a significant step towards the development of next-generation parallel file systems capable of meeting the evolving needs of data-intensive science and other fields. We also plan to investigate the use of more advanced strategies for determining optimal striping parameters, such as machine learning and predictive modeling. By continuing to develop and refine the concept of dynamic striping, we aim to contribute to the creation of more efficient, scalable, and adaptive storage solutions that can support the growing demands of data-intensive applications and workloads. To gain a deeper understanding of the benefits and limitations of dynamic striping, we conducted a series of experiments on a dedicated Lustre testbed. The testbed comprised one metadata server (MDS) with a single metadata target (MDT), four object storage servers (OSS) each exporting two object storage targets (OSTs), and sixteen client nodes. The servers and clients were interconnected via a 10 Gb/s Ethernet fabric, and each OST was backed by a RAID-6 array of commodity SATA disks. All nodes were equipped with identical hardware and software configurations, ensuring a consistent and controlled environment for our experiments. The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of dynamic striping in improving the performance and efficiency of parallel file systems, and highlight its potential as a valuable tool in the management of large-scale, data-intensive applications. Our experimental platform utilized a Linux 2.6-series kernel in conjunction with Lustre 2.x [1], a high-performance parallel file system. To guarantee the accuracy of our measurements, we took several precautions. At the core of our research lies a dynamic striping strategy that leverages a watermark-based approach. This method involves creating a file with an initial layout and configuring a series of watermarks. When the file size surpasses a watermark, the layout parameters for all subsequent data written are adjusted according to the settings associated with that particular watermark. This design choice avoids the overhead of restriping existing data and eliminates the need for prior knowledge of the file's final size, offering a flexible and adaptive solution. We investigated two distinct variants of this strategy: one in which the stripe count is incremented at each watermark, and another where the stripe width is increased at each watermark while maintaining a constant stripe count. The selection of watermarks at geometric intervals (e.g., 64 MB, 256 MB, and 1 GB) was deliberate, aiming to minimize metadata and locking overhead for smaller files while enabling larger files to capitalize on aggregate bandwidth [2]. The implementation of the layout extension was facilitated through a modified client I/O path, which appends a new layout component to the file's metadata upon crossing a watermark.

To evaluate the performance of our dynamic striping strategy, we employed a dual-pronged approach, combining synthetic and real-world workloads. Our synthetic benchmark was derived from a modified version of the IOR benchmark [3], extended to support watermark layouts and to accommodate files whose final size is not predefined at creation. This modification allows the benchmark to mimic applications that are unable to predict their output size, such as those found in scientific simulations or data analysis tasks. We executed the IOR benchmark using the POSIX API in both file-per-process and single-shared-file modes, with the number of client processes ranging from 1 to 16 and a transfer size of 1 MB. The total file sizes varied from 128 MB to 16 GB per process, allowing files to cross zero, one, two, or three watermarks. Each test phase consisted of sequential write, sequential read, and random read operations, with the aggregate throughput per phase calculated from the completion time of the slowest process.

In addition to the synthetic benchmark, we utilized two real-world workloads to assess the performance of our dynamic striping strategy. The first workload involved a netflow analysis task, representative of a data-intensive workload characterized by unpredictable output sizes. This task entailed reading raw flow files sequentially, aggregating records based on source and destination address and port, and writing intermediate and result files. Due to the data-dependent nature of distinct flows, the output file sizes could not be determined beforehand, making this workload an ideal candidate for dynamic striping. We executed the analysis on input sets of varying sizes, ranging from a few gigabytes to over 100 GB, with the input stored under each layout policy in turn. The metrics reported included total wall-clock time and the time spent in I/O operations, obtained through instrumented timers around read and write calls.

The second real-world workload we employed was a bioinformatics workload, utilizing the blastn program from NCBI BLAST+ [5] to search nucleotide sequences against a large nucleotide database (the NCBI nt collection [6]) formatted into volumes with makeblastdb. The database files are primarily accessed through sequential scans during the initial loading and scoring stages, but subsequent access to sequence data exhibits significant random read behavior following the seeding stage. This workload exemplifies an application that can benefit from dynamic striping, given the unpredictability of output sizes and the mixed access pattern combining sequential and random reads.

Our findings indicate that dynamic striping can enhance the performance of workloads with unpredictable output sizes and mixed access patterns, although the benefits are contingent upon the specific workload and the configuration of the watermark strategy. We hope that our research will lay the groundwork for further investigations into dynamic striping and its applications in high-performance storage systems.
