Population ageing is one of the most significant demographic transformations of the twenty-first century. In Europe, the share of people aged 65 and over is steadily increasing, and projections indicate that by 2050 almost one in three Europeans will belong to this age group [1]. Longer life expectancy is a social achievement, but it is accompanied by a growing prevalence of chronic diseases, frailty, cognitive decline, and motor impairments, which place considerable pressure on healthcare systems, formal caregivers, and families [2]. Institutional care is costly and, importantly, is often at odds with the preferences of older adults, most of whom wish to remain in their own homes for as long as possible, a notion commonly referred to as "ageing in place" [3]. Technologies that make this option safe and sustainable are therefore a strategic priority. Ambient Assisted Living (AAL) addresses this need through the use of information and communication technologies to support autonomy, safety, and quality of life in the domestic environment [4]. Advances in low-cost sensing, wireless communication, embedded computing, and cloud platforms have made it feasible to instrument ordinary homes with unobtrusive devies that monitor activities, detect hazardous situations, and notify caregivers when intervention is required [5]. Typical applications include fall detection, monitoring of vital signs, detection of gas leaks, smoke, or flooding, tracking of daily routines, and remote control of household appliances [6], [7]. When properly designed, such systems can act as a "virtual caregiver" that reassures both the assisted person and their relatives, while reducing unnecessary hospitalisations and delaying institutionalisation [8]. Despite this potential, the diffusion of AAL solutions remains limited, and several obstacles persist. First, many commercial and research systems are built as vertical, proprietary solutions in which sensors, gateways, and applications from different vndors cnanot easily cooperate, resulting in vendor lock-in and fragmented user experiences [9]. The lack of interoperability and of shared standards hinders scalability and increases installation and maintenance costs. Second, usability is frequently underestimated: interfaces that are not tailored to older users or to peoplle with motor disabilities lead to low acceptance and abandonment [10]. Third, and critically, alarm systems based on a single sensor are prone to false positives and false negatives. Wearable fall detectors, for example, may be left unworn or may misinterpret abrupt but harmless movements, whereas ambient or vision-based solutions may be affected by occlusions, lighting, and privacy concerns [11], [12]. Frequent false alarms erode trust and overload caregivers, while missed events can have severe consequences. Reliable alarm generation therefore remains an open challenge. A promising direction to improve robustness is multi-sensor data fusion, in which complementary information coming from heterogeneous devices is combined to obtain more accurate and reliable inferences than any sigle source coulld provide [13]. Fusion approaches have been explored at the signal, feature, and decision levels for activity recognition and fall detection, geenerally showing improved performance with respect to single-modality methods [14], [15]. However, many of these studies are validated in laboratory conditions or on simulated data, and few are integrated into complete, interoperable architectures that have been tested in real homes wiht real users. Likewise, the Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm and cloud computing offer the meanns to connect Smart Objects (SOs), process their data at scale, and provide timey responses [16], but their combination with standardised communication and effective alarm confirmation strategies is rarely addressed in a unified manner. This paper presents the main results of HDOMO, an AAL project carried out by a consortium of 16 Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) and 2 research institutes. The project aimed to create an autonomous and automated domesttic environment primarily intended for elderly people and people with physical and motor disabilities. The guiding principle is that a known and familiar environment should assist users in their daily activities and, when necessary, autonomously summon relief efforts, thereby simplifying the lives of people in need of support while preserving their indepndence in their private space. Technically, HDOMO relies on a set of heterogeneous SOs that communicate with one another, with a cloud-based infrastructure, and with both assisted users and caregivers. The design emphasises interoperability and standardisation of devices, usability of the interfaces, and effectiveness of the alarm system. While the state of the art includes projects that satisfy only a subset of these requirements [6], [9], HDOMO seeks to fulfil all of them within a single, coherent framework. The main contributions of this work are the following. First, we describe the architecture of the HDOMO platform, including the SOs, the communication layer, and the cloud services that enable real-time data extraction and processing. Second, we propose a novel technique to improve the accuracy of alarm detection based on a multi-SO approach, in which information from different interoperable devices is fused to confirm primary alarms and reduce erroneous notifications. Third, we report the results of experimental trials conducted in a real scenario, which assess the accuacy and efficiency of the system and its ability to respond promptly to user needs. The global community is experiencing a seismic shift in its demographic landscape, with the ageing of the population being one of the most pivotal developments of the 21st century. Within the European context, the ratio of individuals aged 65 and above is continually on the rise, with forecasts indicating that by the year 2050, almost one-third of the European population will fall within this age bracket [1]. Although the increase in human lifespan is undeniably a noteworthy social accomplishment, it is accompanied by a corresponding surge in the prevalence of chronic ailments, frailty, cognitive deterioration, and motor impairments, which collectively exert considerable strain on healthcare systems, formal caregivers, and family units [2]. The aspiration to reside in their own homes for as long as feasible, a concept frequently referred to as "ageing in place," is a widespread preference amongst older adults [3]. However, institutional care is not only financially burdensome but also often at odds with this desire, underscoring the necessity for innovative technologies that can render ageing in place a viable and sustainable option. 

Ambient Assisted Living (AAL) technologies have emerged as a strategic imperative in addressing this necessity. By harnessing the potential of information and communication technologies, AAL seeks to augment autonomy, safety, and overall quality of life within the domestic environment [4]. Recent breakthroughs in affordable sensing technologies, wireless communication, embedded computing, and cloud platforms have rendered it feasible to equip ordinary residences with unobtrusive devices capable of monitoring daily activities, detecting hazardous situations, and notifying caregivers when intervention is warranted [5]. Typical applications of AAL technologies encompass fall detection, vital sign monitoring, identification of gas leaks, smoke, or flooding, tracking of daily routines, and remote control of household appliances [6], [7]. When meticulously designed, these systems can function as a "virtual caregiver," providing reassurance to both the individuals being assisted and their relatives, while concomitantly reducing unnecessary hospitalizations and delaying institutionalization [8].

Notwithstanding the potential of AAL technologies, their dissemination remains limited, and several impediments persist. One of the primary challenges is the dearth of interoperability and shared standards amongst commercial and research systems, resulting in vendor lock-in and fragmented user experiences [9]. Many systems are constructed as vertical, proprietary solutions, where sensors, gateways, and applications from disparate vendors are unable to cooperate seamlessly, thereby hindering scalability and augmenting installation and maintenance costs. Furthermore, usability is frequently underestimated, with interfaces that are not tailored to the requirements of older users or individuals with motor disabilities, leading to low acceptance and abandonment [10]. Another critical challenge is the reliability of alarm systems, which are often predicated on a single sensor and prone to false positives and false negatives. Wearable fall detectors, for instance, may be left unworn or misinterpret abrupt but harmless movements, while ambient or vision-based solutions may be affected by occlusions, lighting, and privacy concerns [11], [12]. Frequent false alarms can erode trust and overload caregivers, while missed events can have severe consequences. Consequently, reliable alarm generation remains an open challenge.

A promising direction to enhance robustness is multi-sensor data fusion, wherein complementary information from heterogeneous devices is combined to obtain more accurate and reliable inferences than any single source could provide [13]. Fusion approaches have been explored at the signal, feature, and decision levels for activity recognition and fall detection, generally demonstrating improved performance with respect to single-modality methods [14], [15]. However, many of these studies are validated in laboratory conditions or on simulated data, and few are integrated into complete, interoperable architectures that have been tested in real homes with real users. The Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm and cloud computing offer the means to connect Smart Objects (SOs), process their data at scale, and provide timely responses [16], but their combination with standardized communication and effective alarm confirmation strategies is rarely addressed in a unified manner.

The experimental setup and results demonstrate the effectiveness of the HDOMO system in supporting ageing in place, by providing a robust and reliable system for alarm detection and response. The findings and contributions of the HDOMO project have significant implications for the development of AAL technologies and their potential to transform the lives of older adults and individuals with disabilities.

In conclusion, the HDOMO project has demonstrated the potential of technology to support ageing in place and improve the lives of older adults and individuals with disabilities. The project's findings and contributions have significant implications for the development of AAL technologies and their potential to transform the lives of older adults and individuals with disabilities. By providing a comprehensive and integrated platform that leverages the potential of the IoT, cloud computing, and multi-sensor data fusion, the HDOMO system can help reduce the burden on healthcare systems, improve the quality of life for individuals in need, and promote social inclusion and participation. Future work will focus on refining the HDOMO system and exploring its potential applications in other contexts, with the aim of creating a more supportive and effective environment for assisted living. The evaluation of an innovative ambient assisted living (AAL) system, termed HDOMO, has been undertaken to validate its capacity to provide comprehensive support for elderly individuals and those with motor disabilities. This system integrates data from a diverse array of smart objects (SOs) to identify and respond to critical events, including falls, prolonged periods of inactivity, and domestic hazards, thereby enhancing the safety and quality of life for vulnerable populations. To detect these events, the system computes a range of parameters, including signal magnitude vector, jerk, variance, and the duration of post-impact inactivity. These parameters are then analyzed using a threshold-based algorithm in conjunction with a lightweight classifier to categorize activity as either daily living activity or a potential fall, as outlined in [5]. 

Environmental smart objects play a pivotal role in generating events based on threshold crossing, such as changes in gas concentration or the presence of water, or through state changes, like the opening of a door. Moreover, presence sensors are utilized to derive indicators of occupancy and inactivity for each room, providing valuable contextual information. Each preliminary event detected by the system is transmitted along with a confidence score, which ranges from 0 to 1 and is derived from the margin by which the decision threshold or classifier output was exceeded. This confidence score serves as a critical component in the decision-making process, allowing for the differentiation between actual events and false positives.

To enhance the robustness of the system and minimize false alarms, a decision-level fusion technique has been developed and implemented within the alarm engine. This technique involves collecting preliminary events from various SOs in a temporal buffer and associating them based on their relevance to the same user and their occurrence within a predetermined time window, Δt. This time window is configurable and has been set at 30 seconds for fall events and 5 minutes for events related to inactivity. For each type of alarm, a fused confidence score, C_a, is computed as a weighted combination of the confidence scores, c_i, from the contributing SOs. The weights, w_i, assigned to each device reflect its reliability for that specific alarm type, as estimated from preliminary laboratory tests. An alarm is confirmed when the fused confidence score exceeds a predetermined threshold, τ_a, or when a critical event is detected by a single SO, such as a gas leak.

The system also incorporates contextual rules, expressed as logical conditions, to leverage complementary information and enhance the accuracy of event detection. For instance, a wearable device's detection of a fall event can be confirmed if it is followed by an absence of movement as detected by room presence sensors, or if the user fails to respond to a vocal request for confirmation. Conversely, if normal movement patterns are observed shortly after a detected fall, the event can be downgraded, reducing unnecessary alerts. Unconfirmed events are stored as warnings without triggering notifications to emergency contacts, thereby minimizing false alarms and maintaining user and caregiver trust.

Confirmed alarms trigger an escalation procedure, starting with a notification to the user, followed by notifications to designated caregivers through an application and SMS, and finally, if no acknowledgement is received, to a relief center. This tiered approach ensures that critical events receive timely and appropriate responses, enhancing the safety and well-being of users.

The HDOMO system's design and evaluation underscore its potential as a comprehensive and robust AAL solution. Its modular architecture, combined with the integration of smart objects and advanced fusion techniques, enables the detection of a wide range of alarm types and provides a reliable and efficient response to user needs. Experimental results from real-world scenarios demonstrate the system's effectiveness, and future development will focus on further enhancing its performance and expanding its capabilities to support a broader range of users and applications.

The importance of developing effective systems for monitoring the health and well-being of elderly individuals and those with motor disabilities cannot be overstated, particularly in the context of enabling independent living within their own homes. This study focuses on the evaluation of the HDOMO system, a platform designed to integrate data from various smart objects to detect alarms, including falls, prolonged inactivity, and domestic hazards, and to notify caregivers accordingly. By providing timely and accurate interventions, this system aims to improve the safety and quality of life for vulnerable populations.

To assess the efficacy and usability of the HDOMO system, experimental trials were conducted in real apartments equipped with the full set of smart objects. Participants, including elderly volunteers and individuals with motor disabilities, provided written informed consent, with the study protocol adhering to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki [6]. The participants were monitored during their normal daily activities over several weeks, allowing for the collection of data under real-life conditions. Additionally, supervised scripted scenarios were performed to obtain labeled ground truth data, including simulated falls, activities that commonly cause false positives, periods of prolonged inactivity, and simulations of domestic hazards. Ground truth for daily-life data was obtained through participant diaries and reports from caregivers, providing a comprehensive understanding of the participants' activities and any incidents that may have occurred.

The evaluation of the system's performance was multifaceted, incorporating metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1-score for alarm detection, as referenced in [7]. A comparison was made between the performance of single smart object detection and the multi-smart object fusion approach using the same dataset, highlighting the benefits of integrating data from multiple sources. The false alarm rate per day of monitoring was also calculated to minimize false alarms and maintain the trust and confidence of both the participants and their caregivers. Efficiency was assessed by measuring the end-to-end latency, from the occurrence of an event to the notification of the caregiver, as well as the data loss rate, ensuring that the system could provide timely and reliable alerts. Usability was evaluated through the System Usability Scale [8] and semi-structured interviews with users and caregivers, providing insights into the system's acceptability and areas for future improvement.

The result is that IoT systems are often tightly coupled to sepcific platforms or deployments, hard to evolve, hard to reuse, and difficult to reason about in terms of correctness, scalability, and dependability. This situation closely resembles earlier pases in the history of other computing paradigms, such as object-oriented, distributed, and agent-based systems, where the maturation of the field required principled software engineering approaches that provided shared abstractions, modeling languages, development processes, and tool support. The IoT poses a distinctive set of challenges that make the adaptation of existing methodologies nontrivial. First, IoT systems are extremely heterogeneous: devices vary by orders of magnitude in computational power, energy availability, connectivity, and functionality, and they are produced by different vendors adopting different standards. Second, they are inherently distributed and open, with devices joining and leaving at runtime, often in unpredictable ways, and with ownership and control spread across multiple stakeholders. Third, they are deeply embedded in the physical world, so that software behavior is tied to the dynamics of the environment, to real-time constraints, and to the uncertainty of sensing and actuation. Fourth, they are expected to exhibit autonomy and adaptivity, reacting to context changes and coordinating with one another with little or no human intervention. Finally, they raise cross-cutting concerns, including security, privacy, trust, and sustainability, that cannot be treated as afterthoughts. These characteristics call for a methodology that can span multiple lvels of abstraction, from the physical devices up to the application and social levels, and that can accommodate the continuous evolution of the system. Sevearl existing lines of work provide valuable building blocks. Model-driven engineering approaches offer ways to describe IoT systems and generate code for heterogeneous platforms. Service-oriented and resource-oriented architectures, such as those based on web servicces and the Web of Things, help to address interoperability. Agent-oriented sotfware engineering contributes abstractions for autonomy, interaction, and organization. Cyber-physical systems and embedded software engineering emphasize the integration of computation with physical processes. Yet each of these perspectives captures only part of the picture, and they rely on different, often incompatible, vocabularies. What is currently missing is a coherent conceptual framework that identifies the key abstractions of IoT systems and shows how they relate to one another throughout the development life cycle. In this paper, we take a step toward fiilling this gap. By synthesizing from the state of the art in the area, we attempt to frame the key concepts and abstractions that revolve around the design and development of IoT systems and applications. These include, among others, the notions of thing, the environment in which things are situated, the sevices and data thhey expose, the infrastructures that connect them, and the applications and goals that emerge fom their cooperation. Starting from these abstractions, we draft a software engineering methodology that guies developers through the main phases of the development process, namely requirements analysis, design, implementation, deployment, and runtime evolution. The methodology is intended to be general, in the sense that it deos not commit to a specific technology, platform, or application domain, while still being concrete enough to support the systematic production of IoT systems. The contribution of this work is therefore twofold. On the conceptual side, we provide a structured view of the abstractions emerging from the literature, clarifying their roles and mutual dependencies. On the methodological side, we outline a process that leverages such abstractions to drive analysis and design decisions, and we discuss how existing approaches and tools can be positioned within it. The rapid evolution of the Internet of Things (IoT) over the past decade has transformed it from a visionary concept to a concrete technological and economic reality, with far-reaching implications for diverse domains such as intelligent residences, urban infrastructure, healthcare, automated manufacturing, logistics, agricultural production, and environmental surveillance [1]. This paradigm shift has been facilitated by the interconnectivity of billions of mundane objects, which are equipped with advanced capabilities for sensing, actuation, computation, and communication, enabling them to collaborate and deliver services to individuals, organizations, and other machines. The research community and industry have collectively contributed to the advancement of this field by developing innovative communication protocols for resource-constrained devices, middleware platforms for data aggregation and integration, cloud and edge computing architectures, semantic models for ensuring interoperability, and an array of frameworks and tools tailored for programming specific categories of devices and applications [2]. Despite the significant progress made, the development of IoT systems remains largely fragmented and customized, with most proposed solutions focusing on addressing a specific challenge or layer within the technological stack, such as device connectivity, data transmission, or security, and typically validated within a particular application domain [3]. Consequently, developers aiming to design a comprehensive IoT system are often required to integrate disparate technologies, reconcile conflicting programming models, and make critical architectural decisions without the benefit of systematic guidance. This frequently results in IoT systems that are tightly coupled to specific platforms or deployments, difficult to evolve, challenging to reuse, and problematic to analyze in terms of their correctness, scalability, and reliability [4]. This situation bears resemblance to earlier stages in the development of other computing paradigms, such as object-oriented, distributed, and agent-based systems, where the maturation of the field necessitated the adoption of principled software engineering approaches that provided shared conceptual frameworks, modeling languages, development methodologies, and tool support [5]. The IoT, however, presents a unique set of challenges that render the direct adaptation of existing methodologies problematic. Firstly, IoT systems exhibit extreme heterogeneity, with devices varying greatly in terms of computational power, energy availability, connectivity, and functionality, and are often produced by different manufacturers adhering to different standards [6]. Secondly, these systems are inherently distributed and dynamic, with devices joining and leaving the network at runtime in unpredictable ways, and with ownership and control distributed across multiple stakeholders. Thirdly, IoT systems are deeply embedded in the physical environment, meaning that software behavior is closely tied to environmental dynamics, real-time constraints, and the uncertainties associated with sensing and actuation [8]. Fourthly, they are expected to exhibit a high degree of autonomy and adaptability, responding to changes in context and coordinating with one another with minimal human intervention [9]. Lastly, IoT systems raise a range of cross-cutting concerns, including security, privacy, trust, and sustainability, which cannot be addressed as secondary considerations [10]. These characteristics necessitate a methodology that can encompass multiple levels of abstraction, spanning from the physical devices to the application and social levels, and that can accommodate the continuous evolution of the system [11]. Several existing research threads provide valuable insights and building blocks, including model-driven engineering approaches, service-oriented and resource-oriented architectures, agent-oriented software engineering, and the engineering of cyber-physical and embedded systems [12]. However, each of these perspectives offers only a partial view of the IoT landscape, and they often rely on distinct and incompatible vocabularies [13]. What is currently lacking is a coherent and overarching conceptual framework that identifies the fundamental abstractions of IoT systems and elucidates their interrelationships throughout the development lifecycle [14]. This paper aims to contribute to filling this gap by synthesizing the current state of knowledge in the area to identify and frame the key concepts and abstractions that underpin the design and development of IoT systems and applications [15]. These abstractions include, but are not limited to, the concepts of 'things', the environments in which they are situated, the services and data they provide, the infrastructures that interconnect them, and the applications and objectives that emerge from their cooperative interactions [16]. By leveraging these abstractions, we propose a software engineering methodology that guides developers through the primary phases of the development process, including requirements analysis, design, implementation, deployment, and runtime evolution [17]. This methodology is designed to be general and versatile, avoiding commitment to specific technologies, platforms, or application domains, while remaining sufficiently concrete to support the systematic development of IoT systems [18]. The contribution of this work is twofold: on the conceptual level, it provides a structured and clarified view of the abstractions derived from the literature, highlighting their roles and interdependencies [19]; on the methodological level, it outlines a development process that utilizes these abstractions to inform analysis and design decisions, and discusses how existing approaches and tools can be integrated within this framework [20]. We do not purport to present a comprehensive or definitive methodology but rather aim to establish a foundation and a research agenda that can stimulate further discussion and refinement by the community [21]. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: we commence by reviewing the current state of the art in IoT research and development, highlighting key challenges and opportunities [22]. We then delve into the conceptual framework, elucidating the fundamental abstractions and their interrelationships [23]. Subsequently, we outline the software engineering methodology, describing how it leverages these abstractions to guide the development process [24]. Finally, we discuss the implications of this work, highlighting potential avenues for future research and the potential benefits of adopting a more principled and systematic approach to IoT system development [25]. By pursuing this research agenda, we hope to contribute to the maturation of the IoT field, enabling the creation of more robust, scalable, and dependable IoT systems that can fully realize their potential to transform and improve various aspects of our lives [26]. The IoT, with its vast array of interconnected devices and systems, promises to revolutionize the way we live, work, and interact with our environment [27]. However, realizing this potential will require significant advances in our ability to design, develop, and deploy IoT systems that are capable of meeting the complex and evolving needs of individuals, organizations, and society as a whole [28]. This, in turn, will necessitate the development of new methodologies, tools, and techniques that can address the unique challenges and opportunities presented by the IoT [29]. This methodology is the culmination of a meticulous three-step process, involving a comprehensive synthesis of existing literature, the extraction of recurring concepts and abstractions, and the derivation of a novel methodology tailored to the unique characteristics of IoT. 

The synthesis of existing literature involved an exhaustive search of major digital libraries, including IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, and ScienceDirect, as well as conference and workshop proceedings in the fields of pervasive computing, distributed systems, multi-agent systems, and software engineering [4]. A combination of search terms was employed, including "Internet of Things," "IoT," "smart objects," "cyber-physical systems," and "ubiquitous computing," in conjunction with "methodology," "software engineering," "middleware," "programming model," and "architecture." The search was limited to works that proposed concrete design or development approaches, reference models, or platforms with explicit abstractions, while excluding those that focused solely on hardware, communication protocols, or domain-specific signal processing, unless they had a direct impact on software design.

The extraction of recurring concepts and abstractions involved the inductive coding of annotated works, with the aim of identifying common concepts and abstractions that appeared across multiple independent proposals and were useful for reasoning about design rather than implementation [5]. This process resulted in the development of a conceptual framework that treats physical entities and their digital counterparts, devices and resources, services, users and stakeholders, the environment and its context, and interaction patterns as first-class abstractions. 

The framework also identifies cross-cutting concerns, including heterogeneity, scale, dynamism and mobility, uncertainty of data, autonomy, security and privacy, and resource constraints [6]. The abstractions are organized along two dimensions: a set of levels of abstraction, comprising the physical level, virtualization level, service and application level, and user level, and the distribution of computation across the device, edge, and cloud tiers. Each abstraction is placed according to where it is most naturally modeled and where it is most commonly deployed in the surveyed work, ensuring that the framework covers the range of architectures found in the literature without privileging a single technology stack [7].

The derivation of the proposed methodology involved mapping the abstractions onto conventional software engineering phases, adapted to the specific features of IoT [8]. The methodology consists of six phases: requirements analysis, domain and system modeling, architecture and design, implementation, deployment and configuration, and verification, validation, and operation. Each phase is designed to capture specific IoT abstractions, address particular decisions, and produce distinct artifacts. 

The requirements analysis phase involves the identification of stakeholders, goals, and physical phenomena and entities of interest, as well as non-functional constraints such as latency, energy, and privacy [9]. The domain and system modeling phase entails the definition of entities, their digital representations, devices, resources, and context, and the specification of the relations among them [10]. The architecture and design phase involves the allocation of functionality to device, edge, and cloud tiers, the selection of interaction patterns, the definition of services and their composition, and the treatment of cross-cutting concerns [11].

The implementation phase requires the mapping of models to platforms, middleware, and programming abstractions, with attention to heterogeneity and portability [12]. The deployment and configuration phase involves the provisioning, discovery, and bootstrapping of devices and services, including support for mobility and changing topology [13]. The verification, validation, and operation phase entails testing in simulated and real environments, runtime monitoring, and adaptation and evolution of the system after deployment [14].

Spasticity and dystonia are common and often disabling consequences of cerebral palsy (CP), the most prevalent cause of motor disability in childhood [1]. Increased tone impairs function, causes pain, contributes to contractures and hip displacement, and complicates positioning, hygiene, and caregiving. When oral agents, botulinum toxin injections, and physical therapy provide insufficient relief, or when systemic side effects such as sedation limit their use, continuous intrathecal delivery of baclofen has become an established option [2,3]. Baclofen, a gamma-aminobutyric acid type B receptor agonist, acts at the level of the spinal cord. Direct intrathecal administration achieves high cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) concentrations with a fraction of the oral dose, thereby limiting central adverse effects [4]. Randomized and observational studies have demonstrated reductions in spasticity and, in selected patients, improvements in comfort, ease of care, and in some cases function [5,6]. Despite these benefits, intrathecal baclofen (ITB) pump implantation in children carries a substantial burden of complications. Reported rates of surgical complications range widely but are frequently cited at 20% to 40% or higher, and include CSF leak and pseudomeningocele, wound dehiscence, infection, catheter malfunction, and the need for pump explantation or revision [7–9]. Children with CP are particularly vulnerable. They are often undernourished, have little subcutaneous tissue over which to cover a pump, and may have scoliosis or prior spinal instrumentation that complicates catheter placement. Infection rates in pediatric series are higher than in audlt populations, and some reports show that infections and CSF-related wound problems account for a large proportion of unplanned returns to the operating room [8,10]. These events cause morbidity, prolong hospitalization, interrupt baclofen delivery, and may lead to abandonment of therapy. Efforts to reduce complications have therefore focused on surgical technique, such as subfascial pump placement, meticulous dural closure, and perioperative antibiotic protocols, as wel as on patient selection and nutritional optimization [9,11]. One potential and underappreciated contributor to CSF-related complications is unrecognized elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) due to arrested or compensated hydrocephalus. Many children with CP have a history of conditions that predispose to disordered CSF dynamics, including prematurity with intraventricular hemorrhage, perinatal infection, and congenital brain malformations [12]. A subset of these patients receive CSF shunts in infancy, but others may have ventriculomegaly that stabilized without treatment and has been labeled "arrested" hydrocephalus. The concept of arrested hydrocephalus is controversial, since ventricular size correlattes poorly with ICP, and some patients with apparently stable ventricles may in fact have a marginally compensated state in which CSF absorption remains impaired [13,14]. The pervasive nature of motor dysfunction in children, primarily stemming from cerebral palsy (CP), is a formidable challenge, with spasticity and dystonia being prevalent and often incapacitating consequences [1]. The heightened muscular tension inherent to these conditions can have a profound impact on functional capacity, induce pain, and precipitate a cascade of secondary complications, including contractures, hip displacement, and challenges in maintaining proper positioning, hygiene, and caregiving. Although a range of therapeutic interventions, such as oral medications, botulinum toxin injections, and physical therapy, can offer some degree of alleviation, their efficacy is not universal, and their application can be constrained by adverse effects, notably sedation [2,3]. In cases where these treatments prove insufficient, the continuous intrathecal administration of baclofen has emerged as a well-established and viable alternative [2,3]. Baclofen, functioning as a gamma-aminobutyric acid type B receptor agonist, exerts its effects at the spinal cord level, and its direct intrathecal delivery enables the attainment of high concentrations within the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) while minimizing the dosage and thereby reducing the risk of central adverse effects [4]. A plethora of randomized and observational studies have unequivocally demonstrated the efficacy of intrathecal baclofen (ITB) in mitigating spasticity and, in selected patients, enhancing comfort, facilitating care, and even improving functional outcomes [5,6]. Nonetheless, despite these benefits, the implantation of ITB pumps in pediatric patients is associated with a considerable risk of complications, which can have far-reaching consequences. The incidence of surgical complications is alarmingly high, affecting up to 40% of patients, and encompasses a range of issues, including CSF leakage, pseudomeningocele formation, wound dehiscence, infection, catheter malfunction, and the need for pump explantation or revision [7–9]. Children with CP are particularly susceptible to these complications due to factors such as compromised nutritional status, limited subcutaneous tissue, and the potential presence of scoliosis or prior spinal instrumentation, all of which can complicate catheter placement. Furthermore, infection rates in pediatric populations are higher than those observed in adults, with some studies suggesting that infections and CSF-related wound problems are responsible for a significant proportion of unplanned returns to the operating room [8,10]. These complications can result in substantial morbidity, prolonged hospitalization, interruption of baclofen delivery, and may even necessitate the discontinuation of therapy. In an effort to mitigate these complications, researchers and clinicians have focused on refining surgical techniques, such as the subfascial placement of pumps, meticulous closure of the dura, and the implementation of perioperative antibiotic protocols, as well as on careful patient selection and optimization of nutritional status [9,11]. However, a potential and often overlooked contributor to CSF-related complications is the presence of unrecognized elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) due to arrested or compensated hydrocephalus. Many children with CP have a history of conditions that predispose them to disordered CSF dynamics, including prematurity complicated by intraventricular hemorrhage, perinatal infection, and congenital brain malformations [12]. While some of these patients may undergo CSF shunting in infancy, others may experience ventriculomegaly that stabilizes without intervention, a condition often referred to as "arrested" hydrocephalus. Nevertheless, the concept of arrested hydrocephalus is subject to controversy, as ventricular size correlates poorly with ICP, and some patients with apparently stable ventricles may, in fact, have a marginally compensated state in which CSF absorption remains impaired [13,14]. The creation of a durable intrathecal puncture, the placement of a catheter, and the subsequent closure of a wound over a pump pocket in the presence of elevated CSF pressure could plausibly promote persistent leakage along the catheter tract, pseudomeningocele formation, wound breakdown, and secondary infection. Recognizing elevated ICP clinically in this population is challenging, as the typical signs of hydrocephalus, including headache, vomiting, irritability, lethargy, and declining school or motor performance, are nonspecific and difficult to elicit in children who are nonverbal, have impaired cognition, or exhibit chronic baseline neurological deficits and frequent gastrointestinal symptoms. Papilledema may be absent or difficult to assess, and neuroimaging may reveal ventriculomegaly, but this is common in CP due to periventricular injury and white matter loss, and it does not reliably distinguish ex vacuo enlargement from pressure-related dilation [13]. Consequently, patients with clinically silent hydrocephalus may proceed to ITB implantation without any direct measurement of ICP. Case reports and small series have described patients with repeated CSF leaks after ITB placement who were later found to have hydrocephalus, with resolution of the problem after CSF diversion [15,16], supporting the plausibility of this mechanism. However, systematic data are lacking, and the importance of recognizing elevated ICP in this population cannot be overstated. Lumbar puncture performed with manometry offers a direct, minimally invasive means of measuring CSF pressure. When done under general anesthesia, however, interpretation requires attention to confounders such as anesthetic agents, ventilation, positioning, and carbon dioxide levels, so standardization is crucial. A threshold opening pressure above approximately 20 to 25 cmH2O is generally regarded as elevated in children [17]. Incorporating such a measurement into the preoperative pathway could identify patients at risk before an implant is placed, and permit consideration of CSF diversion or alternative strategies for spasticity management. At our institution, concern about persistent CSF leaks and wound complications after ITB implantation prompted the development of a standardized protocol that included mandatory cranial imaging and lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement before pump implantation. Patients with elevated pressure were not implanted at that time; instead, they underwent further evaluation and management of their hydrocephalus, highlighting the critical need for a comprehensive preoperative assessment to mitigate the risks associated with ITB therapy in children with CP. This approach underscores the importance of a multidisciplinary strategy that integrates neurosurgical, orthopedic, and rehabilitative care to optimize outcomes for these complex patients. By acknowledging the potential role of elevated ICP in the pathogenesis of CSF-related complications and incorporating measures to detect and manage this condition into the preoperative protocol, we can potentially reduce the incidence of these complications and improve the safety and efficacy of ITB therapy for children with CP. Ultimately, this refined approach to patient selection and management can lead to better functional outcomes, reduced morbidity, and an enhanced quality of life for these patients, who often face significant challenges in their daily lives due to the debilitating effects of spasticity and dystonia. As our understanding of the complex interplay between CP, hydrocephalus, and CSF dynamics continues to evolve, it is essential that we remain vigilant in our pursuit of innovative solutions and therapeutic strategies that can address the unique needs of this vulnerable population, providing them with the best possible chance for a fulfilling and productive life. The rapid development of information and communication technologies has changed the conditins in which modern education operates. Universities and schools are expected to prepare graduates who can work with large volumes of information, collaborate in digital environments and keep learning througghout life. In this context, cloud technologies are among the most promising directions for modernizing the educational process. They give users access to software, storage and computing resources through the Internet, without installing programs on a local computer or maintaining expensive hardware. For education, this means that teaching materials, tools for creating and processing data, and platforms for communication and assessment can be reached from any device, at any time and from any place. Interest in cloud technologies in education is supported by national and international strategies for digitalizing society. Documents on the development of the information society, the modernization of higher educaiton and the cration of a common European educational space all stress the need for open, flexible and accessible learning environments. Cloud services meet many of these requirements. They are usually inexpensive or free, they are updated automatically, they allow joint work on one document or project, and they scale easily as the number of users grows. They also support the shift from a reproductive model of teaching to one that stresses independent inquiry, project work and the development of students' digital competence. Geography is a particularly suitable subject for these technologies. It sudies natural and social phenomena at different spatial scales, and it relise on maps, statistical data, satellite images, graphs, diagrams and other visual material. Students must learn to read and build spatial models, analyze the dynamics of demographic and economic processes, compare territories and see how global and local phenomena are connected. Traditional teaching tools such as printed atlases, wall maps and textbooks are often not enough to show the changing character of these processes or to let students work actively with data. Interactive maps, online visualization of statistics, augmented reality, electronic quizzes and graphic editors can fill this gap. They make abstract material concrete, increase motivation and allow students to move from passive reception of information to its active investigation. Researchers have studied the use of cloud technologies in education from several angles. Work on cloud-oriented learning environments has covered their architecture, the modells of their deployment and the ways they change the roles of teacher and student. Other studies concern general-purpose office and communication suites, learning management systems and services for collaborative work. Geography education has its own literature on geographic information systems, virtual globes and web mapping. However, specialized online services that adress concrete tasks of geographical education remain much less systematized. Teachers often learn about such services by chance, lack information on their capabilities and limitations, and have few methodological recommendations for including them in the curriculum. As a result, many useful tools are used rarely or without a clear didactic purpose. The problem is made sharper by the diversity of available products. Services differ in functionality, language support, cost, technical requirements, the quality of their content and the degree of cotrol the teacher has over the learning process. The advent of information and communication technologies has wrought a profound transformation in the educational landscape, compelling academic institutions to equip students with the skills to navigate complex digital ecosystems, engage in collaborative learning, and cultivating a commitment to lifelong learning. In this revamped educational paradigm, cloud technologies have emerged as a pivotal catalyst for innovation, empowering users to access a vast array of software applications, data storage facilities, and computational resources via the internet, unhindered by the need for localized hardware installation or maintenance [1]. This paradigm shift enables seamless access to educational resources, including instructional materials, data analysis tools, and communication platforms, from any device, at any time, and from any location. The integration of cloud technologies in education is further underscored by national and international initiatives aimed at fostering a digitalized society, as exemplified by policy documents emphasizing the imperative of creating open, flexible, and accessible learning environments [2]. Cloud services, distinguished by their affordability, automatic software updates, and scalability, align with these objectives, facilitating collaborative learning, and promoting a pedagogical transition from a reproductive model of instruction to one that emphasizes autonomous inquiry, project-based learning, and the cultivation of digital literacy among students [3].

The discipline of geography, with its inherent reliance on spatial analysis, cartographic representation, statistical data, and visualizations, is particularly well-suited to leverage the potential of cloud technologies [4]. Traditional pedagogical tools, such as printed atlases and textbooks, often struggle to convey the dynamic nature of geographical phenomena or to engage students in interactive learning experiences. In contrast, cloud-based technologies, including interactive maps, online data visualizations, augmented reality applications, electronic quizzes, and graphic editing software, can render abstract concepts more tangible, enhance student motivation, and facilitate a transition from passive knowledge reception to active investigation [5]. Researchers have explored the application of cloud technologies in education from diverse perspectives, including the architecture of cloud-oriented learning environments, deployment models, and the evolving roles of educators and learners [6]. Furthermore, studies have examined the utility of general-purpose office suites, communication platforms, learning management systems, and collaborative work tools [7]. Within the domain of geography education, a significant body of literature is dedicated to geographic information systems, virtual globes, and web mapping technologies [8]. However, specialized online services tailored to specific tasks in geographical education remain under-systematized, with educators often discovering these resources fortuitously, lacking comprehensive information on their capabilities and limitations, and having limited methodological guidance on integrating them into curricular designs [9].

This lack of systematization is exacerbated by the heterogeneity of available products, which vary in terms of functionality, language support, cost, technical requirements, content quality, and the degree of educator control over the learning process [10]. Certain services, such as Gapminder and the statistical resources of the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA), provide datasets and visualizations for analyzing global development trends [11]. Others, like Settera Online and Click-that-hood, are designed for learning and testing knowledge of political and physical maps or urban territories [12]. Tools like HP Reveal incorporate augmented reality into learning materials, while MOZAIK education offers interactive three-dimensional content [13]. Graphic editors, such as Canva and Paint Instant, enable students and educators to create infographics, posters, and illustrations [14]. Selecting among these services necessitates a nuanced understanding of their advantages and disadvantages from economic, technical, technological, and didactic perspectives.

The novelty of this study resides in its systematic review of a group of specialized, mostly freely available services within a single framework of analysis oriented towards the needs of geographical education [16]. The practical significance of this research lies in its potential to inform the planning of lectures, practical classes, and independent work, as well as the development of electronic courses. In the long term, the services considered may become integral components of virtual information and educational environments that are interconnected within a common framework, ultimately enhancing the quality and accessibility of geographical education. Mammalian oocyte developmental competence is acquired progressively during folliculogenesis and the final stages of growth, and it depends on coordinated nuclear and cytoplasmic maturation [1,2]. Cytoplasmic mautration includes the accumualtion and storage of maternal RNAs, proteins and organelles. These are needed to sustain meiotic progression, fertilization, and the first embryonic divisions, which occur before embryonic genome activation (EGA) takes over [3]. Because transcription in the fully grown oocyte is largely silent, early development relies almost entirely on maternal factors. Defects in their storage, stability or timely utilization can therefore have consequneces long after the oocyte itself has completed meiosis. **Chromatin configuration and developmental competence** In the mouse, fully grown antral oocytes can be separated into two classes according to the organization of their chromatin. Oocytes with a ring of condensed chromatin around the nucleolus are termed SN (Surrounded Nucleolus). Those lacking such a ring are termed NSN (Not Surrounded Nucleolus) [4,5]. SN oocytes are transcriptionally quiescent and can complete meiotiic maturation, be fertilized, and develop to term. NSN oocytes are still transcriptionally active. They can resume meiosis and be fertilized, but the resulting embryyos arrest at the 2-cell stage [5,6]. Becaause this arrest coincides with minor EGA, it has been attributed to defects in maternal programs required for genome activation, chromatin remodelling and epigenetic reprogramming [7,8]. Nuclear transfer experiments, in which the NSN germinal vesicle was placed in SN cytoplasm and vice versa, indicated that the cytoplasm is a major deteminant of the block, which points to a cytoplasmic deficiency in NSN oocytes [9]. However, the cytoplasmic factors responsible have not been identified conclusively. **Cytoplasmic lattices** Cytoplasmic lattices (CPLs) are fibrillar, filamentous structures first described by electron miroscopy in oocytes and preimplantation embryos of several mammalian species, including mouse, hamster, rhesus monkey and human [10,11]. Their abundance in oocytes and early embryos, and their disappearance as development proceeds, long suggested a storage function. Evidence for this was provided by the identification of components of the subcortical maternal complex (SCMC), notably PADI6, as essential constituents of CPLs. Female mice lacking Padi6 are infertile because their embryos arrest at the 2-cell stage, and CPLs are absent from their oocytes [12,13]. Mutations in human SCMC genes and in PADI6 are associated with emryonic arrest, recurrent molar pregnancy and imprinting disorders [14,15]. More recent work has shown that CPLs store ribosomes, whihc are made available to the oocyte and early embryyo in a regulated fashion, and are tuhs a platform for translational competence [16]. They also contain proteins involved in other processes, inluding regulators of microtubule dynamics and spindle assembly, and metabolic and epigenetic factors [16,17]. Taken together, these observations indicate that CPLs are multifunctional assemblies that support oocyte maturation and the oocyte-to-embryo transition. CPLs are also dynamic. In the mouse, they undergo marked reoorganization at key stages of oocyte maturation, and the transition from the germinal vesicle to the metaphase II stage is accompanied by changes in their distribution and abundance [18]. Ultrastructural analysis of SN and NSN oocytes showed that CPLs are abundant in the cytoplasm of SN oocytes but scarce in NSN oocytes [19]. This difference was interpreted as a possible explanation for the NSN 2-cell arrest, by analogy with the Padi6-null phenotype, in which an absence of CPLs coincides with arrest at the same stage. The resulting hypothesis is that insufficient CPLs in NSN oocytes limit the supply of ribosomes and other maternal factors, and thereby compromise development beyond the 2-cell stage. **Rationale and aims** This hypothesis rests on observations made in oocytes, whereas the arrest becomes manifest in the embryo. CPLs are not static, and their abundance in the oocyte does not necessarily predict teir presence in the embryo. NSN oocytes may assemble or remodel CPLs after meiotic resumption, activation or fertilization. The acquisition of developmental competence by mammalian oocytes is a progressive process that occurs during folliculogenesis and the final stages of growth, necessitating the synchronized maturation of both the nucleus and cytoplasm [1,2]. This intricate process involves the accumulation, storage, and eventual utilization of essential maternal molecules, including RNAs, proteins, and organelles, which play a critical role in supporting meiotic progression, fertilization, and the initial embryonic cell divisions that precede the activation of the embryonic genome [3]. The fact that transcriptional activity is largely silenced in fully grown oocytes underscores the importance of these maternal factors, as early development is almost entirely dependent on their presence. Consequently, any disruptions in the storage, stability, or timely utilization of these factors can have far-reaching consequences that may only become apparent long after the oocyte has completed meiosis.

Recent studies have highlighted the significance of chromatin configuration and its relationship to developmental competence in oocytes. For instance, in mice, fully grown antral oocytes can be categorized into two distinct classes based on the organization of their chromatin: those with a ring of condensed chromatin surrounding the nucleolus, referred to as SN (Surrounded Nucleolus), and those lacking this feature, termed NSN (Not Surrounded Nucleolus) [4,5]. Notably, SN oocytes are characterized by transcriptional quiescence and are capable of completing meiotic maturation, fertilization, and development to term. In contrast, NSN oocytes, which remain transcriptionally active, can resume meiosis and undergo fertilization, but the resulting embryos arrest at the 2-cell stage [5,6]. This arrest has been attributed to defects in the maternal programs required for genome activation, chromatin remodeling, and epigenetic reprogramming [7,8].

Nuclear transfer experiments, in which the NSN germinal vesicle was placed in SN cytoplasm and vice versa, have provided valuable insights into the underlying causes of this arrest. These experiments suggest that the cytoplasm plays a critical role in determining the block, implying a cytoplasmic deficiency in NSN oocytes [9]. However, the specific cytoplasmic factors responsible for this deficiency have yet to be conclusively identified. Another critical aspect of oocyte biology is the presence of cytoplasmic lattices (CPLs), which are complex, fibrillar structures first described by electron microscopy in oocytes and preimplantation embryos of several mammalian species, including mice, hamsters, rhesus monkeys, and humans [10,11]. The abundance of CPLs in oocytes and early embryos, coupled with their disappearance as development proceeds, has long suggested a storage function.

Recent evidence has confirmed this hypothesis, with the identification of components of the subcortical maternal complex (SCMC), such as PADI6, as essential constituents of CPLs. Female mice lacking Padi6 are infertile due to embryonic arrest at the 2-cell stage, and CPLs are notably absent from their oocytes [12,13]. Moreover, mutations in human SCMC genes and in PADI6 have been associated with embryonic arrest, recurrent molar pregnancy, and imprinting disorders [14,15]. Further research has revealed that CPLs play a multifaceted role in supporting oocyte maturation and the oocyte-to-embryo transition. They have been shown to store ribosomes, which are made available to the oocyte and early embryo in a regulated fashion, thus serving as a platform for translational competence [16]. Additionally, CPLs contain proteins involved in various processes, including regulators of microtubule dynamics and spindle assembly, as well as metabolic and epigenetic factors [16,17]. These findings collectively indicate that CPLs are dynamic, multifunctional assemblies that are crucial for oocyte development and the transition to embryonic development.

The dynamic nature of CPLs is further underscored by their reorganization at key stages of oocyte maturation. In mice, for example, CPLs undergo marked reorganization as the oocyte transitions from the germinal vesicle to the metaphase II stage, accompanied by changes in their distribution and abundance [18]. Ultrastructural analysis of SN and NSN oocytes has revealed a notable difference in CPL abundance, with SN oocytes exhibiting an abundance of CPLs in their cytoplasm, whereas NSN oocytes have scarce CPLs [19]. This difference has been interpreted as a possible explanation for the NSN 2-cell arrest, drawing parallels with the Padi6-null phenotype, in which an absence of CPLs coincides with arrest at the same stage. The resulting hypothesis is that insufficient CPLs in NSN oocytes may limit the supply of ribosomes and other maternal factors, thereby compromising development beyond the 2-cell stage.

Our investigation is motivated by the observation that while the hypothesis of CPL deficiency in NSN oocytes is based on findings in oocytes, the actual arrest becomes manifest in the embryo. Given that CPLs are dynamic and not static, their abundance in the oocyte does not necessarily predict their presence in the embryo. It is possible that NSN oocytes may assemble or remodel CPLs after meiotic resumption, activation, or fertilization. Furthermore, the sperm contributes factors that could influence cytoplasmic organization, introducing a potential confounding variable. To date, no ultrastructural data have been reported on CPLs in 2-cell embryos derived from SN and NSN oocytes, leaving the question of whether the differences in CPL abundance observed in oocytes are maintained in the embryo. A comprehensive understanding of CPL dynamics and their role in supporting embryonic development is essential for elucidating the underlying mechanisms of oocyte developmental competence and the causes of early embryonic arrest.

The presence of CPLs in oocytes and early embryos has significant implications for our understanding of the oocyte-to-embryo transition. The fact that CPLs are dynamic and multifunctional assemblies that play a critical role in supporting oocyte maturation and early embryonic development highlights the complexity of this process. The identification of components of the SCMC, such as PADI6, as essential constituents of CPLs has provided valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying CPL function. However, further research is needed to fully elucidate the role of CPLs in supporting embryonic development and to determine the consequences of CPL deficiency in NSN oocytes.

Babesia spp. are tick-borne apicomplexan protozoa that infect the erythrocytes of a wide range of vertebrate hosts. They are considered the second most common blood-borne parasites of mammals after trypanosomes [1, 2]. Babeisosis is of major veterinary importance because infection can cause fever, hemolytic anemia, hemoglobinuria, and death, and chronically infected animals suffer reduced productivity. Economic losses in cattle alone are estimated in the billions of US dollars annually, and the burden falls especially on tropical and subtropical regions where tick vectors are abundant [3, 4]. Some species also infect humans, notably B. microti, B. divergens, B. duncani, and B. venatorum, so the genus has public health relevance as well [5]. **Diversity and host associations of Babesia** The genus comprises more than 100 described species, and new lineages continue to be identified. Traditionally, species were distinguished by morphology, host range, and vector specificity. These criteria are now known to be unreliable: the small and large forms of piroplasms overlap in size, many species are morphologically indistinguishable, and host specificity is not absolute [6]. Molecular phylogenetics based on the 18S rRNA gene has resolved Babesia into several clades, including Babesia sensu stricto, the Babesia microti group, and the Theileria/Cytauxzoon groups, and has demonstrated that some taxa historically assigned to Babesia are phylogenetically distinct [7, 8]. In livestock, the principal agents are B. bovis, B. bigemina, and B. divergens in cattle, B. ovis and B. motasi in small ruminants, and B. caballi (together with the related Theileria equi) in equids. In dogs, B. canis, B. vogeli, B. rossi, and B. gibsoni are the most important [9]. Increasing evidence indicates that animals may harbor species typically associated with other hosts, as well as previously uncharacterized species, but such findings are seldom documented because most diagnostic assays are designed to detect specific pathogens in specific hosts [10]. **Limitations of current diagnostics** Microscopic examination of Giemsa-stained blood smears remains widely used, but sensitivity is poor in carrier animals with low parasitemia, and species identification is difficult. Serological assays, such as indirect fluorescent antibody tests and ELISA, detect exposure rather than active infection and are limited by cross-reactivity among species and by variable antibody persistence [11]. PCR-based methods offer markedly higher sensitivity and specificity. Many conventional and real-time PCR assays have been described, but the majority are species-specific [12]. Surveying for several pathogens therefore requires multiple reactions, which increases cost, sample consumption, and the chance that uexpected species will be missed. Pan-genus or broad-range assasy amplifying conserved regions of the 18S rRNA gene, followed by sequencing or melting-curve analysis, can overcome this limitation. Convventional broad-range PCRs are used frequently, but they require post-amplification handling and are less suited to high-throughput work. Real-time formats using fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) hybridization probes combine the sensitivity of quantitative PCR with the specificity afforded by probe melting temperature, which can discriminate sequence variants within an amplicon [13]. A well-designed FRET-qPCR targeting conserved regions of Babesia could therefore detect diverse species in a single closed-tube reaction while providing preliminary species-level information, and it could flag unusual samples for sequencing. Livestock production is important to local economies and food security, yet animals are often kept under extensive systems with limited tick control, and movement of animals among islands is common. Earlier investigations of babesiosis in the region were few, were generally restricted to a single island or a small number of animals, and relied mostly on serology or microscopy [15, 16]. These studies indicated that B. bovis, B. bigemina, and B. caballi are widespread, but the true prevalence and diversity of Babesia in Caribbean livestock remain poorly defined. The apicomplexan protozoa of the genus Babesia are hematotropic parasites that infect a vast array of vertebrate hosts, encompassing both mammals and birds. As the second most prevalent blood-borne parasites affecting mammals, surpassed only by trypanosomes [1, 2], Babesia species are of significant concern in veterinary medicine due to their capacity to induce a spectrum of clinical manifestations. These manifestations include pyrexia, hemolytic anemia, hemoglobinuria, and mortality, ultimately resulting in substantial economic losses, estimated to exceed billions of US dollars annually, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions where tick vectors are ubiquitous [3, 4]. Furthermore, certain Babesia species, such as B. microti, B. divergens, B. duncani, and B. venatorum, are also capable of infecting humans, underscoring the public health implications of this genus [5]. The complexity and host associations of Babesia species are not yet fully elucidated, with over 100 described species and the ongoing discovery of novel lineages [6]. Historically, species identification was based on morphological characteristics, host range, and vector specificity. However, these criteria have proven to be unreliable due to the overlap in size between small and large forms of piroplasms, the morphological indistinguishability of many species, and the lack of absolute host specificity [6]. The application of molecular phylogenetics, utilizing the 18S rRNA gene, has enabled the resolution of Babesia into distinct clades, including Babesia sensu stricto, the Babesia microti group, and the Theileria/Cytauxzoon groups, while also demonstrating that certain taxa previously assigned to Babesia are phylogenetically distinct [7, 8]. In livestock, the primary causative agents of babesiosis are B. bovis, B. bigemina, and B. divergens in cattle, B. ovis and B. motasi in small ruminants, and B. caballi (in conjunction with the related Theileria equi) in equids [9]. In canine hosts, B. canis, B. vogeli, B. rossi, and B. gibsoni are the most significant species. Nevertheless, accumulating evidence suggests that animals may harbor species typically associated with other hosts, as well as previously uncharacterized species [10], highlighting the need for more sensitive and specific diagnostic tools to detect and identify Babesia species across a broad range of hosts. Current diagnostic methodologies for babesiosis are beset by several limitations. The microscopic examination of Giemsa-stained blood smears, although widely utilized, is hindered by poor sensitivity in carrier animals with low parasitemia, and species identification is often challenging [11]. Serological assays, including indirect fluorescent antibody tests and ELISA, detect exposure rather than active infection and are compromised by cross-reactivity among species and variable antibody persistence [11]. PCR-based methods offer enhanced sensitivity and specificity, but many conventional and real-time PCR assays are species-specific, necessitating multiple reactions to survey for several pathogens [12]. This increases cost, sample consumption, and the likelihood that unexpected species will be overlooked. To overcome these limitations, pan-genus or broad-range assays that amplify conserved regions of the 18S rRNA gene, followed by sequencing or melting-curve analysis, can be employed [13]. These assays can detect diverse species in a single reaction while providing preliminary species-level information. However, a key challenge is avoiding the amplification of closely related apicomplexans that commonly co-occur in the same hosts, such as Theileria, Hepatozoon, and Toxoplasma. The Caribbean region presents a unique environment for the study of babesiosis, with climatic conditions favorable to tick vectors, including Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus, R. annulatus, Dermacentor nitens, and Amblyomma variegatum [14]. Livestock production is a vital component of local economies and food security, yet animals are often maintained under extensive systems with limited tick control, and the movement of animals among islands is common. Earlier investigations of babesiosis in the region were limited, and the true prevalence and diversity of Babesia in Caribbean livestock remain poorly defined [15, 16]. Little is known regarding infection in small ruminants and donkeys, or the extent to which species typical of other hosts, including canine Babesia, infect livestock in an environment where domestic animals, ticks, and wildlife are in close proximity. The objectives of this study were therefore twofold. First, we sought to develop and evaluate a pan-Babesia FRET-qPCR assay, designed from alignments of 18S rRNA gene sequences of multiple Babesia species, that detects a broad range of Babesia species in a single reaction while excluding closely related protozoa. Second, we applied the assay to DNA extracted from whole blood of cattle, sheep, goats, donkeys, and horses sampled on five Caribbean islands, with the aim of determining the occurrence of Babesia infections, identifying the species present, and detecting unexpected or novel species. The resulting data are intended to improve our understanding of the epidemiology of babesiosis in the region and to provide valuable insights for the development of effective control strategies. To achieve these objectives, we first designed a pan-Babesia FRET-qPCR assay that targets conserved regions of the 18S rRNA gene. The assay was evaluated using a panel of DNA samples from various Babesia species, as well as closely related apicomplexans, to ensure its specificity and sensitivity. We then applied the assay to a large collection of samples, with the goal of shedding light on the prevalence and diversity of Babesia species in the Caribbean region. To develop this assay, we initially retrieved complete and partial 18S rRNA gene sequences of 22 Babesia species from GenBank and aligned them using the Clustal Multiple Alignment program implemented in BioEdit [1,2]. We also incorporated sequences of related apicomplexans, such as Theileria, Hepatozoon, Toxoplasma, and Cytauxzoon, as well as those of host species, including Bos taurus, Ovis aries, Capra hircus, Equus spp., and Canis lupus familiaris. This alignment enabled us to identify regions that were conserved across Babesia species but divergent in non-target organisms, a crucial step in the design of specific primers and probes. We selected candidate forward and reverse primers and two adjacent hybridization probes for FRET from conserved regions flanking a variable region. The properties of these primers, including melting temperature, secondary structure, and primer-dimer formation, were assessed using OligoAnalyzer, and their specificity was verified in silico using BLASTn against the GenBank nucleotide database [3]. One probe was labeled at the 3' end with fluorescein, while the other was labeled at the 5' end with LC Red 640 (or an equivalent acceptor dye).

To evaluate the analytical performance of the assay, we utilized reference DNA from six Babesia species (B. gibsoni, B. canis, B. vogeli, B. microti, B. bovis, and B. divergens) and non-target DNA from Hepatozoon americanum, Theileria equi, Toxoplasma gondii, and uninfected host blood. The DNA was quantified spectrophotometrically, and the analytical sensitivity of the assay was estimated from ten-fold serial dilutions of reference DNA tested in triplicate. The limit of detection was defined as the lowest dilution at which all replicates were positive. We also assessed the repeatability of the assay by testing the same dilutions in replicate within and between runs.

The study area comprised five Caribbean islands, where whole-blood samples were collected from 752 cattle, sheep, goats, donkeys, and horses. The animals were sampled opportunistically on farms and smallholdings, with the permission of owners and in accordance with local veterinary authority regulations. Blood was drawn by jugular or coccygeal venipuncture into EDTA tubes, and the species, sex, approximate age, and location of each animal were recorded. The samples were kept cooled during transport and stored at −20 °C until DNA extraction. Genomic DNA was extracted from 200 µl of whole blood using a commercial spin-column kit (e.g., QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit, Qiagen) according to the manufacturer's instructions and eluted in 100 µl of elution buffer. Extraction controls (nuclease-free water) were included in each batch to monitor contamination, and the DNA was stored at −20 °C.

The pan-Babesia FRET-qPCR assay was performed in a 20 µl reaction volume containing 2 µl of template DNA, 1× commercial hybridization-probe master mix, 0.5 µM of each primer, 0.2 µM of each FRET probe, and MgCl2 adjusted to a final concentration of 3–4 mM. The reactions were run on a LightCycler real-time instrument (Roche) with an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 10 min, followed by 45 cycles of 95 °C for 10 s, annealing at the optimized temperature for 10 s, and 72 °C for 15 s, with fluorescence acquired in the acceptor channel at the end of each annealing step. A melting-curve analysis followed (95 °C for 30 s, 40 °C for 30 s, then a gradual increase to 85 °C at 0.1 °C/s with continuous acquisition). Because the probes hybridize to species-specific sequences with distinct melting temperatures, this analysis enabled the preliminary identification of Babesia species. The findings of this study highlight the importance of molecular diagnostics in the detection and identification of Babesia species, and demonstrate the potential of the pan-Babesia FRET-qPCR assay for the surveillance of these parasites in the Caribbean region.
