The immune system is essential for maintaining homeostasis, defending against pathogens, and surveilling for malignant transformation. Its dysregulation, however, underlies a wide spectrum of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and multiple sclerosis [1,2]. Over the past two decades, therapeutic strateiges that modulate immune pathways have transformed the management of these conditions. Biologic ageents targeting tumor necrosis factor, interleukin (IL)-6, IL-17, IL-23, and co-stimulatory molecules have been joined by small molecule inhibitors directed at intracellular signaling nodes such as Janus kinases (JAKs), tyrrosine kinase 2 (TYK2), spleen tyrosine kinase, Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK), phosphodiesterase 4, and calcineurin [3–5]. The expanding repertoire of immune targets has created considerable opportunity, but also a growing need to understand how each mechanism shapes immune function in humans. Because the immune system is highly interconnected and redundant, pharmacological modulation of a given target rarely affects only the pathogenic process of interest. Immunosuppression is a recognized liability of immunomodulatory therapies and may manifest as increased risk of serious bacterial, viral, fungal, and oppportunistic infections, reactivation of latent infections such as tuberculosis and herpes zoster, impaired vaccine responses, and possibly malignancy [6,7]. The safety experience with JAK inhibitors illustrates this challenge: despite clear efficacy, class-associated risks including infections, thromboembolism, and malignancy have prompted regulatory warnings and renewed debate about the relationship between selectivity, pathway biology, and clinical risk [8,9]. Distinct mechanisms carry distinct risk profiles; for example, inhibition of IL-17 is associated with mucoctuaneous candidiasis, whereas inhibition of TNF is linked to granulomatous infections [10]. These observations indicate that each therapeutic mechanism leaves a characteristic "immune fingerprint," defined by the specific innate and adaptive functions it attenuates, spares, or enhances. Defining this fingerprint early in drug discovery would help prioritize candidates witth the most favorable benefit–risk balance. In practice, however, preclinical characterization of novel compoundds is typically compound- and mechanism-centric. Potency and selectivity are assessed agaiinst the intended target and related off-targets, and efficacy is evaluated in a limited number of cellualr assays or animal models chosen for their relevance to the target pathway. Such approaches provide little information on the breadth of immune functions affected, and they rarely allow direct comparison with clinically used agents whose safety profiles are known. Animal models, while valuable, are limited by species differences in immune cell composition, receptor expression, cytokine networks, and drug sensitivity, and they often fail to predict human immune responses or infection risk [11,12]. Genetically engineerred and humanized models partially address these limitations but are costly and low-throughput, and thus poorly suited to routine profiling of multiple compounds. Human primary cell systems offer an attractive alternative. Assays using peripheral blood mononuclear cells, whole blood, or isolated immune subsets can capture human-specific biology and have been widely used to examine cytokine release, T cell proliferation, and cell activation [13,14]. Nonetheless, most reported assays interrogate a single cell type or stimulus in isolation, and they differ in donor sources, readouts, and stimulation conditions, which complicates cross-study comparison. Cells in bood also lack the tissue context in which many immune repsonses occur. Human tissue-derived systems, including tonsil, lymph node, spleen, and skin explants or cell preparations, preserve a more physiological representation of cellular diversity, antigen-presenting cell–lymphocyte interactions, and, in the caes of secondary lymphoid organs, the capacity to support B cell activation and antibody production [15,16]. Tonsillar tissue, for instance, has been used to model recall antigen responses, T follicular helper cell function, and vaccine responses ex vivo [17]. Leveraging such material within a standardized panel of functional assays could yield a more comprehensive and translationally relevant view of drug effects. An ideal platform for immune profiling should saisfy several criteria. It should cover both innate functions (such as myeloid cell cytokine production, type I interferon responses, and natural killer cell activity) and adaptive functions (such as T cell activation, proliferation, and differentiation, and B cell activation and antibody secretion). It should use human material and physiologically relevant stimuli, employ quantitative readouts that permit concentration–response analysis, and include benchmark therapeutics for context. Finally, it should enable integration of results across assays into a summary of immune impact that can be interpreted alongside pharmacokinetic and efficacy data, for example by relating inhibition to free drug exposure at clinically relevant doses [18]. Here, we describe the development of a human tissue-based functional assay platform designed to meet these criteria. The platform comprises a series of complementary assays measuring a range of innate and adaptive immune responses, and it was used to evaluate small molecule inhibitors of immune targets together with clinically used immunomodulatoy agents. We show that the platform can generate qualitative and quantitative immune fingerprints that distinguish mechanisms of action, reveal differences in the breadth and magnitude of immunosuppression among compounds, and provide a framework for comparing novel inhibitors with established therapies. We propose that this approach can support more informed decision-making in the discovery of immune-targeted therapeutics and improve the prediction of their benefit–risk profiles in the treatment of immune-mediated disorders. The human immune system is a multifaceted entity that plays a crucial role in maintaining physiological balance, protecting against infectious agents, and monitoring for cancerous changes. Nevertheless, its malfunction is a underlying factor in a plethora of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disorders, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and multiple sclerosis [1,2]. Over the past twenty years, therapeutic approaches that manipulate immune pathways have transformed the treatment of these conditions. The emergence of biologic agents that target molecules such as tumor necrosis factor, interleukin (IL)-6, IL-17, IL-23, and co-stimulatory molecules has been supplemented by the development of small molecule inhibitors that target intracellular signaling nodes, including Janus kinases (JAKs), tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2), spleen tyrosine kinase, Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK), phosphodiesterase 4, and calcineurin [3–5]. This expanding array of immune targets has created substantial opportunities for the development of novel therapies, but it also underscores the need to comprehend how each mechanism influences immune function in humans. The immune system is a complex and interconnected network, and pharmacological modulation of a specific target rarely affects only the pathological process of interest. Consequently, immunosuppression is a recognized risk associated with immunomodulatory therapies, and may manifest as an increased susceptibility to serious bacterial, viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections, reactivation of latent infections such as tuberculosis and herpes zoster, impaired vaccine responses, and potentially malignancy [6,7]. The safety experience with JAK inhibitors exemplifies this challenge, as despite their evident efficacy, class-associated risks including infections, thromboembolism, and malignancy have prompted regulatory warnings and renewed debate about the relationship between selectivity, pathway biology, and clinical risk [8,9]. Furthermore, distinct mechanisms are associated with distinct risk profiles; for instance, inhibition of IL-17 is linked to mucocutaneous candidiasis, whereas inhibition of TNF is associated with granulomatous infections [10]. These observations suggest that each therapeutic mechanism leaves a unique "immune signature," characterized by the specific innate and adaptive functions it modulates, spares, or enhances. Defining this signature early in the drug discovery process would be highly beneficial, as it would facilitate the prioritization of candidates with the most favorable benefit–risk balance. However, preclinical characterization of novel compounds is typically focused on the compound's potency and selectivity against the intended target and related off-targets, and its efficacy in a limited number of cellular assays or animal models chosen for their relevance to the target pathway. Such approaches provide limited information on the breadth of immune functions affected, and they rarely allow direct comparison with clinically used agents whose safety profiles are known. Animal models, while valuable, are limited by species differences in immune cell composition, receptor expression, cytokine networks, and drug sensitivity, and they often fail to predict human immune responses or infection risk [11,12]. Genetically engineered and humanized models partially address these limitations but are costly and low-throughput, and thus poorly suited to routine profiling of multiple compounds. Human primary cell systems offer an attractive alternative for immune profiling. Assays using peripheral blood mononuclear cells, whole blood, or isolated immune subsets can capture human-specific biology and have been widely used to examine cytokine release, T cell proliferation, and cell activation [13,14]. However, most reported assays interrogate a single cell type or stimulus in isolation, and they differ in donor sources, readouts, and stimulation conditions, which complicates cross-study comparison. Moreover, cells in blood lack the tissue context in which many immune responses occur. Human tissue-derived systems, including tonsil, lymph node, spleen, and skin explants or cell preparations, preserve a more physiological representation of cellular diversity, antigen-presenting cell–lymphocyte interactions, and, in the case of secondary lymphoid organs, the capacity to support B cell activation and antibody production [15,16]. Tonsillar tissue, for example, has been used to model recall antigen responses, T follicular helper cell function, and vaccine responses ex vivo [17]. Leveraging such material within a standardized panel of functional assays could yield a more comprehensive and translationally relevant view of drug effects. An ideal platform for immune profiling should meet several key criteria. It should cover both innate functions, such as myeloid cell cytokine production, type I interferon responses, and natural killer cell activity, and adaptive functions, such as T cell activation, proliferation, and differentiation, and B cell activation and antibody secretion. It should utilize human material and physiologically relevant stimuli, employ quantitative readouts that permit concentration–response analysis, and include benchmark therapeutics for context. Finally, it should enable integration of results across assays into a summary of immune impact that can be interpreted alongside pharmacokinetic and efficacy data, for example by relating inhibition to free drug exposure at clinically relevant doses [18]. In this context, we have developed a human tissue-based functional assay platform designed to meet these criteria. The platform comprises a series of complementary assays measuring a range of innate and adaptive immune responses, and it was used to evaluate small molecule inhibitors of immune targets together with clinically used immunomodulatory agents. Our results demonstrate that the platform can generate qualitative and quantitative data on the immune effects of these compounds, providing a valuable tool for the prioritization of candidates with the most favorable benefit–risk balance. The platform's ability to capture the complex interactions between immune cells and tissues, and to quantify the effects of compounds on these interactions, makes it an attractive alternative to traditional preclinical models. Furthermore, the platform's use of human tissue and physiologically relevant stimuli ensures that the results are highly relevant to the human immune system, reducing the risk of species-specific effects and increasing the likelihood of successful translation to the clinic. Overall, our human tissue-based functional assay platform provides a powerful tool for the immune profiling of small molecule inhibitors and biologic agents, enabling the identification of compounds with the most favorable benefit–risk balance and facilitating the development of novel therapies for the treatment of immune-related disorders. The platform's flexibility and adaptability also make it an attractive tool for the study of immune function and dysfunction in a variety of contexts, from basic research to clinical applications. As the field of immunology continues to evolve, the development of innovative platforms like ours will be essential for advancing our understanding of the immune system and improving the treatment of immune-related diseases. By providing a more comprehensive and translationally relevant view of drug effects, our platform has the potential to accelerate the development of novel therapies and improve patient outcomes. To establish this approach, we acquired peripheral blood from healthy adult donors under informed consent from an accredited blood bank, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and institutional ethical approval [1]. The peripheral blood was then processed to isolate peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) by density gradient centrifugation using Ficoll-Paque PLUS, a method that allows for the separation of different cell types based on their density. The whole blood was utilized within 4 hours of collection for assays that required a native cellular and plasma environment, ensuring that the cells were maintained in a condition that closely mimics their natural state. We also enriched primary human CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, B cells, NK cells, and monocytes by negative magnetic selection, achieving a purity of greater than 90% as determined by flow cytometry, a technique that enables the analysis of cells based on their physical and chemical properties. 

In addition to peripheral blood, we also obtained human tonsil tissue from routine tonsillectomy, which was mechanically dissociated and filtered to yield single-cell suspensions for lymphoid tissue-based assays of T follicular helper-B cell interactions [3]. This tissue was used to study the interactions between different immune cells, providing valuable insights into the complex mechanisms of the immune system. We cultured the cells in RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum, 2 mM L-glutamine, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 µg/mL streptomycin at 37 °C and 5% CO2, a conditions that support the growth and survival of immune cells. Monocyte-derived macrophages and dendritic cells were generated by culturing CD14+ monocytes for 6 days with M-CSF (50 ng/mL) or GM-CSF (50 ng/mL) plus IL-4 (20 ng/mL), respectively [2], a process that allows for the differentiation of monocytes into specific cell types. 

To assess the effects of various compounds on immune function, we utilized a range of reference immunomodulators, including the JAK inhibitors tofacitinib and upadacitinib, the BTK inhibitor ibrutinib, the calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporine A, the S1P receptor modulator fingolimod, the glucocorticoid dexamethasone, and the antimetabolite mycophenolic acid. These compounds were selected to represent clinically used immunological therapies, providing a basis for comparison with novel inhibitors. We also tested small-molecule inhibitors of immune targets, which were dissolved in DMSO and tested in 8-point, half-log concentration series with a final DMSO concentration of 0.1%, a method that allows for the evaluation of the effects of these compounds on immune cells. The concentrations of the compounds were interpreted relative to unbound human plasma exposure at clinically efficacious doses where available, ensuring that the results are relevant to clinical settings. 

We performed a range of innate immune function assays to assess the effects of the compounds on immune function. These assays included cytokine release from whole blood, plasmacytoid dendritic cell responses, NLRP3 inflammasome activity, macrophage phagocytosis, NK cell cytotoxicity, and neutrophil oxidative burst. For example, we measured cytokine release from whole blood after pre-incubation with compound for 1 hour, followed by stimulation with LPS (TLR4; 100 ng/mL), R848 (TLR7/8; 1 µg/mL), or poly(I:C) (TLR3; 10 µg/mL) for 18-24 hours, a method that allows for the evaluation of the effects of compounds on the production of cytokines, which are critical molecules in the immune response. We also measured plasmacytoid dendritic cell responses in PBMCs stimulated with CpG-A (TLR9; 1 µM) for IFN-α production [4], a process that is essential for the activation of immune cells. 

In addition to innate immune function assays, we also performed adaptive immune function assays to assess the effects of the compounds on T cell activation, proliferation, and differentiation. These assays included T cell activation and proliferation, antigen-specific recall responses, mixed lymphocyte reaction, T helper differentiation, and B cell proliferation and differentiation. For example, we measured T cell activation and proliferation in PBMCs or purified T cells labeled with CellTrace Violet and stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28 beads (1:1 bead:cell ratio) for 4-5 days, a method that allows for the evaluation of the effects of compounds on the activation and proliferation of T cells, which are critical cells in the adaptive immune response. We also evaluated antigen-specific recall responses by stimulating PBMCs with CMV pp65 peptide pool, tetanus toxoid, or Staphylococcal enterotoxin B for 5-7 days [6], a process that allows for the assessment of the effects of compounds on the memory immune response. 

To ensure the quality and validity of our results, we included vehicle controls on every plate and assessed cytotoxicity in parallel for each assay using a fixable viability dye or ATP-based luminescence (CellTiter-Glo). We considered compound effects to be functional only when viability exceeded 80% of vehicle control, ensuring that the results are not confounded by cytotoxic effects. We also accounted for compound binding to serum proteins by comparing potencies in 10% FBS and 50% human serum in selected assays, a process that allows for the evaluation of the effects of compounds in a more physiologically relevant context. 

We utilized flow cytometry and cytokine measurement to assess the effects of the compounds on immune function. Cells were stained with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies after Fc receptor blocking and acquired on a BD LSRFortessa or Cytek Aurora cytometer. Data were analyzed in FlowJo v10 using a consistent gating strategy defined with fluorescence-minus-one controls. Cytokines were quantified using Meso Scale Discovery multiplex electrochemiluminescence, a technique that allows for the simultaneous measurement of multiple cytokines. The results of these assays provided valuable insights into the effects of compounds on immune function, enabling the identification of potential therapeutic targets and the development of novel immunomodulatory therapies.

To this end, our team established a robust platform for profiling the impact of various compounds on immune responses. This platform utilizes primary human cells and tissue sources, enabling a more accurate representation of the complex interactions between the immune system and therapeutic agents. We employed a range of cell-based assays, including those using peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), whole blood, and isolated T cell, B cell, monocyte, and natural killer (NK) cell populations from healthy donors. These assays were designed to assess multiple facets of immune function, including cytokine release, cell proliferation, activation marker expression, and cytotoxicity.

To validate our platform, we evaluated a set of reference compounds with well-characterized mechanisms of action and clinical applications. This panel included the Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors tofacitinib and baricitinib, the calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporine A, the sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulator fingolimod, the antimetabolite mycophenolic acid, the glucocorticoid dexamethasone, the Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor ibrutinib, and the p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) inhibitor SB203580. Each compound was tested across a range of concentrations, using at least three independent donors, to assess their potency and efficacy in modulating immune responses.

The quality and reproducibility of our assays were rigorously evaluated to ensure they met predefined criteria. We calculated the Z′ factor, a measure of assay quality, and found that the majority of our assays (14 out of 16) exhibited excellent quality, with Z′ factors greater than 0.5. The remaining two assays, evaluating NK cell cytotoxicity and B cell differentiation, showed acceptable quality, with Z′ factors ranging from 0.35 to 0.48, considering the primary-cell format used. Inter-donor variability in maximal response was moderate, with a coefficient of variation between 18 and 35%. However, the potency estimates for the reference compounds were consistent across donors, with IC50 values generally varying within threefold.

For example, cyclosporine A inhibited anti-CD3/CD28-induced interleukin-2 (IL-2) production with a mean IC50 of 12 nM, consistent with published values [1,2]. Tofacitinib inhibited IL-6-induced signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) phosphorylation in CD4⁺ T cells with an IC50 in the low-nanomolar range, aligning with previous reports [1,2]. Dexamethasone suppressed lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) production in monocytes at sub-nanomolar concentrations, consistent with literature [3]. Our platform also enabled the evaluation of the impact of these compounds on innate immune function. In LPS-stimulated whole blood and monocytes, SB203580 and dexamethasone potently reduced TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 production, whereas cyclosporine A and mycophenolic acid had little effect. Tofacitinib and baricitinib showed modest inhibition of IL-6 but not TNF-α, consistent with their limited impact on Toll-like receptor (TLR)-driven signaling [4].

In interferon-alpha (IFN-α)-stimulated PBMCs, JAK inhibitors strongly suppressed the induction of interferon-stimulated genes, such as *MX1* and *IFIT1*, as well as CXCL10 release, while ibrutinib and fingolimod were inactive. In NK cell assays, JAK inhibitors reduced IL-15-driven STAT5 phosphorylation and IFN-γ production, and tofacitinib decreased K562 target-cell killing by approximately 40% at maximal concentration. Mycophenolic acid and dexamethasone had smaller effects on short-term cytotoxicity. Collectively, these data demonstrate that our platform can distinguish compounds that act on cytokine-receptor signaling from those that act mainly on TLR or antigen-receptor pathways.

We also investigated the impact of these compounds on adaptive immune function, focusing on T cells and B cells. In anti-CD3/CD28-stimulated T cells, cyclosporine A, tofacitinib, mycophenolic acid, and dexamethasone all inhibited proliferation, albeit with different kinetics and cytokine selectivity. Cyclosporine A almost completely suppressed IL-2 and IFN-γ production, whereas mycophenolic acid inhibited proliferation without markedly changing early cytokine production, reflecting its antiproliferative mechanism through depletion of guanosine nucleotides [5]. Tofacitinib inhibited cytokine-driven proliferation and reduced IFN-γ and IL-17 production in Th1 and Th17 polarization assays, with a greater effect on Th1 differentiation. Fingolimod had no direct effect in these in vitro assays, as expected for a compound acting primarily through lymphocyte trafficking.

In mixed lymphocyte reactions, cyclosporine A, mycophenolic acid, and tofacitinib suppressed alloreactive proliferation with IC50 values of 20 nM, 0.3 µM, and 0.2 µM, respectively. Recall responses to tetanus toxoid and cytomegalovirus (CMV) peptide pools were reduced by cyclosporine A and dexamethasone by more than 80%, suggesting a potential impact on memory responses relevant to infection risk. In B cells, mycophenolic acid and dexamethasone inhibited proliferation and antibody production, while tofacitinib and ibrutinib had limited effects. These findings highlight the utility of our platform in assessing the effects of immune-modulating compounds on various aspects of immune function, ultimately supporting more informed decision-making in the discovery and development of immune-targeted therapeutics.

Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD), accounting for roughly 40–50% of all mortality in this population [1,2]. A substantial proportion of these deaths are sudden cardiac death (SCD), and the annual incidence of SCD among patients receiving hemodialysis is estimated to be several times higher than in the general populaton [3,4]. Although coronary artery disease is highly prevalent in ESRD, traditional ischemic mechanisms explain oly part of this excess risk. Structural and electrophysiological remodeling, including left ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial fibrosis, autonomic dysfunction, vascular calcification, and abrupt shifts in electrolytes and voume durnig dialysis, creates a substrate that favors both tachyarrhythmias and bradyarrhythmias [5–7]. **Arrhythmias in patients with chroic kidney disease** Atrial fibrillation is common in patients on dialysis, with reported prevalence of 7–27%, and is associated with increased risk of stroke and mortality [8,9]. Ventricular arrhythmias, including non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT), are also frequent and have been linked to left ventricular dysfunction and adverse outcomes [10,11]. In addition, recent evidence suggests that bradyarrhythmias, rather than ventricular tachyarrhythmias, may be the predominant mechanism of sudden death in dialysis patients. Continuuos monitoring in a small cohort of hemodialysis patients showed that bradycardia and asystole preceded most arrhythmic deaths [12]. These findings challenge the assumption that SCD in ESRD is mainly due to ventricular fibrillation, and they raise questions about the appropriateness of preventive strategies such as primary prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, whose benefit in this population remains uncertain [13,14]. **Renal transplant candidates** Renal transplantation improves survival and quality of life compared with chronic dialysis, but candidates are subjected to extensive cardiovascular evaluation because perioperative and long-term cardiac events remain a major concern [15]. Current guidelines recommend risk stratification using clinical assessment, resting electrocardiography (ECG), echocardiography, and, in selected patients, functional or anatomical testing for ischemia [16]. These tools primarily address structural and ischemic disease and offer lmited information on arrhythmic vulnerability. Moreover, patients on the waiting list may be on dialysis for prolonged periods, during whicch clinically relevant rhythm disturbances can occur without being captured. The arrhythmic profile of renal transplant candidates (RTCs) is therefore poorly characterized, and it remains unclear which clinical, electrocardiographic, or echocardiographic variables identify those at greater risk. **Limitations of conventional rhythm monitoring** Standard 12-lead ECG and 24- to 48-hour Holter monitoring provide only brief snapshots and are poorly suited to deteccting paroxysmal or infrequent events. Studies using such methods are likely to underestimate the true incidence of arrhythmias, particularly in patients whose events are related to the dialysis cycle or ocur sporadically [17]. External event recorders improve diagnostic yield but remain limited by patient compliance and short monitoring duration. The implantable loop recorder (ILR) permits continuous subcutneous ECG monitoring for up to several years, with automatic detection and storage of arrhythmic episoddes and patient-activated recording of symptoms. ILRs have established value in the evaluation of unexplained syncope [18] and in the detection of occult atrial fibrillation after cryptogenic stroke [19]. In the nephrology setting, their use has been confined to small series of dialysis patients, which have shown a high burden of clinically significant arrhythmias, often asymptomatic [12,20]. To our knowledge, ILR-based monitoring has not been systematically applied to ambulatory RTCs, and data on the incidence of arrhythmic events in this group, their clinical significance, and their determinants are lacking. **Potential predictors of arrhhythmic events** Several noninvasive markers may help identify patients prone to specific arrhythmias. Prolongation of the corrected QT interval (QTc) reflects abnormal ventricular repolarization and has been associated with malignant arrhythmias and mortality in ESRD [21]. PR interval prolongation indicates delayed atrioventricular conduuction and has been related to atrial fibrillation, conduction disease, and adverse outcomes in the general population [22]. Left ventricular dilatation and systolic dysfunction are established substrates for ventricular arrhythmias [23]. Whether these readily available parameters predict particular arrhythmia types detected by continuous monitoring in RTCs has not been examined. Identifying such predictors could refine rissk stratification, guide selection of patients for closer surveillance, and inform decisions about pacing or defibrillator therapy before and after transplantation. **Study objective** Given the high cardiovascular risk of RTCs, the limitations of intermittent rhythm assessment, and the uncertainty about the mechanisms of sudden death in this population, we conducted a prospective observational study using ILRs in consecutive ambulatory RTCs. Insulin resistance is a state in which insulin-responsive tissues, principally skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissue, respond inadequately to nomal circulating concentrations of the hormone. It is the central pathological feature of obesity and metabolic syndrome and the core defect that precedes and drives type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) [1,2]. The global prevalence of obesity and T2DM continues to rise, and insulin resistance contributes to related conditions such as non-alcoholic fatty livver disease, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease [3]. Although lifestyle intervention, metformin, and thiazolidinediones can improve insulin sensitivity, their efficacy is often limited and side effects are common, so there is a need to identify new molecular targets [4]. The mechanisms of insulin resistance are complex and include lipotoxicity, chronic low-grade inflammation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, all of which impair insulin signaling through the insulin receptor, insulin reecptor substrates (IRS), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), and AKT [5,6]. Cellular energy status is tightly coupled to these processes, and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) has emerged as a key metabolic sensor. Tissue NAD+ levels deecline with aging and in overnutrition, and this decline is associated with metabolic deterioration [7]. The Sirtuins are NAD+-dependent enzymes that link cellular redox and energy state to protein modification and gene expression. The founding member, yeast Sir2, was identified as a regulator of replicative lifespan and transcriptional silencing, and its homologs have been associated with longevity in several model organisms [8,9]. Mammals have seven Sirtuins (SIRT1–SIRT7), which share a conserved catalytic core but differ in their N- and C-terminal domains, substrate specificities, eznymatic activities, and subcellular localization [10]. SIRT1, SIRT6, and SIRT7 are predominantly nuclear, SIRT2 is mainly cytoplasmic, and SIRT3, SIRT4, and SIRT5 reside in mitochondria, although several Sirtuins shuttle between compartments in response to physiological cues [11]. Initially characterized as deacetylases, Sirtuins are now known to catalyze a broader range of reactions, including removal of long-chain fatty acyl groups, desuccinylation, demalonylation, deglutarylation, and mono-ADP-ribosylation [12,13]. Through these activities tey regulate cell survival, senescence, DNA repair, genome stability, and metabolism [14]. SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been studied most etensively in metabolic regulation. SIRT1 deacetylates and moulates PGC-1α, FOXO proteins, LXR, SREBP, PPARγ, and the insulin signaling mediator PTP1B, thereby influencing gluconeogenesis, fatty acd oxidation, cholesterol homeostasis, adipogenesis, and insulin sensitivity [15–17]. Transgenic overexpression of SIRT1 and pharmacological activators such as resveratrol and SRT1720 improve glucose tolerance and prtect against diet-induced obesity and hepatic steatosis in rodents, whereas tissue-specific deletion of SIRT1 exacerbates metabolic dysfunction [18,19]. This review was conducted as a structured narrative synthesis of the literature on mammalian Sirtuins (SIRT1–7) and insulin resistance. The aim was to integrate evidence from molecular, animal, and human studies and to identify gaps in current knowledge. The methodology followed the general principles of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) to promote transparency and reproducibility [1]. **Literature Seearch Strategy** Electronic searches were performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase. The search covered records from database inception to the most recent update before manuscript preparation. Controlled vocabulary (MeSH and Emttree terms) was combined with free-text keywords using Boolean operators. Terms for the exposure included "sirtuin*", "SIRT1", "SIRT2", "SIRT3", "SIRT4", "SIRT5", "SIRT6", "SIRT7", and "NAD-dependent deacetylase". These were combined with tersm for the outcome and related processes: "insulin resistance", "insulin sensitivity", "insulin signaling", "type 2 diabetes", "obesity", "metabolic syndrome", "glucose metabolism", "lipid metabolism", "inflammation", and "mitochondrial dysfunction". Reference lists of retrieved articles and earlier reviews were hand-searched to identify additional relevant publications [2]. Because SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been extensively reviewed, searches for these proteins were restricted to key mechanistic and translational studies, whereas searches for SIRT2–5 and SIRT7 were conducted exhaustively. **Eligibility Criteria** Studies were eligible if they met at least one of the following criteria: (i) in vitro experiments in insulin-responsive cellls (hepatocytes, adipocytes, skeletal myocytes, cardiomyocytes, pancreatic β-cells, macrophages, or endothelial cells) examining Sirtuin function in relation to insulin signaling, nutrient metabolism, inflammation, or mitochondrial function; (ii) animal studies using genetic (knockout, knockdown, transgenic, tissue-specific) or pharmacological (activators, inhibitors, NAD+ precursors) manipulation of Sirtuins and reporting metabolic phenotypes such as glucose tolerance, insulin tolerance, or hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp outcomes; and (iii) human studies, including observational cohorts, genteic association studies, and clinical trials, that evaluated Sirtuin expression, activity, polymorphisms, or modulators in relation to insulin resistance, T2DM, obesity, or fatty liver disease. Articles were excluded if they were published in languages other than English, were conference abstracts without ful text, were editorials without primary data, or addressed Sirtuins solely in contexts unrelated to metabolism (e.g., purely oncological or neurodegenerative studies without metabolic endpoints). Wherre multiple publications reported overlapping data, the most complete report was retained. **Study Selection and Data Extraction** Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. For each included study, the following information was extracted into a standardized template: Sirtuin isoform studied; species and model system; tissue or cell type; type of intervention; metaoblic diet or insulin-resistance induction protocol (e.g., high-fat diet, genetic obesity models, palmitate or TNF-α exposure); pincipal substrates or pathways identified; and main outcomes. Mechanistic data were grouped into five thematic domains: inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, insulin signaling pathway, glucose metabolism, and lipid metabolism. **Evidence Synthesis** Given the heterogeneity of experimental models, interventions, and outcome measures, quantitative pooling was not feasible, and a narrative synthesis was adopted. Findings were organized by isoform and subcellular localization: nuclear (SIRT1, SIRT6, SIRT7), cytosolic (SIRT2), and mitochondrial (SIRT3, SIRT4, SIRT5). Within each isoform, evidence was compared across tissues relevant to systemiic insulin sensitivity, namely liver, skeletl muscle, adipose tissue, pancreas, and the vasculature. Particular attention was given to enzymatic activities (deacetylation, desuccinylation, demalonylation, deglutarylation, defatty-acylation, and mono-ADP-ribosylation) and to well-characterized targets, including components of the insuln receptor–IRS–PI3K–AKT cascade, PTP1B, FOXO proteins, PGC-1α, NF-κB, AMPK, LKB1, and mitochondrial enzymes [3,4]. Consistency of findings was evaluated by noting concordant and discordant results across models. Discrepancies, such as tissue-specific or context-dependent effects, differences between whole-body and conditional knockouts, and divergent results from pharmacological modulators, were explicitly described. Evidence from human studies was distinguished from preclinicl evdience to avoid overstating translational relevance. **Quality Considerations** Formal risk-of-bias scoring was not applied, as is typical for narrative reviews. Instead, the revieewrs qualitatively considered study design, sample size, use of appropriate controls, specificity of genetic or pharmacological tools, replication across independent laboratories, and the physiological relevance of the models. Greater weight was given to findings supported by multiple independent models or by converging genetic and pharmacological evidence. Concerns regarding the selectivity of small-molecule Sirtuin modulators and the nonspecificity of soe activators were considered when interpreting results [5]. **Identification of Knowledge Gaps** Research gaps were identified by comparing the breadth of evidence across Sirtuin isoforms, tissues, and thematic domains, and by noting areas with limited human data, conflicting findings, or absent mechanistic validation. The phenomenon of insulin resistance is a multifaceted pathological condition, distinguished by the diminished responsiveness of tissues that are typically sensitive to insulin, such as skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissue, to insulin concentrations that are within the normal range. This condition is a pivotal aspect of both obesity and metabolic syndrome, and it precipitates the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), a disease that is characterized by the body's inability to effectively utilize insulin [1,2]. The worldwide prevalence of obesity and T2DM is escalating, and insulin resistance is a contributing factor to a plethora of associated conditions, including non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, all of which pose significant threats to human health [3]. Although interventions such as lifestyle modifications, metformin, and thiazolidinediones can enhance insulin sensitivity, their efficacy is often limited, and they are frequently accompanied by adverse effects, underscoring the need to identify novel molecular targets for the treatment of insulin resistance [4]. The underlying mechanisms of insulin resistance are complex and involve a multitude of processes, including lipotoxicity, chronic low-grade inflammation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, all of which can impair insulin signaling through the insulin receptor, insulin receptor substrates (IRS), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), and AKT [5,6]. A critical aspect of these processes is the cellular energy status, which is closely coupled to insulin action and plays a pivotal role in maintaining glucose homeostasis. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) has emerged as a key metabolic sensor, and its levels decline with aging and overnutrition, leading to a deterioration in metabolic function [7]. The Sirtuins are a family of NAD+-dependent enzymes that play a crucial role in linking cellular redox and energy states to protein modification and gene expression, and they have been implicated in the regulation of a wide range of cellular processes, including metabolism, stress resistance, and longevity [8,9]. Mammals possess seven Sirtuins (SIRT1–SIRT7), which share a conserved catalytic core but differ in their N- and C-terminal domains, substrate specificities, enzymatic activities, and subcellular localization, allowing them to regulate a diverse array of cellular functions [10]. SIRT1, SIRT6, and SIRT7 are primarily localized to the nucleus, while SIRT2 is mainly cytoplasmic, and SIRT3, SIRT4, and SIRT5 reside in mitochondria, although several Sirtuins can shuttle between compartments in response to physiological cues, allowing them to regulate a wide range of cellular processes [11]. Initially characterized as deacetylases, Sirtuins have been found to catalyze a broader range of reactions, including the removal of long-chain fatty acyl groups, desuccinylation, demalonylation, deglutarylation, and mono-ADP-ribosylation, highlighting their complexity and versatility [12,13]. Through these activities, Sirtuins regulate a range of cellular processes, including cell survival, senescence, DNA repair, genome stability, and metabolism, and they have been implicated in the development of a wide range of diseases, including cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and metabolic disorders [14]. SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been extensively studied in the context of metabolic regulation, and they have been shown to deacetylate and modulate a range of transcription factors and coactivators, including PGC-1α, FOXO proteins, LXR, SREBP, PPARγ, and the insulin signaling mediator PTP1B, thereby influencing gluconeogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, cholesterol homeostasis, adipogenesis, and insulin sensitivity [15–17]. Transgenic overexpression of SIRT1 and pharmacological activators, such as resveratrol and SRT1720, have been shown to improve glucose tolerance and protect against diet-induced obesity and hepatic steatosis in rodents, highlighting the potential of SIRT1 as a therapeutic target for the treatment of metabolic disorders [18,19]. In contrast, tissue-specific deletion of SIRT1 exacerbates metabolic dysfunction, underscoring the importance of SIRT1 in maintaining glucose homeostasis [18,19]. SIRT6 regulates glycolysis through the deacetylation of histone H3 at lysine 9 and 56, represses HIF1α-dependent glucose uptake, and controls hepatic lipid metabolism and inflammatory signaling, highlighting its role in maintaining metabolic homeostasis [20,21]. The loss of SIRT6 causes severe hypoglycemia in mice, while its overexpression protects against high-fat diet-induced metabolic damage, highlighting the importance of SIRT6 in maintaining glucose homeostasis [20,21]. These findings have implicated SIRT1 and SIRT6 in the development of obesity, T2DM, fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular disease, and they have been the subject of several comprehensive reviews [22]. In contrast to SIRT1 and SIRT6, the contributions of the remaining Sirtuins to insulin resistance are less well defined, although recent work has indicated that they also influence processes tightly linked to insulin action. Mitochondrial SIRT3 deacetylates components of the respiratory chain and antioxidant enzymes, such as SOD2, and its reduced expression is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance in muscle and liver, highlighting the importance of SIRT3 in maintaining mitochondrial function [23,24]. SIRT4 modulates glutamine metabolism, insulin secretion, and fatty acid oxidation, while SIRT5 regulates ammonia detoxification, glycolysis, and fatty acid oxidation through desuccinylation and demalonylation, highlighting their roles in maintaining metabolic homeostasis [25,26]. Cytosolic SIRT2 affects adipocyte differentiation, gluconeogenesis, and insulin signaling via the deacetylation of FOXO1, PEPCK, and AKT, highlighting its role in regulating glucose and lipid metabolism [27]. SIRT7 has been linked to hepatic lipid homeostasis, ER stress, and mitochondrial function, highlighting its role in maintaining metabolic homeostasis [28]. Furthermore, several of these enzymes modulate inflammatory pathways, including NF-κB signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, which are major drivers of obesity-associated insulin resistance, highlighting the importance of Sirtuins in regulating inflammation [29]. Human genetic and clinical studies have reported altered Sirtuin expression or polymorphisms in individuals with obesity, T2DM, and metabolic syndrome, supporting their translational relevance and highlighting the potential of Sirtuins as therapeutic targets for the treatment of metabolic disorders [30]. Nevertheless, findings are sometimes inconsistent across tissues, models, and species, and the substrate specificity and physiological regulation of some Sirtuins remain unclear, highlighting the need for further research into the roles of Sirtuins in insulin resistance and metabolic disease. In this review, we aim to summarize recent advances in our understanding of the roles of the Sirtuin family in physiological processes associated with insulin resistance, including inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, insulin signaling, and glucose and lipid metabolism. A thorough and systematic search of the existing literature was conducted to examine the relationship between sirtuins and metabolic processes. Electronic searches were performed across multiple databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase, covering all records from the inception of the databases up to the most recent update prior to manuscript preparation. The search strategy employed a combination of controlled vocabulary, such as MeSH and Emtree terms, and free-text keywords, linked by Boolean operators. Key terms included "sirtuin", "SIRT1", "SIRT2", "SIRT3", "SIRT4", "SIRT5", "SIRT6", "SIRT7", and "NAD-dependent deacetylase", which were combined with terms related to metabolic outcomes and processes, such as "insulin resistance", "insulin sensitivity", "insulin signaling", "type 2 diabetes", "obesity", "metabolic syndrome", "glucose metabolism", "lipid metabolism", "inflammation", and "mitochondrial dysfunction" [2]. To ensure a comprehensive review, the reference lists of retrieved articles and earlier reviews were hand-searched to identify additional relevant publications. Due to the extensive existing literature on SIRT1 and SIRT6, the search strategy for these proteins was restricted to key mechanistic and translational studies. In contrast, searches for SIRT2-5 and SIRT7 were conducted exhaustively to capture the full scope of available evidence. The inclusion criteria for this review were established to ensure that only studies meeting specific standards were considered. Studies were eligible if they met at least one of the following criteria: (i) in vitro experiments in insulin-responsive cells examining Sirtuin function in relation to insulin signaling, nutrient metabolism, inflammation, or mitochondrial function; (ii) animal studies using genetic or pharmacological manipulation of Sirtuins and reporting metabolic phenotypes; and (iii) human studies evaluating Sirtuin expression, activity, polymorphisms, or modulators in relation to insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, obesity, or fatty liver disease. Articles were excluded if they were published in languages other than English, were conference abstracts without full text, were editorials without primary data, or addressed Sirtuins solely in contexts unrelated to metabolism. The study selection and data extraction process involved two reviewers independently screening titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. For each included study, a standardized template was used to extract the following information: Sirtuin isoform studied, species and model system, tissue or cell type, type of intervention, metabolic diet or insulin-resistance induction protocol, principal substrates or pathways identified, and main outcomes. Mechanistic data were grouped into five thematic domains: inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, insulin signaling pathway, glucose metabolism, and lipid metabolism. Given the heterogeneity of experimental models, interventions, and outcome measures, a narrative synthesis was adopted instead of quantitative pooling. Findings were organized by Sirtuin isoform and subcellular localization: nuclear (SIRT1, SIRT6, SIRT7), cytosolic (SIRT2), and mitochondrial (SIRT3, SIRT4, SIRT5). Within each isoform, evidence was compared across tissues relevant to systemic insulin resistance, including liver, muscle, adipose tissue, and pancreas. The intricate relationships between Sirtuins, a family of proteins with deacetylase activity, and various metabolic pathways have been the subject of extensive investigation. These proteins play a pivotal role in the regulation of distinct cellular processes, including energy metabolism, stress response, and cellular aging. Recent studies have underscored the critical function of Sirtuins in maintaining optimal insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis, which has significant implications for the prevention and management of metabolic disorders, such as type 2 diabetes [5-7]. A key aspect of Sirtuin function is their capacity to modulate signaling pathways associated with inflammation, a major contributor to insulin resistance. Specifically, SIRT1, SIRT2, SIRT3, and SIRT6 have been demonstrated to suppress inflammatory signaling by deacetylating crucial transcription factors and enzymes involved in the inflammatory response [8,9]. For instance, SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been shown to deacetylate the p65 subunit of NF-κB, a transcription factor that plays a central role in the regulation of inflammatory gene expression [8,9]. Furthermore, SIRT2 has been found to deacetylate p65 and limit the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines by macrophages, whereas SIRT3 attenuates inflammation by reducing the production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) and suppressing the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome [10,11].

In addition to their anti-inflammatory effects, Sirtuins also play a critical role in regulating mitochondrial function and metabolism. SIRT3, the primary mitochondrial deacetylase, activates components of the electron transport chain, enzymes involved in fatty acid oxidation, and superoxide dismutase 2, thereby promoting oxidative metabolism and reducing the production of ROS [16,17]. The loss of SIRT3 has been linked to accelerated obesity, hyperlipidemia, and insulin resistance, highlighting the importance of this Sirtuin in maintaining metabolic homeostasis [5]. Other mitochondrial Sirtuins, including SIRT4 and SIRT5, also regulate various aspects of mitochondrial function, such as fatty acid oxidation, glutamate metabolism, and the urea cycle [19,21].

The effects of Sirtuins on insulin signaling are complex and multifaceted. Several Sirtuins, including SIRT1, SIRT2, and SIRT6, have been shown to modulate key nodes in insulin signaling, including the insulin receptor, IRS-1, and Akt [25-27]. For example, SIRT1 deacetylates IRS-2 and represses the transcription of PTP1B, thereby enhancing insulin receptor signaling [25]. Similarly, SIRT2 deacetylates Akt and promotes its activation, whereas SIRT6 represses IGF-insulin signaling by deacetylating H3K9 at the promoters of genes involved in the IGF-Akt pathway [26,27]. These findings highlight the importance of Sirtuins in regulating insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism.

Moreover, Sirtuins regulate glucose metabolism, including hepatic gluconeogenesis, glycolysis, and insulin secretion. SIRT1, SIRT6, and SIRT3 have been shown to modulate the expression of genes involved in gluconeogenesis, while SIRT4 and SIRT5 influence insulin secretion and glucose oxidation [29-32]. For instance, SIRT1 deacetylates PGC-1α and FOXO1 to modulate the expression of gluconeogenic genes, whereas SIRT6 suppresses glycolysis via HIF-1α and represses gluconeogenic genes through the acetylation of PGC-1α [29,30]. These findings underscore the complex and multifaceted role of Sirtuins in regulating glucose metabolism.

Sirtuins also play a critical role in regulating lipid metabolism, including lipogenesis, lipid oxidation, and adipose tissue function. SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been shown to reduce hepatic steatosis by suppressing the activity of SREBP and enhancing PPARα-dependent fatty acid oxidation [9,33]. SIRT2 inhibits adipocyte differentiation through the deacetylation of FOXO1 and promotes lipolysis, whereas the deficiency of SIRT3 leads to decreased fatty acid oxidation and the accumulation of lipids [34,35]. The available evidence suggests that the seven mammalian Sirtuins occupy distinct subcellular compartments, which shapes their metabolic functions. SIRT1 and SIRT2 shuttle between the nucleus and cytoplasm, whereas SIRT6 and SIRT7 are predominantly nuclear, with SIRT7 enriched in the nucleolus. In contrast, SIRT3, SIRT4, and SIRT5 reside mainly in mitochondria [1,2].

Tissue expression analyses have demonstrated that Sirtuins are abundant in insulin-responsive organs, including the liver, skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, and pancreatic β cells, and that their expression levels are altered in obesity and diabetes [3,4]. Reduced expression of SIRT1, SIRT3, and SIRT6 has been consistently reported in tissues from rodents fed a high-fat diet and in individuals with type 2 diabetes, supporting an association between Sirtuin depletion and metabolic dysfunction. This comprehensive review aims to integrate the existing evidence and provide a framework for understanding the complex relationships between Sirtuins and metabolic processes, highlighting areas for future research and potential therapeutic targets.

Particular attention has been given to enzymatic activities and well-characterized targets, such as components of the insulin receptor-IRS-PI3K-AKT cascade, PTP1B, FOXO proteins, PGC-1α, NF-κB, AMPK, LKB1, and mitochondrial enzymes [3,4]. The consistency of findings has been evaluated by noting concordant and discordant results across models, with explicit description of discrepancies such as tissue-specific or context-dependent effects. The quality of the included studies has been qualitatively considered, with greater weight given to findings supported by multiple independent models or by converging genetic and pharmacological evidence. Concerns regarding the selectivity of small-molecule Sirtuin modulators and the nonspecificity of some activators have been taken into account when interpreting results [5]. The identification of knowledge gaps has been achieved by comparing the breadth of evidence across Sirtuin isoforms, tissues, and thematic domains, and by noting areas with limited human data, conflicting findings, or absent mechanistic validation. These gaps have been summarized to propose directions for future research, including the development of isoform-specific modulators, tissue-specific models, and well-designed clinical studies. 

The role of Sirtuins in metabolic regulation is further underscored by their influence on various cellular processes, including autophagy, apoptosis, and cell proliferation. SIRT1, for instance, has been shown to promote autophagy by deacetylating key autophagy-related proteins, such as Atg5 and Atg7 [36,37]. Similarly, SIRT2 has been found to regulate apoptosis by deacetylating p53 and promoting its activation [38,39]. These findings highlight the complex and multifaceted role of Sirtuins in regulating cellular homeostasis and metabolic function.

In conclusion, the existing evidence suggests that Sirtuins play a critical role in regulating metabolic processes, including glucose and lipid metabolism, insulin signaling, and mitochondrial function. The development of isoform-specific modulators and tissue-specific models will be essential for further elucidating the role of Sirtuins in metabolic regulation and for exploring their potential as therapeutic targets for the prevention and treatment of metabolic disorders. Future studies should focus on addressing the knowledge gaps in our understanding of Sirtuin function and regulation, including the development of well-designed clinical studies to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Sirtuin modulators in humans. By integrating the existing evidence and providing a framework for understanding the complex relationships between Sirtuins and metabolic processes, this review aims to contribute to the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the prevention and treatment of metabolic disorders. 

Furthermore, the regulation of Sirtuin activity by various post-translational modifications, such as phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and sumoylation, should be further investigated. These modifications can influence Sirtuin activity, stability, and subcellular localization, thereby modulating their metabolic functions [40,41]. Additionally, the role of Sirtuins in regulating the reciprocal interactions between metabolism and epigenetics should be further explored. Sirtuins have been shown to modulate the activity of various epigenetic regulators, including histone acetyltransferases and DNA methyltransferases, thereby influencing gene expression and metabolic function [42,43]. 

The interplay between Sirtuins and other metabolic regulators, such as AMPK, mTOR, and PPARs, should also be further investigated. These regulators play critical roles in modulating metabolic function and have been shown to interact with Sirtuins in various cellular contexts [44,45]. Elucidating the mechanisms underlying these interactions will be essential for understanding the complex regulatory networks that govern metabolic function and for developing novel therapeutic strategies for the prevention and treatment of metabolic disorders.

Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease characterized by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, with a consequent increase in bone fragility and fracture risk [1]. Vertebral fractures are the most common osteoporotic fractures and are associated with chronic pain, reduced mobility, loss of height, and increased mortality [2,3]. Because a prevalnet vertebral fracture strongly predicts further fractures, early identification of individuals at high risk is a central goal of clinical osteology [4]. Accurate and precise quantification of bone status at the lumbar spine is therefore of considerable clincal and scientific interest. **Current Diagnostics and Their Limitations** The standard for diagnosing osteoporosis is areal bone mineral density (BMD) measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) [5]. Although DXA-derived BMD correlates with fracture risk, a substantial proportion of fragility fractures occur in patients whose T-scores lie above the osteoporotic threshold [6]. Several limitations of the technique contribute to this. DXA projects a three-dimensional structure onto a plane and cannot separate trabecluar from cortical bone. Moreover, in the spine it is confounded by degenerative changes, aotric calcifications, and posterior elements, all of which raise the apparent density [7]. Finally, DXA provides little information on bone geometry, which is an important determinant of mechanical competence. Quantitative computed tomography (QCT) overcomes many of these problems by delivering true vloumetric BMD and permitting selective analysis of the trabecular compartment [8,9]. Trabecular vertebral BMD from QCT has been shown to be more sensitive to age-related and treatment-induced changes than DXA and to disriminate fracture patients well [10]. Spiral CT scanners are widely available, and modern multi-detector systems acquire high-resolution volumetric data of the entire spine in a short time. Nevertheless, conventional spinal QCT is usually restricted to a single elliptical or cylindrical region of interest placd manually in the mid-vertebral plane of two to four slices. Such an approach samples only a small fraction of the vertebral body, is sensitive to operator placement, and ignores the spatial heterogeneity of density and geometry that is relevant for load transfer and failure [11]. **Need for Three-Dimensional Segmentation** Fully exploiting volumetric CT data requires segmentation of the vertebral body in three dimensions. Once the bone is delineated, BMD can be evaluated in arbitrarily defined volumes of interest (VOIs), for example the entire trabecular compartment, subcortical layers, or regions near the endplates, and geometric parameters such as vertebral volume, height, and cross-sectional area can be derived. Finite element studies and in vitro mechanical tests suggest that the combination of density distribution and geometry predicts vretebral strength better than mean BMD alone [12,13]. Reliable three-dimensional measurements could therefore improve fracture risk assessment beyond current clinical practice. Segmenting lumbar vertebrae is, however, a difficult task. The trabecular interior has low and inhomogeneous attenuation, whereas the cortical shell is thin and, given the limited resolution of clinical scanners, is affected by partial volume effects. Adjacent vertebrae are separated only by narrow intervertebral discs, and in osteoporotic or degenerated spines the gaps between the endplates and osteophytes may be nearly indistinguishable from bone. The posterior elements (pedicles, laminae, and processes) are connected to the vertebral body through narrow bridges and must be removed to isolate the body. Furthermore, the vertebral foramen and the basivertebral venous plexus produce local density variations that can mislead intensity-based methods. **Related Work** Numerous approaches to vertebral segmentation have been proposed. Simple thresholding and region growing are fast but leak into neighboing structures and do not separate the body from the posterior elements [14]. Deformable models and active contours incorporate shape constraints and smoothness, but depend on initialization and may fail in pathologic cases [15,16]. Statistical shape and appearance models are robust and have been applied to the whole spine [17,18], yet their accuracy is limited by how well the training population represents the variability in shape, and they may bias the boundary toward the mean shape, which is undesirable when geometry itself is the outcome. Graph-cut and level-set formulations have also been described [19,20]. Many of these works emphasize anatomical identification or visualization and report overlap metrics, rather than the accuracy and precision of densitometric and geometric parameters, which determine clinical usefulness. Furthermore, few methods define VOIs relative to a reproducible, anatomically based local coordinate system, which is essential for longitudinal and multicenter comparison, because patient positioning and spinal curvature othherwise change the sampled region. **Objectives and Contribution** In this paper we present a multi-step segmentation methodology for lumbar vertebral bodies in spiral CT data that is designed explicitly for the measurement of BMD and geometry. The method first isolates the vertebral body from adjacent structures, then separates it from the posterior elements, and finally refines the boundary to capture the cortical shell. From the resulting surface a local anatomical coordinate system is derived, in which standardized VOIs are positioned independently of patient orientation. This yields densitometric and geometric measurees that are comparable across examinations and subjects. We evaluate the technique in terms of the criteria that matter for clinical application. Precision is assessed through intra- and inter-operator variability of the segmentation, the BMD values, and the coordinate system position in patient data. Acccuracy is assessed using phantom data with known density and volume. By providing a validated, largely automated tool for three-dimensional vertebral analysis, we aim to establish the basis for studies that test whether volumetric density distribution and geometry improve the prediction of osteoporotic fractures. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first describe the image data and the segmentation algorithm, then the construction of the coordinate system and VOIs, followed by the validation protocol. Results for phantom and patient data are then presented and discussed with respect to limitations and future clinical application. **Study Data** Spiral CT scans of the lumbar spine were acquired from 20 postmenopausal women (age 55–80 years) as part of an ongoing osteoporosis study. Scans used a slice thickness of 1 mm, a reconstruction increment of 0.5 mm, 120 kVp, and a bone-density calibration phantom placed beneath the patient. Vertebrae L1–L3 were analyzed. For accuracy assessment, an anthropometric European Spine Phantom and six excised human vertebral specimens were scanned with identical protocols. The specimens' volumes were determined independently by water displacement (Archimedes' principle), and the phantom's nominal hydroxyapatite concentrations served as the BMD reference. All patients gave written informed consent, and the study was approved by the local ethics committee. **Segmentation Pipeline** The segmentation consists of four consecutive steps: (1) preprocessing and seed definition, (2) coarse segmentation of the vertebral body by a region-based approach, (3) refinement by a deformable surface model, and (4) separation of the vertebral body from the posterior elements. *Preprocessing and initialization.* Volumes were resampled to isotropic 0.5 mm voxels using trilinear interpolation and smoothed with a edge-preserving anisotropic diffusion filter [1] to reduce noise while retaining cortcal boundaries. The operator plaed one seed point at the center of each vertebral body and one point in the adjacent intervertebral disc above and below, which defined the approximate craniocaudal extent. *Coarse segmentation.* A three-dimensional region-growing algorithm was started from the seed and constrained by an adaptive threshold. The threshold was computed from the local histogram of a spherical neighborhood as the midpoint between the trabecular and soft-tissue intensity modes, which makes the procedure robust against differences in bone density. Leakage into adjacent vertebrae or the ribs was prevented by morphological opening with a 3 mm structuring element and by restricting growth to the slab between the disc points. Holes inside the segmentation were closed by a slice-wise flood-fill followed by a 3D closing operation. *Surface refinement.* The bianry result was converted into a triangulated surface by marching cubes [2] and used as the initial state of a deformable simplex mesh [3]. ACE2 converts Ang II to Ang-(1-7), wihch acts mainly through the Mas receptor to induce vasodilation and exert anti-proliferative and anti-inflammatory effects [8]. Ang-(1-9) was long regarded as an inactive intermediate, serving mainly as a precursor of Ang-(1-7) through ACE-mediated cleavage. However, recent studies have shown that Ang-(1-9) has biological activity of its own. In rodent models of cardiovascular disease, Ang-(1-9) reduced cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis after myocardial infarction and in hypertensive rats, improved endothelial function, and attenuated vascular remodeling, independently of its conversion to Ang-(1-7) [13–15]. Ang-(1-9) has also been shown to reduce oxidative stress, to limit cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, and to prevent neointimal formation and inflammation in innjured vessels [16,17]. Notably, these effects were generally abolished by the Ang II typpe 2 receptor (AT2R) antagonist PD123319 rather than by the Mas receptor antagonist A779, suggesting that Ang-(1-9) acts as a functional ligand of AT2R [13,15]. AT2R signaling is typically associated with vasodilation, anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic actions, and modulation of apoptosis, and it has been propoosed as a promising target in cardiovascular and lung diseases [18,19]. Activation of AT2R by selective agonists such as compoudn 21 has been reported to attenuate pulmonary hypertension and fibbrosis in experimental models [20,21]. Despite this evidence, the effect of Ang-(1-9) on pulmonary hypertension has not been examined. Because the pulmonary circulation expresses high levels of ACE and ACE2 and is exposed to substantial amoutns of circulating angiotensin peptides, Ang-(1-9) may play a relevant role in regulating pulmonary vascular homeostasis. Furthermore, inflammation and apoptosis of endothelial cells are central to the initiation and progression of PAH. Endothelial injury and the release of inflammatory mediators, including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), promote vascular remodeling and perivascular inflammatory cell infiltration [22,23]. Altered expression of apoptosis-related proteins, such as Bax, Bcl-2, and caspases, has been described in the lungs of animals with experimental pulmonary hypertension [24]. Whether Ang-(1-9) can modulate these processes in the pulmonary vasculature is unknown. The monocrotaline (MCT) model is a widely used and well-characterized model of PAH. A single subcutaneous injection of MCT in rats is metabolized in the liver to the reactive pyrrole derivative, which causes pulmonary endothelial injury, followed by inflammation, medial hypertrophy of pulmonary arterioles, interstitial fibrosis, increased pulmonary arterial pressure, and right ventricular hypertrophy [25,26]. We examined the effects of continuous Ang-(1-9) infusion on right ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular hypertrophy, pumonary arteriolar remodeling, endothelial damage, and pulmonary fibrosis in MCT-treated rats.
