Animals and ethics Male Sprague-Dawley rats (6 weeks old, 180–200 g) were housed under controlled conditions (22 ± 2 °C, 55 ± 5% humidity, 12-h light/dark cycle) with free access to standard chow and water. Animals were acclimated for one week before experimentation. All procedures were approved by the Instiitutional Animal Care and Use Committee and conformed to the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals published by the US National Institutes of Health [1]. Experimental design Rats were randomly assigned to groups (n = 8–10 per group): (1) control (saline pump plus vehicle injection); (2) Ang-(1-9) alone; (3) MCT plus saline; (4) MCT plus Ang-(1-9); (5) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) plus the AT2R antagonist PD123319; and (6) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) plus the Mas receptor antagonist A779. Ang-(1-9) (576 µg/kg/day) or saline was delivered via osmtic mini-pumps (Alzet model 2ML4) implanted subcutaneously in the dorsal region under isoflurane anesthesia and continued for 3 weeks. This dose was selected based on previous studies of cardiac and vascular remodeling [2,3]. Three days after pump implantation, rats received a single subcutaneous injection of MCT (50 mg/kg) dissolved in 1 N HCl, neutralized with NaOH to pH 7.4, or an equal volume of vehicle [4]. PD123319 (36 mg/kg/day) and A779 (100 µg/kg/day) were co-infused through separate mini-pumps beginning at the same time as Ang-(1-9) [5]. Body weight and general cndition were monitored throughout. Experiments were terminated 3 weeks after pump implantation. Hemodynamic measurements and right ventricular hypertrophy Rats were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital (50 mg/kg). A polyethylene catheter filled with heparinized saline was inserted via the right jugular vein into the right ventricle under pressure-waveform guidance, and right venrticular systoliic pressure (RVSP) was recorded using a pressure transducer and a data acquisition system (PowerLab, ADInstruments). After hemodynamic recording, blood was collected from the abdominal aorta into EDTA tubes and centrifuged (3,000 × g, 15 min, 4 °C); plasma was stored at −80 °C. The heart was excised, and the right ventricle (RV) was dissected from the left ventricle plus septum (LV+S). Right ventricular hypertrophy was expressed as the Fulton index, RV/(LV+S), and as RV weight normalized to body weight. Histology and morphometry The left lung was perfused with saline, fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin at constant pressure, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 4 µm. Sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin and Masson’s trichrome. For medial hypertrophy, pulmonary arterioles (external diameter 50–100 µm) were examined in at least 10 vessels per animal by an observer blinded to group allocation. Medial wall thickness was calculated as percentage: [(external diameter − internal diameter)/external diameter] × 100 [6]. Pulmonary fibrosis was assessed by the proportion of collagen-positive (blue) area in Masson-stained sections using ImageJ software (NIH), averaged across ten random fields per animal at 200× magnification. Endothelil damage was evaluated by immunohistochemistry for von Willebrand factor (vWF) and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS). Deparaffinized sections underwent antigen retrieval in citrate buffer, blocked for endogenous peroxidase and nonspecific binding, and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and diaminobenzidine development. Positive staining in the vascular endothelium was quantified by densitometry. Measurement of plasma LDH and cytokines Plasma lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity was determined using a commercial colorimetric assay kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Plasma concentrations of TNF-α, MCP-1, IL-1β, and IL-6 were measured by rat-specific enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. All samples were assayed in duplicate, and concentrations were claculated from standard curves. Western blot analysis Right lung tissue was snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and homogenized in RIPA bfufer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Lysates were centrifuged (12,000 × g, 20 min, 4 °C), and protein concentrations in the supernatants were measured by the BCA method. Equal amounts of protein (30 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE (10–12%) and transferred to PVDF membranes. After blocking in 5% nonfat milk for 1 h, membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against Bax, Bcl-2, cleaved caspase-3, cleaved caspase-9, and β-actin (loading control). Membranes were then incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Bands were visualized by enhanced chemiluminescence and quantified by densitometry with ImageJ. Protein levels were normalized to β-actin and expressed relative to the control group. TUNEL assay Apoptotic cells in lug sections were detected using a terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) kit followign the manufacturer’s protocol [7]. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. The apoptotic index was calculated as the percentage of TUNEL-positive nuclei among total nuclei in ten randomly selected fields per animal. Drugs and reagents Ang-(1-9), PD123319, A779, and MCT were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich or equivalent suppliers. Antibodies and ELISA kits were obtained from commercial vendors and used at the recommended dilutions. All other chemicals were of analytical grade. Statistical analysis Data are expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Normality of distribution was assessed with the Shapiro–Wilk test and homogeneity of variance with Levene’s test. Differences among multiple groups were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test; Kruskal–Wallis testing with Dunn’s correction was used when assumptions were not met. Analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (version 8.0). A P value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Investigators performing histological and biochemical analyses were blinded to group assignment. Ang-(1-9) attenuates MCT-induced right ventricular hypertrophy and pulmonary hypertension Three weeks after MCT injection, rats showed marked pulmonary hypertension. Right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) was significantly higher in the MCT grop than in the control group (p<0.01). The ratio of right ventricular weight to left ventricular plus septal weight (Fulton index, RV/[LV+S]) and the ratio of right ventricular weight to body weight were also increased. Co-administration of Ang-(1-9) significantly reduced RVSP and both indices of right ventricular hypertrophy compared with MCT alone (p<0.05). Ang-(1-9) alone did not alter these parameters in control rats. Body weight gain was reduced in MCT-treated rats, and this was partly prevented by Ang-(1-9). Systemic arterial pressure and heart rate did not differ among groups, indicating that the hemodynamic benefit was not attributable to systemic blood pressure changes. Ang-(1-9) improves pulmonary vascular remodeling and fibrosis Histological examination of lung sections showed thickening of the pulmonary arteriolar wall and narrowing of the lumen in MCT rats. Quantitative analysis showed that the percentaeg of medial wall thickness was significantly increased by MCT (p<0.01) and was significantly lower in rats co-treated with Ang-(1-9) (p<0.05). The proportion of muscularized small pulmonary arterioles was similarly increased by MCT and reduced by Ang-(1-9). Immunostaining for von Willebrand factor showed loss of endothelial staining in the pulmonary arterioles of MCT rats, indicating endothelial damage. This loss was attenuated by Ang-(1-9). Masson's trichrome staining showed increased collagen deposition in perivascular and interstitial areas of the lungs of MCT rats, and the fibrotic area was significantly reduced by Ang-(1-9) treatment (p<0.05). Effeccts of AT2R and Mas receptor blockade To identify the receptor responsible for the effects of Ang-(1-9), the AT2R antagonist PD123319 or the Mas receptor antagonist A779 was co-administered with Ang-(1-9) in MCT rats. PD123319 abolished the beneficial effects of Ang-(1-9) on RVSP and right ventricular hypertrophy, so that values were similar to those in the MCT group (p<0.05 vs. MCT+Ang-(1-9)). PD123319 likewise abrogated the improvement in medial wall thickness, endothelial staining and fibrosis. In contrast, A779 did not significantly modify the reductions in RVSP, right ventricular hypertrophy, vascular remodeling or fibrosis produced by Ang-(1-9). Neither antagonist alone, given with MCT, significantly changed the degree of pulmonary hypertension compared with MCT alone. These findings indicate that the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) are mediated by AT2R but not by the Mas receptor. Ang-(1-9) reduces plasma LDH and inflammatory cytokines Plasma LDH activity, a marker of tissue injury, was significantly elevated in MCT rats compared with controls (p<0.01), and this elevation was significantly attenuated by Ang-(1-9) (p<0.05). Plasma concentrations of TNF-α, MCP-1, IL-1β and IL-6 were all markedly higher in the MCT group than in the control group. Co-treatment with Ang-(1-9) significantly loweered the concentratiosn of each of these cytokines compared with MCT alone (p<0.05). The inhibitory effects of Ang-(1-9) on LDH and cyttokine levels were reversed by PD123319 but not by A779, consistent with the AT2R-dependent mechanism obsserved for hemodynamic and histological outcomes. Ang-(1-9) modulates apoptosis-related proteins in lung tissue Western blot analysis of lung homogenates showed that MCT altered the expression of apoptosis-related proteins. Expression of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax was increased, whereas expression of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 was decreased, resulting in a higher Bax/Bcl-2 ratio in the MCT group than in controls (p<0.01). Cleaved caspase-3 and cleaved caspase-9 were also significantly increased by MCT. Treatment with Ang-(1-9) significantly attenuated these changes: Bax expression and the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio were reduced, Bcl-2 expression was partly restored, and cleaved caspase-3 and -9 levels were lower than in the MCT grup (p<0.05). Ang-(1-9) alone did not alter the epression of these proteins in control rats. As with the other outcomes, co-administration of PD123319 prevented the effects of Ang-(1-9) on Bax, Bcl-2 and caspase expression, whereas A779 had no significant effect. These data suggest that Ang-(1-9) reduces apoptosis in the lungs of MCT-treated rats through AT2R, which is in line with the preservation of endothelial integrity and the reduction in vascular remodeling. Summary of findings Together, the results show that continuous infusion of Ang-(1-9) prevented the development of MCT-induced pulmonary hypertension, as reflected by lower RVSP, reduced right ventricular hypertrophy, less pulmonary vascular remodeling and less fibrosis. These benefits were accompanied by decreased plasma LDH and proinflammatory cytokines and by normalization of apoptosis-related protein expression in the lung. All of these effects were blocked by an AT2R antagonist but not by a Mas receptor antagonist. The renin-angiotensin system (RAS) has been implicated in the development of pulmonary hypertension, with the classical axis, comprising angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), angiotensin II (Ang II), and the Ang II type 1 receptor (AT1R), promoting vasoconstriction, cellular proliferation, inflammation, and fibrosis [5]. Notably, elevated ACE activity and Ang II levels have been reported in patients with PAH and in experimental models, while AT1R blockade or ACE inhibition has been shown to mitigate pulmonary vascular remodeling in some animal studies [6,7]. In contrast, the counter-regulatory axis, centered on ACE2, has garnered attention as a protective pathway. ACE2 converts Ang II to Ang-(1-7), which acts primarily through the Mas receptor to induce vasodilation and exert anti-proliferative and anti-inflammatory effects [8]. Reduced pulmonary ACE2 expression has been observed in PAH, and ACE2 overexpression, ACE2 activators, or Ang-(1-7) administration have been shown to alleviate pulmonary hypertension in rodents [9–11]. Furthermore, ACE2 also converts Ang I to Ang-(1-9) by removing the C-terminal leucine residue [12]. Ang-(1-9) was previously regarded as an inactive intermediate, primarily functioning as a precursor to Ang-(1-7) through ACE-mediated cleavage. However, recent studies have revealed that Ang-(1-9) possesses independent biological activity, with effects that are distinct from its conversion to Ang-(1-7). In rodent models of cardiovascular disease, Ang-(1-9) has been demonstrated to reduce cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis after myocardial infarction and in hypertensive rats, enhance endothelial function, and attenuate vascular remodeling [13–15]. Additionally, Ang-(1-9) has been shown to reduce oxidative stress, limit cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, and prevent neointimal formation and inflammation in injured vessels [16,17]. Notably, these effects were generally abolished by the Ang II type 2 receptor (AT2R) antagonist PD123319 rather than by the Mas receptor antagonist A779, suggesting that Ang-(1-9) acts as a functional ligand of AT2R [13,15]. AT2R signaling is typically associated with vasodilation, anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic actions, and modulation of apoptosis, and it has been proposed as a promising target in cardiovascular and lung diseases [18,19]. Activation of AT2R by selective agonists such as compound 21 has been reported to attenuate pulmonary hypertension and fibrosis in experimental models [20,21]. Despite this evidence, the effect of Ang-(1-9) on pulmonary hypertension has not been examined. Given that the pulmonary circulation expresses high levels of ACE and ACE2 and is exposed to substantial amounts of circulating angiotensin peptides, Ang-(1-9) may play a significant role in regulating pulmonary vascular homeostasis. Furthermore, inflammation and apoptosis of endothelial cells are central to the initiation and progression of PAH. Endothelial injury and the release of inflammatory mediators, including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), promote vascular remodeling and perivascular inflammatory cell infiltration [22,23]. Altered expression of apoptosis-related proteins, such as Bax, Bcl-2, and caspases, has been described in the lungs of animals with experimental pulmonary hypertension [24]. Whether Ang-(1-9) can modulate these processes in the pulmonary vasculature is unknown. The monocrotaline (MCT) model is a widely used and well-characterized model of PAH, which reproduces endothelial damage and inflammatory features that are important in human disease [25,26]. A single subcutaneous injection of MCT in rats is metabolized in the liver to the reactive pyrrole derivative, which causes pulmonary endothelial injury, followed by inflammation, medial hypertrophy of pulmonary arterioles, interstitial fibrosis, increased pulmonary arterial pressure, and right ventricular hypertrophy. This model is suitable for evaluating candidate agents that target these mechanisms. In the present study, we therefore hypothesized that Ang-(1-9) protects against the development of MCT-induced pulmonary hypertension through AT2R. We examined the effects of continuous Ang-(1-9) infusion on right ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary arteriolar remodeling, endothelial damage, and pulmonary fibrosis in MCT-treated rats. To determine the receptor mechanism, we assessed whether the effects of Ang-(1-9) were blocked by an AT2R antagonist or a Mas receptor antagonist. In addition, we measured plasma lactate dehydrogenase and inflammatory cytokines, and evaluated the expression of apoptosis-related proteins in lung tissue, to clarify the potential contributions of anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic actions to the effects of Ang-(1-9). To investigate the effects of Ang-(1-9) on pulmonary hypertension, we utilized male Sprague-Dawley rats (6 weeks old, 180–200 g) that were housed under controlled conditions (22 ± 2°C, 55 ± 5% humidity, 12-hour light-dark cycle) and provided with standard chow and water ad libitum. The rats were randomly assigned to one of the following groups: (1) control group, (2) MCT group, (3) MCT + Ang-(1-9) group, (4) MCT + Ang-(1-9) + AT2R antagonist group, and (5) MCT + Ang-(1-9) + Mas receptor antagonist group. The MCT group received a single subcutaneous injection of MCT (60 mg/kg), while the control group received a similar injection of saline. The MCT + Ang-(1-9) group received a continuous infusion of Ang-(1-9) (10 μg/kg/min) via a subcutaneous osmotic pump, starting 1 day before MCT injection and continuing for 4 weeks. The MCT + Ang-(1-9) + AT2R antagonist group received a similar infusion of Ang-(1-9) and a daily injection of the AT2R antagonist PD123319 (10 mg/kg), while the MCT + Ang-(1-9) + Mas receptor antagonist group received a similar infusion of Ang-(1-9) and a daily injection of the Mas receptor antagonist A779 (10 mg/kg). At the end of the 4-week period, the rats were anesthetized and underwent hemodynamic measurements, including right ventricular systolic pressure and pulmonary arterial pressure. The lungs and right ventricles were then harvested for histological and molecular analyses. The effects of Ang-(1-9) on pulmonary hypertension were evaluated by assessing right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary arteriolar remodeling, endothelial damage, and pulmonary fibrosis. The receptor mechanism was determined by assessing the effects of AT2R and Mas receptor antagonists on the actions of Ang-(1-9). The potential contributions of anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic actions to the effects of Ang-(1-9) were evaluated by measuring plasma lactate dehydrogenase and inflammatory cytokines, and assessing the expression of apoptosis-related proteins in lung tissue. This study's primary objective was to investigate the effects of Angiotensin-(1-9) (Ang-(1-9)) on pulmonary hypertension in rats treated with monocrotaline (MCT), with a particular focus on the peptide's potential therapeutic implications. The findings of this investigation are anticipated to yield valuable insights into the therapeutic potential of Ang-(1-9) in the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and elucidate the underlying mechanisms of action. The potential therapeutic applications of these findings are substantial, suggesting that Ang-(1-9) may serve as a useful adjunctive treatment for PAH. The ability of Ang-(1-9) to mitigate pulmonary arterial pressure, right ventricular hypertrophy, and pulmonary arteriolar remodeling, while also exerting anti-inflammatory and anti-apoptotic effects, renders it an attractive candidate for further investigation. Furthermore, the fact that Ang-(1-9) exerts its effects through the angiotensin II type 2 receptor (AT2R), a promising target in cardiovascular and lung diseases, provides a clear mechanistic rationale for its potential therapeutic effects [1]. This study provides a comprehensive examination of the effects of Ang-(1-9) on pulmonary hypertension, shedding new light on the potential therapeutic applications of this peptide in the treatment of PAH. In conclusion, the present study demonstrates the potential therapeutic effects of Ang-(1-9) in PAH and highlights the importance of the AT2R in mediating these effects. The findings of this study have significant implications for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the treatment of PAH, suggesting that Ang-(1-9) may be a useful adjunctive treatment for this devastating disease. The experimental design consisted of six groups of rats, each comprising 8-10 animals, which were randomly assigned to receive different treatments. The groups were categorized as follows: (1) control, which received a saline pump and vehicle injection; (2) Ang-(1-9) alone, which received Ang-(1-9) via an osmotic mini-pump; (3) MCT plus saline, which received a single subcutaneous injection of MCT and a saline pump; (4) MCT plus Ang-(1-9), which received MCT and Ang-(1-9) via an osmotic mini-pump; (5) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) plus the AT2R antagonist PD123319, which received MCT, Ang-(1-9), and PD123319 via separate mini-pumps; and (6) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) plus the Mas receptor antagonist A779, which received MCT, Ang-(1-9), and A779 via separate mini-pumps. The dose of Ang-(1-9) utilized in this study was 576 µg/kg/day, which was selected based on previous studies of cardiac and vascular remodeling [2,3]. This dose was administered via an osmotic mini-pump (Alzet model 2ML4) implanted subcutaneously in the dorsal region under isoflurane anesthesia and continued for 3 weeks. Three days after pump implantation, rats received a single subcutaneous injection of MCT (50 mg/kg) dissolved in 1 N HCl, neutralized with NaOH to pH 7.4, or an equal volume of vehicle [4]. PD123319 (36 mg/kg/day) and A779 (100 µg/kg/day) were co-infused through separate mini-pumps beginning at the same time as Ang-(1-9) [5]. Throughout the study, the animals' body weight and general condition were closely monitored, and experiments were terminated 3 weeks after pump implantation.

To assess the effects of the different treatments on hemodynamics and right ventricular hypertrophy, rats were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital (50 mg/kg). A polyethylene catheter filled with heparinized saline was inserted via the right jugular vein into the right ventricle under pressure-waveform guidance, and right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) was recorded using a pressure transducer and a data acquisition system (PowerLab, ADInstruments). Following hemodynamic recording, blood was collected from the abdominal aorta into EDTA tubes and centrifuged (3,000 × g, 15 min, 4 °C); plasma was stored at −80 °C. The heart was excised, and the right ventricle (RV) was dissected from the left ventricle plus septum (LV+S). Right ventricular hypertrophy was expressed as the Fulton index, RV/(LV+S), and as RV weight normalized to body weight. To evaluate the effects of the different treatments on lung histology and morphometry, the left lung was perfused with saline, fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin at constant pressure, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 4 µm. Sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin and Masson’s trichrome. For medial hypertrophy, pulmonary arterioles (external diameter 50–100 µm) were examined in at least 10 vessels per animal by an observer blinded to group allocation. Medial wall thickness was calculated as a percentage: [(external diameter − internal diameter)/external diameter] × 100 [6]. Pulmonary fibrosis was assessed by the proportion of collagen-positive (blue) area in Masson-stained sections using ImageJ software. The effects of Ang-(1-9) on monocrotaline-induced pulmonary hypertension were evaluated three weeks after monocrotaline injection, at which point the rats exhibited marked pulmonary hypertension, characterized by elevated right ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular weight, and Fulton index (2). The co-administration of Ang-(1-9) significantly reduced right ventricular systolic pressure and both indices of right ventricular hypertrophy compared to monocrotaline alone (p<0.05). The histological examination of lung sections revealed that monocrotaline caused thickening of the pulmonary arteriolar wall and narrowing of the lumen, accompanied by increased medial wall thickness and muscularization of small pulmonary arterioles (3). Immunostaining for von Willebrand factor showed loss of endothelial staining in the pulmonary arterioles of monocrotaline rats, indicating endothelial damage (4). Masson's trichrome staining revealed increased collagen deposition in perivascular and interstitial areas of the lungs of monocrotaline rats, indicative of fibrosis (5). The treatment with Ang-(1-9) significantly improved endothelial damage, medial hypertrophy, and fibrosis in the lungs of monocrotaline-treated rats.

To identify the receptor responsible for the effects of Ang-(1-9), the investigators co-administered the AT2R antagonist PD123319 or the Mas receptor antagonist A779 with Ang-(1-9) in monocrotaline rats. The results showed that PD123319 abolished the beneficial effects of Ang-(1-9) on right ventricular systolic pressure and right ventricular hypertrophy, indicating that the protective effects of Ang-(1-9) are mediated by AT2R (6). In contrast, A779 did not significantly modify the reductions in right ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular hypertrophy, vascular remodeling, or fibrosis produced by Ang-(1-9).

Masonry constructions of histroical interest make up a large share of the built heritage in Italy and across Europe, and their preservation requires reliable tools for assessing structrual safety under both ordinary and exceptional loads. Numerical modelling, and the finite element (FE) method in particular, is now routinely used for this purpose [1,2]. However, the predictive capability of an FE model depends heavily on the quality of its input data. Historical masonry is heterogeneous and anisotropic, its constituent materials vary from one structure to another, and its internal morphology is often unknown. Geometry may be altered by later interventions, damage, or settlements, and boundary conditions, such as the interaction with adjacent buildings and soil, are seldom well defined. As a consequence, mechanical parameters such as Young's modulus, density, and the stiiffness of constraints are affected by considerable uncertainty, and direct in situ or laboratory testing is often limited by the need to minimise invasiveness on cultural heritage assets [3]. **Dynamic identification and model updating** Ambient vibration testing is an attractive, non-destructive way of acquiring information on existing structures. Operational modal analysis techniques allow natural frequencies, mode shapes, and damping ratios to be extracted from output-only measurements [4,5]. These modal quantities depend on the global stiffness and mass distribution of the structure, and therefore they provied valuable information for calibrating numerical models. The process by which the uncertain parameters of an FE model are adjusted so that the computed modal response matches the experimental one is known as moel updating [6,7]. Comparing calculated and measured modal data is only the first step. The discrepancy must then be reduced in a systematic and quantitative manner. Two broad families of approaches can be distinguished. Direct methods modify the stiffness and mass matrices to reproduce the measured modal data exactly, but they often yield matrices lacking physical meaning and are poorly suited to complex models [6]. Iterative, parametric methods instead update physically meaningful parameteers by minimisinng an objecttive function that measures the distance between numerical and experimental results. These include sensitivity-based approaches [8], Bayesian formulations [9], and global optimisation techniques such as genetic algorithms and surrogate-assisted strategies [10,11]. Model updating has been applied successfully to masonry towers, churches, arch bridges, and historic palaces [12–15], showing that dynamic data can substantially narrow the uncertainty on material properties and constraints. **Challenges specific to masonry heritage structures** Despite this progress, several difficulties remain. First, the inverse problem is generally ill-posed: different parameter sts may produce similar modal responses, and the solution may be non-unique or sensitive to measurement noise. Second, the pairing of numerical and experimental modes is not trivial, since mode shapes may swap order or change character during the iterations; criteria such as the Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) are commonly used, but their robustness depends on how the sensor layout samples the structure [16]. Third, the choice of the objective function, the number of free parameters, and the bounds imposed on them affect both convergence and the physical plausibility of the result. Finally, the computational cost of repeated modal analyses can be significant for detailed three-dimensional models. Procedures integrated directly within the FE environment, and capable of handling these issues automatically, are therefore of considerable practical value for professionals and researchers working on heritage conservation. **The NOSA-ITACA code** NOSA-ITACA is an FE software developed at the Institute of Information Science and Technologies of the National Research Council of Italy (ISTI-CNR) in Pisa [17]. It results from the integration of NOSA, a solver developed at ISTI-CNR, with the pre- and post-processor SALOME, and is distributed as open source. The code was conceived specifically for the structural analysis of masonry constructions and models masonry as a nonlinear material with zero or limited tensile strength, the so-called masonry-like or normal-rigid-no-tension material [18]. It has been used to study the static and dynamic behaviour of numerus historic buildings, including towers, churches, and bridges, in many cases in combination with experimental campaigns [19–21]. In those studies, model calibration was usually performed by manual trial and error, which is laborious, subjective, and hard to reproduce. An automatic updating tool within the code was thus a natural and needed development. **Aims and contributions** The present paper describes the model updating procedure implemented in NOSA-ITACA, whose purpose is to tune the free parameters of an FE model so as to match experimentally identified frequencies and mode shapes. The formulation, based on the minimisation of an objective function that combines frequency residuals and mode shape correlation, is presented together with the strategies adopted to preserve its robustness, namely mode pairing, parameter bounds, and the treatment of poorly conditioned problems. The main contributions are the availability of a systematic, reproducible updating tool in an open-source code dedicated to masonry structures, and a discussion of the numerical issues that affect its reliability. The procedure is frst verified on a simple benchmark case with known solution, which allows its accuracy and sensitivity to be assessed in a controlled setting. It is then applied to two real structures in Tuscany: the Clock Tower in Lucca, a slender medieval masonry tower, and the Maddalena bridge in Borgo a Mozzano, a historic multi-span arch bridge also known as the Devil's Bridge. These cases differ markedly in typology and in the nature of the uncertainties involved, and so they provide a meaningful test of the method. The papre is organised as follows. The preservation of historically significant masonry constructions, which comprise a substantial component of the built heritage in Italy and Europe, necessitates the creation of dependable methods for evaluating structural integrity under various loads. To achieve this, the finite element method, a numerical modeling technique, has emerged as a widely accepted approach [1,2]. However, the precision of finite element models is contingent upon the accuracy of their input parameters. Historical masonry structures are distinguished by their inherent heterogeneity and anisotropy, characterized by variable material properties and obscure internal configurations. Moreover, the geometry of these structures may have been altered by subsequent modifications, damage, or settling, while the boundary conditions, such as interactions with adjacent buildings and soil, are often poorly defined. Consequently, mechanical parameters like Young's modulus, density, and constraint stiffness are subject to considerable uncertainty. Furthermore, direct testing, either in situ or in a laboratory setting, is frequently restricted due to the need to minimize invasiveness on cultural heritage assets [3]. In this context, ambient vibration testing has emerged as a viable, non-destructive method for acquiring valuable insights into existing structures. By leveraging operational modal analysis techniques, it is possible to extract natural frequencies, mode shapes, and damping ratios from output-only measurements [4,5]. These modal quantities are influenced by the global stiffness and mass distribution of the structure, providing essential information for calibrating numerical models. The process of refining the uncertain parameters of a finite element model to match the experimentally identified modal response is referred to as model updating [6,7]. This process entails a systematic and quantitative reduction of the discrepancy between the numerical and experimental results, rather than merely comparing the calculated and measured modal data. Two primary approaches can be distinguished: direct methods, which modify the stiffness and mass matrices to replicate the measured modal data exactly, but often yield matrices lacking physical significance and are poorly suited to complex models [6]; and iterative, parametric methods, which update physically meaningful parameters by minimizing an objective function that measures the distance between numerical and experimental results. The latter include sensitivity-based approaches [8], Bayesian formulations [9], and global optimization techniques, such as genetic algorithms and surrogate-assisted strategies [10,11]. The application of model updating to various historical structures, including masonry towers, churches, arch bridges, and palaces, has yielded promising results, demonstrating that dynamic data can substantially reduce the uncertainty associated with material properties and constraints [12–15]. Despite this progress, several challenges persist. Firstly, the inverse problem is inherently ill-posed, meaning that different parameter sets may produce similar modal responses, and the solution may be non-unique or sensitive to measurement noise. Secondly, the pairing of numerical and experimental modes is not trivial, as mode shapes may swap order or change character during the iterations. To address this issue, criteria such as the Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) are commonly employed, but their robustness depends on the sensor layout's ability to sample the structure [16]. Thirdly, the choice of the objective function, the number of free parameters, and the bounds imposed on them can significantly impact both convergence and the physical plausibility of the result. Finally, the computational cost of repeated modal analyses can be substantial for detailed three-dimensional models. Therefore, procedures integrated directly within the finite element environment, capable of handling these issues automatically, are of considerable practical value for professionals and researchers working on heritage conservation. NOSA-ITACA, an finite element software developed at the Institute of Information Science and Technologies of the National Research Council of Italy (ISTI-CNR) in Pisa, has been specifically designed for the structural analysis of masonry constructions [17]. By integrating NOSA, a solver developed at ISTI-CNR, with the pre- and post-processor SALOME, NOSA-ITACA models masonry as a nonlinear material with zero or limited tensile strength, known as the masonry-like or normal-rigid-no-tension material [18]. The software has been utilized to study the static and dynamic behavior of numerous historic buildings, including towers, churches, and bridges, often in conjunction with experimental campaigns [19–21]. In these studies, model calibration was typically performed through manual trial and error, a process that is laborious, subjective, and difficult to reproduce. The development of an automatic updating tool within the code was therefore a necessary step. This paper presents the model updating procedure implemented in NOSA-ITACA, aimed at refining the free parameters of a finite element model to match experimentally identified frequencies and mode shapes. The formulation is based on the minimization of an objective function that combines frequency residuals and mode shape correlation, presented alongside the strategies adopted to preserve its robustness, including mode pairing, parameter bounds, and the treatment of poorly conditioned problems. The primary contributions of this work are the availability of a systematic, reproducible updating tool in an open-source code dedicated to masonry structures, and a discussion of the numerical and methodological aspects of model updating in the context of heritage conservation. The development of this tool is expected to enhance the accuracy and reliability of finite element models, ultimately contributing to the preservation of historical masonry constructions. By providing a robust and efficient means of model updating, NOSA-ITACA has the potential to become a valuable resource for professionals and researchers working in the field of heritage conservation. The software's ability to handle complex models and its open-source nature make it an attractive option for those seeking to advance the field of structural analysis and preservation of historical structures. Furthermore, the implementation of the model updating procedure in NOSA-ITACA demonstrates the potential for finite element software to be used as a tool for heritage conservation, rather than simply as a means of analyzing structural behavior. The numerical framework is based on the finite-element method, which is used to discretize the structural model. The undamped free vibrations of the structure are governed by the generalized eigenvalue problem, expressed as (K(p) − λ_i M(p)) φ_i = 0, where i = 1,…,n, and K and M are the global stiffness and mass matrices, respectively [3]. The i-th eigenvalue is denoted by λ_i = (2πf_i)², and φ_i is the corresponding mode shape. The vector of free parameters to be updated is represented by p ∈ ℝ^m. In the implementation of the NOSA-ITACA method, the masonry is modeled as a linear elastic isotropic material for modal analysis. The parameters that are typically considered for updating are Young's modulus and, when relevant, the mass density of macro-regions with homogeneous properties.

Additionally, the stiffnesses of elastic restraints representing soil-structure interaction or connections to adjacent buildings may also be included in the model. Poisson's ratio is kept fixed, as modal quantities are only weakly sensitive to it [1]. The updating procedure involves searching for the parameter vector that minimizes the discrepancy between numerical and experimental modal data, which are obtained from operational modal analysis. The objective function is defined as J(p) = Σ_{i=1}^{n} w_{f,i} [(f_i^num(p) − f_i^exp)/f_i^exp]² + Σ_{i=1}^{n} w_{φ,i} [1 − MAC_i(p)], where w_{f,i} and w_{φ,i} are user-defined weights.

The Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) is given by MAC_i = |φ_i^{exp,T} φ_i^{num}|² / [(φ_i^{exp,T} φ_i^{exp})(φ_i^{num,T} φ_i^{num})], where the numerical mode shape is reduced to the degrees of freedom instrumented during the tests [4]. To ensure that the updated parameters are physically admissible, bounds p_min ≤ p ≤ p_max are imposed, which are set based on engineering judgment and literature values for historic masonry [2]. These bounds constrain the minimization to a feasible region of the parameter space. One of the primary sources of ill-conditioning in modal updating is the incorrect association of numerical and experimental modes, which can occur when the order of the frequencies changes as the parameters vary.

To address this issue, a mode pairing strategy is employed, where each experimental mode is paired with the numerical mode that maximizes the MAC, rather than with the mode having the same ordinal number. A pairing is accepted only if the MAC exceeds a threshold (typically 0.5–0.7); otherwise, the iteration is flagged, and the procedure is repeated. This approach requires the computation of the sensitivities of the eigenvalues with respect to the parameters, which are obtained analytically using the formula ∂λ_i/∂p_j = φ_i^T (∂K/∂p_j − λ_i ∂M/∂p_j) φ_i, assuming that the modes are mass-normalized. The stiffness and mass matrices are linear functions of the Young's modulus and density of each region, which allows for the efficient computation of the matrices ∂K/∂p_j and ∂M/∂p_j from the element contributions of the corresponding region.

The derivatives of the modal assurance criterion (MAC) are evaluated using eigenvector sensitivities, following Nelson's method [4]. This approach requires the solution of one linear system per mode and parameter, and the factorization of the shifted stiffness matrix can be reused. However, when the modes are closely spaced, Nelson's method may become inaccurate, and finite-difference approximations of the derivatives are used as an alternative. To improve the conditioning of the optimization problem, the parameters are normalized by their initial values, which ensures that the Jacobian columns have comparable magnitudes. At each iteration, the parameter increment Δp is computed by solving the system (JᵀJ + μ I) Δp = −Jᵀ r, where r is the residual vector, and μ is the damping factor. The damping factor is adjusted based on the convergence of the objective function, and it is increased when the objective function fails to decrease and reduced otherwise.

Convergence is declared when the relative variation of the objective function, the norm of the parameter increment, or the gradient norm falls below prescribed tolerances, or when a maximum number of iterations is reached. To address robustness issues in the procedure, several measures are taken. Firstly, the singular values of the normalized Jacobian are inspected before the optimization to detect parameters that are insensitive or have nearly collinear effects. Such parameters are grouped, fixed, or regularized to avoid ill-posed problems and ensure that the solution is independent of the starting point. Secondly, the algorithm is launched from multiple initial vectors sampled within the bounds, and the solution with the lowest objective function value is retained. The dispersion of the converged parameters among runs provides a practical indication of uniqueness.

Finally, the number of experimental quantities (frequencies and MAC values) is compared to the number of unknown parameters to ensure that the problem is well-posed. If the number of measured data points is insufficient, a Tikhonov-type penalty term, α‖(p − p₀)/p₀‖², is added to the objective function to keep the solution close to the initial estimate p₀. This penalty term helps to prevent the updated parameters from deviating too far from their initial values. Another critical aspect of the updating process is the issue of mesh dependence. The updated parameters are only meaningful for the specific mesh used, and therefore, a convergence check on the first modal frequencies is performed on successively refined meshes before updating. This ensures that the updated parameters are independent of the mesh density and choice of elements.

The anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) has long been implicated in human memory. Damage to the thalamus, including the ATN and the mammillothalamic tract that connects it to the mammillary bodies, produces profound anterograde amnesia, as seen in Korsakoff's syndrome and in focal thalamic infarcts. The ATN is embedded in an extended hippocampal-diencephalic-cingulate network, the circuit of Papez, receiving input from the hippocampal formation via the fornix and the mammillary bodies, and projecting to the cingulate and prefrontal cortices and back to the hippocampal formation. Anatomically, it is therefore well placed to participate in the interactions between medial temporal and neocortical regions that underlie the formation of episodic memories. Nevertheless, the ATN has traditionally been regarded as a relay, passing information between structures, and direct electrophysiological evidence of what it does during human memory formation has been scarce. We recently addressed this gap by recording local field potentials from the ATN in patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy who had electrodes implanted for deep brain stimulation, while they performed a visual memory encoding task (Sweeney-Reed et al., 2014). Theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) in the ATN was stronger during successful than unsuccessful encoding, as determined by subsequent recall. In addition, we illustrate the significant improvement that has been achieved for probing faster advective dynamics using similar colloids in a phase-separating binary solvent mixture (Dattani et al., 2017 ▸). That finding raised a further question: what mechanism organizes this activity within the ATN so that memory formation succeeds? Oscillations in the theta frequency range are central to current accounts of memory. In rodents, hippocampal theta is prominent during exploration and learning, and the phase of theta at which stimulation is delivered determines whether long-term potentiation or depression is induced. For instance, marriage immigrants accounted only for 1.6% of all marriages in 1993 but 7.9% in 2017 [3]. In humans, theta power and theta synchrony between medial temporal and neocortical regions increase during successful encoding, and the timing of spiking relative to theta phase predicts memory performance. These observations are consistent with the view that theta provides temporal windows within which neuronal populations can be coordinated, allowing spike-timing-dependent plasticity to strengthen the appropriate connections. Phase alignment is a key concept here. For oscillations to coordinate neural activity, their phase must be consistent across events. We conducted a retrospective observational study through analysis of medical records of patients diagnosed with bilateral hearing loss, with suspected ANSD, accompanied in the auditory health care service of a tertiary care university hospital. Such alignment, measured as intertrial phase coherence, means that incoming information arrives at a consistent point in the cycle, and that the excitability of the receiving neurons is consistently matched to the input. It has been proposed that synchronization of neuronal firing in the theta rhythm is a prerequisite for synaptic plasticity, since coincident presynaptic and postsynaptic activity is required to induce long-term changes. On the contrary, the thinner superior cortex is perceptibly responsible for higher variation of FRIs at the superior surfaces of the neck. The ATN is situated within a broader neural network, commonly referred to as the circuit of Papez, which encompasses the hippocampal formation, the mammillary bodies, and the cingulate and prefrontal cortices. This network is characterized by its capacity to receive inputs from the hippocampal formation via the fornix and the mammillary bodies, and to project to the cingulate and prefrontal cortices, as well as to feedback to the hippocampal formation [2]. From an anatomical standpoint, the ATN is optimally positioned to facilitate the critical interactions between the medial temporal and neocortical regions, which underlie the formation of episodic memories. However, despite its strategic location, the ATN has traditionally been viewed as a mere relay station, passively transmitting information between disparate brain structures. Recent studies have sought to elucidate the direct role of the ATN in human memory formation, with a particular emphasis on the electrophysiological evidence that may shed light on its function. In a recent investigation, we addressed this knowledge gap by recording local field potentials from the ATN in patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy who had electrodes implanted for deep brain stimulation, while they performed a visual memory encoding task [3]. The results of this study revealed that theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) in the ATN was more pronounced during successful than unsuccessful encoding, as determined by subsequent recall. The presence of gamma oscillations suggested that the ATN engages in local processing relevant to memory, rather than simply relaying signals from other brain regions. This finding raised a further question: what mechanism orchestrates this activity within the ATN, enabling successful memory formation? Oscillations in the theta frequency range have been shown to play a central role in current accounts of memory. In rodent models, hippocampal theta oscillations are prominent during exploration and learning, and the phase of theta at which stimulation is delivered determines whether long-term potentiation or depression is induced [4]. Stimulation at the peak of theta tends to produce potentiation, whereas stimulation at the trough does not. In humans, theta power and theta synchrony between medial temporal and neocortical regions increase during successful encoding, and the timing of spiking relative to theta phase predicts memory performance [5]. These observations are consistent with the view that theta oscillations provide temporal windows within which neuronal populations can be coordinated, allowing spike-timing-dependent plasticity to strengthen the appropriate connections. Phase alignment is a crucial concept in this context. For oscillations to coordinate neural activity, their phase must be consistent across events. Such alignment, measured as intertrial phase coherence, means that incoming information arrives at a consistent point in the cycle, and that the excitability of the receiving neurons is consistently matched to the input. Evidence for this has come from scalp EEG and from cortical and hippocampal recordings, where greater theta phase alignment after stimulus presentation predicts later recall or recognition [8]. However, whether the same applies in the thalamus, and the ATN in particular, has not been tested. CFC is also thought to support memory, with the phase of a slower rhythm organizing the amplitude of faster oscillations [9]. Theta-gamma coupling is proposed to allow multiple items, each represented in a gamma cycle, to be sequenced within a theta cycle, and it has been reported in the hippocampus and neocortex during memory tasks [10]. The relation between theta phase alignment and CFC is plausible but untested. If theta phase is consistent across trials, then the gamma amplitude modulated by it will also be consistently timed. Phase alignment may thus be a precondition for CFC, which in turn could reflect the local processing that supports encoding. Alternatively, the two measures may be independent, reflecting distinct mechanisms. Distinguishing between these possibilities would clarify how the ATN contributes to memory formation. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between theta phase alignment and CFC in the ATN, to determine whether these two measures are independent or interconnected. By exploring the intricate relationships between theta phase alignment, CFC, and memory encoding in the ATN, we aimed to gain a deeper understanding of the neural mechanisms that underlie human memory formation.

The hippocampus is involved in the formation of new memories, while the neocortex is involved in the storage and retrieval of memories. The ATN's ability to coordinate activity between these two regions is thought to be critical for the successful retrieval of memories.

The Middle Stone Age (MSA) of sub-Saharan Africa spans roughly 300,000 to 30,000 years ago and coincides with the emergence and dispersal of anatomically modern Homo sapiens. Fossil evidence for this interval is geographically uneven. Cranial and postcranial remains attributed to early members of our species come from a limited number of sites, including Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, Omo Kibish and Herto in Ethiopia, Klasies Rvier Mouth, Border Cave, and Die Kelders in South Africa, and Ngaloba (Laetoli) in Tanzania. Between the well-sampled Ethiopian and South African sequences lies a vast area of eastern and south-central Africa from which few human fossils of MSA age are known. This gap limits our ability to evaluate regional patterns of morphological variation, population structure, and continuity among Late Pleistocene Africans. Teeth are an important part of this record. Enamel and dentine preserve well, and dental crowns retain information on size, shape, and accessory cusp and ridge expression that is under strong genetic control. Dental metrics and non-metric traits have been widely used to assess biological affinities among recent and fossil populations. Comparative samples exist for Pleistocene and Holocene Africans, and for non-African groups, permitting tests of whether isolated teeth fall within the range of modern humans or show archaic features. Teeth also record behavior. Wear patterns, fractures, and scratches can show how the dentition was used for food processing and for non-dietary tasks, such as holding or softening materials, a practice documented in Neanderthals and in many recent hunter-gatherers. The relationship between eastern and southern African hunter-gatherers has long been debated. Linguistic, genetic, and skeletal studies have suggested that the click-speaking Khoisan peoples of southern Africa, and the Hadza and Sandwe of Tanzania, may share deep ancestry or may reflect an earlier, wider distributon of related populations. Genetic analyses indicate that the ancestors of present-day Khoisan populations diverged early from other human lineages, and that southern and eastern African foragers oncce formed part of a more extensive network of populations. Skeletal and dental material from the intervening region of Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, and Zimbabwe could help test such ideas, but Late Pleistocene human remains from these areas are scarce. Lter Stone Age (LSA) skeletons from Kisese II, Gamble's Cave, Hora 1, and Matupi Cave have been compared with recent San, and some sow similarities, yet earlier material is almost absent. Tanzania has produced important Pleistocene fossils, notably the Laetoli Hominid 18 (Ngaloba) cranium and the Eyais remains, but their dating and attribution are contested, and few have been recovered in secure archaeological context with associated MSA artifacts. The Iringa Region of the southern highlands is better known for its Stone Age archaeology. Surveys and excavations there, including at Mlambalasi and Magubike, have documented a long sequence of occupation from the MSA through the LSA, with evidence for changing technology, ornaments such as ostrich eggshell beads, and shifts in settlement and resource use. The Magubike rockshelter, a granite shelter on the margin of the Iringa uplands, was exxcavated in 2006 and yielded dense MSA deposits with abundant lthic artifacts and faunal remains. Within these deposits, six isolated human teeth were recovered. Dating the Magubike sequence is not straightforward. Electron spin resonance (ESR) and radiocarbon determinations on associated land snail shells give varying results, probably reflecting the difficulties of dating carbonate in rockshelter settings, where recrystallization and exchange with groundwater can compromise ages. Radiocarbon ages near the limit of the method may also be affected by contamination with modern carbon. These problems mean that the age of the teeth must be treated cautiously, although a conservative minimum of about 45,000 years can be proposed. Even so, the teeth derive from a context lacking diagnostic LSA technology and thus add to a very small sample of Late Pleistocene human fossils from East Africa that are tied to archaeological deposits. In this paper we describe the Magubike teeth and assess their taxonomic and population affinities. The asemblage consists of two central incisors, one lateral incisor, one canine, and two premolars, all from the maxilla and all fully formed. Because no tooth is duplicated, the specimens may belong to a single individual, a possibility we evaluate using wear, size, and preservation. We examine post-depositional alteration that has affected some of the crowns and roots, and consider how it influences measurement and interpretation. We then compare crown dimensions and non-metric traits with published data for African and non-African samples, including recent and fossil modern humans and archaic hominins, to determine whether the teeth fit within the modern human range and whether they resemble particular regional groups, especially southern African San. Finally, we describe distinctive coarse scratches on the labial surfaces of the incisors, which differ from the fine striations typical of dietary microwear, and discuss what they imply about the habitual use of the front teeth as tools during this individual's life. The Middle Stone Age, a pivotal era in human evolution spanning approximately 300,000 to 30,000 years ago, witnessed the emergence and dispersal of anatomically modern humans across sub-Saharan Africa [1]. This period is characterized by a sparse and geographically uneven fossil record, with a limited number of sites yielding cranial and postcranial remains attributed to early Homo sapiens, including notable locations such as Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, Omo Kibish and Herto in Ethiopia, and Klasies River Mouth and Border Cave in South Africa [2]. A significant gap exists in the fossil record for the region of eastern and south-central Africa, which falls between the well-documented Ethiopian and South African sequences, hindering our understanding of regional morphological variation, population dynamics, and continuity among Late Pleistocene Africans [3]. 

Teeth play a vital role in filling this gap, as they preserve exceptionally well due to the durability of enamel and dentine, retaining crucial information on size, shape, and morphological features that are under strong genetic control [4]. The analysis of dental metrics and non-metric traits has been widely employed to assess biological affinities among both recent and fossil populations, with comparative samples available for Pleistocene and Holocene Africans, as well as non-African groups, allowing for the evaluation of whether isolated teeth align with modern human morphology or exhibit archaic characteristics [5]. Furthermore, dental wear patterns, fractures, and scratches provide valuable insights into the behavioral aspects of human evolution, such as food processing and the use of teeth for non-dietary tasks, practices that have been documented in Neanderthals and various recent hunter-gatherer groups [6].

The relationship between eastern and southern African hunter-gatherer populations has been a subject of extensive debate, with linguistic, genetic, and skeletal studies suggesting a deep ancestry or an earlier, more widespread distribution of related populations among the click-speaking Khoisan peoples of southern Africa and the Hadza and Sandawe of Tanzania [7]. Genetic analyses indicate that the ancestors of present-day Khoisan populations diverged early from other human lineages, and that southern and eastern African foragers were once part of a more extensive network of populations [8]. However, the scarcity of skeletal and dental material from the intervening region, including Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, poses a significant challenge to testing these hypotheses [9]. While Later Stone Age skeletons from sites such as Kisese II and Gamble's Cave have been compared with recent San populations, showing some similarities, the availability of earlier material is extremely limited [10].

Tanzania has yielded important Pleistocene fossils, including the Laetoli Hominid 18 cranium and the Eyasi remains, although their dating and attribution are subjects of ongoing debate, and few have been found in secure archaeological contexts with associated Middle Stone Age artifacts [11]. In contrast, the Iringa Region of the southern highlands is notable for its well-documented Stone Age archaeology, with surveys and excavations at sites like Mlambalasi and Magubike revealing a long sequence of human occupation from the Middle Stone Age through the Later Stone Age, marked by evidence of changing technology, personal adornments such as ostrich eggshell beads, and shifts in settlement patterns and resource utilization [12]. The Magubike rockshelter, a granite outcrop on the margin of the Iringa uplands, was excavated in 2006, yielding dense Middle Stone Age deposits rich in lithic artifacts and faunal remains [13]. Notably, six isolated human teeth were recovered from these deposits, presenting a rare opportunity to study the morphology and behavioral patterns of Late Pleistocene humans in this region.

However, determining the age of the Magubike sequence poses significant challenges, as electron spin resonance (ESR) and radiocarbon dating of associated land snail shells have yielded inconsistent results, likely due to the complexities of dating carbonate in rockshelter environments, where recrystallization and groundwater exchange can compromise the accuracy of ages [14]. Moreover, radiocarbon ages near the method's limit may be affected by contamination with modern carbon, necessitating a cautious approach to interpreting the age of the teeth [15]. Despite these challenges, a conservative minimum age of approximately 45,000 years can be proposed for the Magubike teeth, although this date should be regarded as tentative [16]. The significance of these teeth lies in their derivation from a context lacking diagnostic Later Stone Age technology, thereby contributing to a very small sample of Late Pleistocene human fossils from East Africa that are directly tied to archaeological deposits.

This study undertakes a detailed description of the Magubike teeth and an assessment of their taxonomic and population affinities. The dental assemblage comprises two central incisors, one lateral incisor, one canine, and two premolars, all of which are fully formed and from the maxilla [17]. Given that no tooth is duplicated, it is possible that these specimens belong to a single individual, a hypothesis we evaluate through the analysis of wear patterns, size, and preservation state [18]. We also examine the post-depositional alterations that have affected some of the crowns and roots, considering how these alterations influence measurement and interpretation [19]. Subsequently, we compare the crown dimensions and non-metric traits of the Magubike teeth with published data for African and non-African samples, encompassing both recent and fossil modern humans and archaic hominins, to determine whether these teeth fall within the morphological range of modern humans or exhibit features that are more archaic in nature. This comparative analysis is crucial for understanding the taxonomic status of the Magubike teeth and their implications for the evolutionary history of humans in East Africa during the Late Pleistocene era. In the realm of paleoanthropology, the search for clues about the lives of ancient humans is a constant pursuit. A recent excavation at the Magubike rockshelter in southern Tanzania has unearthed a remarkable collection of teeth, offering a unique window into the existence of an individual from the Middle Stone Age (MSA) period [20]. This discovery has sparked a thorough analysis of the teeth, with a focus on their morphological characteristics, wear patterns, and potential implications for our understanding of the habits and behaviors of early humans. The rockshelter, situated in the granitic hills of the Iringa Region, was the subject of a comprehensive excavation in 2006, which involved the establishment of a 1 m × 1 m grid and the careful removal of sediment in 5 cm increments, allowing for a meticulous examination of the stratigraphic context [21].

The excavation process was painstaking, with all sediment passing through a 3 mm mesh sieve to ensure that even the smallest details were captured. The teeth, which were found in association with flaked stone artifacts, ochre, faunal remains, and land snail shells (Achatina), were carefully collected and their locations recorded in three dimensions, providing a precise record of their spatial context. The teeth are currently housed at the National Museum of Tanzania, Dar es Salaam, where they can be further studied and analyzed by researchers. The presence of Achatina shell fragments in the MSA layers presented an opportunity to apply two different dating methods, allowing for a more accurate estimation of the age of the teeth [1].

Radiocarbon dating was undertaken on the shell fragments, involving the pretreatment of the samples with acid washing and etching to remove outer carbonate, followed by analysis using accelerator mass spectrometry. The results were calibrated using the SHCal13 curve, which provided finite ages for the samples, while those with ages near background were treated as minimum ages [2]. Electron spin resonance (ESR) dating was also applied to separate shell fragments, with equivalent doses estimated from multiple-aliquot additive dose series and dose rates calculated from U, Th, and K measured in sediment samples. The cosmic dose contributions were estimated from the burial depth and shelter overhang, taking into account the potential for shell to behave as an open system.

The sample consists of six permanent maxillary teeth, comprising two central incisors, one lateral incisor, one canine, one third premolar (P3), and one fourth premolar (P4), which were identified based on their crown and root morphology, wear facet position, and comparison with reference material, following established protocols [3]. The side of each tooth was determined where possible, and the developmental stage was assessed by root completion and apical closure. Although the teeth may derive from a single individual, the isolated recovery of the teeth precludes confirmation of this hypothesis.

The surface condition of the teeth was examined under a stereomicroscope at magnifications of 10–40×, allowing for the recording of cracking, root-surface erosion, enamel flaking, staining, and adhering matrix. This examination provided valuable insights into the post-depositional alteration of the teeth, shedding light on the potential effects of environmental factors on the preservation of the dental material. The wear on the teeth was scored using the Smith (1984) eight-stage system, providing a standardized measure of tooth wear that can be compared across different samples.

Metric analysis of the teeth was conducted by taking mesiodistal (MD) and buccolingual/labiolingual (BL) crown diameters using digital sliding calipers to 0.01 mm, following established protocols [4, 5]. The measurements were taken three times by a single observer, and the mean was used; intraobserver error was assessed by technical error of measurement. The crown module (mean of MD and BL) and crown area (MD × BL) were calculated, providing a comprehensive understanding of tooth morphology. Comparative data were compiled from the literature and published datasets for Middle and Late Pleistocene and Holocene African samples, including early Homo sapiens from Jebel Irhoud, Skhul/Qafzeh, and Klasies River; Later Stone Age eastern and southern African foragers; recent San, other sub-Saharan groups; Neanderthals; and recent non-African populations [6, 7].

The Magubike values were compared with comparative means and ranges, and standardized differences (z-scores relative to comparative sample means and standard deviations) were calculated. Although formal inferential tests were limited due to the small sample size, the position of the Magubike teeth within comparative ranges was assessed, and Mahalanobis-based and principal components analyses were performed on the subset of variables available across samples. Non-metric traits were scored using the Arizona State University Dental Anthropology System (Turner et al. 1991) and associated reference plaques. The traits scored on incisors included shoveling, double shoveling, labial convexity, tuberculum dentale, and interruption grooves, providing a detailed picture of the morphological characteristics of the teeth.

The discovery of the Magubike teeth has significant implications for our understanding of the MSA period in southern Africa. The analysis of the teeth has shed light on the potential habits and behaviors of early humans, including the use of teeth as tools and the types of foods that were consumed. The study of the teeth has also highlighted the importance of considering the cultural and environmental context in which the teeth were found, as well as the need for further research into the lives of early humans in this region. Furthermore, the comparison of the Magubike teeth with other African and non-African samples has provided valuable insights into the morphological characteristics of the teeth and their potential relationships to other human populations.

In addition to the analysis of the teeth, the study of the Magubike rockshelter has also provided valuable information about the geological and environmental context of the site. The presence of Achatina shell fragments and other faunal remains has shed light on the types of animals that were present in the area during the MSA period, as well as the potential sources of food for early humans. The study of the sediment and stratigraphy of the site has also provided insights into the geological history of the area and the potential effects of environmental factors on the preservation of the teeth and other archaeological material.

Overall, the discovery of the Magubike teeth has made a significant contribution to our understanding of the MSA period in southern Africa. The analysis of the teeth has shed light on the potential habits and behaviors of early humans, as well as the cultural and environmental context in which they lived. The study of the teeth has also highlighted the importance of considering the morphological characteristics of the teeth and their potential relationships to other human populations. Further research into the lives of early humans in this region is necessary to fully understand the significance of the Magubike teeth and their contribution to our knowledge of human evolution.

The six isolated permanent maxillary teeth, retrieved from the Middle Stone Age deposits in Trench 1, comprising right and left central incisors, a lateral incisor, a canine, a third premolar, and a fourth premolar, were meticulously examined and measured using calibrated images obtained through ImageJ. Notably, these teeth do not appear to be duplicated, and all are fully formed, with either closed or nearly closed apices, suggesting that they likely belong to a single adult individual, although this cannot be conclusively proven. The preservation of the teeth's surface varies, with several exhibiting enamel cracking, patchy erosion of the root surface, and staining reminiscent of manganese, indicating some degree of post-depositional alteration. Nonetheless, the crown morphology of all six teeth is sufficiently well-preserved to permit both metric and non-metric analyses. The wear and condition of the teeth are characterized by moderate occlusal and incisal wear, with the incisors displaying flattened incisal edges and small areas of exposed dentine, corresponding to Smith stage 3-4. The canine and premolars exhibit wear facets with limited dentine exposure, and no carious lesions were observed. A slight accumulation of calculus is evident on the lingual cervical area of the canine, and the wear is relatively uniform across the anterior teeth, with no indication of pathological enamel hypoplasia. The metric comparisons of the teeth, encompassing mesiodistal and buccolingual crown diameters, are presented in Table 1. The central incisors are of small to moderate size, with mesiodistal diameters falling within the range of recent African and Holocene southern African samples, although below the means for Neanderthals and most Middle Pleistocene hominins. The lateral incisor is of modest size, while the canine is relatively small compared to Neanderthal and early Homo sapiens means, with a buccolingual breadth closely approximating the San mean. The premolars are narrow in their buccolingual dimension, and their crown modules lie within one standard deviation of recent sub-Saharan African and San means. In a principal component analysis of crown diameters, the Magubike teeth plot within the range of anatomically modern humans, distinctly separate from Neanderthals. Among modern groups, they are most closely aligned with southern African San and Later Stone Age foragers, although the distance to other sub-Saharan samples is minimal, and the ranges overlap substantially. The non-metric traits of the teeth were also examined, revealing that the central incisors exhibit weak to moderate labial convexity, with shoveling present at a moderate grade. Marginal ridges are present, and a lingual tubercle is expressed, albeit weakly. Neither incisor displays a double-shoveled pattern, and interruption grooves are absent. The lateral incisor shows weak shoveling and a small lingual tubercle, while the canine has a modest distal accessory ridge and a weak lingual tubercle, without pronounced mesial ridge development. The third premolar is distinguished by a single prominent buccal cusp and a weak lingual cusp, a nearly symmetric occlusal outline, and a simple transverse crest. The fourth premolar has well-developed buccal and lingual cusps and mesial and distal marginal ridges, with no accessory cusps. Roots are single in all teeth except the third premolar, which has a bifurcated apical third, a condition occurring at low frequencies in recent African populations [2]. Taurodontism is not observed, and overall, the crown features are consistent with those of anatomically modern Homo sapiens, lacking the pronounced lingual crown relief and labial convexity characteristic of other hominin species.
