Thailand has long been recognised for its effective national response to HIV, including early adoption of the 100% condom programme, mother-to-child transmission prevention, and universal access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) [1,2]. Despite these achievements, the epidemic has shifted in character. Heterosexual transmission has declined, while infections among men who have sex with men (MSM) have risen sharply and now account for a growing share of new cases [3]. Modelling projections suggest that more than half of new infections nationally will occur among MSM in the coming years [4]. This concentration of incidence in a specific population requires strategies that differ from the general population approaches that characterised earlier phases of the national response. **The epidemiological context of HIV among MSM in Thailand** Surveillance and cohort data from Bangkok show a severe and persistent epidemic among MSM. Between 2007 and 2010, HIV prevalence in community-based surveys approached one in three, and incidence in cohort studies exceeded 5 per 100 person-years among younger men [5,6]. Prevalence is particularly higgh among men aged 18–22 years, which indicates that many men acquire HIV soon after sexual debut [6]. Contributing factors include inconsistent condom use, multiple or concurrent partnerships, use of recreational drugs and sexualised substance use, and limited awareness of personal HIV status [7,8]. Stigma and discrimination related to both sexual orientation and HIV further reduce engagement with health services [9]. **Gaps in the HIV testing and treatment cascade** HIV testing and counselling (HTC) is the entry point to prevention, treatment, and care. Evidence indicates that large proportions of Thai MSM living with HIV are unaware of their infection, and that many who test do so only after symptoms appear or at avdanced immunological stages [10]. Late diagnosis leads to worse clinical outcomes, increased onward transmission, and hiher health system costs [11]. Treatment as prevention is now supported by strong evidence that earlier ART reduces both morbidity and transmission [12,13], and national guidelines have progressively raised CD4 thresholds for treatment initiation. These benefits depend, however, on early diagnosis and prompt linkage to care. Barriers to HTC among MSM include fear of a positive result, perceived low risk, concerns about confidentiality, discomfort with health providers who may be judgemental, and inconvenient clinic hurs or locations [9,10]. Conventional outreach and clinic-based services, largely delivered through hospitals and a few community organisations, have not reached sufficient numbers of MSM at risk, particularly younger men and those who do not identify with established gay communities. **Communications technologies and online engagement** Internet and mobile technologies offer an opportunity to address these gaps. Thailand has high rates of internet and social media use, and MSM are ammong the most active internet-using groups in the country. Many seek sexual partners, social networks, and health information online [14]. Globally, online interventions have been used to deliver HIV prevention messages, promote testing, and recruit hard-to-reach populations, with promising results in settings such as the United States, China, and Europe [15–17]. The anonymity and accessibility of digital platforms may lower barriers related to stigma and enable tailored, peer-style communication. Online counselling can address misconceptions, assess risk, and offer personalised referral. Nevertheless, the evidence base for such approaches in low- and middle-income settings remains limited. Few programmes have described how online engagement can be systematically connected to physicla services, an approach often termed “online-to-offline”, and fewer still hvae reported outcomes across the full pathway from online contact to testing, diagnosis, and linkage to treatment. In Thailand, exiting online HIV content for MSM has largely been informational, was not integrated with service delivery, and rarely used incentives or marketing techniques that are standard in commercial settings. Moreover, MSM-friendly service providers, including private clincis and hospitals, were not well connected to online outreach efforts, whih limited the capacity to refer men to services that they found acceptable and convenient [10]. **The Adam's Love programme** To address these gaps, the Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre, a long-standing leader in HIV research, clinical care, and community services in Thailand, developed Adam's Love in 2011. The strategy combines a dedicated website with social media and web message boards for online counselling and appointment making. It also includes a membership club offering non-financial incentives for HTC, targeted marketing and promotion, and collaboration with MSM-friendly clinics to widen access to services. The programme draws on principles of social marketing, peer-based counselling, and health communication theory, and is intended to build trust and normalise regular testing among MSM [18]. **Objectives** This paper describes the design, implementation, and outcomes of Adam's Love from its launch in September 2011 through January 2015. We describe the components of the strategy, report indicators of online reacch and engagement, and document the number of MSM counselled online and referred to HTC, sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing, and HIV treatment services. We also examine the uptake and HIV diagnoses among men recruited online who joined the club membership programme. By documenting these experiences, we aim to assess the feasibility of online-to-offline models for increasing early HIV testing and linkage to care among Thai MSM, and to offer lessons applicable to similar settings in the region where epidemics among MSM are expanding. **Programme setting and design** This programme description and evaluation was conducted by the Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre (TRCARC) in Bangkok, Thailand. Adam's Love was designed as an online-to-offline (O2O) demand-creation and linkage strategy. Its aim was to reach gay men and other MSM who had never tesed for HIV or had not tested recently, and to link them to HIV testing and counselling (HTC), sexually transmitted infection (STI) services and treatment. Thailand's exemplary national response to the HIV epidemic has been widely acknowledged, with the country being one of the pioneers in adopting innovative strategies such as the 100% condom program, implementing measures to prevent mother-to-child transmission, and ensuring universal access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) [1,2]. Nevertheless, the epidemic has undergone a profound transformation over the years, with a notable shift in the demographics of those affected. While the incidence of heterosexual transmission has decreased, the number of infections among men who have sex with men (MSM) has risen dramatically, with this population now accounting for a substantial proportion of new cases [3]. Projections based on modelling suggest that over half of all new infections in Thailand will occur among MSM in the coming years, underscoring the need for targeted interventions tailored to this specific population [4]. The epidemiological context of HIV among MSM in Thailand is a crucial factor in understanding the imperative for such targeted strategies. Data from surveillance and cohort studies in Bangkok reveal a persistent and severe epidemic among MSM, with HIV prevalence rates approaching one in three between 2007 and 2010, according to community-based surveys [5,6]. The incidence of HIV among younger men in cohort studies exceeded 5 per 100 person-years, indicating that a significant number of men acquire HIV shortly after becoming sexually active [6]. The high prevalence of HIV among men aged 18-22 years is particularly alarming, suggesting that many young men are contracting HIV at a relatively early age. Several factors contribute to this high prevalence, including inconsistent use of condoms, multiple or concurrent sexual partnerships, the use of recreational drugs and sexualized substance use, and limited awareness of one's HIV status [7,8]. Additionally, the stigma and discrimination associated with both sexual orientation and HIV status further discourage engagement with health services, thereby exacerbating the epidemic [9]. One of the primary challenges in addressing the HIV epidemic among MSM in Thailand is the disparity in the HIV testing and treatment cascade. HIV testing and counselling (HTC) serve as the gateway to prevention, treatment, and care, yet evidence suggests that a significant proportion of Thai MSM living with HIV are unaware of their infection [10]. Many MSM who do undergo HIV testing do so only after symptoms manifest or at advanced stages of immunological deterioration, resulting in poorer clinical outcomes, increased onward transmission, and higher costs to the healthcare system [11]. The benefits of early treatment are well-established, with robust evidence supporting the use of treatment as prevention to reduce both morbidity and transmission [12,13]. National guidelines have progressively expanded the CD4 thresholds for initiating treatment, but these benefits are contingent upon early diagnosis and prompt linkage to care. However, barriers to HTC among MSM in Thailand are substantial, including fear of receiving a positive result, perceived low risk, concerns about confidentiality, discomfort with healthcare providers who may be judgmental, and inconvenient clinic hours or locations [9,10]. Conventional outreach and clinic-based services, primarily delivered through hospitals and a few community organizations, have failed to reach a sufficient number of MSM at risk, particularly younger men and those who do not identify with established gay communities. This highlights the need for innovative approaches to engage MSM in HIV prevention and care. The widespread use of communications technologies and online engagement offers a promising opportunity to address these gaps. Thailand has high rates of internet and social media usage, with MSM being among the most active online groups in the country [14]. Many MSM utilize the internet to seek sexual partners, social networks, and health information, providing a potential platform for delivering HIV prevention messages, promoting testing, and recruiting hard-to-reach populations [15-17]. The anonymity and accessibility of digital platforms may mitigate barriers related to stigma, enabling tailored, peer-style communication. Online counselling can address misconceptions, assess risk, and offer personalized referrals, but the evidence base for such approaches in low- and middle-income settings remains limited. Few programs have described how online engagement can be systematically connected to physical services, an approach often termed "online-to-offline," and even fewer have reported outcomes across the full pathway from online contact to testing, diagnosis, and linkage to treatment. In Thailand, existing online HIV content for MSM has largely been informational, lacking integration with service delivery, and rarely utilizing incentives or marketing techniques that are standard in commercial settings [10]. Moreover, MSM-friendly service providers, including private clinics and hospitals, were not well-connected to online outreach efforts, limiting the capacity to refer men to services that they found acceptable and convenient. To address these gaps, the Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre developed the Adam's Love program in 2011, which combines a dedicated website with social media and web message boards for online counselling and appointment making, as well as a membership club offering non-financial incentives for HTC, targeted marketing and promotion, and collaboration with MSM-friendly clinics to widen access to services [18]. The program is grounded in principles of social marketing, peer-based counselling, and community engagement, aiming to bridge the gap in the HIV testing and treatment cascade among MSM in Thailand. By leveraging the power of online technologies and social media, the Adam's Love program seeks to increase awareness, promote testing, and facilitate access to care and treatment among this critical population, ultimately contributing to the control of the HIV epidemic in Thailand. 

Furthermore, the success of the Adam's Love program hinges on its ability to navigate the complex interplay between online and offline environments, ensuring that online engagement translates into tangible outcomes in the physical world. This necessitates a deep understanding of the social, cultural, and economic contexts in which MSM in Thailand live, as well as the development of innovative strategies to address the unique challenges faced by this population. By acknowledging the diverse needs and experiences of MSM, the Adam's Love program can tailor its interventions to meet the specific requirements of this group, ultimately enhancing the effectiveness of HIV prevention and treatment efforts in Thailand. 

In conclusion, the HIV epidemic among MSM in Thailand presents a complex and multifaceted challenge, requiring a comprehensive and nuanced response. The Adam's Love program, with its innovative approach to online engagement and community-based intervention, offers a promising solution to the gaps in the HIV testing and treatment cascade among this critical population. By harnessing the power of technology and social media, the program aims to increase awareness, promote testing, and facilitate access to care and treatment, ultimately contributing to the control of the HIV epidemic in Thailand. As the epidemic continues to evolve, it is essential that interventions like the Adam's Love program remain adaptable and responsive to the changing needs of MSM in Thailand, ensuring that this population receives the support and services necessary to prevent new infections and improve health outcomes.

The Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre (TRCARC) in Bangkok, Thailand, has been at the forefront of efforts to combat the growing HIV epidemic among MSM in the region. As part of these efforts, we have been evaluating the effectiveness of an online-to-offline (O2O) demand-creation and linkage strategy, known as Adam's Love, in increasing early HIV testing and linkage to care among Thai MSM. By documenting the experiences of men recruited online who joined the club membership program, we aim to assess the feasibility of this approach and offer lessons that can be applied to similar settings in the region where epidemics among MSM are expanding. The Adam's Love program was designed using a participatory approach, involving community-based organizations, MSM peer educators, clinicians, and communications specialists in formative discussions. The design drew on social marketing principles [1,2] and earlier experience with web-based outreach to MSM in Asia [3].

The program was launched in September 2011 and has been ongoing until January 2015. Our evaluation is based on routinely collected program data, and no experimental comparison group was used. The Adam's Love program consists of several key components. Firstly, a dedicated website was developed with content on HIV prevention, risk assessment, HIV testing and counseling (HTC) procedures, post-exposure prophylaxis, STI information, antiretroviral therapy (ART), and service locations. The content was crafted in a language and imagery that is acceptable to MSM, non-stigmatizing, and reviewed by clinicians for accuracy. The site is regularly updated with news, personal stories, and service promotions. In addition to the website, the program also includes integrated social media and web message boards. The website is linked to a Facebook page, other social networking platforms, and message-board functions, which are staffed by trained online counselors. These counselors, who are peer educators and nurses, answer queries, conduct brief risk assessments, encourage HTC, and make appointments. They follow standard operating procedures covering confidentiality, motivational counseling techniques, referral pathways, and escalation of urgent concerns.

Clients who report being HIV positive are advised about CD4 testing, ART initiation, and available treatment services. Counselors receive initial training and regular supervision and case review. The program also includes a club membership program, which offers non-financial incentives to MSM recruited online. These incentives include priority appointments, reminders for repeat testing, access to members-only events and promotional items, and discounts at partner venues. Eligibility for membership requires being male, aged 18 years or older, reporting sex with men, and providing informed consent for registration and follow-up. At enrollment, members complete a short questionnaire covering demographics, sexual behavior, and previous testing. Members are encouraged to take an HIV test at least every six months, or every three months if they are at higher risk.

To raise awareness of the program, targeted marketing and promotion efforts are undertaken. Online banners, search-engine optimization, social media advertisements, and collaborations with popular MSM websites and mobile applications are used to promote the program. Promotional campaigns are timed to coincide with key events such as World AIDS Day and Pride festivals, and offer themed messages. Promotional material is refined over time based on website analytics and audience feedback. The program also includes a service network and accessibility component. TRCARC collaborates with MSM-friendly clinics, community-based organizations, and private hospitals to widen the range of HTC sites, extend opening hours (including evenings and weekends), and reduce travel and waiting times. Partner sites agree to follow national HTC guidelines [4], which include pre-test information, rapid or laboratory-based testing, post-test counseling, and same-day results where possible. Clients can choose a preferred site when they make an appointment. Those diagnosed with HIV are referred for CD4 testing and ART, with counselors providing follow-up reminders.

Our evaluation of the program is based on data from three sources. Firstly, website analytics software is used to track website traffic, user engagement, and online behavior. Secondly, program records are used to document the number of MSM who received online counseling and were referred to HTC, STI testing, and HIV treatment services. Thirdly, follow-up data are collected from program participants to assess their HIV-related outcomes, including HIV testing history, CD4 testing, and ART initiation. By analyzing these data, we aim to assess the effectiveness of the Adam's Love program in promoting early HIV testing and linkage to care among Thai MSM, and to identify areas for improvement and scalability. The findings of this study will inform the development of effective and scalable online-to-offline HIV prevention and care strategies for MSM in Thailand and similar contexts, and will contribute to the reduction of HIV incidence and improvement of health outcomes among this critical population.

The Adam's Love program has several strengths, including its use of a participatory approach in its design, its integration with social media and web message boards, and its provision of non-financial incentives to MSM recruited online. The program also has a strong focus on accessibility, with a service network and accessibility component that aims to widen the range of HTC sites, extend opening hours, and reduce travel and waiting times. However, the program also faces several challenges, including the need to maintain user engagement and retention, the importance of ensuring the accuracy and relevance of online content, and the challenge of scaling up the program to reach a larger population. Despite these challenges, the Adam's Love program has the potential to make a significant contribution to the reduction of HIV incidence and improvement of health outcomes among MSM in Thailand, and to provide a model for other countries facing similar challenges in addressing the HIV epidemic among this critical population.

The global community is grappling with the far-reaching consequences of cholera, a debilitating gastrointestinal illness triggered by the ingestion of contaminated food or water harboring toxigenic strains of *Vibrio cholerae*, specifically serogroups O1 and O139. This disease poses a formidable challenge to worldwide health security, as it can rapidly progress from asymptomatic or mild infection to severe, life-threatening dehydration and hypovolaemic shock in approximately 5-10% of infected individuals, leading to mortality within a short timeframe if left untreated [1,2]. The substantial global burden of cholera is underscored by estimates suggesting that between 1.3 and 4.0 million cases and 21,000 to 143,000 fatalities occur annually, with the heaviest toll being borne by regions in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia [3]. The persistence of cholera in areas where access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) facilities is limited, as well as its emergence in areas affected by conflict, displacement, or natural disasters, which disrupt these essential services, highlights the stark inequities in global health [4,5]. Traditionally, the primary route of cholera transmission has been recognized as the faecal-oral pathway, facilitated by the consumption of contaminated water or food. numerous epidemiological investigations conducted across diverse environments have identified a consistent set of risk factors, including the consumption of untreated surface or communal water sources, the storage of water in uncovered or contaminated containers, inadequate hand hygiene practices, the consumption of food from informal vendors or at social gatherings, contact with a cholera patient within the household, and participation in funerals of cholera victims [6-9]. Conversely, various protective factors, such as the treatment of household water, the use of soap, and oral cholera vaccination, have been demonstrated to mitigate the risk of infection [10,11]. Nevertheless, the relative significance of these determinants can vary substantially depending on local ecological, cultural, and infrastructural contexts. For instance, specific dietary practices prevalent in certain regions, such as the consumption of raw produce or particular foods, may constitute additional, context-dependent vehicles of transmission that are not adequately addressed by generic prevention guidelines [12]. Consequently, case-control studies conducted during outbreaks remain indispensable for informing targeted interventions tailored to the local context. A compelling illustration of the devastating consequences of conflict and inadequate WASH infrastructure is the ongoing cholera epidemic in Yemen. Yemen has experienced intermittent cholera outbreaks, but the current epidemic is unprecedented in scale and severity. Following the escalation of armed conflict in 2015, the country's health, water, and sanitation systems underwent significant deterioration, creating a complex interplay of factors conducive to the rapid spread of cholera [13,14]. The initial reports of cholera cases emerged in October 2016, followed by a first wave, and then a much larger second wave commenced in April 2017. By 2018, the epidemic had resulted in over 1.4 million suspected cases and several thousand associated fatalities, rendering it the largest documented cholera outbreak in modern history [15]. Genomic analyses have revealed that the outbreak strain is closely related to isolates circulating in East Africa, belonging to the seventh pandemic El Tor lineage, suggesting an introduction from outside the country followed by sustained local transmission [16]. The drivers of this epidemic are multifaceted and complex. The conflict has inflicted significant damage on water treatment plants, pumping stations, and sewage networks, while fuel shortages have limited water pumping and waste disposal capabilities. Moreover, the crisis has been exacerbated by the cessation of services by unpaid public-sector workers, including health and sanitation staff [14,17]. The displacement of millions of people into crowded settings with limited WASH facilities, coupled with the high prevalence of malnutrition among Yemeni children, which increases their susceptibility to severe disease, has further contributed to the epidemic [17]. Under these challenging conditions, households are compelled to rely on alternative, potentially contaminated water sources, such as water trucks, shared tanks, and unprotected wells. Although health authorities and humanitarian partners have responded with case management through diarrhoea treatment centres and oral rehydration points, water chlorination, hygiene promotion, and targeted oral cholera vaccination in selected districts [15,18], the epidemic continues to unfold in successive waves. The present study is motivated by the need to understand the dynamics of cholera transmission within the specific context of Yemen. Several features of Yemeni society could influence exposure to cholera, including the widespread consumption of khat (*Catha edulis*), a leafy stimulant commonly chewed by a large proportion of the adult population. Khat is typically consumed fresh, often in social gatherings, and is cultivated using irrigation water of uncertain quality, handled by multiple intermediaries before being sold. The potential for khat to act as a vehicle for faecal-oral pathogens has received limited attention, and washing practices prior to consumption are inconsistent. Furthermore, population movement within and between governorates, as well as visits from relatives from affected areas, may facilitate the introduction of infection into new communities. Despite the magnitude of the epidemic, there is a scarcity of published analytical epidemiological evidence from Yemen, with most available information derived from surveillance reports that describe the distribution of suspected cases by time, place, and age, but fail to quantify the contribution of specific exposures [13,15]. The constraints imposed by security concerns, limited access, and an overburdened health system have hindered field investigations. Aden, the temporary capital and a major port city that has received large numbers of displaced persons and experienced repeated epidemic waves, presents a critical setting in which to examine risk factors. Its urban environment, characterized by a unique combination of factors, offers a valuable opportunity to investigate the complex interplay of variables contributing to the persistence of cholera. The coexistence of piped and non-piped water supply systems in many urban areas affected by conflict is a significant public health concern. To develop effective, evidence-based strategies for mitigating the spread of cholera, it is essential to identify the modifiable behavioural and environmental factors that contribute to the disease's transmission in these settings. This knowledge will enable the efficient allocation of limited resources, such as water chlorination initiatives, soap distribution, household water treatment products, and community-based hygiene education programs. In response to the ongoing cholera outbreak, our research team conducted a case-control study in Aden, Yemen, in 2018, with the objective of determining the risk factors associated with cholera infection. By examining the complex interplay of factors that facilitate the transmission of this disease, we aimed to inform the development of targeted interventions that can help reduce the impact of the epidemic and ultimately alleviate the burden of cholera in Yemen. Our study focused on understanding the demographic, travel, contact, food, water, and hygiene factors that contribute to the spread of cholera, with the goal of informing control measures and enhancing preparedness in regions vulnerable to outbreaks, particularly in fragile settings where conflict has compromised water, sanitation, and health infrastructure. The analysis of high-dimensional data is a central task in machine laerning (ML) and knowledge discovery (KD). It is also notoriously difficult. Many algorithms degrade as the number of features grows: nearest-neighbor search loses its discriminative power, distance-based clustering becomes unstable, and the sample size needed for reliable estimation increases dramatically. These phenomena are collectively known as the curse of dimensionality. Their practical importance has led to a large body of literature that investigates their origins and consequences, using tools from statistics, computer science, and mathematics. A recruring observation is that the nominal dimension of a data set, meaning the number of coordinates used to represent each point, is often a poor preditor of how hard the data are to analyze. Data may lie close to a low-dimensional manifold, may be strongly clustered, or may have rapidly decaying variance along most directions. Conversely, data in a low-dimensional ambient space can exhibit behavior typical of high dimension. This motivates the notion of intrinsic dimension: a quantity meant to capture the effective complexity of the data, independent of the particular representation. Numerous estimators have been proposed, among them PCA-based approaches, fractal and correlation dimensions, and nearest-neighbor-based maximum likelihood estimators. They are often useful in practice, but they rest on different assumptions and are usually justified heuristically. They may give inconsistent answers on the same data, and it is rarely clear which properties a reasonable notion of dimension should satisfy. From a mathematical perspective, a particularly illuminating explanation of the dimension curse is the concentration of measure phenomenon. In high-dimensional spaces such as spheres, cubes, or Gaussian spaces, every sufficiently regular function is almost constant on a set of nearly full measure. As a consequence, distances between random points concentrate around a typical value, and the contrast on which many ML algorithms rely vanishes. This link was recognized in the ML/KD literature, and it suggests that intrinsic dimennsion should be tied to concentration properties. Pestov developed this idea into an axiomatic approach: a dimension function for metric spaces with measure should, among other requirements, assign the expected dimension to standard objects, behave monotonically under suitable maps, and reflect the concentration phenomenon through a suitable observable diameter. Gromov's metric measure geometry supplies the framewrk for this, providing the notions of observable diameter, concentration function, and the distance between metric measure spaces. Pestov's approach was developed for idealized objects, namely metrc spaces with probability measures, whereas data sets are finite, may carry additional structure, and are analyzed by algorithms that use only certain featurs of that structure. The present work aims to bridge this gap. We introduce a model of a *geometric data set* that combines a metric measure space, which describes the geometry and distribution of the data, with a family of functions, or features, which describes what a given ML/KD algorithm can observe. This second ingredient makes the model adaptable: different algorithms, for intsance those using only linear functionals, Lipschitz functions, or the outputs of a given class of classifiers, correspond to different feature classes and therefore to different notions of intrinsic dimension. We define isomorphism of geometric data sets and study the set of isomorphism classes. Our first main contribution is structural. We introduce a metric on the set of isomorphism classes, inspired by the Gromov–Wasserstein and box distances, which makes it possible to quantify how close two data sets are, including a finite sample and the underlying distribution from which it is drawn. We also define a partial order, a form of domination, which expresses that one data set is a simplification of another, obtained through feature-preserving maps. We investigate the topological and order-theoretic properties of these objects, including compatibility between the order and the metric. Our second main contribution is an axiomatic treatment of intrinsic dimension for geometric data sets. Building on Pestov's axioms, we formulate requirements for a dimension function: monotonicity with respect to the partial order, continuity or stability with respect to the metric, normalization on reference examples, and consistency with measure concentration. We show that these requirements are mutually compatible by constructing a conncrete dimension function that satisfies them. The function is defined through the concentration behavior of the feature class, via a notion of separattion or observable diameter, and we prove its basic properties, including its behavior under products and its relation to the classical notion of dimension on model spaces. Third, we address computational feasibility. A definition that cannot be evaluated on real data would be of limited value to the ML/KD community. We show that our dimension function can be estmated from finite samples and we describe algorithms for doing so. Experiments on synthetic and real data sets illustrate that the resulting values reflect known intrinsic structure, that they respond sensibly to the choice of feature class, and that they correlate with the performance of specific algorithms, such as nearest-neighbor classification, on the data. A key challenge in this field is understanding the intrinsic structure and properties of the data, particularly in high-dimensional spaces. To address this challenge, a new framework has been developed for analyzing geometric datasets, which are defined as triples consisting of a metric space, a probability measure, and a class of real-valued functions on the space. This framework is grounded in the principles of metric measure geometry and Pestov's axioms, providing a powerful tool for understanding the properties of complex datasets. 

The organization of this work is as follows. Section 2 provides a review of the necessary background from metric measure geometry and Pestov's axioms, which form the foundation of the framework. Section 3 introduces the definition of geometric datasets, their isomorphism classes, and the metric and partial order used to compare them. Section 4 presents the axioms for intrinsic dimension and proves their properties, including monotonicity, continuity, normalization, concentration, and product behavior. Section 5 discusses estimation and computation, and Section 6 reports on experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. Finally, the work concludes with a discussion of limitations and future research directions. 

The framework is based on the concept of a geometric dataset, defined as a triple X = (X, d_X, μ_X), where (X, d_X) is a finite (or more generally compact) metric space, and μ_X is a Borel probability measure on X, accompanied by a class F_X of real-valued functions on X. Two geometric datasets are considered isomorphic if there exists a measure-preserving isometry between the supports of their measures that maps F_X onto F_Y. The set of isomorphism classes of geometric datasets is denoted by 𝒢. For a finite sample x_1,…,x_n, the empirical measure is used, optionally weighted, and the Euclidean metric or another task-appropriate metric is employed for d. To compare datasets of different sizes and ambient spaces, a Gromov-type approach is utilized, based on the Prokhorov and box distances. 

Let X and Y be geometric datasets. A parametrization of X is defined as a Borel map φ: [0,1] → X with φ_*λ = μ_X, where λ is the Lebesgue measure. The observable distance d_conc(X,Y) is defined as the infimum over parametrizations φ, ψ of d_H(φ^*F_X, ψ^*F_Y), where d_H is the Hausdorff distance between the pulled-back function classes, measured in the Ky Fan metric on measurable functions on [0,1]. This distance is of a concentration type, vanishing in the limit for Lévy families, and sensitive to the concentration behavior of the functions in F. It is shown that d_conc is a metric on 𝒢, and sequences of finite samples of a fixed compact geometric dataset converge to it in this metric when the empirical measures converge weakly. 

A partial order on geometric datasets is also introduced, based on the concept of domination. Dataset Y is said to dominate dataset X, written Y ≺ X, if there exists a 1-Lipschitz, measure-preserving map π: X → Y with F_Y ∘ π ⊆ F_X. This relation is reflexive and transitive and is antisymmetric on 𝒢 by an argument based on the rigidity of measure-preserving isometric embeddings of compact spaces. It is proven that ≺ is closed with respect to d_conc, which is necessary for the compatibility of the dimension function with limits. Intuitively, Y ≺ X implies that Y is a "compression" of X that loses no more concentration than the data itself carries. 

The framework is grounded in the concept of intrinsic dimension, a fundamental property of a geometric dataset. Following Pestov, an intrinsic dimension function is a map dim: 𝒢 → [0,∞) satisfying certain axioms, including monotonicity, continuity, normalization, concentration, and product behavior, as discussed in [1]. The consistency of subsets of these axioms is established, and it is shown that they are jointly satisfiable by the function constructed in this work. The construction of the dimension function is based on the principles outlined above, providing a rigorous foundation for understanding the intrinsic properties of complex datasets.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, accounting for nearly one third of all deaths each year [1]. Epidemiological studies have consistently shown that premenopausal women have a lower incidence of coronary heart disease, hypertension, and heart failure than age-matched men, and that this relative protection diminishes after menopause [2,3]. The incidence of cardiovascular events in women rises sharply in the decade following the cessation of ovarian function, eventually approaching that of men [4]. These observations have led to the long-standing hypothesis thhat endogenous ovarian hormones, particularly 17β-estradiol (E2), confer protection against cardiac injury and adverse remodeling. E2 is the most abundant and biologically potent estrogen in premenopausal women. Beyond its classical roles in reproductive physiology, E2 exerts pleiotropic effects on the cardiovascular system, including vasodilation, modulation of lipid metabolism, attenuation of inflammation, and inhibition of vascular smooth muscle proliferation [5,6]. In the myocardium, experimental studies indicate that E2 reduces cardiomyocyte apoptosis, limits infarct size after ischemia-reperfusion injury, attenuates pathological hypertrophy, and preseves mitochondrial function [7-9]. Ovariectomy in animal models aggravatse cardiac dysfunction after pressure overload or myocardial infarction, and these deleterious effects are largely reversed by E2 supplementation [10,11]. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of E2 in maintaining cardiac homeostasis in women of reproductive age. The biological actions of E2 are mediated primarily through estrogen receptors (ERs). Three ER subtypes have been identified in cardiomyocytes: the classical nuclear receptors ERα and ERβ, and the membrane-associated G protein-coupled estrogen receptor GPR30 (also known as GPER) [12,13]. ERα and ERβ are ligand-activated transcription factors encoded by separate genes, and they share a conserved structure comprising a DNA-binding domain and a ligand-binding domain. Upon E2 binding, they dimerize and translocate to the nucleus, where they regulate the transcription of target genes by binding to estrogen response elements or by interacting with other transcription factros such as AP-1 and Sp1 (the genomic pathway) [14]. In addition, a subpopulation of ERα and ERβ localizes at the plasma membrane and in caveolae, where it rapidly activates kinase cascades, including PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, and endothelial nitric oxide synthase signaling, within seconds to minutes (the nongenomic pathway) [15,16]. GPR30 further contributes to rapid estrogen signaling through the activation of adenylyl cyclase, transactivation of the epidermal growth faactor receptor, and mobilization of intracellular calcium [17]. The relative contribution of each receptor subtype to cardioprotection is context dependent, and accumulating evidence suggests that the receptors may act cooperatively or in a compensatory manner depending on the type of cardiac insult [18,19]. Given the apparent cardioprotective effects of E2, hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was initially promoted as a strategy for preventing CVD in postmenopausal women. Early observational studies supported this notion, reporting significant reductions in coronary events amnog HRT users [20]. However, large randomized controlld trials, notably the Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study and the Women's Health Initiative, failed to demonstrate cardiovascular benefit and instead reported increased risks of thromboembolism, stroke, breast cancer, and endometrial cancer [21,22]. Subsequent analyses have proposed the "timing hypothesis," which suggests that the cardiovascular effects of estrogen depend on the age of the patient and the time elappsed since menopause, with benefit observed when therapy is initiated early [23]. Nevertheless, safety concerns, particularly regarding hormone-dependent malignancies, have substantially limited the clinical use of conventional estrogen therapy and stimulated the search for safer alternatives. Phytoestrogens are plant-derived polyphenolic compounds whose structures resemble that of E2 and which can bind to ERs, with a generally higher affinity for ERβ than for ERα [24]. The major classes include isoflavones (genistein, daidzein), lignans, coumestans, and stilbenes such as resveratrol, which are abundant in soybeans, flaxseed, legumes, and grapes [25]. Populations consuming diets rich in these compounds, such as those in East Asia, display a lower incidence of CVD and fewer menopausal symptoms than Western populations [26]. Experimental studies have shown that phytoestrogens can reduce oxidative stress, improve endothelial function, inhibit cardiomyocyte apoptosis, and attenuate cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, in part through ER-dependent activation of PI3K/Akt and related survival pathways [27-29]. Because of their selective receptor binding and weaker estrogenic activity, phytoestrogens may behave as natural selective estrogen receptor modulators, potentially providing cardiovascular benefit with a reduced risk of adverse effects on the breast and uterus [30]. Clinical findings, however, remain inconsistent, reflecting variability in compounds, doses, study populations, and individual metabolism, such as the gut microbial conversion of daidzein to equol [31]. A better understanding of ER-mediated signaling in cardiomyocytes is therefore essential for the rational development of phytoestrogen-based therapies. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of estrogen and ER-mediated genomic and nongenomic pathways that underlie cardioprotection against diverse stresses. We further discuss the clinical implications of ERs and phytoestrogens and provide insights into the potential of phytoestrogens as alternatives in estrogen replacement therapy. This review was conducted as a narrative literature review following the genral principles of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) to promote transparency in literature identification, selection, and synthesis [1]. Because the topic spans basic molecular biology, preclinical models, and clinical studies, a narraive approach was chosen over a formal systematic review or meta-analysis, as heterogeneity in experimental designs, phytoestrogen preparations, doses, and outcome maesures precluded quantitative pooling [2]. **Literature search strategy** Relevant publications were identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase from database inception to the most recent search date. Searches combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text keywords using Boolean operators. Terms were grouped into four conceptual domains: (i) estrogen and receptors ("17β-estradiol", "estrogen receptor alpha", "estrogen receptor beta", "ERα", "ERβ", "GPR30", "GPER"); (ii) cardiac tissue and cell types ("cardiomyocyte", "heart", "myocardium", "cardiac"); (iii) cardiovascular conditions and stresses ("cardioprotection", "ischemia/reperfusion", "myocardial infarction", "hypertrophy", "heart failure", "apoptosis", "oxidative stress", "doxorubicin"); and (iv) phytoestrogens and therapy ("phytoestrogen", "isoflavone", "genistein", "daidzein", "equol", "resveratrol", "coumestrol", "lignan", "flavonoid", "hormone replacement therapy", "estrogen replacement"). Reference lists of key articles and previous reviews were hand-searched to identify additional studies not captured electronically [3]. Cinical trial registries were consulted to identify relevant completed trials on phytoestrogen supplementation and cardiovascular endpoints. **Eligibility criteria** Studies were included if they: (1) investigated the role of E2 or its receptors (ERα, ERβ, GPR30) in cardiomyocytes or cardiac tissue, inccluding genomic and nongenomic signaling; (2) examined cardioprotective effects of phytoestrogens or related compounds with demonstrated ER binding or ER-dependent activity; (3) reported clinical or epidemiological data on estrogen replacement therapy, ER polymorphisms, or phytoestrogen intake in relation to cardiovascular outcomes; or (4) were original research articles, clinical trials, meta-analyses, or high-quality reviews published in English. Priority was given to studies using ER-selective agonists or antagonists, receptor knockout or knockdown models, or ovariectomized animals, as these provide mechanistic evidence for receptor involvement [4]. Exclusion criteria were: studies focusing solely on non-cardiac tisues (e.g., breast, bone, or uterus) without relevance to cardiac signaling; reports on phytoestrogens lacking evidence of ER-related mechanisms; conference abstracts, editorials, and non-peer-reviewed material; and articles lacking sufficient methodological detail to interpret findings. Studies of vascular endothelium and smooth muscle were included selectively when they offered mechanistic insight applicable to cardiomyocyte signaling or helped contextualize clinical outcomes. **Study selection and data extraction** Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance, and full texts of potentially eligible articles were then evaluated against the criteria above. Disagreements regarding inclusion were resolved through discussion among the authors. For each included study, information was extracted on the experimental model (cell line, primary cardiomyocytes, isolated heart, animal species, or human population), the estrogenic compound and dose, the receptor subtype implicated, the cardic insult applied, the signaling pathways assessed, and the principal outcomes. For clinical studies, details on population characteristics (age, menopausal status), intervention duration, and cardiovascular endpoints were recorded [5]. **Thematic organization and synthesis** Extracted evidence was organized into thematic categories reflecting the structure of the review. The first category addressed the biosynthesis, physiology, and cardiac actions of E2, including receptor expression patterns in cardiomyocytes. The second covered receptor-specific signaling: genomic pathways involving ligand-dependent nuclear translocation of ERα and ERβ and transcriptional regulation via estrogen response elements, and nongenomic pathways involing membrane-associated ERs and GPR30, with activation of PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, nitric oxide synthase, and calcium-handling cascades [6,7]. The third examined protective effects against specific insults, including ischemia/reperfusion injury, pressure-overload hypertrophy, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity. The fourth critically appraised clinical evidence on estrogen repllacement therapy, incluuding the divergent findings of large randomized trials and observational studies and the "timing hypothesis" [8]. The fifth evaluated phytoestrogens, grouped by chemical class (isoflavones, stilbenes, lignans, coumestans), with attenttion to relative ER affinity, receptor subtype selectivity, metabolism (e.g., equol production by gut microbiota), and bioavailability [9]. Findings were synthesized qualitatively. Concordant and discordant results across models were compared, and differences were considered in light of species, sex, hormonal status, dose, and treatment timing. Where available, evidence from receptor-selective pharmacological tools and genetic models was weighted more heavily than correlative observations when inferring receptor-specific mechanisms. **Quality considerations and limitations** Formal risk-of-bias scoring was not applied given the narrative design; nevertheless, methodological strengths and weaknesses, such as sample size, presence of appropriate controls, use of physiological versus supraphysiological concentrations, and confounding in observational research, were considered when interpreting findings [10]. The global burden of cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains daunting, with approximately one third of all annual deaths attributed to this condition [1]. A wealth of epidemiological data indicates that premenopausal women exhibit a significantly lower risk of developing coronary heart disease, hypertension, and heart failure compared to their male counterparts of the same age, with this protective effect waning after menopause [2,3]. Notably, the incidence of cardiovascular events in women undergoes a sharp increase in the decade following the cessation of ovarian function, ultimately approaching that observed in men [4]. These findings have led to the longstanding hypothesis that the endogenous ovarian hormone 17β-estradiol (E2) plays a pivotal role in safeguarding against cardiac injury and adverse cardiac remodeling. As the most prevalent and biologically active estrogen in premenopausal women, E2 exerts a multitude of cardiovascular effects, including the promotion of vasodilation, the modulation of lipid metabolism, the attenuation of inflammation, and the inhibition of vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation [5,6]. Experimental studies have demonstrated that E2 exerts cardioprotective effects in the myocardium, including the reduction of cardiomyocyte apoptosis, the limitation of infarct size following ischemia-reperfusion injury, the attenuation of pathological cardiac hypertrophy, and the preservation of mitochondrial function [7-9]. Furthermore, ovarian hormone deprivation in animal models has been shown to exacerbate cardiac dysfunction after pressure overload or myocardial infarction, with these detrimental effects being largely mitigated by E2 supplementation [10,11]. These collective findings underscore the crucial role of E2 in maintaining cardiac homeostasis in women of reproductive age. The biological actions of E2 are primarily mediated through estrogen receptors (ERs), which are expressed in cardiomyocytes. Three distinct ER subtypes have been identified, namely the classical nuclear receptors ERα and ERβ, and the membrane-associated G protein-coupled estrogen receptor GPR30 (also known as GPER) [12,13]. ERα and ERβ are ligand-activated transcription factors encoded by separate genes, and they share a highly conserved structural motif comprising a DNA-binding domain and a ligand-binding domain. Upon binding to E2, these receptors dimerize and translocate to the nucleus, where they regulate the transcription of target genes by binding to estrogen response elements or by interacting with other transcription factors, such as AP-1 and Sp1, thereby activating the genomic pathway [14]. In addition to their genomic effects, a subset of ERα and ERβ receptors localizes to the plasma membrane and caveolae, where they rapidly activate kinase cascades, including the PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, and endothelial nitric oxide synthase signaling pathways, within a timeframe of seconds to minutes, thereby engaging the nongenomic pathway [15,16]. GPR30 further contributes to rapid estrogen signaling through the activation of adenylyl cyclase, the transactivation of the epidermal growth factor receptor, and the mobilization of intracellular calcium [17]. The relative contribution of each receptor subtype to cardioprotection is context-dependent, and accumulating evidence suggests that these receptors may act cooperatively or in a compensatory manner, depending on the nature of the cardiac insult [18,19]. Given the apparent cardioprotective effects of E2, hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was initially promoted as a strategy for preventing CVD in postmenopausal women. Early observational studies supported this notion, reporting significant reductions in coronary events among HRT users [20]. However, large randomized controlled trials, notably the Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study and the Women's Health Initiative, failed to demonstrate a cardiovascular benefit and instead reported increased risks of thromboembolism, stroke, breast cancer, and endometrial cancer [21,22]. Subsequent analyses have proposed the "timing hypothesis," which suggests that the cardiovascular effects of estrogen are contingent upon the age of the patient and the time elapsed since menopause, with benefit observed when therapy is initiated early [23]. Nevertheless, safety concerns, particularly regarding hormone-dependent malignancies, have substantially limited the clinical use of conventional estrogen therapy and stimulated the search for safer alternatives. Phytoestrogens, plant-derived polyphenolic compounds whose molecular structures resemble that of E2, have been proposed as potential alternatives. These compounds can bind to ERs, with a generally higher affinity for ERβ than for ERα [24]. The primary classes of phytoestrogens include isoflavones (genistein, daidzein), lignans, coumestans, and stilbenes, such as resveratrol, which are abundant in soybeans, flaxseed, legumes, and grapes [25]. Populations consuming diets rich in these compounds, such as those in East Asia, exhibit a lower incidence of CVD and fewer menopausal symptoms than Western populations [26]. Experimental studies have demonstrated that phytoestrogens can reduce oxidative stress, improve endothelial function, inhibit cardiomyocyte apoptosis, and attenuate cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, in part through ER-dependent activation of PI3K/Akt and related survival pathways [27-29]. Due to their selective receptor binding and weaker estrogenic activity, phytoestrogens may behave as natural selective estrogen receptor modulators, potentially providing cardiovascular benefit with a reduced risk of adverse effects on the breast and uterus [30]. However, clinical findings on phytoestrogens remain inconsistent, reflecting variability in compounds, doses, study populations, and individual metabolism, such as the gut microbial conversion of daidzein to equol [31]. A more comprehensive understanding of ER-mediated signaling in cardiomyocytes is therefore essential for the rational development of phytoestrogen-based therapies. To ensure the incorporation of high-quality studies, stringent eligibility criteria were established. Studies were deemed eligible if they: (1) investigated the role of estrogen or its receptors in cardiomyocytes or cardiac tissue, encompassing both genomic and nongenomic signaling pathways; (2) examined the cardioprotective effects of phytoestrogens or related compounds with demonstrated estrogen receptor binding or estrogen receptor-dependent activity; (3) reported clinical or epidemiological data pertaining to estrogen replacement therapy, estrogen receptor polymorphisms, or phytoestrogen intake in relation to cardiovascular outcomes; or (4) were original research articles, clinical trials, meta-analyses, or high-quality reviews published in the English language. The process of study selection and data extraction involved an initial screening of titles and abstracts for relevance, followed by a comprehensive evaluation of potentially eligible articles against the predetermined criteria. In the case of clinical studies, data were recorded on population characteristics, such as age and menopausal status, intervention duration, and cardiovascular endpoints [5].

To organize and synthesize the extracted evidence, a thematic approach was employed, categorizing the studies into five primary themes. The first theme addressed the biosynthesis, physiology, and cardiac actions of estrogen, including patterns of receptor expression in cardiomyocytes. The second theme delved into receptor-specific signaling, encompassing both genomic pathways, which involve ligand-dependent nuclear translocation of ERα and ERβ and transcriptional regulation via estrogen response elements, and nongenomic pathways, which involve membrane-associated estrogen receptors and GPR30, with activation of PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, nitric oxide synthase, and calcium-handling cascades [6,7]. The fourth theme critically appraised clinical evidence on estrogen replacement therapy, including the disparate findings of large randomized trials and observational studies, as well as the "timing hypothesis" [8]. The phenomenon of pregnancy loss is a pervasive and intricate issue that affects a substantial proportion of human pregnancies, exerting a profound impact on the physical and emotional welfare of those affected. The spontaneous termination of a pregnancy prior to the stage at which the fetus is capable of surviving outside the womb, referred to as miscarriage or spontaneous abortion, occurs in approximately 15-20% of pregnancies that have been clinically confirmed [1,2]. However, when biochemical pregnancies and losses that occur prior to clinical recognition are taken into account, the actual incidence of pregnancy loss is significantly higher, with estimates suggesting that up to 50% of all conceptions may fail to progress to a viable pregnancy [3]. The majority of isolated miscarriages can be attributed to random chromosomal anomalies in the embryo, which are unlikely to recur. Nevertheless, a subset of women experiences repeated pregnancy losses, a condition known as recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA), recurrent miscarriage, or habitual abortion. Traditionally, RSA has been defined as the occurrence of three or more consecutive pregnancy losses prior to the twentieth week of gestation [4]. However, certain professional organizations, including the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology, have proposed a revised threshold of two or more losses as a criterion for initiating evaluation, acknowledging the substantial emotional toll and the clinical value of earlier investigation [5,6]. According to the traditional definition, RSA affects approximately 1% of couples attempting to conceive, whereas around 2-5% experience two or more losses [2,7]. The risk of subsequent miscarriage increases in conjunction with the number of previous losses and advancing maternal age, rendering a history of repeated loss an independent predictor of further pregnancy failure [8]. Beyond the physical risks, RSA is associated with considerable psychological distress, including anxiety, depression, and grief, as well as a significant burden on healthcare resources [9]. The etiology of RSA is multifaceted and, in many cases, remains incompletely understood. Established causes include parental chromosomal abnormalities, uterine anatomical defects such as septa, fibroids, and intrauterine adhesions, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and other immunological disturbances, infections, thrombophilic states, environmental and lifestyle factors, and endocrine disorders [4,10]. Despite exhaustive evaluation, no underlying cause is identified in approximately half of couples, and this unexplained group continues to pose a significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenge [10]. Endocrine abnormalities are thought to account for roughly 8-12% of cases, making them one of the more common and potentially treatable contributors to RSA [11]. The successful implantation and maintenance of early pregnancy depend on a delicately coordinated hormonal environment. Following ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone and estrogen, which transform the endometrium into a receptive decidua, suppress uterine contractility, and modulate the maternal immune response toward tolerance of the semi-allogeneic conceptus [12]. Thyroid hormones, insulin, prolactin, and androgens also influence follicular development, oocyte quality, endometrial receptivity, and placental function [13]. Disruption of any component of this regulatory network may compromise implantation, trophoblast invasion, or early embryonic development, leading to pregnancy loss. Several endocrine conditions have been implicated in RSA, including polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), the most common endocrinopathy of reproductive-age women, characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and frequently insulin resistance and obesity, which has been associated with an increased risk of early miscarriage [14,15]. Hyperprolactinemia may impair folliculogenesis and corpus luteum function, and dopamine agonist treatment has been reported to improve pregnancy outcome in affected women [16]. Luteal phase defect, an inadequate progesterone-mediated endometrial secretory response, has long been proposed as a cause of implantation failure and early loss, although its diagnostic criteria and clinical significance remain debated [17]. Thyroid dysfunction, both overt and subclinical hypothyroidism as well as thyroid autoimmunity, has been linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes, including miscarriage [18,19]. Diabetes mellitus with poor glycemic control during the periconceptional period increases the risk of miscarriage and congenital malformations through metabolic disturbance of the developing embryo [20]. Hyperandrogenism, whether of ovarian or adrenal origin, may adversely affect endometrial receptivity and early placentation [21]. The relationship between these endocrine disorders and RSA is complex and not fully understood, with studies often yielding conflicting results due to differences in diagnostic criteria, sample sizes, and control populations [14]. It is essential to distinguish cause from association, as in the case of PCOS, where obesity, insulin resistance, and elevated luteinizing hormone may each contribute independently [14]. Likewise, the benefit of interventions such as progesterone supplementation, levothyroxine, metformin, and dopamine agonists remains controversial in some settings [22,23]. The clinical significance of clarifying the role of endocrine dysfunction in RSA cannot be overstated. Many of these conditions are readily detectable and treatable, and appropriate screening and management could improve the live birth rate in affected couples. In this context, the present article provides a comprehensive review of the role of endocrine dysfunction in patients with recurrent spontaneous abortion. Relevant publications were identified through electronic databases, including PubMed and Google Scholar, using key words related to recurrent miscarriage and specific endocrine abnormalities. The findings were then grouped according to the individual disorders, namely PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction, diabetes, and hyperandrogenism. The intricate relationships between these endocrine conditions and RSA are examined in detail, with a focus on the underlying mechanisms, diagnostic challenges, and potential therapeutic strategies. By elucidating the complex interplay between endocrine dysfunction and RSA, this review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the role of endocrine disorders in recurrent pregnancy loss, ultimately informing the development of effective diagnostic and therapeutic approaches to improve outcomes for affected couples. The importance ofIFT analysis in the diagnosis of RSA is also highlighted, as well as the need for a multidisciplinary approach to the management of affected couples. Furthermore, the review discusses the potential benefits and limitations of various interventions, including progesterone supplementation, levothyroxine, metformin, and dopamine agonists, and emphasizes the need for further research to clarify their role in the management of RSA. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between endocrine dysfunction and RSA is essential for the development of effective therapeutic strategies to improve outcomes for affected couples. This involved devising a robust search strategy, delineating explicit criteria for study inclusion, and systematically synthesizing the extracted data (1, 2). The initial phase of our investigation entailed a meticulous search of various electronic databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar, supplemented by additional resources accessible through our institutional library. Our search parameters were calibrated to capture all relevant articles published within the databases from their inception up to the point of our final search, thereby maximizing the breadth of our query. To enhance the sensitivity of our search, we strategically combined controlled vocabulary terms, specifically Medical Subject Headings (MeSH), and free-text terms related to Recurrent Spontaneous Abortion (RSA), endocrine dysfunction, and specific endocrine disorders such as polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperandrogenism, hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction, and diabetes mellitus. The employment of Boolean operators (AND, OR) allowed us to expand our search capabilities, facilitating the identification of articles through combinations such as "recurrent miscarriage AND thyroid" or "recurrent pregnancy loss AND (insulin resistance OR diabetes)." Furthermore, to ensure comprehensiveness, we manually searched the reference lists of pertinent reviews, guidelines, and original studies to uncover any additional publications that might have eluded our electronic search (3).

To maintain consistency and clarity throughout our review, we pre-defined key terms. RSA was defined as three or more consecutive spontaneous pregnancy losses prior to the 20th week of gestation, aligning with traditional definitions (4). However, in acknowledgment of evolving definitions recommended by certain professional societies (5, 6), we also included studies that defined RSA as two or more losses, provided the criteria were clearly articulated and the findings were interpreted with this distinction in mind. Miscarriage was defined as the spontaneous loss of a fetus before viability. Our eligibility criteria were deliberately broad to encompass a wide array of studies examining the relationship between endocrine abnormalities and RSA or recurrent pregnancy loss. This included original research studies (encompassing case-control, cohort, cross-sectional, and randomized controlled studies), meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and clinical practice guidelines that involved human participants and were published in the English language.

The endocrine conditions considered within our review spanned PCOS, hyperandrogenism, hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction (including overt and subclinical hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, and thyroid autoimmunity), and diabetes mellitus, as well as disturbances in glucose metabolism. Studies that exclusively focused on anatomical, genetic, infectious, or immunological causes of RSA without an endocrine component, along with case reports, editorials, conference abstracts lacking full text, and letters devoid of original data, were excluded from our analysis. Additionally, we excluded studies concerned with sporadic single miscarriage, induced abortion, or stillbirth beyond 20 weeks, as well as animal or in vitro studies, unless they provided crucial mechanistic insights. In instances where overlapping datasets were identified, the most complete or most recent report was retained.

The process of study selection was undertaken in two stages. Initially, we screened the titles and abstracts retrieved from our searches for relevance. Full texts of potentially eligible articles were then obtained and assessed against our predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Any disagreements regarding eligibility were resolved through discussion among the authors, with consensus being the ultimate determinant. We placed a premium on recent publications, large well-designed studies, randomized trials, and meta-analyses, while also retaining seminal older studies that provided foundational evidence or addressed gaps in the literature where more contemporary data were scarce.

For each publication included in our review, we extracted detailed information, including the first author and year, country of origin, study design, sample size, characteristics of the study population, diagnostic criteria for the endocrine disorder in question, main findings (such as prevalence in women with RSA, odds ratios or relative risks for pregnancy loss, and pertinent hormonal parameters), and any reported effects of treatment on pregnancy outcomes. We then aggregated the results of our separate searches and categorized them according to the specific endocrine abnormality under consideration, namely PCOS and hyperandrogenism, hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction, and diabetes mellitus. Within each category, the evidence was organized to address epidemiology, proposed pathophysiological mechanisms, diagnostic evaluation, and management strategies (7).

Given the narrative nature of our review, we did not apply a formal quality scoring tool. Instead, we conducted a qualitative assessment of the strength of evidence, taking into account study design, sample size, the presence and adequacy of control groups, the clarity and specificity of diagnostic definitions, and the adjustment for potential confounders such as maternal age, body mass index, and the number of previous pregnancy losses. We noted and discussed discrepancies among studies, such as variations in reference ranges for thyrotropin or differences in the definition of luteal phase defect, as potential sources of heterogeneity. Our findings were synthesized in a descriptive manner, with areas of controversy or insufficient evidence being explicitly identified to guide recommendations for future research (8).

As our review relied solely on previously published data and did not involve direct contact with human participants, the need for ethical approval and informed consent was obviated. Human pose estimation, the task of localizing the body joints of a person in an image or video, is a fundamental problem in computer vision with applications in action recognition, human-computer interaction, surveillance, and animation. Over the past few years, deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have dramatically advanced the accuracy of pose estimation on static images. Among the most successful designs are multi-stage architectures, such as Convolutional Pose Machines and stacked hourglass networks, in which a sequence of CNN stages progressively refines the joint confidence maps predicted by the preceding stage. Each stage takes the image evidence together with the previous belief maps and produces a more accuraet estimate, so that long-range dependencies among joints are implicitly captured through large effective receptive fields. Despite this success on still images, applying these models to vdeos remains unsatisfactory. The most direct approach is to run a single-image model independently on every frame. This has three main drawbacks. First, it is computationally expensive: a multi-stage network must be fully evaluated for each frame, and the cost grows lineary with the number of stages. Second, frame-wise prediction ignores the temporal structure of video. Adjacent frammes show nearly the same pose, yet independent predictions are not constrained to agree, which produces jittering outputs and visible flicker. Third, video frames frequently suffer from motion blur, defocus, self-occlusion, and unusual viewpoints. A model that sees only one frame has no means of recovering from such degradation, whereas a human observer easily infers the hidden or blurred joint position from preceding frames. Together, these problems cause performance degeneration and make the predictions inconsistent over time. Previous attempts to address video pose estimation usually add post-processing or explicit tempporal modeling on top of single-frame networks. Examples include optical flow to propagate predictions between frames, graphical models or tracking-by-detection frameworks that enforce smoothness, and spatio-temporal convolutions over stacked frames. These approaches typically require additional components, such as flow estimators, which are expensive and prone to error under exactly the conditions (blur, occlusion) where help is most needed. They also treat temporal reasoning as separate from the pose network itself, which complicates training and inference. In this paper, we propose a different view. We observe that if the weights of the stages in a multi-stage CNN are shared, the network becomes equivalent to a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) unrolled over stages: each stage applies the same transformation to the previous belief maps and the image features. Under this view, stage-wise refinement is simply a recurrent computation. This observation has two important consequences. First, it decouples the stages from one another. Rather than running every stage on every frame, the recurrence can be unrolled along the time axis of the video, so that eaach new frame needs only one pass through the shared module, with the refinement carried over from earlier frames. This yields a significant speedup when processing video. Second, the recurrent formulation allows us to insert Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units naturally, so that the refinement is performed across vido frames instead of across redundant stages of a single frame. We call the resulting model the LSTM Pose Machine. It consists of a fully convolutional feature extractor, an initial prediction module, and a recurrent refinement module with convolutional LSTM units whose parameters are shared across all frames. At each time step, the network receives the current frame, and the LSTM combines the current image evidence wth its memory of earlier frames and earlier predictions to output the joint confidence maps. The memory cells thus accumulate information about the pose and motion of the person over time. This imposes geometric consistency acrooss frames, because the prediction at one time step is conditioned on the state summarizing the past, and it improves robustness to degraded inputs, since information from clean frames can compensate for blurred or occluded ones. The whole system is trained end to end with supervision on every frame, without optical flow or any other external motion model. We evaluate our approach on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks and show that it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in accuracy while also being considerably faster than repeatedly invoking a multi-stage CNN on each frame. Qualitative results demonstrate that our predictions are visibly more stable and remain accurate under motion blur and occlusion. Beyond reporting performance, we also look inside the network and analyze the memory cells of the LSTM. Our analysis shows that different cells specialize in encoding information such as the motion direction of paritcular body parts and the spatial configuration of the joints, providing insight into why such a memory mechanism benefits pose estimation in video. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows. (1) We show that a multi-stage CNN with shared weights can be rewritten as an RNN, and exploit this to decouple the stages and greatly reduce the computation for video. (2) We introduce LSTM units between frames, yielding a model that enforces temporal and geoometric consistency and handles quality degradation. (3) We achieve state-of-the-art results on two large-scale video benchmarks. (4) We analyze the learned memory cells to explain the behavior of the model.
