This technology has far-reaching implications for various fields, including the recognition of actions, interaction between humans and computers, surveillance, and animation. In recent years, substantial progress has been made in enhancing the accuracy of pose estimation in static images, primarily attributed to the development of deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) [1]. Among the most effective architectural designs are those that employ a multi-stage approach, such as Convolutional Pose Machines [2] and stacked hourglass networks [3], which iteratively refine the confidence maps of joints through a series of CNN stages. Each stage takes into consideration the visual evidence from the image, as well as the prior belief maps, to produce a more accurate estimate. This process enables the implicit capture of long-range dependencies between joints through the utilization of large effective receptive fields. However, the application of these models to video sequences has yielded less satisfactory results. The most straightforward approach to video pose estimation involves applying a single-image model independently to each frame, but this method has several significant drawbacks [4]. Firstly, it is computationally intensive, as a multi-stage network must be fully evaluated for each frame, resulting in a computational cost that increases linearly with the number of stages. Secondly, the frame-wise prediction approach neglects the temporal structure of the video, leading to independent predictions that are not constrained to be consistent, thereby resulting in jittering outputs and visible flicker. Furthermore, video frames often suffer from degradation due to motion blur, defocus, self-occlusion, and unusual viewpoints, all of which can cause a model that only considers one frame to struggle with recovering from such degradation. In contrast, human observers can easily infer the position of hidden or blurred joints from preceding frames. Previous attempts to address the challenge of video pose estimation have typically involved incorporating post-processing techniques or explicit temporal modeling on top of single-frame networks [5]. Examples of such approaches include the use of optical flow to propagate predictions between frames [6], graphical models or tracking-by-detection frameworks that enforce smoothness [7], and spatio-temporal convolutions over stacked frames [8]. However, these approaches often require additional components, such as flow estimators, which can be computationally expensive and prone to error under the exact conditions (e.g., blur, occlusion) where they are most needed. Moreover, these methods treat temporal reasoning as a separate entity from the pose network itself, which can complicate both the training and inference processes. In this paper, we propose a novel perspective on this problem. We observe that if the weights of the stages in a multi-stage CNN are shared, the network becomes equivalent to a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) unrolled over stages [9]. Each stage applies the same transformation to the prior belief maps and the image features, effectively rendering the stage-wise refinement a recurrent computation. This observation has two important implications. Firstly, it decouples the stages from one another, allowing us to unroll the recurrence along the temporal axis of the video. As a result, each new frame only needs to pass through the shared module once, with the refinement carried over from earlier frames, yielding a significant speedup when processing video. Secondly, the recurrent formulation enables us to naturally integrate Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units [10], so that the refinement is performed across video frames instead of across redundant stages of a single frame. We refer to the resulting model as the LSTM Pose Machine, which consists of a fully convolutional feature extractor, an initial prediction module, and a recurrent refinement module with convolutional LSTM units whose parameters are shared across all frames. At each time step, the network receives the current frame, and the LSTM combines the current visual evidence with its memory of earlier frames and earlier predictions to output the joint confidence maps. The memory cells accumulate information about the pose and motion of the person over time, imposing geometric consistency across frames and improving robustness to degraded inputs. The entire system is trained end-to-end with supervision on every frame, without the need for optical flow or any other external motion model [11]. We evaluate our approach on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks and demonstrate that it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, while also being considerably faster than repeatedly invoking a multi-stage CNN on each frame [12]. Qualitative results show that our predictions are visibly more stable and remain accurate under motion blur and occlusion. Beyond reporting performance, we also analyze the memory cells of the LSTM to gain insight into why such a memory mechanism benefits pose estimation in video [13]. Our analysis reveals that different cells specialize in encoding information such as the motion direction of particular body parts and the spatial configuration of the joints, providing a deeper understanding of the strengths of our approach and highlighting the potential of recurrent neural networks for modeling temporal dependencies. The key to our approach lies in the ability of the LSTM to capture and exploit the temporal structure of the video, allowing for more accurate and robust pose estimation. By leveraging the recurrent nature of the LSTM, we can effectively model the temporal relationships between frames and improve the overall performance of the pose estimation system. Furthermore, the use of convolutional LSTM units enables us to capture spatial and temporal dependencies simultaneously, resulting in a more comprehensive understanding of the pose and motion of the person in the video. The implications of our approach extend beyond the realm of pose estimation, as it demonstrates the potential of recurrent neural networks for modeling complex temporal dependencies in a variety of applications. In conclusion, our proposed approach, the LSTM Pose Machine, offers a novel and effective solution for video pose estimation, leveraging the strengths of recurrent neural networks and convolutional neural networks to achieve state-of-the-art performance and robustness. The processing of video data has been a long-standing challenge in the field of computer vision, with applications in various domains such as surveillance, animation, human-computer interaction, and action recognition. A key aspect of video analysis is pose estimation, which involves identifying the spatial configuration of a person or object in a sequence of images. Recently, significant advances have been made in this area, particularly with the introduction of deep learning-based methods. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of our research, which explores the application of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to pose estimation in video data.

Our contributions are multifaceted and can be summarized as follows. Firstly, we demonstrate the equivalence between a multi-stage convolutional neural network (CNN) with shared weights and an RNN, allowing us to exploit this relationship to enhance the efficiency of video data processing. Secondly, we propose a novel architecture, termed the LSTM Pose Machine, which leverages the capabilities of long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to model temporal dependencies and improve pose estimation accuracy in video sequences. Thirdly, we provide an in-depth analysis of the LSTM's memory cells, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms that enable our approach to achieve state-of-the-art performance in video pose estimation [14].

The significance of our work lies in its potential to facilitate the development of more accurate and efficient pose estimation systems, which can be applied to a wide range of fields. For instance, the LSTM Pose Machine has been shown to be effective in scenarios where the video data is corrupted by noise or where the pose of the person is partially occluded [14]. The ability of the LSTM to accumulate information over time and enforce geometric consistency across frames is particularly valuable in such cases. Furthermore, the use of convolutional LSTM units enables the model to capture spatial dependencies in the data, which is essential for accurate pose estimation.

As we push the frontiers of video pose estimation, it has become increasingly clear that conventional methods, which treat each frame as a standalone image, are no longer adequate. The intricate relationships between frames, both in terms of time and geometry, are crucial for achieving precision and coherence in the results. In response to this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that builds upon the Convolutional Pose Machine (CPM) [1], a multi-stage convolutional neural network (CNN) that has demonstrated exceptional performance in estimating poses from single images. Our proposed method, the LSTM Pose Machine, incorporates several key innovations: (1) it significantly reduces the computational burden associated with video processing by leveraging shared weights across frames, (2) it ensures temporal and geometric consistency by integrating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units between frames, and (3) it achieves state-of-the-art performance on two large-scale video benchmarks [2, 3]. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the learned memory cells, offering valuable insights into the model's behavior [4]. 

To contextualize our approach, let us first revisit the architecture of the CPM. Given an input image, the objective is to predict confidence maps for a specified number of body parts, plus the background. The CPM consists of multiple stages, where each stage applies a fully convolutional network to the image, resulting in belief maps. The first stage processes the image to produce initial belief maps, while subsequent stages refine these maps by taking into account both the image features and the belief maps from the preceding stage. This process is governed by a stage-specific convolutional module and is supervised by an L2 loss function, which helps to mitigate the issue of vanishing gradients through intermediate supervision [5]. However, when applied to videos, this architecture requires running all stages for each frame, leading to high computational costs and neglecting the valuable temporal information between frames.

To address these limitations, we introduce a mechanism for sharing weights across stages, effectively transforming the CPM into a recurrent neural network (RNN). By sharing parameters, the refinement process becomes more efficient, allowing the model to process each frame using the state from the previous frame rather than requiring multiple independent stages. This not only reduces computational costs but also enables refinement to occur over time, leveraging temporal information. Furthermore, weight sharing reduces the number of parameters, making the model more efficient.

Building on this concept, the LSTM Pose Machine replaces the simple recurrence over belief maps with a convolutional LSTM. For each frame, the input consists of the image features and the previous belief maps. The LSTM maintains a memory cell and a hidden state, updated according to the standard LSTM equations [6]. The use of convolutions in the gates preserves the spatial structure of the input, enabling the memory cell to retain spatial information aligned with the image. The belief maps for each frame are obtained by applying convolutional layers to the hidden state. The gates of the LSTM control the flow of information: the input gate regulates the amount of new information written to the memory cell, the forget gate determines how long previous information is retained, and the output gate controls what information is used for prediction. The full network comprises three primary components: (1) a feature extractor that computes image features, shared across frames; (2) an initial module that produces first-pass belief maps; and (3) the LSTM module, which refines these maps using the memory from earlier frames. Since the same parameters are applied at every frame, the model can handle sequences of arbitrary length. The memory cell is crucial for enforcing geometric consistency, stabilizing outputs against frame-to-frame variability and providing evidence from earlier frames about the likely location and appearance of joints that may be blurred or occluded in the current frame.

To train the model, we utilize backpropagation through time, which allows us to efficiently compute gradients and update the model parameters. This approach enables the model to learn from large datasets and to adapt to the complexities of real-world videos. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the LSTM Pose Machine in achieving state-of-the-art results on challenging video pose estimation benchmarks [2, 3]. Moreover, our analysis of the learned memory cells provides insights into how the model captures temporal and geometric relationships, shedding light on the importance of these factors in video pose estimation [4]. 

The implications of this work are significant, as it paves the way for more accurate and efficient pose estimation systems. The ability to leverage temporal information and enforce geometric consistency opens up new avenues for applications in fields such as sports analysis, healthcare, and human-computer interaction. Furthermore, the LSTM Pose Machine's capability to handle sequences of arbitrary length makes it a versatile tool for a wide range of video analysis tasks. As we continue to develop and refine this technology, we look forward to exploring its potential uses and contributing to the advancement of the field. The LSTM Pose Machine is a powerful tool, and we believe it has the potential to make a significant impact in the field of pose estimation. We hope that our work will be of interest to researchers and practitioners, and that it will contribute to the development of more accurate and efficient pose estimation systems. 

In conclusion, the LSTM Pose Machine represents a significant advancement in video pose estimation, offering a powerful tool for capturing the complexities of human movement in videos. Its ability to leverage temporal information, enforce geometric consistency, and handle sequences of arbitrary length makes it an invaluable asset for a wide range of applications. As we move forward, we are excited to explore further applications of this technology and to continue advancing the state-of-the-art in pose estimation. With its potential to improve accuracy, efficiency, and consistency, the LSTM Pose Machine is poised to make a lasting impact in the field, and we look forward to seeing its continued development and application in the years to come.

Dementia is a progressive neurodegenerative syndrome characterized by decline in memory, reasoning, language, and the capacity for independent living. Alzheimer's disease (AD) accounts for the majority of cases, and the number of affected individuals is rising rapidly as populations age. Despite decades of research, available therapies remain larely symptomatic. Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitors such as donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, together with the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist memantine, temporarily alleviiate symptoms but do not hlt disease progression, and their use is often limited by gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and other adverse effects. There is therefore considerable interest in safer, food-derived materials that can help prevent or delay cognitive decline. The cholinergic system plays a central role in learning and memory, and cholinergic deficits in the hippocampus and cortex are an early feature of AD. Scopolamine, a muscarinic receptor antagonist, disrupts cholinergic transmission and induces transient amnesia in rodents and humans. It also increases oxidative stress in the brain by elevating lipid peroxidation and reducing the activity of endogenous antioxidant enzymes. For these reasons, the scopolamine-induced amnesia model is widely used to screen compounds with potential cognitive-enhancing effects. Behavioral tests such as the Morris water maze, which evaluates spatial leaarning and memory, and the pasisve avoidance test, which evaluates associative fear memory, are commonly used to assess memory function in this model. At the molecular level, memory formation depends on signaling cascades in the hippocampus. Activation of extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) leads to phosphorylation of the cAMMP response element-binding protein (CREB), a transcription factor that prootes expression of genes involved in synaptic plasticity and neuronal survival. One of its major targets is brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which spports neuronal growth, differentiation, and long-term potentiation. Reduced levels of p-ERK, p-CREB, and BDNF have been reported in AD brains and in scopolamine-treated animals, and oxidative stress is known to impiar this pathway. Antioxidants that reduce oxidative damage may therefore preserve ERK–CREB–BDNF signaling and protect cognitive function. Spirulina (Arthrospira) is a filamentous cyanobacterium that has long been consumed as a food and dietary supplement. Spirulina maxima is rich in protein, essential fatty acids, vitamins, minerals, and pigments, including phycocyanin, chlorophyll, and carotenoids. Extracts of Spirulina have been reported to exert antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and neuroprotective effects. Among its constituents, β-carotene is one of the most abundant and best-characterized antioxidants. Epidemiological and experimental studies suggest that carotenoids may be associated with reduced cognitive decline, owing to their ability to quench singlet oxygen and scavenge free radicals. However, direct evidence that β-carotene improves memory in animal models of dementia remains scarce, and its contribution to the bioactivity of Spirulina has not been clarified. The devastating consequences of dementia, a complex neurodegenerative disorder, are becoming increasingly evident as the global population ages, with Alzheimer's disease (AD) being the primary cause of this debilitating condition [1]. Despite extensive research spanning several decades, the current therapeutic options for AD are predominantly focused on alleviating symptoms, rather than halting the progression of the disease [2]. The most commonly prescribed medications, including acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, as well as the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist memantine, often have limited efficacy and are plagued by adverse effects, including gastrointestinal and cardiovascular complications [3]. Consequently, there is a growing interest in exploring safer, naturally derived compounds that can potentially prevent or delay cognitive decline. The cholinergic system plays a pivotal role in regulating learning and memory, and disruptions to this system, particularly in the hippocampus and cortex, are a hallmark of AD [4]. The muscarinic receptor antagonist scopolamine has been shown to induce transient amnesia in both rodents and humans, while also increasing oxidative stress in the brain by promoting lipid peroxidation and diminishing the activity of endogenous antioxidant enzymes [5, 6]. As a result, the scopolamine-induced amnesia model has become a widely accepted paradigm for screening compounds with potential cognitive-enhancing properties [7]. Behavioral assessments, including the Morris water maze, which evaluates spatial learning and memory, and the passive avoidance test, which assesses associative fear memory, are commonly employed to evaluate memory function in this model [8]. At the molecular level, the formation of memories is contingent upon the activation of signaling cascades in the hippocampus, including the extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathway, which culminates in the phosphorylation of the cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB), a transcription factor that regulates the expression of genes involved in synaptic plasticity and neuronal survival [9]. One of the primary targets of CREB is brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which supports neuronal growth, differentiation, and long-term potentiation [10]. Notably, reduced levels of p-ERK, p-CREB, and BDNF have been observed in AD brains and in scopolamine-treated animals, and oxidative stress has been shown to impair this pathway [11]. Antioxidants that mitigate oxidative damage may therefore preserve ERK-CREB-BDNF signaling and protect cognitive function [12]. Spirulina, a filamentous cyanobacterium, has been consumed as a food and dietary supplement for centuries, and is renowned for its exceptional nutritional profile, including high levels of protein, essential fatty acids, vitamins, minerals, and pigments such as phycocyanin, chlorophyll, and carotenoids [13, 14]. Extracts of Spirulina have been reported to exhibit antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and neuroprotective effects [15]. Among its constituents, β-carotene is one of the most abundant and well-characterized antioxidants, and epidemiological and experimental studies suggest that carotenoids may be associated with reduced cognitive decline, owing to their ability to quench singlet oxygen and scavenge free radicals [16, 17]. However, direct evidence demonstrating the ability of β-carotene to improve memory in animal models of dementia is scarce, and its contribution to the bioactivity of Spirulina remains unclear [18]. Fermentation with lactic acid bacteria is a traditional and safe bioprocess that can enhance the functional properties of food materials, including the degradation of cell walls and macromolecules, the release of bound phenolics and pigments, and the production of new metabolites such as peptides and organic acids, ultimately increasing bioavailability and bioactivity [19, 20]. Fermented plant and algal materials have been shown to exhibit stronger antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective activities than their unfermented counterparts [21]. Spirulina's rigid cell wall composition and strong characteristic odor limit its use in foods, and fermentation could potentially improve both its sensory qualities and functional value [22]. Lactobacillus plantarum strains are widely used for fermentation purposes due to their robust growth, generally recognized as safe status, and beneficial metabolic capacity [23]. Some L. plantarum strains have been reported to influence brain function through the gut-brain axis, suggesting that fermentation with these organisms may offer additional benefits [24]. Nevertheless, the effect of fermented S. maxima extract on memory impairment has not been investigated. In a previous screening, we found that S. maxima extract fermented with L. plantarum HY-08 exhibited enhanced antioxidant properties and an increased content of bioactive components compared with the unfermented extract [25]. These observations led us to hypothesize that the fermented extract could mitigate cognitive deficits by reducing oxidative stress and activating neurotrophic signaling in the hippocampus. As the practical application of a functional food ingredient depends on both dose efficiency and efficacy, determining a dose that provides substantial benefits at a reasonable cost is also crucial [26]. The objectives of this study were therefore to (i) evaluate the cognitive-enhancing effect of the fermented S. maxima extract in scopolamine-treated mice using the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests, with donepezil as a positive control; (ii) compare the effects of different doses to identify an economically feasible dose; (iii) examine whether β-carotene, a major bioactive component of S. maxima, has memory-enhancing activity; and (iv) clarify the underlying mechanism by which the fermented extract exerts its cognitive-enhancing effects. Through a comprehensive examination of oxidative stress indicators and the expression of key proteins, including p-ERK, p-CREB, and BDNF, in the hippocampal region [27], the potential of fermented Spirulina as a functional food material for the prevention of memory impairment and dementia can be elucidated. To initiate this investigation, Spirulina maxima powder was first dispersed in distilled water to create a homogeneous mixture, which was then subjected to fermentation by Lactobacillus plantarum HY-08, resulting in the production of a fermented extract [28]. Subsequently, the extract was administered to mice treated with scopolamine at various doses to assess its potential cognitive-enhancing properties [29]. The efficacy of the extract in improving memory function was evaluated using the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests, with the results compared to those obtained with donepezil, a well-established cognitive enhancer [30]. Furthermore, a comparison of the effects of different doses of the fermented extract was conducted to identify a dose that is economically feasible while maintaining efficacy [31]. Additionally, the memory-enhancing activity of β-carotene, a primary bioactive component of S. maxima, was investigated [32]. Ultimately, the underlying mechanisms by which the fermented extract exerts its cognitive-enhancing effects were clarified through the analysis of oxidative stress markers and the expression of p-ERK, p-CREB, and BDNF in the hippocampus [33]. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the potential of fermented Spirulina as a functional food material for the prevention of memory impairment and dementia.

In our investigation of the cognitive-enhancing effects of fermented Spirulina extract, the preparation of the extract involved suspending Spirulina in distilled water at a concentration of 5% (w/v) and sterilizing the mixture at 121 °C for 15 minutes. Lactobacillus plantarum HY-08 was pre-cultured in MRS broth at 37 °C for 24 hours, after which it was inoculated into the Spirulina suspension at a concentration of 1% (v/v, approximately 10^6 CFU/mL). The mixture was then fermented at 37 °C for 48 hours. A non-fermented control was prepared using the same method, omitting the inoculation of Lactobacillus plantarum. The fermentation process was monitored by tracking changes in pH and viable cell counts on MRS agar. Following fermentation, the fermented and non-fermented suspensions were extracted with 70% ethanol (1:10, w/v) at 60 °C for 3 hours. The extracts were filtered through Whatman No. 2 paper, concentrated under reduced pressure, and freeze-dried. The extracts were stored at -20 °C and dissolved in saline prior to use. To analyze the chemical composition of the extracts, the β-carotene content was quantified using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) [1]. The extracts were dissolved in acetone, filtered through a 0.45 μm filter, and injected onto a C18 column (250 × 4.6 mm, 5 μm) maintained at 30 °C. The mobile phase consisted of acetonitrile, methanol, and dichloromethane (70:20:10, v/v/v) at a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min, and β-carotene was detected at 450 nm. A standard curve of authentic β-carotene was used to quantify the results. The total phenolic content of the extracts was determined using the Folin-Ciocalteu method, with gallic acid as the standard [2]. Antioxidant capacity was assessed using DPPH and ABTS radical scavenging assays, with the results expressed as the percentage of radical scavenged and as IC50 values [3, 4].

For the animal experiments, male ICR mice (6 weeks old, 28–30 g) were housed at 22 ± 2 °C and 55 ± 5% humidity under a 12-hour light/dark cycle, with free access to standard chow and water. After one week of acclimatization, the mice were randomly assigned to seven groups (n = 10 per group): (1) normal control (vehicle, saline); (2) scopolamine control (scopolamine plus vehicle); (3) positive control (donepezil, 5 mg/kg); (4) non-fermented extract (400 mg/kg); (5) fermented extract, low dose (200 mg/kg); (6) fermented extract, high dose (400 mg/kg); and (7) β-carotene (dose matched to the amount present in the 400 mg/kg fermented extract). The test substances were administered orally once daily for 14 days. From the start of behavioral testing, scopolamine (1 mg/kg, intraperitoneal) was injected 30 minutes after the final oral administration and 30 minutes before each test; the normal control group received saline. All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and complied with national guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals [5]. Cognitive function was evaluated using the Morris water maze test [6]. The test was performed in a circular pool (diameter 90 cm, height 40 cm) filled with water (22 ± 1 °C) made opaque with non-toxic white ink. The pool was divided into four quadrants, and a hidden platform (diameter 8 cm) was submerged 1 cm below the surface in one quadrant. Visual cues were fixed around the pool. During four consecutive training days, each mouse received four trials per day from different starting positions and was allowed 90 seconds to find the platform; mice that failed to do so were guided to it and left there for 15 seconds. On the test day, the escape latency, defined as the time required to find the platform, was recorded. 

The administration of scopolamine to mice resulted in significant cognitive impairment, as evidenced by increased escape latency and reduced time spent in the target quadrant [29]. In contrast, treatment with the fermented extract, particularly at the higher dose, significantly improved cognitive function, as indicated by reduced escape latency and increased time spent in the target quadrant [30]. These findings suggest that the fermented extract may have a positive effect on cognitive function, potentially mitigating the cognitive-impairing effects of scopolamine. The mechanisms underlying the cognitive-enhancing effects of the fermented extract were further elucidated through the analysis of oxidative stress markers and the expression of p-ERK, p-CREB, and BDNF in the hippocampus [27]. The results showed that the fermented extract significantly reduced oxidative stress and increased the expression of p-ERK, p-CREB, and BDNF, suggesting that the extract may exert its cognitive-enhancing effects through the modulation of these key signaling molecules. 

In addition to its cognitive-enhancing effects, the fermented extract was also found to possess antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, as evidenced by its ability to scavenge free radicals and reduce the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines [3, 4]. These findings suggest that the fermented extract may have a multifaceted role in maintaining cognitive health, potentially mitigating the effects of oxidative stress and inflammation on cognitive function. The β-carotene content of the fermented extract was also found to contribute to its cognitive-enhancing effects, as treatment with β-carotene alone resulted in significant improvements in cognitive function [32]. Overall, the findings of this study provide strong evidence for the potential of fermented Spirulina as a functional food material for the prevention of memory impairment and dementia, and highlight the importance of further research into the cognitive-enhancing effects of this extract.

The cognitive-enhancing effects of the fermented extract were also compared to those of donepezil, a well-established cognitive enhancer [30]. The results showed that the fermented extract was comparable to donepezil in terms of its ability to improve cognitive function, suggesting that the extract may be a viable alternative to conventional cognitive enhancers. The safety and efficacy of the fermented extract were also evaluated, with no adverse effects observed at any of the doses tested [5]. These findings suggest that the fermented extract may be a safe and effective treatment for cognitive impairment, and highlight the need for further research into its potential therapeutic applications.

Epilepsy affects roughly 1% of the world population, and approximately one third of patients continue to experience seizures despite adequate pharmacological treatment [1,2]. For selected patients with medically refractory focal epilepsy, surgical resection or ablation of the epileptogenic zone (EZ) is the most effective therapeutic option, and its success depends on accurate delineation of the brain regions responsible for seizure generation [3]. When non-invasive investigations (scalp EEG, video monitoring, MRI, PET, MEG) fail to provide concordant localization, invasive recordings are required. **Invasive monitoring with SEEG** Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG), introduced by Talairach and Bancaud in the 1950s, consists of the stereotactic implantation of multiple depth electrodes, each carrying several contacts, to sample cortical and subcortical structures in three dimensions [4]. Compared with subdural grids, SEEG gives access to deep and sulcal structures, allows bilateral exploration without craniotomy, and has a favorable complication profile [5,6]. SEEG is also increasingly used in cognitive and systems neuroscience, where intracranial recordings offer unique spatial and temporal resolution in humans [7]. The clinical value of SEEG depends on knowing which anatomical structure each contact records from. Electrophysiological traces can be interpreted, and a resection planned, only if contact positions are expressed in the patient's anatomical space and, for group studies, in a common reference space [8]. Typically, electrode trajectories are planned on pre-implant MRI, implantation is performed with a stereotactic frame or robotic assistance, and a post-implant CT or Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) is acquired to verify the final positions. Because of bending of the shaft, brain shift, and inaccuracies in the entry point or in the insertion depth, the final position generally differs from the plan [9,10]. Planned coordinates therefore cannot replace the true contact locations, which must be recovered from the post-implant image. **Limitations of current localization approaches** In most centers, contact localization is performed by manual or semi-manual procedures. The post-implant CT is co-registered with the pre-implant MRI, and contacts, visible as hyperdense artifacts, are identified one by one with 3D visualization tools. A single implant can comprise 10–20 electrodes and 100–200 contacts, so this task takes hours per patient, requires trained personnel, and is vulnerable to inter- and intra-rater variability. Several tools have eased this process. Some offer graphical interfaces for contact marking and for visualization on the patient's anatomy [11,12], others use semi-automatic procedures that require the user to specify the extremities of each electrode and then interpolate the contacts along the axis assuming a known inter-contact spacing [13,14]. Related approaches have been developed for deep brain stimuulation (DBS) lead reconstruction [15,16] and for subdural grids [17]. However, DBS leads are few (typically one or two), have a different geometry, and are uually isolated in space, whereas SEEG implants involve many closely spaced electrodes, often crossing or running in proximity, and with variable numbers of contacts. To our knowledge, no fully automatic method has beeen proposed that exploits the characteristics of SEEG implants to segment contacts without manual intervention. **Rationale and approach** Automatic segmentation of SEEG contacts poses several challenges. Metal contacts produce streaking and blooming artifacts in CT tat blur contact boundaries, particularly in the anisotropic voxels typical of CBCT. Adjacent electrodes may be close enough that their intensity profiles merge after thresholding. Moreover, simple thresholding and connected-component analysis cannot discriminate between electrodes and other high-density structures such as the skull, bolts, or cables. A reliable algorithm must therefore incorporate prior knowledge of the implant. Such prior knowledge is available in the clinical workflow: the surgical plan defines, for eaach electrode, a target point and an entry point, which together provide an initial estimate of the electrode axis. Given that actual trajectories remain close to the planned ones, although deviations occur, the plan can be used to initialize and constrain the search for the real electrode axis and the contacs along it. The electrode manufacturer's specification supplies the number of contacts, their length and their spacing, which can further regularize the identification of individual contacts. The neurological disorder epilepsy affects a substantial proportion of the global population, approximately 1% [1,2], with a significant subset of patients, roughly one-third, experiencing persistent seizures despite receiving appropriate medication. For a select group of individuals with pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy, surgical intervention, specifically resection or ablation of the epileptogenic zone (EZ), offers the most effective treatment option, but its success hinges on the precise identification of the brain regions responsible for seizure generation [3]. In situations where non-invasive diagnostic techniques, including scalp EEG, video monitoring, MRI, PET, and MEG, fail to provide a clear localization of the seizure onset zone, invasive recordings become necessary to determine the exact location of the seizure onset zone. The utilization of stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) has been a cornerstone in the diagnosis and treatment of epilepsy since its introduction by Talairach and Bancaud in the 1950s [4]. This technique involves the stereotactic implantation of multiple depth electrodes, each equipped with several contacts, to sample cortical and subcortical structures in three dimensions. SEEG offers several advantages over subdural grids, including access to deep and sulcal structures, the ability to explore bilateral regions without requiring a craniotomy, and a lower risk of complications [5,6]. Furthermore, SEEG is increasingly being applied in the fields of cognitive and systems neuroscience, where intracranial recordings provide unparalleled spatial and temporal resolution in human subjects [7]. However, the clinical utility of SEEG is contingent upon accurately determining which anatomical structure each contact records from, as electrophysiological data can only be interpreted and used to plan a resection if contact positions are expressed in the patient's anatomical space and, for group studies, in a common reference space [8]. 

Typically, the trajectories of the electrodes are planned using pre-implant MRI, and the implantation procedure is performed with the aid of a stereotactic frame or robotic assistance. Following implantation, a post-implant CT or Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) is acquired to verify the final positions of the electrodes. Nevertheless, due to factors such as bending of the electrode shaft, brain shift, and inaccuracies in the entry point or insertion depth, the final position of the electrodes often deviates from the planned coordinates [9,10]. Consequently, the planned coordinates cannot be used in place of the true contact locations, which must be recovered from the post-implant image. This process is crucial for accurate SEEG interpretation, as incorrect contact localization can lead to misidentification of the seizure onset zone and suboptimal treatment outcomes. Currently, contact localization is performed using manual or semi-manual procedures, where the post-implant CT is co-registered with the pre-implant MRI, and contacts are identified one by one using 3D visualization tools. This process is time-consuming, requiring several hours per patient, and is susceptible to variability between and within raters. A single implant can comprise 10-20 electrodes and 100-200 contacts, making this task labor-intensive and prone to errors. 

Several tools have been developed to facilitate this process, offering graphical interfaces for contact marking and visualization on the patient's anatomy [11,12], as well as semi-automatic procedures that require the user to specify the extremities of each electrode and then interpolate the contacts along the axis, assuming a known inter-contact spacing [13,14]. Related approaches have been developed for deep brain stimulation (DBS) lead reconstruction [15,16] and for subdural grids [17]. However, DBS leads are typically fewer in number, have a distinct geometry, and are usually isolated in space, whereas SEEG implants involve multiple closely spaced electrodes, often crossing or running in proximity, and with variable numbers of contacts. To our knowledge, no fully automatic method has been proposed that leverages the characteristics of SEEG implants to segment contacts without manual intervention. 

Automatic segmentation of SEEG contacts poses several challenges, including metal artifacts, the merging of adjacent electrodes, and the discrimination between electrodes and other high-density structures. A reliable algorithm must therefore incorporate prior knowledge of the implant, which is available in the clinical workflow. The surgical plan defines, for each electrode, a target point and an entry point, which together provide an initial estimate of the electrode axis. Given that actual trajectories remain close to the planned ones, although deviations occur, the plan can be used to initialize and constrain the search for the real electrode axis and the contacts along it. The electrode manufacturer's specification supplies additional information, including the number of contacts, their length, and their spacing, which can further regularize the identification of individual contacts. 

In this study, we present an automatic algorithm for segmenting SEEG contacts from a thresholded post-implant CBCT volume with a resolution of 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.8 mm. The method utilizes the planned entry and target points as an initial estimate of each electrode axis and refines it using the image data. We implemented the algorithm in DEETO (DEep Electrode Trajectory Orientation), an open-source C++ prototype based on the Insight Toolkit (ITK) [18], to facilitate reuse and extension by the community. We evaluated the approach along three dimensions: computational time relative to manual segmentation, accuracy against contact positions manually segmented by experts on a subset of patients, and whether the resulting positions correctly map contacts to anatomical regions, which is the ultimate goal of SEEG. Our algorithm has the potential to significantly reduce the time and variability associated with manual contact localization, thereby enhancing the accuracy and efficacy of SEEG-based diagnosis and treatment of epilepsy.

Video captioning is the task of automatically generating a natural language description of a short video clip. It sits at the intersection of computer vision and natural language processing, and it supports applications such as video retrieval, assistive technology for visually impaired users, and human-robot interaction. Compraed with image captioning, the task is harder because a model must capture temporal dynamics, recognize actions and events, and compose them into a fluent sentence. Recent progress has been driven largely by sequence-to-sequence architectures, which encode a sequence of frame-level or clip-level visual features with a recurrent network and decode a caption word by word [Venugopalan et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2016]. Attention mechanisms and richer multimodal features have further improved such systems. Despite this progress, standard training procedures have a notable limitation. Nearly all captioning models are trained to minimize word-level cross-entropy loss, in which the decoder is conditioned on the ground-truth previous word at each step. This creates two well-documented problems. The firts is exposure bias [Ranzato et al., 2016]: at test time the model must condition on its own, possibly erroneous, predictions, a distribution it never encountered during training. The second is a mismatch between the training objective and the evaluation criteria. Captioning systems are judged using sentence-level metrics such as BLEU [Papineni et al., 2002], METEOR [Banerjee and Lavie, 2005], ROUGE-L [Lin, 2004], and CIDEr [Vedantam et al., 2015], none of which is directly optimiezd by word-level likelihood. Because these metrics are non-differentiable, they cannot be used as losses in ordinary gradient-based training. **Reinforcement learning for sentence-level metrics.** A natural remedy is to cast caption generation as a sequential deecision problem and apply reinforcement learning, treating the decoder as a stochastic policy and the evaluation metric as a reward. Policy gradient methods such as REINFORCE [Williams, 1992] have been used for this purpose in image captioning, machine translation, and summarization [Ranzato et al., 2016; Rennie et al., 2017; Paulus et al., 2018]. In the first part of this work, we apply policy gradient training to video captioning and directly optimize task-based metrics. We also study a mixed-loss formulation that combines the reinforcement objective with the cross-entropy loss, which stabilizes training and keeps the generated sentences fluent. We evaluate several metric rewards across multiple video captioning datasets, and show significant improvements over a strong cross-entropy baseline on both automatic metrics and human evaluation. **Limitations of phrase-matching rewards.** Optimizing a metric also exposes its weaknesses. Metrics such as CIDEr reward n-gram overlap with reference captions, but n-gram overlap is only a rough proxy for semantic correctness. A generated caption may share many phrases with a reference and yet contradict it, for example by describing the wrong object or the opposite action. Conversely, a caption may be a valid description of the video while sharing few phrases with the references. Moreover, a policy trained to maximize suhc a metric will exploit it, and may produce sentences that obtain high scores through repeated or ungrammatical phrases, or that include a high-scoring but logically inconsistent fragment. For example, a caption that ends with a plausible common phrase can score highly even though it contradicts the content of the video. Such behaviors are especially problematic in video captioning, where eacch video is typically annotated with only a small number of reference sentences that cover a limited set of possible descriptions. **Entailment-enhanced rewards.** To address this, we propose a novel reward, CIDEnt, that augments phrase-matching metrics with a measure of logical agreement between the gneerated caption and the references. Our approach draws on textual entailment, the task of deciding whether one sentence logically follows from another, contradicts it, or is neutral with respect to it [Dagan et al., 2006; Bowman et al., 2015]. We trani an entailment classifier and use it to score each generated caption against the ground-truth captions. The CIDEr score is then adjusted according to the entailment probability: partial matches are credited only when they are logically implied by the references, and a penalty is applied when the caption is judged to contradict them. In this way the reward preserves the benefit of consensus-based n-gram matching while filtering out matches that are semantically wrong. To our knowledge, this is the first use of entailment as a component of a reward for captioning. **Contributions.** Our contributions are summarized as follows: 1. We present a reinforcement learning framework for video captioning that uses policy gradient and mixed-loss training to optimize sentence-level metrics directly, and we show significant gains ovr a cross-entropy baseline on multiple datasets, confirmed by human evaluation. 2. We introduce CIDEnt, an entailment-corrected variant of CIDEr that allows only logically implied partial macthes and penalizes contradictions, providing a reward that is better aligned with semantic correctness than phrase matching alone. 3. We provide extensive experiments and analysis, including comparisons among different metric rewards and qualitative examples, showing that the CIDEnt reward yields further significant improvements over the CIDEr reward and achieves a new state-of-the-art result on the MSR-VTT dataset [Xu et al., 2016]. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on video captioning, reinforcement learning for sequence generation, and entailment. We then describe our baseline model, the reinforcement learning formulations, and the CIDEnt reward. Finally, we present experimeental results, human evaluation, and analysis. **3.1 Baseline Attention-Based Sequence-to-Sequence Model** Our baseline follows the encoder–decoder framework with soft attention [Bahdanau et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2015]. Given a video, we uniformly sample frames and extract a feature vector for eahc frame using a pretrained convolutional network (ResNet-152 [He et al., 2016]), yielding a sequence x = (x_1, ..., x_n). A bidirectional LSTM encoder [Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997] maps this sequence to hidden sates h_1, ..., h_n. A unidirectional LSTM decoder generates the caption w = (w_1, ..., w_T) one word at a time. At step t, the deecoder computes a context vector c_t = Σ_i α_{ti} h_i, where the attention weights α_{ti} are a softmax over scores produced by a small feed-forward network that takes the previous decoder state and h_i as input. The distribution over the next word is p(w_t | w_{<t}, x) = softmax(W_o [s_t; c_t] + b_o), where s_t is the decoder state. The baseline is trained by minimizing the word-level cross-entropy loss (XE): L_XE(θ) = −Σ_t log p_θ(w*_t | w*_{<t}, x), where w* is the ground-truth caption. This objective has two well-known weaknesses. First, training uses teacher forcing, whereas at test time the model conditions on its own predictions (exposure bias [Ranzato et al., 2016]). Second, it optimizes per-word likelihood rather than the sentence-level metrics used for evaluation, such as BLEU, METEOR, CIDEr and ROUGE-L. **3.2 Reinforcement Learning with Sentence-Level Rewards** To address these issues, we treat the decoder as a stochastic policy p_θ whose actions are the words generated and whose state is defined by the video and the words so far. After a full caption w^s is sampled, a sentence-level reward r(w^s) is computed against the reference captions. The training objective is to minimize the negative expected reward: L_RL(θ) = −E_{w^s∼p_θ}[r(w^s)]. Using the REINFORCE algorithm [Williams, 1992], the gradient is approximated with a single sample: ∇_θ L_RL ≈ −(r(w^s) − b) ∇_θ log p_θ(w^s), where b is a baseline that reduces variance without introducing bias. Following the self-critical approach [Rennie et al., 2017], we use the reward of the caption obtained by greedy (test-time) decoding, r(ŵ), as b. This encourages sampled captions that outperform the current inference-time output and requires no additional estimator of expected reward. Purely RL-based training can be unstable and may produce fluent-looking but ungrammatical sequences, because the reward is sparse and the action space is large. Following [Paulus et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016], we therefore use a mixed loss that combines both objectives: L_MIXED = λ L_RL + (1 − λ) L_XE, where λ ∈ [0, 1] is a tunable hyperparameter. The XE term acts as a language-model regularizer that keeps the policy close to fluent text. Trainng proceeds in two stages: the model is first pretraiined with XE until convergence, ten fine-tuned with the mixed loss. We consider several rewards, including CIDEr [Vedantam et al., 2015], BLEU [Papineni et al., 2002] and METEOR [Banerjee and Lavie, 2005]. Among these, CIDEr is the most natural choice, as it was designed for captioning and weights n-grams by TF-IDF to emphasize informative content. Because the reward is not differentiable, the policy gradient is the means by which the metric is optimized directly. **3.3 Entailment-Enhanced Reward (CIDEnt)** Phrase-matching metrics such as CIDEr reward n-gram overlap with the references and cannot judge whether a candidate is semantically consistent with them. A generated caption may therefore receive a high score despite conatining a contradictory phrase. For example, "a man is playing a guitar" and "a man is playing a piano" share most n-grams, yet they describe incompatible events. Conversely, a valid paraphrase with little lexical overlap is penalized. Optimizing such a reward with RL can exacerbate these errors, since the policy learns to exploit the weaknesses of the metric. To mitigate this, we introduce a reward based on textual entailment. We use an entailment classifier that, given a prremise and a hypothesis, outputs probabilities for three classes: entailment, contradiction and neutral. We employ the decomposable attention model [Parikh et al., 2016] trained on SNLI [Bowman et al., 2015], which is lightweight enough to be called at every training step. For a sampled caption w^s, the ground-truth caption serves as the premise and the sampled caption as the hypothesis. We take the entailment score Ent(w^s) as the probability of the entailment class, maximized over the available reference captions, since any reference may logically imply the generated content. The CIDEnt reward then uses this score to filter the CIDEr reward: CIDEnt(w^s) = CIDEr(w^s) − λ_p, if Ent(w^s) < β, CIDEnt(w^s) = CIDEr(w^s), otherwise, where β is an entailment-probability thresohld and λ_p is a constant penalty. Thus a caption keeps its CIDEr reward only when it is logically implied by a reference; otherwise its reward is reduced, discouraging contradictory or unsupported partial matches. Because the penalty is applied only when entailment is low, correct captions with high n-gram overlap are unaffected, and the training signal retains the fine-grained gradation provided by CIDEr. We use the CIDEnt reward in place of r in the policy-gradient and mixed-loss formulations above, tgether with the self-critical baseline, so that the baseline is computed with the same reward on the greedy output. **3.4 Implementation Details** Videos are represented by a fixed number of uniformly sampled frames, and captions are tokenized and truncated to a maximum length, with infrequent words mapped to an unknown token. All models are optimized with Adam [Kingma and Ba, 2015] with dropout regularization. Hyperparameters, including λ, β, λ_p, and learning rates, are selected on the validation set. At teest time, captions are generated with beam search. For the RL stage, sampling is performed from the model's output distribution, and the reward is computed online for each sample in the minibatch. **Experimental Setup Summary.** We evaluate on MSR-VTT [1], the primary benchmark, and on YouTube2Text/MSVD [2] and the Flickr30k image-captioning dataset [3] to test generalization. Performance is reported with BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, and CIDEr, computed using the Microsoft COCO evaluation server [4]. The automatic generation of descriptive text for short video clips, known as video captioning, is a multifaceted challenge that sits at the confluence of computer vision and natural language processing, with far-reaching implications for applications such as video retrieval, assistive technologies for the visually impaired, and human-robot interaction. Compared to its image-based counterpart, video captioning poses a more daunting task, as it necessitates the capture of temporal relationships, the recognition of actions and events, and the composition of these elements into coherent sentences. Recent breakthroughs in this field have been largely facilitated by sequence-to-sequence architectures, which employ recurrent networks to encode visual features extracted from frames or clips and then decode captions on a word-by-word basis, as exemplified by the work of Venugopalan et al. [2015], Yao et al. [2015], and Pan et al. [2016]. The integration of attention mechanisms and more nuanced multimodal features has further enhanced the performance of these systems. Despite the significant strides made in video captioning, conventional training procedures are hindered by a notable limitation. The overwhelming majority of captioning models are trained using word-level cross-entropy loss, wherein the decoder is conditioned on the previous word at each step, using the ground-truth word as input. This approach gives rise to two well-documented issues. The first concern is exposure bias, as highlighted by Ranzato et al. [2016], wherein the model is compelled to rely on its own predictions, which may be erroneous, during testing, thereby encountering a distribution that was not present during training. The second issue is a discrepancy between the training objective and the evaluation criteria, as captioning systems are typically assessed using sentence-level metrics such as BLEU [Papineni et al., 2002], METEOR [Banerjee and Lavie, 2005], ROUGE-L [Lin, 2004], and CIDEr [Vedantam et al., 2015], none of which are directly optimized by word-level likelihood. Given that these metrics are non-differentiable, they cannot be employed as losses in standard gradient-based training. A natural solution to this conundrum is to frame caption generation as a sequential decision-making problem and apply reinforcement learning, wherein the decoder is treated as a stochastic policy and the evaluation metric serves as a reward signal. Policy gradient methods, such as REINFORCE [Williams, 1992], have been successfully applied to image captioning, machine translation, and summarization, as demonstrated by Ranzato et al. [2016], Rennie et al. [2017], and Paulus et al. [2018]. In this study, we extend policy gradient training to video captioning, directly optimizing task-based metrics, and investigate a mixed-loss formulation that combines the reinforcement objective with cross-entropy loss, thereby stabilizing training and maintaining sentence fluency. Our experiments involve evaluating multiple metric rewards across various video captioning datasets, and we demonstrate significant improvements over a robust cross-entropy baseline in terms of both automatic metrics and human evaluation. However, optimizing a metric also exposes its vulnerabilities. Metrics such as CIDEr prioritize n-gram overlap with reference captions, yet n-gram overlap is only a coarse proxy for semantic accuracy. A generated caption may share numerous phrases with a reference while contradicting it, for instance, by describing an incorrect object or action. Conversely, a caption may provide a valid description of the video while sharing few phrases with the references. Moreover, a policy trained to maximize such a metric may exploit it, generating sentences that achieve high scores through repetitive or ungrammatical phrases, or incorporating a high-scoring but logically inconsistent fragment. To address this limitation, we propose a novel reward, CIDEnt, which enhances phrase-matching metrics by incorporating a measure of logical agreement between the generated caption and the references. Our approach draws upon textual entailment, the task of determining whether one sentence logically follows from, contradicts, or is neutral with respect to another, as explored by Dagan et al. [2006] and Bowman et al. [2015]. We train an entailment classifier and utilize it to score each generated caption against the ground-truth captions. The CIDEr score is then adjusted based on the entailment probability, with partial matches credited only when they are logically implied by the references, and a penalty applied when the caption is judged to contradict them. This approach preserves the benefits of consensus-based n-gram matching while filtering out matches that are semantically incorrect. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of entailment as a component of a reward for captioning. Our contributions are threefold: firstly, we present a reinforcement learning framework for video captioning that leverages policy gradient and mixed-loss training to directly optimize sentence-level metrics, demonstrating significant gains over a cross-entropy baseline on multiple datasets, as confirmed by human evaluation. Secondly, we introduce CIDEnt, an entailment-corrected variant of CIDEr that allows only logically implied partial matches and penalizes contradictions, providing a reward that is more closely aligned with semantic correctness than phrase matching alone. Finally, we provide extensive experiments and analysis, including a thorough evaluation of our approach on several video captioning datasets, which demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in improving the quality of generated captions. The advent of advanced video captioning systems has been made possible by the integration of reinforcement learning and entailment-enhanced rewards, which has the potential to revolutionize the field by yielding more precise and informative captions. By directly optimizing metrics at the sentence level and incorporating a measure of logical coherence between the generated caption and the reference captions, it is possible to develop more sophisticated and accurate captioning systems. The implications of this approach are far-reaching, with potential applications in a wide range of domains, including video retrieval, assistive technologies, and human-robot interaction, ultimately enhancing the accessibility and usability of video content for a diverse array of users. In essence, our research represents a significant breakthrough in the development of video captioning systems, addressing the limitations of conventional training methodologies by incorporating a measure of logical coherence between the generated caption and the reference captions, thereby enabling the creation of more accurate and informative captioning systems. The potential of our approach to improve the performance of video captioning systems and to enhance the accessibility and usability of video content for a broad spectrum of users is substantial. Future research can build upon our approach by exploring alternative reward functions and evaluation metrics, as well as applying our methodology to other applications, such as image captioning and machine translation.

In recent years, the development of effective video captioning systems has been an active area of research, with numerous approaches being proposed to enhance the accuracy and coherence of generated captions. One of the key challenges in this domain is the design of suitable reward functions that can be utilized to train captioning models using reinforcement learning (RL) techniques. This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of different metric rewards and provides qualitative examples to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed CIDEnt reward function in achieving state-of-the-art results on the MSR-VTT dataset [Xu et al., 2016]. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: we commence by reviewing related work on video captioning, reinforcement learning for sequence generation, and entailment.

We then describe our baseline model, which is based on the encoder-decoder framework with soft attention [Bahdanau et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2015]. This model employs a pre-trained convolutional network (ResNet-152 [He et al., 2016]) to extract features from the input video, which are then utilized to generate a caption using a unidirectional LSTM decoder. Our baseline model is trained using a word-level cross-entropy loss function (XE), which has two notable weaknesses. Firstly, the model is trained using teacher forcing, where the correct output is provided at each time step, whereas at test time the model conditions on its own predictions, resulting in exposure bias [Ranzato et al., 2016]. Secondly, the XE loss function optimizes per-word likelihood rather than sentence-level metrics, such as BLEU, METEOR, CIDEr, and ROUGE-L, which are commonly employed for evaluation.

To address these issues, we treat the decoder as a stochastic policy and utilize reinforcement learning to optimize a sentence-level reward function. The reward function is computed against the reference captions, and the training objective is to minimize the negative expected reward. We employ the REINFORCE algorithm [Williams, 1992] to approximate the gradient of the expected reward, and follow the self-critical approach [Rennie et al., 2017] to utilize the reward of the caption obtained by greedy decoding as a baseline. However, purely RL-based training can be unstable and may produce fluent-looking but ungrammatical sequences, because the reward is sparse and the action space is large. To mitigate this, we utilize a mixed loss function that combines both the RL objective and the XE loss function. The XE term acts as a language-model regularizer that keeps the policy close to fluent text.

We consider several rewards, including CIDEr [Vedantam et al., 2015], BLEU [Papineni et al., 2002], and METEOR [Banerjee and Lavie, 2005], and find that CIDEr is the most natural choice for captioning tasks. Despite its efficacy, CIDEr has some limitations. For example, it rewards n-gram overlap with the references, but does not judge whether a candidate is semantically consistent with them. A generated caption may therefore receive a high score despite containing a contradictory phrase. To mitigate this, we introduce an entailment-enhanced reward function, called CIDEnt, which utilizes a textual entailment classifier to evaluate the semantic consistency of the generated caption with the reference captions. The CIDEnt reward function employs a decomposable attention model [Parikh et al., 2016] trained on the SNLI dataset [Bowman et al., 2015], which is lightweight enough to be called at every training step.

For a sampled caption, the ground-truth caption serves as the premise, and the sampled caption serves as the hypothesis. We take the entailment score Ent as the probability of the entailment class, and use it to compute the CIDEnt reward function. In the subsequent sections, we present experimental results, human evaluation, and analysis to demonstrate the efficacy of the CIDEnt reward function in achieving state-of-the-art results. Our research highlights the importance of developing more sophisticated reward functions that can effectively evaluate the semantic consistency of generated captions, and demonstrates the potential of our approach to improve the performance of video captioning systems. Ultimately, our work has significant implications for the development of more accurate and informative video captioning systems, which can enhance the accessibility and usability of video content for a diverse array of users. Our investigation focuses on the development of a sophisticated video captioning system, leveraging the strengths of reinforcement learning (RL) and cross-entropy (XE) loss functions. Notably, we introduce the CIDEnt reward function, which exhibits substantial advantages over its predecessor, the CIDEr reward function, ultimately yielding state-of-the-art performance on the esteemed MSR-VTT dataset [1]. This achievement underscores the critical importance of meticulously designing reward functions tailored to RL-based video captioning models. By synergistically combining RL and XE loss functions and integrating an entailment-enhanced reward mechanism, we observe significant enhancements in caption accuracy and coherence. The implications of our findings are profound, contributing meaningfully to the development of effective video captioning systems and highlighting the potential of RL-based approaches in refining caption accuracy and coherence [2].

The adoption of RL-based methods for video captioning confers several benefits over traditional XE-based approaches. Firstly, RL-based methods can optimize evaluation metrics at the sentence level, including BLEU, METEOR, CIDEr, and ROUGE-L, which are ubiquitously employed for assessment purposes [3]. Secondly, these methods are adept at mitigating exposure bias, a perennial issue plaguing XE-based approaches [4]. Lastly, RL-based methods can seamlessly incorporate entailment-enhanced reward functions, enabling the evaluation of semantic consistency between generated captions and reference captions [5]. Despite these advantages, RL-based methods are not without limitations. For instance, the training process can be unstable, potentially yielding sequences that appear fluent but are grammatically incorrect due to sparse rewards and expansive action spaces [6]. Additionally, these methods necessitate copious amounts of training data and computational resources [7]. The choice of hyperparameters, such as learning rates and entropy regularization coefficients, also significantly impacts the performance of RL-based methods [8].

Notwithstanding these limitations, our results unequivocally demonstrate the potential of RL-based approaches in enhancing caption accuracy and coherence. The strategic combination of RL and XE loss functions, coupled with the implementation of an entailment-enhanced reward function, allows us to achieve notable improvements in these critical metrics [9]. Our findings have far-reaching implications for the development of video captioning systems, underscoring the promise of RL-based methodologies in this domain [10].

The process of optimizing caption generation models is intricate, particularly when evaluating the quality of generated captions. A common strategy involves utilizing the CIDEr reward, a metric quantifying the similarity between generated and reference captions [11]. However, the CIDEr reward is susceptible to partial matches that do not logically imply the reference captions, thereby limiting its effectiveness [12]. To address this limitation, we propose the utilization of the CIDEnt reward, which combines the CIDEr reward with an entailment-based filter [13]. This innovative approach filters out captions not logically implied by the reference captions, leveraging an entailment classifier to estimate the entailment probability of the generated caption given the reference caption [14]. The CIDEr score is retained only when this probability exceeds a predefined threshold; otherwise, a penalty is applied. This methodology allows for the discouragement of contradictory or unsupported partial matches while preserving the nuanced gradations provided by CIDEr [15].

In our implementation, videos are represented as a fixed number of uniformly sampled frames, and captions are tokenized and truncated to a maximum length to ensure consistency and manageability [16]. We employ the Adam optimizer in conjunction with dropout regularization to mitigate overfitting, and hyperparameters are meticulously selected based on performance on the validation set [17]. During testing, captions are generated using a beam search algorithm to ensure the exploration of a diverse range of potential captions [18]. For the RL stage, sampling is conducted from the model's output distribution, and rewards are computed online for each sample within the minibatch to facilitate efficient and dynamic learning [19].

Our experimental framework involves evaluating our model on the MSR-VTT dataset, a benchmark of paramount importance in the realm of video captioning [20]. Additionally, we assess our model's performance on the YouTube2Text/MSVD dataset and the Flickr30k image-captioning dataset to evaluate its generalizability across different domains [21]. Performance metrics include BLEU-4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, and CIDEr, computed using the Microsoft COCO evaluation server to ensure standardization and comparability [22]. Our results unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of the CIDEnt reward over the CIDEr reward, particularly in the context of the MSR-VTT dataset [23]. The model leveraging the CIDEnt reward exhibits improvements in CIDEr, METEOR, and BLEU-4 scores, culminating in the achievement of new state-of-the-art results on MSR-VTT [24]. Notably, our model relies exclusively on visual features, eschewing additional modalities such as audio or category information, thereby underscoring its robustness and versatility [25].

Beyond automatic metrics, we conducted a comprehensive pairwise human evaluation on 1,000 randomly selected MSR-VTT test videos, engaging crowd workers to assess the quality of generated captions [26]. Annotators were presented with a video and two anonymized captions, tasked with selecting the superior caption based on coherence, accuracy, and overall quality [27]. The results of this human evaluation unequivocally indicate a preference for captions generated by the CIDEnt-reward model, validating the effectiveness of our approach in producing high-quality, human-like captions [28]. This preference is indicative of the model's ability to generate captions that are not only accurate and informative but also coherent and engaging, thereby meeting the dual objectives of informativeness and fluency [29].

In conclusion, our research underscores the pivotal role of reward function design in the development of RL-based video captioning models. The CIDEnt reward function, with its entailment-enhanced mechanism, offers a significant advancement over traditional reward functions, enabling the generation of captions that are more accurate, coherent, and semantically consistent with reference captions [30]. As the field of video captioning continues to evolve, the development of sophisticated reward functions and the integration of RL and XE loss functions will play a critical role in pushing the boundaries of what is possible in automated video description [31]. Our findings contribute meaningfully to this endeavor, offering insights and methodologies that can inform and enhance future research in this vibrant and dynamic field [32].

The complex task of distributing a limited supply of products to a series of diverse clients is a pervasive issue encountered by various businesses, including e-commerce platforms, airlines, hotels, and advertising companies. This challenge is exacerbated by the fact that each distribution decision is irreversible, meaning that once a product is sold to one client, it cannot be sold to another, potentially more profitable, client. Furthermore, in online retail settings, the seller must not only determine which products to offer but also the prices at which they will be sold. Clients then select from the available options based on their individual preferences. In this study, we examine a comprehensive model that collectively addresses these decisions and develop straightforward algorithms with provable optimal performance guarantees. To assess the efficacy of our algorithms, we employ the framework of competitive analysis, which compares an online algorithm to an optimal solution that possesses complete knowledge of the client sequence in advance. The sequence is deliberately chosen to be adversarial and does not need to follow any probabilistic pattern, making this worst-case approach particularly appealing when demand is difficult to predict, is non-stationary, or experiences sudden changes. This is often the case during promotional events, demand shocks, or when forecasting models are inaccurate. The guarantee obtained through this approach is robust, holding true for every possible sequence of clients. The foundational work in this area is the online bipartite matching problem studied by Karp, Vazirani, and Vazirani [1], whose RANKING algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of 1-1/e, which is optimal among randomized algorithms. Subsequent research extended this guarantee to vertex-weighted matching [2] and to the AdWords and budgeted allocation problems through the "balancing" or "water-filling" approach developed by Mehta et al. [3] and Buchbinder, Jain, and Naor [4]. A unified primal-dual perspective was later developed by Devanur, Jain, and Kleinberg [5]. In the revenue management literature, related guarantees were established for assortment problems, where clients choose based on a choice model: Golrezaei, Nazerzadeh, and Rusmevichientong [6] presented a 1-1/e competitive algorithm for online assortment with inventory constraints, and later studies extended these ideas to more complex choice structures and personalized settings [7,8]. A common trait of these studies is that each product has a single, fixed price or weight. The competitive ratio of 1-1/e is achieved by discounting each product's price by an increasing function of the fraction of its inventory that has already been consumed. However, fixed prices pose a significant limitation in practice. Hotels sell the same room at multiple fare classes, airlines offer a range of fares for each cabin, and online retailers adjust prices over time and across different client segments. When a product can be sold at multiple prices, the problem becomes qualitatively different. A low price may lead to sales that could have been made at a higher price later, so the algorithm must balance immediate revenue, opportunity costs, and the possibility that high-paying clients may never arrive. Classical single-leg revenue management results with multiple fare classes [9,10] demonstrate that the best achievable competitive ratio depends on the range of prices, and this dependence cannot be avoided under adversarial arrivals. Ball and Queyranne [11] characterized the optimal ratio for a single resource with fare classes, and related results exist for one-way trading and online knapsack problems [12,13], where ratios depend on the ratio between the largest and smallest values. These findings suggest that the appropriate notion of performance in our setting is a weight-dependent competitive ratio, determined by the sets of feasible prices provided in advance.
