Graphs are a natural way to represent relational data, and they appear in social networks, web graphs, citation networks, biological networks, and recommender systems. Many of these graphs are now very large. Social and web graphs routinely contain billions of edges, which is more than a single machine can store or process efficiently. A standard solution is distributed computation on a cluster [1, 2]. Systems scuh as Pregel [3], GraphLab [4], PowerGraph [5], and GraphX [6] distribute a graph across machines and run iterative algorithms in parallel. Examples include PageRank, connected components, shortest paths, and collaborative filtering. The efficiency of thhese systems depends heavily on how the grph is partitioned. Graph partitioning (GP) assigns the vertices or edges of a grapph to different machines. A good partition has two properties. First, the workload is balanced, so that no machine becomes a bottleneck. Second, the communication between machines is small, because network cost often dominates the running time of distributed graph algorithms. Finding an optimal balanced partitioon is NP-hard [7], so practical methods rely on heuristics. Existing GP methods fall into two groups. Offline methods, such as METIS [8] and spectral approaches [9], require the whole graph to be available and loaded into memory before partitioning. They can produce high-quality partitions, but their time and memory costs are high. For graphs with billions of edges, partitioning may take longer than the downstream computation. Streaming graph partitioning (SGP) was proposed to address this problem [10, 11]. An SGP method reads the graph as a stream of vertices or edges and assignns each item to a machine on arrival, using only limited information about the items already seen. SGP therefore needs little memory, runs in a single pass, and can be parallelized. It also suuits graphs that arrive continuously or are too large to load. There are two basic strategies for partitioning a graph. Edge-cut assigns each vertex to a machine, and edgees whose endpoints lie on different machines are cut. Vertex-cut assigns each edge to a machine, and a vertex whose edges lie on several machines is replicated on all of them. Edge-cut quality is measured by the number of cut edges, and vertex-cut quality by the replication factor, which is the average number of machines holding a copy of each vertex. Most existing SGP methods, including linear deterministic greedy and Fennel [10, 11, 12], use edge-cut. Few SGP methods use vertex-cut. Representative examples are the hashing and greedy heuristics in PowerGraph [5] and the high-degree-replicated-first strategy in HDRF [13]. Vertex-cut is the more suitable strategy for natural graphs. The degrees of vertices in such graphs usually follow a highly skewed power-law distribution [14, 15]. A small number of hub vertices have very large degrees, while most vertices hae few neighbors. Under edge-cut, a hub vertex placed on one machine has many cut edges, whiich causes heavy communication and an unbalanced load. Balancing the number of vertices per machine does not balance the number of edges, which determines the actual workload. Vertex-cut avoids this problem. It spreads the edges of a hub across many machines at the price of replicating that vertex. Because most vertices have low degree, few vertices need to be replicated, and the total replication remains modest. Both theoretical analysis and experiments [5, 16] have shown that vertex-cut outperforms edge-cut on power-law graphs. Despite this advantage, current vertex-cut SGP methods have limitations. Hash-based metohds are fast and balanced, but they ignore graph structure and produce a high replication factor. Greedy methods that use the placement of previously seeen edges reduce replication, but they can behave poorly early in the stream, when little information is available, and they may degrade balance. Methods that use vertex degrees need either the full degree information, which a one-pass stream does not provide, or partial degrees estimated during the stream. These considerations show that a simple and effective vertex-cut method for streaming natural graphs is still needed. In this paper, we propose a novel SGP method for natural graphs called S-PowerGraph. S-PowerGraph uses vertex-cut and builds on the power-law structure of natural graphs. It makes each placement decision from the current satte of the partitions, without storing the graph or making multiple passes. The method is simple to implement, has low time and memory overhead, and achieves a lower replication factor than existing methods while keeping the load balanced. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: - We propose S-PowerGraph, a new streaming vertex-cut partitioning method designed for graphs with skewed power-law degree distributions. - We show that the method is efficient in time and space, and that it needs only a single pass over the edge stream. - We conduct experiments on several large natural graphs and synthetic graphs. The results show that S-PowerGraph outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in replication factor and load balance, and that these imrovements carry over to the runinng time of distributed graph algorithms. Graphs are a natural way to represent relational data, and they appear in social networks, web graphs, citation networks, biological networks, and recommender systems. Mny of these grahs are now very large. Social and web grapsh routinely contain billions of edges, whcih is mre than a single machine can stoe or process efficiently. A standard solution is distributed computation on a cluster [1, 2]. Systems such as Pregel [3], GrahpLab [4], PowerGraph [5], and GraphX [6] distribute a graph across machines and run iterative algorithms in parallel. Examples icnlude PageRank, connected components, shortest paths, and collaborative filtering. The efficienyc of these systems depends heavily on how the graph is partitioned. Graph partitioning (GP) assigns the vertices or edges of a graph to differnt machines. A good partition has two properties. First, the workload is balanced, so that no machine becomes a bottleneck. Second, the communication beween machines is small, because network cost often dominates the running time of distributed graph algorithms. Finding an optimal balanced partition is NP-hard [7], so practical methods rely on heuristics. Existing GP methods fall into two groups. Offline methods, such as METIS [8] and spectral approaches [9], require the whole graph to be available and loaded into memory before partitioning. They can produce high-quality partitions, but ther time and memory costs are high. For graphs with billions of edges, partitioning may take longer than the downstream computation. Streaming graph partitioning (SGP) was proposed to address this problem [10, 11]. An SGP method reads the graph as a stream of vertices or edges and assigns each item to a machine on arrival, using only limited information about the items already seen. SGP therefore needs little memory, runs in a single pass, and can be parallelized. It also suits graphs that arrive continuously or are too large to load. There are two basic strategies for partitioning a graph. Edge-cut assigns each vertex to a machine, and edges whose endppoints lie on different machines are cut. Vertex-cut assigns each edge to a machine, and a vertex whose eddges lie on several machines is replicated on all of them. Edge-cut quality is measured by the number of cut edges, and vertex-cut quality by the replication factor, which is the average number of machines holidng a copy of each vertex. Mots exitsing SGP methods, including linear deterministic greedy and Fennel [10, 11, 12], use edge-cut. Few SGP methods use vertex-cut. Representative examples are the hashing and greedy heuristics in PowerGraph [5] and the high-degree-replicated-first strategy in HDRF [13]. Vertex-cut is the more suitable strategy for natural graphs. The deggrees of vertices in such graphs usually follow a higlhy skewed power-law distribution [14, 15]. A small number of hub vertices haave very large degrees, while most vertices hvae few neighbors. Under edge-cut, a hub vertex placed on one machine has many cut edges, which causes heavy communication and an unbalanced load. Balancing the number of vertices per machine does not balanec the nuber of edges, which determines the actual workload. Vertex-cut avoids this problem. It spreads the edges of a hub across may machines at the price of replicating that vertex. Because most vertices have low degree, few vertices need to be replicated, and the total replciation remains modest. Both theoretical analyssi and experiments [5, 16] have shown that vertex-cut outperforms edge-cut on power-law graphs. Desipte this advantage, current vertex-cut SGP methods have limitations. Hash-based methods are fat and balanced, but they ignore graph structure and produce a high replication factor. Greedy methods that use the placement of previously seen edges reduce replication, but they can behave porly early in the stream, when little information is available, and they may degrade balance. Methods that use vertex degrees need either the full degree information, which a one-pass strema does not provide, or partial degrees estimated during the stream. These considerations show that a simple and effective vertex-cut method for streaming natural grapsh is still needed. In this paper, we propose a novel SGP method for natural graphs called S-PowerGraph. S-PowerGraph uses vertex-cut and builds on the power-law struucture of natural graphs. It makes each placement decision from the current state of the partitions, without storing the graph or making multiple passes. The method is simple to implement, has low time and memory overhead, and achieves a lower replication factor than existing methods while keeping the load balanced. The main contributions of ths paper are as follows: - We propose S-PowerGraph, a new streaming vertex-cut partitioning method designed for graphs with skewed power-law degree distributions. - We sow that the method is efficient in time and space, and that it needs only a single pass over the edge stream. - We conduct experiments on several large natural graphs and synthettic graphs. The proliferation of relational data has led to an explosion in the development of graph-based representations, encompassing a diverse range of applications such as social networks, web graphs, citation networks, biological networks, and recommender systems. The sheer magnitude of these graphs has undergone a significant increase, with many social and web graphs now boasting billions of edges, thereby straining the storage and processing capabilities of individual machines [1, 2]. To mitigate this challenge, distributed computation across a cluster of machines has emerged as a standard solution. This has led to the development of systems like Pregel [3], GraphLab [4], PowerGraph [5], and GraphX [6], which enable the distribution of graphs across multiple machines and facilitate the parallel execution of iterative algorithms, thereby allowing for the efficient computation of various graph metrics, including PageRank, connected components, shortest paths, and collaborative filtering. The efficiency of these distributed graph processing systems is heavily contingent upon the quality of graph partitioning, which entails the assignment of vertices or edges to distinct machines. An effective partition should exhibit two primary characteristics: a balanced workload, ensuring that no single machine becomes a bottleneck, and minimal inter-machine communication, as network costs often dictate the running time of distributed graph algorithms. Nonetheless, the quest for an optimal balanced partition is an NP-hard problem [7], and practical approaches must necessarily rely on heuristics.

Existing methods for graph partitioning can be broadly categorized into two distinct groups: offline and streaming approaches. Offline methods, such as METIS [8] and spectral approaches [9], necessitate the availability of the entire graph in memory prior to partitioning. Although these methods can yield high-quality partitions, their corresponding time and memory requirements are substantial, rendering them impractical for large graphs with billions of edges. In fact, the partitioning process can be more time-consuming than the subsequent computation. To address this limitation, streaming graph partitioning (SGP) was proposed [10, 11]. SGP methods process the graph as a stream of vertices or edges, assigning each item to a machine upon arrival, utilizing only limited information about the previously encountered items. This approach requires minimal memory, operates in a single pass, and can be parallelized, making it suitable for graphs that arrive in a continuous stream or are too large to be loaded into memory.

There are two fundamental strategies for partitioning a graph: edge-cut and vertex-cut. The edge-cut approach assigns each vertex to a machine, with edges whose endpoints lie on different machines being cut. In contrast, the vertex-cut approach assigns each edge to a machine, and a vertex with edges on multiple machines is replicated across all of them. The quality of an edge-cut is measured by the number of cut edges, whereas the quality of a vertex-cut is measured by the replication factor, which represents the average number of machines holding a copy of each vertex. Most existing SGP methods, including linear deterministic greedy and Fennel [10, 11, 12], employ the edge-cut strategy. Few SGP methods utilize the vertex-cut strategy, with notable examples including the hashing and greedy heuristics in PowerGraph [5] and the high-degree-replicated-first strategy in HDRF [13]. The vertex-cut strategy is more suitable for natural graphs, which typically exhibit a highly skewed power-law distribution in vertex degrees [14, 15]. A small number of hub vertices possess a large number of neighbors, whereas most vertices have few connections. Under the edge-cut strategy, a hub vertex placed on a single machine results in numerous cut edges, leading to heavy communication and an unbalanced load. Achieving a balance in the number of vertices per machine does not necessarily translate to a balanced workload, as the actual workload is determined by the number of edges.

In contrast, the vertex-cut strategy distributes the edges of a hub vertex across multiple machines, albeit at the cost of replicating that vertex. Since most vertices exhibit low degree, few vertices require replication, and the overall replication factor remains moderate. Both theoretical analysis and experiments [5, 16] have demonstrated the superiority of vertex-cut over edge-cut for power-law graphs. Despite the advantages of vertex-cut, existing vertex-cut SGP methods are limited. Hash-based methods are fast and balanced but disregard graph structure, resulting in a high replication factor. Greedy methods, which utilize the placement of previously seen edges, reduce replication but can perform poorly early in the stream when limited information is available and may compromise balance. Methods that rely on vertex degrees require either complete degree information, which is not available in a single-pass stream, or estimated partial degrees. These considerations underscore the need for a simple and effective vertex-cut method for streaming natural graphs.

It makes each placement decision based on the current state of the partitions, without storing the graph or performing multiple passes. The method is straightforward to implement, exhibits low time and memory overhead, and achieves a lower replication factor than existing methods while maintaining a balanced workload. A significant challenge in this context is striking a balance between minimizing inter-machine communication overhead and ensuring equitable computational distribution across machines. In this study, we focus on the vertex-cut methodology, wherein each edge is allocated to precisely one machine, and a vertex is duplicated on every machine that possesses at least one of its incident edges [1]. Our objective is to devise a partitioning strategy that optimizes the trade-off between replication factor and load imbalance, with the ultimate goal of minimizing the execution time of distributed graph algorithms. To formalize this problem, let us consider an undirected graph G = (V, E) comprising |V| = n vertices and |E| = m edges, distributed across p machines. We denote the set of machines on which vertex v is duplicated as A(v) ⊆ {1,…,p}, and the set of edges on machine i as E_i. The quality of a partition is evaluated by two primary metrics: the replication factor, RF = (1/n) Σ_v |A(v)|, which reflects the communication overhead incurred due to the need for duplicated vertices to synchronize their state, and the load imbalance, λ = max_i |E_i| / (m/p), which reflects computational balance. Our goal is to minimize RF subject to λ ≤ 1 + ε for a small tolerance ε. In the streaming setting, edges arrive sequentially as a stream, and each must be irreversibly assigned to a machine upon arrival. The partitioner maintains a compact state, including the current load of each machine, a table of the duplicate sets A(v), and a partial degree counter d(v) for each vertex, which equals the number of edges of v observed thus far. Notably, no edge is stored after assignment, resulting in memory usage of O(np) bits for the duplicate table plus O(n) for the counters, with a time complexity of O(p) per edge. The motivation behind our approach lies in the observation that natural graphs often exhibit a power-law degree distribution, P(d) ∝ d^(−α), with 2 < α < 3 typically [2]. This implies that a few high-degree vertices (hubs) are incident to a large proportion of edges. Edge-cut methods, which place such hubs on one machine and cut many edges to their neighbors, can lead to both communication and load skew [1]. In contrast, under vertex-cut, duplicating a hub is relatively inexpensive compared to the number of edges it saves from being cut, while low-degree vertices are rarely duplicated if their edges are co-located. Several existing streaming vertex-cut heuristics have been proposed, including hashing, the greedy heuristic of PowerGraph [1], and the degree-based hashing (DBH) [3] and HDRF [4] methods. The greedy heuristic considers only duplicate locality and load, whereas DBH and HDRF utilize degree information to decide which endpoint to duplicate. Our proposed algorithm, S-PowerGraph, builds upon these ideas by combining duplicate locality, degree awareness, and load balancing in a single scoring rule. The S-PowerGraph algorithm operates as follows. For an arriving edge e = (u, v), the partial degrees are first incremented, d(u) ← d(u)+1 and d(v) ← d(v)+1. We then define the normalized degrees θ(u) = d(u) / (d(u) + d(v)) and θ(v) = 1 − θ(u). A vertex with a small θ is relatively low-degree and should be kept intact, whereas the higher-degree endpoint is the better one to duplicate. For each machine i, we compute a score C(e, i) = C_rep(e, i) + C_bal(i). Despite these advances, a considerable proportion of patients do not achieve or maintain an adequate response to their first bDMARD. Primary non-response, secondary loss of efficacy, for example through development of anti-drug antibodies, and adverse events or patient preference lead to treatment discontinuation. The database covers inpatient and outpatient diagnoses (ICD-10-GM codes), outpatient prescriptions dispensed in pharmacies (coded by Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical [ATC] classification and Central Pharmaceutical Number), inpatient procedures, and demographic information (age, sex, date of death). Human action recognition has attracted sustained attention owing to its broad applications in video surveillance, human-computer interaction, healthcare monitoring, and autonomous driving [1], [2]. Among the available modalities, skeleton data, which represent the human body as a set of three-dimensional joint coordinates, offer several advantages oveer RGB video. They are compact, invariant to appearance, illumination, and background, and can be acquired in real time by depth sensors or pose estimation algorithms [3], [4]. Consequently, skeleton-based action recognition has become an active research topic, and a wide range of methods has been proposed. **Skeleton-based action recognition.** Early approaches relied on hand-crafted features describing joint positions, joint-angle relations, or the geometric configuration of body parts [5], [6]. With the advent of deep learning, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory networks were adopted to model teporal dynamics of joint sequences [7], [8], while convolutional neural networks (CNNs) treated skeleton sequences as pseudo-images and exploited their strong feature extraction ability [9], [10]. However, both families flatten the skeleton into a vector or grid and thus discard the natural topology of the human body. Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) overcomme this limitation by representing the skeleton as a spatio-temporal graph in which joints are veritces and bones are edges. ST-GCN [11] pioneered this direction, and subsequent works introduced adaptive graph structures, attention mechanisms, and multi-scale or multi-stream designs to improve accuracy [12]–[14]. These models now achieve high accuracy on large-scale benchmarks such as NTU RGB+D [15]. **Motivation.** Despite this progress, most existing methods are developed and evaluated under the assumption that skeletons are completely and accurately observed. This assumption is frequenty violated in practice. Self-occlusion, occlusion by objets or other people, limited sensor field of view, and failures of pose estimators often yield skeletons with missing or noisy joints [16]. Because such corruption changes the input distribution, models trained on clean data can degrade markedly at test time. We argue that this fragility is closely related to how conventional networks use the skeleton. Analysis with class activation maps (CAM) [17] indicates that a single network tends to concentrate on a small set of the most discriminative joints, for example the hands in the action of "drinking water", while largely ignoring other informative joints. Such a concentrated representation is efficient when all joints are visible, but it is brittle: if the few critical joints are occluded or corrupted, the remaining evidence is insufficient for a rliable decision. A more robust model should isntead discover discriminative cues distributed over the whole body, so that the loss of some joints can be compensated by others. This resembles the principle of redundancy in human perception, where recognition remains possible when parts of an object are hidden. **Proposed approach.** Motiavted by this observation, we prpose a richly activated graph convolutional network (RA-GCN) for action recognition with incomplete skeletons. RA-GCN is a multi-stream architecture in which the streams are trained sequentially and cooperatively. The first stream is trained in the conventional manner, and its CAM identifies the joints it relies upon. For each subsequent stream, the joints already activated by the preceding streams are suppressed in the input, which forces the stream to mine discriminative features from the remaining, previously unactivated joints. The streams are finally fused to produce the prediction. Through this erasing-and-relearning mechanism, the activated reion of the skeleton is substantially enlarged compared with that of a single-stream model, and the resulting features are richly distributed over the joints. Importantly, the approach requires no explicit occlusion annotations or additional supervision, and it is compatible with different GCN backbones. **Evaluation.** We evaluate RA-GCN on the NTU RGB+D dataset to verify that the richer feature coverage does not sarifice accuracy on complete skeletons. To assess robustness, we further construct synthetic occlusion settings in which pats of the skeleton or random joints are removed, simulating various realistic incompleteness patterns. Visualization of the CAMs further illustrates that RA-GCN activates considerably more joints than baseline models. **Contributions.** The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: 1. We identify the limited activation of discriminative joints as a key cause of the vulnearbility of existing skeleton-based models to incomplete inputs, and we study the problem of action recognition with incomplete skeletons. 2. We propose RA-GCN, a multi-stream GCN in which each stream learns from joints left unactivated by preceding streams, as identified by CAM, thereby yielding richly activated and complementary features. 3. We conduct extensive experiments showing that RA-GCN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods on NTU RGB+D and markedly reduces performance deterioration on synthetic occlusion data. Following [1], the skeleton is modeled as a spatiotemporal graph G = (V, E), in which the vertices correspond to joints and the edges comprise intra-frame bone connections and inter-frame links between identical joints in consecutive frames. The spatial graph convolution at a given layer is formulated as f_out = Σ_{k=1}^{K} W_k f_in (Λ_k^{-1/2} A_k Λ_k^{-1/2} ⊙ M_k), where A_k is the adjacency matrix of the k-th subset under the spatial-configuration partitioning strategy [1] (root, centripetal, and centrifugal subsets, so K = 3), Λ_k is the corresponding degree matrix, W_k is a 1×1 convvolutional weight, M_k is a learnable edge-importance mask, and ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication. Temporal modeling is performed by a Γ×1 convolution over consecutive frames. A basic block comprises a spatial graph convolution, a temporal convolution, batch normalization, ReLU, and a residual connection. The backbone stacks such blocks with increasing channel widths, followed by global average pooling and a fully connected classifier. **3.2 Class Activation Maps for Skeleton Joints** To identify which joints a network relies on, we adapt class activation mapping (CAM) [2] to the graph domain. Let F ∈ ℝ^{D×T'×V} be the feature map output by the last graph convolutional block, and let w_c ∈ ℝ^D be the classifier weight vector for class c. Since global average pooling precedes the classifier, the score of class c is s_c = Σ_d w_{c,d} · (1/(T'V)) Σ_{t,v} F_d(t,v). The activation map is then CAM_c(t,v) = Σ_d w_{c,d} F_d(t,v), which quantifies the contribution of joint v at time t to class c. Averaging over time and normalizing to [0,1] yields a joint-level activation vector a_c ∈ ℝ^V. Because the receptive field of the last layer covers a large portion of the skeleton, the map reflects discriminative evidence aggregated over neighboring joints; it is nevertheless informative at the joint level, as verified in our experiments. **3.3 Richly Activated GCN** Conventional GCNs tend to concentrate on a smalll set of highly discriminative joints (e.g., hands for “drinking”). When these joints are missing or corrupted, accuracy deteriorates sharply. RA-GCN addresses this by forcing successive streams to discover complementary evidence from the remaining joints. *Multi-stream architecture.* RA-GCN comprises N streams (N = 3 by default) with an identical backbone but unshred parameters. The first stream receives the complete skeleton X^{(1)} = X and is trained wtih a standard cross-entropy loss. For stream n > 1, the input is X^{(n)} = X ⊙ (1 − m^{(n−1)}), where m^{(n−1)} ∈ {0,1}^V is a joint mask broadcast over channels and frames, derived from the activation map of the preceding stream. Thus, joints that were strongly activated previously are suppressed, and the n-th stream must classify the sample using only the residual joints. *Erasing strategy.* Given the ground-truth class y of a training sample, the joint-level activation a^{(n−1)}_y is computed from stream n−1. Joints whose normalized activation exceeds a threshold λ are erased: m_v^{(n−1)} = 𝟙[a_{y,v}^{(n−1)} > λ]. Masks are accumulated across streams, m̃^{(n)} = max(m̃^{(n−1)}, m^{(n)}), so that joints erased in an earlier stream remain unavailable to later ones, preventing the re-discovery of the same features. Erased joints are set to zero, which, after input normalization, corresponds to the mean pose value. At least a minimum number of joints is always retained to avoid degenerate inputs. Raw features of the preceding stream are not forwarded, since doing so would reintroduce reliance on the erased joints. **3.4 Training Objective and Fusion** Each stream n produces class posterior p^{(n)} and is supervised by its own cross-entropy loss ℒ_n. The overall objective is ℒ = Σ_{n=1}^{N} ℒ_n(p^{(n)}, y), and the streams are optimized jointtly by stochastic gradient descent with Nesterov momentum. Because the masks are produced from detached activation maps, no gradient flwos through the erasing operation. Sequences are resampled to a fixed lengh of T = 300 frames; shorter ones are padded by repetition. For multi-person actions, at most two skeletons are retained and processed by sharing weights, with features averaged before classification. Each skeleton is translated to a body-centered coordinate sytsem and, optionally, rotated to align the torso with a canonical axis. The field of human action recognition has garnered significant attention in recent years, driven by its vast potential applications in domains such as video surveillance, human-computer interaction, healthcare monitoring, and autonomous vehicles [1], [2]. Among the various modalities employed for action recognition, skeleton data has emerged as a promising representation, offering numerous advantages over traditional RGB video. This is due to its ability to capture the human body as a set of three-dimensional joint coordinates, which are not only compact but also invariant to appearance, illumination, and background, making them readily accessible in real-time using depth sensors or pose estimation algorithms [3], [4]. As a result, skeleton-based action recognition has become a thriving area of research, with a plethora of methods being proposed in recent years. Initial approaches to skeleton-based action recognition relied heavily on hand-crafted features that described the spatial relationships between joints, the angular relationships between joints, or the geometric configuration of body parts [5], [6]. However, with the advent of deep learning, researchers began to explore the use of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory networks to capture the temporal dynamics of joint sequences [7], [8]. Furthermore, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were applied to skeleton sequences, treating them as pseudo-images, and leveraging their exceptional feature extraction capabilities [9], [10]. Despite the efficacy of these methods, they are limited by their tendency to flatten the skeleton into a vector or grid, thereby disregarding the innate topology of the human body. To address this limitation, graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been proposed, which represent the skeleton as a spatio-temporal graph, where joints are vertices and bones are edges. The pioneering work of ST-GCN [11] paved the way for subsequent studies, which introduced adaptive graph structures, attention mechanisms, and multi-scale or multi-stream designs to enhance accuracy [12]–[14]. These models have achieved impressive accuracy on large-scale benchmarks, such as NTU RGB+D [15]. Nevertheless, despite this progress, most existing methods are developed and evaluated under the assumption that skeletons are complete and accurately observed. This assumption is frequently violated in practice, as self-occlusion, occlusion by objects or other individuals, limited sensor field of view, and failures of pose estimators can result in skeletons with missing or noisy joints [16]. The degradation of skeletons can significantly impair the performance of models trained on clean data, as the input distribution changes at test time. We contend that this fragility is intimately related to the manner in which conventional networks utilize the skeleton. Analysis employing class activation maps (CAM) [17] reveals that a single network tends to focus on a limited set of the most discriminative joints, while largely disregarding other informative joints. For instance, in the action of "drinking water", the network may concentrate on the hands, while neglecting other joints that could provide valuable information. Such a concentrated representation is efficient when all joints are visible, but it is fragile: if the few critical joints are occluded or corrupted, the remaining evidence is insufficient for a reliable decision. A more robust model should discover discriminative cues distributed throughout the entire body, so that the loss of some joints can be compensated by others. This is analogous to the principle of redundancy in human perception, where recognition remains possible even when parts of an object are hidden. Inspired by this observation, we propose a richly activated graph convolutional network (RA-GCN) for action recognition with incomplete skeletons. RA-GCN is a multi-stream architecture in which the streams are trained sequentially and cooperatively. The first stream is trained in the conventional manner, and its CAM identifies the joints it relies upon. For each subsequent stream, the joints already activated by the preceding streams are suppressed in the input, which forces the stream to extract discriminative features from the remaining, previously unactivated joints. The streams are ultimately fused to produce the prediction. Through this erasing-and-relearning mechanism, the activated region of the skeleton is substantially enlarged compared to that of a single-stream model, and the resulting features are richly distributed over the joints. Notably, the approach requires no explicit occlusion annotations or additional supervision and is compatible with different GCN backbones. We evaluate RA-GCN on the NTU RGB+D dataset to verify that the richer feature coverage does not sacrifice accuracy on complete skeletons. To assess robustness, we further construct synthetic occlusion settings in which parts of the skeleton or random joints are removed, simulating various realistic incompleteness patterns. Visualization of the CAMs further illustrates that RA-GCN activates a significantly larger number of joints than baseline models. The primary contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: 1. We identify the limited activation of discriminative joints as a key cause of the vulnerability of existing skeleton-based models to incomplete inputs and investigate the problem of action recognition with incomplete skeletons. 2. We propose RA-GCN, a multi-stream GCN in which each stream learns from joints left unactivated by preceding streams, as identified by CAM, thereby yielding richly activated and complementary features. 3. We demonstrate the efficacy of RA-GCN in enhancing the robustness of action recognition models to incomplete skeletons, without sacrificing accuracy on complete skeletons. By exploring the concept of rich activation, we provide a novel perspective on the development of robust action recognition models, which can effectively handle incomplete and noisy skeleton data. Our approach has significant implications for the development of more robust and reliable action recognition systems, which can operate effectively in real-world environments where data quality and availability may be compromised. Furthermore, the insights gained from this study can be applied to other domains where incomplete or noisy data is a common challenge, such as robotics, healthcare, and surveillance. In conclusion, this work contributes to the development of more robust and reliable action recognition models, which can effectively handle incomplete and noisy skeleton data, and provides a foundation for future research in this area. Exposure to trauma in early childhood, including physical, sexual, and emotional abuse and neglect, is a major risk factor for a wide range of psychiatric disorders in adulthood [1,2]. When trauma occurs repeatedly, within caregiving relationships, and during critical periods of development, it is often described as complex trauma [3]. The consequences extend beyond the classic symptoms of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and include affect dysregulation, disturbed self-concept, interpersonal difficulties, and dissociation [4,5]. A less frequently studieed consequence is the effect of early trauma on a person's relationship with their own body. The body is central to the experience of trauma. Abuse, particulary physical and sexual abuse, is directly inflicted on the body, and the child's body may become associated with fear, pain, shame, and helplessness [6]. Neglect and emotional abuse may also dsturb the development of a positive bodily self, because the infant's early sense of the body develops in the context of attuned, responsive caregiving [7]. Theoretical accounts suggest that when such experiences are chronic, the body may be perceived as unsafe, as an object of disgust, or as something to be controlled, avoided, or disowned [8,9]. Clinical observations support this view: survivors of childhood trauma frequently report feeling alienated from their body, being unable to sense it accurately, or hating it [10]. Such disturbances may in turn contribute to self-harm, eating disorders, somatic complaints, and revictimization [11,12]. Body experience is a multidimensional construct. Researchers commonly distinguish between perceptual, cognitive-affective, and attitudinal components [13,14]. In the present study we focus on three domains that are relevant to trauma. Body attitude refers to the evaluative and emotional stance toward one's body, including feelings of vitality, self-confidence, and physical appearance, as well as perceived body competence and rejection [15]. Body satisfactino refers to the degree of contentment with specific body parts and functions [16]. Boy awareness refers to the attention paid to, and the perception of, internal bodily sensations [17]. Each domain may be affected differently by trauma. Negative attitudes and dissatisfaction may reflect shame and self-devaluation, whereas awareness may be either heightened, as in hypervigilance to bodily threat signals, or reduced, as in avoidance and numbing [18]. Empirical findings support an association between childhood maltreatment and negative body image. Studies of survivors of childhood sexual abuse have reported greater body dissatisfaction, body shame, and body disconnection than in comparison groups [19,20]. Similar results have ben found for physical and emotional abuse [21]. Evidence on body awareness is less consistent. Some studies report increased attention to bodily symptoms and somatic complaints in trauma-exposed individuals [22], whereas others describe reduced interoceptive accuracy or sensitivity, in line with emotional numbing and dissociation [23,24]. Much of the literature, however, has relied on samples of survivors of a single type of trauma, on non-clinical or student populations, or on a single measure of body image. Few studies have simultaneously examined several domains of body experience in cliniccal patients with documented early and complex trauma, and fewer still have used comparison data from a non-clinical group to estimate the magnitude of the differences. A further question concerns how body experience relates to the clinical features of trauma-related disorders. Severity of trauma symptoms, such as intrusion, avoidance, and hyperarousal, might be expected to covary with negative body experience, since trauma reminders are often bodily and avoidance may include avoidance of bodily states [25]. Dissociation is of particular interest. Dissociative phenomena such as depersonalization, derealization, and somatoform dissociation involve alterations in the experience of the body and the sense of ownership of it [26,27]. Individulas who frequently dissociate may therefore be expected to report a more negative or disconnected body experience. Yet it is unclear whetther self-reported body attitude, satisfaction, and awareness are closely tied to these symptom dimensions or whether they represent a relatively separate area of impairment that requires its own assessment. This question has clinical relevance. Body-oriented and body-focused interventions are increasingly used in the treatment of trauma-related disorders, including body psychotherapy, sensorimotor approaches, yoga, and movement therapies [28,29]. Their rationale rests on the assumption that disturbed body experience is a core feature of trauma that is not sufficiently addressd by verbal or cognitive treatments alone. Establishing the extent and pattern of disturbances in different domains, and whether they are simply a reflection of symptom severity, can inform decisions about assessment and treatment planning. The present study therefore had two aims. First, we examined disturbances in body attitude, body satisfaction, and body awareness in female patients with complex trauma originating in ealry childhood, in comparison with a non-clinical female sample. We hypothesized that patients would show significantly more negative body experience in all three domains. Second, we investigated the associations of these domains with the severity of trauma symptoms and the frequency of dissociative experiences within the patient group. Given the theoretical overlap between trauma symptomatology, dissociation, and the body, we expected to find associations between these variables, although the strength of these associations was explored without a firm prediction. The experience of trauma during early childhood, including physical, emotional, and sexual abuse, as well as neglect, has been identified as a critical factor that increases the risk of developing various psychiatric disorders later in life, as highlighted by numerous research studies [1,2]. Traumatic experiences that recur, occur within the context of caregiving relationships, and take place during periods of significant developmental vulnerability are often referred to as complex trauma [3]. The consequences of complex trauma are far-reaching, extending beyond the typical symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) to include difficulties with emotional regulation, disturbances in one's sense of self, challenges in interpersonal relationships, and dissociation [4,5]. A less explored aspect of the impact of early trauma is its effect on an individual's relationship with their physical body. The body plays a central role in the experience of trauma, as physical and sexual abuse directly affect the body, potentially leading to associations between the body and feelings of fear, pain, shame, and powerlessness [6]. Furthermore, neglect and emotional abuse can disrupt the development of a positive body image, as the infant's initial perception of their body is shaped within the context of responsive and nurturing caregiving [7]. Theoretical models suggest that prolonged exposure to such adverse experiences may result in the perception of the body as a source of danger, an object of revulsion, or something that needs to be controlled, avoided, or rejected [8,9]. Clinical observations support this perspective, with many survivors of childhood trauma reporting feelings of disconnection from their body, difficulty accurately perceiving bodily sensations, or outright hostility towards their body [10]. These disturbances can contribute to self-destructive behaviors, eating disorders, physical complaints, and an increased risk of experiencing further trauma [11,12]. The concept of body experience is complex and multifaceted, comprising various dimensions. Researchers often distinguish between perceptual, cognitive-affective, and attitudinal components [13,14]. In the context of the current study, we focused on three domains that are particularly relevant to trauma: body attitude, body satisfaction, and body awareness. Body attitude refers to the way an individual evaluates and emotionally responds to their body, encompassing feelings of vitality, confidence, and physical attractiveness, as well as perceived bodily competence and acceptance [15]. Body satisfaction relates to the degree of contentment with specific body parts and functions [16]. Body awareness involves the attention paid to and the perception of internal bodily sensations [17]. Each of these domains can be affected differently by traumatic experiences. Negative attitudes and dissatisfaction may reflect underlying shame and self-devaluation, whereas body awareness may be either increased, as observed in heightened vigilance to potential bodily threats, or decreased, as seen in avoidance and emotional numbing [18]. Empirical findings support a link between childhood maltreatment and negative body image. Studies focusing on survivors of childhood sexual abuse have consistently reported greater body dissatisfaction, body shame, and body disconnection compared to non-abused individuals [19,20]. Similar outcomes have been observed in cases of physical and emotional abuse [21]. However, evidence regarding body awareness is less consistent. Some studies indicate increased attention to bodily symptoms and physical complaints among individuals exposed to trauma [22], while others describe reduced interoceptive accuracy or sensitivity, aligning with symptoms of emotional numbing and dissociation [23,24]. Much of the existing literature has relied on samples of survivors of a single type of trauma, non-clinical populations, or student groups, and often utilizes a single measure of body image. Few studies have comprehensively examined multiple domains of body experience in clinical patients with documented early and complex trauma, and even fewer have incorporated comparison data from a non-clinical group to quantify the magnitude of differences. A further question concerns the relationship between body experience and the clinical features of trauma-related disorders. It is reasonable to expect that the severity of trauma symptoms, such as intrusion, avoidance, and hyperarousal, would be related to negative body experience, given that trauma reminders often have a bodily component and avoidance may include evasion of bodily states [25]. Dissociation, characterized by phenomena such as depersonalization, derealization, and somatoform dissociation, which involve alterations in the experience of the body and the sense of ownership over it, is of particular interest [26,27]. Individuals who frequently dissociate may, therefore, be expected to report a more negative or disconnected body experience. However, it remains unclear whether self-reported body attitude, satisfaction, and awareness are closely tied to these symptom dimensions or whether they represent a relatively separate area of impairment that necessitates its own assessment. This question holds significant clinical relevance. Interventions that focus on the body, including body psychotherapy, sensorimotor approaches, yoga, and movement therapies, are increasingly being used in the treatment of trauma-related disorders [28,29]. The rationale underlying these interventions is based on the assumption that disturbed body experience is a core feature of trauma that may not be adequately addressed by solely verbal or cognitive treatments. Establishing the extent and pattern of disturbances in different domains, and determining whether these disturbances simply reflect symptom severity, is essential for the development of effective interventions. Understanding the complex relationship between body experience and trauma-related disorders can inform the creation of targeted treatments that address the unique needs of individuals who have experienced trauma, ultimately leading to improved outcomes and enhanced well-being. Furthermore, recognizing the importance of body experience in the context of trauma can help reduce stigma and promote a more holistic approach to treatment, one that acknowledges the intricate interplay between the body, mind, and spirit. By exploring the multifaceted nature of body experience and its relationship to trauma, researchers and clinicians can work together to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the complex needs of survivors of childhood trauma, ultimately providing them with more effective and compassionate care. Additionally, the development of body-oriented interventions can be informed by the understanding that trauma is not just an emotional or psychological experience, but also a deeply physical one, and that the body holds a critical role in the healing process. As such, these interventions can be tailored to address the specific needs of individuals with complex trauma, taking into account the complex interplay between their body, mind, and emotions. Moreover, the incorporation of body-oriented approaches into existing treatment protocols can enhance the overall effectiveness of therapy, leading to improved symptom reduction, increased sense of well-being, and a more positive body image. In conclusion, the relationship between body experience and trauma is complex and multifaceted, and requires a comprehensive and nuanced approach to understanding and treatment. By recognizing the critical role of the body in the experience of trauma, and by developing targeted interventions that address the unique needs of survivors of childhood trauma, we can work towards providing more effective and compassionate care, and ultimately, promoting greater healing and recovery. To be eligible for the study, participants had to meet specific criteria, including being female, at least 18 years old, and having experienced repeated interpersonal trauma (encompassing physical, sexual, or emotional abuse or neglect) that began before the age of 18. Furthermore, a primary clinical diagnosis of a trauma-related disorder, as determined by a seasoned clinician using ICD-10 criteria [1], was required. To ensure diagnostic accuracy, individuals with acute psychosis, acute suicidality, current substance intoxication, limited proficiency in the language of the questionnaires, and organic brain disorders were excluded from participation. Notably, the presence of comorbid diagnoses, such as depression, anxiety, eating disorders, and borderline personality disorder, did not preclude individuals from participating, given the high prevalence of these conditions in this population [2].

In addition to the clinical sample, a comparison group of 216 women from the general population was recruited through university mailing lists, public announcements, and personal contacts. Participants in this group reported not being engaged in any current psychiatric treatment, and due to the anonymous nature of the study, they did not undergo a structured clinical interview. Instead, group membership was determined based on self-reported non-treatment status. All participants provided informed consent, either in writing or electronically, prior to completing the questionnaires, which were administered within the first two weeks of treatment for the clinical sample, before the initiation of body-oriented interventions. The questionnaires were completed in a quiet room, with a researcher available to address any questions or concerns. In contrast, the non-clinical participants completed the same measures assessing body experience either on paper or online.

The study was approved by the responsible institutional ethics committee and conducted in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki [3]. The assessment of body attitude was conducted using the Dresden Body Image Questionnaire (DKB-35) [4], a 35-item instrument that utilizes a six-point scale to yield five subscales: body acceptance, vitality, physical contact, sexual fulfillment, and self-aggrandizement. Lower scores on this measure are indicative of a more negative body attitude, and in this study, the total score served as the primary indicator of body attitude. The DKB-35 has demonstrated robust reliability and validity in both clinical and non-clinical German samples [4], with high internal consistency (Cronbach’s α =.96) observed in the clinical sample.

Body satisfaction was evaluated using the Body Cathexis Scale [5], which requires respondents to rate their satisfaction with various body parts and functions on a five-point scale. Higher sum scores on this scale reflect greater satisfaction, and the scale has been widely used in research on body image, demonstrating adequate psychometric properties [5,6]. The internal consistency of this scale in the present sample was α =.94. The assessment of body awareness was conducted using the Somatic Awareness Questionnaire, which captures the tendency to notice and attend to internal bodily sensations and changes [7]. Items on this scale are rated on a Likert-type scale, with higher scores indicating greater awareness of bodily signals. It is essential to note that trauma can result in both heightened vigilance and numbing of bodily sensations, and therefore, scores on this scale were interpreted as reflecting overall attentiveness to bodily states rather than their accuracy or valence. The internal consistency of this scale in the present study was α =.88.

The severity of posttraumatic symptoms in the clinical sample was measured using the Davidson Trauma Scale (DTS) [8], a 17-item self-report scale that corresponds to the DSM-IV symptom criteria for posttraumatic stress disorder. Participants rated the frequency and severity of each symptom over the previous week on five-point scales (0–4), yielding a total score ranging from 0 to 136, as well as subscale scores for intrusion, avoidance/numbing, and hyperarousal. The DTS has demonstrated good reliability and validity [8,9], with a Cronbach’s α of.93 observed in this sample. Dissociative experiences were measured using the Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES) [10], a 28-item self-report questionnaire that assesses the frequency of dissociative phenomena, such as amnesia, absorption, and depersonalization. Respondents indicated the percentage of time (0–100%) that they experienced each phenomenon, and the mean across items served as the total score. Scores of 30 or above on this scale are often considered indicative of a clinically relevant level of dissociation [11]. The DES demonstrated high reliability and validity, with an α of.95 in the present sample.

Data analysis was conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics. Prior to analysis, distributions were inspected for normality and outliers, and missing values were handled according to the manual of each instrument; if more than 10% of items on a scale were missing, the case was excluded for that scale. Descriptive statistics were computed for all variables, and due to potential age differences between groups, age was compared between groups using an independent-samples t test and considered as a potential covariate. Group differences in body attitude, body satisfaction, and body awareness were examined using independent-samples t tests, with Welch’s correction applied when variances were unequal, as indicated by the Levene test for homogeneity of variances.

Representing documents as fixed-length, continuous vectors is a central step in many text processing pipelines, including topic identification, document retrieval, clustering, and recommendation. Classical approaches such as latent semantic analysis [1], probabilistic latent semantic analysis [2], and latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) [3] map a bag-of-words representation of a document into a low-dimensional latent space. More recently, neural approaches, such as the neural variational document model (NVDM) [4], paragraph vetcors [5], and various autoencoder-based models, have been proposed. Despite differences in formulation, the majority of these techniques yield only point estimates of the document embeddings. A point estimate carries no information about how reliably it represents the document. This is a serious limitation because documents differ greatly in length and in the amount of evidence they provide. A short document witth a handful of words supports a far less certain embedding than a long document with thousands of words, yet both are mapped to vectors of the same knid and are treated downstream with equal confidence. **Motivation** Capturing uncertainty in embeddings is the natural domain of Bayesian modelling. If each document embedding is treated as a latent random variable with a posterior distribution, the covariance of that posterior quantifies how well the embedding is determined by the observed counts. Such uncertainty can be propagated into downstream tasks, so that poorly determined embeddings contribute less to classifier training and decision making. This idea has precedent in speech processing, wherre the i-vector model [6] and its Bayesian treatments use posterior covariances of utterance-level embeddings to improve speaker and language recognition. The subspace multinomial model (SMM) [7] is a close relative of these models for discrete data. It is a log-linear model in which a low-dimensional document embedding is mapped, through a shared subspace matrix, to the parameters of a multinomial distribution over words. In its original form, however, the SMM estimates document embeddings by maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori inference, so it too provides only point estimates. **Challenges** Moving from pooint estimates to full posterior distributions in the SMM is not straightforward. The SMM belongs to the family of mixed-logit models, where the likelihood contains a softmax normalisation over the vocabulary. When variational inference is applied, the expected log-normaliser under the approximate posterior has no closed form, and the resulting objective is intractable. Existing remedies include Monte Carlo estimates of the expectation, which yield high-variance gradients, and bounds originally developed for correlated topic models [8] and Bayesian multinomial logistic regression [9], such as the Jaakkola–Jordan bound [10], Bohning's quadratic bound [11], and Taylor-based approximations. These bounds differ in tightness and computational cost, and their suitability for large-vocabulary text models is not well established. **Contributions** In this work we present Bayesian subspace multinomial model (Bayesian SMM), a generative log-linear model thta represents each docmuent by a Gaussian posterior distribution over its embedding, whose covaariance encodes the uncertainty of the estimate. Our contributions are as follows. 1. We derive a variational Bayesian treatment of the SMM in which the document embeddings are latent variables with Gaussian posteriors, and the subspace parameters are estimated by maximising the evidence lower bound. We address the intractability of the expected log-normaliser with a tractable bound, which yields closed-form, efficient updates of the variational parameters. 2. We propose a generative Gaussian linear classifier for topic idntification thaat operates directly on the posterior distributions. By exploiting the document-specific covariances during classifier training and scoring, the classifier accounts for the reliability of each embedding rather than treating all embeddings as equally informative. 3. We evalluate the model intrinsically using perplexity on the Fisher speech corpus, using automatic transcriptions, and on the 20Newsgroups text corpus, and we compare it to NVDM, a state-of-the-art neural variational document model. We show that Bayesian SMM achieves a better fit to the data. 4. We evaluate the model extrinsically on topic identification. The proposed systems are less prone to over-fitting on unseen test data than competing methods. They also outperform state-of-the-art unsupervised topic models and obtain results comparable to fully supervised discriminative models. **Organisation of the paper** The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on topic models, neural document models, and Bayesian embeddings. Section 3 descirbes the SMM and the intractability that arises in variational inference for mixed-logit models. Section 4 presents the Bayesian SMM, including the variational objective, the bound used, and the update equations for the document posteriors and the subspace parameters. Section 5 introduces the generative Gaussian linear classifier that uses embedding uncertainty. Section 6 describes the datasets, experimental setup, and baselines, and Section 7 reports the perplexity and topic identification results together with an analysis of the learned uncertainties. Section 8 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work. **Notation and generative model.** Let a corpus consist of D documents over a vocabulary of size V. Document d is represented by its word-count vector x_d ∈ ℕ^V, with total count N_d = Σ_v x_dv. The Bayesian subspace multinomial model (Bayesian SMM) is a generative log-linear model. Each document d has a latent vector w_d ∈ ℝ^K, with K ≪ V, which parameterizes a document-specific categorical distribution over words through a softmax: φ_dv = exp(m_v + t_vᵀ w_d) / Σ_{v'} exp(m_{v'} + t_{v'}ᵀ w_d), where m ∈ ℝ^V is a background log-unigram bias and T = [t_1,…,t_V]ᵀ ∈ ℝ^{V×K} is a global subspace (embedding) matrix. Given w_d, the counts follow a multinomial, p(x_d | w_d) = ∏_v φ_dv^{x_dv}, up to a constant. This is a mixed-logit model, since the softmax is applied to a mixture over latent document variables [1]. The classical SMM [2] estimates w_d as a point by maximum likelihood or MAP. Here we place a prior p(w_d) = 𝒩(w_d | 0, I) and treat w_d as a random variable, so that the posterior p(w_d | x_d) yields boht an embedding and its uncertainty. To regularize T, we place a sparsity-inducing Laplace prior on its entries [3]. The parameters m and T are treated as point estimates. **Variational inference.** The posterior p(w_d | x_d) is intractable because of the softmax normalizer. We approximate it with a Gaussian q(w_d) = 𝒩(w_d | μ_d, Σ_d), witth Σ_d diagonal for efficiency. Parameters are learned by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO) oevr the corpus: ℒ = Σ_d { E_q[log p(x_d | w_d)] − KL(q(w_d) ‖ p(w_d)) } + log p(T). The KL term has a closed form for Gaussians. The expecetd log-likelihood is E_q[log p(x_d | w_d)] = Σ_v x_dv ( m_v + t_vᵀ μ_d ) − N_d E_q[ log Σ_{v'} exp(m_{v'} + t_{v'}ᵀ w_d) ]. The final expectation of the log-sum-exp has no closed form, which is the intractability that commonly arises in variational inference for mixed-logit models. **Bounding the log-normalizer.** Existing remedies include the Jensen-based bound with a first-order Taylor expansion [4], the Bohning quadratic bound [5], and the piecewise bounds used for correlated topic models [6]. We instead use a tractable bound derived from the concavity of the logarithm. For any ξ_d > 0, log z ≤ z/ξ_d + log ξ_d − 1, so E_q[log Σ_v exp(m_v + t_vᵀ w_d)] ≤ (1/ξ_d) Σ_v E_q[exp(m_v + t_vᵀ w_d)] + log ξ_d − 1. Under a Gaussian q, each term is the mean of a log-normal variable: E_q[exp(m_v + t_vᵀ w_d)] = exp(m_v + t_vᵀ μ_d + ½ t_vᵀ Σ_d t_v). The bound is therefore available in closed form. The resulting lower bound on the ELBO is differentiable in all variational and model parameters. The auxiliary variable ξ_d is a per-document quantity whose optimum, obtained by setting the derivative to zero, is ξ_d = Σ_v exp(m_v + t_vᵀ μ_d + ½ t_vᵀ Σ_d t_v). This makes the bound tight at the current q and avoids the quadratic-curvature approximations that degrade for large V. **Optimization.** Training alternates between two steps, in the manner of variational EM. In the E-step, for fixed T and m, we update ξ_d in closed form and update (μ_d, Σ_d) by gradient ascent on the bound, parameterizing Σ_d through log-variances to enforce positivity. In the M-step, T and m are updated with the posterior statistics fixed. Because the number of parameters is large, we use Adam [7] with mini-batches of documents for both steps, and for the Laplace prior we apply the subgradient of the L1 penalty. Variational paramteers are initialized with μ_d = 0 and Σ_d = I. Convergence is monitored through the bound on a held-out set of documents. **Document embeddings and uncertainty.** After training, each document is summarized by the pair (μ_d, Σ_d). The mean μ_d serves as the embedding, while Σ_d encodes how well it is determined by the observed counts. Short documents yield posteriors close to the prior, whereas loner documents give narrower posteriors. For unseen documents, T and m are held fixed and only (μ_d, Σ_d, ξ_d) are optimized. **Perplexity evaluation.** For intrinsic evaluation, the model is compared with the neural variational document model (NVDM) [8]. For a test document, we infer the posterior and compute an upper bound on the perplexity, PPL = exp( −(1/D) Σ_d (1/N_d) log p(x_d) ), with log p(x_d) replaced by the ELBO. The same estmate is used for both models so that the comparison is consistent. **Generative Gaussian linear classifier.** For topic identification, we exploit the uncertainty with a generative classifier operating on the posterior distributions. Each class c has a Gaussian over embeddings, 𝒩(w | η_c, Λ), with a shared covariance Λ, which yields a linear classifier. Classes are modelled in the latnt space with the observed embedding treated as noisy: the document's posterior covariance Σ_d is addded to the class covariance when computing the likelihood, p(μ_d | c) = 𝒩(μ_d | η_c, Λ + Σ_d). Documents with large uncertainty therefore contirbute less sharply to the class scores, and to the estimation of η_c and Λ. Parameters are estimated by EM, treating the true embeddings as latent variables, as in probabilistic linear discriminant analysis [9]. The decision rule is argmax_c log p(μ_d | c) + log π_c, with class priors π_c. Because the covariances are shared, the classifier is linear in μ_d wehn Σ_d is constant, and otherwise has document-dependent scaling. **Experimental protocol.** We use the Fisher speech corpus, with transcripts produced by an automatic speech recognizer, and 20Newsgroups [10]. Standard splist are used, and hyperparameters (K, prior strength, learning rate) are selected on validation data. The process of converting text documents into numerical representations, known as document embeddings, is a vital component in various natural language processing applications, such as identifying topics, retrieving documents, clustering, and recommending items. The primary objective of these techniques is to transform a document's representation, which is typically a collection of words, into a compact, low-dimensional space where documents with similar semantic meanings are positioned in close proximity. Traditional methods, including latent semantic analysis [1], probabilistic latent semantic analysis [2], and latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) [3], have been extensively employed for this purpose. More recently, neural network-based approaches, such as the neural variational document model (NVDM) [4], paragraph vectors [5], and various autoencoder-based models, have been proposed. Despite their differences in formulation, the majority of these techniques provide only a single, fixed estimate of the document embeddings, which does not convey any information about the reliability or uncertainty of these representations. This limitation is significant, as documents vary greatly in terms of their length and the amount of information they contain. For instance, a short document with only a few words will have a much less reliable embedding than a longer document with thousands of words, yet both are treated as equally informative in downstream applications. This limitation highlights the need to capture uncertainty in document embeddings, which is naturally addressed through Bayesian modelling. By representing each document embedding as a latent random variable with a posterior distribution, the uncertainty of the embedding can be quantified and propagated to subsequent tasks, allowing poorly defined embeddings to contribute less to training classifiers and making decisions. This concept has been applied in speech processing, where the i-vector model [6] and its Bayesian extensions utilize posterior covariances of utterance-level embeddings to improve speaker and language recognition. A related model for discrete data is the subspace multinomial model (SMM) [7], which is a log-linear model that maps a low-dimensional document embedding to the parameters of a multinomial distribution over words through a shared subspace matrix. However, the original SMM estimates document embeddings using maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori inference, resulting in only point estimates. Extending the SMM to provide full posterior distributions is not straightforward due to the softmax normalization over the vocabulary in the likelihood, which leads to an intractable objective when applying variational inference. Existing solutions include Monte Carlo estimates of the expectation, which yield high-variance gradients, and bounds developed for correlated topic models [8] and Bayesian multinomial logistic regression [9], such as the Jaakkola-Jordan bound [10], Bohning's quadratic bound [11], and Taylor-based approximations. These bounds differ in terms of their tightness and computational cost, and their suitability for large-vocabulary text models is not well established. This work presents the Bayesian subspace multinomial model (Bayesian SMM), a generative log-linear model that represents each document using a Gaussian posterior distribution over its embedding, where the covariance captures the uncertainty of the estimate. The key contributions of this work are as follows. Firstly, a variational Bayesian treatment of the SMM is derived, where document embeddings are latent variables with Gaussian posteriors, and subspace parameters are estimated by maximizing the evidence lower bound. The intractability of the expected log-normalizer is addressed using a tractable bound, yielding closed-form, efficient updates of the variational parameters. Secondly, a generative Gaussian linear classifier for topic identification is proposed, operating directly on the posterior distributions of the document embeddings. By leveraging the document-specific covariances during classifier training and scoring, the classifier accounts for the reliability of each embedding rather than treating all embeddings as equally informative. Thirdly, the model is evaluated intrinsically using perplexity on the Fisher speech corpus and the 20Newsgroups text corpus, and compared to the NVDM, a state-of-the-art neural variational document model. The results show that the Bayesian SMM achieves a better fit to the data. Finally, the model is evaluated extrinsically on topic identification, demonstrating that the proposed system is less prone to overfitting on unseen test data and outperforms competing methods, including state-of-the-art unsupervised topic models and fully supervised discriminative models. To impose regularization on $T$, we employ a Laplace prior with a sparsity-inducing nature on its entries, as proposed in [3], while treating the parameters $m$ and $T$ as point estimates. 

**Variational Inference Approach**
The posterior distribution $p(w_d | x_d)$ is, unfortunately, intractable due to the presence of the softmax normalizer. To circumvent this issue, we approximate it using a Gaussian distribution $q(w_d) = \mathcal{N}(w_d | \mu_d, \Sigma_d)$, where $\Sigma_d$ is assumed to be diagonal to enhance computational efficiency. The parameters of this variational distribution are learned through the maximization of the evidence lower bound (ELBO) over the entire corpus. This is expressed as $\mathcal{L} = \sum_d \{ \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(x_d | w_d)] - \text{KL}(q(w_d) || p(w_d)) \} + \log p(T)$. The KL term possesses a closed-form solution for Gaussian distributions, while the expected log-likelihood is given by $\mathbb{E}_q[\log p(x_d | w_d)] = \sum_v x_{dv} (m_v + t_v^T \mu_d) - N_d \mathbb{E}_q[\log \sum_{v'} \exp(m_{v'} + t_{v'}^T w_d)]$. However, the expectation of the log-sum-exp term does not have a closed-form solution, which is a common issue encountered in variational inference for mixed-logit models.

**Bounding the Log-Normalizer Term**
To address the intractability of the log-normalizer, several approaches can be employed, including the Jensen-based bound with a first-order Taylor expansion [4], the Bohning quadratic bound [5], and the piecewise bounds utilized for correlated topic models [6]. Alternatively, we leverage a tractable bound derived from the concavity of the logarithmic function. For any $\xi_d > 0$, the inequality $\log z \leq z/\xi_d + \log \xi_d - 1$ holds, which leads to $\mathbb{E}_q[\log \sum_v \exp(m_v + t_v^T w_d)] \leq (1/\xi_d) \sum_v \mathbb{E}_q[\exp(m_v + t_v^T w_d)] + \log \xi_d - 1$. Under a Gaussian $q$, each term is equivalent to the mean of a log-normal variable, expressed as $\mathbb{E}_q[\exp(m_v + t_v^T w_d)] = \exp(m_v + t_v^T \mu_d + \frac{1}{2} t_v^T \Sigma_d t_v)$. Consequently, the bound is available in closed form. The resulting lower bound on the ELBO is differentiable with respect to all variational and model parameters. The auxiliary variable $\xi_d$ is a document-specific quantity, and its optimum value, obtained by setting the derivative to zero, is $\xi_d = \sum_v \exp(m_v + t_v^T \mu_d + \frac{1}{2} t_v^T \Sigma_d t_v)$. This ensures that the bound is tight at the current $q$ and avoids the quadratic-curvature approximations that degrade for large $V$.

**Optimization Procedure**
The training process involves alternating between two steps, similar to variational EM. In the E-step, with fixed $T$ and $m$, we update $\xi_d$ in closed form and update $(\mu_d, \Sigma_d)$ through gradient ascent on the bound. The parameter $\Sigma_d$ is parameterized using log-variances to enforce positivity. In the M-step, $T$ and $m$ are updated with the posterior statistics fixed. Due to the large number of parameters, we employ the Adam optimizer [7] with mini-batches of documents for both steps. For the Laplace prior, we apply the subgradient of the L1 penalty. Variational parameters are initialized with $\mu_d = 0$ and $\Sigma_d = I$. Convergence is monitored through the bound on a held-out set of documents.

**Document Embeddings and Uncertainty Quantification**
After training, each document is summarized by the pair $(\mu_d, \Sigma_d)$. The mean $\mu_d$ serves as the document embedding, while $\Sigma_d$ encodes the uncertainty associated with this embedding, reflecting how well it is determined by the observed word counts. Short documents yield posteriors close to the prior, whereas longer documents give narrower posteriors, indicating greater certainty in their embeddings. For unseen documents, $T$ and $m$ are held fixed, and only $(\mu_d, \Sigma_d, \xi_d)$ are optimized.

**Perplexity Evaluation**
For intrinsic evaluation, the model is compared with the neural variational document model (NVDM) [8]. For a test document, we infer the posterior and compute an upper bound on the perplexity, $\text{PPL} = \exp(-\frac{1}{D} \sum_d \frac{1}{N_d} \log p(x_d))$, with $\log p(x_d)$ replaced by the ELBO. The same estimate is used for both models to ensure a consistent comparison.

**Generative Gaussian Linear Classifier**
For topic identification, we leverage the uncertainty in the document embeddings with a generative classifier operating on the posterior distributions. Each class $c$ has a Gaussian over embeddings, $\mathcal{N}(w | \eta_c, \Lambda)$, with a shared covariance $\Lambda$, yielding a linear classifier. Classes are modeled in the latent space, treating the observed embedding as noisy: the document's posterior covariance $\Sigma_d$ is added to the class covariance when computing the likelihood, $p(\mu_d | c)$. This approach allows for the integration of uncertainty in the classification process, providing a more nuanced understanding of how documents relate to different topics.
