Cryptococcosis is a life-threatening mycosis caused by basidiomycetous yeasts of the Cryptococcus neoformans/Cryptococcus gattii species complex [1,2]. Infection follows inhalation of desiccated yeast cells or spores, which establish a primary pulmonary focus and, in susceptible hosts, disseminate hematogenously to the central nervous system, causing meningoencephalitis [3]. Cryptococcosis is responsible for an estimated one million cases annually worldwide, with a high mortality rate, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa [4]. Historically, C. neoformans has been considered an opportunistic pathogen of immunocompromised individuals, especcially patients with HIV/AIDS, whereas C. gattii has been associated with disease in apparently immunocompetent hosts [5,6]. **Epidemiology and population structure of C. gattii** C. gattii was originally restricted to tropical and subtropical regions and associated with Eucalyptus speciees [7]. Thiis view changed after the outbreak on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, in 1999, which spread to the mainland of Canada and the Pacific Northwest of the United States [8,9]. The outbreak was dominated by molecular typpe VGII, including the hypervirulent VGIIa/b genotypes, and generated considerable interest in the mechanisms underlying the enhanced virulence of these strains, such as tubular mitochondrial morphology, increased intracellular proliferation within macrophages and altered host immune responses [10,11]. Bsed on molecular typing, C. gattii is classified into four major types, VGI to VGIV [12], and recent genomic analyses have proposed that these lineages may represent distinct cryptic species [13]. Capsular serotypes B and C are both founnd in C. gattii. Serotype B includes types VGI, VGII and VGIII, whereas serotype C corresponds mainly to VGIII and VGIV [12]. VGIV is the most frequent type in HIV-infected patients in sub-Saharan Africa, while VGIII has been reported in both clinical and environmental samples from Latin America and in HIV-positive patienst in California [14,15]. Despite this clinical relevance, the vast majority of experimental studies have focused on serotype B isolates, particularly VGI and VGII. Consequently, the pathogenic properties of serotype C strains reman poorly characterized. **Virulence determinants in Cryptococcus** The pathogenic potential of Cryptococcus species depends on several well-characterized virulence factors. The polysaccharide capsule, composed mainly of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) and glucuronoxylomannogalactan (GXMGal), is the main determinant; it inhibits phagocytosis, modulates cytokine responses and protects against oxidative stress [16,17]. Capsule synthesis requires the products of the CAP genes (CAP10, CAP59, CAP60 and CAP64), whose deletion results in acapsular, avirulent mutants [18]. Capsule size and structure are highly variable among isolates and are regulated by environmental conditions, and GXM structural differences affetc recognition by monoclonal antibodies and the host immune response [19,20]. Melanin, produced through laccase-mediated oxidation of diphenolic compounds, protects fungal cells against oxidative and nitrosative damage, antifungal drugs and host effector mechanisms [21]. In addition, chitin and chitooligomers in the cell wall and capsule contribute to cell integrity, capsule architecture and the interaction with host chitinases, which have beeen linked to the modulation of immune responses and to disease susceptibility [22,23]. Other factors, including extraclelular enzymes such as ureaase and phospholipase, and the ability to grow at 37 °C, are also essential for survival and dissemination in the host [3,24]. Phenotypic variability in these traits among isolates of the same species has been correlated with differences in virulence in animal models [25,26]. In the case of C. gattii, the hypervirulence of VGII strains has been related to their capacity to proliferate rapidly in lung tissue and to evade immune surveillance [10,27]. However, whether similar mechanisms operate in serotype C isolates, or whether VGIII and VGIV lineages differ in their virulence profiles, is unknown. The fungal infection cryptococcosis poses a significant threat to human life, as it is caused by the pathogenic yeasts of the Cryptococcus neoformans/Cryptococcus gattii species complex, which can be lethal if left untreated [1,2]. Upon inhalation of desiccated yeast cells or spores, a primary site of infection is established in the lungs, and in individuals with compromised immune systems, the fungus can disseminate through the bloodstream to the central nervous system, resulting in a severe inflammatory response known as meningoencephalitis [3]. With approximately one million reported cases worldwide each year, cryptococcosis is a major public health concern, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where the mortality rate is alarmingly high [4]. Historically, Cryptococcus neoformans has been viewed as an opportunistic pathogen that primarily affects individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS, whereas Cryptococcus gattii has been associated with disease in individuals who appear to be immunocompetent [5,6]. However, recent studies have led to a significant shift in our understanding of the epidemiology and population structure of C. gattii. Initially, C. gattii was thought to be confined to tropical and subtropical regions, where it was often found in association with Eucalyptus species [7]. Nevertheless, this perspective changed dramatically after the outbreak on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, in 1999, which subsequently spread to the mainland of Canada and the Pacific Northwest region of the United States [8,9]. The outbreak was dominated by the molecular type VGII, including the highly virulent VGIIa/b genotypes, which sparked a surge of interest in the underlying mechanisms that contribute to the enhanced virulence of these strains, such as the unique tubular morphology of their mitochondria, their ability to proliferate rapidly within macrophages, and their capacity to modulate the host immune response [10,11]. Based on molecular typing, C. gattii can be classified into four major categories, designated VGI to VGIV [12], and recent genomic analyses have suggested that these lineages may represent distinct, yet cryptic, species [13]. Notably, both capsular serotypes B and C are found in C. gattii, with serotype B encompassing types VGI, VGII, and VGIII, and serotype C corresponding primarily to types VGIII and VGIV [12]. Interestingly, VGIV is the most frequently encountered type in HIV-infected patients in sub-Saharan Africa, while VGIII has been detected in both clinical and environmental samples from Latin America and in HIV-positive patients in California [14,15]. Despite the significant clinical relevance of these molecular types, the vast majority of experimental studies have focused on serotype B isolates, particularly VGI and VGII, leaving a substantial knowledge gap in our understanding of the pathogenic properties of serotype C strains. This gap in our knowledge is particularly concerning, as elucidating the virulence determinants of C. gattii is essential for the development of effective treatment strategies and improving patient outcomes. The pathogenic potential of Cryptococcus species is dependent on several well-characterized virulence factors, including the polysaccharide capsule, which is composed primarily of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) and glucuronoxylomannogalactan (GXMGal) [16,17]. The capsule is the primary determinant of virulence, as it inhibits phagocytosis, modulates cytokine responses, and protects the fungus against oxidative stress. The synthesis of the capsule requires the products of the CAP genes, including CAP10, CAP59, CAP60, and CAP64, and the deletion of these genes results in the formation of acapsular, avirulent mutants [18]. The size and structure of the capsule are highly variable among isolates and are regulated by environmental conditions, and differences in GXM structure can affect recognition by monoclonal antibodies and the host immune response [19,20]. In addition to the capsule, melanin, which is produced through the laccase-mediated oxidation of diphenolic compounds, plays a crucial role in protecting fungal cells against oxidative and nitrosative damage, antifungal drugs, and host effector mechanisms [21]. Other essential factors that contribute to the virulence of Cryptococcus species include chitin and chitooligomers in the cell wall and capsule, which are involved in cell integrity, capsule architecture, and the interaction with host chitinases, and have been linked to the modulation of immune responses and disease susceptibility [22,23]. Furthermore, extracellular enzymes, such as urease and phospholipase, and the ability to grow at 37 °C, are also critical for the survival and dissemination of the fungus within the host [3,24]. Phenotypic variability in these traits among isolates of the same species has been correlated with differences in virulence in animal models [25,26]. In the case of C. gattii, the hypervirulence of VGII strains has been attributed to their capacity to proliferate rapidly in lung tissue and evade immune surveillance [10,27]. However, whether similar mechanisms operate in serotype C isolates, or whether the VGIII and VGIV lineages differ in their virulence profiles, remains unknown. Some studies have suggested that VGIII and VGIV isolates are generally less virulent in mice than VGII isolates [28,29], but these findings are based on a limited number of strains, and a systematic comparison of the phenotypic attributes and virulence of these lineages is lacking. Given the significant clinical importance of VGIV in Africa and VGIII in the Americas, and the scarcity of experimental data on these lineages, a comprehensive analysis of the phenotypic diversity of serotype C isolates is necessary. Elucidating how variation in capsule properties, cell wall composition, pigment production, and antigenic structure translates into differences in virulence may provide valuable insights into the pathogenesis of infections caused by these molecular types and the factors that determine tissue tropism, particularly the ability to colonize the central nervous system. In the present study, we conducted a comparative analysis of three serotype C C. gattii isolates, including one VGIII (ATCC 24066) and two VGIV (WM 779 and 106.97) isolates, with respect to capsule dimensions, expression of CAP genes, chitooligomer distribution, induction of host chitinase activity, pigment production, and reactivity to various stimuli. By examining the phenotypic diversity of these isolates, we aim to contribute to a deeper understanding of the pathogenic properties of serotype C C. gattii and the factors that influence their virulence, ultimately informing the development of effective treatment strategies for cryptococcosis. The study of the pathogenic mechanisms of C. gattii is a complex and multifaceted field, and further research is needed to fully elucidate the virulence determinants of this fungus. Nevertheless, by exploring the phenotypic diversity of serotype C isolates, we can gain a better understanding of the factors that contribute to the pathogenesis of cryptococcosis and develop more effective strategies for the prevention and treatment of this devastating disease. Ultimately, the goal of this research is to improve our understanding of the complex interactions between the host and the fungus, and to develop novel therapeutic approaches that can effectively target the virulence factors of C. gattii. By achieving this goal, we can hope to reduce the burden of cryptococcosis on public health and improve the outcomes of patients infected with this fungus. The importance of this research cannot be overstated, as cryptococcosis remains a major public health concern, particularly in regions with limited resources and high HIV prevalence. By advancing our knowledge of the pathogenic mechanisms of C. gattii, we can develop more effective strategies for the prevention and treatment of this disease, and ultimately improve the lives of millions of people worldwide. Cryptococcus gattii is a highly pathogenic fungus that causes severe disease in humans, particularly those with compromised immune systems. To better understand the virulence mechanisms of this fungus, we undertook a comprehensive study of serotype C isolates, which are known to exhibit distinct molecular types. Specifically, we investigated the phenotypic characteristics and virulence potential of three serotype C isolates, including their growth rates, capsule sizes, melanin production, and reactivity with GXM-binding monoclonal antibodies [1]. We also assessed the expression of CAP genes, which are involved in capsule formation, and the distribution of chitooligomers in the cell wall and capsule. Our findings provide valuable insights into the pathogenic potential of serotype C isolates and their ability to cause disease in mammalian hosts.

To initiate our study, we characterized the three serotype C isolates, namely 106.97 (molecular type VGIV), WM 779 (VGIV), and ATCC 24066 (VGIII), which were previously distinguished through URA5-RFLP analysis [1]. We cultured these isolates under standard laboratory conditions to evaluate their growth rates, capsule sizes, and melanin production. The isolates were stored at −80 °C in a 20% glycerol solution to maintain their viability and were revived on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 30 °C as needed. We then cultured the yeast cells in Sabouraud broth for 24 hours at 30 °C with constant shaking at 200 rpm, followed by washing in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and quantification using a Neubauer chamber.

To induce capsule formation, we cultured the cells in a minimal medium consisting of 15 mM glucose, 10 mM MgSO₄, 29.4 mM KH₂PO₄, 13 mM glycine, and 3 µM thiamine, with a pH of 5.5, for 48 hours at 37 °C, as previously described [2]. We employed a counterstaining technique with India ink to assess the capsule thickness, which was defined as the distance between the cell wall and the outer edge of the India ink exclusion zone. Using ImageJ software, we measured the cell body diameter and capsule thickness in at least 50 cells per isolate, allowing us to calculate the capsule-to-cell ratio as the capsule thickness divided by the cell body radius.

We also examined the expression of genes associated with capsule formation, including CAP10, CAP59, CAP60, and CAP64. To do this, we extracted total RNA from yeast cells grown in minimal medium using a mechanical disruption/TRIzol protocol, treated the RNA with DNase I, and then synthesized cDNA using oligo(dT) primers and reverse transcriptase. Quantitative PCR with SYBR Green was performed to quantify the transcript levels of these genes, normalizing them to the housekeeping gene ACT1 and expressing them relative to isolate ATCC 24066 using the 2^−ΔΔCt method [3]. This analysis was conducted in technical duplicate across three independent biological replicates.

Furthermore, we investigated the distribution of chitooligomers and chitin staining in the cells. We detected chitooligomers by incubating fixed cells with wheat germ agglutinin conjugated to fluorescein isothiocyanate (WGA-FITC) at a concentration of 10 µg/mL for 1 hour at 37 °C, as previously described [4]. Following incubation, we washed the cells, mounted them, and imaged them using fluorescence microscopy. We qualitatively scored the fluorescence patterns, including signals at budding sites, the cell body, and the capsule, in at least 100 cells per isolate. Additionally, we quantified the fluorescence intensity using ImageJ software.

To assess melanin production, we spotted 10^6 cells onto minimal medium agar containing 1 mM L-DOPA and incubated them at 30 °C and 37 °C in the dark for up to 7 days. We documented the pigmentation and measured the melanin content using a spectrophotometric assay. We also evaluated the ability of the isolates to induce host chitinase activity and their reactivity with GXM-binding monoclonal antibodies. These experiments provided a comprehensive understanding of the phenotypic characteristics of the serotype C isolates and laid the foundation for the subsequent virulence studies.

The virulence of the serotype C isolates was evaluated in a murine model of intranasal infection. Mice were infected with each of the three isolates, and their survival rates, fungal burdens in the lungs and brain, and immune responses were monitored. The results of these experiments will provide valuable insights into the pathogenic potential of serotype C isolates and their ability to cause disease in mammalian hosts. By comparing the virulence of VGIII and VGIV isolates, we can determine whether these molecular types differ in their ability to infect and colonize the central nervous system, and whether they exhibit distinct virulence profiles.

In conclusion, the study of serotype C C. gattii isolates is essential for understanding the pathogenesis of cryptococcosis and for developing effective treatment strategies. By characterizing the phenotypic diversity of these isolates and evaluating their virulence in a murine model, we can gain insights into the mechanisms underlying the enhanced virulence of certain molecular types and identify potential targets for therapeutic intervention. The results of this study will contribute to a better understanding of the biology of C. gattii and will have significant implications for the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of cryptococcosis. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the molecular type of C. gattii isolates when developing treatment strategies and emphasize the need for further research into the pathogenesis of this fungus.

The results of our study demonstrate that serotype C C. gattii isolates exhibit distinct phenotypic characteristics, including growth rates, capsule sizes, and melanin production. We also found that the isolates differ in their ability to induce host chitinase activity and their reactivity with GXM-binding monoclonal antibodies. These findings suggest that the molecular type of C. gattii isolates may influence their virulence potential and ability to cause disease in mammalian hosts. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms underlying the virulence of C. gattii and to develop effective treatment strategies for cryptococcosis.

In summary, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the phenotypic characteristics and virulence potential of serotype C C. gattii isolates. Sickle cell disease (SCD) is the most common life-limiting genetic disease among African Americans, affecting more than 100,000 people in the United States and millions worldwide [1,2]. It results from a single nucleotide substitution in the β-globin gene that produces hemoglobin S. Under deoxygenated conditions, hemoglobin S polymerizes, causing red blood cell rigidity, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion. Beyond these primary events, chronic hemolysis, endothelial dysfunction, and persistent inflammation contribute to progressive multi-organ injury [3,4]. Although advances in newborn screening, penicillin prophylaxis, vaccination, and hydroxyurea therapy have substantially improved survival in childhood, pulmonary complications remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality across the lifespan [5,6]. Pulmonary disease in SCD encompasses a broad spectrum of acute and chronic conditions, including acute chest syndrome (ACS), pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, nocturnal hypoxemia, thromboembolic disease, and obstructive airway disease [7,8]. ACS, defined by a new pulmonary infiltrate accompanied by fever, respiratory symptoms, or hypoxemia, is the second most common cause of hospitalization and a leading cause of death among patients with SCD [9]. Recurrent ACS is itself associated with the development of chronic lung disease, creating a cycle of progressive pulmonary injury [10]. Understanding modifiable risk factors for ACS and other pulmonary complications is therefore a priority. Asthma has long been recognized as one of these potential risk factors. Early observational studies described an association between asthma and ACS, pianful vaso-occlusive episodes, and early mortality in SCD [11–13]. In the Cooperative Study of Sickle Cell Disease, children with a physician diagnosis of asthma experienced a higheer incidence of ACS and pain episodes than those without, and asthma was associated wth an increased risk of early death in adults [11,12]. Subsequent studies have supported these findings, although results have not been uniform, and the strength of associations varies with how asthma is defined [14,15]. The mechanisms linking asthma to SCD complications are not fully elucidated but may include airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction-induced hypoxia, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and systemic inflammatory amplification that promotes sickling and vascular adhesion [16,17]. More recently, attention has turned to wheezing, even in the absence of a formal asthma diagnosis, as a possible marker of disease severity in SCD. Longitudinal data from infant and childhood cohorts deemonstrate tht wheezing is common in young children with SCD and is associated with higher rates of ACS, pain, and hospitalization [18,19]. These observations suggest that wheezing may reflect a distinct SCD-related phenotype, rather than simply representing coexisting atopic asthma. Indeed, wheeze in SCD may arise from multiple processes, including pulmonary vascular congestion, fat or thromboembolism, prior pulmonary infarction, infection, and airway hyperresponsiveness, in addition to classic allergic airway inflammation [20]. Establishing a diagnosis of asthma in patients with SCD is therefore challenging. According to national and international guidelines, asthma is diagnosed on the basis of a history of recurrent respiratory symptoms such as wheeze, cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea, together with objective evidence of variable airflow obstruction that is typically reversible with bronchodilators [21,22]. In SCD, however, several of these features are highly prevalent and frequently occur in isolation. Wheezing has been reported in up to approximately 30–50% of children with SCD, exceeding the prevalence in the general African American population [18,23]. Obstructive patterns on spirometry are common, yet many patients also display restrictive physiology or mixed defects, complicating interpretation [24,25]. Airway hyperresponsiveness, measured by methacholine or exercise challenge, has been described in a substantial proportion of children with SCD, including many without clinical asthma [26,27]. Bronchodilator responsiveness is likewise frequent, even among patients with no history of wheeze [28]. Consequently, the relationships among symptoms, physiologic abnormalities, and clinical asthma remain pooryl defined, and the true prevalence of asthma in SCD is uncertain, with estimates ranging from approximately 10% to more than 40% depending on the definition and population studied [29,30]. This diagnostic ambiguity has practical consequences. Underdiagnosis may deprive patients of effective controller therapy, whereas overdiagnosis may expose them to unnecessary medications and divert attention from other treatable causes of respiratory symptoms. Management is further complicated by limited evidence: patients with SCD have been largelly excluded from asthma clinical trials, and recommendations rely heavily on extrapolation from the general population [31]. Particular concerns include the potential risks of systemic corticosteroids, which have been associated with rebound pain crises and readmission in SCD, and the uncertain role of β-agonists and other asthma therapies in this population [32,33]. Whether biologic therapiies or disease-modifying treatments such as hydroxyurea alter airway outcomes also remains unknown. Given these gaps, a critical appraisal of current knowledge is warranted. In this review, we summarize: (1) the epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway responsiveness among patients with SCD; (2) the evidence supporting associations of these features with SCD morbidity; (3) current understanding of the pathophysiology of airway inflammation in SCD; (4) existing approaches to the diagnosis and management of asthma in SCD; and (5) future research diections needed to improve respiratory outcomes in this vulnerable population. A narrative approach was chosen over a formal systematic review or meta-analysis because the available studies differ substantially in design, population, case definitions, and outcome measures, which limits quantitative syynthesis [1,2]. The review was structured around five predefined themes: (1) epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway responsiveness; (2) associations with SCD-related morbidity and mortality; (3) pathophysiology of airway inflammation; (4) current approaches to the diagnosis and management of asthma in SCD; and (5) future research directions. **Search strategy** We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for articles publihed from database inception through the date of the final search. Search terms combined controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text keywords for the condition and the respiratory outcomes: "sickle cell disease," "sickle cell anemia," "hemoglobin SS," "hemoglobin SC," "asthma," "wheeze," "wheezing," "airway obstruction," "airway hyperresponsiveness," "bronchial hyperreactivity," "bronchodilator response," "pulmonary function," "spirometry," "acute chest syndrome," "vaso-occlusive pain," and "inhaled corticosteroids." Boolean operators were used to combine the concepts. Additional searches addressed inflammatory mechanisms, including "eosinophil," "IgE," "atopy," "cytokine," "hemolysis," "nitric oxide," and "leukotriene." Reference lists of key articles, prior reviews, and consensus guidelines were hand-searched to identify additional relevant publications [3,4]. Studies were eligible if they reported at least one of the following: prevalence or incidence of physician-diagnosed asthma or wheezing; spirometric or plethysmographic measures of airflow obstruction; bronchodilator responsiveness or bronchial provocation testing; associations between these respiratory phenotypes and clinical outcomes (pain episodes, acute chest syndrome [ACS], hospitalization, or mortality); biomarkers of airway or systemic inflammation; or theapeutic interventions for asthma or wheezing in SCD. Basic science and translational studies, including murie models, were included when they informed mechanisms of airway inflammation in SCD. We excluded articles not published in English, conference abstracts without full-text data, case reports, and studies focusing exclusively on pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, or sleep-disordered breathing without relevant airway outcomes. Disagreements regarding inclusion were resolved by discussion among the authors. For each included study, we extracted the following information where available: study design, setting, sample size, age group, SCD genotype, definitions used for asthma, wheeze, airway obstruction, and AHR, methods of pulmonary function testing, comparison groups, principal findings, and adjustment for confounders. For epidemiologic data, we compared prevalence estimates across studies and with those of the general African American population, taking into account age, geography, and case definition. For studies of morbidity, we emphasized those that used longitudinal designs and adjutsed for relevant covariates such as age, genotype, hydroxyurea use, and hemoglobin level, and we highlighted where evidence derived from single-center or retrospective studies might be subject to selection and ascertainment bias. For mechanistic evidence, we distinguished human studies from animal and in vitro studies. Elevated urinary leukotriene E4 and neutrophil activation were noted in children with SCD, particularly those with wheeze [21]. Together these findings suggest that airway disease in SCD is heterogeneous, with both asthma-like and SCD-specific inflammatory phenotypes. **Diagnosis and management** Current guidelines from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute recommend that asthma in SCD be diagnosed using the same criteria as in the general population: a history of recurrent respiratory symptoms plus demonstrable reversible airflow obstruction on spirometry [23]. Consequently, the guidelines encourage objective testing, ideally by a pulmonary or asthma specialist, particularly when symptooms are atypical [23]. Management evidence is sparse. The global prevalence of sickle cell disease (SCD), a genetic disorder affecting millions worldwide, including over 100,000 individuals in the United States, underscores the need for continued research into its pathophysiology and clinical manifestations [1,2]. The condition arises from a single nucleotide substitution in the β-globin gene, leading to the production of abnormal hemoglobin, which polymerizes under deoxygenated conditions, resulting in red blood cell dysfunction, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion. However, the repercussions of SCD extend far beyond these initial events, as the cumulative effects of chronic hemolysis, endothelial dysfunction, and persistent inflammation contribute to progressive injury in multiple organs [3,4]. Despite significant advancements in early detection and therapeutic interventions, including newborn screening, prophylactic antibiotics, vaccination, and hydroxyurea therapy, which have substantially improved survival rates in childhood, pulmonary complications remain a major contributor to morbidity and mortality across the lifespan of individuals with SCD [5,6]. The spectrum of pulmonary disease in SCD is broad, encompassing acute and chronic conditions such as acute chest syndrome (ACS), pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, nocturnal hypoxemia, thromboembolic disease, and obstructive airway disease [7,8]. ACS, characterized by new pulmonary infiltrates accompanied by fever, respiratory symptoms, or hypoxemia, is a leading cause of hospitalization and mortality among patients with SCD, with recurrent episodes contributing to the development of chronic lung disease [9,10]. Understanding the risk factors for ACS and other pulmonary complications is essential for developing effective management strategies. One potential risk factor that has been recognized is asthma, with early observational studies highlighting an association between asthma and increased incidence of ACS, painful vaso-occlusive episodes, and early mortality in SCD [11-13]. For instance, the Cooperative Study of Sickle Cell Disease found that individuals with a physician-diagnosed asthma experienced higher rates of ACS and pain episodes, with asthma also being associated with an increased risk of early death in adults [11,12]. Subsequent studies have supported these findings, although the results have been inconsistent, and the strength of associations varies depending on the definition of asthma used [14,15]. The mechanisms underlying the link between asthma and SCD complications are not fully elucidated but may involve airway inflammation, hypoxia resulting from bronchoconstriction, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and systemic inflammatory amplification that promotes sickling and vascular adhesion [16,17]. More recently, attention has focused on wheezing, even in the absence of a formal asthma diagnosis, as a potential marker of disease severity in SCD. Longitudinal data from infant and childhood cohorts demonstrate that wheezing is common in young children with SCD and is associated with higher rates of ACS, pain, and hospitalization [18,19]. These observations suggest that wheezing may represent a distinct phenotype in SCD, rather than simply indicating coexisting atopic asthma. Indeed, wheezing in SCD may arise from multiple factors, including pulmonary vascular congestion, fat or thromboembolism, prior pulmonary infarction, infection, and airway hyperresponsiveness, in addition to classic allergic airway inflammation [20]. Diagnosing asthma in patients with SCD is challenging due to the overlap of symptoms and physiologic abnormalities. According to established guidelines, asthma is diagnosed based on a history of recurrent respiratory symptoms such as wheezing, cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea, combined with objective evidence of variable airflow obstruction that is typically reversible with bronchodilators [21,22]. However, in SCD, these features are highly prevalent and often occur in isolation, complicating diagnosis. Wheezing has been reported in up to 30-50% of children with SCD, exceeding the prevalence in the general African American population [18,23]. Obstructive patterns on spirometry are common, yet many patients also display restrictive physiology or mixed defects, further complicating interpretation [24,25]. Airway hyperresponsiveness, measured by methacholine or exercise challenge, has been described in a substantial proportion of children with SCD, including those without clinical asthma [26,27]. Bronchodilator responsiveness is also frequent, even among patients without a history of wheezing [28]. Consequently, the relationships among symptoms, physiologic abnormalities, and clinical asthma remain poorly defined, and the true prevalence of asthma in SCD is uncertain, with estimates ranging from approximately 10% to over 40% depending on the definition and population studied [29,30]. This diagnostic ambiguity has significant practical implications, as underdiagnosis may deprive patients of effective controller therapy, while overdiagnosis may expose them to unnecessary medications and divert attention from other treatable causes of respiratory symptoms. Management is further complicated by limited evidence, as patients with SCD have been largely excluded from asthma clinical trials, and recommendations rely heavily on extrapolation from the general population [31]. Particular concerns include the potential risks of systemic corticosteroids, which have been associated with rebound pain crises and readmission in SCD, and the uncertain role of β-agonists and other asthma therapies in this population [32,33]. The impact of biologic therapies or disease-modifying treatments such as hydroxyurea on airway outcomes also remains unknown. Given these knowledge gaps, a comprehensive review of current understanding is warranted. This review aims to provide a detailed examination of the epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway responsiveness among patients with SCD, as well as the evidence supporting associations between these features and SCD morbidity, highlighting the need for further research into the complex relationships between SCD and respiratory complications [1-33]. The intricate relationship between sickle cell disease (SCD) and asthma is a pressing concern, warranting a comprehensive examination of the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms and the complexities of diagnosing and managing asthma in patients with SCD [1]. This discussion aims to elucidate the multifaceted nature of asthma in SCD, exploring its epidemiological, pathophysiological, and clinical aspects, as well as the challenges and future directions in its diagnosis and treatment [2]. The coexistence of asthma and SCD presents a formidable challenge, as the symptoms and physiological alterations associated with both conditions can overlap, complicating diagnosis and management [3]. A profound understanding of the interplay between these conditions is crucial for developing effective strategies to improve patient outcomes [4].

SCD, characterized by the production of abnormal hemoglobin, leads to recurrent episodes of pain, infection, and other complications, with asthma being a significant comorbidity that can significantly alter the disease's course [5]. The presence of asthma in SCD patients can exacerbate symptoms and contribute to the development of complications, underscoring the need for a thorough comprehension of its epidemiology, pathophysiology, and clinical manifestations in this population [6]. The epidemiological landscape of asthma in SCD is complex, with asthma being a common comorbidity that impacts the disease's progression, yet its diagnosis is hindered by overlapping symptoms and physiological abnormalities [7]. Therefore, elucidating the epidemiological aspects of asthma in SCD is essential for providing optimal care to patients with this condition [8].

Furthermore, the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the relationship between asthma and SCD are not fully elucidated, although it is evident that asthma can worsen SCD symptoms and contribute to complications [9]. The airway inflammation seen in asthma can interact with the vascular and hemodynamic alterations characteristic of SCD, potentially leading to increased morbidity [10]. Thus, further research into the pathophysiology of airway inflammation in SCD and the development of effective diagnostic and therapeutic strategies is imperative [11].

The clinical presentation of asthma in SCD patients is varied and can include symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath, which can also be attributed to other conditions, making accurate diagnosis challenging [12]. A comprehensive understanding of these clinical manifestations is vital for the optimal management of asthma in the context of SCD [13]. The management of asthma in SCD requires a multifaceted approach, taking into account the unique physiological and pathological characteristics of SCD, as well as the potential interactions between asthma therapies and SCD [14]. 

In conclusion, the association between asthma and SCD is intricate and multifaceted, with asthma being a common comorbidity that can significantly impact the course of SCD [15]. The diagnosis and management of asthma in SCD are complicated by overlapping symptoms and physiological alterations, necessitating a profound understanding of the epidemiology, pathophysiology, and clinical manifestations of asthma in this population [16]. Further research is crucial to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the relationship between asthma and SCD and to develop effective diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, ultimately aiming to improve outcomes for patients with SCD [17]. By advancing our understanding of the complex interplay between SCD and asthma, we can work towards developing more effective management strategies and improving the quality of life for individuals affected by these conditions [18]. 

Ultimately, this narrative review underscores the importance of considering the complexities of SCD and asthma in the diagnosis and management of patients with these conditions, emphasizing the need for continued research into the epidemiology, pathophysiology, and clinical manifestations of asthma in SCD [19]. Collaborative efforts to enhance our understanding of these conditions will be pivotal in improving patient outcomes and reducing the burden of SCD and asthma on individuals and communities [20]. The future of SCD and asthma management lies in the development of targeted therapeutic strategies that address the unique needs of patients with these comorbid conditions, requiring ongoing research and clinical innovation [21]. By shedding light on the intricate relationship between SCD and asthma, we hope to contribute to the development of more effective diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, ultimately enhancing the care provided to patients with these conditions [22]. 

References to the complexities and the need for future studies in this area are clear [23], with an emphasis on the importance of interdisciplinary approaches to address the multifaceted challenges posed by SCD and asthma [24]. The path forward involves a commitment to research, clinical innovation, and patient-centered care, aiming to alleviate the burden of these conditions and improve the well-being of affected individuals [25]. As our understanding of the relationship between SCD and asthma evolves, so too will our ability to provide tailored, effective care to those who need it most [26]. 

The integration of knowledge from various disciplines, including hematology, pulmonology, and epidemiology, will be essential in addressing the complex interplay between SCD and asthma [27]. Furthermore, the development of novel therapeutic strategies and diagnostic tools will require a deep understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying these conditions [28]. By fostering a collaborative environment that encourages research and innovation, we can accelerate progress in the management of SCD and asthma, leading to better outcomes for patients and a reduction in the healthcare burden associated with these conditions [29].

In exploring the intricacies of asthma in SCD, it becomes evident that a one-size-fits-all approach is insufficient, and personalized care strategies are needed [30]. The variability in disease presentation, severity, and response to treatment among SCD patients with asthma necessitates a tailored approach, considering the unique characteristics of each patient [31]. This personalized approach will not only improve patient outcomes but also enhance the efficiency of healthcare resources, reducing unnecessary interventions and focusing on the most effective treatments for each individual [32].

The role of healthcare providers in managing SCD and asthma is crucial, requiring not only a deep understanding of these conditions but also the ability to communicate effectively with patients and coordinate care across different specialties [33]. Patient education and empowerment are also vital, enabling individuals to take an active role in managing their conditions and making informed decisions about their care [34]. By promoting a patient-centered approach and supporting ongoing research and innovation, we can work towards a future where SCD and asthma are managed effectively, and patients can lead fulfilling lives with minimal disruption from these conditions [35].

As we move forward in our understanding and management of SCD and asthma, it is essential to acknowledge the disparities and inequalities that exist in healthcare access and outcomes for individuals with these conditions [36]. Addressing these disparities will require a multifaceted approach, involving policy changes, educational initiatives, and community-based programs aimed at improving healthcare access and quality for underserved populations [37]. By recognizing and addressing these challenges, we can ensure that advancements in the management of SCD and asthma benefit all individuals affected by these conditions, regardless of their background or socioeconomic status [38].

In conclusion, the relationship between SCD and asthma is complex and multifaceted, requiring a comprehensive and personalized approach to diagnosis and management [39]. Through continued research, innovation, and a commitment to patient-centered care, we can improve outcomes for individuals with these conditions and reduce the burden of SCD and asthma on individuals and communities [40]. The future of SCD and asthma management is promising, with potential avenues for improvement including the development of novel therapeutic strategies, advances in diagnostic technologies, and a greater emphasis on personalized and equitable care [41]. As we strive to enhance our understanding of these conditions and develop more effective management strategies, we are motivated by the potential to significantly improve the lives of individuals affected by SCD and asthma [42]. The intersection of sickle cell disease (SCD) and respiratory health is a complex and multifaceted field of study, encompassing various aspects such as mortality rates, the pathological mechanisms underlying airway inflammation in SCD, current diagnostic and therapeutic approaches to managing asthma in SCD patients, and potential avenues for future research aimed at enhancing respiratory outcomes in this vulnerable population. To comprehensively identify pertinent studies, a rigorous search strategy was employed, combining both controlled vocabulary and free-text keywords related to SCD, asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR). The search terms utilized included "sickle cell disease," "sickle cell anemia," "hemoglobin SS," "hemoglobin SC," "asthma," "wheeze," "airway obstruction," "airway hyperresponsiveness," "bronchial hyperreactivity," "bronchodilator response," "pulmonary function," "spirometry," "acute chest syndrome," "vaso-occlusive pain," and "inhaled corticosteroids." Additionally, Boolean operators were used to combine these concepts, and supplementary searches were conducted to address inflammatory mechanisms, incorporating terms such as "eosinophil," "IgE," "atopy," "cytokine," "hemolysis," "nitric oxide," and "leukotriene." The search spanned multiple databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, from their inception to the date of the final search. Furthermore, a manual search of the reference lists of pivotal articles, prior reviews, and consensus guidelines was performed to identify additional relevant publications [3,4]. The ClinicalTrials.gov database was also queried to identify ongoing or recently completed trials pertinent to future directions in SCD and respiratory health. 

The criteria for study inclusion were deliberately broad to capture a wide range of research relevant to respiratory outcomes in SCD. Eligible studies included original research articles (encompassing prospective and retrospective cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, case-control studies, and clinical trials), registry analyses, and clinical practice guidelines that reported on respiratory outcomes in both children and adults with SCD. To be included, studies had to report at least one of the following: the prevalence or incidence of physician-diagnosed asthma or wheezing; spirometric or plethysmographic measures of airflow obstruction; bronchodilator responsiveness or bronchial provocation testing; associations between these respiratory phenotypes and clinical outcomes (such as pain episodes, acute chest syndrome [ACS], hospitalization, or mortality); biomarkers of airway or systemic inflammation; or therapeutic interventions for asthma or wheezing in SCD. Basic science and translational studies, including murine models, were also included when they provided insights into the mechanisms of airway inflammation in SCD. However, studies not published in English, conference abstracts without full-text data, case reports, and studies focusing exclusively on pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, or sleep-disordered breathing without relevant airway outcomes were excluded. General population asthma guidelines were reviewed to contextualize diagnostic and therapeutic approaches [5,6].

The process of selecting studies and extracting data was rigorous and systematic. Initial screening of titles and abstracts was followed by a full-text review of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements regarding inclusion were resolved through discussion among the authors. For each included study, a comprehensive range of information was extracted, including study design, setting, sample size, age group, SCD genotype, definitions used for asthma, wheeze, airway obstruction, and AHR, methods of pulmonary function testing, comparison groups, principal findings, and adjustment for confounders. The variability in definitions of asthma across studies (e.g., parental report, physician diagnosis, medication use, or administrative codes) was noted, and the definition used in each study was recorded and considered when interpreting prevalence estimates [7]. Similarly, the definition of airway obstruction (whether by the forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity ratio relative to the lower limit of normal or by fixed thresholds) and the reference equations used were noted, acknowledging the impact of race-specific equations on interpretation [8].

The synthesis and appraisal of findings were qualitative, organized within each of the thematic domains. Epidemiologic data were compared across studies and with those of the general African American population, taking into account age, geography, and case definition. When examining studies of morbidity, emphasis was placed on those that used longitudinal designs and adjusted for relevant covariates such as age, genotype, hydroxyurea use, and hemoglobin level. Evidence derived from single-center or retrospective studies that might be subject to selection and ascertainment bias was highlighted. For mechanistic evidence, human studies were distinguished from animal and in vitro studies. Although a formal risk-of-bias assessment or pooled quantitative analysis was not performed, the strength of evidence was evaluated based on study size, design, and consistency of findings across cohorts [2].

In the section on diagnosis and management, recommendations from national asthma guidelines and SCD-specific expert panel recommendations were compared, identifying areas where evidence specific to SCD was lacking and recommendations were extrapolated from the general population [5,6,9]. Particular attention was given to the role of spirometry, bronchodilator reversibility testing, and methacholine challenge in distinguishing asthma from isolated wheeze or AHR in SCD, as well as to the safety and efficacy of corticosteroids, considering reports of rebound pain and ACS after systemic steroid exposure [10]. Finally, gaps in knowledge identified across the preceding sections were used to generate proposed future directions, including prospective phenotyping, biomarker development, and clinical trials of asthma therapies, which are critical for advancing the understanding of the complex relationships between SCD and respiratory health and ultimately improving outcomes for individuals with SCD.

This comprehensive review underscores the complexity of respiratory health in SCD and highlights the need for tailored diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. The variability in study findings and the gaps in current knowledge emphasize the necessity for further research, including prospective studies and clinical trials, to address the unique challenges posed by SCD. By exploring the intersection of SCD and respiratory health through a comprehensive and systematic approach, this work aims to inform clinical practice, guide future research, and ultimately enhance the management and outcomes of individuals with SCD and respiratory complications. The future directions proposed here are designed to stimulate investigation into critical areas of need, fostering a deeper understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying asthma and other respiratory conditions in SCD, and paving the way for more effective and personalized therapeutic strategies [11]. Through such efforts, it is anticipated that significant improvements can be made in the respiratory health and overall well-being of individuals with SCD, a population that faces numerous challenges and complexities in managing their condition. 

In conclusion, the interplay between SCD and respiratory health is intricate and demands a nuanced approach, considering the multifaceted nature of SCD and its implications for respiratory function. The identification of key areas for future research and the proposal of targeted investigations into the mechanisms, diagnosis, and management of respiratory conditions in SCD represent critical steps towards enhancing outcomes for affected individuals. By building upon the foundations laid by existing research and addressing the gaps in current knowledge, it is possible to envision a future where the respiratory health of individuals with SCD is better understood, managed, and optimized, leading to improved quality of life and reduced morbidity and mortality associated with respiratory complications in this vulnerable population. As such, continued research and clinical efforts are imperative to unravel the complexities of SCD and respiratory health, with the ultimate goal of developing evidence-based, personalized care strategies that can effectively mitigate the burden of respiratory disease in SCD.

Such data arise naturally in applications such as estimating how many users own a certain item and what average rating they give it. ## Challenges of Key-Value Data under LDP Key-value data cannot be handled by applying existing mechanisms independently to keys and values. First, the key and value are correlated: a value is meaningful only if its key is present, and perturbing them separately wastes the privacy budget and yields biased estimates. Second, a user typically holds many keys, so the data are high-dimensional and sparse, and the privacy budget must be split across potentially many coordinates, degrading utility. Third, the value domain is continuous or ordinal, requiring perturbation that preserves unbiased aggregates. PrivKV [12] was the first work to formalize LDP for key-value data, perturbing each pair by a sequence of value and key randomization steps and supporting frequency and mean estimation. Subsequent refinements, such as interactive variants, reduce estimation error [12], [13]. Nevertheless, existing mechanisms still suffer from considerable variance when the privacy budget is small or the key domain is large, and the correlation between key and value perturbation is not fully exploited. A further limitation is that current methods deliver only marginal statistics: the frequency of each key and the mean of the values of each key. Many downstream tasks require conditional information. Naive Bayes classification, decision-tree induction, association-rule mining, and recommendation systems all depend on conditional probabilities or conditional means, such as the probability that a user holds key B given that she holds key A, or the mean value of key B among users holding key A [14], [15]. Estimating such quantities under LDP is challenging because the conditioning event itself is observed only through noisy reports, and errors in the condition compound errors in the target statistic. ## Our Contributions In this paper, we address these gaps by designing new perturbation mechanisms for key-value data and by building conditional analysis on top of them. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. **New key-value perturbation mechanisms.** We propose a family of LDP mechanisms that jointly perturb the key and value of a pair while satisfying ε-LDP under a unified privacy budget. The mechanisms are designed so that unbiased estimators of key frequency and value mean can be derived in closed form, and we analyze their estimation variance, showing improved accuracy over existing approaches. 2. **Conditional frequency estimation.** We introduce a method for estimating the conditional frequency of one key given another from perturbed reports, enabling the recovery of conditional probabilities and marginal statistics for key analysis. We prove the estimator's unbiasedness and bound its error. 3. **Conditional mean estimation.** We develop an estimator of the mean of the values associated with one key, conditioned on the presence of another key, supporting richer value analysis than marginal means. 4. **Support for learning tasks.** We show how the released conditional statistics can be used directly in downstream learning tasks, and illustrate this with classification based on conditional probabilities. 5. **Extensive evaluation.** We conduct experiments on synthetic datasets with varied distributions and on real-world rating datasets. The results show that our mechanisms achieve lower error in frequency and mean estimation than state-of-the-art competitors across a wide range of privacy budgets and key-domain sizes, and that conditional estimates remain accurate enough to be useful. ## Organization The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Large-scale data collection from individuals underpins personalized services, public-health surveillance, and the training of modern machien learning models. At the same time, the data that users contriibute are frequently sensitive, and centralized collection exposes them to breaches, misuse, and untrusted curators. Differential privacy (DP) [1] offers a rigorous guarantee that the output of an analysis is insensitive to any single individual's record, but its standard formulation presumes a trusted aggregator. Local differential privacy (LDP) [2], [3] removes this assumption: each user perturbs her data on her own device before transmission, so the aggregator never observes raw values. Because of this strong threat model, LDP has been deployed in industrial sysems such as Google's RPAPOR [4], Apple's iOS and macOS telemetry [5], and Microsoft's telemetry collection [6]. Most of the LDP literature considers simple data types. Substantial progress has been made on categorical frequency estimation [4], [7], [8], heavy-hitter identification [9], and mean estimation for numerical attributes [10], [11]. Real-world data, however, are often richer. In particular, key-value data, the basic data model of NoSQL stores, appear in user-profile databases, e-commerce logs, and smart-device records. A key-value pair couples a categorical key (e.g., a poduct or an app) with a numerical value (e.g., a rating or usage time). Such data arise naturally in applications scuh as estimating how many users own a certain item and what average rating they give it. ## Challenges of Key-Value Data under LDP Key-value data cannot be handled by applying existing mechanisms independently to keys and values. First, the key and value are correlated: a value is meaningful only if its key is present, and perturbing them separately wastes the privacy budget and yields biased estimates. Second, a user typically holds many keys, so the data are high-dimensional and sparse, and the privacy budget must be split across potentially many coordinates, degrading utility. Third, the value domain is continuous or ordinal, requiring perturbation that preserves unbiased aggregates. PrivKV [12] was the first work to formalize LDP for key-value data, perturbing each pair by a sequence of value and key randomization steps and supporting frequency and mean estimation. Subsequent refinements, such as interactive variants, reduce estimation error [12], [13]. Nevertheless, existing mechanisms still suffer from considerable variance when the privacy budget is small or the key domain is large, and the correlation between key and value perturbation is not fully exploited. A further limitation is that current methods deliver only marginal statistics: the frequency of each key and the men of the values of each key. Many downstream tasks require conditional information. Naive Bayes classification, decision-tree induction, association-rule mining, and recommendation systems all depend on conditional probabilities or conditionl means, such as the probability that a user holds key B given that she holds key A, or the mean value of key B among users holding key A [14], [15]. Estimating such quantities under LDP is challenging because the conditioning event itself is observed only through noisy reports, and errors in the condition compound errors in the target statistic. ## Our Contributions In this paper, we address these gapps by designing new perturbation mechanisms for key-value data and by building conditional analysis on top of them. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. **New key-value perturbation mechanisms.** We propose a family of LDP mechanisms that jointly perturb the key and value of a pair while satisfying ε-LDP under a unified privacy budget. The mechanisms are designed so that unbiased estimators of key frequency and value mean can be derived in closed form, and we analyze their estimation variance, showinng improved accuracy over existinng approaches. 2. **Conditional frequency estimation.** We introduce a method for estimating the conditional frequency of one key given another from perturbed reports, enabling the recovery of conditional probabilities and marginal statistics for key analysis. We prove the estimator's unbiasedness and bound its error. 3. **Conditional mean estimation.** We develop an estimator of the mean of the values associated wiht one key, conditioned on the presence of another key, supporting richer value analysis thhan marginal means. 4. **Support for learning tasks.** We show how the released conditional statistics can be used directly in downstream leanring tasks, and illustrate this with classification based on conditional probabilities. 5. **Extensive evaluation.** We conduct experiments on synthetic datasets with varied distributions and on real-world rating datasets. The rsults shoow that our mechanisms achieve lowwer error in frequency and mean estimation than state-of-the-art competitors acoss a wide range of privacy budgets and key-domain sizes, and that conditional estimates remain accurate enough to be useful. ## Organization The remaindre of the paper is organized as follows. An untrusted aggregator wishes to estimate (i) the key frrequency f_k, (ii) the mean value m_k of each key, (iii) the conditional frequency f_{k|c} = Pr[key k | codition c], and (iv) the conditional meean m_{k|c} = E[v | key k, condition c], where c is a predicate on a sceond key or attribute held by the same user. Each user perturbs the pir locally with a randomized mechanism M satisfying ε-LDP [2]: for all inputs x, x′ and outputs y, Pr[M(x)=y] ≤ e^ε Pr[M(x′)=y]. By sequential copmosition [3], when a user's report is split into components with budgets ε₁ and ε₂, the overall guarantee is (ε₁+ε₂)-LDP. We build on randomized response (RR) [4] for categorical data and on stochastic rounding for numerical data [5]. A value v is discretized to v* ∈ {−1,1} with Pr[v*=1] = (1+v)/2, which is unbiased, and v* is then flipped by RR with keep probability e^{ε₂}/(e^{ε₂}+1). Our design aims to remove thsi coupling. **Key-Value Perturbation Mechanism** Each user encodes its input as a d-dimensional vector in which a held key k carries the discretized value v* ∈ {−1,1} and every other entry is 0. A report is generated by sampling one coordinate j and perturbing only that coordinate, so the outpt domain is {−1,0,1}. The sampling sep is analogous to the one in [6], and the estimator is rescaled by d to correct for it. For the sampled coordinate with true entry x ∈ {−1,0,1}, the mechanism outputs y wtih probability Pr[y | x] = p if y = x, and q = (1−p)/2 otherwise, with p = e^ε/(e^ε+2). The ratio p/q = 2e^ε/(1−p)… more precisely, p/q = 2e^ε/2 = e^ε after normalization, so the mechanism satisfies ε-LDP, since any two inputs differ only by the ratio p/q. Using a three-way mechanism over the joint key-value domain spends the whole budget once rather than splitting it between key and value, which gives lowwer variance thna sequential perturbation at equal ε. **Unbiased Estimators** Let n_y(j) be the number of reports that sample coordinate j and output y ∈ {−1,0,1}, and let N_j be the number of reports sampling j. Defining the debiased counts ĉ₊ = (n₊ − qN_j)/(p−q), ĉ₋ = (n₋ − qN_j)/(p−q), where n₊ and n₋ denote the counts of outputs +1 and −1 on coordinate j, we have E[ĉ₊] = c₊ and E[ĉ₋] = c₋, the true counts of users holding key j with discretized value +1 and −1 respectively. The key frequency estimator is f̂_j = (ĉ₊ + ĉ₋)/N_j, and the mean estimator is m̂_j = (ĉ₊ − ĉ₋)/(ĉ₊ + ĉ₋). The mean estimator is a ratio of unbiased quantities and is therefore asymptotically unbiased; a second-order Taylor epxansion shows the bias is O(1/(n f_j)). This is simple and asymptotically unbiased, but the variance grows with |A|d. *Split-budget encoding.* The user spends ε_a on a (using generalized RR [7]) and ε_k = ε − ε_a on the key-value pair. The increasing reliance on individualized services, disease surveillance, and artificial intelligence has fueled the necessity for aggregating vast amounts of personal data. Nevertheless, the confidentiality concerns surrounding user-contributed data make individuals vulnerable to cyber threats, data misuse, and unreliable data handlers. To mitigate these risks, a robust framework known as differential privacy (DP) [1] has been established, ensuring that data analyses are unaffected by any single individual's data entry. However, the conventional DP paradigm presupposes a trustworthy data aggregator, which is not always the case. Local differential privacy (LDP) [2], [3] addresses this limitation by empowering users to distort their data locally before transmitting it, thereby precluding the aggregator from accessing raw data. The robust threat model underlying LDP has led to its integration into various industrial systems, including Google's RAPPOR [4], Apple's iOS and macOS telemetry [5], and Microsoft's telemetry collection [6]. Despite the advancements in LDP, the majority of existing research focuses on simple data structures, such as estimating categorical frequencies [4], [7], [8], identifying high-frequency data points [9], and estimating numerical attribute means [10], [11]. However, real-world data often exhibit complex structures, particularly in the form of key-value pairs, which serve as the fundamental data model for NoSQL databases. Key-value pairs are ubiquitous in various applications, including user-profile databases, e-commerce logs, and smart-device records, where a categorical key (e.g., a product or application) is paired with a numerical value (e.g., a rating or usage duration). Estimating the frequency of a specific item and its average rating are examples of applications that rely on key-value pairs. Handling key-value data under LDP poses significant challenges. Firstly, the correlation between keys and values means that perturbing them independently would not only compromise the privacy budget but also yield biased estimates. Secondly, users typically possess multiple keys, resulting in high-dimensional and sparse data that necessitates dividing the privacy budget across numerous coordinates, ultimately degrading data utility. Thirdly, the value domain is often continuous or ordinal, requiring perturbation methods that preserve unbiased aggregate estimates. The pioneering work on LDP for key-value data, PrivKV [12], perturbs each pair through a sequence of value and key randomization steps, supporting frequency and mean estimation. Subsequent refinements, including interactive variants, have reduced estimation errors [12], [13]. Nevertheless, existing mechanisms still suffer from considerable variance when the privacy budget is limited or the key domain is large, and the correlation between key and value perturbation is not fully exploited. Furthermore, current methods only provide marginal statistics, such as key frequencies and value means, which may not be sufficient for various downstream tasks. Many applications, including naive Bayes classification, decision-tree induction, association-rule mining, and recommendation systems, rely on conditional information, such as conditional probabilities or conditional means. For instance, estimating the probability that a user possesses key B given that they possess key A, or the mean value of key B among users holding key A [14], [15], is essential for these tasks. However, estimating such quantities under LDP is challenging because the conditioning event itself is observed only through noisy reports, and errors in the condition compound errors in the target statistic. In this study, we address these gaps by introducing novel perturbation mechanisms for key-value data and constructing conditional analysis frameworks upon them. Our primary contributions can be summarized as follows. Firstly, we propose a family of LDP mechanisms that jointly perturb the key and value of a pair while satisfying ε-LDP under a unified privacy budget. These mechanisms enable the derivation of unbiased estimators of key frequency and value mean in closed form, and we analyze their estimation variance, demonstrating improved accuracy over existing approaches. Secondly, we introduce a method for estimating the conditional frequency of one key given another from perturbed reports, enabling the recovery of conditional probabilities and marginal statistics for key analysis. We prove the estimator's unbiasedness and bound its error. Thirdly, we develop an estimator of the mean of the values associated with one key, conditioned on the presence of another key, supporting richer value analysis than marginal means. Fourthly, we demonstrate how the released conditional statistics can be used directly in downstream learning tasks, illustrating this with classification based on conditional probabilities. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on synthetic datasets with diverse distributions and on real-world rating datasets, showing that our mechanisms achieve lower error in frequency and mean estimation than state-of-the-art competitors across a wide range of privacy budgets and key-domain sizes, and that conditional estimates remain accurate enough to be useful. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is an extracorporeal blood purification technique that removes large molecular weight substances from the circulation, such as autoantibodies, immune complexes, paraproteins, and toxins, and replaces the removed plasma with albumin solutions or fresh frozen plasma. It is established as first-line or adjunctive therapy in a wide range of neurological, hematological, renal, and immune-mediated diseases, including thrombotic microangiopathies, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenic crises, anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and humoral rejection after transplantation. Plasma can be separated either by centrifugation or by membrane filtration. In membrane-based TPE, blood is pumped through a hgihly permmeable plasmafilter, and the separated plasma is discarded and replaced. Any extracorporeal circuit exposes blood to artificial surfaces and thereby activates the coagultaion cascade and platelets, with a risk of clotting of the filter and lines. Clotting reduces the efficacy of the procedure, causes blood loss, and increases costs and workload. Anticoagulation is therefore needed. Unfractionated heparin is the most widely used agent in membrane-based TPE, but its use is limited by the risk of bleeding, which is particularly relevant in patients with thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, recent surgery or biopsy, uremic platelet dysfunction, or active vasculitis with hemorrhagic lesions. Heparin may also induce heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and its effect is varialbe and difficult to predict. Moreover, TPE itself removes coagulation factors and may alter the response to heparin. Low molecular weight heparins and other agents such as argatroban or nafamostat have been used, but they share a systemic effect and are costly or not universally available. Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) was developed to confine the anticoagulant effect to the extracorporeal circuit. Citrate chelates ionized calcium, a cofactor essential for several steps of the coagulation cascade, so that infuusing citrate at the beginning of the circuit decreases ionized calcium and prevents clotting. Part of the citrate-calcium complex is removed in the effluent, and the remainder returns to the patient, where it is rapidly metabolized by the liver, skeletal muscle, and kidney cortex to bicarbonate, releasnig calcium. Insufficient citrate yields inadequate reduction of ionized calcium in the circuit, and thus filter clotting. Our investigation focused on devising a personalized approach to managing citrate and calcium supplementation during therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) procedures, a crucial aspect of patient care in the intensive care and nephrology units [35]. A key objective was to assess the efficacy and safety of our protocol, with particular attention to maintaining circuit patency and ensuring systemic ionized calcium and acid-base balance. This prospective observational study aimed to address the limitations currently inherent in the management of regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) during TPE, providing a more tailored approach to anticoagulation therapy in this context. Conducted in a university hospital setting, the study protocol received approval from the local ethics committee, with informed consent obtained from all patients or their relatives when necessary. The study encompassed 14 adult patients undergoing a total of 47 TPE sessions for standard clinical indications, excluding those with severe hepatic dysfunction, pregnancy, or a known allergy to circuit materials. Each TPE session utilized a hollow-fiber plasmafilter, with treatment parameters such as blood flow, plasma removal rate, and session duration determined by the treating physician based on the patient's plasma volume. Vascular access was established via a double-lumen dialysis catheter, and the replacement fluid, either 4% albumin or fresh frozen plasma, was administered post-plasmafilter, without systemic anticoagulation. The occurrence of circuit clotting and any premature session terminations were meticulously recorded. To achieve effective anticoagulation, trisodium citrate was continuously infused into the arterial line pre-plasmafilter using a dedicated volumetric pump [1], while calcium chloride was administered through a separate line into the patient's venous return, via a central venous route distinct from the dialysis catheter, to counteract citrate-bound calcium loss in the removed plasma and the citrate returned to the patient [2]. Our primary goal was to reduce the ionized calcium concentration in the blood entering the plasmafilter to a level that inhibits clotting, without exposing the patient to excessive citrate levels. To monitor the effectiveness of citrate anticoagulation, blood samples were collected at standardized intervals: pre-session, at fixed intervals during treatment, and post-session. These samples were drawn from both the post-plasmafilter port, indicative of circuit ionized calcium, and from the patient, reflecting systemic levels. Ionized calcium, pH, bicarbonate, base excess, sodium, and lactate were analyzed using a blood gas analyzer equipped with ion-selective electrodes [3]. Additional parameters, including hematocrit, total calcium, magnesium, albumin, and coagulation parameters, were obtained from routine pre-treatment laboratory analyses. Hypocalcemia was defined as a systemic ionized calcium level below a predetermined threshold (<0.9 mmol/l), considered significant if it necessitated intervention beyond protocol adjustments or was symptomatic [4]. Acid-base disturbances were identified by deviations in pH and bicarbonate from normal ranges. A calcium supplementation algorithm was developed a priori to manage calcium levels, with the calcium infusion rate initiated in proportion to the citrate infusion rate and adjusted based on systemic ionized calcium measurements at each time point [5]. The infusion rate was increased if systemic ionized calcium levels fell below the target range and decreased if levels rose above it, aiming to maintain systemic ionized calcium within physiological ranges throughout and at the end of the session. During the discovery phase, citrate was initially infused at a fixed rate relative to blood flow, then adapted based on the post-plasmafilter ionized calcium measured at the first time point, with target ranges derived from literature on regional citrate anticoagulation in continuous renal replacement therapy [6]. Citrate infusion rates were adjusted if post-plasmafilter ionized calcium levels exceeded or fell below the target. The final citrate infusion rate required to achieve the target, along with the corresponding pre-filter ionized calcium concentration, was recorded for each session. The relationship between circuit clotting and pre-filter ionized calcium was examined to define the concentration range that effectively prevents circuit coagulation. To develop a citrate prescription equation, we analyzed the determinants of the required blood citrate concentration, considering pre-session patient and treatment variables, including hematocrit, systemic plasma ionized calcium, total calcium, albumin, blood flow, plasma flow, and replacement fluid type [7]. Given that citrate chelates calcium in the plasma phase, plasma flow entering the filter was calculated from blood flow and hematocrit. We then mathematically modeled the citrate dose needed to adjust plasma ionized calcium from baseline to target levels, using the citrate-ionized calcium chelation relationship observed in the discovery data [8]. Variables significantly improving the model fit were retained. The resulting equation enabled the calculation of the required citrate dose based on patient and treatment characteristics, facilitating personalized citrate anticoagulation during TPE. This approach not only aids in maintaining circuit patency but also ensures the safety of the patient by minimizing the risk of hypocalcemia and acid-base disturbances.
