The complexities of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) are multifaceted and far-reaching, encompassing a broad spectrum of hip anomalies that range from mild dysplasia of the acetabulum and femoral head subluxation to severe, high-riding dislocation. The prevalence of DDH exhibits significant variability, with reported rates differing substantially across different geographic locations, ethnic groups, and diagnostic criteria. While estimates of dislocation incidence are approximately 1 per 1,000 live births, the inclusion of milder forms of instability and radiographic dysplasia can increase this rate to over 10 per 1,000 [1,2]. The importance of early detection and intervention in DDH cannot be overstated, as prompt treatment with a harness or abduction splint during the neonatal period or early infancy is often effective in achieving successful outcomes [3]. However, in many instances, inadequate or incomplete screening leads to delayed presentation, with children often not being diagnosed until after they have begun walking, at which point established dislocation or residual dysplasia may be present. Furthermore, even in cases where initial reduction is successful, residual acetabular dysplasia may persist [4,5]. The long-term consequences of untreated or inadequately treated DDH are well-documented and can have a profound impact on the health and quality of life of affected individuals. The abnormal distribution of load across the joint resulting from persistent acetabular insufficiency can lead to labral damage and premature osteoarthritis, rendering dysplasia a primary cause of secondary hip arthrosis in young adults [6,7]. The capacity for spontaneous remodeling of the acetabulum declines with age, and beyond approximately 18 to 24 months, this process is generally considered unreliable [8]. In children over 2 years of age, the likelihood of successful closed reduction diminishes, and open reduction, often combined with femoral shortening and pelvic osteotomy, is typically necessary to achieve a stable, concentric joint [9,10]. Various pelvic osteotomies have been developed to address acetabular deficiency in children, including redirectional procedures such as the Salter, Steel, Tönnis, and Ganz osteotomies, which involve rotating the acetabulum as a single unit, and reshaping procedures such as the Pemberton and Dega osteotomies, which alter the volume and configuration of the acetabular roof by hinging it through the iliac cortices [11–13]. Salter's innominate osteotomy provides anterior and lateral coverage but requires a stable, concentric reduction and may increase intra-articular pressure through medialization and lengthening of the limb [14]. The Pemberton osteotomy, a pericapsular procedure, reduces acetabular volume and relies on a flexible triradiate cartilage [12]. Each technique has its specific indications and limitations, and no single procedure has been demonstrated to be superior across all patterns of dysplasia. The Dega osteotomy, first described in 1953, is an incomplete transiliac osteotomy that extends from the outer cortex of the ilium toward the triradiate cartilage, leaving the inner cortex intact at the hinge [15]. The acetabular roof is then levered downward and secured with a bone graft. The osteotomy can be modified to increase anterior, lateral, or posterior coverage, depending on the site of the deficiency, making it an attractive option for the varied acetabular deformities seen in DDH, including those associated with neuromuscular disease [16,17]. Since its original description, the procedure has undergone refinement by several authors and has experienced renewed interest due to its versatility, relatively low morbidity, and avoidance of internal fixation in many cases [18,19]. Nonetheless, most published reports on the Dega osteotomy are limited by short or medium-term follow-up, involve small or mixed series, or combine different etiologies, and the English-language literature on its long-term outcome in idiopathic DDH remains limited [20,21]. Long-term data are particularly crucial in DDH, as the ultimate goal of treatment extends beyond radiographic normalization in childhood to include the preservation of a painless, functional hip into adulthood. Radiographic indices such as the acetabular index, center-edge angle, and Sharp angle may appear satisfactory at skeletal maturity, yet degenerative changes may emerge decades later [22]. Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head is a significant complication of treatment, especially after open reduction, and is a major determinant of poor outcome [23,24]. Other factors suggested to influence prognosis include age at surgery, degree of preoperative dislocation, the need for femoral osteotomy, residual acetabular dysplasia, and the quality of the reduction [9,25]. However, the relative importance of these predictors for the long-term survival of the hip after a Dega osteotomy has not been clearly established. The assessment of acetabular morphology and femoral head coverage has also evolved over time. Plain radiographs can be challenging to interpret in young children due to variable ossification and projection, and computed tomography has been used to define the three-dimensional pattern of acetabular deficiency and to verify reduction [26]. However, whether such imaging adds prognostic or operative value in children undergoing Dega osteotomy is uncertain. This multicenter study, conducted at three tertiary pediatric orthopedic centers, sought to investigate the long-term outcomes of this procedure in a cohort of children under the age of 8 years. The study was approved by the institutional review board at each center, and informed consent was obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all prospectively enrolled patients. For retrospective cases, consent for the use of anonymized data was obtained in accordance with local regulations, ensuring adherence to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The study population comprised children who underwent a Dega osteotomy for DDH between January 1988 and October 2000. A total of 17 hips were identified retrospectively from hospital records and radiographic archives, while 41 hips were enrolled prospectively after the introduction of a standardized protocol. To be eligible for inclusion in the study, patients had to meet specific criteria: (1) a diagnosis of DDH, encompassing acetabular dysplasia, subluxation, and complete dislocation; (2) age at surgery between 2 and 8 years; (3) a Dega osteotomy performed as part of the index procedure; and (4) a minimum follow-up of 13 years. Exclusion criteria included teratologic or neuromuscular dislocations, syndromic conditions (e.g., arthrogryposis, myelomeningocele), previous surgery on the affected hip, and incomplete clinical or radiographic records. Following the application of these criteria, 58 hips in 48 children (ten bilateral cases) were included in the study. Demographic data, laterality, age at diagnosis, previous treatment (such as Pavlik harness, closed reduction, or traction), and age at surgery were documented for each patient. Dislocations were graded according to the Tönnis classification [1], a widely used system that categorizes hip dislocations into four grades, ranging from mild to severe. The Tönnis classification provides a standardized framework for evaluating the severity of hip dislocation. The surgical technique employed in this study was based on the original description by Dega [2] and modified by later authors [3]. The procedure involved an anterior iliofemoral (Smith-Petersen) incision, followed by the splitting of the iliac apophysis and subperiosteal exposure of the lateral wall of the ilium down to the capsule. A curved incomplete osteotomy was then performed through the lateral cortex from just above the anterior inferior iliac spine toward the posterior limb of the triradiate cartilage, preserving the medial cortex and the continuity of the sciatic buttress. The acetabular roof was levered downward and outward with a curved osteotome to redirect the acetabulum, and the osteotomy was held open with a wedge-shaped bone graft. The graft was typically harvested from the iliac wing, although in some cases, a bank allograft was utilized. Kirschner wires were employed for fixation at the surgeon's discretion. In cases where the femoral head was dislocated, open reduction was performed through the same incision, involving capsulotomy, resection of the ligamentum teres and pulvinar, release of the transverse acetabular ligament, and capsulorrhaphy. Adductor tenotomy and psoas release were performed as necessary to facilitate reduction and prevent complications. Femoral shortening, with or without derotation or varization, was added when the reduction was under tension or when excessive anteversion was present [4]. The proliferation of multi-homed devices, such as smartphones equipped with both WiFi and cellular interfaces and servers connected to several networks, has created an opportunity to use multiple network paths simultaneously. Traditional TCP binds a connection to a single pair of IP addresses and therefore a single path, leaving additional connectivity idle and offering no resilience when the actvie path degrades. Multipath TCP (MPTCP) [1], standardized by the IETF in RFC 6824 and later revised in RFC 8684, addresses this limitation. It extends TCP so that a single transport connnection can be split into several subflows, each traversing a different path, while remaining transparent to applications. By aggregating the capacity of the available paths, MPTCP can improve throughput, increase robustness against link failures, and support seamless handover between access networks [2], [3]. Despite these benefits, MPTPC must still provide the same service guarantee as TCP: a reliable, in-order byet stream delivered to the application. Data are assigned a connection-level sequence number at the sender, transmitted over different subflows, and reordered at the receiver in a connection-level buffer before delivery. When paths differ in delay and bandwidth, as is typical for heterogeneous combinations succh as WiFi and LTE, packets sent later on a fast path may arrive before packets sent earlier on a slow path. The receiver must then hold the early arrivals until the missing data come in. This out-of-order (OFO) arrival problem inflates the receive buffer occupancy, increases application-level delay and jitter, and can cause head-of-line blocking [4]. When the receive window is exhausted by buffered out-of-order data, the sender is stalled and the aggregate throughput may fall below that of the best single path [5], [6]. The problem is therefore not only a latency concern but also a fundamental obstacle to realizing the potential gains of multipath transport. The paacket scheduler, which decides on which subfllow each pacekt is transmitted, plays a central role in mitigating this problem. The defualt scheduler in the Liunx MPTP implementation, minRTT, selects the available subflow with the smallest smoothed round-trip time that has spce in its congestion window [7]. Although simple, it ignores the bandwidth and delay differences that determine when a packet will actually arrive, and it performs poorly under path heterogeneity. Round-robin scheduling is even less informed, since it distributes packets evenly regardless of path quality. Numerous alternatives have been proposed. Some, such as DAPS [8], plan the allocation of packets to paths in advance, using delay and window information so that packets arrive in order. Others, such as BLEST [9], estimate whether using a slow subflow will blokc the connection-level send window and skip that subflow when blocking is likely. ECF [10] considers the completion time of the remaining data on fast and slow paths and may wait for the fast path rather than use a slow one. Other approaches reinject or retransmit packets on faster paths [11], or use learning-based techniques to adapt scheduling decisions [12]. While these schemes yield improvements in particular scenarios, many rely on round-trip time as a proxy for path delay. The use of RTT is problematic for in-order delivery. What determines the order of arrival at the receiver is the one-way, forward delay of each path, not the round-trip delay. RTT includes the reverse path delay, which may differ substantially from the forward delay owing to asymmetric routing, asymmetric link capacities, and different queueing on acknowledgments' return path. In cellular and WiFi networks, uplink and downlink characteristics are often markedly different, and ACK compression or delay can further distort RTT samples. A scheduler guided by RTT may thus mispredict arrival times and dispathc packets in an order that causes reordering. Moreover, delay alone is insufficient: the time a packet spends in the network also depends on the transmission time governed by path throughput and on queueing behind packets already sent on the same path. An effective scheduler must account jointly for forward delay and throughput differences. Motivated by these observations, we propose the forward-delay-based packet scheduling (FDPS) algorithm for MPTCP. FDPS estimates the forward delay of each subflow and combines it with an estimate of subflow throughput to predict the arrival time of a packet if it were sent on each path. The sender then dispatches pakets so that those with earlier sequence numbers are expected to arrive earlier, and so that the arrival sequence at the receiver closely follows the transmission sequence. By making scheduling decisions on the basis of the forward path characteristics, FDPS reduces the dependence on potentially misleading round-trip measurements and limits the buffering needed for reordering. Second, we design FDPS, which uses estimated forward delay and troughput differences among paths to schedule packets. Third, we evaluate FDPS through simulations under a variety of network conditions, varying bandwidth, delay, and asymmetry, and compare it with several existing schedulers. The proliferation of multi-homed devices, such as smartphones equipped with both WiiFi and cellular interfaces and servers connected to several networks, has created an opportunity to use multiple network paths simultaneously. Traditional TCP binds a connection to a single pair of IP addresses and therefore a single path, leaving additional connectivity idle and offering no resilience when the active path degrades. Multipath TCP (MPTCP) [1], standardized by the IETF in RFC 6824 and later revised in RFC 8684, addresses this limitation. It extends TCP so that a single transport connection can be spplit into several subflows, each traversing a different path, while remaining transparent to applications. By aggregating the capacity of the available paths, MPTCP can improve throughput, increase robustnness against link failures, and support seamless handover between access networks [2], [3]. Despite these benefits, MPTCP must still provide the samme service guarantee as TCP: a reliable, in-order byte stream delivered to the application. Data are assigned a connection-level seqeunce number at the sender, transmitted over different subflows, and reordered at the receiver in a connection-level buffer before delivery. When paths dfifer in delay and bandwidth, as is typical for heterogeneous combinations such as WiFi and LTE, packets sent later on a fast path may arrive beforre packets sennt earlier on a slow path. The reciever must then hold the early arrivals until the missing data come in. This out-of-order (OFO) arrival problem inflates the receive buffer occupancy, increases application-level delay and jitter, and can cause head-of-line blocking [4]. When the receive widnow is exhausted by bufferd out-of-order data, the sender is stalled and the aggregate throughput may fall below that of the best single path [5], [6]. The problem is therefore not only a latency cocnern but also a fundamental obstacle to realizing the potential gainns of multipath transport. The packt scheduler, which decidees on which subflwo each packet is transmitted, plays a central role in mitigating this problem. The default scheduler in the Linux MPTCP implementation, minRTT, selects the available subflow with the smallest smoothed round-trip time that has space in its congestion window [7]. Although simple, it ignores the bandwidth and delay differences that determine when a packket will actually arrive, and it performs poorly under path heterogeneity. Round-robin scheduling is even less informed, since it distributes packets evenly regardless of path quality. Numerous alternatives have been proposed. Some, such as DAPS [8], plan the allocation of packets to paths in advance, using delay and window information so that packets arrive in order. Others, such as BLEST [9], estimate whether using a slow subflow will block the connection-level send window and skip thhat subfolw when blocking is likely. ECF [10] considers the completion time of the remaining data on fast and slw paths and may wait for the fast path rather than use a slow one. Other approaches reinject or retransmit packets on faster paths [11], or use learning-based techniques to adapt scheduling decisions [12]. While these schemes yield improvements in particulra scenarios, many rely on round-trip time as a proxy for path delay. The use of RTT is problematic for in-order delivery. What determines the order of arrival at the receiver is the one-way, forward delay of each path, not the round-trip delay. RTT includes the reverse path delay, which may differ substatially from the forward delay owing to asymmetric routing, assymmetric link capacities, and different queueing on acknowledgments' return path. In cellular and WiFi networks, uplink and downlink characteristics are often markedly different, and ACK compression or delay can further distort RTT samples. A scheduler guided by RTT may thus misredict arrival times and dispatch packets in an order that causes reordering. Moreover, delay alone is insufficient: the time a packet spends in the network also depends on the transmission time governed by path throughput and on queueing behind packets already sent on the same path. An effective scheduler must account jointy for forward delay and throughput differences. Motivated by thse observations, we propose the forward-delay-based packet scheduling (FDPS) algorithm for MPTCP. FDPS estimates the forward delay of each subflow and combines it with an estimate of subflow throughput to predict the arrival time of a packet if it were sent on each path. The sneder then dispatches packets so that those with earlier sequence numbers are expected to arriive earlier, and so that the arrival sqeuence at the receiver closely follows the transmission sequence. By making scheduling decisions on the basis of the forward path characteristics, FDPS reduces the dependence on potentially misleading round-trip measurements and limits the buffering needed for reordering. The main contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we analyze why RTT-based and delay-agnostic scheduling lead to out-of-order arrivals in heterogeneous multipath environments. Second, we design FDPS, which uses estimated forward delay and throughput differencees among paths to scchedule packets. Third, we evaluate FDPS through simulations under a vaariety of network conditions, varying bandwidth, delay, and asymmetry, and compare it with several existing schedulers. The results show that FDPS substantially improves in-order arrival at the receiver, reducing the reordering burden relative to the baselines. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Our system model consists of an MPTCP connection with multiple subflows between a sender and a receiver, following the architecture outlined in RFC 6824 [1]. A connection-level data sequence number (DSN) is used to order the byte stream across subflows, and the scheduler assigns each DSN-mapped segment to a subflow with available congestion window space.

Upon arrival, the receiver reorders segments in a shared receive buffer before delivering them to the application. However, if a segment arrives with a DSN greater than the next expected one, it is considered out of order and must wait in the buffer, potentially causing head-of-line blocking and throttling throughput when the buffer is limited [2], [3]. To mitigate this issue, FDPS employs a forward delay estimation mechanism. For each subflow, the one-way forward delay is the time from transmission at the sender to arrival at the receiver, consisting of propagation delay, transmission delay, and queueing delay. While using the smoothed round-trip time as a proxy for the forward delay is common [4], this approach is inadequate on asymmetric paths and when reverse-path congestion inflates ACK delays. Therefore, FDPS directly estimates the forward component of the delay.

The forward delay estimation in FDPS involves the receiver stamping each arriving segment with its local clock and returning the stamp in a TCP option carried on the ACK, similar to the TCP timestamp option [5]. The sender records the send time of each segment and computes a relative forward delay, which equals the forward delay plus an unknown constant clock offset. The sender maintains the minimum observed value of the relative forward delay for each subflow, which approximates the propagation delay plus the transmission delay when queues are empty. The queueing-inclusive delay is then estimated by subtracting the minimum observed value from the relative forward delay. This yields a delay estimate of each path relative to the fastest one, which is smoothed using an exponentially weighted moving average [6].

To avoid ambiguity, samples from retransmitted segments are discarded. Throughput is estimated per subflow as the ratio of the congestion window to the smoothed round-trip time, giving the sending rate that the congestion controller currently permits. This estimate is smoothed over a window of the most recent ACKs to dampen short-term oscillations. The scheduling rule in FDPS is designed to ensure that packets arrive in order. Suppose the scheduler is about to send a segment on a subflow at time t. The expected arrival time is calculated based on the estimated delay, the amount of data already queued or in flight, and the sending rate. The scheduler aims to assign consecutive DSNs arrival times that are monotonically non-decreasing. To achieve this, FDPS maintains the largest expected arrival time among segments already scheduled and selects the subflow whose expected arrival time is closest to, but not earlier than, the largest expected arrival time.

Smoking and other mucosal insults, as well as periodontal infection, have been proposed as triggers of citrullination that precede joint involvement [10]. A growing number of citrullinated autoantigens have been identified in the rheumaotid joint, including fibrin(ogen), vimentin, α-enolase, and type II collagen [11–14]. Citrullinated proteins and PAD enzymes are abundant in the inflamed synovium, and ACPA can form immune complexes with these antigens, activating complement and Fc receptor-bearing cells and thereby amplifying inflammation [15]. The chronic autoimmune disorder known as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is marked by the inflammation of synovial joints, which, if left untreated, can lead to the progressive degradation of articular cartilage and bone, ultimately resulting in significant disability [1]. A key characteristic of RA is the production of a diverse array of autoantibodies, including rheumatoid factor, which targets the Fc region of IgG, and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA) [2,3]. These ACPA can be detected in the sera and synovial fluids of approximately 60-70% of RA patients, often appearing years before the onset of clinical symptoms. Furthermore, ACPA have been linked to a more severe and erosive disease course, which is why ACPA seropositivity is a crucial factor in the current classification criteria for RA [4,5]. The process of citrullination, which involves the conversion of arginine residues to citrulline by calcium-dependent peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs), plays a critical role in the development of ACPA [6,7]. This post-translational modification can alter the structure and function of proteins, leading to the creation of neoepitopes that can evade the immune system's tolerance mechanisms. Although citrullination is a physiological process that occurs during various cellular processes, including apoptosis, differentiation, and inflammation, it is not unique to RA. However, in individuals with a genetic predisposition, particularly those carrying HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles, citrullinated peptides are presented to CD4+ T cells with higher affinity, supporting the activation of B cells and the production of ACPA [8,9]. Environmental factors, such as smoking and periodontal infection, have been proposed as potential triggers of citrullination that precede joint involvement [10]. A growing number of citrullinated autoantigens have been identified in the rheumatoid joint, including fibrin(ogen), vimentin, α-enolase, and type II collagen [11-14]. These citrullinated proteins and PAD enzymes are abundant in the inflamed synovium, and ACPA can form immune complexes with these antigens, activating complement and Fc receptor-bearing cells, thereby amplifying inflammation [15]. Moreover, ACPA that react with cartilage-derived citrullinated epitopes have been shown to induce or enhance arthritis in experimental models, suggesting that antigens within the cartilage itself may be pathogenically relevant targets [16]. One such antigen is aggrecan, a large aggregating proteoglycan that is one of the most abundant macromolecules in articular cartilage. Aggrecan provides compressive resistance to cartilage through its highly charged glycosaminoglycan chains and consists of three globular domains (G1, G2, and G3) and an extended interglobular and glycosaminoglycan-attachment region [17]. The N-terminal G1 domain of aggrecan binds to hyaluronan and link protein, anchoring the molecule within the extracellular matrix. Aggrecan has long been recognized as an arthritogenic autoantigen, and immunization of BALB/c mice with human cartilage PG induces a progressive, erosive polyarthritis (proteoglycan-induced arthritis, PGIA) that resembles human RA, with the production of autoantibodies and T cell-dependent disease [18,19]. Additionally, T cell responses to human PG, particularly to peptides from the G1 domain, have been detected in RA patients [20,21]. More recent studies have demonstrated that T cells from RA patients respond to citrullinated aggrecan peptides, and that citrullinated epitopes within the G1 domain bind with high affinity to shared-epitope-containing HLA-DR molecules [22,23]. Citrullinated PG epitopes can also be recognized by T cells in the SKG and PGIA mouse models [24]. These findings suggest that citrullinated aggrecan may serve as a joint-specific target of both T and B cell responses, which could help explain the localization of the autoimmune attack to the joints, despite the systemic distribution of ACPA and citrullinating enzymes. Despite the evidence, a fundamental question remains unanswered: whether the aggrecan molecule is actually citrullinated in vivo in human cartilage. Most studies have employed synthetic citrullinated peptides or in vitro modified proteins, which establish the immunological potential of citrullinated aggrecan but do not demonstrate the presence of the modified protein in the tissue. Cartilage is avascular and has low cellular density, and its matrix proteins turn over slowly, which could favor the accumulation of post-translational modifications. Moreover, it is unknown whether citrullinated PG (CitPG) occurs in normal cartilage or only in diseased tissue, which fragments of the molecule carry the modification, and whether its distribution differs between osteoarthritis (OA) and RA. Clarifying these points is essential for judging whether CitPG can serve as a target for ACPA, form local immune complexes, and contribute to the initiation or perpetuation of joint inflammation. In the present study, we sought to determine whether citrullinated aggrecan is present in human articular cartilage and to characterize its molecular features. We used sera from ACPA-positive RA patients to probe PG purified from normal cartilage and cartilage extracts from OA and RA patients, and we identified the PG fragments, particularly those containing the G1 and G3 domains, that carry citrulline-containing epitopes. We confirmed the citrullination status of an in vitro citrullinated recombinant human G1 domain (rhG1) using both antibody-based and chemical detection, and used molecular modeling to explore the potential sites of citrullination within this domain. Finally, we quantified CitPG-specific serum autoantibodies by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and compared the immunohistochemical localization of CitPG in cartilage from OA and RA patients to better understand its role in the pathogenesis of RA. The presence of citrullinated aggrecan in human cartilage could provide a critical link between the autoimmune response and the joint-specific damage observed in RA. By elucidating the molecular features of citrullinated aggrecan and its role in the immune response, we may uncover new targets for therapeutic intervention and improve our understanding of the complex mechanisms underlying this debilitating disease. The identification of citrullinated aggrecan as a potential target of the autoimmune response in RA could also lead to the development of novel diagnostic markers and therapeutic strategies, ultimately improving the outcomes for patients with this disease. Furthermore, the study of citrullinated aggrecan could provide valuable insights into the pathogenesis of other autoimmune diseases, where similar mechanisms of post-translational modification and immune recognition may be at play. Cartilage specimens were sourced from tissue donors without a history of joint disease, as well as from patients undergoing surgical procedures for osteoarthritis (OA) or rheumatoid arthritis (RA). These specimens were stored at -80 °C pending analysis, while serum samples were collected from RA patients who met the 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria [1]. The ACPA status of these patients was ascertained using a commercial anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP2) ELISA, and samples were subsequently categorized as ACPA-positive (ACPA+) or ACPA-negative (ACPA-). Sera from ACPA-negative healthy individuals or OA patients served as controls, and all sera were aliquoted and stored at -80 °C to preclude repeated freeze-thaw cycles. The extraction and purification of proteoglycan from cartilage involved the use of a combination of guanidine hydrochloride and sodium acetate buffer, followed by dialysis and CsCl density-gradient ultracentrifugation [2]. The high-density fraction (A1) was harvested, and aliquots underwent deglycosylation using chondroitinase ABC, keratanase, and endo-β-galactosidase to expose the core protein and its constituent fragments. Protein concentration was quantified using the BCA assay. Additionally, we employed a mammalian expression system to produce a recombinant human G1 domain of aggrecan (rhG1), which was purified by nickel-affinity chromatography [3]. The purity of the rhG1 was verified by SDS-PAGE with Coomassie staining, and the protein was utilized in subsequent in vitro citrullination experiments. In these experiments, rhG1 (and, in parallel, purified native PG) was incubated with rabbit skeletal muscle peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD) in the presence of calcium and DTT, and the reaction was terminated with EDTA [4]. Control samples were processed in an identical manner, albeit without enzyme or calcium. To confirm citrullination, we employed both antibody-based and chemical methodologies. The antibody-based approach involved the transfer of proteins onto PVDF membranes, which were then probed with anti-modified citrulline antibody, followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibody [4]. The chemical method utilized the colorimetric diacetyl monoxime-thiosemicarbazide assay to quantify citrulline in the samples against an L-citrulline standard curve [5]. Absorbance was measured at 530 nm. Furthermore, dot blot and Western blot experiments were conducted to detect the presence of CitPG in cartilage extracts and sera. For dot blots, purified PG, cartilage extract, or rhG1 was applied to nitrocellulose membranes, while for Western blots, native or deglycosylated samples were separated on SDS-polyacrylamide gels and transferred to PVDF or nitrocellulose membranes. Membranes were blocked with non-fat dry milk or BSA in TBS-Tween and incubated with individual ACPA+ or ACPA- sera overnight at 4 °C. Bound IgG was detected with HRP-conjugated anti-human IgG and enhanced chemiluminescence. The quality of the model was evaluated by QMEAN scores and Ramachandran plots, and the solvent accessibility of each arginine residue was calculated using PyMOL and the NACCESS algorithm. Bound IgG was detected with HRP-conjugated anti-human IgG and TMB substrate, and absorbance was measured at 450 nm. Background signal from uncoated wells was subtracted, and reactivity to CitrhG1 was compared with reactivity to unmodified rhG1. The study of autoantibodies in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) has been a subject of significant interest in recent years, with considerable attention focused on the development of novel diagnostic and therapeutic modalities. The investigation of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) has focused intently on the role of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs), which are known to be pivotal in the disease's pathogenesis and serve as a distinctive marker of the condition. This study delved into the interaction between ACPA-positive (ACPA+) RA sera and proteoglycans (PGs) isolated from normal human cartilage, aiming to elucidate the specific recognition patterns and the nature of the epitopes involved. To initiate this inquiry, PG was purified from extracts of normal human articular cartilage and then probed with sera from ACPA+ RA patients, ACPA-negative (ACPA–) RA patients, and healthy controls, utilizing dot blot analysis as described in previous research [1]. The results showed that all ACPA+ sera tested yielded distinct signals with the purified PG, with the intensity of these signals increasing in direct proportion to the amount of PG applied, thus indicating a dose-dependent reactivity. Conversely, signals obtained from ACPA– or control sera were minimal, hovering at or below background levels, suggesting that ACPA+ sera exhibit a specific affinity for epitopes located on the PG molecule. 

To further decipher the characteristics of these epitopes, the PG was subjected to enzymatic treatment with chondroitinase ABC, keratanase, and endo-β-galactosidase, aimed at removing the glycosaminoglycan chains, as outlined in earlier studies [2]. Notably, this enzymatic treatment did not eradicate the reactivity of ACPA+ sera, pointing to the conclusion that the epitopes recognized by these antibodies are embedded within the core protein of the PG and are neither obscured by nor dependent on the glycosaminoglycan side chains. This observation aligns with preceding research indicating that ACPAs are capable of recognizing citrullinated epitopes on proteins [3]. 

The next phase of the investigation involved analyzing cartilage extracts from osteoarthritis (OA) and RA patients using Western blotting techniques, as referenced in prior work [4]. It was observed that ACPA+ sera reacted with multiple fragments of PG in both OA and RA extracts, with the most prominent bands corresponding to molecular masses consistent with fragments containing the G1 domain. This finding was corroborated by reprobing with an anti-G1 monoclonal antibody, which specifically targets the G1 domain. Bands corresponding to higher apparent mass, indicative of the intact core protein, were less intense and less consistently observed. The variability in band patterns among specimens could be attributed to differences in the degree of in vivo proteolytic fragmentation. Notably, serum from an ACPA– individual failed to exhibit specific reactivity with any of the extracts, and the omission of primary serum or the use of secondary antibody alone resulted in no signal, thereby underscoring the specificity of the ACPA+ sera for citrullinated PG fragments. These outcomes collectively demonstrate that citrullinated PG (CitPG) fragments are detectable in both degenerative and inflammatory arthritic cartilage.

To verify the in vitro citrullination of the recombinant human G1 domain, rhG1 was treated with peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD) and the resulting citrullination was verified through two independent methodologies [5]. Firstly, after chemical modification with 2,3-butanedione monoxime/antipyrine under acidic conditions, the PAD-treated rhG1 was detected using an anti-modified citrulline antibody, whereas untreated rhG1 yielded no signal. Secondly, the PAD-treated rhG1 reacted positively with an anti-citrulline antibody, whereas the untreated protein did not, further confirming the successful citrullination. Coomassie staining revealed that PAD treatment did not cause noticeable degradation of the protein, and the loading of the treated and untreated preparations was equivalent, ensuring that the observed differences were due to citrullination rather than protein degradation. ACPA+ sera reacted vigorously with citrullinated rhG1 but only weakly, if at all, with the unmodified protein, while ACPA– sera did not differentiate between the two forms. This pattern of reactivity was consistent across several individual ACPA+ sera, although the titers varied among patients. Additionally, a G3 domain-containing PG fragment also reacted with ACPA+ sera following citrullination, indicating that citrullinated epitopes are present in at least two globular domains of PG.

Finally, to evaluate which arginine residues in the G1 domain could potentially be accessible to PAD, molecular modeling techniques were employed [6]. A structural model of the human G1 domain, encompassing the Ig-like, link module A, and link module B subdomains, was utilized to identify potential citrullination sites. Among the arginine residues within the domain, a subset was found to reside in solvent-exposed loops or flexible regions that could be accommodated within the PAD active site, suggesting their potential for citrullination. Others were found to be buried within the β-sheet core or engaged in salt bridges, making them less likely to be modified in the native fold. The exposed candidates were dispersed across all three subdomains, with several clustered in the link-module regions. The in silico conversion of these residues to citrulline resulted in the removal of positive charges and alterations in local electrostatic surfaces without major changes in the backbone conformation, suggesting that multiple sites within the G1 domain can be citrullinated and could contribute to the polyclonal ACPA response against PG.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that ACPA+ RA sera specifically recognize citrullinated epitopes on PG purified from normal human cartilage. These recognized epitopes are located within the core protein and are not masked by, or dependent on, the glycosaminoglycan side chains. The presence of citrullinated PG fragments in both degenerative and inflammatory arthritic cartilage, along with the presence of citrullinated epitopes in at least two globular domains of PG, underscores the complex nature of ACPA recognition. Molecular modeling suggests that multiple sites within the G1 domain can undergo citrullination, potentially contributing to the polyclonal ACPA response against PG. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of the pathogenesis of RA and the role of ACPAs in the disease. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have moved from specialized military platforms to widely available tools for civilian applications, including surveillance, agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and emergency resonse [1], [2]. In disaster operations, UAVs are especially attractive because they can be deployed quickly, can reach areas that are dangerous or inaccessible to ground crews, and can provied situational awareness within the critical first hours after an event such as an earthquake, flood, or wildfire [3]. As the cost of small multirotor and fixed-wing platforms decreases, attention has turned from the operation of a single vehicle to the coordinated use of many vehicles. Swarms of UAVs can cover large areas in parallel, provide redundancy against individual vehicle failures, and support tasks such as search and rescue, damage assessment, and communication relay [4], [5]. Despite these advantages, operating multiple UAVs introduces substantial challenges for human operators. A single operator supervising several vehicles must manage task allocation, moniitor vehicle states, interpret sensor data, and respond to changing conditions, often under time pressure and stress [6]. The design of efective user interfaces and operating procedures for such multi-vehicle systems remains an open research problem, and poor interface design has been linked to reduced operator performance and an increased risk of mishaps [7]. Training personnel to use these systems is similarly demanding. Real-world flight tests are expensive, weather dependent, and constrained by regulations, and they may place vehicles, bystanders, and property at risk. Disaster scenarios in particular are difficult to rperoduce safely and repeatably in the field. Simulation offers a practical means of addressing these limitations. Simulated environments allow researchers to prototype and compare interface designs, evaluate human-swarm interaction strategies, and train operators in a cnotrolled and repeatable setting at low cost [8]. A variety of simulators have been developed for robotics and UAV research, including Gazebo, AirSim, and others built on general-purpose game or physics engines [9], [10]. These tools often provide high-fidelity physics and sensor models, but they can be complex to configure and are not always oriented toward the study of operator interaction with large teams of vehicles in disaster response contexts. Conversely, simulators designed for human-in-the-loop studies and training frequently simplify vehicle dynamics, for example by allowing vehicles to move instantaneously between positions or to follow idealized straight-line paths at constant speed. Suhc simplificatoins can be adequate for studying high-level decision making, but they may give operators an inaccurate impression of how real vehicles respond to commands. The result is a gap between simulated and real operation, which can lead to negative training transfer and to interface designs that perform well in simulation but poolry in the field [11]. The Reno Rescue Simulator (RRS) was developed to support research on human interaction with swarms of UAVs in search-and-rescue and disaster scenarios. It provides a virtual environment in which an operator can issue commands to multiple simulated vehicles, view imagery and sensor information, and carry out mission tasks such as locating survivors. However, the motion of vehicles in the original simulator was represented in a simplified manner, which limited the realism of the user experience and the applicability of findings to real systems. Because the perceived responsiveness, turning behavior, and path-following characteristics of a UAV strongly influence how operators plan and issue commands, more faithful motion models are an important step toward a useful training and prototyping platform [12]. In this paper, we present the integration of a model-based waypoint navigation controller into the Reno Rescue Simulator. Waypoint navigation is a common method of commanding UAVs, in which an operator or plnner specifies a sequence of positions that the vehicle must visit, and an onoard controller computes the control inputs required to follow the path [13]. Model-based controllers use a mathematical representation of vehicle dynamics to compute these inputs, producing motion that reflects physical constraints such as limited acceleration, finite turning rates, and inertia. By embedding such a controller within the simulator, vehicles respond to operator commands in a manner more consistent with real platforms, and the interface through which operators assign waypoints becomes a more representative model of actual ground control systems. The contributions of this work are as follows. First, we describe the design and implementation of a waypoint navigation controller based on a dynamic model of the UAV and its integration into the architecture of the Reno Rescue Simulator, including the interface between the user-facing components and the vehicle control layer. Second, we show how the controller supports simultaneous operation of multiple vehicles, enabling swarm-level scenarios relevant to disaster operations. Third, we discuss potential uses of the resulting simulator, including interface prototyping, operator training, mission rehearsal, and human-subject experimentation. We also consider how such a simulator might support real-world UAV operations, for instance by allowing operators to preview planned missions, anticipate vehicle behavior, and test contingency plans before committing physical asets to a hazardous environment. The transformative journey of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) from their origins as specialized military assets to their current status as versatile tools for a wide range of civilian applications has been nothing short of remarkable. Presently, UAVs are being leveraged in diverse settings, encompassing surveillance, agricultural monitoring, infrastructure assessment, and emergency response efforts [1], [2]. Within the domain of disaster management, UAVs have emerged as particularly invaluable assets, as they can be rapidly deployed to areas that are inaccessible or pose a hazard to ground-based teams, thereby providing critical situational awareness in the aftermath of catastrophic events such as seismic activities, floods, or wildfires [3]. The diminishing costs associated with small multirotor and fixed-wing platforms have led to a paradigm shift, from the operation of individual vehicles to the coordination of multiple UAVs. This swarm-based approach enables the coverage of extensive areas in a parallel manner, offers redundancy in the event of individual vehicle failures, and facilitates tasks such as search and rescue operations, damage assessment, and communication relay [4], [5]. Nevertheless, the operation of multiple UAVs presents significant challenges for human operators, who must manage task allocation, monitor vehicle status, interpret complex sensor data, and respond to evolving conditions, often under stringent time constraints and high levels of stress [6]. The development of effective user interfaces and operating protocols for such multi-vehicle systems remains an open and complex research challenge, with poorly designed interfaces having been linked to diminished operator performance and an increased likelihood of adverse events [7]. Moreover, the training of personnel to utilize these systems is a formidable task, as real-world flight tests are costly, weather-dependent, and subject to regulatory constraints, and may pose risks to vehicles, bystanders, and property. Disaster scenarios, in particular, are challenging to replicate safely and consistently in real-world settings. Simulation offers a viable solution to these limitations, allowing researchers to prototype and evaluate interface designs, assess human-swarm interaction strategies, and train operators in a controlled, repeatable, and cost-effective environment [8]. A variety of simulation tools have been developed for robotics and UAV research, including Gazebo, AirSim, and other platforms built on general-purpose game or physics engines [9], [10]. While these tools often provide high-fidelity physics and sensor models, they can be complex to configure and may not be optimized for the study of operator interaction with large teams of vehicles in disaster response contexts. Conversely, simulators designed for human-in-the-loop studies and training often simplify vehicle dynamics, for example by allowing vehicles to move instantaneously between positions or to follow idealized straight-line paths at constant speed. Such simplifications may be adequate for studying high-level decision-making processes but can provide operators with an inaccurate understanding of how real vehicles respond to commands, leading to a disconnect between simulated and real-world operation, negative training transfer, and interface designs that perform well in simulation but poorly in actual field conditions [11]. To address these challenges, the Reno Rescue Simulator (RRS) was developed to support research on human interaction with swarms of UAVs in search-and-rescue and disaster scenarios. The RRS provides a virtual environment in which an operator can issue commands to multiple simulated vehicles, view imagery and sensor information, and perform mission tasks such as locating survivors. However, the original simulator represented vehicle motion in a simplified manner, limiting the realism of the user experience and the applicability of findings to real-world systems. Given that the perceived responsiveness, turning behavior, and path-following characteristics of a UAV significantly influence how operators plan and issue commands, more realistic motion models are essential for creating a useful training and prototyping platform [12]. This paper presents the integration of a model-based waypoint navigation controller into the Reno Rescue Simulator. Waypoint navigation is a common method of commanding UAVs, where an operator or planner specifies a sequence of positions that the vehicle must visit, and an onboard controller computes the necessary control inputs to follow the path [13]. Model-based controllers utilize a mathematical representation of vehicle dynamics to compute these inputs, resulting in motion that reflects physical constraints such as limited acceleration, finite turning rates, and inertia. By incorporating such a controller within the simulator, vehicles respond to operator commands in a manner more consistent with real-world platforms, and the interface through which operators assign waypoints becomes a more representative model of actual ground control systems. The contributions of this work are threefold. Firstly, we describe the design and implementation of a waypoint navigation controller based on a dynamic model of the UAV and its integration into the architecture of the Reno Rescue Simulator, including the interface between the user-facing components and the vehicle control layer. Secondly, we demonstrate how the controller supports the simultaneous operation of multiple vehicles, enabling swarm-level scenarios relevant to disaster operations. Thirdly, we discuss the potential applications of the resulting simulator, including interface prototyping, operator training, mission rehearsal, and human-subject experimentation, as well as its potential to support real-world UAV operations, for instance by allowing operators to rehearse missions in a virtual environment before deployment. The implications of this work extend to the broader context of UAV operation, where the development of realistic and effective simulation tools can play a critical role in enhancing operator performance, reducing the risk of adverse events, and ultimately saving lives in disaster response scenarios. Furthermore, the integration of model-based controllers into simulation platforms like the RRS can facilitate the development of more sophisticated autonomous systems, where UAVs can operate with greater degrees of independence and decision-making capability, thereby expanding their potential applications and benefits in a wide range of fields. As the field of UAV research continues to evolve, the importance of simulation-based training and prototyping will only continue to grow, highlighting the need for further innovations in simulator design, vehicle modeling, and human-machine interaction. The potential for simulation to bridge the gap between theoretical models and real-world operations, and to provide a safe and controlled environment for the testing and evaluation of new concepts and technologies, is vast and largely untapped. By leveraging advances in simulation technology, researchers and practitioners can work together to create more effective, efficient, and safe UAV systems, and to unlock the full potential of these versatile and powerful tools. Ultimately, the development of sophisticated simulation platforms like the RRS, and the integration of model-based controllers into these systems, represents a critical step forward in the pursuit of more capable, more reliable, and more effective UAVs, and holds significant promise for the future of disaster response, search and rescue, and a wide range of other applications where these systems can make a meaningful difference. The capability to preview and rehearse planned missions, predict the behavior of vehicles, and test emergency plans in a virtual setting is crucial for effective disaster response operations. The evolution of the Reno Rescue Simulator (RRS) with the incorporation of a model-based waypoint navigation controller marks a significant milestone in the realm of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) research and disaster response. By creating a more realistic and immersive simulation environment, the RRS enables researchers and operators to gain a deeper understanding of the complexities involved in human-swarm interaction, ultimately leading to the development of more effective strategies for UAV deployment in disaster scenarios. Additionally, the RRS offers a secure and controlled environment for training operators, thereby reducing the risk of accidents and enhancing overall performance. As the role of UAVs in disaster response continues to expand, the need for advanced simulation tools like the RRS will become increasingly critical. By facilitating the development of more effective interface designs, operator training protocols, and mission planning strategies, the RRS can play a vital role in enhancing the safety and efficacy of UAV operations in disaster response scenarios.

In the context of search and rescue operations, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have proven to be invaluable assets, offering unprecedented capabilities in navigating and surveying hazardous environments. However, the effective deployment of UAVs in such scenarios is contingent upon the development of sophisticated simulation tools that can accurately model their behavior and interaction with human operators. This paper aims to address this challenge by presenting an enhanced version of the Reno Rescue Simulator (RRS), a multi-agent, game-engine-based environment designed to simulate UAV operations in disaster scenarios. The RRS was selected as the foundation for this work due to its adaptability and potential for customization [1]. The original RRS featured a kinematic model of UAV motion, where each vehicle moved towards its assigned target at a constant speed with instantaneous changes in direction. Nevertheless, this model does not accurately reflect the dynamic constraints of real-world multirotor aircraft, which are subject to physical limitations and environmental factors such as wind. To address this limitation, we replaced the kinematic model with a model-based waypoint navigation controller, enabling the simulation of more realistic vehicle behavior.

The development of this controller involved several key steps, including the design of the simulator architecture, the vehicle dynamics model, the controller design, swarm-level integration, and the evaluation procedure. The architecture of the RRS is organized into three distinct layers: a scenario layer that defines the terrain, hazards, and victim locations; an agent layer that encapsulates the state and behavior of each UAV; and a user interface layer that provides a map view and accepts operator commands. The simulation advances in fixed time steps of 10 ms for physics and control updates, while rendering and interface updates run at the display frame rate. This decoupling of rates ensures numerical integration stability, regardless of the rendering load. The new controller was implemented as a replaceable module within the agent layer, allowing for seamless switching between the original kinematic model and the new dynamic model without altering the scenario or interface layers.

A critical component of the RRS is the vehicle dynamics model, which simulates the behavior of each UAV as a quadrotor rigid body with twelve states: position, velocity, Euler angles, and body angular rates. The translational dynamics of the UAV are governed by Newton's second law, while the rotational dynamics follow Euler's equations with a diagonal inertia matrix. Parameters such as mass, arm length, inertia, maximum thrust, and drag coefficient were set to values representative of a commercially available small quadrotor platform [2]. Actuator limits were enforced by saturating thrust and commanded torques, and first-order motor lag was included to prevent unrealistically abrupt control changes. Additionally, optional wind disturbance was modeled as a steady component plus a low-pass-filtered stochastic gust added to the drag term [3]. The waypoint navigation controller employs a standard cascaded structure, comprising an outer position loop and an inner attitude loop [2], [4]. The outer loop computes a desired acceleration from the position and velocity errors relative to the active waypoint, while the inner loop applies proportional-derivative control to track the desired angles and yaw rate. Gains were initially selected by pole placement on the linearized model and then tuned in simulation to achieve a damped response with limited overshoot and no sustained oscillation.

The integration of the controller with the swarm-level behavior of the UAVs is a crucial aspect of the RRS. Each UAV runs its own controller instance, and the operator interacts with the group through high-level commands. Group commands, such as moving to a location or sweeping a region, are decomposed into per-vehicle waypoint lists. Regions are partitioned into parallel lanes assigned to the nearest available vehicles, in a manner that ensures efficient and coordinated coverage. The RRS also allows for the simulation of various environmental conditions, such as wind and obstacles, which can significantly impact the behavior of the UAVs. By simulating these conditions, researchers and operators can develop more effective strategies for UAV deployment in disaster scenarios.

Additionally, the RRS can be used to train operators in a safe and controlled environment, reducing the risk of accidents and improving overall performance. Cancer is a heterogeneous group of diseases driven by the accumulation of genomic alterations that confer selective advantages to cells, including sustained proliferation, evasion of cell death and the capacity to invade and colonize distant tissues. Ovre the last decade, large-scale sequencing initiatives such as The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) have profiled thousands of tumors across dozens of cancer types. These efforts hvae produced extensive catalogues of somatic mutations, copy number alterations, gene fusions and expression changes, and have enabled the identification of hundreds of cancer driver genes using methods that search for signals of positive selection, such as recurrence, functional impact bias or clustering of mutations in protein sequence and structure. Such cohort-level analyses have been invaluable for understanding the landscape of cancer genomics. However, they describe the properties of populations of tumors, and their conclusions do not translate directly to the individual patient. A typical tumor carries from tens to thousands of somaatic coding mutations, and only a handful of them, sometimes just one or none, affect known driver genes. The remaining alterations are usually considered passengers, although some may be rare drivers, may modulate the effect of the main drivers, or may represent unexplored therapeutic opportunities. Moreover, tumors of the same histological type frequently differ in their molecular makeup, and the same gene can play different roles, as oncogene or tumr suppressor, depending on the tissue. Interpreting the alterations found in a single patient therefore requires placing them in the context of the tumor type, the available knowledge on driver genes, and the functional and structural consequences of each variant. Precision oncology aims precisely at this goal: matching each patient with the therapy most likely to be effective on the basis of the molecular characteristics of the tumor. Clinical sequencing, from targeted gene panels to whole exomes and genomes, is becoming increasingly common, and molecular tumor boards are being established in many hospitals. Nevertheless, translating a list of variants innto clinically meaningful information remains a major bottleneck. Several resources address parts of this problem. Databases such as COSMIC, cBioPortal and the ICGC Data Portal provide access to mutation data and cohort-level exploration; OncoKB, CIViC, the Caancer Genome Interpreter and My Cancer Genome curate evidence on the oncogenic effect and clinical actionability of variants and on drug responses; and tools such as IntOGen compile cancer driver genes derived from large cohorts. Yet these resources typically differ in scope, in the nomenclature and annotations they use, and in whether they emphasize the cohort or the individual. Clinicians and researchers must often connsult several of them and integrate the results manually, which is time-consuming and prone to inconsistency. A further limitation is that most interpretation strategies treat genes as isolated entities. Proteins function within complex networks of physical interactions, and the consequences of a mutaiton depend on its cellular environment. A mutation may disrupt a protein-protein interface and rewire specific interactions, affect a catalytic or ligand-binding site, or destabilize the fold. Network-based approaches have shown that cancer genes tend to occupy particular positions in the interactome and that mutations in different genes can converge on the same pathways or complexes. Likewise, three-dimensional structural information, whether experimental or derived from homology modelling, allows mutations to be mapped onto functional regions, pockets and interfaces, providing mechanistic hypotheses about their impact and, potentially, about druggability. Incorporating these layers ino the interpretation of personal cancer genomes remains uncommon in accessible tools. Another challenge is the need for a coherent view that combines complementary perspectives. A cohort-centric view answers questions such as how frequently a gene is mutated in a tmor type, whether it is a recognized driver, and what the typical patterns of co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity are. A patient-centric view asks which of the mutations in a given tumor are likely to be functionally relevant, how they relate to each otheer in terms of pathways and interactions, and whether there is evidence of clinical actionability. Bridging both views allows an individual profile to be compared with relevant cohorts, helpng to distinguish expected from unusual alterations and to prioritize variants for follow-up. Here we present Cancer PanorOmics, a web-based resource designed to provide a comprehensive, multi-layered view of personal cancer genomes. In addition, the resource maps mutations onto the human interactome to reveal their cellular context, and onto protein structures, wih quasi-atomic detail whenever available, to highlight potential functional consequences. By combining these perspectives in a single, accessible interface, Cancer PanorOmics aims to facilitate the interpretation of individual tumors and, together with appropriate genetic counselling and medical advice, to contribute to the identification of actionable alterations that can guide clinical decision-making. The notion of cancer as a singular entity has given way to a more nuanced understanding, recognizing it as a multifaceted and diverse group of disorders. At its core, cancer is driven by the gradual accumulation of alterations in the genome, which impart cells with a selective advantage, enabling unbridled proliferation, evasion of programmed cell death, and the ability to infiltrate and colonize distant tissues [1]. Over the past decade, groundbreaking advancements in our comprehension of the genomic topography of cancer have been facilitated by large-scale sequencing endeavors, notably The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC) [2, 3]. These initiatives have meticulously cataloged thousands of tumors across numerous cancer types, yielding exhaustive repositories of somatic mutations, copy number variations, gene fusions, and expression alterations. Through the analysis of these datasets, researchers have successfully identified hundreds of cancer driver genes by employing methodologies that detect signals of positive selection, such as the recurrence of mutations, bias in functional impact, or the clustering of mutations within protein sequences and structures [4, 5]. Although these analyses at the cohort level have been instrumental in elucidating the landscape of cancer genomics, they possess a significant limitation: they describe the characteristics of tumor populations, and their findings do not directly translate to the individual patient [6]. A typical tumor harbors anywhere from tens to thousands of somatic coding mutations, with only a handful, occasionally just one or none, affecting recognized driver genes [7]. The majority of these alterations are generally considered passengers, although some may represent rare drivers, modulate the effects of primary drivers, or signify unexplored therapeutic avenues [8]. Furthermore, tumors of the same histological classification frequently exhibit differences in their molecular composition, and the same gene can assume disparate roles, functioning as either an oncogene or a tumor suppressor, contingent upon the tissue context [9]. Therefore, interpreting the alterations present in a single patient necessitates situating them within the context of the tumor type, available knowledge on driver genes, and the functional and structural consequences of each variant [10]. Precision oncology seeks to address this challenge by pairing each patient with the most efficacious therapy based on the molecular characteristics of their tumor [11]. The practice of clinical sequencing, encompassing targeted gene panels to whole exomes and genomes, is becoming increasingly prevalent, and molecular tumor boards are being established in numerous hospitals [12]. Nonetheless, the translation of a list of variants into clinically relevant information remains a substantial bottleneck [13]. Several resources address aspects of this challenge, including databases such as COSMIC, cBioPortal, and the ICGC Data Portal, which provide access to mutation data and facilitate cohort-level exploration [14, 15, 16]. Additionally, resources like OncoKB, CIViC, the Cancer Genome Interpreter, and My Cancer Genome curate evidence on the oncogenic effects and clinical actionability of variants, as well as drug responses [17, 18, 19, 20]. Tools such as IntOGen compile cancer driver genes derived from large cohorts [21]. However, these resources often differ in scope, nomenclature, annotations, and whether they emphasize the cohort or the individual, necessitating clinicians and researchers to consult multiple resources and manually integrate the results, a process that is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies [22, 23]. A further limitation of current interpretation strategies is their tendency to treat genes as isolated entities, disregarding the fact that proteins function within complex networks of physical interactions [24]. The consequences of a mutation are contingent upon its cellular environment, and a mutation may disrupt a protein-protein interface, rewiring specific interactions, affect a catalytic or ligand-binding site, or destabilize the protein fold [25]. Network-based approaches have demonstrated that cancer genes tend to occupy specific positions within the interactome, and mutations in different genes can converge on the same pathways or complexes [26]. Similarly, three-dimensional structural information, whether experimentally derived or predicted through homology modeling, enables the mapping of mutations onto functional regions, pockets, and interfaces, providing mechanistic hypotheses about their impact and potential druggability [27]. Incorporating these layers into the interpretation of personal cancer genomes remains an uncommon feature in accessible tools [28]. Another significant challenge is the need for a coherent view that integrates complementary perspectives [29]. A cohort-centric view addresses questions such as the frequency of gene mutations in a tumor type, whether a gene is a recognized driver, and the typical patterns of co-occurrence and mutual exclusivity [30]. In contrast, a patient-centric view seeks to identify which mutations in a given tumor are likely to be functionally relevant, how they relate to each other in terms of pathways and interactions, and whether there is evidence of clinical actionability [31]. Bridging both views enables the comparison of an individual profile with relevant cohorts, facilitating the distinction between expected and unusual alterations and the prioritization of variants for follow-up [32]. To address these challenges, we introduce Cancer PanorOmics, a web-based resource designed to provide a comprehensive, multi-layered view of personal cancer genomes [33]. The platform integrates data and annotations for 26 tumor types, including cancer driver predictions, mutation frequencies and patterns, and clinical and scientific evidence on variants, genes, and pathways, aiming to facilitate a more nuanced understanding and treatment of cancer at the individual level. The realm of cancer therapy has witnessed significant advancements with the emergence of personalized treatment approaches, made possible by the development of comprehensive resources such as Cancer PanorOmics [34]. This platform enables users to delve into the intricacies of tumor biology at the cohort level, while also allowing for the submission of individual tumor variants to generate patient-specific reports [35]. Moreover, the tool provides a detailed mapping of mutations onto the human interactome, as well as onto protein structures, to elucidate the potential functional consequences of these genetic alterations [36]. By integrating these multiple perspectives into a single, user-friendly interface, Cancer PanorOmics aims to facilitate the interpretation of cancer genomes and support the development of tailored therapeutic strategies [37]. The interpretation of individual tumors is a complex task, necessitating a comprehensive understanding of the underlying genetic alterations that drive their growth and progression. To address this challenge, we have developed a framework that combines diverse data types and analytical approaches to identify actionable genetic alterations that can inform clinical decision-making. This framework is built upon a foundation of publicly available data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC), which provides a rich resource for exploring the genetic landscape of 26 distinct tumor types. To define our cohorts, we gathered somatic mutation, copy number, and clinical data from these public repositories, utilizing cBioPortal and the corresponding data portals to retrieve and process the data. We defined tumor types based on the primary site and histology of the cohort, and mapped variants to the GRCh37/hg19 reference genome, adjusting coordinates as necessary. For the purpose of our analysis, we focused on point mutations and short insertions/deletions in coding regions, excluding synonymous variants from driver identification but retaining them for background mutation rate estimation. To identify genes that drive cancer development, we employed a combination of complementary methods that detect signals of positive selection, including OncodriveCLUST, OncodriveFM, MutSigCV, and dNdScv-like approaches [1]. Each method was applied separately to every tumor type, and p-values were corrected for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Genes with a q-value of less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant, and results from individual methods were integrated using a rank-based combination. Genes were assigned a confidence tier based on the number of methods supporting them, and were also cross-referenced with the Cancer Gene Census and curated lists of known drivers to identify previously described cancer genes. To further classify drivers, we examined the distribution of missense and truncating mutations, annotating them as oncogenes or tumor suppressors. We also annotated variants from personal genomes, supplied as VCF or MAF files or as a list of gene/protein changes, using the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor. Annotations included consequence type, affected transcript and protein position, and functional impact was estimated using SIFT, PolyPhen-2, and the Mutation Assessor score. These scores were combined into a consensus categorization, and population frequencies from the 1000 Genomes Project and gnomAD were used to filter likely germline polymorphisms. Variants with an allele frequency above 1% were labeled as common polymorphisms. In addition to variant annotation, we also queried the recurrence of each variant in tumor cohorts and in COSMIC. Our framework provides two complementary views: a cohort-centric view, in which users select a tumor type and explore its driver genes, mutation frequencies, mutual exclusivity, and co-occurrence patterns, as well as the distribution of mutations along protein domains; and a patient-centric view, in which each mutated gene in the submitted genome is placed in the context of the selected tumor type. In this view, the system reports whether the gene is a driver in that tumor type, whether the exact variant or the same residue is recurrently mutated, and the predicted impact. Genes and variants are ranked by a score combining driver status, recurrence, functional impact, and presence in clinical evidence databases, prioritizing putative drivers over passenger events. To provide clinical and scientific evidence, we drew on a range of resources, including the Cancer Genome Interpreter catalog of validated oncogenic mutations, CIViC, OncoKB-compatible public resources, and DGIdb [2]. Evidence was classified by level (approved therapies, clinical trials, case reports, and preclinical data) and by the nature of the association (sensitivity, resistance, or prognosis). Alterations were matched to evidence at the level of the exact variant, the gene, or the mutation type, and matches were annotated by tumor type, distinguishing evidence from the same tumor type from evidence extrapolated from other tumors. Relevant literature was linked through PubMed identifiers, and drug-target relationships were retrieved from ChEMBL and DrugBank. To explore the cellular environment of mutations, we constructed a human protein-protein interaction network by integrating curated experimental interactions from BioGRID, IntAct, HPRD, and Reactome [3]. Only interactions supported by direct experimental evidence were retained, and mutated genes from a patient were mapped onto this network. First-order neighbors, shared interactors, and connected components were computed using NetworkX, and the network was annotated with driver status, mutation frequency in the tumor type, and drug targets. Over-represented pathways among the mutated genes were identified using a hypergeometric test, and the results were visualized using a network layout algorithm. By integrating these various analytical approaches, our framework provides a comprehensive platform for the interpretation of cancer genomes and the identification of actionable genetic alterations that can inform personalized cancer therapies.
