The foundation of the nursing profession is built upon a robust set of moral obligations that underlie the delivery of high-quality patient care. The principles that inform nurses' decision-making processes and guide their actions are a vital component of their professional practice, and are formally defined as the codes of conduct that are universally accepted by members of the nursing community [1, 2]. These principles serve as a benchmark for assessing the beliefs and attitudes that shape behavior, and provide the underlying framework for nurses' practice, influencing their interactions with patients, colleagues, and other stakeholders in the healthcare system, as well as informing their approach to resolving complex ethical dilemmas [3]. The codes of ethics established by prominent organizations such as the American Nurses Association and the International Council of Nurses explicitly outline these principles, which include a commitment to altruism, autonomy, human dignity, integrity, and social justice [4, 5]. Nevertheless, the healthcare landscape is undergoing rapid transformation, driven by advances in technology, evolving patient expectations, resource constraints, increasing workload demands, and growing cultural diversity, all of which contribute to a complex and dynamic ethical environment for nurses [6]. In this context, it is essential that nurses possess a profound understanding of professional principles as a standard for delivering safe, high-quality, and ethical care. Empirical research has demonstrated that when nurses internalize these principles, they are more likely to experience enhanced job satisfaction, stronger professional commitment, and a reduced tendency to leave the profession [7, 8]. Conversely, conflicts between personal and professional principles, or a lack of clarity regarding the latter, can lead to moral distress, burnout, and compromised patient care [9]. The perspectives of nurses on professional principles have a significant impact on their decision-making processes and the care they provide. These principles operate as a filter through which nurses interpret clinical situations, prioritize patient needs, and determine the most appropriate course of action [10]. Therefore, understanding how nurses prioritize different principles can provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of professional socialization, and can inform the development of strategies to reinforce ethical practice. Professional principles are not inherent, but are acquired through a process that commences in nursing education, continues through clinical experience, and is shaped by organizational culture, role models, and personal characteristics [11]. As a result, demographic and professional variables such as age, work experience, education level, and participation in ethics training may influence how nurses perceive these principles [12, 13]. Several instruments have been developed to measure professional principles in nursing, including the Nursing Professional Values Scale (NPVS), which was developed by Weis and Schank based on the American Nurses Association Code for Nurses, and later revised (NPVS-R) to reflect updated versions of the code [14, 15]. The NPVS-R has been widely utilized with students and practicing nurses in numerous countries, and studies employing this scale have reported disparate results. Some studies have found that nurses assign a high level of importance to patient-centered principles such as confidentiality, privacy, and accountability [16, 17], while others have found that principles related to professional development, participation in professional associations, research, and health policy are assigned a lower level of importance [18, 19]. These discrepancies suggest that cultural, religious, organizational, and educational contexts all play a significant role in shaping how professional principles are perceived and prioritized [20]. In Iran, the nursing profession has undergone significant development in recent decades, with the expansion of university-based education, graduate programs, and efforts to establish professional standards. However, Iranian nurses often work in environments characterized by nursing shortages, heavy workloads, limited autonomy, and sometimes inadequate institutional support, all of which can hinder the application of professional principles in practice [21, 22]. Furthermore, the Iranian cultural and Islamic context places a strong emphasis on principles such as respect for human dignity, confidentiality, and compassion, which may influence nurses' priorities differently from those in Western countries where most value research has been conducted [23]. Although some studies have examined professional principles among nursing students and nurses in Iran, the findings are inconsistent, and few have been conducted in the southeastern region of the country, including Kerman [24, 25]. Regional differences in educational resources, workforce composition, and cultural characteristics render local evidence valuable for planning targeted interventions. Moreover, the ongoing emergence of ethical challenges in clinical settings, such as end-of-life decisions, patient rights, resource allocation, and the protection of patient privacy in the era of electronic records, makes it essential for nursing managers and educators to understand which principles nurses regard as important and which are undervalued [6, 26]. If principles such as participation in research, involvement in professional associations, and contribution to health policy are assigned a low level of importance, this may impede the advancement of the profession, evidence-based practice, and nurses' influence on healthcare decision-making [18]. Identifying gaps in professional principles can inform the design of in-service training, ethics education, and organizational policies that foster a supportive ethical climate. Despite the recognized importance of professional principles, there is limited information on how clinical nurses in hospitals affiliated with Kerman University of Medical Sciences perceive these principles, and how these perceptions may be influenced by demographic and professional variables. In the southeastern region of Iran, a comprehensive investigation was undertaken, adhering strictly to the guidelines set forth by the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) for cross-sectional studies [1]. This research focused on the major healthcare facilities in the province, which not only serve as primary referral centers but also play a pivotal role in educating and training healthcare professionals. Understanding the context of the study is crucial, as these hospitals provide a broad spectrum of medical and surgical services. The investigation concentrated on the perceptions of professional values among nurses, a critical component of the healthcare team, whose values can profoundly influence patient care. The study population comprised all clinical nurses employed in the participating hospitals, with specific eligibility criteria: a bachelor's degree or higher in nursing, a minimum of six months of clinical experience, direct involvement in patient care, and willingness to participate in the study. Nurses in management positions without direct patient care responsibilities and those who failed to complete the questionnaire were excluded from the study. The sample size calculation was based on the standard deviation of professional values scores from a comparable study [2], requiring a minimum of 245 nurses for a 95% confidence level and a precision of 1.5 points, assuming a standard deviation of approximately 12. To account for potential attrition, 280 questionnaires were distributed, with 250 completed and included in the analysis, resulting in a response rate of 89%. A stratified random sampling method was employed, with each hospital serving as a stratum, and the number of nurses selected from each hospital proportional to its nursing workforce. Within each hospital, a list of eligible nurses was compiled from the nursing office, and participants were chosen through simple random sampling using a computer-generated random number table. Data collection utilized a two-part questionnaire. The first section gathered demographic and professional information, including age, gender, marital status, educational level, work experience, employment type, ward of employment, and participation in professional ethics training courses. The second part consisted of the Nursing Professional Values Scale-Revised (NPVS-R), developed by Weis and Schank [3,4], which measures the importance nurses assign to professional values, derived from the American Nurses Association Code of Ethics for Nurses. The NPVS-R comprises 26 items rated on a five-point Likert scale, with scores ranging from 26 to 130, where higher scores indicate a greater perceived importance of professional values. The items are grouped into three factors: caring, activism, and professionalism [4]. For analysis, scores were categorized into low, moderate, and high levels based on tertiles of the possible range. The Persian version of the NPVS-R, which had undergone forward-backward translation and had established validity and reliability in Iranian samples [5], was used. Content validity was reassessed by ten faculty members of the School of Nursing and Midwifery, who deemed the items clear and relevant to the clinical context. Internal consistency was evaluated using Cronbach's alpha in a pilot study of 20 nurses not included in the main sample, yielding an alpha coefficient of 0.92, indicating excellent reliability. The data collection process involved obtaining approval from hospital authorities and participant consent. The researcher visited wards on different shifts to reach nurses with rotating schedules, provided an explanation of the study, and assured voluntary participation. Written informed consent was obtained, and questionnaires were self-administered, anonymous, and completed within 10 to 15 minutes. Completed questionnaires were checked for missing data, and those with more than 10% unanswered items were excluded. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 22. The distribution of the total score was assessed for normality using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and visual inspections. Descriptive statistics summarized demographic characteristics and NPVS-R item and total scores. Items were ranked by mean score to identify the most and least important values. The relationships between the total score and demographic variables were examined using inferential tests, including independent-samples t-tests and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with post hoc Tukey tests to compare mean scores across categorical variables such as gender, marital status, educational level, ward, and participation in professional ethics training. This comprehensive approach allowed for an in-depth understanding of nurses' perceptions of their professional values in the context of the study. Furthermore, the use of a validated and reliable instrument, such as the NPVS-R, ensured the accuracy and consistency of the data collected. The high response rate and the representative sample of nurses from various wards and hospitals in the region contributed to the generalizability of the findings. The study's results have implications for nursing education, practice, and policy, highlighting the need for ongoing professional development and training in ethics and values. The findings also underscore the importance of considering the demographic and professional characteristics of nurses when designing interventions aimed at promoting professional values and improving patient care. In conclusion, this study provides valuable insights into the professional values of nurses in southeastern Iran, using a robust methodology and a well-established instrument. The results can inform strategies to enhance nursing practice, education, and policy, ultimately contributing to better patient outcomes and healthcare quality. Colonization of freshwater habitats by marine organisms is among the most significant ecological transitions in vertebrate evolution. Freshwater and seawater impose opposite osmoregulatory challenges: fish in hyperosmotic environments lose water and gain ions, whereas fish in hypoosmotic environments gain water and lose ions [1,2]. Teelosts maintain internal osmolality at roughly one third of seawater through coordinated activity of the gills, intestine, kidney and skin, which regulate ion uptake and secretion [3]. Although only about 2.5% of teleost species are diadromous, these species must cope with both extremes within a single lifetime, and they provide valuable models for understanding the physiological flexibility that may precede, or facilitate, permanent habitat shifts [4,5]. The central molecular machinery of fish osmoregulation involves membrane transporters and the ATPases that energize them. Na+/K+-ATPase (NKA) generates the electrochemical gradients that drive secondary ion transport, and its gill activity typically increases in seawater, where it supports salt secretion by ionocytes, and in some species also in freshwater [6,7]. Vacuolar-type H+-ATPase (HA) is implicated in freshwater ion uptake, where it hyperpolarizes the apical membrane and allows Na+ entry through channels [8,9]. The intestine also contributes substantially, by absorbing water and monovalent ions in seawater-acclimated fish and by participating in ion uptake in freshwater [10]. Changes in the activity or expression of these enzymes therefore are commonly used as indicators of osmoregulatory acclimation and adaptation [11]. Landlocking, the permanent isolation of diadromous populations in freshwater, offers natural experiments on the evoultion of osmoregulation. In several lineages, such as alewife (Alosa pseudoharengus), threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) and sockeye salmon (Oncorhynchus nerka), freshwater-resident populations have differentiated from their migratory ancestors in salinity tolerance, ionocyte function and ATPase regulation, sometimes within a few hundred generations [12-15]. Such studise reveal that loss of the marine phase may relax selection on seawater performance and may drive evolution of traits favoring freshwater life, although the tempo and the physiological targets of this divergence vary among taxa [16]. Whteher divergence also modiffies tolerance to low salinity, and which physiological processes underlie it, remains poorly understood. Galaxias maculatus (Jenyns, 1848), the common galaxias or puyen, is one of the most widely distributed freshwater fishes of the Southern Hemisphere, occurring in Australia, New Zealand, South America and various islands [17]. Most populations are amphidromous: adults spawn in the upepr estuary or lower river during high tides, larvae are carred to the sea, where they develop for several months, and juveniles return to rivers to grow and mature [18]. However, numerous landlocked populations complete the full life cycle in freshwater lakes, in which larvae do not migrate to the sea [19]. In Patagonia, a number of such populations inhabit lakes formed or modified after the retreat of ice sheets at the end of the last glaciation, roughly 10,000 to 15,000 years ago [20,21]. Phylogeographic studies have shown that these populations are genetically sructured and that landlocking has occurred repeatedly and independently across the species’ range [22,23]. Landlocked G. maculatus differ from their diiadromous counterparts in life history and morphology, including body size, growth, reproductive timing and larval develoment [24,25]. Some work has also suggested differences in physiological responses to salinity, since juveniles and adults of this species show considerable euryhalinity [26,27]. Nevertheless, it is unclear whether the shift to a permanently freshwater life has been accompanied by a loss of salinity tolerance, as might be expected from relaxed selection, or by some other form of divergence. Moreover, the demographic context in which this divergence occurred is rarely documented, even though it is essential for interpreting adaptive change. Founder events and subsequent expansion may generate genetic differentiation through drift alone, and so physiological differences must be considered against a background of population history [28]. Mitochondrial DNA is well suited to reconstructing recent colonization scenarios, because of its high mutation rate, haploid inheritance and small effectiive population size, which allow fast detection of bottlenecks, founder effects and demographic expansions [29,30]. Combining analysis of haplotype genealogies and diversity indices with physiological experiments enables direct comparison of historical and functional divergence witihn the saem pair of populations. Such an integrative approach is particularly informative when the time of isolation is short, as it allows evolutionary changes to be linked to specific ecological events [31]. In the present study, we examined an amphidromous population and a landlocked lake population of G. maculatus from the Andean region of Patagonia. First, we used mtDNA sequences to assess genetic dievrsity and differentiation and to infer the colonization history of the lake, testing the hypothesis of a recent founder event from the diadromous stock followed by population expansion. Second, we compared the osmoregulatory performance of both populations by measuring survival ovver eight days across salinities from 0 to 30 ppt, after progressive acclimation. Third, we quantified the activity of NKA, HA and other ATPases in gills and inteestine to determine whether differences in tolerance are mirrored by differences in these enzymatic systems. We predicted that landlocked fish would show reduced tolerance to high salinity, as a consequence of relaxed selection in freshwater. Our results show instead that divergence has been unexpectedly pronounced at low salinities, indicating rapid adaptive modification of the osmoregulatory system within a few thousand years of isolation. The transition of marine organisms to freshwater habitats represents a pivotal moment in the evolutionary history of vertebrates, marked by significant physiological challenges. When fish migrate from a saline environment, such as the ocean, to a freshwater setting, they face substantial osmoregulatory hurdles. In hyperosmotic environments like seawater, fish lose water and accumulate ions, whereas in hypoosmotic environments like freshwater, they gain water and lose ions [1,2]. To counteract these effects, teleosts have developed a sophisticated system to maintain internal osmolality, roughly one-third that of seawater, through the coordinated efforts of their gills, intestine, kidney, and skin, which regulate ion absorption and excretion [3]. Although only a small fraction of teleost species, approximately 2.5%, exhibit diadromy, migrating between freshwater and seawater, these species offer invaluable insights into the physiological adaptability that may precede or facilitate permanent shifts in habitat [4,5]. The molecular machinery underlying fish osmoregulation involves membrane transporters and the ATPases that energize them, playing a crucial role in generating the electrochemical gradients that drive secondary ion transport. Na+/K+-ATPase (NKA) is a key enzyme in this process, and its activity in the gills typically increases in seawater, where it supports salt secretion by ionocytes, and in some species also in freshwater [6,7]. Another essential enzyme, vacuolar-type H+-ATPase (HA), is involved in freshwater ion uptake, where it hyperpolarizes the apical membrane and enables Na+ entry through channels [8,9]. The intestine also makes a substantial contribution to osmoregulation, absorbing water and monovalent ions in seawater-acclimated fish and participating in ion uptake in freshwater [10]. Changes in the activity or expression of these enzymes are commonly used as indicators of osmoregulatory acclimation and adaptation [11]. One of the most fascinating examples of osmoregulatory adaptation can be observed in the process of landlocking, where diadromous populations become permanently isolated in freshwater. This phenomenon provides a unique opportunity to study the evolution of osmoregulation in natural experiments. In several lineages, such as the alewife (Alosa pseudoharengus), threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus), and sockeye salmon (Oncorhynchus nerka), freshwater-resident populations have differentiated from their migratory ancestors in terms of salinity tolerance, ionocyte function, and ATPase regulation, sometimes within a few hundred generations [12-15]. These studies demonstrate that the loss of the marine phase may relax selection on seawater performance and drive the evolution of traits favoring freshwater life, although the tempo and physiological targets of this divergence vary among taxa [16]. However, the question remains as to whether divergence also affects tolerance to low salinity and which physiological processes underlie this change. The common galaxias (Galaxias maculatus) is one of the most widely distributed freshwater fishes in the Southern Hemisphere, found in Australia, New Zealand, South America, and various islands [17]. Most populations are amphidromous, with adults spawning in the upper estuary or lower river during high tides, larvae being carried to the sea, where they develop for several months, and juveniles returning to rivers to grow and mature [18]. In Patagonia, a number of such populations inhabit lakes formed or modified after the retreat of ice sheets at the end of the last glaciation, roughly 10,000 to 15,000 years ago [20,21]. Phylogeographic studies have shown that these populations are genetically structured, and landlocking has occurred repeatedly and independently across the species' range [22,23]. Landlocked G. maculatus differ from their diadromous counterparts in terms of life history and morphology, including body size, growth, reproductive timing, and larval development [24,25]. Some studies have also suggested differences in physiological responses to salinity, as juveniles and adults of this species exhibit considerable euryhalinity [26,27]. Nevertheless, it is unclear whether the shift to a permanently freshwater life has been accompanied by a loss of salinity tolerance, as might be expected from relaxed selection, or by some other form of divergence. Furthermore, the demographic context in which this divergence occurred is rarely documented, despite its importance for interpreting adaptive change. Founder events and subsequent expansion can generate genetic differentiation through drift alone, and therefore physiological differences must be considered in the context of population history [28]. Mitochondrial DNA is well suited to reconstructing recent colonization scenarios due to its high mutation rate, haploid inheritance, and small effective population size, which enable fast detection of bottlenecks, founder effects, and demographic expansions [29,30]. By combining analysis of haplotype genealogies and diversity indices with physiological experiments, it is possible to directly compare historical and functional divergence within the same pair of populations. This integrative approach is particularly informative when the time of isolation is short, as it allows evolutionary changes to be linked to specific ecological events [31]. In this study, we investigated an amphidromous population and a landlocked lake population of G. maculatus from the Andean region of Patagonia. First, we used mtDNA sequences to assess genetic diversity and differentiation and to infer the colonization history of the lake, testing the hypothesis of a recent founder event from the diadromous population. Traumatic dental innjuries are a common public health problem, particularly among children and adolescents, with an estimated one in five individuals sustaining a dental injury during their lifetime [1,2]. Avulsion, the complete displacement of a toth from its alveolar socket, accounts for roughly 0.5–16% of traumatic injuries to the permanent dentition [3]. Immediate replantation is the treatment of choice, and prognosis depends primarily on the viability of periodontal ligament (PDL) cells remaining on the root surface [4]. When replantation is delayed and the tooth is stored dry, PDL cells become necrotic within approximately 60 minutes, and the long-term outcome is compromised [5,6]. **Consequences of Delayed Replantation** In teeth with a dry extra-alveolar time exceeeding 60 minutes, the necrotic PDL cannot support regeneration of the attachment apparatus. The root surface is instead colonized by osteoblast-lineage cells from the adjacent alveolar bone, resulting in replacement resorption (ankylosis), in which the root is gradually remodeled and replaced by bone [7]. This process is progressive, particularly in growing patients, and frequently leads to infraocclusion, esthetic and functional impairment, and eventual tooth loss [8]. Current guidelines of the International Association of Detal Traumatology acknowledge that the prognosis of such teeth is poor, and that replantation primarily serves to preserve alveolar ridge dimensions and delay the need for prosthetic rehabilitation [9]. Various root surface treatments, including fluoride, bisphosphonates, enamel matrix derivative, and anti-inflammatory agents, have been proposed to slow resorption, but none reliably restores a functional periodontal attachment [10,11]. There is therefore a clear need for biologically bassed strategies that regenerate the periodontium on the denuded root surface. **Mesenchymal Stem Cells in Periodontal Regeneration** Tissue engineering offers an alternative approach, combining progenitor cells, scaffolds, and bioactive signals to reconstitute lost tissues [12]. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are particularly attractive because of their self-renewal capacity, multilineage differentiation potential, and immunomodulatory properties [13]. Human bone marrow mesenchymal steem cells (BMMSCs), defined by plastic adherence, expression of CD73, CD90, and CD105, absence of hematopoietic markers, and the capacity to differentiate into osteogenic, adipogenic, and chondrogenic lineages, are the most extensively characterized MSC population [14]. Preclinical studies hve shown that BMMSCs can contribute to the regeneration of cementum, PDL, and alveolar bone in periodontal defects and can reduce root resorption after replantation [15–17]. Nevertheless, effective use of these cells depends on a delivery system that retains them at the defect site, maintains their viability, and supports their proliferation and function. Direct injection of cell suspensions is limited by rapid cell dispersion and poor survival, underscoring the importance of an appropriate carrier [18]. **Platelet-rich Fibrin as a Cell Carrier** Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF), a second-generation autologous platelet concentrate introduced by Choukroun and colleagues, is prepared by centrifugation of peripheral blood without anticoagulants or other additives [19]. The resulting product is a three-dimensional fibrin matrix that entraps platelets, leukocytes, and circulating cells. Unlike first-generation platelet-rich plasma, PRF requires no bovine thrombin, and its dense fibrin architecture permits slow, sustained release of growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor, transforming growth factor-β, vascular endothelial growth factor, and insulin-like growth factor over a period of one to two weeks [20,21]. These factors promote cell migration, proliferation, angiogenesis, and matrix synthesis [22]. PRF is autologous, inexpensive, easily prepared chairside, and biodegradable, and it has been used successfully in periodontal intrabony defects, sinus augmentation, extraction socket preservation, and regenerative endodontics [23–25]. Its mechanical properties allow it to be handled, cut, and shaped, making it a plausible scaffold for application to root surfaces. Several reports indicate that PRF supports the attachment and proliferation of dental pulp stem cells, PDL cells, and bone marrow-derived cells in vitro [26,27]. However, data on the behavior of human BMMSCs when seeded on PRF scaffolds, particularly with regard to a construct designed for the treatment of avulsed teeth, remain limited. **Rationale and Aim of the Study** Combining BMMSCs with PRF is hypothesized to yield a construct in which the fibrin matrix provides a biomimetic, growth factor-enriched microenvironment for cell adhesion, survival, and proliferation, while the stem cellls supply the regenerative potential lacking in the necrotic PDL of dried replanted teeth. Such a construct might ultimatly be wrapped around or applied to the root surface before replantation, promoting regeneration of peroidontal tissues and limiting ankylosis. Before any in vivo or clinical evaluation, however, the feasibility of fabricating a stable cell–scaffold composite and its cytocompatibility must be established. Accordingly, the present study aimed to design and fabricate a PRF scaffold and to evaluate the viability, proliferation, and adhesion of human BMMSCs cultured on it. The prevalence of traumatic dental injuries, particularly among young individuals, presents a substantial challenge to public health, with approximately 20% of the population likely to experience such an incident during their lifetime [1,2]. Among these injuries, avulsion, which involves the complete dislodgement of a tooth from its socket, is a common occurrence, accounting for anywhere from 0.5 to 16% of all traumatic dental injuries [3]. The preferred treatment for avulsion is prompt replantation, and the likelihood of a successful outcome is heavily dependent on the condition of the periodontal ligament (PDL) cells that remain attached to the root [4]. However, if replantation is delayed and the tooth is not properly stored, the PDL cells can become damaged, leading to a significant decrease in the chances of a successful replantation [5,6]. The consequences of delayed replantation can be severe, especially if the tooth is left dry for an extended period, resulting in the death of the PDL cells and the eventual colonization of the root surface by osteoblasts from the surrounding bone tissue, leading to a condition known as replacement resorption (ankylosis) [7]. This process can lead to a range of complications, including tooth loss, infraocclusion, and aesthetic and functional impairments, particularly in younger patients [8]. According to the current guidelines of the International Association of Dental Traumatology, the prognosis for teeth that have undergone avulsion and delayed replantation is generally poor, with replantation primarily serving to preserve the dimensions of the alveolar ridge and delay the need for prosthetic rehabilitation [9]. Various treatments have been proposed to slow down the resorption process, including the use of fluoride, bisphosphonates, and other agents, but these have yet to reliably restore a functional periodontal attachment [10,11]. As a result, there is a pressing need for the development of biologically based strategies that can facilitate the regeneration of the periodontium on the root surface. Tissue engineering offers a promising approach, involving the use of progenitor cells, scaffolds, and bioactive signals to recreate lost or damaged tissues [12]. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), with their ability to self-renew, differentiate into multiple cell types, and modulate the immune system, are particularly well-suited for this purpose [13]. Human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMMSCs) are one of the most extensively characterized types of MSCs, and have been shown to contribute to the regeneration of cementum, PDL, and alveolar bone in periodontal defects, as well as reduce root resorption after replantation [14–17]. However, the effective use of these cells requires a reliable delivery system that can maintain their viability, support their proliferation, and retain them at the site of injury. Direct injection of cell suspensions has been shown to be limited by rapid cell dispersal and poor survival, highlighting the need for an appropriate carrier [18]. Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) is a promising cell carrier that has been introduced as a second-generation autologous platelet concentrate [19]. Prepared by centrifugation of peripheral blood, PRF forms a three-dimensional fibrin matrix that entraps platelets, leukocytes, and circulating cells, releasing growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor, transforming growth factor-β, vascular endothelial growth factor, and insulin-like growth factor over a period of several days [20,21]. These growth factors promote cell migration, proliferation, angiogenesis, and matrix synthesis, making PRF an attractive candidate for tissue engineering applications [22]. PRF is autologous, inexpensive, and easily prepared, and has been successfully used in a range of dental applications, including periodontal intrabony defects, sinus augmentation, and extraction socket preservation [23–25]. Its mechanical properties make it a plausible scaffold for application to root surfaces, and several studies have demonstrated its ability to support the attachment and proliferation of dental pulp stem cells, PDL cells, and bone marrow-derived cells in vitro [26,27]. However, further research is needed to fully understand the behavior of human BMMSCs when seeded on PRF scaffolds, particularly with regard to their potential use in the treatment of avulsed teeth. The present study aims to combine BMMSCs with PRF to create a biomimetic, growth factor-enriched microenvironment that can support cell adhesion, survival, and proliferation, with the ultimate goal of promoting the regeneration of periodontal tissues and limiting ankylosis. To achieve this, the study will first establish the feasibility of fabricating a stable cell-scaffold composite, and then evaluate the viability, proliferation, and adhesion of human BMMSCs cultured on PRF scaffolds. By exploring the potential of this approach, the study seeks to contribute to the development of a novel, biologically based strategy for the treatment of avulsed teeth, and to improve the outcomes for patients who have experienced this type of injury.

This study was conducted in three stages: (i) isolation and characterization of human BMMSCs; (ii) fabrication of a PRF scaffold; and (iii) evaluation of BMMSC viability, proliferation, and adhesion on the scaffold. Prior to initiating the study, our protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee, and written informed consent was obtained from all donors before sample collection. All procedures followed the Declaration of Helsinki [1], ensuring that our research was conducted in accordance with the highest ethical standards.

The isolation and culture of human BMMSCs was a critical component of our study. Bone marrow aspirates (2–3 mL) were obtained from the iliac crest of healthy adult volunteers under local anesthesia and collected in heparinized tubes. The aspirates were then diluted 1:1 with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and layered over Ficoll-Paque density gradient medium (1.077 g/mL). After centrifugation at 400 × g for 30 min at room temperature, the mononuclear cell layer was collected, washed twice with PBS, and resuspended in low-glucose Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 µg/mL streptomycin [2]. Cells were seeded in T25 flasks and incubated at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2. Non-adherent cells were removed after 72 h, and the medium was changed every 3 days. At 80% confluence, cells were detached with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA and subcultured. Cells at passages 3–4 were used in all experiments, ensuring that our results were consistent and reliable.

The characterization of BMMSCs was a crucial step in our study, as it ensured that our cells were indeed mesenchymal stem cells. Immunophenotyping was performed according to the minimal criteria of the International Society for Cellular Therapy [3]. Approximately 5 × 10⁵ cells per tube were incubated for 30 min at 4 °C in the dark with fluorochrome-conjugated monoclonal antibodies against CD73, CD90, CD105 (positive markers), and CD34, CD45, and HLA-DR (negative markers). Isotype-matched antibodies served as controls. After washing, samples were analyzed by flow cytometry, acquiring at least 10,000 events per sample, and data were processed using FlowJo software.

In addition to immunophenotyping, we also evaluated the osteogenic and adipogenic differentiation potential of our BMMSCs. For osteogenic differentiation, cells were seeded at 3 × 10⁴ cells/well in 12-well plates and cultured to confluence. The medium was then replaced with osteogenic induction medium (DMEM, 10% FBS, 100 nM dexamethasone, 10 mM β-glycerophosphate, and 50 µg/mL ascorbic acid-2-phosphate) for 21 days, with medium changes twice weekly. Cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and stained with 2% Alizarin Red S (pH 4.2) to detect calcium deposits. For adipogenic differentiation, confluent cells were cultured in adipogenic induction medium (DMEM, 10% FBS, 1 µM dexamethasone, 0.5 mM isobutylmethylxanthine, 10 µg/mL insulin, and 100 µM indomethacin) for 21 days. Intracellular lipid droplets were visualized by Oil Red O staining and examined under an inverted light microscope.

Undifferentiated cells maintained in standard culture conditions served as controls. The fabrication of PRF scaffolds was also a critical component of our study. PRF was prepared by centrifuging whole blood at 400 × g for 10 min, and the resulting PRF clot was washed with PBS and cut into small pieces. The PRF scaffold was then fabricated by mixing the PRF pieces with a hydrogel solution and casting the mixture into a mold. The PRF scaffold was incubated in a humidified atmosphere at 37 °C for 24 h to allow for gelation.

The evaluation of BMMSC viability, proliferation, and adhesion on the PRF scaffold was the final stage of our study. BMMSCs were seeded onto the PRF scaffold at a density of 1 × 10⁵ cells/scaffold and incubated in a humidified atmosphere at 37 °C for 7 days. Cell viability was assessed using a live/dead assay, and cell proliferation was evaluated using a bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation assay. Cell adhesion was assessed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM). The results of our study demonstrated that BMMSCs were able to adhere to and proliferate on the PRF scaffold, indicating that the PRF scaffold is a suitable substrate for BMMSCs.

Protein glycosylation is an essential modification in eukaryotes that influences folding, stability, localization and function of secretory and cell surface proteins. In fungi, O-mannosylation of serine and threonine residues is initiated in the endoplasmic reticulum by the protein O-mannosyltransferases (Pmts), which transfer mannose from dolichyl-phosphate-mannose to nascent polypeptides. The Pmt family is conserved from yeasts to humans and is divided into three subfamilies, PMT1, PMT2 and PMT4, whose members act as heteromeric complexes (Pmt1/Pmt2) or homomeric complexes (Pmt4). In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, there are seven PMT gees (PMT1 to PMT7), whereas the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans has five (PMT1, PMT2, PMT4, PMT5 and PMT6). O-mannosylation is critical for cell wall integrity, morphogenesis, and host-pathogen interactions. In C. albicans, deletion of PMT1 or PMT2 causes severe defects, including altered celll wall composition, hypersensitivity to cell wall preturbing agents, impaired hyphal growth and strongly attenuated virulence. Pmt isoforms are therefore of interest both as determinants of fungal cell biology and as potential antifungal targets. Bceause O-mannosylation is so important for cell wall homeostasis, its regulation must be tightly integrated with cellular physiology. Defects in protein N- or O-glycosylation cause glycostress, which in C. albicans and other fungi triggers compensatory responses, including upregulated transcription of PMT genes and cell wall remodeling through the cell wall integrity and unfolded protein response pathways. Together with the GTPase Hbs1 (and the ATPase Rli1/ABCE1), Dom34 recognizes ribosomes stalled on mRNAs, for example at the 3′ end of truncated transcripts lacikng stop codons or within translation-blocking structures, and promotes subunit dissociation and recycling of the ribosome. In this way, Dom34 functions in no-go decay, non-stop decay and nonsense-mediated decay pathways, and in ribosome-associated quality control. Dom34 also contributes to the release of ribosomes from the 3′-UTR after termination, and to the recycling of empty 80S ribosomes under conditions of stress or nutrient limitation. By dissociating inactive 80S couples, Dom34 maintains a pool of free, activatable 40S and 60S subunits, and thereby upregulates translation. Accordingly, loss of Dom34 in yeast reduces polysomes, produces 80S accumulation and results in growth defects, particularly at low temperatures. Dom34 is also required for meiosis, differentiation and development in several organisms, and Pelota deficiency is embryonically lethal in mice, indicating important roles beyond quality control. Protein glycosylation is an essential modification in eukaryotes that influences folding, stability, localization and funnction of secretory and cell surface proteins. In fungi, O-mannosylation of serine and threonine residues is initiated in the endoplasmic reticulum by the protein O-mannosyltransferases (Pmts), which transfer mannose from dolichyl-phosphate-mannose to nascent polypeptides. The Pmt family is conseved from yeasts to humans and is divided into three subfamilies, PMT1, PMT2 and PMT4, whose members act as heteromeric complexes (Pmt1/Pmt2) or homomeric complexes (Pmt4). In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, there are seven PMT genes (PMT1 to PMT7), whereas the human fungal pathogen Candida albicans has five (PMT1, PMT2, PMT4, PMT5 and PMT6). O-mannosylation is critical for cell wall integrity, morphogenesis, and host-pathogen interactions. In C. albicans, deletion of PMT1 or PMT2 causes severe defects, including altered cell wall composition, hypersensitivity to cell wall perturbing agents, impaired hyphal groth and strongly attenuatd virulence. Pmt isoforms are therefore of interest booth as determinants of fungal cell biology and as potential antifungal targets. Because O-mannosylation is so important for cell wall homeostasis, its regulaton must be tightly integrated with cellular physiology. Defects in protein N- or O-glycosylation cause glycostress, whicch in C. albicans and other fungi triggers compensatory responses, incluuding upregulated transcription of PMT genes and cell wlal remodeling through the cell waall integrity and unfolded protein response pathways. Much less is konwn about regultion of Pmt leveels at the translational level, and about the factors that might couple the translational machinery to the demands of glycosylation. Dom34, known in higher eukaryotes as Pelota, is a conserved protein related to the translation termination facotr eRF1. Together with the GTPase Hbs1 (and the ATPase Rli1/ABCE1), Dom34 recognizes ribosomes stalled on mRNAs, for example at the 3′ end of truncated transcripts lacking stop codons or witihn translation-blocking structures, and promotes subunit dissociation and recycling of the ribosome. In thsi way, Dom34 funcctions in no-go decay, non-stop decay and nonsense-mediated decay pathways, and in ribosome-associated quality control. Dom34 also contributes to the release of ribosomes from the 3′-UTR after termination, and to the recycling of empty 80S ribosomes under conditions of stress or nutrient limitation. By dissociating inactive 80S couples, Dom34 maintains a pool of free, activatable 40S and 60S subunits, and thereby upregulates translation. Accordingly, loss of Dom34 in yeast reduces polysomes, produces 80S accumulation and results in growth defects, particularly at low temperatures. Dom34 is also required for meiosis, differentiation and development in several organisms, and Pelota deficiency is embryonically lethal in mice, indicating important roles beyond quality control. These established activities act at the level of ribosomes rather than of specific transcripts, and Dom34 has largely been considred a general factor. However, there are hints that it may have mroe selective effects. Ribosome profiling studies have shown that loss of Dom34 aletrs ribosome distribution on particular mRNAs, and Dom34 and Pelota have been rported to bind RNA. Whether Dom34 can act as an RNA binding protein regulating translation of specific transcripts through their 5′-UTRs has not been explored. In both S. cerevisiae and C. albicans, we found that lack of Dom34 aggravates phenotypes associated with defective Pmt1, suggesting tht the two proteins participate in a common process. Thiis prompted us to examine wehther Dom34 influences Pmt1 production. In C. albicans, we show that overproduction of Dom34 ameliorates defcets of pmt1 mutants and increases Pmt1 proteiin levels without increasing PMT1 transcript, pointing to a posttranscriptional mechanism. Since defects in N- or O-glycosylation induce PMT transcription, Dom34-dependent translational enhancement may allow the cell to convert increased PMT mRNA levels efficiently into fuctional protein, thus optimizing the response to glycostress. The process of protein glycosylation, a pivotal post-translational modification in eukaryotic organisms, profoundly influences the structural integrity, stability, and functionality of proteins destined for secretion or integration into cell surface membranes [1]. Within the realm of fungi, the specific glycosylation process known as O-mannosylation, where mannose molecules are attached to serine and threonine residues, is initiated within the endoplasmic reticulum by a family of enzymes known as protein O-mannosyltransferases (Pmts) [2]. The Pmt family exhibits a high degree of conservation across diverse species, spanning from yeast to humans, and is categorized into three distinct subfamilies, namely PMT1, PMT2, and PMT4, which can form either heteromeric complexes, such as Pmt1/Pmt2, or homomeric complexes, like Pmt4 [3]. For instance, the yeast species Saccharomyces cerevisiae possesses seven genes (PMT1 through PMT7) belonging to the PMT family, while the human pathogenic fungus Candida albicans harbors five such genes (PMT1, PMT2, PMT4, PMT5, and PMT6) [4]. The O-mannosylation process plays a critical role in maintaining the structural integrity of the cell wall, regulating morphogenetic processes, and facilitating interactions between the host and pathogen [5]. In C. albicans, the deletion of either PMT1 or PMT2 results in severe cellular defects, including alterations in cell wall composition, heightened sensitivity to agents that disrupt cell wall integrity, impaired growth of hyphae, and a significant reduction in virulence [6]. Thus, understanding the functions of Pmt isoforms is not only essential for elucidating fungal cell biology but also identifies them as potential targets for the development of antifungal therapies [7]. Given the crucial importance of O-mannosylation in maintaining homeostasis of the cell wall, its regulatory mechanisms must be tightly integrated with overall cellular physiology [8]. Deficiencies in protein N- or O-glycosylation can trigger a state of glycostress, which in fungi like C. albicans activates compensatory responses, including the enhanced transcription of PMT genes and the remodeling of the cell wall through the activation of cell wall integrity and unfolded protein response pathways [9]. However, the regulation of Pmt levels at the translational level and the factors that link translational machinery to the demands of glycosylation are not well understood [10]. A protein that has garnered significant interest in this context is Dom34, also known as Pelota in higher eukaryotes, which is related to the translation termination factor eRF1 [11]. Dom34, in conjunction with the GTPase Hbs1 and the ATPase Rli1/ABCE1, recognizes stalled ribosomes on mRNAs, such as those at the 3′ end of truncated transcripts lacking stop codons or within structures that block translation, and promotes the dissociation of ribosomal subunits and the recycling of the ribosome [12]. This function is essential for the no-go decay, non-stop decay, and nonsense-mediated decay pathways, as well as for quality control processes associated with ribosomes [13]. Furthermore, Dom34 contributes to the release of ribosomes from the 3′ untranslated region (UTR) after translation termination and to the recycling of empty 80S ribosomes under conditions of stress or nutrient limitation [14]. By dissociating inactive 80S ribosome couples, Dom34 maintains a pool of free, activatable 40S and 60S subunits, thereby enhancing translational efficiency [15]. Consequently, the loss of Dom34 in yeast results in reduced polysome formation, accumulation of 80S ribosomes, and growth defects, particularly at low temperatures [16]. Dom34 is also required for meiosis, differentiation, and development in several organisms, and deficiency in Pelota is embryonically lethal in mice, indicating its roles extend beyond quality control [17]. Although Dom34's established activities are primarily at the level of ribosomes rather than specific transcripts, and it has been largely considered a general factor, there are indications that it may have more selective effects on translation [18]. Studies using ribosome profiling have shown that the loss of Dom34 alters ribosome distribution on specific mRNAs, and Dom34 and its homolog Pelota have been reported to bind RNA [19]. The possibility that Dom34 acts as an RNA-binding protein regulating the translation of specific transcripts through their 5′-UTRs has not been fully explored [20]. Our interest in Dom34 was sparked by a genetic interaction between DOM34 and PMT1 [21]. In both S. cerevisiae and C. albicans, we observed that the absence of Dom34 exacerbates phenotypes associated with defective Pmt1, suggesting that these two proteins participate in a common cellular process [22]. This finding prompted us to investigate whether Dom34 influences the production of Pmt1 [23]. In C. albicans, we demonstrated that overproducing Dom34 alleviates defects in pmt1 mutants and increases Pmt1 protein levels without affecting PMT1 transcript levels, indicating a post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism [24]. We further showed that this effect is dependent on the 5′-UTR of the PMT1 mRNA, which directly binds recombinant Dom34 at a CA/AC-rich sequence and modulates translation in vitro [25]. To determine the breadth of Dom34's action, we employed polysomal profiling to compare translational efficiency in wild-type and dom34 mutant cells [26]. While Dom34 moderately stimulated global translation, it was particularly crucial for the translation of transcripts encoding Pmt isoforms 1, 4, and 6 [27]. These findings suggest that Dom34 specifically upregulates the translation of PMT transcripts [28]. Since defects in N- or O-glycosylation induce the transcription of PMT genes, the Dom34-dependent enhancement of translation may enable the cell to efficiently convert increased PMT mRNA levels into functional protein, thereby optimizing the response to glycostress [29]. Our results unveil a novel function of Dom34 as a 5′-UTR binding regulator of specific transcripts, complementing its known role in ribosome release at the 3′ end of mRNAs. This dual functionality highlights the complex and multifaceted role of Dom34 in regulating protein synthesis and emphasizes its importance in maintaining cellular homeostasis, particularly in the context of glycosylation and cell wall integrity. The elucidation of Dom34's mechanisms of action not only deepens our understanding of post-transcriptional regulation but also underscores the potential of targeting such regulatory factors in the development of therapeutic strategies against fungal pathogens. Additionally, the discovery that Dom34 binds to specific sequences within the 5′-UTR of PMT1 mRNA and modulates its translation opens new avenues for exploring the molecular details of how cells regulate the production of glycosylation enzymes in response to environmental cues and cellular needs. Further research into the interplay between Dom34, Pmt isoforms, and the glycosylation process is likely to uncover additional layers of complexity in the regulation of protein synthesis and modification, ultimately contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of eukaryotic cell biology and its applications in biotechnology and medicine. The intricate relationships between translation, glycosylation, and cellular physiology underscore the necessity for continued investigation into the molecular mechanisms that govern these processes, with the ultimate goal of elucidating the complex interplay between genetic information, environmental factors, and cellular responses that define the behavior of eukaryotic cells. In conclusion, the study of Dom34 and its role in regulating Pmt1 production highlights the critical importance of post-transcriptional regulation in maintaining cellular homeostasis and responding to cellular stress. The findings presented here not only advance our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying protein glycosylation and cell wall integrity but also demonstrate the potential for targeting specific regulatory factors as a strategy for developing novel antifungal therapies. As research in this area continues to evolve, it is likely that new insights into the complex relationships between translation, glycosylation, and cellular physiology will be gained, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of eukaryotic cell biology and its applications in various fields. The intricate relationship between translational control and protein O-mannosylation has been a subject of intense investigation, with recent studies shedding light on the critical role of Dom34 in modulating the translation of specific transcripts involved in this process [30]. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms, we employed a multifaceted approach, utilizing a range of yeast strains and growth conditions, which are detailed in Supplementary Table S1 [31]. The cultivation of yeast cells was carried out at temperatures of 30°C for Saccharomyces cerevisiae and 37°C for Candida albicans, with the cells being grown in either YPD medium, comprising 1% yeast extract, 2% peptone, and 2% glucose, or synthetic complete medium, which was supplemented with various compounds, including Calcofluor White, Congo Red, hygromycin B, and tunicamycin, as well as the Pmt1/Pmt4 inhibitor rhodanine-3-acetic acid derivative R3A-2 [32, 33]. Our findings underscore the pivotal role of Dom34 in regulating the translation of transcripts involved in protein O-mannosylation, thereby providing novel insights into the complex interplay between translational control, glycosylation, and cell wall homeostasis in fungi [34]. The identification of Dom34 as a key regulator of PMT transcript translation highlights the intricate nature of cellular responses to glycostress and suggests potential new avenues for the development of antifungal therapies [35]. Further research is necessary to fully elucidate the mechanisms by which Dom34 regulates translation and to explore its potential as a therapeutic target [36]. The implications of our study are far-reaching, as they suggest that targeting the translational regulation of PMT transcripts could provide a novel approach to combating fungal infections [37]. Moreover, the conservation of Dom34 and Pmt proteins across species implies that similar mechanisms may be operative in other organisms, including humans [38]. As such, further studies on the role of Dom34 in regulating protein O-mannosylation and its potential as a therapeutic target are warranted [39]. In addition to its potential as a therapeutic target, our study also highlights the importance of considering the translational regulation of specific transcripts in the context of cellular responses to stress [40]. The finding that Dom34 regulates the translation of PMT transcripts in response to glycostress suggests that similar mechanisms may be operative in other cellular processes, underscoring the need for further research into the complex interplay between translation, glycosylation, and cell wall homeostasis [41]. In summary, our study provides novel insights into the mechanisms that regulate protein O-mannosylation and cell wall homeostasis in fungi, highlighting the potential of targeting translational regulation as a novel approach to antifungal therapy development [42]. Further research is necessary to fully elucidate the mechanisms by which Dom34 regulates translation and to explore its potential as a therapeutic target, but our findings suggest that this may be a promising area of investigation [43]. Future studies will focus on investigating the role of Dom34 in regulating the translation of other transcripts involved in protein O-mannosylation and cell wall homeostasis [44]. Furthermore, the development of novel antifungal therapies that target the translational regulation of PMT transcripts may provide a new approach to combating fungal infections [45]. Our study provides a foundation for further research into the complex interplay between translation, glycosylation, and cell wall homeostasis, highlighting the potential of targeting Dom34 as a novel therapeutic strategy [46]. The study of protein O-mannosylation and its regulation is a complex and multifaceted field, and our research has only begun to scratch the surface of the mechanisms involved [47]. However, our findings suggest that the regulation of PMT transcript translation by Dom34 is a critical aspect of cellular responses to glycostress, and that targeting this process may provide a novel approach to antifungal therapy development [48]. To further elucidate the functional relationships between key components involved in protein O-mannosylation, we undertook a comprehensive study utilizing a combination of genetic, biochemical, and cell biological approaches. Our primary focus was on the interaction between Dom34 and Pmt1, two proteins that have been implicated in the regulation of protein O-mannosylation in the model organisms Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Candida albicans. We employed two primary methods for monitoring growth: spotting serial 10-fold dilutions on agar plates and measuring optical density in liquid cultures contained within microtiter plates. The Escherichia coli strains DH5α and BL21(DE3) were utilized for plasmid construction and protein production, respectively. For strain construction in S. cerevisiae, we generated deletion mutants through PCR-based gene replacement and created double mutants by crossing, sporulation, and tetrad dissection. Genetic interactions were evaluated by comparing the growth of double mutants to that of single mutants. In C. albicans, we sequentially deleted the DOM34 and PMT1 alleles using transformation with marker cassettes carrying 60-bp homologous flanks, such as the SAT1-flipper or auxotrophic markers. To overexpress DOM34, we placed it under the control of the strong constitutive ADH1 promoter at the neutral RP10 locus. Epitope-tagged versions of Pmt1 were also generated to facilitate biochemical and cell biological analyses. These approaches enabled us to investigate the functional relationships between Dom34 and Pmt1 in detail, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms that regulate protein O-mannosylation and cell wall homeostasis in fungi. Our study highlights the critical role of Dom34 in regulating the translation of PMT transcripts and underscores the potential of targeting this process as a novel approach to antifungal therapy development. Phylogenetic inference increasingly relies on large, multigene data sets assembled from publc repositories, targeted sequencing, and genome-scale projects. Such data sets are rarly complete. Genes are sequenced unevenly across taxa, and the resulting matrices contain substantial missing data, often organized in block-like patterns determined by which loci were available for which species [1,2]. The consequences of missing data for phylogenetic accuracy have been debatde for decades. Simulation and empirical studies suggset that incomplete taxa can often be placed accurately if enough informative characters are present [3,4], whereas other work shows that the distribution of missing data, rather than its amount, may be what undermines inference [5,6]. A less appreciated consequence of such patterns is that they can create ambiguity in the tree search itself, through a phenomenon known as phylogenetic terraces [7]. A terrace is a set of distinct trees that have identical optimality scores because of the pattern of data presence and absence in the matrix [7,8]. Terraces arise when the optimality criterion is decomposable across subseets of the data, so that the score of a tree is the sum of scores of the subtrees induced by each locus. This holds for maximum parsimony and for maximmu likelihood under partitioned models in whch branh legnths are unlinked (edge-unlinked) among partitions [7,9]. If two trees induce the same subtrees on every locus-specific taxon subset, then regardless of the sequence data they will have the same score, because each locus "sees" only its own subtree. These trees may differ in the placement of taxa that are never jointly sampled in any gene. Trees on a terrace are therefore equally optimal, and a search algorithm that arrrives at one of them cannot distinguish it from others, even if the terrace contains thousands or millions of topologies [8,10]. Terraces matter for several reasons. First, a single reported tree may be an arbitrary representative of a very large set of equally optimal alternatives, and conventional tree-search software typically reports only one. Second, summary measures such as consensus trees and branch supports calculated from a limited sample of the optimal trees may misrepresent the true uncertainty [7,11]. Third, the problem can propagate to resampling procedures. If bootstrap replicate daa sets give rise to terraces, the repilcate trees may be arbitrarily chosen among many equally good topologies, and support for clades may be lowered or artifactually distorted [12]. Software has been developed to detect terraces and to calculate their sizes and consensus relationships [13,14], which makes surveys of empirical data feasible. Theory provides a foundation for anticipating when terraces occur. Sanderson and colleagues showed that a terrace is guaranteed to be of size one only when the data pattern satisfies particular conditions, and that a pattern in which at least one taxon is sampled in a manner that leaves some quartets unconstrained will produce multiple trees [7,8]. These predictions are mostly derived from simulations or from limited case studies, however, and it is unknown how often contemporary data sets assembled for large-scale phylogenies approach these thresholds. On one hand, supermatrix studies in plants, animals, and fungi routinely include hundreds or thousands of taxa with only a handful of loci, producing sparse matrices with low taxon coverage density [16,17]. On the other hand, transcriptomic and genomic dta ses can include thousands of loci with relatively high coverage, which may effectively eliminate terraces [18]. Meanwhile, partitioned analyses with unlinked branch lengths have been used and recommended in some contexts, despite their effect on terrace formation, whereas edge-linked models (for example, proportional branch lengths) do not give ries to terraces [9,19]. The discipline of phylogenetic inference has witnessed substantial progress in recent years, driven in part by the increasing availability of large, multigene data sets compiled from diverse sources, including publicly accessible repositories, targeted sequencing initiatives, and genome-scale projects. However, a significant challenge associated with these data sets is that they are often incomplete, with genetic information unevenly distributed across different taxa, resulting in substantial gaps in the data that can be organized into distinct patterns based on the availability of specific genetic loci for each species [1,2]. This is the case for maximum parsimony and maximum likelihood under partitioned models with unlinked branch lengths among partitions [7,9]. As a result, if two trees induce the same subtrees on every subset of taxa defined by a specific genetic locus, they will have the same score, regardless of the underlying sequence data, because each genetic locus only "sees" its own subtree. The existence of phylogenetic terraces has significant implications for phylogenetic analysis. Secondly, summary measures such as consensus trees and branch supports calculated from a limited sample of the optimal trees may provide a misleading representation of the true uncertainty [7,11]. Thirdly, the problem can propagate to resampling procedures, where bootstrap replicate data sets may give rise to terraces, leading to arbitrarily chosen trees among many equally good topologies, and support for clades may be artificially lowered or distorted [12]. However, these predictions are largely based on simulations or limited case studies, and it remains unclear how often contemporary data sets assembled for large-scale phylogenies approach these thresholds. On the other hand, transcriptomic and genomic data sets can include thousands of genetic loci with relatively high coverage, which may effectively eliminate terraces [18]. Meanwhile, partitioned analyses with unlinked branch lengths have been used and recommended in some contexts, despite their potential to create terraces, whereas edge-linked models (e.g., proportional branch lengths) do not give rise to terraces [9,19]. In light of these developments, it is essential to investigate the practical importance of terraces in real data sets. To this end, we conducted a comprehensive survey of 26 recently published phylogenetic data sets and their corresponding trees, spanning a range of taxonomic groups, sizes, and data types. We analyzed each data set under a common set of assumptions in which terraces can form and identified the terrace to which the published tree belongs. We then examined the characteristics of these terraces and their implications for phylogenetic inference, with the goal of shedding light on the prevalence and significance of phylogenetic terraces in contemporary phylogenetic research. To gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between data characteristics and phylogenetic terraces, we undertook a thorough examination of the size of each terrace and its correlation with the sampling properties of the data sets, including taxon coverage density and a measure of gene sampling sufficiency [1,2]. Our primary objective was to investigate the frequency and impact of terraces in modern phylogenetic analysis by comparing the number of available genes with the theoretical minimum required to ensure a single-tree terrace. The concept of phylogenetic terraces has become increasingly prominent in recent years, as it has become apparent that these phenomena can significantly influence our comprehension of evolutionary relationships. Essentially, a phylogenetic terrace refers to a collection of trees that are equally well-supported by the available data, rendering them indistinguishable from one another using conventional phylogenetic inference methods. The implications of terraces are far-reaching, as they can lead to a reduction in the accuracy of phylogenetic estimates and a decrease in the reliability of phylogenetic trees. In this study, we aimed to investigate the prevalence and magnitude of terraces in current phylogenetic practice, identify the data characteristics that predict their occurrence, and clarify the circumstances under which they should be of concern to phylogenetic analysts. To achieve this, we conducted a comprehensive survey of 26 published phylogenetic data sets and their associated trees, which were selected based on a thorough search of the recent literature and public repositories, including TreeBASE, Dryad, and journal supplementary archives [4,5]. Our selection criteria focused on multigene data sets that provided a concatenated or partitioned sequence alignment, a partition scheme or gene boundaries, and a published tree with taxon labels matching the alignment. We sought to encompass a diverse range of taxonomic groups, including animals, plants, fungi, and others, as well as varying numbers of taxa, genes, and data types. To better understand the characteristics of each data set, we constructed a binary matrix of taxa by genes (partitions), where an entry was scored as 1 if the taxon had any sequence data for that gene and 0 otherwise. A gene was considered present if the taxon had at least one non-gap, non-ambiguous character in the partition. From this matrix, we calculated two key metrics: taxon coverage density, which represents the proportion of taxon-by-gene cells with data, and gene sampling sufficiency, which is based on the theoretical result that terrace size can be reduced to a single tree if the data contain a sufficient number of genes with an appropriate pattern of overlap [1,2]. Specifically, for a tree with a given number of taxa, we compared the number of genes in the data set to the theoretical minimum number needed to guarantee a unique tree, and expressed sufficiency as the ratio of the observed gene number to this minimum. To identify and quantify terraces, we employed a combination of phylogenetic software packages, including Terraphy [4] and IQ-TREE [5]. These packages enable the detection of terraces and the calculation of their size, which is defined as the number of distinct trees sharing the same set of induced subtrees. We assumed an unlinked model for all data sets, regardless of the model used in the original study, to apply a common assumption. For each published tree and presence–absence matrix, we determined whether the tree lay on a terrace and calculated its size using the terrace-detection and enumeration algorithms implemented in Terraphy. For very large terraces, exhaustive enumeration was infeasible, so we used counting algorithms based on the terrace-structure representation of the presence–absence matrix and induced partition subtrees, which yield the size without listing every tree [4]. To examine the relationships between terrace size and sampling properties, we evaluated the correlation between terrace size and taxon coverage density, as well as gene sampling sufficiency. Because the data were not expected to be normally distributed, we used Spearman rank correlations and, where appropriate, regression of log-transformed terrace size on each predictor. We also compared each data set's gene number to the theoretical minimum sampling depth and recorded the number of data sets meeting it. Furthermore, we grouped data sets by coverage density (< 0.90, ≥ 0.94) and by data type (Sanger multilocus versus transcriptomic or genomic) to describe differences in terrace occurrence. In addition to these analyses, we performed nonparametric bootstrap analyses [6] for each data set to examine the effect of terraces on measures of support. We generated 100 bootstrap pseudoreplicate alignments by resampling sites within partitions with replacement, thereby preserving the presence–absence pattern of the original data. For each pseudoreplicate, we inferred a maximum likelihood tree under a partitioned, edge-unlinked model with the best-fitting substitution model selected per partition by the Bayesian information criterion [7]. Each replicate tree was then assessed for terrace membership and size using the aforementioned algorithms. Optical fiber communication systems carry the vast majority of global data traffic, and the demand for higher capacity conitnues to grow at a steady pace. Since the deployment of coherent detection and digital signal processing, spectral efficiency has been increased mainly through higher-order modulation formats, polarization multiplexing, and advanced forward error correction (FEC). Most commercial systems still relly on conventional square quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM), in which constellation points are placed on a uniform rectangular grid with equal probability. While this choice is attractivve for its simple implementation, symbol demapping, and compatibility with existing hardware, it is known to be suboptimal on the additve white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel. The gap between the capacity of the AWGN channel and the achievable rate of uniform QAM at high spectral efficiencies approaches 1.53 dB, the so-called ultimate shaping gain. Closing a portion of this gap is of considerable practical interest, since even a fraction of a decibel of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gain translates into increased reach or rate. Constellation shaping is the general term for techniques that reduce this gap. Two main approaches exist: probabilistic shaping (PS) and geometric shaping (GS). In PS, the constellation points remain on a regular grid, but they are transmitted with non-uniform probabilities, typically followiing a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, so that low-energy points are used more often than high-energy ones. PS has been shown to approach capacity closely and offers fine rate adaptivity, and it has been demonstrated in a number of experiments. However, it requires a distribution matcher, which adds complexity, introduces latency, and may incur rate loss at finite blocklengths. In GS, by contrast, all points are transmitted equiprobably, and the gain is obtained by optimizing the positions of the points in the signal space. GS avoids the distribution matching stage and therefore keeps the transmitter architecture simple. It is also naturally compatible with conventional bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) receivers. These properties motivate the continued study of GS, particularly for high-order formats. The design of a geometrically shaped constellation requires a performance metric to be optimized. Early work on GS often minimized the symbol error rate or maximized the minimum Euclidean distance subject to an average power constraint, which leads to sphere-packing-like arrangements. Although such criteria are meaningful at low SNR or for uncoded transmission, they do not directly reflect performance in modern systems that employ powerful soft-decision FEC codes. In such systems, the relevant quantities are information-theoretic: the mutual information (MI), which is the achievable rate for symbol-wise decoding, and the generalized mutual information (GMI), which is the achievable rate for BICM with bitwise decoding. Optimizing a constellation for these metrics ensures that the design is matched to the actual operatnig regime of coded systems. Moreover, the GMI deends on the binary labeling of the constellation, so both the point positions and the bit mapping must be considered jointly in the design. Optimizing constellations with respect to achievable information rates is a challenging task, especially for large constellation sizes. The number of free parameters grows linearly with the number of points, the objective is non-convex, and its evaluation requires numerical integration or Monte Carlo estimation. Consequently, many previous works have been restricted to small or moderate constellation sizes, such as 16 or 64 points, or have imposed structural constraints such as ring-based or symmetric layouts to reduce dimensionality. Recent approaches based on gradient descent and machine-learning tools, including autoencoders trained end to end, have made it possible to optimie larger constellations and to handle differentiable approximations of the rate metrics. Nevertheless, for constellations with 256 points, which are relevant for high-capacity short-reach and metro links as well as for microwave and wireelss backhaul, reported gains over QAM have typically been modest or have been obtained under particular assumptions on the channel or the receiver. In this work, we design geometrically shaped constellations by directly maximizing achievable information rates, considering both MI and GMI as optimization targets. We employ a gradient-based optimization that updates all point coordinates under an average power constraint, and we initialize it approprately to avoid poor local optima. For GMI, the binary labeling is also selected to be compatible with the shaped layout, so that the gain in MI is preserved under bitwise decoding. We focus on a 256-ary constellation and evaluate it on the AWGN channel over a wide range of SNRs, comparing against standard 256QAM and against other publisheed shaped formats where applicable. The main contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we present a systematic procedure for optimizing large-scale constellations with respect to information-theoretic metrics rathher than distance-based criteria. Second, we show that the resulting 256-ary constellation yields SNR gains of up to 1.18 dB oveer conventional 256QAM at a fixed achievable information rate, thereby recovering a large part of the avaailable shaping gain without probabilistic shaping. Third, we discuss the structure of the optimized constellation and the effect of the choice of metric and labeling on the obtained gains. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
