The exponential growth of global data exchange has created an unprecedented need for enhanced capacity in optical fiber communication networks. Following the introduction of coherent detection and digital signal processing, the main strategies for boosting spectral efficiency have involved the adoption of advanced modulation formats, polarization multiplexing, and sophisticated forward error correction (FEC) techniques [1]. Despite these developments, most commercial systems still rely on traditional square quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM), where constellation points are arranged in a uniform grid with equal probability of occurrence. Although this approach is appealing due to its simplicity, ease of implementation, and compatibility with existing infrastructure, it is well-established that it falls short of optimal performance in the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel [2]. The disparity between the capacity of the AWGN channel and the achievable rate of uniform QAM at high spectral efficiencies approaches 1.53 dB, a phenomenon referred to as the ultimate shaping gain [3]. Closing a portion of this gap is of significant practical interest, as even a small improvement in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) can lead to increased transmission distances or data rates. Constellation shaping techniques aim to address this gap, and two primary methods exist: probabilistic shaping (PS) and geometric shaping (GS) [4]. PS involves transmitting constellation points with non-uniform probabilities, typically following a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, where low-energy points are used more frequently than high-energy ones [5]. PS has been shown to closely approach capacity and offers fine-grained rate adaptivity, with numerous experiments demonstrating its effectiveness [6]. However, it requires a distribution matcher, which introduces complexity, latency, and potential rate loss at finite block lengths [7]. In contrast, GS involves transmitting all points with equal probability, with the gain achieved by optimizing the positions of the points in the signal space [8]. GS avoids the need for distribution matching, maintaining a simple transmitter architecture, and is inherently compatible with conventional bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) receivers [9]. These properties motivate the continued exploration of GS, particularly for high-order formats. The design of a geometrically shaped constellation requires the optimization of a performance metric. Early research on GS often focused on minimizing the symbol error rate or maximizing the minimum Euclidean distance subject to an average power constraint, resulting in arrangements resembling sphere packing [10]. Although such criteria are meaningful at low SNR or for uncoded transmission, they do not directly reflect performance in modern systems that employ powerful soft-decision FEC codes [11]. In such systems, the relevant quantities are information-theoretic: the mutual information (MI), which represents the achievable rate for symbol-wise decoding, and the generalized mutual information (GMI), which represents the achievable rate for BICM with bitwise decoding [12]. Optimizing a constellation for these metrics ensures that the design is tailored to the actual operating regime of coded systems. Furthermore, the GMI depends on the binary labeling of the constellation, so both the point positions and the bit mapping must be considered jointly in the design [13]. Optimizing constellations with respect to achievable information rates is a challenging task, particularly for large constellation sizes. The number of free parameters grows linearly with the number of points, the objective is non-convex, and its evaluation requires numerical integration or Monte Carlo estimation [14]. Consequently, many previous studies have been limited to small or moderate constellation sizes, such as 16 or 64 points, or have imposed structural constraints, such as ring-based or symmetric layouts, to reduce dimensionality [15]. Recent approaches based on gradient descent and machine learning tools, including autoencoders trained end to end, have facilitated the optimization of larger constellations and the handling of differentiable approximations of the rate metrics [16]. Nevertheless, for constellations with 256 points, which are relevant for high-capacity short-reach and metro links, as well as for microwave and wireless backhaul, reported gains over QAM have typically been modest or have been obtained under specific assumptions regarding the channel or receiver [17]. This study focuses on designing geometrically shaped constellations by directly maximizing achievable information rates, considering both MI and GMI as optimization targets. A gradient-based optimization is employed, updating all point coordinates under an average power constraint, and initialized appropriately to avoid poor local optima [18]. For GMI, the binary labeling is also selected to be compatible with the shaped layout, ensuring that the gain in MI is preserved under bitwise decoding [19]. The study concentrates on a 256-ary constellation and evaluates it on the AWGN channel over a wide range of SNRs, comparing against standard 256QAM and other published shaped formats where applicable [20]. The primary contributions of this paper are threefold. First, a systematic procedure is presented for optimizing large-scale constellations with respect to information-theoretic metrics rather than distance-based criteria. Second, it is demonstrated that the resulting 256-ary constellation yields SNR gains of up to 1.18 dB over conventional 256QAM. This achievement has significant implications for the design of high-capacity optical communication systems, where even small improvements in SNR can lead to substantial increases in transmission reach or data rate. By leveraging geometric shaping techniques, system designers can create more efficient and effective communication systems, ultimately supporting the growing demands of global data exchange. Furthermore, the approach presented in this study can be extended to other constellation sizes and modulation formats, enabling the widespread adoption of geometric shaping techniques in optical communication systems. Our investigation commences with an examination of transmission over a memoryless additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel, wherein the received signal $Y$ is constituted by the sum of the transmitted symbol $X$ and circularly symmetric complex Gaussian noise $N$. The transmitted symbol $X$ is selected from a constellation $C$ comprising $M = 256$ points, with the average signal power constrained to $E[|X|^2] = P$, and the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) defined as $P/\sigma^2$. Unless explicitly stated otherwise, symbols are assumed to be equiprobable, implying that any shaping gain is exclusively attributable to the geometric configuration of the constellation, rather than probabilistic shaping. Two achievable rates are utilized as design metrics in this study: the mutual information (MI) and the generalized mutual information (GMI). The mutual information, given by $I(X;Y) = \log_2 M - (1/M) \sum_i E_N[\log_2 \sum_j \exp(-(|c_i - c_j + N|^2 - |N|^2)/\sigma^2)]$, represents the achievable rate for symbol-wise decoding with an optimal soft-decision decoder [1]. The generalized mutual information, applicable to bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) with binary labeling, is expressed as $GMI = \sum_{k=1}^m [1 - (1/M) \sum_i E_N[\log_2 (\sum_j \exp(-|c_i - c_j + N|^2/\sigma^2) / \sum_{j \in S(k, b_k(i))} \exp(-|c_i - c_j + N|^2/\sigma^2))]]$, where $S(k,b)$ denotes the subset of constellation points whose $k$-th label bit equals $b$ [2]. These expectations are evaluated using Gauss-Hermite quadrature in two dimensions, with verification via Monte Carlo simulations employing $10^5$ noise samples per point. The mutual information serves as an upper bound, independent of labeling, while the generalized mutual information captures the penalty associated with binary labeling and the practical BICM receiver. By optimizing both metrics separately, we obtain constellations suited to coded modulation with multilevel/nonbinary codes (MI) and BICM (GMI), thereby enabling an exploration of the trade-offs between these two design strategies.

To parameterize the constellation, we note that it is described by $2M$ real parameters, corresponding to the in-phase and quadrature coordinates of each point. In order to reduce the dimensionality of the search space and enforce a symmetric structure, we impose four-fold rotational symmetry, resulting in only $M/4 = 64$ free points, with the remaining points determined by rotation. This yields $128$ real degrees of freedom. Additionally, a variant with mirror symmetry about the real axis was tested to further reduce the dimensionality. Following each update, the constellation is renormalized to satisfy the average power constraint and recentred to have zero mean. The optimization procedure aims to maximize the chosen rate (MI or GMI) at a fixed target SNR, with the constellation serving as the variable. Given that the objective is smooth in the point coordinates, we employ gradient-based optimization. Gradients are obtained through automatic differentiation of the quadrature-evaluated rate expression. The Adam optimizer is used with an initial learning rate of $10^{-2}$, decayed to $10^{-4}$, and batches of noise samples are redrawn at each iteration when stochastic estimates are utilized. Due to the non-convex nature of the landscape, with numerous local optima, we employ multiple initializations: square 256-QAM, a hexagonal-like arrangement, concentric-ring layouts, and random perturbations of these. The best result among all runs is retained. Optimization is carried out for target SNRs spanning the region in which the 256-QAM rate lies between 5 and 7.5 bits/symbol. The constellation optimized at one SNR is used as the starting point for the neighboring SNR to promote continuity (warm starting). For GMI optimization, the labeling must also be chosen. Given a geometry, we initialize with binary reflected Gray labeling extended to the two-dimensional layout and then apply the binary switching algorithm, which iteratively swaps labels of pairs of points to minimize a bit-error-oriented cost. Geometry and labeling are optimized in alternation: several gradient steps on the coordinates with fixed labels, followed by a labeling refinement, until the GMI improvement falls below $10^{-4}$ bits/symbol.

These include population-based averaging, in which a large population implicitly smooths the noise [7]; modified selection schemes and thresholding [8]; and explicit resampling, in which each candidate solution is evaluated several times and the mean is used as the fitness estimate [9,10]. Resampling is perhaps the most widely used approach because it is simple, applicable to any algorithm, and reduces the variance of the estimate by a factor equal to the number of samples. Its cost is equally clear: each resample consumes part of a finite evaluation budget, so the designer must trade accuracy of individual estimates against the number of search steps that can be performed. Determining how many resamples to use, and whether the number should be static or adaptive, has motivated a substantial body of both empirical and theoretical work [11,12]. **Runtime analysis and First Hitting Time** The theoretical study of such trade-offs is largely carried out through runtime analysis, which derives bounds on the expected number of fitness evaluations required by an algorithm to solve a given problem [13,14]. In the noiseless setting, runtime is almost universally defined as the First Hitting Time (FHT): the number of evaluations until the optimum is first sampled. This definition is natural and mathematically convenient, and it has underpinned many results for simple algorithms such as the (1+1) EA on benchmark functions like OneMax and LeadingOnes [13]. An algorithm is deemed to have succeeded the moment the optimum is evaluated, even if the algorithm cannot recognise that it has done so. Because the fitness observations are corrupted, the algorithm may immediately reject the optimum, and then wander away from it indefinitely. The FHT criterion ignores this behaviour. More fundamentally, the criterion presupposes knowledge that is unavailable in practice. In a real application the optimal solution and its objective value are unknown; if they were known, no search would be needed. Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) and related randomised seach heuristics have been applied successuflly to a wide range of optimisation problems in engineering, logistics, machine learning and design [1,2]. Their performance on real-world problems is, however, frequuently complicated by uncertainty. Measurements may be corrupted by sensor error, simulations may be stochastic, and human evaluators may be inconsistent. In such settings the fitness function returns a noisy observation of the true objective value, and an algorithm that treats this observation as exact may accept inferior solutions, discard superior ones, and ultimately fail to converge [3,4]. Optimisation under noise has therefore become an established research area within evolutionary computation [5,6]. **Coping with noise** A variety of strategies have been proposed for noisy optimisation. These include population-based averaging, in which a large population implicitly smooths the noise [7]; modified selection schhemes and thresholding [8]; and explicit resampling, in which each candidate solution is evaluated several times and the mean is used as the fitness estimate [9,10]. Resampling is perhaps the most widely used approach because it is simple, applicable to any algorithm, and reduces the variiance of the estimate by a factor equal to the number of samples. Its cost is equally clear: each resample consumes part of a finite evaluation budget, so the designer must trade accuracy of individual estimates against the number of search steps that can be performed. Determining how many resamples to use, and whether the number should be static or adaptive, has motivated a substantial body of both empirical and theoretical work [11,12]. **Runtime analysis and First Hitting Time** The theoretical study of such trade-offs is largely carried out through runtime analysis, which derives bounds on the expected number of fitness evaluations required by an algorithm to solve a given problem [13,14]. In the noiseless setting, runtime is almost universally defined as the First Hitting Time (FHT): the number of evaluations until the optimum is first sampled. This definition is natural and mathematically convenient, and it has underpinned many results for simmple algorithms such as the (1+1) EA on bencmhark functions like OneMax and LeadingOnes [13]. It has also been carried over to noisy domains, where analyses have characterised the noise levels under which algorithms such as the (1+1) EA, ant colony optimisers and population-based EAs retain polnomial runtime, and how resampling alters thhose thresholds [15–18]. Under noise, however, the FHT is problematic. An algorithm is deemed to have succeeded the moment the optimum is evaluated, even if the algorthm cannot recognise that it has done so. Because the fitness observations are corrupted, the algorithm may immediately reject the optimum, and then wander away from it indefinitely. The FHT criterion ignores this behaviour. More fundamentally, the criterion presupposes knowledge that is unavailable in practice. In a real application the optimal solution and its objective value are unknown; if they were known, no search would be needed. A practitioner cannot halt the algorithm upon encountering the optimum, but must instead choose a stopping rule, typically a fixed budget, and accept whatever solution the algorithm returns at that point. The quality of that returned solution, rather than the moment at which an optimal solution happened to be sampled, is wat matters operationally. **Final solution quality** This paper argues that the evaluation of noisy optimisation algorithms should instead focus on final solution quality: the true fitness (or the gap to the optimum) of the solution returned after a fixed evaluation budget. This measure aligns with how algorithms are deployed, accounts for the algorithm's ability to retain and recognise good solutions under noise, and naturally incorporates the cost of strategies such as resampling, since the budget is shared between sampling and search. It is also consistent with established practice in the empirical benchmarking of optimisers, where fixed-budget and anytime performance views are advocated [19,20], and with fixed-budget perspectives developed in runtime analysis [21]. Despite this, the FHT remains the dominant measure in noisy runtime analysis, and the consequences of this choice have not been examined systematically. **Contributions and structure** The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we articulate why FHT is an inappropriate performance criterion for noisy optimisation, identifying the specific mechanisms by which it can overestimate the quality of an algorithm. Second, we propose and formalise final solution quality under a fixed evaluation budget as an alternative. Third, we present cases, both analytical and empirical, in which the two criteria yield markedly different conclusions about the relative merits of noisy optimisation algorithms and of resampling strategies; in particular, we show that an algorithm or parameter setting ranked favourably by FHT can perform poorly in terms of the solution it returns, and vice versa. We do not claim that FHT results are mathematically incorrect, but that their practical interpretation as indicators of real-world algorithm quality is unreliable. In such settings the fitness function returns a noisy observation of the true objective value, and an algorithm that treats this observation as exact may accept inferior solutions, disacrd superior ones, and ultimately fail to converge [3,4]. Optimisation under noise has therefore become an established rsearch area withhin evloutionary computation [5,6]. **Coping with noise** A variety of strategies have been proposed for noisy optimisation. Thsee iclude population-based averaging, in which a large population implicitly smooths the noise [7]; mdified selection schemes and thresholding [8]; and explicit resampling, in which each candidate solution is evaluated several times and the mean is used as the fitness estimate [9,10]. Resampling is perhaps the moost widely used approach because it is simple, applicable to any algorithm, and reeduces the variance of the estimate by a factro equal to the nuumber of samples. Its cost is equally clear: each resample consumes part of a finitte evaluation budget, so the designer must trade accuracy of individual estimates against the number of search steps that can be performed. Determining how many resamples to use, and whether the number should be static or adaptive, has motivated a substantial body of both empirical and theoretical work [11,12]. **Runtime analysis and First Hitting Time** The theoretical study of such trade-offs is largely carried out through runtime analysis, which derives bounds on the expected number of fitness evaluations required by an algorithm to solve a gven problem [13,14]. In the noiseless setting, runtime is almoost univresally defined as the First Hittign Time (FHT): the nummber of evaluations until the optimuum is first sampled. This definition is natural and mathematically convenient, and it has underpinned many results for simple alogrithms such as the (1+1) EA on benchmark functions like OneMax and LeadingOnes [13]. It has also been carried over to noisy domains, whree analyses have characterised the noise levels under which algorithms such as the (1+1) EA, ant colony optimisers and population-based EAs retain polynomial runtime, and how rsampling alters those thresholds [15–18]. Under noise, however, the FHT is problematic. An algorithm is deemed to have scceeded the moment the optimum is evaluated, even if the algorithm cannot recognise that it has done so. Because the fitenss observations are corrupted, the algorithm may immediately reject the optimum, and then wander away from it indefinitely. The FHT criterion ingores this behaviour. More fundamentally, the criterion presupposes knowledge that is unavailable in practice. In a real application the optimal solution and its objective value are unknown; if they werre known, no search would be needed. A practitioner cannot hlt the algoritthm upon encountering the optimum, but must instead choose a stopping rule, typically a fixed budget, and accept whatever solution the algorithm reeturns at that point. Ths measure aligns with how algorithms are deployed, accounts for the algorithm's ability to rteain and recognise good soluutions under noise, and naturally incorporates the cost of strategies such as resampling, since the budget is shared betwen samplig and search. The utilization of evolutionary algorithms and their associated stochastic search methodologies has yielded significant successes in resolving a diverse array of optimization problems spanning multiple disciplines, including engineering, logistics, machine learning, and design [1,2]. Nevertheless, the efficacy of these algorithms in real-world applications is frequently hindered by the presence of uncertainty, which can emanate from various sources such as sensor inaccuracies, stochastic simulations, or inconsistent human assessments. Consequently, the fitness function yields a distorted observation of the actual objective value, potentially leading to the acceptance of suboptimal solutions, the rejection of superior ones, and ultimately, the failure to converge [3,4]. Optimization under uncertainty has thus emerged as a prominent area of research within the realm of evolutionary computation [5,6]. Mitigating the effects of noise in optimization is crucial, and numerous strategies have been proposed to address this issue, including population-based averaging, which implicitly reduces noise through the use of a large population [7]; modified selection schemes and thresholding [8]; and explicit resampling, where each candidate solution is evaluated multiple times, and the mean of these evaluations is employed as the fitness estimate [9,10]. Resampling is arguably the most widely adopted approach due to its simplicity, versatility, and ability to diminish the variance of the estimate by a factor proportional to the number of samples. However, the cost of resampling is also evident: each additional sample consumes a portion of the limited evaluation budget, necessitating a trade-off between the accuracy of individual estimates and the number of search iterations that can be performed. Determining the optimal number of resamples and whether this number should remain static or be adapted has motivated a substantial body of both empirical and theoretical research [11,12]. Theoretical investigations of these trade-offs are predominantly conducted through runtime analysis, which establishes bounds on the expected number of fitness evaluations required by an algorithm to resolve a given problem [13,14]. In the absence of noise, runtime is nearly universally defined as the First Hitting Time (FHT): the number of evaluations required until the optimum is first encountered. This definition is natural and mathematically convenient, underpinning numerous results for simple algorithms, such as the (1+1) EA, on benchmark functions like OneMax and LeadingOnes [13]. It has also been applied to noisy domains, where analyses have characterized the noise levels under which algorithms, including the (1+1) EA, ant colony optimizers, and population-based EAs, retain polynomial runtime, and how resampling alters these thresholds [15–18]. However, the FHT is problematic in the presence of noise. An algorithm is considered successful the moment it encounters the optimum, regardless of whether it can recognize this achievement. Due to the corruption of fitness observations, the algorithm may immediately reject the optimum and then diverge from it indefinitely. The FHT criterion overlooks this behavior. More fundamentally, it presupposes knowledge that is unavailable in practice. In real-world applications, the optimal solution and its objective value are unknown; if they were known, no search would be necessary. Practitioners cannot halt the algorithm upon encountering the optimum but must instead select a stopping rule, typically a fixed budget, and accept the solution returned at that point. The quality of the returned solution, rather than the moment at which an optimal solution was sampled, is what matters operationally. This paper posits that the evaluation of noisy optimization algorithms should instead focus on the quality of the final solution: the true fitness (or the gap to the optimum) of the solution returned after a fixed evaluation budget. This measure aligns with the deployment of algorithms, accounts for the algorithm's ability to retain and recognize good solutions under noise, and naturally incorporates the cost of strategies such as resampling, as the budget is shared between sampling and search. It is also consistent with established practices in the empirical benchmarking of optimizers, where fixed-budget and anytime performance views are advocated [19,20], and with fixed-budget perspectives developed in runtime analysis [21]. Despite this, the FHT remains the dominant measure in noisy runtime analysis, and the implications of this choice have not been systematically examined. The contributions of this paper are threefold. Firstly, we elucidate why the FHT is an inappropriate performance criterion for noisy optimization, identifying the specific mechanisms by which it can overestimate algorithm quality. Secondly, we propose and formalize the final solution quality under a fixed evaluation budget as an alternative criterion. Thirdly, we present analytical and empirical cases in which the two criteria yield markedly different conclusions regarding the relative merits of noisy optimization algorithms and resampling strategies; in particular, we demonstrate that an algorithm or parameter setting ranked favorably by FHT can perform poorly in terms of the solution it returns, and vice versa. We do not assert that FHT results are mathematically flawed but rather that their practical interpretation as indicators of real-world algorithm quality is limited. The primary focus of this work is to provide a comprehensive understanding of the limitations of the FHT and the benefits of adopting a final solution quality criterion in the context of noisy optimization. By exploring the theoretical and empirical implications of these two criteria, we aim to contribute to the development of more effective and robust optimization algorithms capable of performing well in real-world applications. Furthermore, we anticipate that our findings will have significant implications for the design and evaluation of optimization algorithms, highlighting the need for a shift in focus from the FHT to more practical and meaningful measures of algorithm performance. Ultimately, this shift in focus will enable the creation of more efficient and reliable optimization algorithms, better equipped to handle the complexities and uncertainties of real-world problems. Additionally, the adoption of a final solution quality criterion will facilitate the development of more sophisticated and adaptive optimization algorithms, capable of learning and improving their performance over time. As the field of optimization continues to evolve, the importance of developing algorithms that can effectively handle noise and uncertainty will only continue to grow, making the need for a robust and practical evaluation criterion all the more pressing. The evaluation of an algorithm's performance in the presence of noise is a complex task, particularly when the fitness function is noisy and each evaluation counts towards the overall budget, including any repeated evaluations due to resampling. This study examines the performance of three widely-studied algorithms in the literature on noisy runtime analysis: the (1+1) EA with resampling, the (μ+λ) EA, and the Compact Genetic Algorithm (cGA). 

The (1+1) EA with resampling operates by generating an offspring $y$ at each generation through the independent bit-flip mutation of the parent $x$ with a probability of $1/n$. Both the parent and the offspring are evaluated $k$ times, and the offspring replaces the parent if its mean noisy fitness is superior or equal to that of the parent. The resampling parameter $k$ is tested with values of 1, 5, 20, and 100, as well as a dynamic $k$ that increases with the generation counter. 

In contrast, the (μ+λ) EA utilizes a population size where $\mu = \lambda$, set to either 5 or 10. Each individual within the population is evaluated $k$ times per generation, and selection is based on the sample means, with truncation selection applied. The use of populations in the (μ+λ) EA is motivated by their inherent robustness to noise without the need for resampling, as noted in previous research [4]. 

The Compact Genetic Algorithm (cGA), on the other hand, maintains a probability vector with a hypothetical population size $K$ of 20, 50, or 100, and boundary values are set at $[1/n, 1-1/n]$. At each iteration, two samples are drawn and evaluated $k$ times. Theoretical analyses have shown that the cGA exhibits robustness to noise [5]. Each of these configurations is run on every problem instance and under various noise settings, enabling a comprehensive comparison of the algorithms' performance.

To assess the performance of these algorithms, two key metrics are employed: the First Hitting Time (FHT) and the Final Solution Quality (FSQ) after a predetermined evaluation budget. The FHT is defined as the number of fitness evaluations required until a solution $x$ that satisfies $f(x) = n$ is found. The algorithm terminates upon reaching this condition, utilizing oracle knowledge of the optimum, a common approach in runtime analysis [1,6]. If the optimum is not reached within the maximum budget $B$, the run is considered censored at $B$. The study reports the mean, median, and success rate of the FHT, with adjustments for censoring by using the restricted mean and the expected running time estimate [7].

The Final Solution Quality metric involves running the algorithm for the full budget $B$ and returning a solution based on a recommendation rule that does not rely on $f$. For the (1+1) EA, the current parent is returned; for the (μ+λ) EA, the individual with the highest sample mean in the final population is selected; and for the cGA, the solution is obtained by rounding the probability vector. After the run, the true fitness $f(x_{returned})$ is computed in a noise-free evaluation. The study reports the mean and median normalized true fitness $f(x)/n$, the proportion of runs resulting in an optimal solution, and the mean Hamming distance to the optimum, which aligns with the simple-regret notion in noisy optimization [8].

The distinction between FHT and FSQ is significant because an algorithm may visit the optimum but subsequently accept a worse solution due to noise, leading to a discrepancy between the two metrics. By tracking both, the study can quantify the frequency of such occurrences. Additionally, the number of generations where the optimum was held as the incumbent and whether it was held at the end of the budget are recorded for each run.

The experimental protocol is designed to ensure a thorough comparison of the algorithms. The budget is set to $B = 200 \cdot n^2$ evaluations for OneMax and $400 \cdot n^2$ for LeadingOnes, which is sufficiently large for noise-free algorithms to find the optimum. Each configuration is repeated 100 times with independent random seeds, and the same seeds are used across all measures to prevent differences in conclusions due to sampling variation. The algorithms are ranked based on their performance, allowing for conclusions to be drawn about their relative strengths and weaknesses.

In the subsequent sections, a detailed analysis of the experimental results will be presented, providing insights into the performance of the algorithms under various noise settings and problem sizes. The goal is to offer a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each algorithm, shedding light on the implications for the design and analysis of noisy optimizers. The pursuit of efficient and effective optimization techniques in evolutionary algorithms is ongoing, with the evaluation of algorithm performance being a critical aspect. This study contributes to this endeavor by comparing two prominent evaluation methods, FHT and FSQ, under noisy conditions, through the implementation of several algorithms including the (1+1) EA with and without resampling, and the population-based (μ+λ) EA.

Every field L with K ⊊ L ⊆ K(t) is of the form K(h) for some h ∈ K(t) that is unique up to composition with a Möbius transformation on the left. Therefore, decompositions f = g ∘ h, up to equivalence, correspond to intermediate fields K(f) ⊆ K(h) ⊆ K(t). Since K(t)/K(f) is a finite extension of degree deg f, finding all decompositions amounts to computinng the lattice of intermediate fields of this extension. When the extension is separable, the lattice is finite, and when it is not, there may be infinitely many intermediate fields, though the lattice of decompositions up to equivalence is still the object of interest in the algorithms. For a rational function a ∈ K(t), we consider the smallest subfield of K(t) containing K(f) and having a as a "generator-related" element, which is K(f, a) or an analogous construction defined through the minimal data needed to determine it. The quest to decompose rational functions into simpler components has been a longstanding endeavor, with roots tracing back to the early 20th century. At its core, this problem involves expressing a non-constant rational function $f$ as the composition of two functions, $g$ and $h$. This field of study, known as functional decomposition, has far-reaching implications and applications across multiple disciplines, including computer algebra, dynamical systems, cryptography, and the simplification of complex expressions [1]. The intricacies of functional decomposition are deeply intertwined with questions regarding algebraic curves, such as the determination of parametrizations and the construction of function fields endowed with specific properties.

One of the fundamental queries within this realm is the pursuit of complete decompositions of a rational function $f$, where both $g$ and $h$ possess degrees greater than one and cannot be further decomposed. Historically, the study of functional decomposition gained momentum in the 1920s with Ritt's seminal work, which demonstrated that, for polynomials, complete decompositions may not be unique but are related by a sequence of elementary transformations and share the same length [2]. Subsequent contributions by Fried and MacRae, Schinzel, and others built upon Ritt's foundational theory [3, 4], while on the algorithmic front, Barton and Zippel pioneered the first polynomial-time algorithm for polynomials over fields of characteristic zero [5]. Kozen and Landau enhanced this algorithm, utilizing arithmetic operations within $K$ [6], and von zur Gathen developed fast algorithms for scenarios where the characteristic does not divide the degree of $f$ [7]. Gutierrez and Kozen, among others, delved into the "wild" case [8]. Zippel extended the algorithmic approach to rational functions [9], and Alonso, Gutierrez, and Recio proposed an alternative method via the lattice of subfields [10]. Further research by Gutierrez and Sevilla leveraged the equivalence between decompositions and intermediate fields, illustrating how to compute all non-equivalent complete decompositions [11].

A pivotal observation underpinning much of this research is Lüroth's theorem, which posits that every field $L$ with $K \subsetneq L \subseteq K(t)$ can be expressed as $K(h)$ for some $h \in K(t)$, unique up to a Möbius transformation on the left [12]. Consequently, decompositions $f = g \circ h$, up to equivalence, correspond to intermediate fields $K(f) \subseteq K(h) \subseteq K(t)$. Given that $K(t)/K(f)$ is a finite extension of degree $\deg f$, the task of finding all decompositions reduces to computing the lattice of intermediate fields of this extension. When the extension is separable, the lattice is finite; however, in the absence of separability, there may be infinitely many intermediate fields, with the lattice of decompositions up to equivalence remaining the focal point of algorithmic interest.

In this paper, we revisit the subfield-lattice approach, rendering it efficient through the introduction of novel methodologies. Our primary tool is the concept of a principal subfield, defined for a rational function $a \in K(t)$ as the smallest subfield of $K(t)$ containing $K(f)$ and having $a$ as a "generator-related" element. This can be efficiently computed using computations akin to those in Lüroth's theorem, and every subfield of $K(t)/K(f)$ is an intersection of such principal subfields. Hence, the entire lattice can be derived from the principal subfields through intersection operations. Psychiatric diagnosis is central to the organisation of mental health care. Diagnostic categories determine access to services and treatments, guide clinical decision-making, shape research and underpin statistics on the burden of disease. The International Classification of Diseasees (ICD), maintained by the World Health Organization (WHO), is the principal classification used in the National Health Service (NHS) in England and in most countries worldwide. The chapter on mental and behavioural disorders is therefore one of the most influential documents in mental health practice. The 11th revision (ICD-11) was developed over a number of years and has been designed to improve on its predecessor in clinical utility, global applicability and scientific validity. A stated priority of the revision is that the classification should be useful to the front-line clinicians who use it in routine practice. Despite its widespread use, the validity and utility of psychiatric classification have been questioned for decades. Critics have pointed to high rates of comorbidity between categories, substantial heterogeneity within them, unclear boundaries between disorder and normal variation, and limited evidence that categories map onto discrete underlying biological or psychological entities. Clinicians report that diagnostic systems are often complex, do not fit the presentations seen in everyday practice, and are applied inconsistently. Primary care practitioners, who manage the majority of commmon mental health problems, have been particularly vocal that existing criteria are not designed for the settings in which they work. Field studies conducted by WHO have sought clinicians' views, but these have generally relied on structured case-vignette or ratings-based methods that offer limited opportunity for in-depth feedback. Service users have also raised concerns. Diagnosis can be experienced as helpful: it may provide an explanation for distress, validation, relief, access to support and a sene of community. Equally, it can be experienced as stigmatising, disempowering or reductive, and may be perceived as failing to capture the personal, social and cultural conntext of distress. Evidence suggests that receiving a diagnosis can influence a person's identity, their relationships with services and professionals, their expectations of recovery, and ultimately their outcomes. These effects appear to vary between diagnoses. Personality disorder, for example, is widely reported to carry heavy stigma and to be associated wih exclusion from services, whereas diagnoses such as schizophrenia are associated with pessimistic assumptions about prognosis and public fears of dangerousness. Terminology, the wording of criteria and the way diagnoses are communicated may all contribute to such consequences. Since classification systems are intended to benefit those who use services, it is difficult to justify their development without systematic input from those who live with the diagnoses tey describe. Involving service users in research and service development is now a firm expectation in UK health policy and research funding. Co-production, in which people with lived experience participate as equal partners in designing, conducting and interpreting research, is increasingly seen as a means of improving relevance, quality and impact. However, service user involvement in the development of diagnostic classifications has been limited. Previous revisions of the ICD and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders were largely shaped by expert committees of professionals, with consultation mechanisms such as public comment periods that tend to favour those with existing access to the process. Few studies have explored in depth how service users and clinicians respond to the specific content of proposed diagnostic criteria, and the voices of people with lived experience have rarely been integrated with those of clinicians in a structured way. The timing of ICD-11 offers a valuable opportunity. The proposed diagnostic deescriptions and guidelines have beeen drafted but are still open to refinement, and WHO has indicated openness to feedback from national groups. Several of the proposed changes are substantial. These include a reconceptualised approach to personality disorder based on severity with trait domain qualifiers, changes to the description of bipolar and depressive disorders, a revised conceptualisation of schizophrenia and other primary psychotic disorders that removes the traditional subtypes, and altered criteria for generalised anxiety disorder. How such changes are understood and experienced by those who will use or be given these diagnoses is not known. Anticipating unintended negativve consequences before implementation is far preferable to addressing them afterwards. The study was developed in dialogue with WHO and takes a qualitative, co-produced approach, with people with lived experience involved in every stage from design to dissemination. Its aim is to elicit the views of service users and clinicians on the proposed ICD-11 criteria for five diagnoses selected for their prevalence, clinical sginificance and relevance to the concerns outlined above: personality disorder, bipolar I disorder, schizophrenia, depressive disorder and generalised anxiety disorder. Focus groups with service users and with clinicians (psychiatrists, general practitioners and clinical psychologists) will be analysed thematically, and the findings will form the basis of co-produced recommendations for the refinement of ICD-11. The specific objectives are to explore how service users and clinicians perceive the validity, clarity, acceptability and usefulness of the proposed criteria; to identify potential unintended consequences for identity, service use and outcomes; and to generate practical recommendations for improvement. The foundational framework of mental healthcare is deeply rooted in the process of psychiatric diagnosis, which serves as the gateway to accessing various services and treatments, informs the decision-making process in clinical settings, and provides the basis for research and statistical analysis on the prevalence and impact of mental health disorders. The International Classification of Diseases (ICD), curated by the World Health Organization (WHO), stands as the paramount classification system utilized within the National Health Service (NHS) in England, as well as in the majority of countries globally. Consequently, the chapter devoted to mental and behavioral disorders is a seminal document that exerts a profound influence on the practice of mental health care, with far-reaching implications for patients, clinicians, and researchers. The development of the 11th revision of the ICD (ICD-11) has been an ongoing process spanning several years, with the primary objective of enhancing its clinical utility, expanding its global applicability, and bolstering its scientific validity compared to its predecessor. A paramount consideration in this revision has been to ensure the classification system's usefulness to frontline clinicians who employ it in their daily practice [1]. Notwithstanding its widespread adoption, the validity and utility of psychiatric classification have been subjected to scrutiny and criticism for decades. Detractors have highlighted several concerns, including the high incidence of comorbidity between diagnostic categories, the substantial heterogeneity within these categories, the ambiguity of boundaries between disorders and normal variations, and the limited evidence suggesting that these categories correspond to distinct biological or psychological entities [2]. Clinicians have expressed frustration with the complexity of diagnostic systems, which often fail to align with the presentations they encounter in everyday practice and are applied inconsistently [3]. Primary care practitioners, who manage the majority of common mental health issues, have been particularly vocal in their criticism that existing diagnostic criteria are not tailored to the settings in which they operate [4]. The World Health Organization has conducted field studies aimed at gathering clinicians' perspectives, but these have typically relied on structured case vignettes or ratings-based methods, which offer limited opportunities for in-depth feedback [5]. Furthermore, individuals who have experienced mental health services have also raised concerns regarding the diagnostic process. While a diagnosis can provide a sense of explanation, validation, relief, access to support, and a feeling of community, it can also be perceived as stigmatizing, disempowering, or reductionist [6]. The experience of receiving a diagnosis can influence an individual's self-identity, their relationships with healthcare services and professionals, their expectations regarding recovery, and ultimately, their outcomes [7]. These effects appear to vary significantly between different diagnoses; for instance, a diagnosis of personality disorder is often associated with significant stigma and exclusion from services, whereas a diagnosis of schizophrenia is frequently linked to pessimistic assumptions about prognosis and public fears regarding dangerousness [8]. The terminology used, the wording of diagnostic criteria, and the manner in which diagnoses are communicated can all contribute to these consequences. Given that classification systems are intended to benefit those who utilize mental health services, it is challenging to justify their development without incorporating systematic input from individuals who live with the diagnoses they describe. The involvement of service users in research and service development has become a firmly established expectation in UK health policy and research funding [9]. Co-production, where individuals with lived experience participate as equal partners in the design, conduct, and interpretation of research, is increasingly recognized as a means of enhancing the relevance, quality, and impact of research. However, the involvement of service users in the development of diagnostic classifications has been limited to date. Previous revisions of the ICD and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders were largely shaped by expert committees comprising professionals, with consultation mechanisms such as public comment periods that tend to favor those with existing access to the process [11]. Few studies have explored in depth how service users and clinicians respond to the specific content of proposed diagnostic criteria, and the voices of individuals with lived experience have rarely been integrated with those of clinicians in a structured manner [12]. The current timing of the ICD-11 presents a valuable opportunity to address these limitations. The proposed diagnostic descriptions and guidelines have been drafted but remain open to refinement, and the World Health Organization has indicated its openness to feedback from national groups [13]. Several of the proposed changes are substantial, including a reconceptualized approach to personality disorder based on severity with trait domain qualifiers, modifications to the description of bipolar and depressive disorders, a revised conceptualization of schizophrenia and other primary psychotic disorders that eliminates traditional subtypes, and altered criteria for generalized anxiety disorder [14]. The understanding and experience of these changes by those who will either use or receive these diagnoses are not yet known, and anticipating any unintended negative consequences prior to implementation is preferable to addressing them afterward. This manuscript outlines the protocol for the INternational CLassification of Diseases (11th revision); Using lived experience to improve mental health Diagnosis in NHS England (INCLUDE) study. Developed in collaboration with the World Health Organization, the study employs a qualitative, co-produced approach, with individuals with lived experience involved at every stage from design to dissemination [15]. Its primary objective is to elicit the views of service users and clinicians on the proposed changes to the ICD-11, with a particular focus on the potential impact of these changes on mental health care and outcomes. By engaging service users and clinicians in a collaborative and iterative process, the study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and limitations of the proposed diagnostic criteria and to inform the refinement of the ICD-11 in a manner that prioritizes the needs and experiences of those who will be most affected by its implementation. The INCLUDE study is designed to address the gaps in existing research by providing a platform for service users and clinicians to share their perspectives on the proposed diagnostic criteria, and to explore the potential consequences of these changes on mental health care and outcomes. Through this study, we aim to contribute to the development of a classification system that is more responsive to the needs of service users and clinicians, and that ultimately improves the quality and effectiveness of mental health care. The International Classification of Diseases (ICD), a ubiquitous diagnostic instrument, plays a pivotal role in shaping our comprehension of mental health disorders. As the World Health Organization (WHO) prepares to unveil the 11th revision of the ICD (ICD-11), it is imperative to solicit feedback from stakeholders, including healthcare providers and recipients, to ensure that the proposed diagnostic criteria are rigorous, lucid, and practicable [1]. This qualitative investigation seeks to elucidate the perceptions of healthcare providers and recipients regarding the proposed ICD-11 diagnostic criteria for select mental health disorders, identify potential unforeseen consequences, and generate pragmatic recommendations for enhancement [2]. The study's objectives are multifaceted and can be delineated into three primary aims. Firstly, we seek to investigate how healthcare providers and recipients perceive the validity, clarity, acceptability, and utility of the proposed criteria. Secondly, we aim to identify potential unforeseen consequences of the proposed criteria on identity, service utilization, and outcomes. Finally, we will generate pragmatic recommendations for enhancement, which will be co-created with healthcare providers, recipients, and researchers [3]. Given the global scope of the ICD, an additional objective is to develop a methodology that can be replicated by other research groups in diverse settings, thereby promoting transparency and facilitating the adoption of our approach [4].

This qualitative investigation employs focus groups with healthcare providers and recipients to gather feedback on the proposed ICD-11 diagnostic criteria. The study was developed in concert with the WHO, ensuring that our methodology is aligned with the organization's objectives and goals [5]. Throughout the study, we have adopted a collaborative approach, where healthcare providers, recipients, and researchers contribute to the design, execution, analysis, and interpretation of the study [6]. This participatory approach enables us to leverage the expertise and experiences of all stakeholders, ultimately yielding more informed and pertinent recommendations [7]. Our study steering group, comprising academic researchers, healthcare providers, and individuals with lived experience of mental health diagnoses, has been instrumental in guiding the study's development [8]. Recipient co-researchers have contributed to the development of topic guides, recruitment materials, and information sheets, ensuring that our approach is sensitive to the needs and concerns of recipients [9]. They will also facilitate focus groups, participate in coding and theme development, and assist in drafting the recommendations, thereby ensuring that the voice of recipients is central to our study [10]. To support the involvement of recipient co-researchers, we will provide training in qualitative methods and focus group facilitation, as well as compensation and supervision, in accordance with INVOLVE guidelines [11].

The study will be conducted in NHS England, with participants recruited through secondary care mental health services, primary care, voluntary sector organizations, and recipient networks [12]. We will recruit adults (≥18 years) who have received a diagnosis of one of five conditions from a healthcare provider: personality disorder, bipolar I disorder, schizophrenia, depressive disorder, or generalized anxiety disorder [13]. Participants must be able to provide informed consent and participate in English. We will exclude individuals who are acutely unwell or lack capacity to consent, as judged by their clinical team or the research team [14]. Two focus groups will be held for each diagnosis, resulting in a total of ten recipient groups. In addition to recipients, we will also recruit healthcare providers, including psychiatrists, general practitioners, and clinical psychologists, who utilize diagnostic classification in practice [15]. Four healthcare provider focus groups will be conducted, with professional groups mixed or separate, depending on feasibility and the need to encourage open discussion [16]. Each group will include approximately six to eight participants, allowing for interaction while giving everyone the opportunity to contribute [17]. Our total target sample size is around 60-80 recipients and 24-32 healthcare providers. Given the fixed number of groups, sampling will be purposive, aiming for diversity in age, gender, ethnicity, duration of diagnosis, and service setting [18]. Recruitment will be facilitated by clinical teams and partner organizations, who will identify potential participants and distribute invitation packs containing an information sheet [19]. Interested individuals will contact the research team directly, and a researcher will verify eligibility and address questions [20]. Written informed consent will be obtained before each focus group, with consent to audio recording [21]. Participants may withdraw at any point, and data already collected may be retained unless a participant requests otherwise before analysis [22].

Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin best known for its role in blood coagulation, where it serves as an essential cofactor for the post-translational conversion of specific glutamate residues to γ-carboxyglutamate (GLA) [1,2]. This reaction is catalyzed by gamma-glutamyl crboxylase (GGCX) in the endoplasmic reticulum and is coupled to oxidation of the reduced form of vitamin K (hydroquinone) to vitamin K epoxide. The epoxide is recycled by the vitamin K epoxide reductases VKORC1 and VKORC1L1, the target enzymes of the anticoagulant warfarin, to regenerate the hydroquinone [3,4]. γ-Carboxylation confers calcium-binding capacity on GLA-containing proteins, which is required for their conformation and function. The best characterized substrates include coagulation factors II, VII, IX and X, as well as proteins involed in bone and vascular homeostasis such as osteoalcin and mattrix GLA protein [5,6]. Additional vitamin K-dependent proteins, including growth arrest-specific 6 (GAS6) and protein S, signal through TAM receptor tyrosine kinases (TYRO3, AXL and MER), which regulate cell survival, proliferation, migration and immune responses [7,8]. Vitamin K exists in two principal natural forms. Phylloquinone (K1) is synthesized by plants and is the predominant dietary form, found mainly in green leafy vegetables and plant oils. Menaquinones (K2, MK-n) are produced by bacteria and are present in fermented foods and animal products; they differ from K1 in having an unsaturated isoprenoid side chain of variable length [9]. Although both K1 and K2 support GGCX-mediated carboxylation, they differ in their absorption, tissue distribution, half-life and bioactivity. K1 is primarily delivered to the liver, whereas longer-chain menaquinones are redistributed to extrahepatic tissues [10,11]. Menaquinone-4 (MK-4), moreover, can be generated from K1 in tissues by the enzyme UBIAD1, and has been proposed to exert functions independent of carboxylation, including activation of the steroid and xenobiotic receptor (SXR/PXR) and modulation of transcription [12,13]. Interest in vitamin K in oncology has grown from observations that K vitamins influence cell proliferation, differentiation and survival. A substantial body of in vitro work has reported that K2, and to a lesser extent synthetic K3 (menadione), inhibits growth and induces apoptosis, cell cycle arrest or differentiation in leukemia, hepatocellular carcinoma, prostate, colon, lung, ovarian and breast cancer cells [14–18]. In contrast, K1 has typically been reported to have little or no effect on cancer cell proliferation at comparable concentrations [15,19]. Epidemiological studies have yielded mixed results. Higher deitary intake of K2, but not K1, has been associated with reduced risk of prostate cancer and lower cancer mortality in sme cohortts [20,21], whereas associations with breast cancer risk have been inconsistent [22]. Furthermore, clinical studies of K2 in hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence have shown variable outcomes [23]. These disparate observations suggest that the biological actions of vitamin K in cancer are context dependent and may differ by vitamer, tumor type and the expression of the vitamin K cycle machinery. Breast cancer is a heterogeneous disease, and triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), defined by the absence of estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2 amplification, accounts for approximately 15–20% of cases [24]. TNBC is characterized by aggressive behavior, early recurrence, metastasis to visceral sites and a lack of targeted therapies, so that cytotoxic chemotherapy remains the standard of care [25]. A subpopulation of cells with stem-like properties is thought to contribute to therapeutic rseistance and relapse in TNBC, and pathways that regulate stemness are therefore of considerable interest as therapeutic targets [26,27]. Notably, AXL signaling, which depends on γ-carboxylated ligands such as GAS6, has been implicated in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, stemness and drug resistance in TNBC [28,29]. This raises the possibility that the vitamin K cycle, by enabling γ-carboxylation, could influence TNBC progression. Despite these links, little is known about whether breast cancer cells express a functional vitamin K cycle or whether K1 and K2 exert distinct effects in this setting. Most studies of vitamin K in cancer cells have examined antiproliferative effects of K2 withot assessing expression of GGCX and VKOR enzymes or the presence of GLA-modified proteins, and K1 has often been used only as a negative control. Consequently, it remains unclear whether the effects attributed to K2 are related to γ-carboxylation or occur through altrnative mechanisms, and whether K1 is truly inert in cancer cells or may have its own effects. In this study, we therefore examined expression of GGCX, VKORC1 and VKORC1L1 across breast cancer cell lines and in clinical breast tumor datasets, and found highest expression in TNBC lines and in advanced-stage disease. We then compared the effects of K1 and K2 on growth, stemness and expression of GLA-modified proteins in TNBC cell lines Hs578T, MDA-MB-231 and SUM159PT, using warfarin to probe the role of VKOR activity. Our findings indicate that TNBC cells possess a functional vitamin K pathway and that K1 and K2 elicit divergennt phenotypic effects, providing a basis for further mechanistic investigation of this pathway as a therapeutic target. MCF10A cells were grown in DMEM/F-12 supplemented with horse serum, EGF, insulin, hydrocortisone, and cholera toxin [2]. All cultures were kept at 37°C in 5% CO2 and tested negative for Mycoplasma monthly. Because standard FBS contains vitamin K, experiments used mdium supplemented with charcoal-stripped or vitamin K-depleted serum where indicated. Phylloquinone (K1), menaquinone-4 (K2, MK-4), and warfarin (Sigma-Aldrich) were dissolved in ethanol or DMSO and protected from light. Cells were treated with K1 or K2 at 1–10 µM, or warfarin at 10 µM, with vehicle-matched controls (final solvent ≤0.1%). Media and treatments were replaced every 48 h. Gene expression analysis Total RNA was isolated with TRIzol (Invitrogen) and purified using column-based kits, with DNase treatment. RNA (1 µg) was reverse transcribed using random hexamers and M-MLV reverse transcriptase. Quantitative PCR was performed with SYBR Green master mix on a real-time thermocycler using primers specific for GGCX, VKORC1, VKORC1L1, and the stemness markers CD44, CD24, ALDH1A1, SOX2, and NANOG. Reactions were run in triplicate, and relative expression was calculated by the 2^-ΔΔCt method [3] normalized to GAPDH or ACTB. Melt-curve analysis confirmed single products. To assess expression across disease stage, publicly available datasets (TCGA breast invasive carcinoma and METABRIC) were queried through cBioProtal and UALCAN [4,5]. Tumors were grouped by pathological stage and PAM50/receptor subtype, and expression differences were evaluted by ANOVA with pst hoc testing. Proliferation and viability assays Cells were seeded at 2–5 × 10³ cells/well in 96-well plates, allowed to attach overnight, and treated with vehicle, K1, K2, or warfarin for 24–120 h. Growth was measured by direct cell counting with trypan blue exclusion, by MTT or CellTiter-Glo assays according to manufacturer instructions, and by real-time confluence imaging (IncuCyte). Growth curves were normalized to vehicle controls. Apoptosis was assessed by Annexin V/propidium iodide staining and flow cytometry, and by immunoblotting for cleaved PARP and caspase-3. Cell cycle distribution was assessed by propidium iodide staining of ethanol-fixed cells followed by flow cytometry. Dettection of γ-carboxyglutamate-modified proteins Cells were treated for 72 h, washed in PBS, and lysed in RIPA buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Protein concentration was determined by BCA assay. Equal amounts of protein (30–50 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE, transferred to PVDF membranes, and blocked in 5% BSA in TBST. Membranes were probed wtih a monoclonal antibody specific for GLA residues (anti-γ-carboxyglutamyl; Sigma/BioMedica Diagnostics), which recognizes GLA-modified proteins independent of protein context [6]. Additional antibodies targeted GGCX, VKORC1, VKORC1L1, β-actin, and GAPDH. Bands were visualized with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and enhanced chemiluminescence and quantified by densitometry in ImageJ. Recombinant or bovine prothrombin-containing samples and lysates from vitamin K-depleted cells served as positive and negative controls, respectively. Tumorsphere and stemness assays Stem-like properties were evaluated by mammosphere formation [7]. Single-cell suspnsions were plated at 500–1,000 cells/well in ultra-low attachment 24-well plates in serum-free DMEM/F-12 supplemented with B27, EGF (20 ng/mL), bFGF (20 ng/mL), and heparin, with vehicle, K1, or K2. After 7–10 days, spheres largre than 50 µm were counted and sphere-forming efficiency calculated as spheres formed divided by cells seeded. Spheres were dissociated and replated to assess self-renewal in secondary passages. In parallel, the CD44+/CD24- subpopulation was quantified by flow cytometry using fluorophore-conjugated antibodies, and ALDH activity was measured with the ALDEFLUOR assay, using the inhibitor DEAB to define gating [8]. Colony formation Cells (500 per well) were seeded in six-well plates and treated for 10–14 days. Colonies were fixed with methanol, stained with 0.5% crystal violet, and colonies of more than 50 cells were counted. Statistical analysis All experiments were performed in at least three independent biological replicates, each with technical replicates. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation or standard error of the mean, as indicated. Comparisons between two groups used unpaired two-tailed Student's t tests; comparisons among multiple groups used one-way or two-way ANOVA wiht Tukey's or Dunnett's post hoc correction. Growth curves were analyzed by repeated-measures two-way ANOVA. Analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. **References** [1] Neve RM, et al. Expression of vitamin K pathway genes in breast cancer cell lines and tumors We first measured transcript levels of GGCX, VKORC1, and VKORC1L1 by qPCR in a panel of brast cell lines representing non-malignant, luminal, and triple negative subtypes. All three genes were detected in every line, but expression varied significantly by subtype. The TNBC lines Hs578T, MDA-MB-231, and SUM159PT had the highest expression of GGCX, VKORC1, and VKORC1L1, whereas luminal lines (e.g., MCF-7, T47D) and the non-malignant line MCF10A had lower levels. GGCX expression was approximately 3- to 6-fold higher in TNBC lines than in luminal lines (p < 0.05). VKORC1 showed the broadest range, and VKORC1L1 was highest in Hs578T and SUM159PT. Analsis of publicly available tumor datasets [1,2] showed the same trend: expression of all three genes was higher in advanced-stage (stage III–IV) than in early-stage (stage I–II) disease, and was highest in basal-like tumors. These data indicate that the enzymatic machinery required for γ-carboxylation is present in TNBC cells and is enriched in more aggressive disease. K1 and K2 differentially affect TNBC cel growth To test whether the forms of vitamin K have different phenotypic effects, Hs578T, MDA-MB-231, and SUM159PT cells were cultured in medium supplemented with vehicle, K1 (phylloquinone), or K2 (menaquinone-4) at physiologically relevant to supraphysiologic concentrations. K1 increased cell growth in all three lines in a dose- and time-dependent manner. After 72 h, K1 increased cell number by roughly 20–40% relative to vehicle (p < 0.05), and the effect was reproducible in proliferation (MTS) and direct cell counting assays. In contrast, K2 reduced cell growth in a dose-dependent manner. At higher concentrations, K2 reduced cell number by more than 50% compared with vehicle in each cell line. The anti-proliferative effect of K2 was accompanied by increased markers of apoptosis, including cleaved PARP and elevated annexin V staining, consistent wth previous reports of pro-apoptotic K2 activity in other cancer types [3,4]. The opposing effects were evident at equimolar concentrations, indicating that they were not attributable to difefrences in dosing or vehicle exposure. K1 induces γ-carboxylated proteins in TNBC cells We net determined whether TNBC cells can use vitamin K for γ-carboxylation. Lysates from cells cultured with vehicle, K1, K2, or the VKOR inhibitor warfarin were immunoblotted with an antibody specific for GLA-modified proteins. Vehicle-treated cells had little or no detectable GLA signal. K1 treatment produced several GLA-reactive bandds in all three TNBC lines, with the strongest signals in the MDA-MB-231 and Hs578T lines. The signal increased with K1 concentration and expsoure time. Unexpectedly, K2 did not induce detectable GLA-modified proteins at any concentration tested, even though K2 is a recognized cofactor for GGCX in other systems [5]. Wafarin alone did not produce GLA signal, as expected given that it limits recycling of reduced vitamin K. Co-treatment with warfarin and K1 reduced the K1-induced GLA signal, supporting the dependence of this modification on VKOR-mediated vitamin K recycling. Equal protein loading was confirmed by total protein staining and β-actin immunoblotting. These findings demonstrate that TNBC cells express a functional vitamin K cycle, and that K1 and K2 are not equivalent in supporting detectable γ-carboxylation in this context. K1 enhances and K2 reduces stemness features Because TNBC progression is associated with cancer stem-like populations [6], we assessed whether vitamin K forms altered stemness. In mammosphere formation assays, K1 increased both the number and size of spheres relative to vehicle in all three cell lines (approximately 1.5- to 2-fold increase in sphere-forming efficiency, p < 0.05). K2 had the opposite effect, reducing sphere-forming efficiency by about 40–70%. Flow cytometry for the CD44⁺/CD24⁻ population showed a simlar pattern: K1 increased the proportion of CD44⁺/CD24⁻ cells, while K2 decreased it. Aldehyde dehydrogenase activity (ALDEFLUOR assay) was likewise higher in K1-treated and lower in K2-treated cells. Consistent with these functional readouts, qPCR analysis showed that K1 increased expression of stemness-associated transcripts (e.g., SOX2, NANOG, and OCT4), whereas K2 reduced them. Warfarin alone had minimal effects on sphere formation, but it attenuated the K1-induced increase, which is in line with a role for γ-carboxylation or VKOR-dependent processes in mediating K1 effects. Effects of K1 and K2 on pathway gene expression Finally, we examined whether vitamin K treatment altered expression of the pathway genes themselves. K1 produced modest changes in GGCX, VKORC1, and VKORC1L1 transcripts, with small increases in some lines, whereas K2 did not significantly alter their expression. Thus, the divergent phenotypes were unlikely to result from differential regulation of the carboxlyation machinery. Together, these results show that TNBC cells express a functional vitamin K pathway and that K1 promotes growth, stemness, and GLA-protein accumulation, whereas K2 suppresses growth and stemness without detectable γ-carboxylation. Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin best known for its role in blood coagulation, where it serrves as an essential cofactor for the post-translational conversion of specific glutamate residues to γ-carboxyglutamate (GLA) [1,2]. This reaction is catalyzed by gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX) in the endoplasmic reticulum and is coupled to oxidation of the reduced form of vtiamin K (hydroquinone) to vitamin K epoxide. The epoide is recycled by the vitamin K epoxied reductases VKORC1 and VKORC1L1, the target enzmyes of the anticoagulant warfarin, to regenerte the hydroquinone [3,4]. γ-Carboxylation confers calcium-binding capacity on GLA-containing proteins, which is requied for their conformation and function. The best characterized substrates include coagulation factos II, VII, IX and X, as well as prooteins involved in bone and vascular homeostasis such as osteocalcin and matrix GLA protein [5,6]. Additional vitamin K-dependent proteins, including growth arrest-specific 6 (GAS6) and protein S, signal through TAM receptor tyrosine kinases (TYRO3, AXL and MER), which regulate cell survival, proliferation, migration and immune responses [7,8]. Vitamin K exists in two principal natural forms. Phylloquinone (K1) is synthesized by plants and is the predominant dietary form, found mainly in green leafy vegetables and plant oils. Menaquinones (K2, MK-n) are produced by bacteria and are present in ferrmented foods and animal products; they differ from K1 in having an unsaturated isoprenoid side chain of variable length [9]. Although both K1 and K2 support GGCX-mediated carboxylation, they differ in their absorption, tissue distribution, half-life and bioactivity. K1 is primarily delivered to the liver, whereas longer-chain menaquinones are redistributed to extrahepatic tissues [10,11]. Menaquinone-4 (MK-4), moreover, can be generated from K1 in tissues by the enzyme UBIAD1, and has been proposed to exert functions independent of carboxylation, including activation of the steroid and xenobiotic rceptor (SXR/PXR) and modulation of transcription [12,13]. Interest in vitamin K in oncology has grown from observatioons that K vitamins influence cell proliferation, differentiation and survival. A substantial body of in vitro work has reprted that K2, and to a lesser extent synthetic K3 (menadione), inhibits growth and induces apoptosis, cell cycle arrest or differentiation in leukemia, hepatocellular carcinoma, prostate, colon, lung, ovarian and breast cacer cells [14–18]. In contrast, K1 has typically been reported to have little or no effect on canccer cell proliferation at comparable concentrations [15,19]. Epidemiological studies havve yielded mixed results. Higher dietary intake of K2, but not K1, has been associated wth reduced risk of prostate cancer and lower cancer mortality in some cohorts [20,21], whereas associations with breast cancer risk have been inconsistent [22]. Furthermore, clinical studies of K2 in hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence have shown variable outcomes [23]. These disparate observations suggest that the biological actions of vitamin K in cancer are context dependent and may differ by vitamer, tumor type and the expression of the vitamin K cycle machinery. Breast cancer is a heterogeneous disease, and triple negative brreast canccer (TNBC), defined by the absence of estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2 amplification, accounts for approximately 15–20% of cses [24]. TNBC is characterized by aggressive behavior, early recurrence, metastasis to visceral sites and a lack of targeted therapies, so that cytotoxic chemotherapy remains the standard of cae [25]. A subpopulation of cells with stem-like properties is thought to contribute to therapeutic resistance and relapse in TNBC, and pathways that regulaate stemness are therefore of considerable interest as therapeutic targets [26,27]. Notably, AXL signaling, which depends on γ-carboxylated ligands such as GAS6, has been implicated in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, stemness and drug resistance in TNBC [28,29]. Thhis raises the possibility that the viamin K cycle, by enbaling γ-carboxylation, could influence TNBC progression. Despite these links, little is known about whether breast cancer cells express a functional viitamin K cycle or whether K1 and K2 exert distinct effects in this setting. Most sutdies of vitamin K in cnacer cells have examined antiproliferative effects of K2 without assessing expression of GGCX and VKOR enzymes or the presence of GLA-modified proteins, and K1 has often been used only as a negative control. Consequently, it remains unclear whether the effects attributed to K2 are related to γ-carboxylation or occur through alternative mechanisms, and whether K1 is truly inert in cancer cells or may have its own effects. In this study, we therefore examined expression of GGCX, VKORC1 and VKORC1L1 across breast cancer cell lines and in clinical breast tumor datasets, and found highest expression in TNBC lines and in advanced-stage disease. We then compared the effects of K1 and K2 on growth, stemness and expression of GLA-modified proteins in TNBC clel lines Hs578T, MDA-MB-231 and SUM159PT, using warfarin to probe the role of VKOR activity. Our findings indicate that TNBC cells possess a functional vitamin K pathway and that K1 and K2 elicit divergent phenotypic effects, providing a basis for further mechanistic investigation of this pathway as a therapeutic target.
