This enzymatic reaction, which is facilitated by the enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX) within the endoplasmic reticulum, is intimately linked to the oxidation of vitamin K hydroquinone to its epoxide form. Subsequently, the epoxide is regenerated to its reduced form through the actions of vitamin K epoxide reductases, specifically VKORC1 and VKORC1L1, which are targeted by the anticoagulant warfarin [3,4]. The resulting γ-carboxylation reaction imparts calcium-binding properties to Gla-containing proteins, thereby modulating their conformation and functionality. Notable substrates of this reaction include coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins involved in bone and vascular homeostasis, such as osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein [5,6]. Beyond its established function in coagulation, vitamin K has also been implicated in various cellular signaling pathways that regulate cellular survival, proliferation, migration, and immune responses. For instance, growth arrest-specific 6 (GAS6) and protein S, both of which are vitamin K-dependent proteins, interact with TAM receptor tyrosine kinases (TYRO3, AXL, and MER) to modulate cellular processes [7,8]. These signaling pathways are essential for maintaining tissue homeostasis and preventing disease progression. Vitamin K exists in two primary natural forms: phylloquinone (K1) and menaquinones (K2, MK-n). Phylloquinone, synthesized by plants, is the predominant dietary form, primarily found in green leafy vegetables and plant oils. In contrast, menaquinones, produced by bacteria, are present in fermented foods and animal products, distinguished by an unsaturated isoprenoid side chain of varying length [9]. Although both K1 and K2 support GGCX-mediated carboxylation, they exhibit distinct differences in absorption, tissue distribution, half-life, and bioactivity. K1 is primarily targeted to the liver, whereas longer-chain menaquinones are redistributed to extrahepatic tissues [10,11]. Menaquinone-4 (MK-4), which can be generated from K1 in tissues via the enzyme UBIAD1, has been proposed to exert functions independent of carboxylation, including activation of the steroid and xenobiotic receptor (SXR/PXR) and modulation of transcriptional activity [12,13]. In recent years, the potential role of vitamin K in oncology has garnered significant interest. A substantial body of in vitro research has demonstrated that K2, and to a lesser extent synthetic K3 (menadione), inhibits growth and induces apoptosis, cell cycle arrest, or differentiation in various cancer cell types, including leukemia, hepatocellular carcinoma, prostate, colon, lung, ovarian, and breast cancer cells [14–18]. In contrast, K1 has typically been reported to have minimal or no effect on cancer cell proliferation at comparable concentrations [15,19]. Epidemiological studies have yielded mixed results, with some suggesting that higher dietary intake of K2, but not K1, is associated with reduced risk of prostate cancer and lower cancer mortality [20,21]. However, associations with breast cancer risk have been inconsistent [22], and clinical studies of K2 in hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence have shown variable outcomes [23]. These disparate findings suggest that the biological actions of vitamin K in cancer are context-dependent and may vary by vitamer, tumor type, and the expression of vitamin K cycle machinery. Breast cancer is a heterogeneous disease, with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) accounting for approximately 15–20% of cases [24]. TNBC is characterized by aggressive behavior, early recurrence, metastasis to visceral sites, and a lack of targeted therapies, rendering cytotoxic chemotherapy the standard of care [25]. A subpopulation of cells with stem-like properties is thought to contribute to therapeutic resistance and relapse in TNBC, and pathways regulating stemness are therefore of considerable interest as therapeutic targets [26,27]. Notably, AXL signaling, which depends on γ-carboxylated ligands such as GAS6, has been implicated in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, stemness, and drug resistance in TNBC [28,29]. This raises the possibility that the vitamin K cycle, by enabling γ-carboxylation, could influence TNBC progression. In the realm of cancer research, the investigation of cell lines and culture conditions is a vital aspect, as it enables the development of accurate models for studying the disease. To this end, our laboratory acquired several human breast cancer cell lines, including Hs578T, MDA-MB-231, SUM159PT, MCF-7, and T47D, as well as the non-tumorigenic mammary epithelial line MCF10A, from reputable sources such as ATCC and Asterand. To verify the authenticity of these cell lines, we employed short tandem repeat profiling, a widely accepted method for verifying the identity of cell lines [1]. The culture conditions for each cell line were meticulously optimized to mimic the in vivo environment as closely as possible. For instance, Hs578T and MDA-MB-231 cells were maintained in a specialized medium, Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium (DMEM), supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), while SUM159PT cells required a more customized medium, Ham's F-12, with 5% FBS, insulin (5 µg/mL), and hydrocortisone (1 µg/mL). Similarly, MCF-7 and T47D cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 with 10% FBS [1]. In contrast, the non-tumorigenic MCF10A cells were grown in a DMEM/F-12 medium supplemented with horse serum, epidermal growth factor (EGF), insulin, hydrocortisone, and cholera toxin [2]. All cell cultures were maintained at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2 and were regularly tested for Mycoplasma contamination to ensure the integrity of our experiments. Given that standard FBS contains vitamin K, which can influence the results of experiments involving this vitamin, we used medium supplemented with charcoal-stripped or vitamin K-depleted serum where indicated. Phylloquinone (K1), menaquinone-4 (K2, MK-4), and warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist, were dissolved in ethanol or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and protected from light to prevent degradation. Cells were treated with K1 or K2 at concentrations ranging from 1 to 10 µM, or with warfarin at 10 µM, with vehicle-matched controls to account for any potential effects of the solvent, which was limited to ≤0.1% in all experiments. The media and treatments were replaced every 48 hours to maintain a consistent environment.

Gene expression analysis is a crucial component of understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying cancer. Total RNA was isolated from the cells using TRIzol (Invitrogen) and purified using column-based kits, with DNase treatment to eliminate any residual DNA. The RNA (1 µg) was then reverse-transcribed using random hexamers and M-MLV reverse transcriptase. Quantitative PCR was performed using SYBR Green master mix on a real-time thermocycler, with primers specific for genes of interest, including GGCX, VKORC1, VKORC1L1, and stemness markers such as CD44, CD24, ALDH1A1, SOX2, and NANOG. Reactions were run in triplicate to ensure reliability, and relative expression levels were calculated by the 2^-ΔΔCt method [3], normalized to either GAPDH or ACTB. To gain insights into the expression of these genes across different stages of breast cancer, we queried publicly available datasets, including The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) breast invasive carcinoma and Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium (METABRIC), through cBioPortal and UALCAN [4,5]. Tumors were grouped based on their pathological stage and PAM50/receptor subtype, and differences in gene expression were evaluated using analysis of variance (ANOVA) with post hoc testing to account for multiple comparisons.

Proliferation and viability assays are essential for understanding how different treatments affect cell growth. Cell growth was measured by direct cell counting with trypan blue exclusion, by MTT or CellTiter-Glo assays according to the manufacturer's instructions, and by real-time confluence imaging using the IncuCyte system. Growth curves were normalized to vehicle controls to facilitate comparisons. Apoptosis, a key mechanism of cell death, was assessed by Annexin V/propidium iodide staining and flow cytometry, as well as by immunoblotting. Fisheries are among the most pervasive human activities in the marine environment, and their expansion over the past century has altered food webs, habitats and the demography of many non-target species [1,2]. Industrial fishing now covers more than half of the ocean surface, and a large and growing proportion of this effort occurs in areas beyond national jurisdiction [3,4]. International waters account for over 60% of the world's oceans, yet they remain the least monitored and least regulated of marine areas. Management relies on regional fisheries management organisations, whose capacity to enforce regulations is limited by the vast sclae of the area and by incomplete reporting of catch, effort and bycatch [5,6]. Consequently, how fisheries in these regions shape ecosystem processes is surprisingly poorly understood. Monitoring of fishing activity at sea has traditionally depended on logbooks, onboard observers and, moe recently, vessel monitoring systems (VMS) and the Automatic Identification System (AIS). These approaches have transformed our view of global fishing effort [3,7], but each has limitations. Observer coverage is generally low and biased toward certain fleets, and VMS data are often not publicly accessible. AIS transmissions can be switched off or spoofed, and vessels engaged in illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing have a strong incentive to avoid detection [8,9]. Satellite-based radar and optical imagery can detect non-broadcasting vessels, but coverage is intermittent, limited by cloud and resolution, and costly to apply across ocean basins [10]. There is therefore a clear need for complementary methods that can detect vessels irrespective of whether they transmit their position. Seabirds are among the taxa most affected by fisheries. Many species are attracted to vessels, where they exploit discards, offal and baited hooks, and this behavior brings them into contact with fishing gear [11,12]. Incidental mortality in longline and trawl fisheries is considered the primary threat to albatrosses and large petrels, and it has contributed to the fact that albatrosses are now among the most threatened groups of birds, with most species listed as threatened or near-threatened [13,14]. At the smae time, access to fishery waste may provide a food subsidy that influences foraging behavior, diet, breeding success and population dynamics [15,16]. Quantifying the interaction between seabirds and fisheries is therefore essential both for assessing bycatch risk and for understanding the wider ecological consequences of fishing. Most assessments of this interaction havve been based on the spatial overlap between the distributions of tracked birsd and the distributions of fishing effort, derived from VMS or AIS data [17,18]. Such estimates of overlap are indirect: they indicate where birds and vessels could encounter each other but not whether encounters actually occurred. Overlap analyses are also constrained by the resolution and completeness of the fisheries data, and they are likely to underestimate exposure in international waters where vessel data are sparse or absent [19]. Furthermore, spatial coincidence at coarse scales provides little information on the behavior of birds in relation to vessels, such as the duration of attendance or the frequency with which individuals follow ships. Direct obseravtions of seabird–vessel interactions are needed to resolve these uncertainties. Recent advances in biologging provide such an opportunity. Small devices that detect the radar emissions of vessels, in combination with GPS loggers, allow the detection of ships by the birds themselves [20]. Because the marine radars carried by most vessels operate continuously, particularly at night and in poor visibility, such devices can record encounters between birds and vessels, including those from vessels that do not transmit AIS, and can thus reveal the true extent of overlap. Initial deeployments on albatrosses and other seabirds in restricted regions have shown that this approach can detect IUU activity and quantify encounter rates [20,21]. Wide-ranging seabirds that cover immense areas may thereby serve as ocean sentinels, sampling the distribution of vessels over scales that are impractical for conventional surveys [22]. The wandering albatross (*Diomedea exulans*) is an ideal model for this approach. It is a wide-ranging, long-lived species that exploits the winds of the Southern Ocean to travel thousands of kilometers during foraging trips, and individuals are known to be attracted to fishing vesses [23,24]. Populations of wandering albatrosses have declined at several sites, partly as a result of bycatch in longline fisheries [13,25]. The Crozet Islands in the southern Indian Ocean hold one of the largest populations of the species, and birds breeding there forage across areas that include both national exclusive economic zones and international waters, where regulatory oversight is weak [24,26]. Desite decades of tracking, how often these birds actually encounter vessels, and where, remains unknown. Here, we used loggers combining GPS and radar detection, deployed on wandering albatrosses breeding at the Crozet Islands, to measure the true extent of overlap between albatrosses and fishing vessels. Our objectives were to (i) quantify the area patrolled by breeding albatrosses and the distances reached from the colony; (ii) determine the proportion of birds that detected vessels and the frequency of detections; (iii) compare detections with the distribution of vessels broadcasting AIS to estimate the proportioon of non-broadcasting vessels; and (iv) generate estimates of the intensity of fishing and the distribution of vessels in international waters. We predicted that encounter rates would be higher than expected from overlap analyses based on AIS and VMS, particularly in ares beyond national jurisdiction. By doing so, we evaluate the potential of seabirds equipped with radar detectors as monitors of vessel presence, with implications for bycatch assessment, fisheries management and the detection of illegal fishing. The profound impact of fishing operations on the health of marine ecosystems has become a paramount concern, as the substantial expansion of the industry over the past century has had far-flung repercussions for the intricate networks of species interactions, the integrity of habitats, and the population dynamics of numerous non-target species [1,2]. The magnitude of industrial fishing activities is nothing short of astonishing, with current operations encompassing more than half of the world's oceanic surface, and a considerable proportion of these efforts concentrated in areas beyond the jurisdiction of national governments [3,4]. These international waters, which comprise over 60% of the global ocean, remain the most poorly monitored and least regulated of all marine areas, with their management reliant on regional fisheries management organizations that often face significant challenges in enforcing regulations due to the vast expanse of the area and the incomplete reporting of catch, fishing effort, and bycatch [5,6]. Consequently, our comprehension of the ways in which fisheries in these regions influence ecosystem processes is surprisingly limited. Traditional approaches to monitoring fishing activities at sea, such as the use of logbooks, onboard observers, and vessel monitoring systems (VMS) and the Automatic Identification System (AIS), have revolutionized our understanding of global fishing effort [3,7]. Nevertheless, each of these methods has its own set of limitations. The coverage of observers is often sparse and biased towards specific fleets, while VMS data are frequently inaccessible to the public. Furthermore, AIS transmissions can be intentionally disabled or falsified, and vessels engaged in illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing have a strong incentive to avoid detection [8,9]. The use of satellite-based radar and optical imagery can detect vessels that do not broadcast their position, but such coverage is intermittent, limited by cloud cover and resolution, and prohibitively expensive to apply across entire ocean basins [10]. This underscores the need for complementary approaches that can detect vessels regardless of whether they transmit their location. Seabirds are among the taxa most severely impacted by fisheries, with many species drawn to vessels where they exploit discarded catch, offal, and baited hooks, thereby bringing them into contact with fishing gear [11,12]. The incidental mortality of seabirds in longline and trawl fisheries is a major concern, with albatrosses and large petrels being particularly vulnerable [13,14]. In fact, albatrosses are now considered one of the most threatened groups of birds, with most species listed as threatened or near-threatened. At the same time, access to fishery waste can provide a food subsidy that influences foraging behavior, diet, breeding success, and population dynamics [15,16]. Quantifying the interaction between seabirds and fisheries is therefore essential for assessing bycatch risk and understanding the broader ecological consequences of fishing. Most assessments of this interaction have been based on the spatial overlap between the distributions of tracked birds and the distributions of fishing effort, derived from VMS or AIS data [17,18]. However, these estimates of overlap are indirect, indicating only where birds and vessels could potentially encounter each other, rather than confirming whether encounters actually occurred. Moreover, overlap analyses are constrained by the resolution and completeness of the fisheries data, and are likely to underestimate exposure in international waters where vessel data are sparse or absent [19]. Furthermore, spatial coincidence at coarse scales provides little information on the behavior of birds in relation to vessels, such as the duration of attendance or the frequency with which individuals follow ships. Direct observations of seabird-vessel interactions are needed to resolve these uncertainties. Recent advances in biologging technology have provided a new opportunity to address this knowledge gap. Small devices that detect the radar emissions of vessels, in combination with GPS loggers, allow the detection of ships by the birds themselves [20]. Because marine radars carried by most vessels operate continuously, particularly at night and in poor visibility, these devices can record encounters between birds and vessels, including those from vessels that do not transmit AIS, and can thus reveal the true extent of overlap. Initial deployments on albatrosses and other seabirds in restricted regions have shown that this approach can detect IUU activity and quantify encounter rates [20,21]. Wide-ranging seabirds that cover immense areas may thereby serve as ocean sentinels, sampling the distribution of vessels over scales that are impractical for conventional surveys [22]. The wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans) is an ideal model species for this approach. As a wide-ranging, long-lived species that exploits the winds of the Southern Ocean to travel thousands of kilometers during foraging trips, individuals are known to be attracted to fishing vessels [23,24]. Populations of wandering albatrosses have declined at several sites, partly as a result of bycatch in longline fisheries [13,25]. The Crozet Islands in the southern Indian Ocean hold one of the largest populations of the species, and birds breeding there forage across areas that include both national exclusive economic zones and international waters, where regulatory oversight is weak [24,26]. Despite decades of tracking, the frequency and location of encounters between these birds and vessels remain unknown. In this study, we used loggers combining GPS and radar detection, deployed on wandering albatrosses breeding at the Crozet Islands, to measure the true extent of overlap between these birds and fishing vessels, and to quantify the frequency and location of their encounters. By doing so, we aimed to provide novel insights into the interactions between seabirds and fisheries, and to inform the development of effective conservation and management strategies for these iconic species. Our approach also highlights the potential of seabirds as indicators of the impact of fisheries on marine ecosystems, and demonstrates the value of combining cutting-edge technology with rigorous scientific research to address the complex challenges facing our oceans. The implications of our findings are far-reaching, and underscore the need for continued innovation and collaboration in the pursuit of sustainable and responsible fisheries management. Ultimately, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between seabirds, fisheries, and the marine environment, and provides a foundation for the development of more effective conservation and management strategies for these critically important species. By exploring the complex interactions between seabirds and fisheries, we can gain a more nuanced understanding of the impacts of human activities on marine ecosystems, and work towards a more sustainable future for our oceans. The use of biologging technology, in particular, offers a powerful tool for monitoring and managing the interactions between seabirds and fisheries, and has the potential to inform the development of more effective conservation and management strategies for these species. As we continue to face the challenges of managing the world's oceans, it is essential that we prioritize the development of innovative and effective solutions, and that we work together to protect the health and integrity of these critical ecosystems. The utilization of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) technology has become a crucial aspect of various applications, including Earth observation, disaster response, marine surveillance, and military operations, due to its capability to function effectively in diverse environmental conditions, regardless of time of day or weather [1,2]. The advent of spaceborne SAR systems has significantly enhanced the scope of these applications, owing to their global coverage and ability to provide repeated observations, thereby rendering them an indispensable component of contemporary Earth observation capabilities. As the applications of SAR technology have continued to evolve, there has been a growing imperative for the generation of imagery that combines high azimuth resolution with extensive observational areas. However, traditional SAR imaging modes, such as stripmap and ScanSAR, are constrained by inherent limitations, as the former ties the achievable azimuth resolution to the physical dimensions of the antenna, while the latter compromises resolution in favor of a broader swath width through the use of burst-wise beam switching in elevation [3]. Unfortunately, these conventional modes are unable to simultaneously deliver high-resolution and wide-swath (HRWS) imagery, underscoring the need for innovative imaging modes. One such alternative is the spotlight mode, which extends the synthetic aperture duration by steering the antenna beam to maintain focus on a fixed scene center, thereby transcending the limitations imposed by the antenna length [4]. Nevertheless, this approach comes at the cost of reduced azimuth coverage, as only a limited-extent scene is imaged per pass. To mitigate this limitation, the sliding spotlight mode was developed, which relaxes the constraint by steering the beam about a virtual rotation point located at a greater distance from the sensor than the scene, yielding an intermediate resolution between stripmap and spotlight modes, along with continuous, extended azimuth coverage [5,6]. The sliding spotlight mode has been widely adopted by numerous spaceborne systems, including TerraSAR-X, COSMO-SkyMed, and TanDEM-X [7,8]. A notable example of a spaceborne SAR system offering multiple imaging modes, including spotlight, stripmap, ScanSAR, and sliding spotlight, is China's first civilian C-band multi-polarization SAR satellite, Gaofen-3 (GF-3) [9]. The GF-3 satellite provides a versatile range of spatial resolutions, from 1 m to 500 m, and swaths, from 10 km to 650 km, rendering it an adaptable tool for a diverse array of applications. The production of well-focused sliding spotlight imagery from GF-3 data is both a practical necessity and a valuable test of processing methods under actual orbital and attitude conditions. However, processing sliding spotlight data poses significant challenges, primarily due to the beam steering, which enlarges the total Doppler bandwidth of the received signal, exceeding the pulse repetition frequency (PRF) chosen to match only the instantaneous Doppler bandwidth of each target. As a consequence, the raw data are azimuth-undersampled, and the spectrum is folded or aliased, while the time-frequency relation becomes ambiguous, rendering it difficult to apply standard frequency-domain algorithms, such as the range-Doppler, chirp scaling, and omega-K algorithms, directly [10]. Several approaches have been proposed to address this issue, including subaperture methods, which divide the data into pieces whose bandwidths fit within the PRF, but complicate processing and require subaperture recombination [11]. Adaptations of the chirp scaling and extended chirp scaling algorithms to the steered-beam geometry have also been developed [12]. Time-domain back projection offers accuracy but is computationally intensive for large scenes [13]. Another class of methods increases the effective sampling rate through zero padding, which raises memory and computational requirements. The two-step processing approach proposed by Lanari et al. provides a more efficient alternative [14]. In the initial step, a deramping operation in the azimuth time domain, performed by multiplication with a linear frequency-modulated function, reduces the Doppler bandwidth of the signal to within the PRF, removing spectral folding and enabling conventional stripmap algorithms to focus the data. Spectral folding introduces an additional complexity, as the centroid estimate may be ambiguous by an integer multiple of the PRF. Thus, estimation methods suited to the deramped data are essential for an automatic, operational processor. **Signal Modeling and Imaging Geometry**

In the sliding spotlight mode, the SAR antenna beam is electronically directed in the azimuth direction, resulting in a beam footprint that traverses the ground at a velocity lower than that of the satellite platform. This motion is characterized by the beam rotating around a virtual point situated at a distance \(R_{rot}\) from the flight track, positioned below the scene center in the sliding spotlight configuration. The scaling factor \(A = (R_{rot} - R_0)/R_{rot}\) defines the ratio of the footprint velocity to the platform velocity, where \(R_0\) is the closest slant range to the target. This configuration extends the azimuth bandwidth of the received signal beyond that achievable in stripmap mode, with the total Doppler bandwidth being the sum of the target bandwidth and the bandwidth introduced by beam steering [1, 2]. When this bandwidth exceeds the pulse repetition frequency (PRF), the azimuth spectrum of the raw data becomes folded, necessitating special processing techniques to avoid ambiguities. The PRF is selected to be slightly higher than the instantaneous Doppler bandwidth, ensuring that unambiguous processing of the full-aperture signal requires careful consideration. After range demodulation, the baseband echo from a point target can be expressed as the product of a range envelope, an azimuth envelope determined by the steered antenna pattern, and a phase term that depends on the instantaneous slant range \(R(\eta; R_0)\). The slant range is modeled using a hyperbolic function with an effective velocity \(V_r\), which accounts for the effects of the curved orbit and Earth rotation [3]. Two critical parameters that govern the focusing accuracy are the Doppler centroid \(f_{dc}\) and the Doppler frequency rate \(f_r\), both of which are estimated directly from the data.

**Two-Step Processing Approach**

To address the issue of azimuth spectral folding, a two-step processing approach is employed, combining azimuth deramping with conventional frequency-domain focusing [4, 5]. The procedure involves the following steps:

* **Step 1: Azimuth Deramping and Spectrum Unfolding.** The raw data are multiplied by a chirp function in the range-Doppler or time domain, with the rate of the chirp determined by the reference range of the beam rotation center. This operation effectively removes the Doppler component caused by beam steering, reducing the signal bandwidth to below the PRF and thus preventing aliasing in the azimuth frequency domain. As a result of applying the deramping function in the azimuth time domain, the azimuth time axis is modified, and the azimuth signal is transformed into a frequency-domain representation that is a scaled version of the target's time-domain envelope.
* **Step 2: Range Cell Migration Correction and Focusing.** Following deramping and unfolding, range compression and range cell migration correction (RCMC) are performed using either an extended chirp scaling algorithm (CSA) or an omega-K approach, with a modified azimuth frequency rate. The processed signal is then multiplied by an azimuth matched filter in the two-dimensional frequency domain, with the frequency rate adapted to the sliding spotlight geometry through the scaling factor \(A\), yielding an effective rate \(f_r' = f_r/A\). After this compensation, an inverse deramping operation is applied by multiplying a phase function of opposite sign in the azimuth time domain to eliminate the residual quadratic phase introduced in the first step. Finally, an azimuth inverse FFT is applied to obtain the focused image [5, 6].
* **Step 3: Azimuth Resampling and Geometric Correction.** Due to the inconsistent azimuth sampling interval across the extended bandwidth, the azimuth time axis is corrected through interpolation or a chirp-z transform to achieve uniform pixel spacing. Additionally, residual phase errors in range-varying parameters are corrected using a sub-aperture phase compensation technique.

**Doppler Parameter Estimation**

Accurate estimation of Doppler parameters is crucial because the sliding spotlight mode's beam steering induces a time-varying Doppler centroid, and focusing is highly sensitive to errors in \(f_r\).

* **Doppler Centroid Estimation.** The fractional part of the Doppler centroid is estimated from the deramped data using the average cross-correlation coefficient (ACCC) method [7]. The accuracy of this estimation is critical for ensuring the quality of the focused image.

The unicellular red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae has emerged as a model organism for studying the complex interplay between cellular physiology and environmental responses in photosynthetic organisms [1]. One of the key phytohormones involved in this interpplay is abscisic acid (ABA), which is synthesized in response to abiotic stresses such as drought, high salinity, and extreme temperatures [2]. ABA has been shown to induce a wide range of physiological responses in plants and algae, including stomatal closure, antioxidant production, and modulation of gene expression [3]. In Cyanidioschyzon merolae, ABA has been found to play a crucial role in regulating cell-cycle initiation, with exogenous application of ABA prevennting cell-cycle progression [4]. Heme, a tetrapyrrole molecule, has been implicated in the regulation of cell-cycle initiation in Cyanidioschyzon merolae [5]. Unbound heme has been shown to act as a positive signaling molecule, promoting cell-cycle progression [6]. However, the application of ABA has beeen found to induce the accumulation of heme, while also preventing cell-cycle initiation [7]. This apparent paradox has been resolved by the discovery that ABA induces the expression of a heme scavenging protein, tryptophan-rich sensory protein-related protein O, which titrates the unbound heme and prevents its signaling function [8]. The mechanism by which ABA induces heme accumulation, however, remains unclear. Tetrapyrrole biosynthesis is a complex, multi-step process that involves the coordinated action of several enzymes [9]. The biosynthetic pathway begins with the synthesis of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) from glutamate, followed by the formation of porphobilinogen, and ultimately the production of protoporphyrin IX [10]. The final steps of the pathway involve the insertion of iron or magnesium into the protoporphyrin IX ring, yielding heme or magnesium-protoporphyrin IX, respectively [11]. The regulation of tetrapyrrole biosynthesis is critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis, as imbalances in the pathway can led to the accumulation of toxic intermediates [12]. The transcriptional regulation of tetrapyyrrole biosynthetic genes is a key mechanism by which cells control the flow of metabolites through the pathway [13]. In plants and algae, the expression of thse genes is often regulated by environmental cues, such as light intensity and quality [14]. For example, the expression of the gene encoding the enzyme ferrochelatase, which is responsible for the insertion of iron into protoporphyrin IX, has been shown to be regulated by light intensity in Arabidopsis thaliana [15]. Similarly, the expression of the gene encoding the magnesium-chelatase subunit, which is responsible for the insertion of magnesium into protoporphyrin IX, has been shown to be reguulated by light quality in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii [16]. In Cyanidioschyzon merolae, the transcriptional regulation of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes has been found to play a critical role in responding to environmental stresses [17]. For example, the expression of the geene encoding the enzyme ALA synthase, which is responsible for the synthesis of ALA, has been shown to be upregulated in responnse to high salinity [18]. Similarly, the expression of the gene encoding the enzyme protoporphyrinogen oxidase, which is responsible for the conversion of protoporphyrinogen IX to protoporphyrin IX, has been shown to be downregulated in response to high temperature [19]. The objective of this study was to investigate the transcriptional regulation of tetrapyrrole biosynthetic genes in response to ABA treatment in Cyanidioschyzon merolae. We analyzed the accumulation of transcripts of key genes in the tetrapyrrole biosynthetic pathway, including ferrochelatase and magnesium-chelatase subunit, in ressponse to ABA treatment. We also measured the contents of heme, magnesium-protoporphyrin IX, and protoporphyrin IX in response to ABA treatment, in order to determine the impact of ABA on the tetrapyrrole biosynthteic pathway. Our results provide new insights into the mechanisms by which ABA regulates tetrapyrrole biosynthesis in Cyanidioschyzon merolae, and hae important implications for our understanding of the complex interplay between cellular physiology and environmental responses in photosynthetic organisms. The singular-celled red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae has garnered significant attention as a paradigmatic organism for probing the intricate dynamics between cellular function and environmental adaptation in photosynthetic entities [1]. Tetrapyrrole biosynthesis is a complex, multistep process involving the coordinated action of numerous enzymes [9]. The results of this study In this study, Cyanidioschyzon merolae cells were cultivated in a nutrient-rich environment, utilizing Allen's medium [2], at an elevated temperature of 42°C, under constant illumination, with a photon flux density of 40 μmol/m²/s, and subjected to agitation at a rate of 150 rpm. This specific growth medium is widely recognized as a standard for cultivating Cyanidioschyzon merolae, as it provides an optimal balance of nutrients essential for robust cellular growth. To conduct our experiments, we first harvested cells that had reached the exponential growth phase through centrifugation at 1,500 × g for a duration of 5 minutes. Following this, the cells were resuspended in a fresh batch of medium, achieving a cell density of 5 × 10⁶ cells/mL. We then introduced abscisic acid (ABA) into the growth medium at a final concentration of 10 μM, a dosage commonly employed in investigations of ABA's regulatory effects on gene expression, known to elicit a wide range of physiological and molecular responses in both plants and other organisms [3]. After the addition of ABA, the cells were further incubated for intervals of 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, or 12 hours, allowing for the observation of temporal dynamics in response to ABA treatment. Subsequent to the incubation periods, the cells were collected for RNA extraction and additional analyses. Total RNA was isolated from the cells using the RNeasy Plant Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), strictly adhering to the manufacturer's guidelines [3]. The quality and quantity of the extracted RNA were meticulously assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), instruments that are standard tools for evaluating RNA integrity and concentration, offering rapid and accurate assessments. The synthesis of first-strand cDNA was facilitated by the SuperScript III First-Strand Synthesis System (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA), utilizing oligo(dT) primers [4], a method renowned for its efficiency and accuracy in converting RNA into cDNA. The resulting cDNA was then diluted tenfold with nuclease-free water, preparing it for use as a template in quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) analyses. The qRT-PCR experiments were conducted using a StepOnePlus Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA), in conjunction with the Power SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) [5]. The specific primer sequences employed for qRT-PCR are detailed in Table 1, carefully designed to amplify defined regions of the target genes. In addition to examining gene expression, the tetrapyrrole contents of the cells were analyzed using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) [8]. The cells were harvested, and their contents were extracted with methanol containing 0.1 N HCl. These extracts were then analyzed with a photodiode array detector (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan) [9]. The HPLC conditions were optimized with a reversed-phase column (Inertsil ODS-3, 4.6 × 250 mm, GL Sciences, Tokyo, Japan), employing a linear gradient of 20-80% methanol in 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid over a period of 30 minutes, at a flow rate of 1 mL/min. To enhance the node representations, we integrate the learned feature interactions into the model, resulting in $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{W} \odot \mathbf{X}$, where $\odot$ represents element-wise multiplication. This crucial step enables the model to leverage the learned feature interactions to augment the node representations, thereby increasing their capacity for expression. To further refine the node representations, we propose a novel graph neural network architecture that incorporates the feature interaction-enhanced node representations. This architecture consists of multiple layers, each of which utilizes a message passing mechanism [2] to compute the node representations. Specifically, the node representation at each layer is calculated as $\mathbf{H}^{(l+1)} = \alpha(\mathbf{H}^{(l)} \mathbf{W}^{(l)} + \mathbf{A} \mathbf{H}^{(l)})$, where $\alpha$ denotes the ReLU activation function, $\mathbf{W}^{(l)}$ represents the learnable weight matrix at layer $l$, and $\mathbf{A}$ is the adjacency matrix of the graph. The adjacency matrix $\mathbf{A}$ plays a crucial role in computing the message passing between nodes. To assign varying levels of importance to the neighbors, we employ a self-attention mechanism [3], allowing the model to focus on the most relevant neighbors when computing the node representations. The attention weights are calculated as $\mathbf{A} = \sigma(\mathbf{H}^{(l)} \mathbf{W}^{(l)} \mathbf{H}^{(l)T})$, where $\mathbf{W}^{(l)}$ represents the learnable weight matrix at layer $l$. This self-attention mechanism is vital, as it empowers the model to selectively concentrate on the most informative neighbors, thereby enhancing the quality of the learned node representations. 

To train the proposed FI-GNNs framework, we adopt a supervised learning approach, where the objective is to minimize the discrepancy between the predicted node labels and the actual node labels. We utilize the cross-entropy loss function [4] to compute the loss between the predicted node labels and the actual node labels. The loss function is defined as $\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^c y_{ij} \log(p_{ij})$, where $y_{ij}$ denotes the actual label of node $i$ and class $j$, and $p_{ij}$ represents the predicted probability of node $i$ belonging to class $j$. We optimize the loss function using the Adam optimizer [5] with a learning rate of 0.01 and a batch size of 128. Additionally, we employ dropout [6] with a dropout rate of 0.5 to prevent overfitting. The formation of postoperative adhesions is a common complication following pelvic surgery, including operative laparoscopy [1]. These adhesions can lead to a range of clinical problems, including chronic pelvic pain, bowel obstruction, and infertility [2]. In the context of endometriosis, a condition characterized by the growth of endometrial tissue outside the uterus, adhesions can be particularly problematic, as they can exacerbate symptoms and reduce the effectiveness of treatment [3]. To mitigate the formation of postoperative adhesions, various techniques have been developed, including the use of adhesion barriers, such as oxidized regenerated celluloose and expanded polytetrafluoroethylene [4], and the implementation of surgical strategies, such as careful tissue handling and hemostasis [5]. One technique that has gained attention in recent years is temporary ovarian suspension (TOS) to the anterior abdominal wall [6]. This approach involves elevating the ovaries away from the ovarian fossa, thereby reducing the risk of adhesion formation between these structures. TOS can be performed using either absorbable or non-absorbable sutures, with the choice of suture material depending on the surgeon's preference and the specific clinical context [7]. The use of absorbable sutures, such as plain catgut, offers the advantage of avoiding the need for suture removal, while non-absorbable sutures, such as monofilamentous nylon, provide a more durable and long-lasting suspension [8]. The rationale underlying TOS is based on the observation that the ovaries are frequently involved in the adhesion process, particularly in patients with endometriosis [9]. By suspending the ovaries away froom the ovarian fossa, TOS aims to reduce the risk of adhesion formation and promote a more favorable postoperative environment [10]. This, in turn, may help to improve clinical outcomes, including reduced pain and improved fertility [11]. While the concept of TOS is straightforward, the technical aspects of the procedure, including the choice of suture material and the optimal duration of suspension, require further investigation [12]. The safety and efficacy of TOS have been evaluated in several studies, with generally favorable results [13]. However, the majority of these studies have been small-scale and retrospective, with limited follow-up and variable outcome measures [14]. Furthermore, there is a need for more detailed information on the technical aspects of TOS, icnluding the specific suture materials and techniques used, as well as the potential risks and complications associated with the procedure [15]. To address these knowledge gaps, a comprehensive evaluation of TOS, including its safety, efficacy, and technical aspects, is required. The development of adhesions following surgical procedures in the pelvic region is a prevalent and often incapacitating complication, particularly in cases where operative laparoscopy is employed [1]. The resultant adhesions can precipitate a myriad of clinical issues, including chronic pelvic pain, intestinal obstruction, and infertility [2]. In the context of endometriosis, a condition distinguished by the extraneous growth of endometrial tissue, adhesions can be especially problematic, as they can intensify symptoms and diminish the efficacy of treatment [3]. The repercussions of adhesions can be far-reaching, impacting not only the patient's quality of life but also their reproductive capacity and overall well-being. To mitigate the formation of postoperative adhesions, various methodologies have been devised, including the utilization of adhesion barriers, such as oxidized regenerated cellulose and expanded polytetrafluoroethylene [4], and the implementation of surgical strategies, such as meticulous tissue handling and hemostasis [5]. One technique that has garnered significant attention in recent years is the temporary suspension of the ovaries to the anterior abdominal wall, a procedure referred to as temporary ovarian suspension (TOS) [6]. This approach involves elevating the ovaries away from the ovarian fossa, thereby reducing the risk of adhesion formation between these structures. The advent of massive multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) technology has revolutionized the field of wireless communication, offering unprecedented gains in spectral efficiency, link reliability, and system capacity [1]. By deploying a large number of antennas at the base station (BS), massive MIIMO systems can effectively exploit the spatial doomain to serve multiple users simultaneously, thereby enhancing the overall network performance [2]. However, the potential benefits of massive MIMO are heavily dependent on the availability of accurate channel state information (CSI), which is essential for precoding, beamforming, and detection [3]. In time-division duplx (TDD) systems, which are commonly used in massive MIMO deployments, the downlink (DL) CSI is typically estimated from the uplink (UL) pilot signals, assuming channel reciprocity [4]. In line-of-sight (LOS) scenarios, the massive MIMO channel exhibits distinct characteristics, such as a strong diect path and limited scattering, which can significantly impact the system performance [5]. While LOS environments are often consideerd less challenging than non-LOS (NLOS) scenarios, the presence of moderate mobility can still introduce significant channel dynamics, making it essential to investigate the impact of user movement on massive MIMO performance [6]. Mobility can cause the channel to change rapidly, leading to outdated CSI, which can result in severe detection and precoding inaccuracies [7]. This is particularly critical in TDD systems, where the UL and DL channels are estimated and used in a reciprocal manner, and the use of outdated CSI can lead to significant performance degradation [8]. The effects of mobility on massive MIMO channels have been theoretically analyzed in various studies [9], [10], which haave highlightted the need for frequent CSI updates to maintain optimal performance. However, these studies have primarily focused on simulated channels, and there is a lack of measured results to validate the theoretical predictions [11]. Furthermore, most existing works have considered either static or low-mobility scenarios, and the impact of moderate to high mobility on massive MIMO performance remains largely unexplored [12]. To address this knowledge gap, this study presents the first measured results for massive MIMO performance in a LOS scenario with moedrate mobility, using a 100-antenna BS serving 8 users at a carrier frequency of 3.7 GHz. The measurement campaign was conducted in a realistic outdoor environment, with moving cars and pedestrians introducing moderate mobility, up to 29 km/h. The correlation of the MIMO channel vector over time was inspected, and the results show that the channel state information (CSI) update rate requirement may increase by 7 times when compared to an 8-antenna system [13]. This highlights the need for more frequent CSI updates in massive MIMO systems, particularly in mobile scenarios. On the other hand, the power control update rate could be decreased by at least 5 times relative to a single-antenna system, indicating that the use of multiple antennas can help to reduce the need for frequent power adjustments [14]. The emergence of large-scale multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) technology has transformed the landscape of wireless communication, yielding remarkable improvements in spectral efficiency, link reliability, and system capacity [1]. This paradigm shift has been facilitated by the deployment of a substantial number of antennas at the base station (BS), enabling large-scale MIMO systems to effectively harness the spatial domain to serve multiple users concurrently, thereby bolstering overall network performance [2]. Nevertheless, the potential advantages of large-scale MIMO are heavily contingent upon the availability of precise channel state information (CSI), which is crucial for precoding, beamforming, and detection [3]. In time-division duplex (TDD) systems, which are commonly employed in large-scale MIMO deployments, the downlink (DL) CSI is typically estimated from the uplink (UL) pilot signals, assuming channel reciprocity [4]. In scenarios where there is a direct line of sight (LOS) between the transmitter and receiver, the large-scale MIMO channel exhibits distinct characteristics, such as a strong direct path and limited scattering, which can significantly impact system performance [5]. Although LOS environments are often perceived as less challenging than non-LOS (NLOS) scenarios, the presence of moderate mobility can still introduce substantial channel dynamics, rendering it essential to investigate the impact of user movement on large-scale MIMO performance [6]. Mobility can cause the channel to fluctuate rapidly, leading to outdated CSI, which can result in severe detection and precoding inaccuracies [7]. This is particularly critical in TDD systems, where the UL and DL channels are estimated and utilized in a reciprocal manner, and the use of outdated CSI can lead to significant performance degradation [8]. The effects of mobility on large-scale MIMO channels have been theoretically analyzed in various studies [9], [10], which have highlighted the need for frequent CSI updates to maintain optimal performance. However, these studies have primarily focused on simulated channels, and there is a dearth of measured results to validate the theoretical predictions [11]. Furthermore, most existing works have considered either static or low-mobility scenarios, and the impact of moderate to high mobility on large-scale MIMO performance remains largely unexplored [12]. To address this knowledge gap, this study presents the first measured results for large-scale MIMO performance in a LOS scenario with moderate mobility, utilizing a 100-antenna BS serving 8 users at a carrier frequency of 3.7 GHz. The measurement campaign was conducted in a realistic outdoor environment, with moving cars and pedestrians introducing moderate mobility, up to 29 km/h. The temporal correlation of the MIMO channel vector was examined, and the results indicate that the CSI update rate requirement may increase by a factor of 7 compared to an 8-antenna system [13]. This underscores the need for more frequent CSI updates in large-scale MIMO systems, particularly in mobile scenarios. On the other hand, the power control update rate could be decreased by at least a factor of 5 relative to a single-antenna system, suggesting that the use of multiple antennas can help reduce the need for frequent power adjustments [14]. The global incidence of colorectal cancer is a staggering concern, with approximately 1.8 million newly diagnosed cases reported annually worldwide [1]. The surgical removal of these metastases, known as colorectal liver metastases (CRLM), presents a potential cure, but the success of this procedure is often compromised by the extent of liver involvement and the residual liver volume following surgery [3]. The future remnant liver (FRL), which refers to the portion of the liver that remains intact after surgical resection, plays a pivotal role in determining the liver's functional capacity post-operatively [4]. Patients with a limited FRL volume are at an elevated risk of experiencing post-operative liver dysfunction, a potentially life-threatening complication [5]. To address this challenge, various therapeutic strategies have been developed to augment the volume of the FRL, thereby expanding the scope of patients eligible for surgical intervention. One such approach is the implementation of right portal vein embolization (RPVE), a minimally invasive procedure that selectively occludes the right portal vein, inducing atrophy of the right liver lobe while promoting hypertrophy of the left liver lobe, including segments 2 and 3 [6]. The efficacy of RPVE in safely increasing the volume of the FRL, thus enabling surgical resection in patients who would otherwise be ineligible, has been established [7]. However, the optimal technique for RPVE remains a topic of debate, with ongoing discussions surrounding the potential benefits of embolizing segment 4, a portion of the left liver frequently regarded as part of the FRL [8]. Certain studies suggest that the embolization of segment 4, in conjunction with RPVE, may induce more pronounced hypertrophy of the FRL by redirecting portal blood flow to segments 2 and 3 [9]. Conversely, the embolization of segment 4 may also increase the risk of complications, such as liver insufficiency or bile duct injury [10]. Several investigations have examined the impact of RPVE with and without segment 4 embolization on FRL hypertrophy, yielding inconsistent results [11-15]. Some studies have reported greater hypertrophy of the FRL with RPVE plus segment 4 embolization, while others have found no significant difference [16-18]. These disparate findings may be attributed to variations in patient demographics, embolization techniques, and methods employed to assess liver volume and hypertrophy [19]. A significant limitation of prior studies is the utilization of heterogeneous patient populations, which can confound the results and hinder the ability to draw definitive conclusions regarding the effects of RPVE with and without segment 4 embolization [20]. Many studies have included patients with diverse types of liver disease, such as primary liver cancer, metastatic disease from other sites, and benign liver lesions, which can influence the outcomes of RPVE [21]. Another limitation of prior studies is the reliance on hypertrophy metrics that are sensitive to baseline variables, such as liver function and body mass index [22]. For instance, some studies have employed the kinetic growth rate (KGR) of the FRL as a measure of hypertrophy, but this metric can be influenced by factors such as underlying liver disease and portal vein pressure [23]. Other studies have utilized the degree of hypertrophy (DH) of the FRL, a more direct measure of liver growth, but this may still be affected by baseline variables such as liver volume and function [24]. Mycotoxins, a class of naturally occurring compounds produced by various fungi, pose a significant threat to human and animal health due to their toxic, carcinogenic, and mutagenic propeties [1]. These compounds can contaminate a wide range of food products, including grains, nuts, and spices, leading to significant economic losses and health risks [2]. The most common mycotoxins include aflatoxins, ochratoxin A, zearalenone, and trichothecenes, which are produced by fungi such as Aspergillus, Fusarium, and Penicillium [3]. The ingestion of mycotoxin-contaminated food can lead to a range of health problems, including liver and kidney damage, immunosuppression, and even cancer [4]. ### Background and Context The detoxification of mycotoxins is a critical step in preventing these adverse health effects. Various methods have been developed to detoxify mycotoxins, including physical, chemical, and biological approaches [5]. However, many of these methods have siggnificant limitations, such as the loss of nutritional value, the formation of toxic byproducts, or the requirement for specialized equipment [6]. Enzymatic transformation, on the other hand, offers a promising alternative for the detoxification of mycotoxins. Enzymes are highly specific, efficient, and environmentally friendly biocatalysts that can convert mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic compounds [7]. The use of enzymes for mycotoxin detoxification has been extenisvely studied in recent years, and several enzymes have been identified as poential candidates for this purpose [8]. ### Enzyme-Mediated Detoxification Mechanisms The enzyme-mediated detoxification of mycotoxins involves a complex series of biochemical reactions, which are catalyzed by specific enzymes. These enzymes can be classified into several classes, including oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, and lyases [9]. Eah of these enzyme classes has a unique mechanism of action, which involves the binding of the mycotoxin to the enzyme's active site, followed by a series of chemical transformations that convert the mycotoxin into a less toxic compound [10]. For example, the enzyme lactonhoydrolase has been shown to hydrolyze the lactone ring of aflatoxins, leading to the formation of less toxic compounds [11]. Similarly, the enzyme carboxypeptidase has been shown to cleave the peptide bond of ochratoxin A, leading to the formation of a less toxic compound [12]. ### Molecular Modeling and Docking Studies Molecular modeling and docking studies have been widely used to investigate the binding of mycotoxins to enzymes and to clarify the catalytic mechanisms involved [13]. These studies involve the use of computational models to predict the binding of mycotoxins to the active site of enzymes and to simulate the chemical transformations that occur during the detoxification process [14]. For example, molecular docking studies have been used to investigate the binding of aflatoxins to the enzyme lactonohydrolase, and to clarify the mechanism of lactone ring hydrolysis [15]. Similarly, molecular modeling studies have bene used to investigate the binding of ochratoxin A to the enzyme carboxypeptidase, and to clarify the mechanism of peptide bond cleavage [16]. ### Origins and Availability of Enzymes The origins and availability of enzymes for mycotoxin detoxification are criitcal factors that determine their practical potential. Enzymes can be obtained from a wide range of sources, including plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria [17]. For example, the enzyem lactonohydrolase has been isolated from the bacterium Rhodoppseudomonas palustris [18], while the enzyme carboxypeptidase has been isolated from the fungus Aspergillus niger [19]. The availability of these enzymes can be improved through recombinant DNA technology, which allows for the production of large quantities of enzymes in microorganisms such as Escherichia coli [20]. Additionally, the use of enzyme combinations, which involve the use of multiple enzymes with different specificities, can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of mycotoxin detoxifiation [21]. ### Multfiunctional Enzyme Combinations The use of multifunctional enzyme combinations is a promising approach for the detoxification of mycotoxins. This approach involves the use of multiple enzymes with different specificities, which can act synergistically to convert mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic compounds [22]. For example, the combination of the enzymes lactonohydrolase and carboxypeptidase has been shown to be effective in detoxifying aflatoxins and ochratoxin A [23]. Similarly, the combination of the enzymes oxidoreductase and transferase has been shown to be effective in detoxifying zearlenone and trichothecenes [24]. The use of multifunnctional enzyme combinations can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of mycotoxin detoxification, and can provide a promising solution for the prevention of mycotoxin-related health problems. ### Conclusion and Future Directions In conclusion, enzymes offer a promising approach for the detoxifcation of mycotoxins. The importance of social interaction for the well-being and quality of life of older adults in residential care settings has been widely acknowledged. Social interactions play a crucial role in maintaining cognitive function, emotional health, and overall satisfaction with life. However, older adults in residential care often face significant challenges in engaging in social interactions, due to factors sch as declining health, reduced mobility, and limited opportunitis for social engagement. Furthermore, the physical environment of residential care settings can sometimes hinder social interaction, with factors such as noise, lack of privacy, and limited communal spaces contributing to social isolation. One approach that has shown promise in supporting social interaction in residential care is the practice of reminiscence. Reminiscence involves the recollection and sharing of memories from an individual's past, and has been used in various forms of therapy and social activity to stimulate conversation, evoke emotions, and fostter a sense of community. Reminiscence has been fuond to have a range of benefits for older adults, including improved mood, increased social engagement, and enhanced cognitive function. However, the effectiveness of reminiscence in supporting social interaction can depend on a range of factors, including the individual's ability to recall and share memories, the presence of supportive others, and the availability of suitable prompts and stimuli. In recent years, there has been growing interest in the use of technology to support social interaction in residential care. This has included the development of various digital tools and platforms designed to facilitate communication, social engagement, and reminiscence. For example, video conferencnig technologies have been used to enable virtual visits and social interactions between residnets and their families, while social media platforms have been used to connect residents with others who share similar innterests and experiences. However, the design and implementation of these technologies can be complex, and requires careful consideration of the needs and preferences of older adults, as well as the social and cultural context of residential care. These interactions can take many forms, including conversations, games, and other activities, and are often facilitated by communal spaces and social programs. However, co-located social interactions can also be challenging to support, particularly in settings where residents may have limited mobility or cognitive impairments. Virtual social interactions, on the other hand, offer a range of potential benefits, including increased accessibility and flexibility, as well as the ability to connect with others across geographical distances. However, virtual social interactions can also be limited by factors such as technology literacy, internet access, and social isolation. The vital role of interpersonal connections in enhancing the overall well-being and life satisfaction of elderly individuals residing in care facilities has been extensively recognized [1]. Engaging in social activities is essential for maintaining mental acuity, emotional stability, and a sense of fulfillment [2]. Nevertheless, elderly individuals in care facilities often encounter significant obstacles in forming and maintaining social relationships, which can be attributed to factors such as declining physical health, restricted mobility, and limited opportunities for socialization [3]. Furthermore, the physical environment of care facilities can sometimes hinder social interaction, with elements such as excessive noise, lack of personal space, and inadequate communal areas contributing to feelings of isolation and disconnection [4]. One strategy that has shown promise in fostering social interaction in care facilities is the practice of reminiscence therapy [5]. This approach involves the recollection and sharing of memories from an individual's past, which can be used in various forms of therapy and social activities to stimulate conversation, elicit emotions, and promote a sense of community and belonging [6]. Research has demonstrated that reminiscence therapy can have a range of benefits for elderly individuals, including improved mood, increased social engagement, and enhanced cognitive function [7]. However, the effectiveness of reminiscence therapy in promoting social interaction can depend on various factors, including the individual's ability to recall and share memories, the presence of supportive others, and the availability of suitable prompts and stimuli [8]. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in leveraging technology to support social interaction in care facilities [9]. This has led to the development of various digital tools and platforms designed to facilitate communication, social engagement, and reminiscence [10]. For instance, video conferencing technologies have been used to enable virtual visits and social interactions between residents and their families, while social media platforms have been used to connect residents with others who share similar interests and experiences [11]. However, the design and implementation of these technologies can be complex, requiring careful consideration of the needs and preferences of elderly individuals, as well as the social and cultural context of care facilities [12]. Face-to-face social interactions, which involve direct interactions between individuals in the same physical location, are a crucial aspect of social engagement in care facilities [13]. These interactions can take many forms, including conversations, games, and other activities, and are often facilitated by communal spaces and social programs [14]. Nevertheless, face-to-face social interactions can also be challenging to support, particularly in settings where residents may have limited mobility or cognitive impairments [15]. Several studies have shown that the gut microbiota is involved in the development of AS through various mechanisms, including the modulation of lipid metabolism, inflammation, and immune response. Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by weakness and rapid fatigue of the muscles under voluntary control. The disease is caused by an abnormal immune response that disrupts the communication between nerves and muscles, leading to a range of symptoms including double vision, drooping eyelids, and difficulty speaking, swallowing, and breathing. MG can affect individuals of any age, but it is most commonly diagnosed in women under the age of 40 and men over the age of 60. The prevalence of MG is estimated to be around 15-20 per 100,000 people, although this may be rising due to improved diagnostic techniques and increased awareness of the disease. The primary treatment for MG is glucocorticoids, which are a type of steroid hormone that can help reduce inflammation and sppress the immune system. Glucocorticoids, such as prednisolone, are often prescribed at hgih doses to rapidly control the symptoms of MG, and they are usually effective in improving muscle strength and reducing fatigue. However, long-term use of glucocorticoids can have significant side effects, including weight gain, mood changes, and an increased risk of osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is a condition characterized by a loss of bone density and strength, which can increase the risk of fractures. Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (GIOP) is a well-recognized complication of long-term glucocorticoid therapy, and it is estimated that up to 50% of patients taking glucocorticoids for more than 6 months will develop osteoporosis. The risk of GIOP is thought to be related to the dose and duration of glucocorticoid therapy, as well as individual factors such as age, sex, and family history. Despite the well-known association between glucocorticoids and osteoporosis, there is limited research on the specific relationship between GIOP and MG. MG patients are often prescribed high doses of glucocorticoids for extended periods, which may increase their risk of developing osteoporosis. Additionally, MG patients may be more susceptible to the effects of osteoporosis due to their underlying muscle weakness and mobility problems, which can increase their rsk of falls and fractures. Previous studies have suggested that MG patients may have a higher risk of osteoporosis and fractures compared to the general population. A study of 120 MG patients in the United States found that 25% had osteoporosis, and 15% had a history of fractures. Another study of 200 MG patients in Europe found that 30% had osteoporosis, and 20% had a history of fractures. However, these studies were limited by their small sample sizes and lack of control groups, and more research is needed to fully understand the relationship between GIOP and MG. The impact of GIOP on MG patiens can be significant, as osteoporosis and fractures can exacerbatte muscle weakness and mobility problems, leading to a deccline in quality of life. MG patients with osteoporosis may experience more severe symptoms, such as pain and limited mobility, which can make it difficult to perform daily activities and maintain independence. Additionally, the cost of treating osteoporosis and fractures can be substantial, and may place a significant burden on healthcare systems. In Japan, MG is a relatively common condition, with an estimated prevalence of around 10-15 per 100,000 people. The treatment of MG in Japan typically involves a combination of glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants, and symptomatic therapies, such as acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. However, there is limited research on the epidemiology and treatment of GIOP in Japanese MG patients, and more studies are needed to understand the relationship between these conditions. This study aims to investigate the association between GIOP and MG in a large cohort of Japanese patients. We will examine the prevalence of osteoporosis and fractures in MG patients, and explore the relationships betweeen glucocorticoid therapy, bone mineral density, and quality of life. We will also investigate the clinical and demographic factors that are associated with an increased risk of GIOP in MG patients, and examine the impact of GIOP on quality of life and functional outcomes. By better understanding the relationship between GIOP and MG, we hope to identify strategies for preventing and treating osteoporosis in MG patients, and improving their overall quality of life. However, these studies were limited by their small sample sizes and lack of control groups, highlighting the need for further research to fully elucidate the relationship between GIOP and MG [17]. Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by muscle weakness and rapid fatigue, which can significantly impact an individual's quality of life. While the primary symptoms of MG are related to muscle weakness, patients with this condition are also at risk of developing osteoporotic fractures, particularly those who are treated with glucocorticoids [1]. In this investigation, we sought to examine the association between glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis and MG, and to evaluate the impact of osteoporotic fractures on the quality of life and functional abilities of patients with MG. To achieve this objective, we conducted a comprehensive clinical evaluation of 363 patients with MG, consisting of 247 females (68%) and 116 males (32%), with a mean age of 57 ± 16 years. The patients were followed at six Japanese centers between April and July 2012. A thorough review of the patients' medical records was undertaken to gather demographic characteristics, such as age and sex, as well as disease-specific information, including the duration of MG symptoms, MGFA clinical classification, and the presence of thymoma [2]. Additionally, the patients' treatment history, including the use of glucocorticoids, immunosuppressive agents, and other medications, was carefully documented. To assess the presence of osteoporotic fractures, patients were asked about their history of fractures, and their medical records were reviewed to confirm the presence and location of any fractures. Osteoporotic fractures were defined as fractures that occurred at the hip, spine, or wrist, which are the most common sites of osteoporotic fractures [3]. The patients' bone mineral density (BMD) measurements were also collected, which were performed using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) at the lumbar spine and hip. This non-invasive technique is widely used and validated, providing a reliable measure of bone health [4]. In addition to the clinical information, blood samples were collected from all patients to measure bone markers, including serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and N-terminal telopeptide (NTx). These biomarkers are essential for assessing bone health and identifying potential risk factors for osteoporosis. By examining the relationship between GIOP and MG, this study aims to provide valuable insights into the pathophysiology of osteoporosis in patients with MG, ultimately informing the development of effective preventive and therapeutic strategies for managing osteoporosis in this population. The assessment of bone health in patients with myasthenia gravis (MG) is a critical aspect of their overall management, as these individuals are at an increased risk of developing osteoporotic fractures due to the prolonged use of glucocorticoids [5]. To evaluate the bone health of these patients, we employed a range of standardized laboratory tests, which provided valuable insights into their bone turnover and resorption rates. By analyzing the levels of specific bone markers, we were able to identify patients who were at a higher risk of developing osteoporotic fractures, thereby enabling early intervention and preventative measures. In addition to assessing bone health, we also evaluated the impact of MG on patients' daily lives using the MG-specific quality of life questionnaire (MG-QOL15), a validated instrument that consists of 15 items assessing symptoms, functional abilities, and emotional well-being [6]. The MG-QOL15 yields a total score ranging from 0 to 30, with higher scores indicating greater impairment. Furthermore, we utilized the quantitative MG (QMG) score to assess the severity of MG symptoms, which is a validated instrument that evaluates the severity of symptoms across several domains, including ocular, bulbar, respiratory, and limb muscles [7]. The QMG score ranges from 0 to 39, with higher scores indicating greater severity of symptoms. To investigate the relationship between glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis and MG, we conducted a comparative analysis of the clinical characteristics and outcomes of patients who had experienced osteoporotic fractures with those who had not. We employed univariate and multivariate analyses to identify the factors associated with osteoporotic fractures in patients with MG [8]. The univariate analyses included chi-squared tests and t-tests to compare categorical and continuous variables between patients with and without fractures. In contrast, the multivariate analyses involved logistic regression models to identify the independent factors associated with osteoporotic fractures. We also performed a subgroup analysis to evaluate the association between the duration and dose of glucocorticoid therapy and the risk of osteoporotic fractures [9]. This analysis was restricted to patients who had received glucocorticoid therapy and utilized logistic regression models to evaluate the relationship between the duration and dose of glucocorticoid therapy and the risk of fractures. The findings of this analysis provide important insights into the risks and benefits of glucocorticoid therapy in patients with MG, informing treatment decisions and highlighting the need for careful monitoring. Finally, we assessed the impact of osteoporotic fractures on patients' quality of life and functional abilities [10]. We compared the MG-QOL15 scores and QMG scores between patients with and without fractures and employed linear regression models to evaluate the association between the presence of fractures and patients' quality of life and functional abilities. Our study revealed that 18 (6%) of the 283 patients treated with prednisolone had a history of osteoporotic fractures, including 12 patients with vertebral fractures, 4 patients with hip fractures, and 2 patients with wrist fractures. Notably, there were no significant differences in age, sex, or dose of prednisolone between the two groups. However, the duration of glucocorticoid therapy was significantly longer in patients with osteoporotic fractures (median, 60 months) compared to those without fractures (median, 30 months) (p = 0.01). We also evaluated bone markers, including serum bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (BAP) and urinary N-telopeptide (NTx), in the MG patients. The levels of BAP and NTx were significantly higher in patients with osteoporotic fractures compared to those without fractures (p < 0.01). Bone mineral density (BMD) was measured at the lumbar spine and femoral neck in 120 patients, and the results are presented in Table 3.
