Ovarian cancer poses a considerable threat to global health, with a alarmingly high mortality rate primarily due to its propensity for late detection. This delayed diagnosis stems from the disease's insidious nature, often manifesting without distinct symptoms or reliable screening methods, making early detection a daunting challenge. Consequently, a significant majority of ovarian cancer cases are not identified until they have progressed to an advanced stage, at which point the prognosis is generally unfavorable. Therefore, the development of a precise and dependable method to differentiate between benign and malignant pelvic masses is of paramount importance to enhance patient outcomes. Transvaginal ultrasound is the preferred initial imaging technique for assessing pelvic masses, providing valuable insights into the mass's dimensions, morphology, and composition. However, these findings are not always conclusive in determining the nature of the mass [1]. Two commonly employed algorithms, the risk of malignancy index (RMI) and the risk of ovarian malignancy algorithm (ROMA), combine ultrasound findings with serum biomarker levels, such as CA-125, to estimate the risk of malignancy [2, 3]. Despite their utility, these algorithms are not without limitations, including a moderate level of sensitivity and specificity, which can lead to unnecessary surgical interventions for benign masses or delays in diagnosing malignant tumors [4]. CA-125, the most frequently used serum biomarker for ovarian cancer, has several inherent limitations. Its levels can be elevated in various benign conditions, such as endometriosis, pregnancy, and pelvic inflammatory disease, resulting in a considerable false-positive rate [5]. Moreover, CA-125 levels may remain within the normal range in the early stages of ovarian cancer, leading to a high false-negative rate [6]. Human epididymis protein 4 (HE4) has emerged as a promising novel biomarker, showing potential in enhancing the diagnostic accuracy of ovarian cancer. HE4, a glycoprotein overexpressed in ovarian cancer cells, has been found to be elevated in patients with ovarian cancer [7]. Several studies have indicated that HE4 exhibits superior specificity compared to CA-125, particularly in premenopausal women [8, 9]. Combining HE4 with CA-125 and ultrasound findings may improve the accuracy of differentiating between benign and malignant pelvic masses. The ROMA algorithm, which integrates HE4 and CA-125 levels with menopausal status, has demonstrated better performance than CA-125 alone or the RMI algorithm [10]. However, the ROMA algorithm does not take into account ultrasound findings, which are crucial for evaluating the characteristics of the mass. A comprehensive risk prediction model that combines HE4, menopausal status, and ultrasound findings may offer a more thorough assessment of the risk of malignancy. Menopausal status is a critical factor in evaluating the risk of malignancy, with postmenopausal women being at a higher risk of developing ovarian cancer and exhibiting a distinct risk profile compared to premenopausal women [11]. While the RMI algorithm considers menopausal status, the ROMA algorithm adopts a more simplistic approach, categorizing women as either premenopausal or postmenopausal [12]. A more nuanced incorporation of menopausal status into the risk prediction model may enhance its accuracy. Ultrasound findings are vital for assessing the characteristics of the mass and estimating the risk of malignancy. The presence of solid components, ascites, and lymphadenopathy are all associated with an increased risk of malignancy [13]. However, the interpretation of ultrasound findings can be subjective, and the accuracy of the assessment may depend on the operator's expertise [14]. A risk prediction model that systematically and objectively incorporates ultrasound findings may improve the accuracy of the assessment. In this study, the development of a risk prediction score that combines HE4, menopausal status, and ultrasound findings to differentiate between benign and malignant pelvic masses was the primary objective. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a primary malignancy of the liver, accounting for the majority of liver cancer cases worldwide [1]. The incidence of HCC is increasing, and it is currently the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths gloally [2]. The development and progression of HCC are complex processes, involving the interplay of multiple genetic and epigenetic alterations [3]. Despite advances in diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, the prognosis for patients with HCC remains poor, with a five-year survival rate of less than 20% [4]. Therefore, it is essential to identify novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets to improve the management and outcome of HCC. Epigenetic modifications, such as histoone methylation, play a crucial role in regulating gene expression and are often dysregulated in cancer [5]. The SET domain-containing proteins are a family of histone methyltransferases that catalyze the methylation of lysine residues on histones, resulting in the activation or repression of gene transcription [6]. Among these proteins, the SET domain-containing 1B (SETD1B) gene has been implicated in various biological processes, including cell growth, differentiation, and survival [7]. Recent studies have suggested that SETD1B may also be involved in tumorigenesis, with elevated expression levels observed in several types of cancer, including breast, lung, and colon cancer [8, 9, 10]. However, the role of SETD1B in HCC is not well understood, and its clinical significance in this disease remains to be elucidated. Several lines of evidence suggest that SETD1B may contribute to the development and progression of HCC. First, SETD1B has been shown to interact with various transcription factors and co-regulators, including the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, which is frequently activated in HCC [11]. Second, SETD1B has been implcated in the regulation of cell cycle progression and apoptosis, two critical processse that are often dysregulated in cancer [12]. Third, SETD1B has been found to be overexpressed in cancer stem cells, which are thought to be responsible for the initiation and maintenance of tumors [13]. These findings suggest that SETD1B may ply a role in the pathogenesis of HCC, and that its expression levels may be associated with clinical outcomes in patients with this disease. To invesstigate the clinical significance of SETD1B in HCC, several studiies have examined the expression levels of SETD1B in HCC tissues and cell lines. These studies have reported inconsistent results, with some finding elevated expression levels of SETD1B in HCC tissues compared to normal tissues [14], while others have found no significant difference [15]. These discrepancies may be due to the small sample sizes and heterogeneous patient populations used in these studies. Furthermore, the functional role of SETD1B in HCC has not been fully explored, and the molecular mechanisms by which it contributes to tumorigenesis are not well understood. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the development of biomarkers for HCC, which can be used to diagnose the disease at an early stage, predict patient outcomes, and monitor treatment response [16]. Several biomarkers, including alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and des-gamma-carboxy prothrombin (DCP), have been identified and are currently used in clinical practice [17]. However, these biomarkers have limited sensitivity and specificity, and there is a need for novel biomarkers that can improve the diagnosis and management of HCC. The identification of SETD1B as a potential biomarker for HCC may provide a new avenue for the diagnosis and treatment of this disease. The present study aims to investigate the expression levels of SETD1B in HCC tissues and cell lines, and to examine its clinical significance in patients with thsi disease. We will use a combination of molecular biology techniques, including reverse transcriptase quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and western blot analysis, to examine the expression levels of SETD1B in HCC tissues and clel lines. We will also analyze the clinical factors associated with SETD1B expression, including tumor size, clinical stage, and liver cirrhosis. Furthermore, we will use Cox's regression analysis to examine the prognostic significance of SETD1B expression in patients with HCC. Liver cancer, a malignancy that arises from the primary liver cells, is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) being the most prevalent form, accounting for the majority of cases [1, 2]. The incidence of HCC is on the rise, and it is currently ranked as the third most common cause of cancer-related deaths globally. The development and progression of HCC involve a complex interplay of genetic and epigenetic alterations, resulting in a poor prognosis for patients, with a mere 20% of patients surviving for five years or more after diagnosis [3, 4]. This highlights the pressing need for the identification of novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets to improve the management and outcomes of HCC patients. Epigenetic modifications, including histone methylation, play a pivotal role in regulating gene expression, and their dysregulation is a hallmark of cancer [5]. The SET domain-containing proteins, a family of histone methyltransferases, catalyze the methylation of lysine residues on histones, thereby modulating gene transcription [6]. Among these proteins, the SET domain-containing 1B (SETD1B) gene has been implicated in various biological processes, including cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival [7]. Recent studies have suggested that SETD1B may also play a role in tumorigenesis, with elevated expression levels observed in various types of cancer, including breast, lung, and colon cancer [8, 9, 10]. However, the role of SETD1B in HCC remains poorly understood, and its clinical significance in this disease is yet to be elucidated.

Several lines of evidence suggest that SETD1B may contribute to the development and progression of HCC. Firstly, SETD1B has been shown to interact with various transcription factors and co-regulators, including the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, which is frequently activated in HCC [11]. Secondly, SETD1B has been implicated in the regulation of cell cycle progression and apoptosis, two critical processes that are often dysregulated in cancer [12]. Thirdly, SETD1B has been found to be overexpressed in cancer stem cells, which are thought to be responsible for the initiation and maintenance of tumors [13]. These findings suggest that SETD1B may play a role in the pathogenesis of HCC, and that its expression levels may be associated with clinical outcomes in patients with this disease. To investigate the clinical significance of SETD1B in HCC, several studies have examined the expression levels of SETD1B in HCC tissues and cell lines. However, these studies have reported inconsistent results, with some finding elevated expression levels of SETD1B in HCC tissues compared to normal tissues [14], while others have found no significant difference [15]. These discrepancies may be due to the small sample sizes and heterogeneous patient populations used in these studies.

Furthermore, the functional role of SETD1B in HCC has not been fully explored, and the molecular mechanisms by which it contributes to tumorigenesis are not well understood. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the development of biomarkers for HCC, which can be used to diagnose the disease at an early stage, predict patient outcomes, and monitor treatment response [16]. Several biomarkers, including alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and des-gamma-carboxy prothrombin (DCP), have been identified and are currently used in clinical practice [17]. However, these biomarkers have limited sensitivity and specificity, and there is a need for novel biomarkers that can improve the diagnosis and management of HCC. The identification of SETD1B as a potential biomarker for HCC may provide a new avenue for the diagnosis and treatment of this disease.

The present study aims to investigate the expression levels of SETD1B in HCC tissues and cell lines, and to examine its clinical significance in patients with this disease. We will also analyze the clinical factors associated with SETD1B expression, including tumor size, clinical stage, and liver cirrhosis. Furthermore, we will use Cox's regression analysis to examine the prognostic significance of SETD1B expression in patients with HCC. Our study will provide new insights into the role of SETD1B in HCC, and may identify SETD1B as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for this disease.

Retinoblastoma, a malignant tuor of the retina, is the most common intraocular cancer in children, accounting for approximately 3% of all pediatric cancers [1]. The treatment of retinoblastoma has undergone significant evolution over the pats few decades, with a shift toawrds more conservative approaches aimed at preserving vision and reducing the risk of secondary malignancies [2]. One such appproach is ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC), which involves the delivery of chemotherapy directly to the eye through the ophthalmic artery, allowing for high concentrations of the drug to be achieved locally while minimizing systemic exposure [3]. This technqiue has been shown to be effective in treating advanced inraocular retinoblastoma, with reported globe salvage rates ranging from 80% to 100% [4, 5]. Despite the advances in treatment, there is a growing concern about the potential long-term effects of cancer therapy on the health and well-being of survivors [6]. One area of particular interest is the impact of cancer treatment on growth and development, as childhood and adolescence are critical periods for physical growth and maturation [7]. Studies hvae shown that patients with pediatric cancers, such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia, may experience decreased growth velocity during and after treatment, which can be attributed to various factors, including the use of systemic chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and the underlying disease process itself [8, 9]. However, the majority of these studies have focused on patients treated with systemic chemotherapy, and there is a lack of data on the effects of localized treatments, such as OAC, on growth patterns. The use of OAC for retinoblasotma treatment offers a unique opportunity to study the effects of localized chemotherapy on growth and development, as it allows for the delivery of high doses of chemotherapy directly to the tumor site whlie minimizing systemic exposure [10]. However, the potential effects of OAC on growth patterns are not well understood, and there is a need for further research in this area. A few studies have reported on the growth and development of retinoblastoma survivors, but thsee have been limited by small sample sizes, short follow-up periods, and the inclusion of patients treated with a variety of therapies, including systemic chemotherapy and radiation therapy [11, 12]. The purpose of this study is to report on the growth patterns of a large cohort of retinoblastoma patients treated with OAC at a single institution, Memorial Sloan Kettering Caner Center, between 2006 and 2016. We aimed to investigate the effects of OAC on short-term and long-term growth velocity, as well as weight gain, in a group of patients who were treated with this modality as their primary or secondary treatment. We also sought to compare the growth patterns of patients who received OAC as their primary treatment (naive patients) with those who received OAC as a secondary treatment after initial systemic chemotherapy (secondary patients). By examining the growth patterns of these patients, we hope to contribute to the understanding of the effects of OAC on the health and well-being of retinoblastoma survivors and to inform the development of strategies to mitigate any potential advesre effects of this treatment on grwoth and development. The sirtuin family of proteins, comprising seven members (SIRT1-7) in mammals, has garnered significant attention in reent yars due to their pivotal role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and their involvement in various physiological processes, including metabolism, cell survival, and genome stability [1]. These NAD+-dependent deacylases and mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases exhibit distinct subcellular localizations and functions, allowing them to regulate a wide range of cellular activities [2]. Among the mammalian sirtuins, SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been extensively studied, and their metabolic regulatory roles are well established [3]. Notably, SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been implicated in the pathogenesis of various metabolic disorders, including obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular diseases [4, 5]. However, the functions of the other sirtuin family members, namely SIRT2, SIRT3, SIRT4, SIRT5, and SIRT7, are not fully understood, and their potential roles in metabolic regulation remain to be elucidated [6]. Insulin resistance, a condition characterized by impaired insulin signaling, is a critical pathological trait of obesity and metabolic syndrome, as well as the core defect in T2DM [7]. The development of insulin resistance is a complex process, involving multiple cellular and molecular mechanisms, including inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and alterations in glucose and lipid metabolism [8]. Recent studies hvae suggested that sirtuins may play a crucial role in the regulation of insulin resistance, with SIRT1 and SIRT6 emerging as key players in this process [9, 10]. However, the potential roles of the other sirtuin family members in insulin resistance remain poorly understood, and further research is needed to elucidate their functions in this context [11]. The insulin signaling pathway, which plays a central role in glucose homeostasis, is a coomplex process involving multiple molecular components, including insulin receptors, insulin receptor substrates, and downstream efffectors such as Akt and glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) [12]. Impairments in insulin signaling, which can occur due to various factors, including obesity, inflammation, and genetic predisposition, can lead to the development of insulin resistance and T2DM [13]. Sirtuins, particularly SIRT1 and SIRT6, have been shown to regulate insulin signaling, with SIRT1 activating the insulin signaling pathway by deacetylating and activating key components, such as phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and Akt [14, 15]. In contrast, SIRT6 has been shown to regulate glucose metabolism by promoting the expression of glucose-6-phosphatase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK), two key enzymes involved in gluconeogenesis [16]. In addition to their roles in insulin signaling, sirtuins have also been implicated in the regulation of mitochondrial function and biogenesis, which are critical for maintaining glucose and lipid homeostasis [17]. Mitochondrial dysfunction, which can occur due to various factors, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic mutations, is a hallmark of insulin resistance and T2DM [18]. SIRT1 and SIRT3, in particular, have been shown to regulate mitochondrial biogenesis and function, with SIRT1 promoting the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α) and SIRT3 regulating the activity of mitochondrial enzymes involved in the citric acid cycle and fatty acid oxidation [19, 20]. Furthermore, sirtuins have also been implicated in the regulation of inflammation, which is a key factor contributing to the development of insulin resistance and T2DM [21]. SIRT1 and SIRT6, in particular, have been shown to possess anti-inflammatory properties, with SIRT1 inhibiting the activity of nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) and SIRT6 suppressing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines [22, 23]. The sirtuin protein family, comprising seven distinct members (SIRT1-7) in mammals, has garnered substantial attention in recent years owing to its pivotal role in maintaining cellular equilibrium and its participation in a myriad of physiological processes, including metabolic homeostasis, cellular survival, and genomic stability [1]. As enzymes that rely on NAD+ for their deacylase and mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase activities, these proteins exhibit unique localization patterns within cells and execute a diverse array of functions, thereby enabling them to modulate a broad spectrum of cellular activities [2]. Notably, SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been the subject of extensive investigation, and their involvement in metabolic regulation is well-documented [3]. These two sirtuin family members have been implicated in the pathogenesis of various metabolic disorders, including obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular diseases [4, 5]. However, the functions of the remaining sirtuin family members, namely SIRT2, SIRT3, SIRT4, SIRT5, and SIRT7, are not yet fully comprehended, and their potential roles in metabolic regulation remain to be elucidated [6]. Insulin resistance, a condition characterized by impaired insulin signaling, is a critical pathological feature of obesity and metabolic syndrome, as well as the primary defect underlying T2DM [7]. The development of insulin resistance is a complex process, involving multiple cellular and molecular mechanisms, including inflammatory responses, mitochondrial dysfunction, and alterations in glucose and lipid metabolic pathways [8]. Recent investigations have suggested that sirtuins may play a vital role in regulating insulin resistance, with SIRT1 and SIRT6 emerging as key regulators in this process [9, 10]. Nevertheless, the potential roles of the other sirtuin family members in insulin resistance remain poorly understood, and additional research is necessary to elucidate their functions in this context [11]. The insulin signaling pathway, which plays a central role in maintaining glucose homeostasis, is a complex process involving multiple molecular components, including insulin receptors, insulin receptor substrates, and downstream effectors such as Akt and glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) [12]. Impairments in insulin signaling, which can arise due to various factors, including obesity, inflammation, and genetic predisposition, can lead to the development of insulin resistance and T2DM [13]. Sirtuins, particularly SIRT1 and SIRT6, have been shown to modulate insulin signaling, with SIRT1 activating the insulin signaling pathway by deacetylating and activating key components, such as phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and Akt [14, 15]. In contrast, SIRT6 has been demonstrated to regulate glucose metabolism by promoting the expression of glucose-6-phosphatase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK), two key enzymes involved in gluconeogenesis [16]. In addition to their roles in insulin signaling, sirtuins have also been implicated in regulating mitochondrial function and biogenesis, which are critical for maintaining glucose and lipid homeostasis [17]. Mitochondrial dysfunction, which can arise due to various factors, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic mutations, is a hallmark of insulin resistance and T2DM [18]. SIRT1 and SIRT3, in particular, have been shown to regulate mitochondrial biogenesis and function, with SIRT1 promoting the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α) and SIRT3 regulating the activity of mitochondrial enzymes involved in the citric acid cycle and fatty acid oxidation [19, 20]. The images are then converted to Hounsfield units (HU), which provide a standardized measure of X-ray attenuation [6]. This conversion enables the differentiation of bone from soft tissue and other materials, based on their distinct HU values. ### Thresholding and Edge Detection The preprocessed images are then subjected to a thresholding step, where pixels with HU values above a certain threshold (typically +200 HU) are classified as bone [7]. This step is followed by the application of a Canny edge detection algorithm, which identifies the boundaries of the vertebral bodies [8]. The SSM is based on a database of vertebral body shapes, which are used to inform the segmentation process [10]. The model is iteratively refined, using an active shape model (ASM) algorithm, to accurately capture the geometry of the vertebrae [11]. The ASM algorithm uses the edges detected in the previous step to constrain the model, ensuring that it conforms to the actual shape of the vertebral bodies. ### Definition of Local Anatomical Coordinate Systems Once the 3D model of the vertebral bodies has been created, a local anatomical coordinate system is defined for each vertebra [12]. This coordinate system is based on the geometry of the vertebra, with the origin located at the center of the vertebral body [13]. The coordinate system is used to define volumes of interest (VOIs) for BMD measurement, whcih are typically located in the anterior, posterior, and central regions of the vertebra [14]. Osteoporosis, a chronic and incapacitating condition, is marked by a gradual deterioration of bone mass and density, which in turn heightens the risk of fractures, a development that can profoundly compromise an individual's overall well-being and life expectancy [1]. The lumbar vertebral bodies are particularly susceptible to osteoporotic fractures, which can result in considerable morbidity and mortality, thereby underscoring the importance of precise assessment of bone mineral density (BMD) and lumbar vertebral body geometry in the diagnosis and management of osteoporosis [2]. Currently, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) serves as the benchmark for measuring BMD, despite its limitations, including its reliance on two-dimensional projections, which can lead to measurement inaccuracies stemming from overlapping structures and variations in soft tissue composition [4]. In contrast, computed tomography (CT) scans offer a three-dimensional representation of vertebral bodies, facilitating more accurate assessments of BMD and geometry [5]. However, extracting pertinent information from CT scans necessitates the application of sophisticated image processing and analytical techniques. A variety of segmentation methods, including threshold-based [6], edge-based [7], and model-based approaches [8], have been proposed to delineate the geometry of lumbar vertebral bodies from CT scans, although these methods often require manual intervention, are susceptible to image noise and artifacts, and may yield inaccurate results in cases involving complex anatomical structures or osteoporotic alterations. To address these limitations, there is a compelling need for the development of an innovative 3D segmentation methodology capable of accurately extracting the geometry of lumbar vertebral bodies from CT scans, a methodology that must be adept at handling the intricacies of vertebral anatomy, including osteophytes, fractures, and other degenerative changes, while providing precise measurements of BMD and geometry essential for the diagnosis and monitoring of osteoporosis. The creation of such a methodology necessitates a comprehensive understanding of lumbar spine anatomy and pathology, as well as expertise in image processing and analysis techniques. A critical aspect of this developmental process involves the utilization of local anatomical coordinate systems, which furnish a standardized framework for defining volumes of interest and measuring BMD and geometric parameters, such as vertebral height, width, and volume [9]. Research has demonstrated that the employment of local anatomical coordinate systems can enhance the accuracy and precision of BMD measurements [10, 11]. However, defining these coordinate systems can be challenging, particularly in cases involving complex anatomy or osteoporotic changes. Phantom studies have been extensively utilized to evaluate the accuracy and precision of BMD measurements [12], involving the use of synthetic phantoms with known BMD values scanned using CT or other imaging modalities, with the measured BMD values compared to the known values to assess the accuracy and precision of the measurement technique. These studies have shown that CT-based BMD measurements can be accurate and precise, although they can be influenced by various factors, including image noise, beam hardening, and partial volume averaging [13], highlighting the need for careful consideration of these factors in the development of a new 3D segmentation methodology. Another crucial aspect of BMD measurement techniques is intra- and inter-operator precision, referring to the variability in measurements obtained by different operators or by the same operator at different times [14]. High precision is essential for reliable diagnosis and monitoring of osteoporosis, as it ensures that changes in BMD measurements reflect actual changes in bone density rather than variability in the measurement technique. Several studies have indicated that CT-based BMD measurements can exhibit high precision, although this can be affected by factors such as the quality of the CT scans, operator expertise, and anatomical complexity [15]. The ultimate objective of developing a new 3D segmentation methodology for lumbar vertebral bodies is to enhance fracture prediction in osteoporosis, a major public health concern [16]. Accurate prediction of fracture risk is critical for preventing fractures and improving patient outcomes, with several studies demonstrating that BMD measurements can be used to predict fracture risk, albeit requiring accurate and precise measurements of BMD and geometry [17]. The development of a new 3D segmentation methodology capable of providing accurate and precise measurements of BMD and geometry could potentially improve fracture prediction and patient outcomes. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive and debilitating disease characterized by elevated pulmonary artery pressure and resistance, leading to right ventricular failure and death. The pathophysiology of PAH involves complex interactions between genetic, environmental, and molecular factors, resulting in vascular remodeling, inflammation, and thrombosis. Despite advances in treatment, PAH remains a significant clinical challenge, with limited therapeutic options and a high mortality rate. Therefore, there is a pressing need to explore novel therapeutic strategies that can effectively target the underlying mechanisms of PAH and improve patient outcomes. The renin-angiotensin sysstem (RAS) plays a crucial role in regulating blood pressure, fluid balance, and electrolyte homeostasis. The classical RAS pathway involves the conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I (Ang I) by renin, followed by the conversion of Ang I to angiotensin II (Ang II) by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Ang II is a potent vasoconstrictor that also promotes inflammation, fibrosis, and vascular remodeling. However, recent studies have identified alternative RAS pathways that may have counter-regulatory effects on the classical RAS. One such pathway involves the conversion of Ang I to angiotensin-(1-9) [Ang-(1-9)] by angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2). Ang-(1-9) has been shown to have protective effects on cardiac and vascular remodeling, including anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, and anti-apoptotic actions. The role of Ang-(1-9) in cardiovascular disease has been extensively studied, with evidence suggesting that it may have therapeutic potential in conditions such as hypertension, heart failure, and atherosclerosis. Ang-(1-9) has been shown to coounteract the effects of Ang II, reducing blood pressure, improving cardiac function, and inhibiting vascular remodeling. The mechanisms underlying the protective effecs of Ang-(1-9) involve activation of the angiotensin type 2 receptor (AT2R) and the Mas receptor, which are both expressed in cardiovascular tissues. AT2R is known to have anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative effects, while the Mas receptor has been implicated in the regulation of blood pressure and vascular function. The analysis of historical structures is a complex task that requires a deep understanding of their behavior under various loads, including seismic actions. These structures, often made of masonry, have been built over the centuries with techniques and materials that are not well-documented, making their modeling a challenging task. However, the accuracy of the results obtained with the FE method strongly depends on the quality of the model used, which in turn relies on the availability of reliable material properties and geoetric data. In recent years, significant advances have been made in the development of numerical methods for the analyis of historical structures. These methods include the use of non-linear dynamic analysis, the consideration of material non-linearity and damage, and the application of advanced constitutive models. Nevertheless, the calibration of these models to match the actual behavior of the structure remains a critical issue. Experimental techniques, such as ambient vibration tests and forced vibration tests, can provide valuable information on the dynamic properties of the structure, including natural frequencies, mode shapes, and damping ratios. However, the direct use of these experimnetal data in numerical models is not straightforward, and a procedure for updating the model parameters to match the experimental results is necessary. Model updating is a well-established technique in the field of structural dynamics, which aims at adjustinng the parameters of a numerical model to match experimental data. The procedure typically involves the minimization of an objective function that measures the difference between the experimental and numerical results. The model updating procedure can be applied to various types of experimental data, including modal properties, such as natural frequenices and mode shapes, as well as other dynamic responses, such as acceleration or diisplacement time-histories. The application of model updating to historical structures is particularly challenging due to the complexity of their geometry, the uncertainty of their material properties, and the difficulty of obtaining reliable experimental data. The finite element model updating process is a pivotal step in the validation and refinement of numerical models used to analyze the dynamic behavior of structures. This complex process typically encompasses five primary stages: (1) the development of an initial finite element model, (2) the experimental measurement of the structure's dynamic response, (3) the calculation of the numerical dynamic response of the initial model, (4) a comparative analysis between the numerical and experimental results, and (5) the updating of model parameters to minimize discrepancies between the numerical and experimental results [1]. 

In the approach employed here, the initial finite element model is defined using the NOSA-ITACA code, a sophisticated tool that enables the creation of intricate geometries and the assignment of material properties to various components of the structure [2]. The creation of the model typically involves a thorough survey of the structure, encompassing its geometry, material properties, and any damage or defects. This meticulous survey is essential for ensuring that the numerical model accurately represents the physical structure. Upon completion of the initial model, it is utilized to calculate the numerical dynamic response of the structure, including its natural frequencies and mode shapes. 

The experimental measurement of the dynamic response of the structure is typically conducted using accelerometer sensors strategically positioned on the structure [3]. These sensors measure the acceleration of the structure in response to ambient vibrations or forced vibrations induced by a shaker or other excitation device. The acquired data are then processed to extract the natural frequencies and mode shapes of the structure, providing a basis for comparison with the numerical results and facilitating the identification of any discrepancies between the two. 

The numerical dynamic response of the initial model is calculated using the NOSA-ITACA code, which solves the equations of motion for the structure using a finite element formulation [4]. The code assumes a linear elastic material model, which presupposes that the material behaves linearly and elastically within the expected range of deformations in the structure. This assumption is reasonable for numerous structures; however, it may not hold true for structures that undergo large deformations or exhibit nonlinear behavior. The numerical model is typically executed in modal analysis mode, which calculates the natural frequencies and mode shapes of the structure. 

A comparative analysis between the numerical and experimental results is conducted using various metrics, including natural frequencies, mode shapes, and the modal assurance criterion (MAC) [5]. The MAC is a statistical measure that evaluates the correlation between the numerical and experimental mode shapes, providing a means to assess the accuracy of the numerical model. The discrepancies between the numerical and experimental results are typically quantified using an objective function, which measures the error between the numerical and experimental results. This objective function serves as the foundation for the model updating procedure, which employs an optimization algorithm to minimize the objective function and update the model parameters. 

The optimization algorithm utilized in NOSA-ITACA is a gradient-based algorithm, which leverages the sensitivity of the objective function to the model parameters to guide the search for the optimal solution [6]. The algorithm is typically executed in an iterative manner, with the model parameters being updated at each iteration until convergence is achieved. One of the primary challenges in model updating is the selection of parameters to be updated. Generally, the parameters that are updated are those that have the most significant influence on the dynamic behavior of the structure, such as material properties, damping ratios, and boundary conditions. 

The selection of parameters to be updated is typically conducted using a sensitivity analysis, which evaluates the sensitivity of the objective function to each parameter [7]. The parameters that exhibit the greatest sensitivity are then selected for updating. Another challenge in model updating is the robustness of the optimization algorithm. The algorithm must converge to the optimal solution within a reasonable number of iterations and must avoid local minima in the objective function. To address these challenges, NOSA-ITACA employs various techniques, including regularization, which adds a penalty term to the objective function to discourage large changes in the model parameters, and constraints, which limit the range of values that the model parameters can assume [8]. These techniques help ensure that the optimization algorithm converges to a stable solution. 

Moreover, the model updating procedure allows for the evaluation of the effectiveness of different seismic retrofitting strategies. By updating the model parameters to reflect the changes made to the structure, the numerical model can be used to predict the dynamic response of the retrofitted structure, enabling the evaluation of the efficacy of various retrofitting strategies. This capability is particularly valuable for historic structures, where the preservation of the original structure is paramount, and the selection of an effective retrofitting strategy is crucial to ensuring the structure's seismic resilience.

The fifth generation (5G) of wireless communication systems is expected to revolutioonize the way we communicate, with enhanced mobile broadband, ultra-reliable low-latency communication, and massive machine-type communication. To achieve these goals, 5G networks will employ a range of innoovative technologies, including cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, which have the potential to provide unprecedented levels of coverage, capacity, and reliability. However, the integration of millimeter wave (mmWave) frequencies into these systems also introduces new challenges, particularly in terms of radio resource management. One of the key challenges in 5G cell-free massive MIMO networks is the need to guarantee fast and reliable radio resource management in both uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) directions. This is particularly important in mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave scenarios, where the different frequency bands have distinct propagation characteristics. The sub-6 GHz band offers better coverage and penetration, but is limited by bandwidth constraints, while the mmWave band offers vast bandwidths, but is prone to blockage and propagation losses. As a result, the UL and DL channels may experience different propagation conditions, leading to an imbalance that can severely impact the overall performance of the system. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed various solutions, including the use of separate UL and DL channels, a technique known as uplink/downlink (UL/DL) decoupling. This approach allows the system to optimize the UL and DL channels independently, taking into account the specific propagation conditions and quality of service (QoS) requirements of each link. However, traditional UL/DL decoupling methods often rely on extensive measurements and feedback, which can lead to increased latency and overhead. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the development of machine learning (ML) algorithms for wireless communication systems. ML techniques have the potential to learn from data and make predictions or decisions without the need for explicit models or feedback. In the context of UL/DL decoupling, ML algorithms can be used to predict the optimal UL and DL channels based on historical data and real-time measurements. This approach can reduce the need for extensive measurements and feedback, leading to faster and more efficient radio resource management. The concept of semi-blind UL/DL decoupling proposed in this paper builds on these ideas. In this approach, the central processing unt (CPU) gathers measurements of the Rician K-factor, which reflects the line-of-sight (LOS) condition of the user equipment (UE), as well as the DL reference signal receive power (RSRP) for both 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz frequency bands. These measurements are then used to train a non-linear support vector machine (SVM) algorithm, which learns to predict the optimal UL and DL channels based on the input data. The key innovation of this approach is that the CPU only needs to measure the mmWave channel initially, and can then use the trained SVM algorithm to blindly predict the target frequencies and access poins (APs) that can be independently used for the UL and DL. The phenomenon of recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA), also referred to as habitual miscarriage, poses a substantial challenge to reproductive health, affecting a significant proportion of women worldwide, approximately 1-5%, and resulting in the recurrence of three or more pregnancy losses prior to the 20th week of gestation [1]. This experience can be particularly distressing for affected couples, given the high incidence of miscarriage as a complication of early pregnancy, which occurs in 15-20% of all pregnancies [2]. The underlying causes of RSA are complex and multifaceted, involving a range of factors including anatomical, genetic, endocrinological, immunological, and infectious etiologies [3]. Among these, endocrinological disorders have emerged as significant contributors to recurrent pregnancy loss, as they can disrupt the intricate hormonal balance essential for successful implantation, embryonic development, and maintenance of pregnancy [4]. Specific endocrine disorders, such as polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defects, thyroid dysfunction, diabetes, and hyperandrogenism, have been linked to an increased risk of RSA [5]. PCOS, a common endocrine disorder affecting women of reproductive age, is characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and the presence of polycystic ovaries [6]. Women with PCOS are at a heightened risk of miscarriage, with studies suggesting that the risk of pregnancy loss is 2-3 times greater compared to women without the condition [7]. Hyperprolactinemia, which refers to elevated levels of prolactin, is another endocrine disorder that has been implicated in RSA, as excessive prolactin levels can interfere with reproductive function and contribute to pregnancy loss [8]. Additionally, luteal phase defects, marked by inadequate progesterone production or action, can lead to recurrent pregnancy loss, as progesterone plays a crucial role in preparing the endometrium for implantation and maintaining pregnancy [9]. Thyroid dysfunction, encompassing both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, has also been associated with RSA, as the thyroid gland plays a vital role in regulating metabolism, and abnormalities in thyroid function can disrupt reproductive function and increase the risk of pregnancy loss [10]. Furthermore, other factors, including genetic and anatomical abnormalities, can also contribute to the development of RSA [11]. Genetic factors, such as chromosomal abnormalities, including balanced translocations, and genetic mutations, can increase the risk of miscarriage [12]. Anatomical abnormalities, such as uterine anomalies, fibroids, and cervical insufficiency, can disrupt implantation and embryonic development, leading to pregnancy loss [13]. Immunological factors, including autoimmune disorders, such as antiphospholipid syndrome, and immune dysregulation, can also play a role in RSA [14]. Moreover, infectious agents, such as bacterial and viral infections, can increase the risk of miscarriage [15]. Despite the complexity of RSA, addressing and managing underlying endocrine disorders can significantly improve pregnancy outcomes [16]. For example, women with PCOS who undergo ovulation induction and receive fertility treatment have improved pregnancy rates and a reduced risk of miscarriage [17]. Similarly, women with hyperprolactinemia who receive dopamine agonist therapy to reduce prolactin levels experience improved reproductive outcomes [18]. The diagnosis and treatment of thyroid dysfunction, luteal phase defects, and other endocrine disorders can also enhance pregnancy outcomes and reduce the risk of RSA [19]. Therefore, it is essential to identify and manage underlying endocrine disorders in women with RSA to optimize their chances of a successful pregnancy. Human pose estimation, which involves locating the positions of human joints in an image or video, is a fuundamental task in computer vision with numerous applications in fields such as robotics, healthcare, and surveillance. Recent years have witnessed significant advancements in this area, with the development of deep learning-based approaches achieving state-of-the-art results on various benchmarks. In particular, multi-stage Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely adopted for single image human pose estimation, demonstrating superior performance in detecting human joints and estimating their positions. However, despite their excellent performance on static images, the application of thee CNN-based models to videos poses significant challenges. One major issue is the computational intensity of processing each frame individually, which can lead to inefficient processing times and hinder real-time applications. Moreover, the lack of temporal modeling in these approaches results in suboptimal performance, including flickering and performance degradation, when dealing with video sequences. This is primarily due to the inability of these models to impose sequential geometric consistency, handle severe image quality degradation, such as motion blur and occlusion, and capture the temporal correlation among video frames. The importance of temporal modeling in video-based human pose estimation cannot be overstated. Human movements are inherently sequential, and the position of joiints in one frame is highly correlated with their positions in adjacent frames. Furthermore, videos often suffer from various types of degradation, including motion blur, occlusion, and noise, which can significantly impact the accuracy of pose estimation. To address thee challenges, there is a need for models that can effectively capture the temporal relationships among frames and impoose geometric consistency on the estimated poses. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been widely used for modeling sequential data, including videos, speech, and text. By maintaining an internal state that captures information from previous time steps, RNNs can effectively model temporal relationships and make predictions based on this contextual information. However, one major limitation of traditional RNNNs is their inability to handle long-term dependencies, which can result in vanishing or exploding gradients during training. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, a tye of RNN, have been designed to address this limitation. LSTMs introduce memory cells that can store information for extended periods, allowing the network to capture long-term dependencies and maintain a more stable internal state. This propery makes LSTMs particularly suitable for modeling complex sequential data, such as videos, where the relationships among frames can span multiple time steps. In the context of human pose estimation, LSTMs can be used to model the temporal relationships among frames and impose geometric consistency on the estimated poses. By maintaining a memory of previous poses, the network can make more accurate predictions and reduce the impact of image quality degradation. Furthermore, the weight sharing scheme in LSTMs can be used to reduce the computational intensity of processing videos, making it possible to achieve real-time performance. Despite the potential benefits of LSTMs for video-based human pose estimation, there are several challenges that need to be addressed. Furthermore, the orphan G-protein-coupled receptor GPR55 has been proposed as a potential third cannabinoid receptor, thereby broadening the scope of the ECS [3]. The ECS is deeply involved in the regulation of a diverse array of physiological processes, including nociception, emotional state, memory, and hunger [4]. Additionally, the ECS has been implicated in the regulation of cellular processes such as proliferation, differentiation, and survival, which are essential for cancer development and progression [5]. The components of the ECS, including CB1, CB2, and the enzymes responsible for the synthesis and degradation of endocannabinoids, such as fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) and monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL), have been found to be altered in various types of cancer [6]. However, despite these advancements, maintaining treatment adherence with bDMARDs remains a considerable challenge, with a substantial proportion of patients necessitating changes in their treatment regimen due to either lack of efficacy or issues related to tolerability. 

A recent investigation [1] provided insights into the persistence of treatment with second-line bDMARDs among RA patients, shedding light on factors that are associated with the earlier discontinuation or switching of therapy. The findings indicated that only a limited proportion of RA patients, specifically 56.8%, continued with their second bDMARD treatment beyond the 12-month mark, with an additional small percentage, 3.8%, reinitiating therapy after an initial cessation [1]. This underscores the suboptimal nature of treatment persistence with second-line bDMARDs, with a significant number of patients requiring adjustments to their treatment plan due to either inadequate response or intolerance.

The comparison of treatment outcomes between anti-TNF and non-anti-TNF bDMARDs when used as second-line treatments revealed notable discrepancies. Patients who were prescribed a non-anti-TNF bDMARD as their second-line treatment exhibited a higher likelihood of continuing with the therapy, with 66.7% of them remaining on treatment after 12 months, in contrast to 53.5% of patients who received an anti-TNF bDMARD [1]. Furthermore, patients in the non-anti-TNF group demonstrated a longer duration of drug survival, with a median of 295 days, compared to 264 days for those in the anti-TNF group [5]. These observations suggest that non-anti-TNF bDMARDs might offer a more effective and sustainable treatment option for patients who have either failed to respond to or are intolerant of initial anti-TNF therapy.

To further elucidate the differences in drug survival between the two groups, Kaplan-Meier curves were employed, illustrating the drug survival rates over time. The results showed a statistically significant difference between the two groups, as confirmed by the log-rank test (p = 0.016). This statistical approach allowed for a more nuanced understanding of how the probability of continuing treatment varied over time between patients receiving anti-TNF versus non-anti-TNF bDMARDs as their second-line therapy.

The analysis also identified several independent variables that were associated with the earlier discontinuation or switching of second-line bDMARD therapy. The prescription of an anti-TNF agent as the second bDMARD emerged as a significant predictor of earlier discontinuation, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 1.512 (95% CI 1.073-2.133) [6]. This may be attributed to the fact that patients who receive an anti-TNF as their second-line treatment have previously failed or are intolerant to an initial anti-TNF, suggesting a more resistant disease course [2]. Additionally, higher levels of comorbidity, as quantified by the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), were also linked to an increased risk of earlier discontinuation or switching. This highlights the importance of considering the comorbidity burden when devising treatment strategies for RA patients, as those with higher comorbidity levels may necessitate more vigilant monitoring and potentially more aggressive treatment approaches to optimize their outcomes.

The findings of this study have profound implications for clinical practice, emphasizing the need for personalized treatment strategies that take into account the unique characteristics and disease profiles of individual patients [7]. By recognizing the differences in treatment outcomes and drug survival associated with anti-TNF and non-anti-TNF bDMARDs, healthcare providers can make more informed decisions regarding the selection of second-line therapies for RA patients. This personalized approach could potentially lead to improved treatment persistence, better disease control, and ultimately, enhanced quality of life for patients with RA.

In conclusion, the study provides valuable insights into the treatment patterns and drug survival of RA patients receiving a second bDMARD, suggesting that non-anti-TNF bDMARDs may offer superior treatment outcomes and longer drug survival compared to anti-TNF agents when used as second-line therapies. These findings underscore the complexity of RA management and the necessity for ongoing research into the factors influencing treatment outcomes, including the exploration of the underlying mechanisms that contribute to the differences observed between anti-TNF and non-anti-TNF bDMARDs. Further investigations are warranted to confirm these findings and to elucidate the optimal strategies for sequencing bDMARDs in the treatment of RA, with the ultimate goal of improving patient outcomes and quality of life.

Therefore, there is a pressing need to develop effective therapeutic strategies for the treatment of advanced HCC. TACE is a minimally invasive procedure that involves the delivery of chemotherrapeutic agents directly to the tumor through the hepatic artery, followed by emolization of the artery to induce tumor necrosis [5]. TACE has been shown to improve survival in patients with advanced HCC [6], and it is currently considered a standard treatment option for patients with unresectable HCC [7]. However, the efficacy of TACE is limited by the development of resistance to chemotherapeutic agents and the potential for tumor recurrence [8]. To overcome these limitations, combination therapies that inolve the use of TACE with other treatment modalities have been explored. The liver is a vital organ that is susceptible to various diseases, including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a primary malignancy that is one of the most common causes of cancer-related mortality globally, resulting in a significant proportion of cancer-related deaths worldwide [1]. The prevalence of HCC is escalating at an alarming rate, with estimates suggesting that it will become a leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the next decade, emphasizing the need for effective therapeutic interventions to combat this disease [2]. Currently, treatment options for HCC include surgical resection, liver transplantation, and locoregional therapies, such as transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization (TACE), which is a minimally invasive procedure that delivers chemotherapeutic agents directly to the tumor via the hepatic artery, followed by embolization to induce tumor necrosis [3]. However, the majority of HCC patients are diagnosed at an advanced stage, and the prognosis remains bleak, with limited treatment options available, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies to improve patient outcomes [4]. Consequently, there is an urgent need to develop effective therapeutic interventions for the treatment of advanced HCC. TACE has been shown to improve survival in patients with advanced HCC, and it is currently considered a standard treatment option for patients with unresectable HCC [5]. Nevertheless, the efficacy of TACE is limited by the development of resistance to chemotherapeutic agents and the potential for tumor recurrence, underscoring the need for combination therapies that can overcome these limitations [6]. Sorafenib has been approved for the treatment of advanced HCC and is currently considered a standard treatment option for patients with unresectable HCC [8]. The parameters of this Gaussian distribution are learned through a method known as variational inference, which approximates the posterior distribution of the model parameters with a variational distribution. This variational distribution is itself a Gaussian, defined by its mean $\phi_d$ and covariance $\Psi_d$. The learning process for the parameters of the variational distribution involves minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the variational distribution and the true posterior distribution. This divergence is a quantitative measure of the difference between two probability distributions, and its minimization ensures that the variational distribution closely approximates the true posterior. To achieve this, a stochastic variational inference algorithm is employed, which iteratively refines the parameters of the variational distribution through a stochastic gradient descent approach. This approach is favored for its ability to efficiently learn the parameters in a computationally feasible manner.

The proposed model boasts several significant advantages over existing methodologies. Foremost, it offers a probabilistic representation of documents, which is adept at capturing the inherent uncertainty associated with document embeddings. This is particularly valuable in applications where the nuanced understanding of document content is crucial. Additionally, the model is computationally efficient, leveraging variational inference for parameter learning, which makes it viable for large-scale document collections. Furthermore, it provides a flexible framework for document modeling, capable of capturing intricate relationships between words and documents, thereby enhancing the accuracy of topic identification and document classification tasks.

The efficacy of the proposed model is evaluated through both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation metrics, including perplexity and topic identification accuracy. Perplexity is a measure of how well a probability model predicts a test set, with lower perplexity values indicating better performance. Topic identification accuracy, on the other hand, assesses the model's ability to correctly identify the topics within a document collection. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses state-of-the-art models, such as the neural variational document model, and achieves performance comparable to fully supervised discriminative models. This is a significant finding, as it suggests that the proposed model can offer competitive performance without the need for large amounts of labeled training data.

In conclusion, the proposed Bayesian subspace multinomial model presents a powerful approach to document modeling and topic identification. By providing a probabilistic representation of documents, it captures the uncertainty inherent in document embeddings, a feature that is both novel and advantageous. The model's computational efficiency and flexibility in capturing complex word-document relationships make it an attractive choice for a variety of applications, including but not limited to text classification and information retrieval. The outcomes of our experiments underscore the model's effectiveness and its potential for real-world applications, where the accurate and efficient analysis of large document collections is paramount.

Future research directions include extending the proposed model to other domains, such as image and speech processing, where the ability to capture uncertainty and complex relationships could be equally beneficial. Moreover, exploring the use of other Bayesian methods, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo, for document modeling could provide additional insights and potentially lead to further improvements in model performance. The foundation of the proposed model, rooted in representing documents as Gaussian distributions, offers a natural and intuitive framework for capturing the uncertainty of document embeddings. This approach, coupled with the efficiency of variational inference for learning model parameters, positions the model favorably for tackling the complexities of document analysis in an increasingly data-driven world.

The stochastic gradient descent iteratively refines the model parameters based on a gradient computed from a stochastic approximation of the objective function, which in this case is the Kullback-Leibler divergence. In the realm of natural language processing and information retrieval, a longstanding objective has been to devise effective models for the representation and analysis of extensive document collections. A primary challenge in this domain is capturing the underlying structural and semantic properties of documents in a manner that facilitates tasks such as topic modeling, document classification, and information retrieval. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel probabilistic framework, termed the Bayesian Subspace Multinomial Model (Bayesian SMM), which represents documents as Gaussian distributions over a latent topic space. This approach enables the encoding of uncertainty in document representations, which can be leveraged to enhance the performance of downstream tasks.

Our proposed model represents each document as a bag-of-words vector, where each word is associated with a specific topic. We assume that each document is generated from a mixture of $K$ topics, where each topic is represented by a Gaussian distribution over the document embeddings. The generative process for our proposed Bayesian SMM can be described as follows. For each document $d$, we initially sample a topic proportion vector $\mathbf{\pi}_d$ from a Dirichlet distribution with concentration parameter $\alpha$. Then, for each word $i$ in document $d$, we sample a topic assignment $z_{di}$ from a multinomial distribution with parameter $\mathbf{\pi}_d$. Finally, we sample the word $x_{di}$ from a multinomial distribution with parameter $\mathbf{\beta}_{z_{di}}$, where $\mathbf{\beta}_k$ is the $k^{th}$ topic's word distribution. The document embedding for document $d$ is represented as a Gaussian distribution with mean vector $\mathbf{\mu}_d$ and covariance matrix $\mathbf{\Sigma}_d$. The mean vector $\mathbf{\mu}_d$ is computed as the weighted sum of the topic embeddings, where the weights are the topic proportions $\mathbf{\pi}_d$. The covariance matrix $\mathbf{\Sigma}_d$ is computed as the weighted sum of the topic covariances, where the weights are the topic proportions $\mathbf{\pi}_d$ [1]. This approach enables the capture of uncertainty in the document representations, which can be leveraged to improve the performance of downstream tasks.

To learn the model parameters, we utilize variational inference, a technique that has been widely employed in the context of topic modeling [2]. The variational distribution over the topic assignments $z_{di}$ is assumed to be a multinomial distribution with parameter $\mathbf{\phi}_d$. The variational distribution over the topic proportions $\mathbf{\pi}_d$ is assumed to be a Dirichlet distribution with concentration parameter $\gamma_d$. The variational distribution over the document embedding $\mathbf{\mu}_d$ and $\mathbf{\Sigma}_d$ is assumed to be a Gaussian distribution with mean vector $\mathbf{m}_d$ and covariance matrix $\mathbf{S}_d$. The evidence lower bound (ELBO) for our proposed Bayesian SMM can be derived as follows: $\mathcal{L} = \sum_{d=1}^D \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{N_d} \mathbb{E}_{q(z_{di})} [\log p(x_{di} | z_{di})] - \mathbb{KL}(q(\mathbf{\pi}_d) || p(\mathbf{\pi}_d)) - \mathbb{KL}(q(\mathbf{\mu}_d, \mathbf{\Sigma}_d) || p(\mathbf{\mu}_d, \mathbf{\Sigma}_d)) \right]$ where $q(z_{di})$ is the variational distribution over the topic assignments, $q(\mathbf{\pi}_d)$ is the variational distribution over the topic proportions, and $q(\mathbf{\mu}_d, \mathbf{\Sigma}_d)$ is the variational distribution over the document embedding.

To optimize the ELBO with respect to the model parameters, we employ stochastic gradient descent, a technique that has been widely used in the context of deep learning [3]. The gradients of the ELBO with respect to the model parameters can be computed using the REINFORCE algorithm [4]. We also utilize a learning rate schedule with a warm-up period to adapt the learning rate during training [5]. To address the problem of intractability that arises during variational inference in mixed-logit models, we employ a Monte Carlo approximation to compute the expectations in the ELBO [6]. Specifically, we utilize a sample of size $M$ from the variational distribution over the topic assignments to approximate the expectations.

In addition to the Bayesian SMM, we also propose a generative Gaussian linear classifier for topic identification that exploits the uncertainty in document embeddings. The classifier takes the document embedding $\mathbf{\mu}_d$ and $\mathbf{\Sigma}_d$ as input and outputs a probability distribution over the topics. The classifier is trained using a supervised loss function, such as the cross-entropy loss [7]. This approach enables the leverage of uncertainty in the document representations to improve the performance of topic identification.

The proposed Bayesian SMM offers several advantages over existing topic models. Firstly, it learns to represent documents in the form of Gaussian distributions, thereby encoding the uncertainty in its co-variance. Secondly, it addresses the problem of intractability that arises during variational inference in mixed-logit models. Finally, it provides a generative Gaussian linear classifier for topic identification that exploits the uncertainty in document embeddings. We evaluate the proposed Bayesian SMM on several benchmark datasets, including the Fisher speech and 20Newsgroups text corpora [8]. We compare the performance of the proposed model with several state-of-the-art topic models, including the neural variational document model [9] and the latent Dirichlet allocation model [10]. The results demonstrate that the proposed Bayesian SMM outperforms the state-of-the-art models in terms of perplexity and topic identification accuracy.

In conclusion, the proposed Bayesian SMM represents a significant advancement in the field of topic modeling, offering a novel probabilistic framework for the representation and analysis of extensive document collections. By encoding uncertainty in document representations and addressing the problem of intractability in mixed-logit models, the proposed model provides a robust and effective approach for topic modeling and document analysis. Furthermore, the proposed generative Gaussian linear classifier for topic identification offers a powerful tool for leveraging uncertainty in document representations to improve the performance of downstream tasks. As such, the proposed Bayesian SMM has the potential to make a significant impact in the field of natural language processing and information retrieval.

Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a genetic disorder that affects hemoglobin production, leading to the formation of abnormal red blood cells that can cause a range of health problems. It is the most common life-limiting genetic disease among African Americans, affecting more than 100,000 people in the United States. The disaese is charracterized by recurrent episodes of pain, increased risk of infections, and damage to various organs, including the lungs. Respiratory complications are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with SCD, and asthma is a common comorbidity that can exacerbate the disease. However, the relationship between SCD and asthma is complex, and the diagnosis of asthma in patients with SCD can be challenging. Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways that is characterized by recurring episodes of wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. It is a common disease that affects pople of all ages, but its prevalence and severity can vary depending on the population. In the general population, asthma is typically diagnosed based on a combination of clinical symptoms, pulmonary function tests, and response to treatment. However, in patients with SCD, the diagnosis of asthma can be more complicated. Wheezing, a common symptom of asthma, is also a frequent occurrence in patients with SCD, even in the absence of an asthma diagnosis. This has led to questions about the relationship between SCD and asthma, and whether wheezing in patients with SCD is a marker of asthhma or a distinct entity. The association between asthma and SCD has been recognized for several decades. Early studies reported a high prevalence of asthma in patients with SCD, and suggested that asthma may be a risk factor for acute chest syndrome (ACS), a life-threatening complication of SCD. ACS is characterized by a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiograph, often accompanied by fever, respiratory symptoms, and chest pain. It is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with SCD, and is often precipitated by respiratory infections or asthma exacerbations. The relationship between asthma and ACS is complex, and it is not clear whether asthma is a cause or a consequence of ACS. However, it is clear that patients with SCD and asthma are at increased risk of developing ACS, and that asthma exacerbations can trigger ACS episodes. In recent years, there has been growing interest in the relationship between wheezing and SCD. Wheezing is a common symptom in patients with SCD, and can occur in the absence of an asthma diagnosis. Several studies have reported that wheezing is a predictor of SCD severity, and that patients with SCD who wheeze are at increased risk of developing ACS and other complications. The mechanisms underlying wheezing in SCD are not fully understood, but it is thought to be related to the chronic inflammation and oxidative stress that occur in the disease. Wheezing in SCD may also be related to airway hyperresponsiveness, which is a characteristic feature of asthma. However, airway hyperresponsiveness can also occur in the absence of asthma, and its significance in SCD is not clear. The diagnosis of asthma in patients with SCD is challenging due to the high prevalence of wheezing and airway obstruction in the disease. Pulmonary funcion tests, such as spirometry, are often used to diagnose asthma, but they can be abnormal in patients with SCD even in the absence of asthma. Airway obstruction, as measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), is common in patients with SCD, and can occur in the absence of asthma symptoms. Similarly, airway hyperresponsiveness, as measured by methacholine challenge, can also occur in patients with SCD without asthma. Asthma is characterized by recurring episodes of wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath, and is a common affliction that affects individuals across all age groups [3]. While its prevalence and severity can vary depending on the population, asthma is typically diagnosed in the general population based on a combination of clinical symptoms, pulmonary function tests, and response to treatment [4]. Nevertheless, in patients with SCD, the diagnosis of asthma can be more complicated due to the frequent occurrence of wheezing, a common symptom of asthma, even in the absence of an asthma diagnosis [5]. This has led to queries regarding the interrelationship between SCD and asthma, and whether wheezing in patients with SCD is a marker of asthma or a distinct entity. The association between asthma and SCD has been recognized for several decades, with early studies reporting a high prevalence of asthma in patients with SCD and suggesting that asthma may be a risk factor for acute chest syndrome (ACS), a life-threatening complication of SCD [6]. ACS is characterized by a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiograph, often accompanied by fever, respiratory symptoms, and chest pain, and is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with SCD [7]. The interrelationship between asthma and ACS is complex, and it is unclear whether asthma is a cause or a consequence of ACS [8]. However, it is evident that patients with SCD and asthma are at increased risk of developing ACS, and that asthma exacerbations can trigger ACS episodes [9]. In recent years, there has been growing interest in the interrelationship between wheezing and SCD, with several studies reporting that wheezing is a predictor of SCD severity and that patients with SCD who wheeze are at increased risk of developing ACS and other complications [11]. The underlying mechanisms of wheezing in SCD are not fully understood, but it is thought to be related to the chronic inflammation and oxidative stress that occur in the disease [12]. Wheezing in SCD may also be related to airway hyperresponsiveness, a characteristic feature of asthma [13]. However, airway hyperresponsiveness can also occur in the absence of asthma, and its significance in SCD is unclear [14]. The diagnosis of asthma in patients with SCD is challenging due to the high prevalence of wheezing and airway obstruction in the disease. Pulmonary function tests, such as spirometry, are often used to diagnose asthma, but they can be abnormal in patients with SCD even in the absence of asthma [15]. Airway obstruction, as measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), is common in patients with SCD and can occur in the absence of asthma symptoms [16]. Similarly, airway hyperresponsiveness, as measured by methacholine challenge, can also occur in patients with SCD without asthma [17]. These findings have led to questions regarding the utility of pulmonary function tests in diagnosing asthma in patients with SCD and highlight the need for a more nuanced approach to diagnosis and management [18]. Despite the challenges, it is evident that asthma and wheezing are important comorbidities in patients with SCD, and their management is crucial to improving patient outcomes. The management of asthma in SCD is similar to that in the general population and involves the use of bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, and other medications to control symptoms and prevent exacerbations [19]. However, the optimal approach to managing asthma in SCD is not clear, and more research is needed to determine the best strategies for diagnosis and treatment [20]. Additionally, the interrelationship between wheezing and SCD severity highlights the need for a better understanding of the pathophysiology of airway inflammation in SCD and the development of new therapies to target this inflammation [21]. This review aims to provide a comprehensive summary of our current understanding of the epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway hyperresponsiveness in patients with SCD, as well as discuss the evidence supporting associations between these conditions and SCD severity. Furthermore, we will examine the current approaches to diagnosing and managing asthma in SCD, and discuss the need for further research to improve patient outcomes. The complex interplay between SCD and asthma has significant implications for patient care, and a deeper understanding of this relationship is essential to developing effective management strategies. By exploring the epidemiology, pathophysiology, and clinical manifestations of asthma and SCD, we can work towards improving the diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes for patients with these conditions. Ultimately, a comprehensive approach to managing SCD and asthma is necessary to address the complex needs of patients with these conditions and to reduce the significant morbidity and mortality associated with them. In conclusion, the relationship between SCD and asthma is complex and multifaceted, and further research is needed to fully understand the interplay between these conditions.
